documents.t: Produce a native NuGet package from a small SDK-style library.
Build a small Rust command-line application and run the delivered executable.
Build and run a small Go command without build YAML or module dependencies.

Run oyzu install --frozen, oyzu run list, oyzu build --plan, oyzu build --isolated --full and oyzu inspect dist. Native go.work owns both modules. Run the delivered service executable and expect Hello from the workspace library. Change the shared implementation to return Updated workspace library., build again, and run the newly collected executable. The output must change without downloading a public substitute for the contained module. Native Go supplies the relationship; this is not two unrelated Oyzu targets.
Build a Java application through Gradle and consume its delivered JAR.
Package a small Helm chart and render its delivered archive without a cluster.

Provision the documented npm/Node captured executor and Docker first. Run oyzu build --isolated --full, inspect dist, and run the delivered index.cjs. Repeat the same build output must agree with the changed build while actions execute freshly. Do not delete shared caches to manufacture a miss.
documents.s: Observe cache reuse and source invalidation

documents.t: Compile a conventional Java application into a JAR and run its class from the delivered archive.

Run oyzu install --frozen, oyzu build --plan, oyzu build and oyzu inspect dist. Maven evaluates the parent and orders the shared library before the application. Select both delivered JAR paths from the bundle and run java -cp "" example.Hello. Expect Hello from the reactor library. The checkout POMs and local dependency remain native Maven configuration. Oyzu's public CLI is organized by workflow. oyzu --help works offline without a platform account or project checkout. oyzu <command> --help and oyzu help <command> show nested options. One source of truth The detailed references linked below are copied at build time from the owning CLI source documents. This overview helps you navigate; it is not a second definition of flag behavior.

Intent Example Details Discover tasks oyzu run list Tasks Preview a build oyzu build --plan Local builds Build native outputs oyzu build Build receipts Review past executions oyzu history Build bundles Inspect tool needs oyzu pin --dry-run Tool commands View effective settings oyzu config show Configuration Explore cache behavior oyzu cache status Action cache

oyzu --help oyzu build --help oyzu --json config show Public commands default to human-readable text and accept global --json for structured results. Formatting choices do not change authorization, policy or exit status. The CLI help and CLI output references cover the precise current behavior, terminal/CI differences, and output envelopes.

A useful build system answers not only what ran, but also why that work was selected.
documents.s: Projects, targets and the build graph

documents.t: Oyzu begins with native evidence such as package manifests and scripts. It applies known builder rules and configuration to plan required work. A dependency graph then constrains which actions can run concurrently. Project manifests and configuration | v Discovery and selection | v Planned targets/actions | +------+------+ | | v v Action A Action B | | +------+------+ | v Artifact/report This diagram is conceptual. The number and type of actions depend on the actual project, supported ecosystem and chosen build plan.

If an upstream action fails, its consumers may become blocked. An independent target can still complete successfully. Correct reporting keeps those outcomes disjoint and avoids making a blocked task look as if its command ran and failed.

The default is convention-first. Use build.yaml for explicit exceptions, and oyzu.toml for tools and environment configuration. These files have distinct purposes. Try it: Preview a build then read the build tasks reference.

Caching avoids work only when the recorded inputs and outputs are suitable for reuse. The central question is not whether a result was cached, but whether it is appropriate for the current invocation.

Concept What it means Work executed now Native actions ran during this invocation Reused action output A previously captured result was admitted under the current cache rules Reused test evidence Test results from a prior run were associated with the current build; fresh tests did not execute

Depending on the supported action class, cache decisions can consider source inputs, configuration, tools, target variants and declared action dependencies. Incomplete inputs or unsupported paths should cause conservative behavior rather than incorrect reuse. The local action cache reference describes the actual implemented scope and its limits. This concept page must not be interpreted as a claim of fully hermetic distributed caching.

A receipt records whether an outcome was newly produced or reused and points to relevant evidence. Without that distinction, a fast cached build can be mistaken for independently verified fresh work. Use it: Cache guide and Build evidence.
A build result should support investigation after the terminal scrollback is gone.

Invocation — the current command request and observation interval. Plan/actions — what was selected and which work was actually executed, reused, blocked or cancelled. Artifact set — paths and identities for produced outputs. Reports — supported test, coverage or other collected results, with actual provenance. Manifest and events — retained machine-readable records where the current implementation supports them. The producing build identity and current invocation identity are not interchangeable.

A successful receipt does not imply tests ran when only older evidence was reused. A report with no measurable coverage must not be represented as positive coverage. A blocked action did not independently fail its own native command. Observation loss is uncertainty, not proof of a terminal state. An illustrative command or diagram is not a tested capture.
oyzu history oyzu history <invocation-id> --json See build bundles for history/retention constraints, CLI output for the result envelope, and read the receipt for a first-pass explanation.

Its canonical recipe owns the source, tool requirements, commands and revision-specific evidence. Explore the catalog for workspaces, features and generated-source examples. Read the Rust reference for current adapter behavior and build results for recorded outcomes. This existing route remains available for incoming links.

Build your project. Manage its tools. Run its tasks. No account required. Oyzu is an opinionated, batteries-included developer platform. The standalone CLI can discover native project conventions, select tools, preview a build and record its outputs and evidence. Early implementation Oyzu is in active development. Some capabilities and host/tool combinations remain experimental. Use the capability summary and canonical CLI reference before relying on a particular integration.
Install Oyzu from an available source checkout. Discover tasks, preview work and build. Manage project tools. Understand results, reuse and evidence.
documents.s: Your path to a first build

documents.t: oyzu run list oyzu build --plan oyzu build These commands require no account or managed service. oyzu build --plan is a preview, not execution.
Task-oriented guides for specific workflows. CLI reference for precise command behavior. Concepts to understand what Oyzu is doing. Limitations for what is not yet verified.
You can use Oyzu directly inside an existing supported native project. Start with a project whose normal native build prerequisites are available.
oyzu run list Oyzu reads supported project conventions and displays the tasks it can discover. The actual list depends on the current repository and native ecosystem.

oyzu build --plan The plan previews intended work and unresolved requirements without executing a build. Inspect the selected toolchain, builders and targets. If Oyzu chooses something unexpected, see discovery and selection.
oyzu build Oyzu runs the applicable native builders. A successful run includes a receipt identifying its actual actions, artifacts, tests and evidence. Outputs vary by project and supported builder.

oyzu history A bounded history of retained build summaries is available; use the invocation or run identifier with oyzu history <id> --json for structured inspection. Evidence availability depends on retention. Read understand the build result before interpreting cached test evidence as freshly executed tests. Prefer small configuration Supported projects use native-manifest discovery. Add build.yaml for explicit builder or artifact intent only when conventions are insufficient. Put tool requirements in oyzu.toml and resolved identities in oyzu.lock.
Run a discovered task. Understand the build graph. Troubleshoot a failed build.

The current documented installation path is building the CLI from a source checkout. A public one-line installer or package-manager formula is not yet documented as a supported distribution method. Source access The source repository is currently private. You need authorized checkout access to follow this procedure. Public binary installation instructions should be added only when an actual published distribution is verified.

A supported Rust toolchain and Cargo. A checkout of the Oyzu CLI repository. Native tools required by your particular project; automatic installation is implemented for qualified providers, not every tool. See current capabilities and tool management reference for important limits.

From the Oyzu repository root: cargo build --locked The development executable is: Platform Location Windows target\debug\oyzu.exe Linux / macOS target/debug/oyzu You can invoke it by absolute path or put the containing directory on your PATH. Validate the executable: oyzu --version oyzu --help The current version string identifies a local build and source identity. It is not a claim of production release eligibility.

Open the target project in your terminal and follow your first build. The CLI's regular workflows do not require a platform account. If you receive a tool or configuration error, consult troubleshooting rather than assuming every ecosystem is automatically provisioned.
The final receipt answers three different questions: what was requested, what ran or was reused, and what evidence remains available.
A completed build reports its result, duration, action outcomes and evidence references. On failure, prefer the root cause and recovery path over scrolling through unrelated successful tasks.

Wording Meaning Executed actions Native work actually ran during the invocation Reused results Oyzu reused previously retained evidence or outputs under the applicable cache rules Tests run now Tests executed during the current build Reused test evidence A prior report is associated with the current outcome; tests did not run now Blocked action Downstream work was prevented by a dependency failure Unknown action state The available observation does not establish a terminal result Reused test evidence is not fresh test execution. If there is no measurable coverage, do not turn a collected report into a positive coverage percentage.

oyzu history oyzu history <invocation-id> --json Build manifests and retained JSONL events can correlate an invocation with recorded actions and available artifacts. Retention and support vary. See the CLI output contract, build bundles and evidence model.
The homepage terminal panel is explicitly illustrative. The production website should only label a transcript captured when its source revision, platform, invocation and process bytes are available.
documents.s: A recorded example versus an illustration

documents.t: Oyzu coordinates project tool requirements and their environment variables with the native tasks that need them. Provider and platform coverage remains bounded.
oyzu pin --dry-run Inspect the requirement inventory and prospective changes before recording tool identities.

oyzu pin oyzu install oyzu pin resolves and records selected identities. oyzu install installs qualified locked tools. Unsupported providers or unavailable network inputs still require preparation; do not interpret every successful lock as proof that all binaries are installed.

oyzu which cargo Substitute a command known to the current project. For a shell integrated with Oyzu, use the documented shell setup: oyzu shell install bash The CLI also documents zsh and PowerShell options, and shims for noninteractive environments. See shell activation for path precedence and tool commands for exact supported subcommands.

Caching is useful only when a reused result is still valid for the requested work. Oyzu's current implementation contains an experimental local action cache with limited scope; it is not a claim of a complete distributed cache.
oyzu cache status Read the action cache reference for the relevant store, supported actions, retention rules and exact output.
oyzu build --no-cache This is useful when investigating unexpectedly reused outputs. It does not prove that every dependency input has been hermetically captured.

oyzu build --explain oyzu cache explain These commands expose available cache/execution explanations within the currently implemented scope. Consult the reference for input and output details rather than assuming remote cache support.

A reused test report is reused evidence. It must not be presented as tests having run now. Inspect the result receipt's fresh/reused distinction and producing run. Read the cache concept for the broader model and build results for receipt semantics.
Oyzu can operate without an account. CI needs an explicitly provisioned executable, native tools and inputs supported by your target project.

The following is a workflow outline, not a qualified copy-and-paste workflow for every runtime or hosted runner: # Illustrative job steps — adjust tool versions and native dependencies steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable - name: Compile Oyzu run: cargo build --locked - name: Inspect build plan run: ./target/debug/oyzu build --plan - name: Build the project run: ./target/debug/oyzu build For Windows, use the matching .exe path. A repository building Oyzu itself is not the same as a separate target repository—set the working directory accordingly.

oyzu --json config show Global --json provides a machine-readable output envelope while preserving native command exit status. Its exact schema, task forwarding rules and known limitations are in CLI output.

Retain the build receipt and relevant artifacts. Don't relabel historical test evidence as fresh tests. Validate the exact toolchain and runner environment; hosted CI support is not demonstrated by a local success alone. Related: build logging, build bundles, limitations.
Oyzu begins with the conventions of your native ecosystem, instead of requiring a new build definition for every project.
oyzu run list oyzu build --plan Review what Oyzu discovered, including its toolchain and builder choices. No build actions execute during the plan.

Some projects have multiple supported package managers, custom outputs or additional artifact relationships. In those cases, create a small build.yaml expressing the necessary exception, rather than duplicating the native project's existing scripts and configuration. Tool requirements live in oyzu.toml, and resolved identities live in oyzu.lock. Their precedence and effects are documented in configuration.

Read discovery and selection for the ranking rules and builder selection hints. Unsupported or ambiguous selections should produce a reason and recovery route—not silently pick a different native build. Evidence and limitations A discovered task does not guarantee that all of its native tools, platform targets or offline dependencies are supported. Verify the plan and consult the specific ecosystem reference before assuming a successful build. Next: Run tasks or build your first project.

Oyzu's standalone workflows do not require a platform account. Remote execution and connected services are optional extensions. Experimental client, not a deployed service guarantee The documented remote client has been tested with controlled client fixtures. It has not been qualified against a production remote queue, worker fleet or artifact transfer service. Do not infer that a configured endpoint exists or is available.
oyzu build --help The current remote-runs reference documents the experimental build --remote client, requirements, token handling, pushed-commit rule, logs, cancellation, and failure behavior.

A reliable remote result needs to identify the requested work, acknowledged execution, which observations were received, known terminal states, and any gaps after reconnect. Loss of observation must not be silently converted into success or failure. See build evidence and current limitations. Remote-cost telemetry, production availability and actual worker capacity must be verified against a deployed service when one exists.
documents.s: What remote evidence should tell you

documents.t: Use Oyzu to discover tasks exposed by your project and then invoke them through one consistent command surface.
oyzu run list The result reflects your project's native manifests, supported tooling and any explicit task configuration.
oyzu run <task-name> Replace <task-name> with a name returned by run list. Do not type the angle brackets. The selected task can have native hooks and dependencies that affect its execution.

oyzu run --help oyzu --json run list See build tasks for hook order, native output streams, failures and execution effects. Use CLI output to understand structured results. Task names depend on project discovery There is no universal list of run task names that works in every repository. Start with the actual task inventory rather than copying a guessed task.
When a command fails, start with its named cause and recovery action. The successful actions surrounding it are not necessarily relevant.
oyzu build --plan Inspect chosen builders and tools. Check discovery and selection for ambiguity resolution, and configuration for scopes and overrides.

oyzu pin --dry-run oyzu tools current Check whether the provider and version are in the currently implemented tool-management scope. Locking a tool identity does not guarantee an offline distribution is present.
oyzu build --explain oyzu cache status For a diagnostic run that avoids cache reuse: oyzu build --no-cache Review cache limitations before inferring distributed cache behavior.

Consult the receipt and retained logs; root failures are distinct from blocked dependents. Some outcomes can remain unknown if observation was lost, particularly through the experimental remote client. oyzu history oyzu history <invocation-id> --json Retained invocation lookup is bounded; missing historical evidence is not proof of earlier success. See CLI output and build bundles.

Search is local to the documentation website. If it does not return results, check that JavaScript is enabled and the index assets loaded. A published site cannot answer questions about unpublished internal documents.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/acquisition-transport.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The experimental dependency broker provides the approved HTTP fetch boundary used by captured builder preparation. Native managers retain lockfile interpretation, dependency resolution and package integrity verification. The broker fetches bytes from admitted routes; it does not run a resolver or install tools. This reference describes the current engine transport, not the planned corporate agent or a complete managed registry service.

Builder preparation supplies explicit source routes. A route binds an identifier, HTTPS origin/path prefix and optional host-held authorization header. HTTP is allowed only for loopback test/local endpoints. Credential-bearing base URLs, query/fragment-bearing bases and encoded path escapes are rejected. Every request and redirect destination must match an admitted route. A redirect uses the destination route's credentials; the original token never follows it implicitly. A route can be marked redirect-only: it admits a hop that another route redirected to, but a request that starts there is SOURCE_DENIED. The Go builder's only such route is https://storage.googleapis.com/proxy-golang-org-prod/, where proxy.golang.org sends large module zips (such as google.golang.org/api); go.sum still pins every zip. Upstream fetches honor the standard proxy environment (see Proxy and trust settings); route admission and credential rules apply identically with or without a proxy. Offline preparation containers use a private file channel to request downloads; they receive status, content type, source identity and body bytes, without upstream authorization or response headers such as cookies. Native Maven and Gradle adapters translate their loopback repository requests into this channel. Admitted standalone sources are currently selected by adapters; arbitrary private registries, corporate connector discovery and general managed credential refresh remain separate unfinished integrations. oyzu build performs acquisition before freezing the execution plan. Later build actions use prepared inputs and denied networking. Retries described here occur only during approved acquisition; a missing input or integrity failure during offline execution never triggers a download fallback. Development commands such as oyzu run install retain their documented host/native execution behavior and are not made isolated by this broker.

The broker's upstream HTTP client (tool metadata and archives, helper archives and captured-build dependency fetches) reads the standard environment of the process that runs oyzu: Variable Effect HTTPS_PROXY / https_proxy Proxy for HTTPS routes (CONNECT tunnel) HTTP_PROXY / http_proxy Proxy for HTTP routes ALL_PROXY / all_proxy Fallback when the scheme-specific variable is unset NO_PROXY / no_proxy Hosts, domains and CIDR ranges that bypass the proxy SSL_CERT_FILE PEM bundle of additional trust anchors for corporate TLS inspection; the built-in public roots stay trusted Loopback destinations (localhost, 127.0.0.0/8, ::1) always bypass the proxy, so local endpoints and their host-held authorization never go through it. Local agent, native-session and npm-session endpoints are separate clients and remain proxy-free. Proxy URLs may carry credentials and are never printed. A set but invalid proxy URL or an unreadable/empty SSL_CERT_FILE fails with PROXY_INVALID, TRUST_BUNDLE_UNREADABLE or TRUST_BUNDLE_INVALID; there is no silent direct fallback. Admitted routes still decide which origins may be contacted; a proxy adds a path, not authority. Through a TLS-inspecting proxy the proxy can see request headers, including route authorization, so configure only a proxy you trust with that route's credential. Proxy authentication beyond credentials in the proxy URL, PAC files, system proxy stores and per-route proxies are not supported. Verification: unit tests cover variable parsing, invalid values and secret redaction. On Linux, oyzu install of Node 22.15.0 through an authenticated-egress HTTPS proxy succeeded with this support and failed with SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE without it, with HTTP 403 when HTTPS_PROXY was removed, and with TRUST_BUNDLE_UNREADABLE for a bad SSL_CERT_FILE. The corporate CA proof adds TLS inspection with mitmdump and independent empty stores for all three controls. Linux result (pending execution; replace the placeholders only after running): Node 22.15.0 installed through the inspecting proxy with its additional CA: <RESULT>; without SSL_CERT_FILE, TLS failed with no successful direct fallback: <RESULT>; with an unrelated CA, TLS failed: <RESULT>. The proxy observed the positive archive download: <RESULT>. Windows/macOS behavior and real HTTP_PROXY/ALL_PROXY qualification remain open.

One logical fetch has at most two retries in addition to its initial attempt. The retry count and a 45-second network deadline are shared across redirect destinations; redirecting does not renew either budget. The existing maximum of five HTTP redirect-chain requests remains bounded separately. Each actual request also consumes the session's 4096-request allowance, including retries and redirects. The HTTP library's automatic protocol retries are disabled so they cannot silently extend this budget. These are per-fetch broker bounds. A native manager can submit another logical request; its own retry behavior remains native and is constrained by the session and enclosing acquisition limits. This is not a per-package attempt counter or a persistent upstream cooldown shared across requests. Retryable upstream statuses are 408, 429, 502, 503 and 504. Connection/request/body transport failures can also retry; partial transfers are discarded before a fresh request. A complete response still goes through its adapter's integrity checks. Statuses such as 401, 403, 404 and 500 are returned immediately. Denied routes, invalid redirects and resource-limit failures are terminal in the broker. Package checksum failures remain terminal at their adapter boundary. Backoff is 200 ms, then 400 ms. A supplied Retry-After delay or HTTP date sets a longer minimum wait, using the standard HTTP semantics. Invalid headers or waits that cannot fit the remaining deadline return the current upstream failure instead of retrying early. A timeout may exhaust the whole deadline before any retry is possible. There is no new project setting for these bounds. A delivery edge that is still filling an artifact from its publisher answers 503 with Oyzu-Fill: pending and Retry-After (problem code FILL_PENDING). That answer is not an ordinary failure: the client waits the Retry-After seconds (1 to 30, default 5), asks again with a fresh 45-second deadline and does not count it as one of the two retries, for up to 15 minutes per logical fetch. A large first download through an organization's edge therefore waits for the edge to finish verifying the artifact instead of failing. Without the header a 503 is an ordinary retryable status. Requests send Accept: text/html unless the source serves a JSON API, in which case the source declares application/json (the Adoptium JDK catalog rejects the default with 406). Successful-response bodies are limited to 256 MiB each and 1 GiB read per session. Bytes from partial/failed attempts count toward the session total. Upstream error bodies are discarded without reading or relaying them; clients receive a fixed message containing the HTTP status. These are broker payload bounds, not a claim about total TCP traffic or native resolver memory use. Native acquisition has additional enclosing execution limits.

The private channel now preserves the difference between denied access and unavailable transport. Broker-generated failures include a sanitized errorCode and a fixed body, with no requested URL, query, token or upstream error text: HTTP status Broker code Meaning and next step 400 REQUEST_INVALID Malformed channel input; correct the adapter/request contract 403 SOURCE_DENIED No approved route permits the request or redirect; fix the declared source integration 413 BYTE_LIMIT Payload/session bounds exceeded; inspect dependency size and acquisition scope 429 REQUEST_LIMIT Session request allowance exhausted; inspect resolution scope rather than retrying that exhausted session 502 SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE Transport failed after eligible retries; check availability/connectivity and rerun preparation 502 REDIRECT_INVALID, REDIRECT_LIMIT Invalid or excessive redirect chain; correct the source endpoint 504 SOURCE_TIMEOUT Network deadline expired; investigate the source/connectivity before rerunning Upstream HTTP failures retain their actual status and a redacted body; they do not acquire a fabricated broker code. Native managers determine how they display those statuses. Maven now requests native error stack traces (-e) to retain nested resolution causes in failed-build diagnostics; debug logging (-X) is not enabled. A failed preparation produces no successful dependency snapshot or executable build plan. A later explicit build prepares fresh inputs and evidence. Previously, the channel reported every internal failure as 403. Consumers must handle non-success statuses generally rather than assuming every unsuccessful request is a permission denial. The optional errorCode field is additive; existing native clients still receive the original status/body fields. This does not change successful dependency records or artifact identities. For broker-generated BYTE_LIMIT, the private response additionally provides limitScope (response, session, or artifact), observedBytes, and limitBytes. These numeric facts identify the exhausted existing bound without exposing the request URL, response body, or headers. The pnpm archive adapter includes them in its sanitized failed-preparation diagnostic; it also reports the count and stored bytes of publisher metadata captured before archive acquisition. Neither field changes the configured limits or permits a failed preparation to produce a snapshot. The channel serves up to eight requests at once. One thread claims request files in arrival order and a pool of eight fetchers answers them; the pool shares one session's 4096-request and 1 GiB allowances, so concurrency does not raise either bound. The bundled clients use it: the npm, pnpm and Yarn adapters keep up to eight registry fetches in flight and record packages in lock order whichever fetch finishes first, npm seeds its private cache with one native npm cache add per 16 tarballs or 16 MiB of archives, whichever comes first, instead of one per package (the command unpacks every archive it is given at once into the worker's 512 MiB /tmp, and 200 archives of a large project ran it out of space; its memory also grows with the number of archives, and 64 or more small archives exceeded a 2 GiB worker), Go asks go mod download for the whole module set in one call, the Python adapter splits a locked, hashed export across four pip download --no-deps processes before the resolving download, and Cargo capture on the host fetches index entries and crate archives eight at a time with the same routes and shared allowances, then checks them in lock order. A request still has its 55-second client wait, so more than eight slow upstream requests can queue behind each other, and this does not eliminate every acquisition outage. Active blocking requests are not immediately interruptible on session shutdown. General cancellation, queue scheduling and managed retry-policy delivery remain work. A successful retry does not authenticate a dependency or establish release eligibility.

When native npm cache add fails, the diagnostic names the one-based seed batch, archive count and compressed bytes. It keeps the native exit status and signal, and recognized spawn error codes, numeric errno and syscall names when available. For example, a silent exit can report npm cache seed batch 1 (16 archives; 4066624 bytes): npm cache add failed (244): status=244; signal=none. The npm adapter can also read the final 16 KiB of a newly created private npm debug log for recognized OS error codes and errno numbers, and fixed syscall names. Raw debug text, arguments, configuration values and URLs are excluded from these additional fields. Earlier commands' logs are ignored, and missing or unreadable logs do not replace the original failure. Existing native stdout/stderr behavior is preserved. The temporary cache and its logs are removed through the existing cleanup path; the adapter does not retain raw debug logs in the build bundle. A status such as 244 alone does not establish an out-of-memory cause. Use the reported native cause and worker evidence to decide whether the problem is resource pressure, filesystem access or another native failure. These diagnostics do not retry npm, change the 16-archive/16-MiB seed limits, or alter offline and lifecycle restrictions. Run oyzu exec -- node --test tooling/test-npm-native-diagnostics.mjs for the failure/privacy and cache-seeding regressions; their fixture transport requires no registry access.

Resolved artifact set installs reuse this transport with one source per per-host route (artifact sets). Two additions apply only to that caller: a source marked redirects = "server" treats any 3xx as ROUTE_REDIRECT_UNEXPECTED (not followed), and a client-followed redirect hop that no route permits fails ROUTE_REDIRECT_UNROUTABLE instead of SOURCE_DENIED; a hop to a host with its own rule is fetched from that rule's destination. With no tools route configured, hops may reach any https host. Other callers keep SOURCE_DENIED and the redirect rules above. Redirect targets and their query strings are never stored or reported.

Native tool preparation also sends the admitted nextest/LLVM-coverage release archives through this broker. Public helper acquisition admits GitHub and its release-assets redirect origin; configured tool connectors replace that public route and do not receive an automatic public fallback. The tool adapter validates the pinned recipe against its admitted metadata before download, and the store verifies the archive digest before extraction. This is archive installation, not arbitrary Cargo package resolution or source compilation. See native helper installation. Pinned distribution inputs (Rust, and the Node, Go, Python, JDK and Maven archives) opt into sequential 8 MiB HTTP range requests. Each range is one bounded logical fetch under the retry, 45-second deadline, redirect and source-authorization rules above. Total artifact size is capped at 512 MiB, because a JDK archive is about 200 MB, with every transferred byte charged to the shared 1 GiB session budget. Unpinned responses keep the 256 MiB limit. Large progressing artifacts can therefore take longer than 45 seconds overall without permitting an individual stalled request to wait indefinitely. Range responses must match the requested offsets and body lengths, be contiguous, and agree on the total size. A server may ignore the first range and return a complete response under the ordinary deadline. It may not return a full response after partial segments. Malformed or inconsistent ranges fail as SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE; oversize totals fail as BYTE_LIMIT. The Rust adapter checks the final locked SHA-256 before making any input available to rustup. This is neither persistent partial-download caching nor a change to native manager requests. Other fetch callers keep the ordinary single-response contract.

cargo test --locked --test integration broker:: uses real local HTTP servers to verify retryable statuses, partial-body replacement, retry exhaustion, terminal statuses, authorization on retries/redirects, a retry budget shared across hosts, error-body redaction and channel failure classification. Owner-local tests verify delay/date/deadline decisions and terminal byte/request limits. These checks run in the Windows, macOS and Linux CLI jobs before captured scenarios. The httpdate dependency owns HTTP-date parsing instead of a handwritten parser. Version 1.0.3 is MIT OR Apache-2.0, declares Rust 1.56 support and uses portable standard-library time types; its lock entry is generated by Cargo. It does not change route authorization or clocks used for monotonic request deadlines. See implementation status for completed checks. Controlled HTTP failures prove transport behavior; they do not establish the cause or resolution of an unrelated Maven Central incident. Actual Java/native scenario success remains separate CI evidence.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/action-cache.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Status: experimental. Implements the first milestone of the draft OEP-0011 (local cache) and, since 2026-10-10, a standalone development-scope remote OCI cache for per-action results (handoff K3). The proposal stays draft until maintainer review. Managed-platform cache policy, signing and every CI trust claim are later milestones and are not implemented here. A repeat oyzu build skips targets whose inputs have not changed and restores their earlier results. Nothing is configured: users never write cache keys or per-language cache paths. Reuse is local to one user on one machine, and every output says plainly that a restored result was not executed now. When known, reuse.source records the serving local or remote tier, independently of the original producing run. Receipts separate reused test evidence from fresh tests. An unavailable cache is distinct from explicit --no-cache; permitted native execution continues with a warning and fresh action evidence. Lookup metadata distinguishes hit, miss, rejected restoration and unavailable store; it does not change cache admission.

The unit of reuse depends on what Oyzu knows about the target: Per action for targets whose actions carry a stage contract (today node/package on the captured path). Each action (for example api:version, api:build, api:package) has its own key and result; see Per-action reuse. The target's group record is kept as a view that lists its action results, so an unchanged repeat still restores the whole target in one step. Per target group for every other builder: one key per target, restoring all its actions together or none. The actions of one target share a single private workspace. For native npm applications with dependencies, the target group includes the prepare action (npm ci). A hit restores the successful group without reinstalling dependencies. A miss installs into the private target workspace before pre-build hooks. This adds an action to native plan/manifest records; the install retains the selected build's admitted environment, including task overrides, without changing other operations' environments. Existing results with the earlier action definition miss naturally. No cache format change or manual clearing is needed. Captured npm installation retains its existing per-action admission and may still run on an unchanged build.

Before action lookup, npm validates native metadata and captures locked dependency bytes with lifecycle scripts disabled. This script-free acquisition can reuse a local preparation result. Its key binds the complete admitted source and target tree, exact worker image/platform, currently admitted tools, runtime adapter, command/environment, configuration and public broker routes. A source, lock, tool, route or configuration change requires a new capture. Tool admission still runs before lookup; restored files and the complete tree are verified before use. The builder revalidates its captured native facts and makes current version and recipe decisions afterward. This does not cache the later offline install or lifecycle scripts. Unbounded actions and hooks retain their existing execution rules. The preparation journal records reused acquisition as not executed now, with its original capture time and key. Dependency evidence describes the same captured bytes. Preparation entries share the local store, lease, 10 GiB retention budget and oyzu cache status/prune/clear operations with action results. They are not uploaded to remote action caches. Missing, damaged or unreadable entries fall back to fresh acquisition; partially restored trees are discarded. --no-cache, cache.local = false and contract verification disable preparation reuse. Managed configuration, secret environment values and authenticated acquisition routes are ineligible. Offline builds may reuse previously captured inputs after current admission; a miss follows the ordinary acquisition/offline rules. Only npm's script-free acquisition currently opts in. No cache migration or manual clearing is required. Native builder actions can also bind exact prepared-resource files. The plan's dependency input records those files and their content-tree digest; execution mounts and revalidates that same selection even with --no-cache. An absent selection keeps the whole prepared input, while an empty selection exposes an empty directory. Export-only injected defaults may be omitted from commands that do not consume them; explicit native or user values remain effective. Authored replacements clear these native bindings. The bounded Go application path additionally isolates native tests in fresh original-capture workspaces and empty report output roots. Their ephemeral writes are discarded; the collector retains the actual roots until report gates finish and captures validated reports into the invocation bundle. Reused reports retain their original producer evidence. Generated/artifact workspace consumers and --verify-contract with private roots are currently unsupported on that path. Native runtime qualification remains in the Go proof record. A reused target or action keeps: its artifacts, byte for byte (each is re-verified against its recorded digest); its original JUnit, coverage and other reports and their producer evidence; the original run identifier, key and completion time, in a reuse record (for an action reused individually, the run in which that action really executed). A target is stored only after all of its actions succeeded and its reports were collected. Failed, blocked and cancelled targets are never stored. Not cached by default (the target simply runs, and the output says why): targets containing authored tasks or task overrides that do not ask to be cached, and targets whose hooks ([tasks."api:pre_build"]) declare no outputs, because their effects are not visible to Oyzu. An authored task with cache = true and outputs is cached (see Authored tasks); a hook that declares outputs is followed on targets reused action by action (see Hooks); targets with hooks on a path that reuses a target only whole (the native host path, and captured targets without stage contracts): restoring the target would skip its hooks, which run on every build; targets using secret environment values ({ secret = "…" }). Declared source inputs are captured and included in the target scope on both native and captured paths (see Declared inputs). They do not by themselves prevent reuse. Built-in builders declare their own actions, so their stages are cacheable without configuration.

Captured executor path: oyzu build and oyzu build --affected on targets that use it (for example node/package). This needs the Docker executor the captured path already requires and its provisioned toolchain images. Native host path: builds that run on the host with Oyzu-provisioned tools (node/app dist applications, Go, Rust, Python wheels) reuse unchanged targets the same way; see Native host builds. Targets built by a host-coordinated image worker are not cached yet and say so. Direct oyzu run task executions are never cached. Standalone use needs no account. Ephemeral CI runners start with an empty local store; with a remote OCI cache configured they reuse per-action results other checkouts pushed. A remote hit is a development result, not trusted CI evidence. Existing regression verification is Linux (see Verification). The bounded shared-source baseline also measured Windows-host/Linux-Docker seed/repeat reuse and native package results. Shared edits conservatively re-execute unrelated work there; full Windows/macOS cache qualification remains pending. The bounded Linux shared-source proof passed; its named remaining qualification cases stay explicit in that record.

On Windows, action tracking can observe native symbolic links and the Linux symlink reparse points (WSL format 2) created by Docker in a captured workspace. The shared workspace copier preserves the original link form in native control views for these Linux links; native Windows link recreation remains unsupported. Tracking records the target without following it, so pnpm links can remain available to later native actions. A delta containing links still cannot be restored from the action cache. Other reparse formats fail explicitly; this does not admit symlinks in captured source or relax dependency/artifact containment. No project setting or cache migration is required. See the bounded pnpm workspace proof.

oyzu build # first build executes and stores; repeats reuse oyzu build --affected HEAD # Git-selected targets also reuse unchanged results oyzu build --full # quality stages and their reports are reused too oyzu build --no-cache # run every action; read and write nothing oyzu cache status # where the store is, how large, how many entries oyzu cache clear # remove every cached result (bundles are untouched) oyzu build --explain # after the build, why each stage was reused or ran oyzu cache explain api # why target api's key (and its stages' keys) last changed Every oyzu cache command is headless, reads no project beyond configuration, and supports the global --json flag before or after the subcommand. Example (EX-033 declared-targets project, Linux, one run each): $ oyzu build # cold ✓ Build succeeded 4 targets · 4 executed · 9.4s $ oyzu build # unchanged repeat ↺ api build reused was 1.2s ✓ Build succeeded 4 targets · 4 reused · 1.8s $ echo "// edit" >> api/src/greeting.mjs && oyzu build ✓ Build succeeded 4 targets · 3 reused · 1 executed · 3.1s

Status: experimental, node/package on the captured path. Draft design: stage/action contract (steps A and B of OEP-0020 slice S5). Nothing is configured; step B added one flag, build --verify-contract (its name is provisional until the maintainer confirms it). Planning attaches a stage contract to each action of an analyzed target (extensions["oyzu.dev/stage-contract"] in plan.json): the reads, writes, environment names and tools the static analysis found for the stage, the actions it follows, the fallback rung and whether its outputs are bounded (no unknown write). A target whose actions all carry a contract is reused action by action: Step Behavior Lookup the target's group record is tried first (unchanged target: one step). On a miss, each action is looked up when it becomes ready Action key the action's own frozen definition (command, environment, working directory, platform, limits, report contracts, configuration digest), the target scope digest, toolchain, builder, variant, platform, prepared dependencies (only for an action that reads them), materialized artifacts and the output digests of the earlier actions of the target it follows Action result the files the action published to the bundle (artifacts, reports), the records describing them, and its observed workspace changes (created and modified files with digests, deleted files, new directories) Reuse records enter the manifest as succeeded with a reuse record; reports are parsed again and gated by the current contract; the workspace changes are restored before the next action that has to execute, so dependents see the files executing it would have left. A fully reused target never touches its workspace Early cutoff a re-run action that produces the same workspace changes leaves its dependents' keys unchanged, so they are still reused Always runs an action without bounded outputs (a stage contract with an unknown write) is never reused on its own; it runs every time and its observed output still feeds what follows. A target holding such an action is not restored whole Storing results are committed only after the whole target succeeded and its reports were collected; the group view is written last and lists actionResults (action id and key) Keys: target scope, or the contract's reads for a confined action. An action's key hashes the target scope unless the action is confined (next section); a confined action hashes only the source entries its contract reads. The configuration digest is part of every action, so changing an execution setting such as --full re-keys all actions (see Deferred). A builder with no analysis, and any target containing an authored task or task override that does not set cache = true with outputs, or a hook without declared outputs, keeps the group behavior and wording described above. A symbolic link or special file created by an action makes its changes unrestorable: the action still runs and feeds its dependents but is not stored. The manifest records each action's outcome (reused, executed, always-run) under manifest.extensions["oyzu.dev/action-cache"].targets.<target>.actions; executed actions also carry their actionKey.

Status: experimental (stage/action contract step C), per-action targets only (node/package on the captured path). A hook ([tasks."api:pre_build"], post_<stage>) that declares outputs no longer makes its target not-cached: [tasks."api:pre_build"] argv = ["node", "hook.mjs"] outputs = ["generated"] # workspace paths, directories or globs the hook writes Aspect Behavior The hook runs on every build; it is never restored and its record never carries reuse. The per-action record shows it as always-run Its output the files it actually changed are recorded (like any action's workspace changes) and their digest enters the key of every later action of the target, so a hook that writes something else re-runs what follows it and a hook that writes the same bytes leaves it reused Target outcome reused when every other action was reused (the hook running does not count against it); otherwise executed. The target's group record is not stored, as for any always-run action Undeclared effects a hook that changes a file outside its declared outputs is not followed: nothing of the target is stored and the target outcome carries a rejected note naming the files, so the next build executes it again No outputs unchanged: the target is not-cached ("hooks without declared outputs"). --no-cache is unchanged Whole-target path on the native host path, and on captured targets without stage contracts, a target is restored only whole, which would skip its hooks. Such a target is not-cached ("runs hooks, which run on every build, and its actions are not reused one by one here") and its hooks run on every build. (Before this was fixed, a hook that declared outputs on that path was restored without running on an unchanged repeat.) On hosts without view support (Windows today) no action is confined, so every action keeps the target-scope key and any source edit, including a hook edit, re-runs the whole target; the hook still runs every build and an unchanged repeat is still reused. The hook_reuse and generated_source scenarios assert confined (and the selective reuse that depends on it) only where views are supported and the target-scope behavior elsewhere; every other assertion runs unchanged on all hosts. Hook outputs are relative to the hook's working directory (the target, unless cwd says otherwise), written with / or \; the cache resolves them against the project root before judging the files the hook changed. Editing a hook script is a source edit: it changes the target scope, so it re-runs the target-scope-keyed actions and any confined action whose reads include the script (the default lint and format-check read every JavaScript and TypeScript file of the target). Whether it also changes the development version, which is in every action's environment, depends on the hook: Hook Development version A comment-only edit of its script (same output) pre_build with outputs, on a builder that finalizes versions (Node) finalized after the hook (below): the script leaves the version scope and what the hook wrote enters it keeps the version; the confined api:build is reused. api:test re-runs in EX-033 because its contract reads api/** any other hook (pre_test, post_build, …), or another builder the script stays in the version scope changes the version, which re-keys every action of the target Version finalization after hooks (OEP-0011 handoff K2, captured path): Planning moves the target's version action after its followed pre_build hooks, so nothing that writes the version runs before them, and records every action in plan.json with the pre-hook source version (the version scope without the hook's script). The target record carries extensions["oyzu.dev/version-finalization"] with the hooks and the actions that follow them. The actions before the hook (prepare, the hook itself) run with the pre-hook source version. When the hooks succeed, the files under their declared outputs are digested (from the workspace, not the cache, so --no-cache gives the same result) and folded into the version. The target is planned again with that version, and the actions after the hooks run from this post-hook plan: the same actions and edges, with the final version in their environment, artifact names and target record. It is written to plans/<target>.post-hooks.json (evidence kind post-hook-plan); plan.json is never changed. The manifest's target record is the post-hook one, and manifest.extensions["oyzu.dev/version-finalization"].<target> gives preHookVersion, version, hookOutputs, planPath and planDigest. A hook edit that changes what the hook writes changes the version and the package. A script stays in the version scope when it is not named as an argument of the hook's command (for example run = "node hook.mjs" through a shell) or when a builder stage reads or writes it; such an edit then changes the version as before. The hook still runs on every build. Limits: the hook's other reads stay in the source scope as usual; a package that ships the hook script without the analysis seeing it (an npm package with no files field) gets a new package under the same version after a script-only edit, the same limit the test-only exclusion has; other builders, other hook phases and the native host path are not finalized. An authored task such as EX-010's api:test is reused around a hook when it sets cache = true (next section). Limits: effects outside the workspace (network, global state) are invisible and are the hook author's to declare away.

Status: experimental (OEP-0011 handoff K1). An authored task or task override is not cached by default, because its effects are not visible to Oyzu. It opts in with the existing cache and outputs task fields: [tasks."api:test"] run = "node --test" cache = true inputs = ["src/**", "test/**"] # optional; may only add to the target scope outputs = [".events"] # workspace paths, directories or globs the task writes Aspect Behavior Opt-in cache = true and at least one outputs entry. The plan marks the action cacheable: true and records the declaration in extensions["oyzu.dev/authored-cache"]. Hooks always run: cache on a hook is ignored Key the task's own frozen definition (command, environment names, working directory, report contracts, configuration digest) and the target scope, as for a builder stage; so editing a file in the target, or the task itself, re-runs it. It is never keyed on, or confined to, the builder's analysis of a stage it replaces inputs relative to the task's directory. Entries inside the target are already covered by its scope. An entry outside the target is a scope the cache does not model yet: the target is not-cached ("declares inputs outside its target (…), which are not scoped yet") rather than keyed on less than the task reads Per-action targets (captured node/package) the task is a reusable action. Its observed workspace changes are its result and must lie inside its declared outputs; changes outside them store nothing for the target and the outcome carries a rejected note naming the files, as for a hook. Around a hook it is reused while the hook's output digest is unchanged and re-runs when that output changes (EX-010) Whole-target path (native host, other builders) the target is reused whole when every action is a builder stage or a cached authored task; reports are restored and re-gated. Declared outputs are not checked there: the private workspace is discarded after the build and nothing runs after a restored target. A target with hooks is not cached on this path (see the hooks section) cache = true without outputs not-cached with the reason "<task> sets cache = true but declares no outputs, so it is not cached" --no-cache, cache.local = false unchanged: nothing is reused or stored Limits: a task that leaves nothing in the workspace must still name an output (for example the directory its tool writes logs to); reusing an authored task around hooks needs per-action reuse, which only captured node/package targets have; inputs outside the target are not honored; a command that a builder does not recognize for report instrumentation keeps today's reporting behavior (on the native path such an override fails its report gate whether or not it is cached).

Status: experimental (stage/action contract step B). Prerequisites: the captured executor path and a Unix host (views recreate installed command shims as symbolic links; Linux was run, macOS was not). Windows has no view support yet, so narrow keys stay off there and every action keeps its target-scope key. A narrow key is only sound if the action cannot see anything the key left out. Oyzu therefore keys an action on its contract's reads only when the action also runs confined to them: Step Behavior Eligible the contract is confinable: the analysis modeled that stage's own command (stage-specific facts exist), no fact of the stage is an unbounded unknown (a bounded one adds its bound to the reads; see bounded unknowns), and its outputs are bounded. For an analyzed Node package these are build and test from its scripts, and the builder's own commands: the version stamp (version), the npm install (prepare), npm pack (package) and the default ESLint and Prettier checks (lint, format-check) of a package without such scripts. A builder command's facts name it (runner) and apply only to an action running that command, so pnpm and Yarn installs and packs, workspace plans, application packages, Biome and authored replacements keep the target-scope key. See builder-owned stages Key the digest of the captured source entries the contract's reads select, plus the output digests of every earlier action of the target (not only the ones it names) except a check ordered before it only to share the workspace (see checks that run at once), the frozen action, toolchain, prepared dependencies and materialized artifacts. Editing a file the stage does not read leaves its key unchanged only when the edit also leaves the development version unchanged: a test-only file, or the script of a pre_build hook whose version is finalized after it. Any other edit in the target changes the version, which is in every action's environment, so it re-keys every action View before the action runs, the executor builds a private view of the target workspace holding only the declared reads, what the earlier actions its key follows created, and the artifacts materialized for it, and mounts it as /workspace. Files outside it do not exist for the action Merge when the action ends, what it created, changed or deleted in the view is merged back into the target workspace, so the next action and the change tracker see what an unconfined run would have left Not confined any action without a contract, with an unbounded unknown fact or an unknown write, on a builder without analysis, on the native host path, and on hosts without view support. Each keeps the target-scope key; narrow keys never exist without confinement The EX-033 api target, oyzu build --full, after appending a comment to api/test/greeting.test.mjs: · api:build Reused from an earlier run · not executed now · originally ran … (key 0452eeca9fb2) › api:test Running Cache active · 3 targets reused Since the builder's own stages are confined too (2026-10-10), the same edit also reuses api:version, api:prepare and api:package (it packs only files: ["dist"]) and re-runs api:lint and api:format-check, which read every JavaScript file of the target. manifest.extensions["oyzu.dev/action-cache"].targets.<target>.confined lists the actions run confined, and actions shows each one's outcome. --no-cache and cache.local = false disable result lookup and storage, while eligible actions keep the same private views and predecessor effects. A fresh oracle therefore executes the same admitted file boundary as a reusable run. Disabling reuse does not expose undeclared files.

Status: experimental (OEP-0020 NSA-02, 2026-10-10; design: bounded unknowns). An unknown fact may carry a bound: the files, globs, task environment or installed packages the construct cannot read outside of. A stage whose unknown facts are all bounded has the rung widened: its contract's reads gain each bound, it stays confinable, and it runs confined with a narrow key like any other. One unbounded unknown keeps the whole stage on the target-scope key, unconfined, as before. Bound Covers Example Hard what the tool's own rules allow npm pack files entries (the package directory), an unexpanded test pattern (the runner's root), a computed environment mode (<envDir>/.env*), a missing relative import (the files resolution probes), a tsconfig extending a package (installed packages and the configuration's directory), computed process.env access and Nitro provider detection (the task's environment) Heuristic where a tool usually stays a command with no tool profile (prettier, biome, oxlint, tsup) or an unmodeled subcommand or flag of a modeled one (next lint, ng test, vitest --coverage): its directory, the files directly in each directory above it, and installed packages. Task runners (turbo, nx, lerna, ultra, wireit) are never bounded A bound that relies on installed packages counts only for an action that reads the prepared dependencies, which key them. If a confined widened action reads outside its bound, it fails with the path and the inputs declaration that fixes it (below); declared inputs add to the bound but never bound an unbounded unknown. oyzu build --plan shows the rung (scope: widened) and each bound in the Why column of the Unknown (widens scope) group; --why <path> answers covered-by-bound for a path only a bound covers.

Status: experimental (parallel block WS2, 2026-10-10). The check stages of one target (test, lint, format-check, scheduled by --full or CI) leave nothing another check consumes, so the plan marks the edge between two consecutive ones as order only (extensions["oyzu.dev/order-only"] on the later action). A hook between them, or a declared depends_on, keeps the edge a real dependency. When build.jobs is above 1, the executor starts a check as soon as what it really needs (for example build) has finished, beside the checks ordered before it, if all of these hold: the check runs confined (its contract is confinable, the host has view support, and --verify-contract is not set); every action of its target already running is a check running confined; no two of them declare writes that could meet (a glob counts as its literal directory). Otherwise it waits for its turn as before. Order-only edges change three things, in serial and parallel runs alike, so both give the same keys and outputs: Behavior View a check's view leaves out what the checks ordered before it left, even where its read globs match, and checks that may overlap get copied files instead of hard links, so one check's in-place write cannot reach another Key a check's key follows the actions its view shows, not the checks ordered before it; package still follows every check Failure a failed check no longer blocks the next check; it still blocks package and everything after it A check that finishes before the checks ordered ahead of it is recorded after them, so the target workspace changes in plan order. The build prints overlapping checks as running at the same time. Not covered: the independent-targets pipeline still runs one action per target at a time (each branch holds one worker), the native host path and Windows have no views, and oyzu run stays serial.

For a captured target whose complete final selected commands are bounded, cacheable and confinable, the development source suffix now uses the positive read boundary of its shipping commands, together with captured configuration and lock paths and declared inputs. A check's reads stay included if its writes can feed a shipping command, including through another check. This can keep an unrelated target's version unchanged after a shared-source edit that none of its commands reads. It uses the same rule with reuse enabled or disabled. This final binding currently requires Unix view support. Targets with hooks, authored replacements, source projections, materialized artifact inputs or cross-target prerequisites retain their established conservative version scope. Missing or unstable final command evidence also keeps that scope atomically; preparation is not rerun. See version inference. A development snapshot version (1.2.3-dev.g<digest>) is written into package.json by the version action, so it is an input of every later action. The earlier conservative path derived from the whole target scope, which made build impossible to reuse after any edit. It now derives from the same scope minus files that only a quality stage (test, lint, format-check) is known to read exactly: a file the analysis lists as an exact read of test and that no other stage reads, writes or is covered by. An unknown fact of a shipping stage (build, package) counts as reading its bound, or every file when it has none, so a test-only file a computed import of build may reach stays in the version. The reads of the builder's own commands (npm pack packing a package without files, for example) do not count here, so modeling those stages did not change any version. A test-only edit therefore changes neither the version nor the artifact names; a new test file, which only a glob finds, still does. This holds for a target at the project root too (EX-031). When several targets share the directory holding a file, such as a package and an image at the root, the file is left out only if every one of them reads it only from a quality stage; otherwise each version still covers it. The script of a followed pre_build hook also leaves its own target's scope (not when another target shares that directory), and what the hook wrote is folded in after it runs (version finalization). Tagged and history-derived versions are unchanged. The version reaches every action as OYZU_VERSION, so any other edit in the target re-keys all of them.

If a confined action fails and its output names a file that exists in the target but not in the view, the build reports the stage, the path, the missing fact and the smallest fix, in human, NO_COLOR and --json output (diagnostic confined-read-outside-contract; structured detail in manifest.extensions["oyzu.dev/contract-violations"]): ERROR api:build read extra.txt, which its stage contract does not declare, so the confined view hid it. Missing fact: reads-path extra.txt Fix: declare it as an input of api in build.yaml: inputs: ["api/extra.txt"] (Or make the reference static so the analysis sees it.) The fix is to declare the path (see Declared inputs): the declaration in the message is relative to build.yaml, as inputs are, while the read path is shown as the target's own files write it. --json carries the same declaration as fix.declare.inputs. Making the reference static removes the need for it. Disabling the cache preserves the admitted view. The file is found by scanning the action's output for paths, so a tool that fails without printing the path is reported only as a failed action. The builder's node --test stage writes JUnit and coverage to report files, which do not carry a test file's own error output, so it also runs the spec reporter on the action's stderr: a test file that reads an undeclared file is explained like any other stage. The behavior is the same when targets run in parallel; see the parallel soundness gate.
documents.s: When a confined action reads something undeclared

documents.t: A target's inputs in build.yaml name extra source paths it reads (files or directories, relative to build.yaml; see target workspaces). On the captured path each one: joins the target's input scope, so the target-scope key and the development snapshot version cover it; joins the reads of every stage contract of the target (source: "build.yaml", confidence exact), so a confined action sees it and its narrow key covers it. A target-level input therefore also re-keys test when the file changes, even if only build reads it; only adds. It never removes an inferred read, and it never makes an action confinable: an action whose contract has an unbounded unknown fact keeps the target-scope key whatever is listed. An input that leaves the workspace (the directory holding build.yaml) or names no captured file is a CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE error before anything runs, so a typo cannot silently declare nothing. Globs are not accepted; a directory covers everything beneath it. --affected does not yet treat a change under another target's declared input as affecting the declaring target.

oyzu build --verify-contract # also: --json, --full The flag name is provisional (confirmed direction, name pending maintainer confirmation). It cannot be combined with --no-cache or --plan. A normal build runs; additionally, for every confined action: the action starts from a copy of its target workspace and runs confined, as usual; the same action runs again from an identical copy with the whole target visible; the results are compared: exit code, every workspace file created, changed or deleted, and the artifacts collected. Test and coverage report files are not compared, because they carry timing. Equal results pass. If they differ, Oyzu runs the action again with subsets of the hidden files (at most twelve extra runs) to find a minimal set that explains the difference, and names those files and the declaration that fixes them: Contract check failed · 8 confined actions run again with their whole target visible · 7 equal · 1 diverged · 20 not confined (not checked) api:build Diverged · also reads optional.json · declare inputs: ["api/optional.json"] A divergence fails the build, also when independent targets run in parallel (diagnostic contract-diverged; manifest.extensions["oyzu.dev/contract-verification"] carries status, counts and one record per action). The check reuses and stores nothing (it uses a throwaway store), does not use a tracer and does not run on the native path. It runs each confined action at least twice with copies of the workspace, so it is slow on large installed trees. Actions that are not confined are counted, not checked. If the search stops at its budget the record says minimal: false.

Status: experimental (OEP-0011 milestones 2 and 3, handoffs K3 and K4; registry sign-in added 2026-10-10). Unsigned: a CI repository is trusted only because its registry refuses writes without the CI credential (see CI and development repositories); no producer is verified. Verified on Linux against zot 2.1.18 (anonymous), CNCF Distribution 3.1.2 behind a registry token service with an S3-API store, and a Harbor 2.13.1 proxy-cache project in front of that registry. The entry format is frozen (2026-10-10, under its v1alpha1 identifiers); design: the object-count rules. # oyzu.toml (project): where results are shared [cache] remote = "oci://registry.example.com/team/oyzu-cache" cache.remote and cache.ciRemote are accepted only in user/global, machine or administrative scope. Project/local files that set either key fail with a scope diagnostic. Use OYZU_CACHE_REMOTE and OYZU_CACHE_CI_REMOTE for invocation or CI configuration; they override ordinary files and remain subject to administrative constraints. These restrictions apply even to trusted project folders. # user configuration: this machine also publishes what it builds [cache] write = true A registry that requires sign-in is supported through the registry token flow. The credential is an environment variable, never a setting: export OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN=… # the token your registry's token endpoint accepts In a CI job that offers OIDC ID tokens the way GitHub Actions does (OYZU_ID_TOKEN_URL and OYZU_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN, which the Oyzu runner sets), leave OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN unset: the client signs in with the job's own ID tokens and asks for a new one when it needs it (see sign-in below). Reading is on by default once cache.remote is set (cache.read = true); writing is off until cache.write = true. Both are per-machine preferences; neither changes an action key, so readers and writers share entries. A loopback host (localhost, 127.0.0.0/8, ::1) is reached over plain HTTP, every other host over HTTPS with the shared proxy and trust settings. The remote is used only while the local cache is active: --no-cache, cache.local = false and --verify-contract use no remote. What is shared: per-action results on targets reused action by action (captured node/package and node/app targets with stage contracts), and whole-target results on targets reused only whole (the native host path, other builders), one entry under the target key. A per-action target's group view is never pushed; a client rebuilds it locally from the action results, so an unchanged repeat after a remote hit makes no registry request. In the build record a whole-target entry is listed under the target's id where an action id would be. Step Behavior Lookup after a local miss, one GET of the manifest under the action's tag. On a hit, the config and the layer it names (two blob GETs). No blob HEAD, no tag listing Verify manifest shape, media types and key annotation; config and layer size and SHA-256; the uncompressed archive's SHA-256; every archive entry against its name; the set of entries against the blobs the config references. Only then is the result committed to the local store, and the unchanged local restore verifies it again Push after an action's (or whole target's) result is committed locally and cache.write is true: one GET of the tag (racing-writer check), config and layer uploads (POST + PUT each), then the manifest PUT under the tag, which is the only write that makes the entry visible Offer a reused result when a build reuses a result this machine produced and never sent to this remote (stored before the remote was configured, or while it was down), it is pushed the same way, always after the tag GET, even with immutable tags (it is usually there already). The store then marks it sent (pushed/<remote>/<key>), so later reuses ask nothing. Results that came from a remote, and results written before the format freeze (no keyComponents), are not offered. Recorded with "reused": true Racing writers equal output identity (artifact digests and workspace changes; reports excluded, they carry timing) converges and writes nothing; a different one is a conflict: recorded, never replaced Sign-in and redirects: The credential is first sent as a bearer token. The first 401 carrying a Bearer challenge names the registry's token endpoint. It is used only when it is on the registry's own origin (scheme, host and port); otherwise the request is a denial and the credential is never sent elsewhere. The client then asks that endpoint for one token per repository, before its first request there, with OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN as the Basic password (user name oyzu), or with no credential when the variable is unset or empty. Tokens ask for pull, plus push when cache.write is true. A rejected or expired token is fetched again once; a second refusal is a denial. Without OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN, when OYZU_ID_TOKEN_URL and OYZU_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN are both set, the Basic password is a CI job ID token instead: GET $OYZU_ID_TOKEN_URL with ?audience=<configured registry origin> (scheme, host and non-default port) and the request token as a bearer, answered with {"value": "<jwt>"}. The ID token is reused until 30 seconds before its exp, then fetched again, and fetched once more when the token endpoint refuses it. ID tokens live minutes (five on Oyzu runners), so a build that pushes for longer than that keeps signing in to each shard it reaches later. The request token goes only to that URL; neither is recorded. Each fetch is counted as GET id token in the request counts. With the sharded layout below, a build asks for at most one token per shard it touches (7 for EX-034's seven actions). A blob response may redirect to another host, for example a registry that serves large blobs from a separate blobs hostname through short-lived signed links. Redirects are followed without the Authorization header when they change origin, at most 5, and never from HTTPS to HTTP. An empty Docker-Content-Digest header (Harbor's proxy cache sends one on its first fetch) is treated as no claim; the manifest is still checked against its key annotation and every blob. Layout (frozen 2026-10-10 under its draft identifiers): repository <prefix>/v1alpha1/<first two key hex>, tag lookup-<64-hex key>, an OCI image manifest with artifactType application/vnd.oyzu.action-result.v1alpha1, the action-result descriptor as config (application/vnd.oyzu.action-result.config.v1alpha1+json) and one layer (application/vnd.oyzu.tree.v1alpha1.tar+zstd) holding every blob the descriptor references, named sha256/<hex>, sorted, mode 0644, owner and time 0. Annotations: dev.oyzu.action.key, dev.oyzu.action.output and, on the layer, dev.oyzu.tree.uncompressed-digest. Failures never change the pipeline: Situation Behavior 404 under the tag miss; the action runs (and is pushed when writing) 5xx, 408, 429, timeout, connection failure retried, at most 3 attempts with exponential backoff and jitter; then the remote is off for the rest of the build and everything computes 401 / 403 after sign-in (one token renewal), not retried: remote off for the build, no other route is tried. A wrong OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN, no credential where one is required and a read-only credential with cache.write = true all end here; the build computes and succeeds 409 / 412 on the manifest PUT the registry refused to replace the tag: a conflict, not retried, the entry there is kept and not read back; the remote stays on Digest, size or shape mismatch, missing blob, conflicting config entry rejected, its bytes quarantined in the local store's quarantine/ (remote-<key>-<part>), the action runs. The remote entry is not repaired Push failure the build succeeds; the record says why the entry was not pushed Push interrupted before the manifest PUT uploaded blobs stay unreferenced; nothing is visible under the tag The build record gains manifest.extensions["oyzu.dev/action-cache"].remote: location, read, write, status (active, unavailable with reason, or unusable for a cache.remote the client cannot use), counts of hits, pushed, converged, conflicts and rejected, the requests sent by kind, and per target the actions in each of those lists. A result materialized from the remote carries extensions["oyzu.dev/remote-origin"] in the local store. The summary line adds the remote part, for example remote 7 reused · 0 pushed.
