A project can name a second repository that only CI writes: # oyzu.toml (project) [cache] ciRemote = "oci://registry.example.com/team/oyzu-cache/ci" # CI writes, everyone reads remote = "oci://registry.example.com/team/oyzu-cache/dev" # optional: developers share here immutableTags = true # the registry never replaces a tag write = true # CI ignores user configuration Build Reads (after a local miss) Writes (with cache.write) CI (the execution context detects a CI provider or CI) cache.ciRemote only; cache.remote is recorded as skipped cache.ciRemote Anywhere else cache.ciRemote, then cache.remote cache.remote only; never cache.ciRemote No cache.ciRemote cache.remote, as before cache.remote What makes the CI repository trusted is the registry, not Oyzu. The registry must refuse writes to it without the CI credential; detecting CI only narrows what a build accepts and grants nothing. A build that sets CI without the credential is refused (403), keeps building and writes nothing. A CI build never reuses a developer's upload: it does not read cache.remote, and a result in its local store that came from a development remote is looked up again in the CI repository. A remote hit is recorded with its scope (ci or development), in the hit list and in the local result's remote-origin. Nothing is signed, so a hit from the CI repository says where it was read, not who produced it. The registry credential is OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN or, without it, the CI job's ID tokens (never a setting). OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN is sent as a bearer token on every request to the configured registry host, over HTTPS or to a loopback host, and dropped when a redirect leads elsewhere (blob storage). When the registry answers with a token-flow challenge instead, it is exchanged for a per-repository token as described under sign-in above. It is never written to a record or a log. Immutable tags. cache.immutableTags = true says every configured cache repository refuses to replace a tag, as the platform build cache registry does. A push then skips the racing-writer read, so a pushed action costs 6 requests instead of 7, and a refused manifest PUT (409 or 412) is the conflict. Do not set it for a registry that replaces tags: the last writer would then win silently. Without it the read stays, which is how customer-run registries are used; a refusal there is still a conflict. Either way a tag is only how an entry is found: a hit is used only after the digests its manifest names verify.

Measured on EX-034 (oci-standalone, one node/app target, oyzu build --full, seven cacheable actions), counted from zot's own request log, 2026-10-10: Build Manifest GET Blob GET Upload POST Blob PUT Manifest PUT Total Cold push (7 executed, 7 pushed) 14 0 14 14 7 49 Warm hit, second checkout, empty store (7 reused) 7 14 0 0 0 21 Partial hit, test-only edit (1 reused, 6 executed and pushed) 13 2 12 12 6 45 Unchanged repeat after a warm hit 0 0 0 0 0 0 Objects per entry: 3 (config, layer, manifest; the manifest PUT also writes the one tag). Per action: a hit costs 3 requests, a miss that pushes costs 7 (lookup, racing-writer check, 2 × 2 uploads, manifest). Measured against the format as frozen on 2026-10-10. Behind a signed-in registry and its storage. The same build against CNCF Distribution 3.1.2 with its S3 driver on SeaweedFS 4.48, behind a registry token service whose front redirects blobs of 1 KiB or more to a separate blobs host (the platform's development registry stack), 2026-10-10. Client requests are what the build record counts; storage operations are the S3 API calls Distribution made, from SeaweedFS's counters, grouped the way Cloudflare R2 bills them (Class A: PUT, POST, COPY, LIST; Class B: GET, HEAD; DELETE is free): Build Client requests of which token S3 Class A S3 Class B S3 total Cold push (7 executed, 7 pushed) 57 7 183 115 324 Warm hit, empty store (7 reused) 29 7 0 37 37 Partial hit (1 reused, 6 pushed) 53 7 150 99 269 Through a Harbor proxy-cache project, first read (7 reused) 29 7 0 74 74 Through Harbor, second read (7 reused) 29 7 0 28 28 What this shows: Sign-in adds one token request per shard the build touches and one challenged request per build (the extra manifest GET): 8 requests on EX-034. A hit stays cheap in storage: 4 Class B operations per entry, plus one per redirected blob, because the front lets Distribution open a blob before it redirects. A push costs about 25 Class A operations per entry in Distribution's S3 layout (171 to 183 for the 7 entries across runs, depending on which directories already exist), against the 3 objects the entry consists of: upload sessions are S3 multipart uploads moved into place by copy, and every blob and manifest also writes link files and lists directories. This confirms the audit's concern about stock registries on R2. At R2's list price it is about $0.0001 per pushed entry. The maintainer accepted it for now (2026-10-10) rather than serving the cache's few OCI calls directly over object storage (about 3 writes per entry); either serves the same frozen entries. Harbor revalidates every read with the upstream registry (one HEAD and one GET of the manifest per entry), so a pull-through saves blob traffic, not manifest requests.

Sign-in uses only OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN, as a bearer token or through the registry token flow, or a CI job's ID tokens through the token flow (no Basic auth to the registry itself, credential helpers, Docker configuration or login command, and no OAuth2 POST token form); no capability probes, so immutable tags are declared, not detected; no signing or producer verification; no batched lookup (rule 7: an action's key includes the outputs of the actions it follows, so lookups can be grouped only across actions whose predecessors have all resolved), minimum entry size (rule 3) or strict tag enumeration (rule 6); no remote retention or pruning; a damaged remote entry is rejected by every reader but never repaired or replaced; an entry pushed before the format freeze (no keyComponents in its config) is rejected like a damaged one; entries above 256 MiB are not pushed; transfers are sequential, so the four-transfer parallel limit is not exercised; verified only on Linux against zot, Distribution behind a token service and a Harbor proxy-cache project (no Artifactory, Nexus, Docker Hub, GHCR, Windows or macOS); no CACHE-04 or any producer trust: a remote hit says which run produced it, never that this run executed it.

A target's action key is a SHA-256 over frozen plan values and captured inputs only: Input Notes The target's actions command, environment, working directory, platforms, limits, report contracts, configuration digest (scheduling settings such as build.jobs and transport settings are not part of it) Scoped source digest the target's own directory, the directories of every target it declares as a prerequisite (depends_on, materialize, task dependencies — the same edges --affected uses) and every file no target owns (root build.yaml, oyzu.toml, locks) Toolchain identity the resolved image's content digest, not its tag Prepared dependencies the dependency snapshot's content (lock digests, prepared tree, manager identity), not where or when it was prepared Builder identity the builder's digest Materialized inputs the digests of artifacts consumed from producer targets, available only after producers finish Host paths, run identifiers, timestamps, credentials, the number of parallel jobs and the whole-tree source digest never enter a key, so a serial build, a --jobs N build and a host with a different core count share hits. Different checkouts, worktrees and branches therefore share hits: a second checkout at a different path reused all four EX-033 targets in the measured run. Changing any of those inputs for a target re-runs exactly that target; the rest are reused. unused stayed reused across every EX-033 edit, and an API-only edit left shared, web and unused reused.
documents.s: Inputs and what invalidates a target

documents.t: The native path has no plan of captured inputs, so its key is built from what the host build actually saw: Input Notes The target's actions command line (per-invocation locations such as temporary output directories become fixed tokens), environment variable names, working directory, report contracts, configuration digest — never environment values or host paths Source the target's private source projection digest: its own directory plus any explicitly declared inputs. Isolation makes this sound by construction — the build cannot read anything outside the projection Tools the digest of oyzu.lock (the resolved tool identities) and the host platform Builder the Oyzu executable's digest; for a target an external builder plugin builds, also that plugin's identity Materialized inputs the digests of artifacts consumed from producer targets Because tools are identified through the lock, a tool that is not in the lock (for example a system C compiler used by cgo, or sh) is not part of the key; use --no-cache after changing such a tool. A restored native target also keeps its materialization receipts. Promoted local binaries (.oyzu/bin) are refreshed from the restored artifact exactly as after an execution.

The cache trusts the declared target graph, like --affected. An action that reads another target's directory without a declared edge is invisible to the key: the checked-in future-syntax variants/targets/build.yaml declares no edges, so editing shared/ does not invalidate api or web, although their build scripts copy ../shared. Measured: api, web and unused were reused after a shared edit, while oyzu build --no-cache rebuilt them. Native cross-root dependency discovery (the fixture's "inferred" relationships) is not implemented; the runnable overlay used by the regression tests declares depends_on: [shared] for api and web, and there a shared edit re-runs shared, api and web. Declare relationships in build.yaml, or use --no-cache, for builds that read across target directories.

A target built by an external builder plugin (a plugins.development or plugins.packages binding) is reused like a built-in target. Core writes the plugin's verified identity on the target record as extensions["oyzu.dev/builder-plugin"] and binds it into the target and action keys next to the Oyzu executable digest: {"reference":"go/app","source":"package","package":"oyzu/go","version":"0.1.0", "release":"sha256:…","executableDigest":"sha256:…","runtime":{"os":"linux","arch":"amd64","abi":null}} {"reference":"go/app","source":"local-development","executableDigest":"sha256:…", "runtime":{"os":"linux","arch":"amd64","abi":null}} runtime uses the plugin package vocabulary (linux/darwin/windows, amd64/arm64, gnu/musl/msvc). A development executable's ABI is not known and is recorded as null. On a host outside that vocabulary a development binding records the raw operating system and architecture names. A changed plugin executable, package release or version, runtime or reference re-runs the target and explain reports builder identity changed; reverting it reuses the earlier result. How the selection was made (resolved now, locked) is provenance, not identity, and never changes a key. The plugin cannot add to the record. A plugin-built target never shares a key with the built-in builder it replaces. A development binding's digest covers only the bound file. When that file is not a native executable (no ELF or Mach-O header, and not a PE image with an .exe name and a valid PE signature: a wrapper script or a .cmd file, for example), what it runs is outside the key, so its targets are not-cached with the reason "is built by a development plugin binding that is not a native executable …". Bind the plugin executable itself to reuse its results. A native wrapper executable is reused on its own digest alone: a program it starts is outside the key, so rebuild or rebind the wrapper after changing what it runs. Package entrypoints are native payloads verified at installation. Plugin-built results stay in the local store: no cache.remote or cache.ciRemote is asked for or given them, and --slice refuses the target (EXTERNAL_BUILDER) because a handoff repository cannot carry them. The other exclusions are unchanged: --no-cache, cache.local = false, --verify-contract, secret environment values and hooks without declared outputs keep the target out of the cache, and tools are admitted before the lookup. Remote sharing of plugin-built results is a named follow-up. Unused execution-only settings (for example build.jobs, and --full, which sets the full-checks mode) are part of the configuration digest and therefore also invalidate every key, including each action's; narrowing that is deferred hardening.

The live Build section marks every restored action with ↺ (the word reused without color) and reused in place of executed, and the final summary tallies it apart from executed work (2 targets · 3 reused · 1 executed). The per-target reuse origin and the Action cache facts (now a Cache line) are shown with -v and in JSON; the final receipt appends reused from an earlier run, not run now to test and coverage lines that come from restored reports. In the build bundle a reused action keeps status: "succeeded" so every gate applies unchanged, and gains: "actionKey": "sha256:…", "reuse": { "actionKey": "sha256:…", "originalRunId": "…", "originalCompletedAt": "2026-10-07T08:43:02Z", "originalDurationMs": 812 } manifest.extensions["oyzu.dev/action-cache"] records the mode, whether the cache was active or disabled (and why) and each target's outcome: reused, executed (with stored and, when a damaged entry was replaced, rejected), or not-cached with the reason. The draft schema's cached action status is not used: it would hide a reused action from gates that read succeeded. Journal events (logs/events.jsonl) use the finish status reused; logs for reused actions are not recreated. A hit never grants authority and never skips a gate. On restore, every report is parsed again from its retained bytes and judged by the current action's contract (for example the coverage minimum). A report that fails there rejects the entry and the target executes normally, so the real failure appears through the usual path. Mandatory preflight, policy and required-check enforcement are unchanged.

Two read-only views answer "why did this stage run or get reused?" (OEP-0020 inspection tier B). Both name the first key component that differs from the last build of the same target or stage, so a miss points at what changed rather than only saying it missed. Every key is derived from named components, compared in this order: Component What it covers Parts named on a change builder the builder id and digest (an Oyzu upgrade changes it) — platform, variant the target platform and variant — toolchain the toolchain identity: image content digest or resolved tool lock, host platform — dependencies the prepared-dependency identity (for Node, node_modules) — source the scoped source digest and its rung: the whole target scope, or a confined action's predicted reads — definition the frozen action definitions, field by field and the environment variable by variable: argv, env.<NAME>, cwd, limits, report contracts, configuration digest, input mounts api:build env.MODE (group key) or env.MODE (action key) materialized digests of artifacts consumed from producer targets the artifact id upstream output digests of the earlier actions of the target an action follows the action id definition leaves input digests out. source comes before it because an action's environment can carry values derived from its source, such as the development version, so a source edit changes both. When several components differ, the first is the reason and the rest are listed after it with their parts (see the examples below). The key itself stays the only thing that decides reuse; components only explain it. Recorded data. Every stored result carries its components in the top-level keyComponents field, an ordered list of {name, digest, parts?} (source also records rung); they travel with a remote entry because the entry's config is the descriptor. (Results written between WS2 and the format freeze kept them in extensions["oyzu.dev/key-components"].) Independently of storage, each lookup records the subject's key in history/<sha256 of subject>.json under the store: the latest key with the run that first and last used it, and the distinct key before it (kind: "action-key-history"). Subjects are a target's group key and, for targets reused action by action, each action's key. History is written even when nothing is stored (a failed build, an always-run target), is a few kilobytes per subject, is removed by oyzu cache clear and is not subject to retention. oyzu build --explain. After the receipt, at most eight recorded action decisions, with an omitted count and the manifest available for complete detail. Selection and execution/reuse have separate labels; a blocked or failed action keeps its outcome cause instead of being described as executed merely because the cache was disabled. An illustrative expanded entry is: Why each stage ran or was reused api:build — Executed Recorded selection: api (requested) Reuse: source files in scope changed Source comparison: run previous-observation changed: shared/greeting.mjs (reads-source) Native provenance: applications/api/build.mjs:2 (path, exact) This example describes the candidate evidence shape, not a passing captured qualification. Reused entries retain their original producing run, which may precede the invocation whose results were restored most recently. Other reasons: no earlier build of it is recorded in this cache (first build, or after cache clear); inputs unchanged since run …, but no result is stored (not stored, evicted or cleared); the stored result was rejected: … (damaged entry); a hook runs on every build…; a reused result fetched from a remote says so. A stage of a target that is reused or run whole shares the target's reason; a target that is not cacheable shows its not-cached reason. --explain conflicts with --plan and --remote. It changes only the human output: the reasons are always in the manifest, under manifest.extensions["oyzu.dev/action-cache"].targets.<target> as explain ({reason, changed?, previousRunId?, sourceChanges?}, where changed lists every differing component with its label, changed parts and, for source, a rung change) and, per action, actionExplain.<action>, so --json output carries them without the flag. A failed local result lookup is recorded as lookup: unavailable, with its actual filesystem/lease cause and execution fallback. It is distinct from a stored result rejected by artifact/report validation. The target's unavailable detail and action explanation preserve that distinction; successful execution still means target success. Retained summaries include the material limitation even if the configured cache tier was initially active. Explicit --no-cache remains a recorded disabled choice, rather than an unavailable lookup. Captured source inventories are retained once per captured context in the existing cache history metadata; observations hold a context reference and input-scope identity. They do not add file-digest ledgers to every action or affect keys, selection, admission or execution. sourceChanges compares the actual previous observation's captured identities under the engine's effective confined read set or existing coarse target scope, including additions/removals. Hashing and comparison share the same coarse membership owner. paths retains the comparison and native selector provenance. Exact reads are labeled reads-source, approximate bounds bounded-read, and unmodeled relationships scope-input. A source location is read provenance, not proof of a longer import chain. sourceChanges.status is available, unavailable or scope-changed. Unavailable inventories, missing context and changed boundaries never produce guessed filenames. Broad/group scopes retain their conservative membership; native selectors annotate actual changes without narrowing a key. Windows has no confined action views, but captured coarse-scope file comparisons are available. Native builds without captured context retain their target-level reasons. An affected-selection Git baseline and a previous cache-key observation may differ; their contexts remain separate. Explicit --no-cache writes no source history metadata. These inventories follow existing cache-history retention and are removed by cache clear; recorded invocation causes remain in finalized bundles. The complete Linux qualification passed 84 explanation observations; see the explanation record for exact commands, identities and platform limits. oyzu cache explain <target>. Reads the store's key history for a target id (its group key and every recorded action of it) or a single action id such as api:build. For each it shows the latest key, the runs that first and last used it, whether a result is stored for it and the first component that differs from the key before it. It reads no project and runs nothing, so it works between builds and on another checkout sharing the same store. An unknown name exits non-zero with no key history for <name> in this cache. $ oyzu cache explain api Cache key explanation api api (whole target) Key 3608cd663130 · since run 26520-… · last seen run 26520-… (2026-10-10T10:04:22Z) Result stored · the next build with these inputs reuses it Changed since run 25996-…: source files in scope changed (also: action definition: api:build env.OYZU_VERSION, api:build env.PROOF_VALUE added and 7 more) api:build (stage) Key f700515a6d9c · since run 26520-… · last seen run 26520-… (2026-10-10T10:04:23Z) Result stored · the next build with these inputs reuses it Changed since run 23970-…: source files in scope changed (also: action definition: env.OYZU_VERSION, env.PROOF_VALUE added and 1 more; output of an earlier action: api:version) A stage's previous run can be older than the target's: a build that restores a target whole does not look its actions up. --json returns kind: "action-cache-explain" with subjects[] (id, kind, target, actionKey, firstRunId, lastRunId, lastSeenAt, stored, previous, reason, changed). Limits. Keys still contain aggregate source digests. File details require the separately retained captured comparison and supported effective scope described above. Cache history keeps two distinct keys per subject, so cache explain compares its latest keys, not an arbitrary older invocation. For a finalized invocation use history, which reads the recorded manifest without redoing analysis or consulting current cache state. Concurrent builds sharing one store may interleave history writes (each write is atomic; the later one wins). Native host builds explain at target level only.

Control Effect oyzu build --no-cache no lookup and no storage for this invocation; the summary shows disabled (--no-cache) cache.local = false same, from configuration (default true) cache.dir absolute directory replacing the default location; user or system scope only — a project oyzu.toml or oyzu.local.toml that sets it is rejected (CONFIG_SCOPE). User-scope configuration is ignored in CI, as for other user settings oyzu cache status / clear inspect or empty the store; status also reports the Docker image budget oyzu build --explain, oyzu cache explain <target> explain why stages were reused or ran; read-only | cache.remote, cache.read, cache.write | the remote OCI cache: destination, lookup (default on) and publishing (default off) | | cache.ciRemote, cache.immutableTags | the CI repository and whether the registry refuses to replace tags (default off) | See configuration. No other flag, command or setting exists; keys and cache paths are never user-authored.

Host Default store Linux $XDG_CACHE_HOME/oyzu/actions (fallback ~/.cache/oyzu/actions) macOS ~/Library/Caches/Oyzu/actions Windows %LocalAppData%\Oyzu\cache\actions The location is per user and shared across projects. It holds blobs/sha256/ (raw file bytes), results/<key>.json (descriptors), quarantine/ (rejected data) and tmp/. A group descriptor and an action descriptor each follow the draft action-result contract (key, recipe digest, input digests, output tree, reports, platforms, enforced properties, producer evidence) with the per-target detail under extensions, so a remote store can reuse the same shape. Locally the output tree is a tree manifest blob plus one blob per file, not a compressed archive.

At the end of a build, if the store exceeds 10 GiB, least-recently-used results are evicted until it fits and blobs no remaining result references are removed. A hit refreshes an entry's recency. Eviction touches only the cache directory: bundles in dist hold their own copies and are never affected. The budget is fixed in this milestone; there is no setting for it. Builds take a shared cross-process lease on store.lock at the first cache read or write and retain it through blob/descriptor publication and deferred restores. Opening an unused store creates neither its directory nor its lock file. Disabled cache runs and runs with nothing cacheable leave the store untouched; end-of-build retention also skips an unused store. Clear and eviction require an exclusive lease. oyzu cache clear fails with a retry diagnostic while a build uses that cache; it leaves active staging and unpublished blobs alone. Retry after the build finishes. End-of-build eviction reports a retention warning on contention, so the store may temporarily exceed its budget; a later build can retry retention. Accessing a store during maintenance reports that it is busy; builds can proceed without that cache, while cache commands return an error. An unsuccessful first lease attempt stays unavailable for that store handle; a subsequent invocation can retry. Do not delete store.lock to resolve contention: the persistent file is the coordination point, and the OS releases a process's lease when it exits. The lease protects cooperating Oyzu processes, not external deletion or filesystems without working OS locks. No new setting or cache-format migration is required.

Cache capture hashes file bytes while copying them into private staging and uses that digest for the workspace delta and blob identity. Size and modification-time checks reject observed source changes during the copy. Restore likewise hashes while staging the copy. All files in an action's deferred workspace delta are verified before accepting the hit, and those private verified copies are retained until apply; apply does not reopen or re-hash the cache blobs. Each destination is replaced only after staging succeeds, preserving the previous file when a blob is missing or corrupt. A cross-filesystem restore can require an additional copy into destination-local staging, without another digest pass. Artifact and report records reuse the digests verified during restore. Directory artifact verification and native report gates still run; this is not a claim that every build file is hashed only once. There is no new option. Corrupt cache data is rejected/quarantined and recomputed as below; disk or permission failures need space/access repaired before retrying. Multi-file apply is not a transactional workspace rollback on later filesystem errors. This applies to build outputs, not installed-tool verification or launch. No capture/restore throughput numbers have been measured for this change.

Situation Behavior No entry the target executes and is stored Damaged blob or descriptor, mismatched key, unreadable entry rejected, quarantined, the target executes and replaces it; the summary notes the rejection Report gate fails on restore entry rejected; the target executes normally Cache location missing, unwritable or unusable the build runs normally and stores nothing; no pipeline change is needed cache.local = false / --no-cache everything executes Cancelled or failed build independently valid completed actions can remain reusable; failed/interrupted actions and failed target groups have no success descriptor Writes are atomic (stage, then rename), and a descriptor is published only after every blob it references. Maintenance uses the leases described above. The completed-action recovery qualification records the failure/retry/test-only-repair/fresh-comparison proof, missing aggregate evidence and interruption cases, plus native standalone OCI restoration into an empty local store. Windows partial-reuse precision remains unqualified. An eligible action seals its outputs, workspace changes/deletions and owned reports at its actual completion/report boundary. Later writers and target failure cannot replace those captured bytes. Required missing or malformed action reports prevent its publication; aggregate target obligations still gate target success. Restored evidence retains the original producer and is checked against current report requirements. The real four-run failed-target recovery and standalone OCI recovery case passed; remaining finite and preservation qualification is recorded in the bounded recovery record. Maintenance regression tests cover competing-process clear/eviction, human/JSON busy errors, corrupt-blob destination preservation and deferred restore from retained verified bytes. These new tests have not run on the desktop; see verification status.

Contracts change in place at v1alpha1; no version was added. The manifest action gained the optional reuse object, plan actions now set cacheable: true for builder-declared stages (the field existed and was always false), and the manifest and plan schemas accept extensions on artifacts, which the implementation already emitted. Development snapshot versions are now scoped to each target's inputs. Previously the -dev.g… suffix came from the whole captured tree, so any edit renamed every target's outputs. It now derives from the same per-target scope as the key, so an unrelated edit no longer changes a target's version, artifact name or OYZU_VERSION. Tagged and history-derived versions are unchanged. Dependency evidence still records the whole-tree source digest. Upgrading Oyzu invalidates entries (the builder digest is part of the key); nothing is migrated and old entries age out by retention. Python application targets pass the whole-tree digest to the build in the environment (OYZU_SOURCE_DIGEST); they are safe but miss on any edit until that is scoped. Native Python builds now set PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1. Previously the first build wrote __pycache__ files into the verified Python installation, and every later build failed with installed payload differs from receipt (also on main), which made repeat native Python builds, and therefore reuse, impossible.

Parallel builds block P4. Linux x86_64 (cloud container), Docker 29.8.2, Node 22 toolchain image, debug build of the compiled CLI: python tooling/test-build-scenarios.py --cli target/debug/oyzu --suite node --only parallel-soundness # longer stress: OYZU_STRESS_TARGETS=10 OYZU_STRESS_ROUNDS=6 OYZU_STRESS_SEED=20261010 The registered parallel-soundness check builds a project of N independent npm packages (default 6) with --full --jobs N and asserts: a parallel build has the same action keys, outcomes, artifacts and confined actions as a serial one; in each seeded round (default 3, seed printed for replay) an undeclared read seeded into the build or test stage of random targets (the first round always seeds a test stage) fails exactly the seeded actions, and every seed is reported with confined-read-outside-contract, the right action, path and fix, while no unseeded action reports a violation; a running action never sees a sibling target's workspace; and --verify-contract reports exactly the seeded divergences. Each round records how many actions overlapped across targets and within one target, so the check shows which concurrency it exercised. Result: passed, 9 seeded undeclared reads over 3 rounds (seed 7) each failed exactly their action and the 8 build seeds were explained; a 10-target, 6-round run (seed 20261010) failed exactly all 30 seeds and explained the 12 build seeds. Up to 5 actions overlapped across targets (worker-memory admission bounds it below --jobs) and 1 within a target, since parallel stage admission (P2) had not landed. Re-run on 2026-10-10 after node --test gained the spec reporter on stderr (6 targets, 3 rounds, seed 200643300): passed, all 9 seeds explained, 5 of them in test stages. Fixed by this gate: build.jobs was part of the configuration digest, so every key changed with --jobs (or the host's core count, its default) and a serial build was never reused by a parallel one; and branches of independent targets dropped contract violations and --verify-contract records when collected, so a divergence did not fail a parallel build.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/affected-builds.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu build --affected <git-ref> is experimental target-level selection for a local Git baseline. It compares the captured source bytes with that commit, selects changed targets and their declared consumers, then includes the prerequisites needed to build them. It does not reuse cached actions or artifacts. oyzu build --affected HEAD --plan oyzu build --affected origin/main oyzu inspect dist The reference must already exist locally. Oyzu does not fetch it. Git must be available on PATH; selected builds require the same explicitly provisioned images and dependencies as ordinary builds. --affected cannot be combined with positional target selection. Omitting it preserves the existing full-build behavior. No new project configuration is required.

Comparison uses raw committed Git blobs and the immutable source snapshot, including deletions and executable-bit changes. Projects nested inside a Git repository are compared with their corresponding subtree. The same source exclusions apply to both sides, so generated dist, .oyzu, dependency and other excluded directories do not trigger builds. Checkout filters and line-ending conversion can make working bytes differ from committed bytes; such differences count as changes. A changed file selects every enclosing discovered target. The selection follows consumers of depends_on, materialize.from and resolved cross-target task prerequisites transitively. Existing selection then adds required producers and admitted task/hook dependencies. Every selected target receives its normal applicable checks and packaging stages. A native workspace remains one target; this does not select individual native members or infer arbitrary cross-project file reads. Declare inter-target dependencies for those relationships. The frozen plan and manifest record extensions["oyzu.dev/selection"] with mode: "affected", requested impacted targets, the final selected set and excluded targets. Its affected object records the reference, resolved baseline commit, source digest, changed paths, per-target reasons and any full-build fallback. These are selection facts, not release eligibility or trusted CI evidence. The default human build view renders them as a Selection section (changed, dependents and unaffected counts, the base and its short commit, or a Not narrowed notice with the recorded fallback code); see Result output. Nothing is recomputed for display. Execution follows plain-build rules: when every selected target is native-eligible the selection runs on the host with no container, otherwise the captured executor is used. The recorded selection is the same either way. An empty change set always takes the captured path, which writes the empty bundle without starting a container. If nothing changed, --plan returns an empty read-only preview without replacing dist. A build writes a successful, inspectable empty bundle with no tools, actions or artifacts; previous bundles retain normal history behavior. Excluded targets are not represented as successful builds, and old artifacts are not copied into the new bundle.

--affected works in a clone made with git clone --filter=blob:none, which has the full history but only the file contents a checkout needs. That is how the platform's planner checks out a commit before running oyzu build --remote --plan --affected <merge-base> (see planning a remote run). Baseline files unchanged since the merge base are already present. Git fetches the blobs of files that changed from the clone's remote on demand, so the planner needs read access to the repository; if the fetch fails, the baseline is unavailable and the conservative full selection below applies. Git fetches those blobs one at a time, so a very large change is slower to plan; prefetching them in one request is later hardening.

Oyzu selects the full workspace when the local baseline cannot be read, when an input is new relative to it, when a changed input has no target owner, or when recognized build/configuration/lock metadata changes. Root tasks with cross-target prerequisites also force full selection when inputs change. Managed configurations currently force full selection until policy-aware narrowing is implemented. The recorded fallback explains these decisions; fetch a missing baseline yourself and rerun if appropriate. Selection does not grant network access, bypass validation, change source files or establish authorization. Source discovery and validation still cover the whole workspace. Baseline reads need no network, but normal selected-target preparation can require approved acquisition routes. Git object limits or unsupported baseline entries also cause full selection. Fallback can therefore require toolchains even when a no-change build would not. Changes to external configuration, tools or environment are not inferred from Git. Use a full build when those inputs change. Action-level caching, native member-level impact, automatic CI baseline discovery and policy-controlled narrowing remain unfinished. Git metadata never grants signing or production publication authority.

The compiled Windows CLI passed no-change plan/build/inspection for both repository-root and nested project roots, plus rejection of conflicting positional selection. Rust tests cover owners, transitive consumers, deletion, immutable capture and conservative fallbacks. tooling/test-affected-selection.py runs after CLI compilation in the three-host task matrix; cross-host results remain pending. The Linux Node suite registers affected-targets against the EX-033 declared-target variation: no-change output, API-only selection with its producer, shared-input consumers, snapshot packages and required reports. Its captured-build result remains pending. The separate registered action-cache check covers this fixture's reuse and exact invalidation; see local action cache. Reuse trusts the declared edges, so the checked-in project without depends_on is not invalidated by edits to shared/ (documented limit there).

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/ant.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The java/ant builder captures conventional/custom Ant projects and exports versioned JARs. Native oyzu run test is a separate host workflow that produces test and coverage evidence without packaging a JAR. These paths share the native Ant reporting integration; a direct-test pass does not qualify captured delivery.

oyzu build --isolated --full oyzu inspect dist Docker and the explicitly provisioned oyzu-toolchain/ant:1.10.18-jdk17 image are prerequisites. The image supplies Ant, JDK 17, JUnit 4.13.2, Hamcrest 1.3, JaCoCo 0.8.13 and Java quality tools. Rebuild it with the current compiled worker after launcher changes. There is no native host-build adapter; host direct tests do not remove the captured build's executor/image requirements. --isolated selects captured execution; --full requests test and quality operations in addition to build/archive/package. Isolation alone does not request all checks. Plain local oyzu build retains the shared fast defaults; explicitly required checks still apply. Ant selects native archive targets and contained JAR paths from admitted metadata evaluation rather than inventing a project layout. Native arbitrary downloads and projects with ivy.xml are not supported captured dependency acquisition; Ivy is explicitly refused. The bundle contains versioned JARs and current evidence for selected checks. Native failures or missing required reports block exported artifacts and retain available reports in the failed bundle. An opaque override that exits zero with optional reports absent remains incomplete reporting; a [checks] section with tests = "required" and coverage = "required" makes those reports mandatory (check levels). See direct reporting acceptance for the shared distinction between command success and verified evidence.

Ant projects with a conventional test target can run oyzu run test to produce native test and coverage evidence in a test-only dist/ bundle. The direct adapter reuses the captured builder's Ant listener, JUnit formatter and JaCoCo integration. It does not create a new test framework or require an Oyzu configuration file for the conventional case. oyzu run list oyzu run test oyzu inspect dist For an existing custom target, a task replacement selects it: [tasks.test] argv = ["ant", "verify-contract"] One literal ant <target> command is instrumented, including the equivalent literal shell spelling used in the custom example. Compound shell commands and arbitrary replacements retain their bodies and must produce the required JUnit and JaCoCo reports themselves, using the assigned OYZU_TEST_REPORT and OYZU_COVERAGE_REPORT paths. Extra forwarded arguments to the automatic adapter are currently unsupported and fail explicitly. Target-qualified names and pre/post hooks use the common task engine. A failed test skips its success-only post hook. Discovery always supplies an implicit builder-owned test slot. A root [tasks.test] replacement in a single-target project selects a custom Ant target while retaining report obligations through the shared task owner resolution. Without a native test target or a replacement, execution fails with Ant's missing-target error; discovery does not fabricate a test suite.

Provision a JDK with java and javac, Ant and JaCoCo before execution. Set JAVA_HOME to the JDK or put both executables on PATH. Set ANT_HOME to the Ant distribution and JACOCO_HOME to a directory containing jacocoant.jar and jacocoagent.jar. JUnit projects also need their normal test libraries; the CI fixture puts JUnit and Hamcrest in Ant's lib directory. Native libraries are loaded from that directory. The adapter compiles its owned Java integration into a temporary directory and launches Ant using the host's classpath separator. It does not install tools or download dependencies. The CI provisioner supplies checksum-pinned Ant 1.10.18, JaCoCo 0.8.13, JUnit 4.13.2 and Hamcrest 1.3: python tooling/provision-ant-reporting.py --destination /absolute/path/ant-reporting python tooling/test-ant-direct.py --cli /absolute/path/oyzu --tools /absolute/path/ant-reporting The first command is explicit online test setup, outside product execution. The second additionally needs tooling/design-requirements.txt. CI uses JDK 17 and runs the probe after compiling the CLI on Windows, Linux and macOS; registration alone is not verified platform support.

The manifest links JUnit outcomes and JaCoCo application coverage. Native JUnit suites retain individual tests and skipped cases. Conventional forked Java assertion programs produce one case per invocation. These programs require fork="true" and failonerror="true". Coverage follows the existing adapter's conventional src ownership and observed javac output; test classes are excluded. Builds without line debug data retain the available instruction counters rather than inventing line coverage. Arbitrary source layouts, alternate task implementations and JUnit Platform integration require further work or explicit reports. Direct tests keep native project version properties, execute the target's compilation prerequisites, and can update native build output. They do not package snapshot artifacts or run lint/format checks. oyzu build --isolated --full projects snapshot versions, requests quality gates and collects JAR artifacts. Both paths use the same native reporting implementation; captured execution retains its fixed tool locations and isolation. Captured builds use shared version inference over the native version property and applicable Git history. Ant's model is queried again with the chosen version/oyzu.version user properties before planning. The versioned artifact name, bundle version and exported JAR Implementation-Version agree. Native qualifiers are preserved when they cannot participate in SemVer inference; exact tag intent still produces a snapshot without release authority. Missing tools, compilation errors, native test failures, missing or invalid reports and unmet coverage constraints fail the command. Available current reports remain in the failed bundle; correct the native prerequisite or project and rerun. The shared collector owns report validation, hook ordering, bundle history and inspection. See direct test reports for existing-output preservation and host provenance. Host tasks can access the host network and ambient environment; these reports do not prove hermetic execution.

tooling/test-ant-direct.py exercises the authored conventional/custom Ant examples and a native JUnit fixture through the compiled CLI: task discovery, real tests, current JUnit/JaCoCo, unchanged source/configuration, hooks, failed assertions and bundle inspection. tooling/test-ant-reporting.py separately checks the underlying native adapter. Current measured outcomes are recorded in implementation status; captured JAR acceptance and direct test acceptance are distinct. The captured ant scenario uses the same fixtures and requests isolated/full execution. It checks native application-only coverage, versioned JAR manifests, delivered-JAR execution (including native JUnitCore), unchanged source and repeated plan/artifact identity. Native assertion, custom-target, JUnit and explicitly required-report failures must block artifacts. The normalized-flow qualification record owns its reproducible command, exact candidate/tool identities and current execution limits. The targeted Linux group passed conventional/custom/JUnit captured builds, independent delivered-JAR execution, required reports, repeatability, source preservation and failure gates. All three direct-test fixtures also passed. These bounded fixtures do not establish broader layouts, frameworks or additional platform support. Both probes passed locally on Windows with JDK 17.0.20.1, Ant 1.10.18 and JaCoCo 0.8.13, using the pinned CI prerequisite bundle. The direct CLI step passed on Linux, macOS and Windows at 343c682 in run 37052623343 (jobs 110991301336, 110991301392 and 110991301544 respectively). The existing captured Java suite passed at 039f83a, before this shared-launcher change; the changed captured launcher still needs its CI regression run. The compiled Oyzu worker owns process sequencing and native report composition. Native Java integrations remain embedded assets; Python is not required to execute these builder operations. Rebuild captured images after updating the worker.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/artifact-sets.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Status: experimental, client side only. Implements the consumer half of the draft ingested artifact set client contract. Every flag, code and position below is provisional; the draft is not accepted. Most checks use sets hand-built from the contract schema (tests/fixtures/artifact-sets). On 2026-10-10 the client read real producer output (oyzu tools resolve + tools evidence for terraform v1.16.5, aqua: record ids), found it eligible on all three platforms, wrote the lock and downloaded and verified the Linux artifact, and install --frozen replayed it from the lock. SETC P1 is not claimed. Installing from the signed tool index is the supported path; this flag reads a set file directly. Platforms: developed and checked on Linux x86-64; Windows and macOS are unverified. A resolved artifact set names, per (tool, version, platform), the URLs, archive facts and verification evidence of a community-recipe tool. This client reads one, decides whether each platform's record is usable, maps accepted records into oyzu.lock, downloads and verifies the host artifact, and later replays the lock without the set. No account is needed and recipes are never evaluated by install or tools info. # Eligibility only: nothing is written or downloaded oyzu install --dry-run --artifact-set terraform.verified.json oyzu:terraform@1.16.5 oyzu --json tools info --artifact-set gh.verified.json aqua:cli/cli@2.102.0 --details # Pin a record by its digests.full, lock all pinned platforms, download and verify the host artifact oyzu install --artifact-set go-task.verified.json --artifact-set-digest sha256:<digests.full> \ oyzu:go-task/task@3.54.0 # Replay from the lock alone (the set file may be gone); --offline reuses the verified cache oyzu install --frozen
documents.s: Installing from resolved artifact sets (client slice)

documents.t: Flag Meaning --artifact-set FILE A set document (JSON, format: 1, kind: "artifact-sets"); repeatable. Accepted by install SPEC and tools info; with --frozen it cross-checks the lock --artifact-set-digest sha256:D Pins one record by its digests.full; repeatable. With none, each file is a local set anchored by its holder --connector-bindings FILE Host binding file for routes (below) The spec is oyzu:<name>@version (a curated name), oyzu:owner/name@version, aqua:owner/name@version or recipe:owner/name@version. It matches records whose tool.id is aqua:owner/name (what the producer writes and the schema requires) or recipe:owner/name (earlier hand-built sets). core: records (Oyzu's own providers) are read but not installable from a set (LOCK_ID_UNREPRESENTABLE). The version matches version.requested (v1.16.5) or version.normalized (1.16.5). -g/--local are not supported for sets (project lock only).

Document-level rejections (no record is used, nothing is written): size over 16 MiB, malformed JSON or a duplicate key, format other than the integer 1 or a wrong kind (SET_FORMAT_UNSUPPORTED), unknown envelope fields, more than 4096 records, a duplicate record, or records not sorted by (tool.id, version.requested, platform) (SET_SCHEMA_INVALID). Record-level checks (an invalid record is unusable; other records stay usable): closed fields and enums, https URLs without userinfo, fragment, backslash, dot-segment or encoded separator, evidence[].lock_kind equal to the method's fixed mapping, evidence roles present in urls[], verified.lock present exactly when verification is ok, 1 MiB per record, and recomputed digests.declared / digests.full (domain oyzu.artifact-set.v1, canonical JSON; full is the record without digests, declared also drops verified and tier) — a difference is SET_DIGEST_MISMATCH. A set is not self-authenticating: a record needs an anchor.
documents.s: What the client requires of a set

documents.t: One result per platform. Checks run in a fixed order and every failing check contributes its denials: Check Meaning Codes E1 tool-admitted tools.allowed CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED (rule, scope and source from configuration) E2 set-integrity record valid, anchored, fresh SET_FORMAT_UNSUPPORTED, SET_SCHEMA_INVALID, SET_DIGEST_MISMATCH, SET_UNANCHORED, SET_ANCHOR_EXPIRED, SET_DISAGREEMENT E3 record-status resolved passes; unsupported is unavailable; error is invalid the ingest reason code, verbatim E4 evidence-floor tier and evidence floors TIER_BELOW_FLOOR, EVIDENCE_BELOW_FLOOR, EVIDENCE_VERIFIER_UNAVAILABLE, EVIDENCE_ORIGIN_NOT_ACCEPTED E5 routes every urls[] entry and evidence egress host routes ROUTE_UNROUTABLE, ROUTE_EGRESS_UNROUTABLE (all items listed) E6 lock-representable install only LOCK_ID_UNREPRESENTABLE, DIGEST_NOT_SHA256, ARCHIVE_FORMAT_UNSUPPORTED, PLATFORM_ABI_UNSUPPORTED Outcomes: eligible, denied (a rule someone can change), unavailable (the set says no asset; not an error, omitted from the lock and listed as unavailablePlatforms; selecting that platform fails TOOL_PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE) and invalid (the set is not usable evidence). E2 or E3 failures mark later checks skipped. Exit status is 1 for denied, invalid and an unavailable host platform; argument errors use 2. Human output leads with the outcome, then Platforms, Reasons and a "Denied by" table with rule, scope, reason and remedy; --details adds every check and route (tools info --details). --json prints the same result object (outcome, results[].checks/denials/routes, code, written). Secrets, query strings and redirect targets never appear. Scope names follow configuration: administrative scopes print as managed, built-in marks rules defined by the contract. Floors are not user-settable yet: the default requires the verified tier and sets no evidence floor. They are exercised by library tests only (open decision 3).

Precedence: the lock, then an anchored set, then a local set; there is no recipe-evaluation fallback. A record matching a --artifact-set-digest pin has a pin anchor; with no pins every record is local. With pins, only matching records are candidates: the host platform must match, other platforms that no pin matches are left out of the lock. Two anchored records of one snapshot_digest with different digests.declared fail closed with SET_DISAGREEMENT (both digests shown, neither used); a different snapshot is not a disagreement. In managed mode local sets are ineligible by default (SET_UNANCHORED, remedy: use the catalog); writes are rejected in managed mode. Catalog index anchors and valid_until freshness are implemented in the evaluator, but nothing feeds them: organization catalogs are read by index resolution (tool catalog), not by this flag.

A tools route in registries.routes whose scope is an exact host (for example github.com) routes that host; its connectorId selects a host binding: format = 1 [connectors.corp-github] base_url = "http://127.0.0.1:8080/gh/" # https in production; http only for loopback tests redirects = "server" # or "client" (default) authorization_env = "CORP_AUTH" # optional; never printed Destination = destination origin + prefix + the set URL's own path and query, byte for byte. No tools route at all: standalone implies direct identity routes for the set's hosts and follows redirect hops to any https host. Any tools route (even a per-tool one) is closed world: only listed hosts route; two rules for a host are ROUTE_RULE_CONFLICT. redirects = "server": one request; a 3xx reply is ROUTE_REDIRECT_UNEXPECTED and is not followed. client: each hop must have its own rule (ROUTE_REDIRECT_UNROUTABLE otherwise) and is fetched from that rule's destination. A redirect target is never stored, logged or printed. Routes are administrative-only configuration like the rest of registries.routes.

An accepted, verified record becomes a version-1 lock entry without a schema change: id = recipe:<package> (the client's own namespace for set-installed tools, whether the record says aqua:<package> or recipe:<package>), version = version.normalized, digest/size from verified.artifact, source_id = artifact URL host, artifact_id = percent-decoded file name, verification copied from verified.lock, resolution.inputs.artifact = the set's artifact URL and digest, backend_digest from the snapshot digest (provisional). Direct and mirror installs produce byte-identical locks. Digests must be lowercase sha256:<64 hex>; nothing is repaired. A publisher sha512 is covered by the sha256 the set recorded at ingest (not shown separately in the lock). install --frozen finds locked recipe: tools, downloads (or reuses the verified cache) and checks size and digest through the tool store; with --artifact-set it also fails with TOOL_LOCK_STALE when an anchored record disagrees with the lock.

Tests use hand-built fixtures and resealed copies with producer ids; real producer output has been consumed by hand once (above), not in CI. Installing downloads and verifies the artifact into the tool store cache but does not extract it, publish a receipt or shim, or write [tools] configuration; a recipe tool is not yet runnable. One layout fact (the first declared file) feeds layout_digest; multi-file layouts are the installer's. Evidence is not re-verified at install (digest comparison only). GitHub attestations are verified by the producer (tools evidence), not by this client. No catalog source, no index freshness input, no tier/evidence settings (floors are hard-wired), no update for sets. Windows and macOS unrun.

cargo test --lib artifact_set (parser, routes, eligibility, selection, lock mapping and loopback fetch tests), cargo test --test integration artifact_set (compiled CLI, no network) and tooling/test-artifact-set-client.py (real GitHub bytes, loopback mirror needing root for the administrative route file). See implementation status and the qualification record.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/auth.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Status: experimental client. oyzu auth login|status|logout and the shared credential provider implement the initial client contract of the draft connected-client authentication companion. The OEP stays a draft. They are verified against a local conformance fake (oyzu auth conformance); they have not been run against a real identity provider, a real platform or each operating system's credential store. The platform surfaces they rely on (protected-resource metadata, the registered oyzu-cli client and the self access-context route) are built separately; until a platform serves them these commands report discovery as unsupported.
documents.s: Platform sign-in and the credential provider

documents.t: Sign a person in to a platform account once, keep the session in the operating system's protected credential store, and let oyzu build --remote, oyzu run --remote, oyzu secrets and oyzu release check use it. Everything else Oyzu does stays local and needs no account.

platform.url and platform.account in user, machine or administrative configuration (a project or local file is refused, so a checkout cannot choose where credentials go): oyzu config set --global platform.url https://platform.example.com oyzu config set --global platform.account payments A platform that publishes OAuth protected-resource metadata (RFC 9728) naming exactly one issuer that allows the device authorization grant (RFC 8628) for the registered public client oyzu-cli, and the draft self access-context route. For login: a terminal where you can read a code and approve it in a browser (any browser, on any device). A protected credential store: macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, or a running Linux Secret Service provider (GNOME Keyring, KWallet). There is no plaintext fallback; without a store login stops before asking you to approve anything.

Command Does oyzu auth login Discover the issuer, show a verification address and code, wait for approval, confirm you are an active member of platform.account, then store the session oyzu auth status Show the platform, account and local session state: absent, active, refreshing, reauthentication-required or logged-out. Reads local state only and asks no server oyzu auth logout Fence renewal, delete this account's local session, then ask the issuer to revoke it and report that separately oyzu auth conformance Run the client conformance suite against a local fake; needs no account Login discovery, step by step: GET /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource (with the platform URL's path appended when it has one). resource must equal platform.url and exactly one authorization_servers entry is accepted; zero, several or a mismatch stop the login. The issuer's RFC 8414 metadata (else its OpenID configuration). Its issuer must equal the advertised one; the device authorization and token endpoints (and a revocation endpoint if offered) must be HTTPS (HTTP only for a loopback host), carry no credentials, query or fragment, and sit on the issuer's own origin. The device grant must be advertised and public clients (none authentication) allowed. No bearer is sent to any of this and no redirect is followed. The device grant for client oyzu-cli: no client secret, password grant or dynamic registration; no scope parameter (the issuer's session defaults) and never offline_access. The verification address must be on the issuer's origin or it is not shown. Polling honors the issuer's interval and slow_down and is bounded to 15 minutes. GET /api/v1/access-context?account=<platform.account> with the new access token: the response must be oyzu.access/1 and name an active membership of exactly that account. Another membership is never a fallback. An account that needs stronger authentication is reported as AUTH_STEP_UP_REQUIRED; a missing membership as AUTH_NOT_A_MEMBER. Either way the sign-in is revoked and nothing is stored. Only then is the session stored, so a cancelled, denied, expired or failed login leaves no usable partial session. The device code is never shown or logged.

secrets, release check and --remote obtain their credential from one provider. Selection is deterministic and never falls through to another identity after a failure: Situation Result platform.authentication.provider is workload, private-key or execution AUTH_PROVIDER_UNSUPPORTED (not implemented yet) Provider environment OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN is required; without it AUTH_PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE Provider session The stored session; with OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN also set, AUTH_PROVIDER_CONFLICT No provider selected, OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN set That bearer, as supplied: never stored, refreshed or replaced No provider selected, stdin and stderr are terminals The stored session No provider selected, unattended (CI, scripts, agents) AUTH_PROVIDER_REQUIRED; a stored session is never used implicitly A bearer the platform rejects is reported (*_UNAUTHENTICATED); it is not replaced by a stored session. An explicit session selection is human authority, not an automation identity. The credential is delivered only to the origin of platform.url. A request to any other origin (a redirect, a download link from a checkout) gets none.

Setting Values Meaning platform.authentication.provider session, environment, workload, private-key, execution; absent Host-owned provider selection, see above. Contains no credential. Environment input OYZU_PLATFORM_AUTH_PROVIDER. User, machine or administrative scope only OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN stays a credential, not a setting.

Refresh state and the cached access token are separate protected entries, keyed by platform, issuer, client, subject and account. Selection metadata (issuer, subject, state, expiry) is a small non-secret file under the user data directory (auth/), created private. Renewal takes a per-session cross-process lock plus an in-process single flight, rereads state after waiting and renews only if still needed, so concurrent commands renew once. Before a refresh credential is spent it is marked pending. If the answer is lost (timeout, crash, failed store write) the session is ended (AUTH_REFRESH_AMBIGUOUS, AUTH_STORE_FAILED) and you are asked to sign in again; a possibly spent rotating credential is never retried. A rejected renewal also ends the session (AUTH_REAUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED). An issuer outage or an unreachable network leaves the session untouched. logout starts a new session epoch under the commit lock before deleting, so a renewal already in flight cannot recreate the session; it discards its result and revokes the credential it just received. A new login also starts a new epoch. Local removal can succeed while remote revocation is unavailable; the record says so (remote: refused|unreachable|not-advertised). Access tokens already issued stay valid until they expire. A separately supplied OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN is unaffected.

Human output leads with the outcome. --json prints one record: auth-login, auth-status, auth-logout or auth-conformance, holding session facts only. The verification address and user code go to standard error and only when it is a terminal, so JSON on standard output stays machine-readable; without a terminal login fails with AUTH_INTERACTION_REQUIRED before any request.

Exit status is 1 on failure. Codes: AUTH_NOT_CONFIGURED, AUTH_INTERACTION_REQUIRED, AUTH_STORE_UNAVAILABLE (start or unlock the store), AUTH_STORE_FAILED, AUTH_DISCOVERY_UNSUPPORTED, AUTH_DISCOVERY_UNAVAILABLE, AUTH_DISCOVERY_INVALID, AUTH_DISCOVERY_AMBIGUOUS, AUTH_ISSUER_MISMATCH, AUTH_ISSUER_UNTRUSTED, AUTH_REDIRECT_REFUSED, AUTH_GRANT_UNSUPPORTED, AUTH_DEVICE_EXPIRED, AUTH_DEVICE_UNTRUSTED, AUTH_LOGIN_DENIED, AUTH_LOGIN_CANCELLED, AUTH_NOT_A_MEMBER, AUTH_STEP_UP_REQUIRED, AUTH_CONTEXT_UNAVAILABLE, AUTH_LOGIN_REQUIRED, AUTH_REAUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED, AUTH_REFRESH_AMBIGUOUS, AUTH_ISSUER_UNREACHABLE, AUTH_ISSUER_CHANGED, AUTH_DESTINATION_MISMATCH, AUTH_AUDIENCE_UNSUPPORTED and the provider codes above. Commands that use the provider report *_UNAUTHENTICATED when no credential is available. Recovery for a session that cannot be renewed is always oyzu auth login.

Tokens, device codes and refresh credentials never appear in output, logs, configuration, command arguments, error text or the metadata file; debug formatting is redacted and credential handles cannot be serialized. No plaintext credential file exists. The conformance suite's file-backed store holds synthetic credentials for its own fake and is not selectable by a command. A coding agent or unattended job does not inherit a developer's session. Do not give an agent a person's OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN; a copied bearer still identifies that person.

oyzu auth conformance (or oyzu --json auth conformance) starts a fake issuer and protected resource on loopback and runs the real client against it, with synthetic credentials and stores and real child processes for refresh contention. It exits 1 if any scenario fails. Covered client-side criteria of the authentication contract: Criterion Covered AUTH-CLIENT-01 Device login, membership validation, an authorized call, revoked membership denying a fresh call and login (against the fake) AUTH-CLIENT-02 Provider selection without fallback, unattended refusal, one renewal for concurrent callers, expiry and logout AUTH-CLIENT-03 Store failure, cancelled, denied and expired login, foreign verification address, destination binding, no partial session AUTH-CLIENT-06 / 07 Self-context subset: step-up challenge, no implicit membership fallback, independent accounts, local state versus authority, remote revocation reported separately AUTH-CLIENT-08 Ambiguous, mismatched or untrusted metadata and endpoints, redirects, checkout-selected settings AUTH-CLIENT-09 Two-process contention, failed replacement store, ambiguous renewal, refresh racing logout AUTH-TEL-01 / 03 (client side) No credential in output, errors, debug text or state files Not covered: AUTH-CLIENT-04, 05 and 10 (server-side or later work), a real identity provider, real per-OS credential stores, and a real platform remote build with membership revocation. Those need a platform and each operating system, and are not claimed.

The OS store implementation compiles for macOS, Windows and Linux but has not been exercised on each here; Linux additionally needs a Secret Service provider in the session. workload, private-key and execution providers, loopback PKCE login, account switching beyond re-running login for another platform.account, and a local background agent are not implemented. Pagination of the self access-context response follows an optional next_cursor; the exact wire shape awaits the platform implementation. The subject of the access-context response may be a string or an object with an id.

oyzu exec -- cargo test --locked --test integration authentication runs the compiled CLI (help opens no store or network, status/logout without a session, provider selection and no fall-through against real consumers, supplied-bearer mode, conformance). oyzu exec -- cargo test --locked --lib auth:: runs the library suite, including the full conformance scenarios. Neither qualifies a real identity provider, platform or OS store.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/build-bundles.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu build finalizes its results under the workspace's dist/. The bundle contains the manifest, frozen plan when planning succeeded, execution envelope, native logs, retained reports and collected snapshot artifacts. A failed build can still produce a useful bundle; consult manifest.json for actual outcomes. oyzu inspect (no argument: this project's dist/) or oyzu inspect dist checks recorded content integrity and does not establish trusted CI identity or release eligibility.

Every artifact a target produces, and that target's reports, is written below dist/<target>/<platform>/ (build intent BIN-07). The platform is the canonical os/arch name (linux/x86_64, windows/arm64, darwin/arm64), with -<abi> on the architecture only when the platform was declared or requested with an ABI that is not the OS's naming default (linux/arm64-musl; see below); output a builder declares platform-independent uses any instead: dist/ manifest.json plan.json envelope.json logs/ cli/windows/x86_64/oyzu.exe cli/windows/x86_64/oyzu-shim.exe cli/windows/x86_64/reports/junit.xml docs/windows/x86_64/application-0.1.0/ The layout is the same for local, multi-platform and CI builds, so bundles for different platforms merge without collisions. Which platform a target uses: Build Platform directory Native host build The host (windows/x86_64 on 64-bit Windows) Isolated (captured) build The platform the toolchain image builds for, such as linux/x86_64, or the target's one declared platform (platforms) Captured worker under a native build (Docker image targets) The worker's platform Builder declares the output platform-independent (independent artifact compatibility) any; no built-in builder declares this for a whole target yet OCI image index any; the index spans its member platforms Node applications, including static dist/ and Vite sites, stay per target platform as before (maintainer decision of 2026-10-18); an explicit opt-in for platform-neutral Node output is a follow-up. The manifest and plan record each artifact's bundle-relative path (cli/windows/x86_64/oyzu.exe); consumers such as oyzu inspect, publication, the action cache and bundle handoff read that path and never assume a layout. Plan target records carry the directory as the oyzu.dev/output extension. reports is reserved: no artifact may be named reports, because it is the target's report directory. A builder-internal file, such as Docker's intermediate container/image.tar, also lives in the platform directory; Vite's vite-state.json stays at dist/<target>/. Each artifact record also carries profile: development or optimized, the build profile its producing commands actually used, shown on its Outputs row. Which profile a target builds follows where its output goes, build.optimized and --optimized/--no-optimized (optimized builds); the target records the decision as extensions["oyzu.dev/optimization"]. optimized is recorded only for an artifact the optimizing profile actually changes: Rust binaries, native or isolated (cargo build --release; .crate source archives stay development), and .NET packages (--configuration Release). Builders whose output optimization does not change keep development. When the target's build or the artifact's producer is an authored task replacing the builder's command, the artifact is development. Platform and executor. Each target record's platform is the platform it was built for (canonical os/arch[/abi]), with the ABI its toolchain resolved when the OS has several ({"os":"linux","arch":"arm64","abi":"musl"}; Rust records it today); its artifacts' compatibility carries the same platform. The dist/<target>/<platform>/ directory uses the published form of the declared or requested platform: an ABI appears only when it is not the OS's default, as a sibling folder that never nests inside another (--platform linux/arm64/musl writes dist/<target>/linux/arm64-musl/, linux/arm64/gnu writes dist/<target>/linux/arm64/), so builds of both ABIs merge into one tree without collisions when the ABI is declared or requested. The folder follows the declared or requested platform, not the resolved ABI, which is known only after planning: a target declaring linux/arm64 that is cross-built to musl lands in dist/<target>/linux/arm64/ although its asset is -musl and its evidence path linux/arm64-musl, and a native GNU build and a musl cross build of that undeclared ABI share one folder. Declare the ABI (linux/arm64/musl) to keep them apart; a folder that follows the resolved ABI is a recorded follow-up, and extensions["oyzu.dev/platforms"] records how it was built: target (the logical target every platform variant shares), declared (the platforms the target declares), declaredExecutors, platform and executor ({"kind":"host"}, {"kind":"cross-toolchain","toolchain":"rust-lld","target":"aarch64-unknown-linux-musl"} or {"kind":"container"}), and one rows entry per declared or requested platform with selected, executor or reason, and the runner that builds it on its own host. Image-worker targets record target, declared, platform and the container executor. Publication reads declared to refuse an incomplete platform set. An executor other than the host is part of the target's action-cache identity. See platforms and executors. Executable verification. An artifact the builder declares a native executable (Rust and Go binaries; an external plugin's executable flag only promotes a file to .oyzu/bin and is not verified) is verified statically when it is collected, on the native and isolated paths: the file must be a valid executable for its target platform (an ELF, Mach-O, including a universal binary's matching slice, or PE header), name that platform's architecture, and contain every loadable segment or section it declares (not empty or truncated). The artifact is never run, so cross-built artifacts are verified too. The record carries extensions["oyzu.dev/executable"]: platform from planning and, once verified, verified.format (elf, mach-o, pe) and verified.architecture. A failure is EXECUTABLE_INVALID: artifact <id> is not a valid <platform> executable: <cause> and fails the build; the artifact keeps its ordinary kind (file). Known architectures are x86_64, arm64, 386, arm, riscv64, ppc64le and s390x; another is refused as unknown. Limitations: a Python wheel whose compatibility is inspected after the build stays in the target's platform directory even when it turns out to be py3-none-any. A direct oyzu run <target>:test places reports under the host platform. A native artifact named reports is refused with a reserved-name error before the build runs.

When a frozen plan exists, inspection also requires matching manifest target records and declared artifact target/variant identities. Relabeling a runtime variant in the manifest without changing the corresponding plan is rejected. A target finalized after declared generator hooks must match its existing recorded post-hook plan. Inspection verifies that plan's bytes, base, fresh successful hooks, native version identity and unchanged context; only declared version followers may change their version values. Missing or altered finalization evidence fails inspection. Runtime-specific reports remain attributable through their concrete target records; see runtime matrices. This consistency check does not authenticate either record. A successful bundle must contain every planned artifact and every required successful action and report. Inspection reuses the report collector's native parsers and current plan gates, including coverage policy, instead of accepting stored summaries alone. Missing required records, changed bytes or a failing native report fail inspection. Reused reports retain their original producer. For an OCI image artifact, inspection additionally verifies that the archive's actual OS/architecture matches its target record. Collection enforces the same check, including after custom test or packaging tasks. A valid archive digest alone cannot establish that the image was built for the requested platform. See Docker target selection; structural image checks do not prove application execution on that target.

An invocation holds an operating-system file lock on .oyzu/build.lock through staging and finalization. Another cooperating build in that workspace fails before execution with a workspace-lock diagnostic. The existence of the lock file alone does not indicate a live build: the operating-system lock is authoritative and is released when its owning process exits. Different workspace roots have independent locks. The engine creates its staging directory under .oyzu/bundle-* on the destination filesystem. It admits an existing dist only when it is a directory containing an Oyzu build manifest. A preexisting application-owned dist must be preserved or moved by its owner before building; Oyzu does not delete it. State, lock, bundle marker and destination paths reject symbolic links, including dangling links, and Windows reparse points. History paths receive the same checks before use. The invocation records the existing manifest's content identity, or the absence of a destination. Immediately before finalization it rechecks that state. A newly created destination, changed manifest, invalid destination or existing history slot stops finalization instead of overwriting it. This is a change check, not a proof that every byte in the older bundle remained unchanged.

When records are finalized, the previous dist is moved to .oyzu/history/<new-run-id>, and the staged directory becomes dist. No reports or artifacts are appended to the old manifest. If the second rename fails, Oyzu attempts to restore the prior bundle. If restoration also fails, the diagnostic identifies the history path containing the previous bundle. Native builds retire the previous bundle's claimed artifacts into history even when the new build fails. They do not copy those artifacts back into dist as unclaimed files, which would prevent a later successful retry. Unrelated native files remain preserved and collision-protected; .oyzu/bin stays at the last successful build. Test-only output preservation retains its separate contract. If an older bundle already records old binaries as unclaimed host output, preserve or relocate that bundle before rebuilding: a matching filename alone does not authorize replacement. A finalization error retains the new staging directory and includes its exact path in the error. Inspect that path directly when its records are complete: oyzu inspect .oyzu/bundle-EXAMPLE Use the path from the diagnostic, not the literal example name. Preserve the conflicting destination and resolve the filesystem problem before rebuilding. Retained staging directories are not automatically considered successful builds or reused as input. An ordinary abandoned staging scope is cleaned up; read-only --plan creates no staging scope.
