Failures while writing records, abrupt termination and full disks can leave incomplete evidence; a retained directory alone does not prove a valid bundle. The filesystem publication step does not contact a registry or require network access. It adds no configuration or UI dependency. --plan is a read-only preview; it performs no image/dependency preparation and never replaces dist.

The executable plan's existing target extensions retain the final native placement facts under oyzu.dev/execution (needsDaemon, executionPlatform) and the separate result/effect facts under oyzu.dev/slice (transferable, repeatable, reason, detail). A transferable contract is not an actual cache hit. Missing bounded native result coverage keeps transferability false; safe repetition additionally requires supported confined commands. These facts do not grant authority to repeat hooks or unknown effects. Coupled work can remain one invocation without new user placement configuration. Experimental implementation for #479: a successful --slice --handoff <repository> offers its sealed complete bundle before filesystem publication, in addition to existing computation-result handoffs. The selected plan, envelope, logs, directory/file artifacts and native reports travel together. The registry is required for this explicit slice flow; ordinary local finalization remains offline. The existing v1alpha1 OCI layout is extended in place: Part Binding Repository and tag <handoff>/v1alpha1/<first two manifest-digest hex>:bundle-<64 hex> Artifact type application/vnd.oyzu.build-bundle.v1alpha1 Config Canonical manifest.json bytes, application/vnd.oyzu.build-manifest.v1alpha1+json; SHA-256 equals the tag identity Layer One application/vnd.oyzu.build-bundle.v1alpha1.tar+zstd archive containing the other bundle entries Annotations dev.oyzu.build.manifest names the config digest; dev.oyzu.bundle.uncompressed-digest names the raw tar digest Archive entries are sorted portable paths with zero uid/gid/mtime, regular files at 0644/0755 and directories at 0755, including empty artifact directories. Links are rejected by the existing snapshot owner. Config plus compressed layer and the expanded tar each have a 256 MiB bound. The existing OCI client supplies authentication, transport retries and immutable publication. An identical entry converges; a different or corrupt entry at that identity fails. Upload retries reuse the sealed bytes without native command replay. If delivery still fails, the invocation records HANDOFF_PUSH_FAILED and exit 5 while preserving its actual successful action outcomes. Its ordinary bundle evidence retains the successful config, compressed layer and OCI entry bytes for a private transfer-only retry. That retry validates all retained identities and leaves the finalized failed invocation immutable. It does not authorize a new execution or make an unverified platform attempt successful. This transport does not authenticate the producer or decide run-wide completion. The platform must accept the live attempt and verify complete selected obligations. See the qualification record for measured transport coverage and the still-pending real-service proof.

oyzu history oyzu history <invocation-id> oyzu history <run-id> --json oyzu inspect <bundle-directory> --json history reads the current dist/manifest.json and finalized manifests under .oyzu/history/. It looks up the recorded identity inside each manifest, because a history directory is named for the replacing run. Old bundles lacking invocationId remain selectable by their runId. It performs no installation, network calls, execution or artifact hashing; inspect separately verifies a named complete bundle. Invalid identifiers fail with INVOCATION_ID_INVALID; missing identities fail with INVOCATION_NOT_FOUND and a listing next action. Listing returns at most twenty summaries, ordered by available envelope start time, plus omitted counts and up to eight incomplete-bundle notices. A selected summary contains reconciled action counts, fresh/reused/unknown-origin test totals, warnings, at most eight exceptional actions and eight diagnostics, bounded diagnostic excerpts, available reuse provenance and evidence paths. It also contains at most eight recorded action decisions (decisions, with omittedDecisions), the recorded selection, and cache status/reason. Nested inventories keep at most eight entries with adjacent *Omitted counts; selection reason/variant maps also retain at most eight keys with omission counts. Recorded cacheLimitations retain unavailable local/remote tiers and selectionFallback retains a fallback reason independently of warning diagnostics. Each decision preserves its actual outcome, execution/reuse reason, available captured-source comparison and original producer. Human history and build --explain share this projection; the complete manifest retains omitted details. It does not include native log bodies or environments. Missing event/plan/action logs are explicitly unavailable. The complete manifest and available files can be opened using the returned paths. Summary availability is not artifact verification or proof that a journal contains every execution event. Later source/configuration changes or cache clear do not rewrite these selected invocation decisions. History never substitutes current preview analysis or the latest cache-key history. Older or incomplete records without file comparison detail explicitly report it unavailable, preserving known outcomes and producer provenance. A reused test report remains evidence of earlier execution. A plan or manifest target whose configuration a policy constraint changed records extensions["oyzu.dev/policy-overrides"]: one entry per override with the setting, the effective value, the constraint (source, kind of lock, minimum, maximum or required, bound, selector), what it replaced (value, source relative to the project root, scope) and the human note (see policy constraints and selectors). The constraint's label is org policy, admin policy or, for the root oyzu.toml's project constraints (source oyzu.toml [constraints]), project constraint. A release build's target whose check a nearer folder lowered below a farther [context.release] value records extensions["oyzu.dev/release-lowerings"]: one entry per check with the setting, the value used, its source (app/oyzu.toml:2), the releaseValue and its releaseSource (oyzu.toml:5), relative to the farther file's folder (per-context values). The checks summary projects captured target oyzu.dev/build-checks facts: selected action IDs, logical operations and native report kinds, explicit omitted operations, and outcomes joined to the finalized action records. targets keeps eight rows, with omission counts; aggregate counts include all recorded rows. tests on each target is selected, not-requested or unknown. Only a valid complete captured selected array establishes absence of selected tests; missing or malformed historical selection remains unknown. Current configuration and report counts never fill that gap. Aggregate checks.status is recorded when every target has captured selection, partial for a mix, and unknown when none do; unknownTargets retains the count. Test totals remain split by fresh/reused/unknown origin. Each bucket adds zeroTestReports for collected native reports explicitly recording total: 0. Missing passed, failed or skipped facts make that aggregate field null, rendered unavailable; a bucket with no reports also has unknown numeric totals. Zero tests, native skips, missing required reports and absent evidence remain distinct. Human receipts and history use the same shared check projection; build JSON retains the full target selection and report facts in its manifest. This is local build/test-bundle history, governed by existing filesystem access and bundle retention. Nothing is uploaded or granted to another user. There is no automatic history expiry or deletion command; bundles remain until their owner explicitly removes them. An operation ending before bundle creation has no retained entry. Abrupt termination, sink/write failures, incomplete staging, externally removed bundles and interactive native streams can leave partial or missing evidence. Remote run history and general command transcripts remain unimplemented; remote portal links are the available inspection route.

When an external builder is bound (see plugin packages), the plan, execution envelope and manifest each carry extensions["oyzu.dev/plugins"]: one record per bound reference with its source (package or local-development), identity and executableDigest. The plan digest covers the plan's copy. oyzu inspect fails with plugin records differ from plan or … from envelope when the manifest's or envelope's copy is missing or edited. Like every inspect check this is integrity of recorded content, not proof of who produced it.

Rust tests cover lock contention, first/repeated finalization, history retention, ordinary staging cleanup, changed or newly created destinations, history collisions, invalid run IDs, incomplete staging records and retained failure evidence. Windows tests create real directory junctions and verify rejection without modifying the target. Unix symlink checks run in the Linux/macOS test jobs. The existing captured-build suites exercise the same lifecycle with native artifacts, repeated builds and failed-build reports; consult implementation status for revision-specific evidence. The two renames are not a power-loss-safe transaction. There is no automatic journal recovery if the process or machine stops between them. Path checks and locks also do not make the store race-free against a hostile process with permission to replace directories. Inspection verifies recorded outputs separately from these destination checks. Remote storage and automatic history retention limits remain unfinished. The direct Node/Python/Go test workflow reuses this transaction with host output preservation. Unlike captured builds, it can admit native application output in dist, copy that output into the new test-only bundle and retain the original directory in history. These bytes have a separate integrity inventory and are not new build artifacts. It removes prior engine report/evidence claims from the current bundle, preserves their original bytes in history, and rejects reserved-path collisions. Other direct test profiles remain to be integrated.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/build-logging.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu build presents a pipeline in the terminal: phases, parallel targets, commands, live output and an evidence-based final receipt. Presentation never changes the task graph, execution policy or required checks. oyzu build oyzu build api web worker oyzu build --output plain oyzu build --output interactive oyzu build --plan oyzu build --json > result.json 2> events.jsonl

--output auto is the default and uses compact linear preparation, named work and one final receipt. --output plain uses the same flow: no alternate screen, fixed panes, input handling or whole-screen redraws. On capable terminals, active operations show a labeled header and the last eight output lines beneath it; routine successful steps collapse; slow steps and exceptions stay in scrollback. Redirected streams are strictly append-only. Colors are independent of interactivity (ui.color=auto|always|never); nonempty NO_COLOR takes precedence, and CLICOLOR_FORCE can style a pipe without enabling redraw. GitHub Actions uses the same bounded linear view with balanced phase groups. --output interactive requires terminal stdin/stderr and allows inspecting the dashboard even in CI. --json and quiet logging take precedence over either option. In JSON mode, stdout contains the final manifest/plan JSON and stderr contains JSON-line events only. No project configuration is needed. The dashboard uses Crossterm's Windows/macOS/Linux terminal support. Only explicit interactive selection initializes the dashboard and can report its setup errors. Windows GNU builds using an older bundled GNU linker can encounter import-table incompatibility with terminal dependencies; the local proof uses the provisioned LLVM MinGW linker explicitly. Standard CI compilation remains registered on all three hosts; see implementation status for actual verification.

The explicit dashboard follows Prepare, Build and Collect. During preparation it shows verified/pending tool counts and up to two pending tools, without claiming that external prerequisites are installed. Completed setup collapses when execution starts. Optional quality tools stay out of a fast-build summary. p reveals requested versions, observed setup/context facts and the selected work's stage/output details. Setup facts use a height-dependent budget of at most eight rows, disclose omitted detail and point to detailed logs or oyzu build --plan --json. The live pane remains available with large tool inventories. The project header, elapsed time, phase indicators and platform overview stay in place. Selected platforms appear before dependency preparation starts, with readable OS/architecture names. Each row shows its current operation and elapsed time. Active rows also show how long output has been quiet. Preparation is tracked separately from planned build actions. One live pane shows the selected step's seven most recent output lines. Its last lines remain visible during silence, alongside time since the last output. New parallel work does not steal focus from a running step. Warnings and failures remain pinned above the pane. Native output is retained even when Oyzu does not recognize its content; detailed history preserves redacted command arguments, observed timing and event details. Successful process exit can show Checking outputs until collection validates the action. Color reinforces status symbols and labels. NO_COLOR disables color, including an explicit force; the frozen ui.color configuration supports auto, always and never. Status remains readable without color. Key Action Up / Down Select the previous/next preparation or build step Enter Expand or collapse the live output pane a Follow active work automatically p Toggle bounded preparation/context and selected-work details d / l Toggle detailed multiplexed log history Escape Return to the compact live pane Page Up / Page Down Scroll the selected/all log view Left / Right Pan long log/command lines horizontally f / End Follow new output again q Restore terminal input, hide the dashboard and continue the build with plain logs (including during resize) n Inspect the next failed task without automatic focus changes Ctrl+C Restore the terminal and request cooperative interruption; exit 130 A failed command or final action failure raises a notice without changing the selected task; n selects a failed task explicitly. Successful process exit does not establish action success: reports/artifacts can fail validation later. Blocked tasks expose their prerequisite reason. The interface does not require input to finish. Terminal resizing recalculates panel sizes. Very small terminals show a resize hint. Output is clipped to display cells rather than wrapping into the pinned header; horizontal panning reveals long lines. Interactive scrollback uses a temporary disk spool with in-memory line offsets, retaining early output without holding every output byte in memory. It is removed when the view closes. Raw build logs and the event journal remain the durable record. The alternate screen restores the previous terminal at normal completion or error, then prints the permanent receipt. q restores the screen immediately without cancelling work. Ctrl+C uses the build cancellation lifecycle below.

The first Ctrl+C requests cooperative build cancellation; its notice uses the invocation logger, including JSONL framing and correlation. A second Ctrl+C, or expiry of the ten-second grace period, forces exit. Forced cleanup gives all tracked container removals one shared five-second deadline; on Windows, tracked child process-tree termination shares that budget. Unfinished cleanup clients are killed and reaped asynchronously rather than waited on indefinitely. Oyzu names containers or process trees whose removal failed or remained pending, then exits with status 130 even when Docker does not respond. These budgets are fixed. Forced exit is best effort: it can leave containers, process trees and incomplete staging evidence, and does not promise a finalized failure bundle. After the daemon recovers, inspect the reported names and remove leftovers before retrying; use bundle recovery for retained build state. Emergency cleanup messages go to stderr even with --json; they are not a final JSON result. The authored stuck-Docker regression is Unix-specific; neither it nor the cross-platform cleanup tests ran on this desktop. See verification status.

oyzu build prints one build as named sections (see Result output for the reader's view). The live stream on stderr carries the title, Prepare, Plan and Build; the final receipt on stdout carries Outputs, Warnings, the summary line and Details. A section appears only with its first row and is never printed empty. Title. The heading event keeps its recorded text. The linear view shortens its subtitle (windows/x86_64 (host) · local · fast) and right-aligns it, wrapping below the title when the width is short. Prepare. Every preparation step prints as one row: mark, name, detail, and the duration followed by · N warnings when work raised them. The warning count joins a step to its scope (a step named docs dependencies ran the scope docs:dependencies). While a step runs it shows under the heading with a spinner (.. without color). The Tools row summarizes the pinned tools (2 tools pinned · 0 installed now) and lists each beneath it with its version, whether it was already installed or installed now, and the detected requirement that needs it, then why the build has it: detected from Cargo.toml (a builder found it) or pinned in docs-site/oyzu.toml · not detected for docs (only a folder pin selected it), followed by the detected toolchain components and host prerequisites. Best-effort detection (Rust: prost-build/tonic-build in Cargo.lock → protoc) lists a detected tool (detected from Cargo.lock), pinned or not (an unpinned one is resolved to the detection's version hint, else the latest stable release, locked in oyzu.lock and installed), and adds ! attention rows for a detected tool that is unknown, has no usable checksum or cannot be resolved or installed (pin it in oyzu.toml or silence it with tools.ignore; the build continues, only an explicit pin fails), a missing host prerequisite, or a package that fetches a tool outside the lock; they warn and never fail the build. tools.ignore silences a detection (shown only with -v). When another build holds the workspace, a Build lock row waits for it, naming its process and start time, instead of failing; Ctrl-C stops the wait. Selection. Only when the build is not simply every declared target, a Selection section prints after Prepare, from the recorded selection record (mode, requested, selected, excluded, prerequisites) and affected evidence; nothing is recomputed. For --affected the heading says compared with <ref> at <short commit> and the rows are changed (targets and changed paths), dependents and unaffected (not built · -v lists them); long name lists end in +N and -v lists all. A conservative fallback prints ! Not narrowed with a short reason, recorded reason: <code>, selected all N targets and a to narrow line only for the codes with a known fix (unowned-input, baseline-unavailable); it is an attention notice, not a failure. An explicit request prints requested and, when prerequisites were pulled in, required. When every target is selected the section is omitted. -q hides it. Plan. The plan table waits until preparation and Selection have been shown, then prints once under Plan; if no action runs it prints when the view closes. With a Selection the trailer reads N of M targets, and an affected build adds a final why column (changed or uses <target>) unless the table would overflow. The table has a row per target (a row per platform for one target on several platforms, headed 1 target · N platforms), a column per declared stage (format, lint, test, build, package, then others), cells run, skip or -, and one dim footnote per skip reason. Above twelve rows, identical rows are counted (29 targets); -v lists every target. A table wider than the terminal becomes one record per row. Stage facts come from the inventory event's stagePlans; stages whose status is unavailable also read skip, with their reason in a footnote. Stage plans that arrive after execution has started are not added. Build. The heading opens when execution starts. Each finished action prints one row: mark, target (without the platform when every target shares it), stage, the redacted command shortened to the remaining width with … (an internal builder worker shows builder operation), executed, reused or failed, and the duration right-aligned. Rows of a narrow terminal keep the command on a second line instead of dropping it. A failed action's native cause prints before its row. An action reused from retained evidence has the mark ↺ (word reused), is never counted as executed, and shows was <duration>: the recorded duration is that of the run that produced it, not time spent now. Starts print nothing in redirected output; the ten-second heartbeat still reports long waits. Failure. A failed action's row says failed (FAIL). Its native cause is not printed where it happens: the view keeps the first error context (else the last eight lines) and the receipt prints it once under ── Failure: <target> · <stage> ── with the exit code, the retained log path and Next oyzu build <target>; at most three blocks, then + N more failed actions. If nothing was captured the recorded error diagnostics are the cause. A preparation failure prints Failure: preparation · <target> from the error diagnostics and no Build section. Blocked and waiting. A blocked task event gives one row, ⊘ target stage needs target · stage, taken from the event's reason; only the first three print and finish adds + N more blocked · -v lists them. In a live terminal pane a queued action with unfinished prerequisites (plan dependsOn) shows ○ … waits for …, at most three and + N more waiting. Collapse. With more than twelve planned actions and without -v, clean executed and reused successes are counted into one ✓ N finished · R reused · E executed line (printed when the view closes, and live in the pane with N of M finished); warned, failed and blocked actions keep rows. The Build heading then carries the action count, because an append-only stream cannot update it. Redirected and CI logs. Output that is redirected, or a build in a detected CI context, is appended and never redrawn. Each action prints one start line (00:12 .. api build started) and one end line with its outcome and duration, both led by the dim elapsed mm:ss since the invocation began; blocked rows carry it too. In a build that collapses (more than twelve actions) only the end lines and the tally remain. The ten-second heartbeat is one line, 00:31 still running: api build 10s · auth-lib test 12s · 6 waiting (at most three running actions, then + N more), and replaces the earlier Progress, Work and Running … lines among the Build rows; -v keeps the older lines. CI group markers around the phases are unchanged. An interactive terminal keeps the live pane and prints no elapsed prefix. Directories. The build tells the view where each selected target lives through Log::target_directories, a presentation call outside the event stream, so JSON events are unchanged. Builds across more than one top-level directory group the plan, Outputs and the summary by directory as described in Result output; the receipt reads the same directories from the manifest's target path. Narrow and no color. Below about 60 columns, or without color, marks are padded words and rules are short; every table has a record form that loses no value: the plan table (one record per target), Outputs (the target and size, then the whole path on the next line), Selection (counts, then the names below) and Build rows (the command, elided with …, moves below the row). Redirected output always renders at 100 columns. Terminal width comes from the console, so a narrow layout cannot be forced through COLUMNS. Quiet. With -q the view prints no native excerpts; the receipt prints the Failure blocks, Warnings and the summary line only. Warnings once. With the default verbosity native warnings and WARN diagnostics are not printed where they happen: the receipt's Warnings (N) section lists each distinct one, owner first (target and tool, for example docs · npm). Errors are never deferred. -v keeps warnings inline as well. NATIVE_WARNING is shown only with -v; Oyzu-owned codes are always shown. No color. Without color the mark is a word padded to a common width (ok, reused, warn, FAIL) and rules use dashes. Terminal controls in every value are escaped before display. Quiet. -q hides the title and sections; warnings and the summary line remain in the receipt. Only a real local oyzu build selects the sectioned view, because only it prints the receipt that lists warnings once; --plan, --check, remote runs, oyzu run, scan and the dashboard keep their existing renderers. JSON events, --json stdout and exit status do not change.

The operation heading identifies the project, host/platform selection, execution mode and requested checks. In the sectioned build view the scope and affected facts are the Selection section described above; the legacy renderer keeps a compact scope record naming up to three selected targets and counting the rest, with the baseline, overlapping category counts and any conservative fallback. Planner facts remain authoritative. Routine queued/included stage rows do not produce per-stage lines; the plan table above carries them. In the legacy (non-sectioned) renderer deliberate skips are neutral, grouped by reason, naming up to three affected stages in each group, with up to three distinct reasons and an inspection route for further detail. Unavailable/unknown stages receive attention separately; up to eight such records appear, followed by an explicit omission and oyzu build --plan --json inspection route. -v shows additional stage/context records in the same linear design. The old Preflight, Selection, Stages and About this build sections have been removed from the linear renderer, including its verbose path. Explicit build --plan remains a read-only inspection view with its own grouped plan tables. Concurrent plans preserve active work and register every target's readable label, including targets beyond the visible budget. JSON inventory stagePlans, action selection, dependencies, checks, caching and execution policy are unchanged. The linear view uses status, subject and activity records, without table headers mixed into preflight updates. Installation progress includes the requested version when available. Routine checks and reused tool readiness collapse by default; actual acquisition and explicit installation results remain visible. System prerequisites explicitly say they are checked during compilation. Unselected optional tools stay out of the summary. Native preflight uses named steps for configuration, tool preparation, dependencies, output bundle, compiler cache, source evidence, CLI identity and report preparation. Running steps use ›, explicitly completed steps use ✓, and interrupted-by-error preparation uses ✗; stopping a progress heartbeat is not a completion signal. On capable terminals active rows redraw. Fast successful preparation collapses; steps lasting at least ten seconds and failures remain visible. Completed slow work stays successful; duration alone does not turn it into a warning. Dependency readiness removes its running row, and entering execution retires preparation. Redirected output appends named long-wait feedback and remains readable without color. Report contracts and binding readiness share one completion row. Execution/isolation context remains in context facts and the build heading, not repeated · build progress prose. Structured JSON events and journal records retain these transitions; stdout, native child streams and exit status retain their existing contracts. Each active build subprocess has a short preview immediately beneath its operation header. This applies uniformly to formatting, linting, tests, compilation, custom hooks and tool installation through the shared logging lifecycle. The latest eight lines scroll within that preview and use dim text when color is enabled. Successful operations collapse into receipt totals; slow action completions may remain visible. Failed operations retain the first useful eight-line diagnostic context, or their last eight lines when no diagnostic marker is recognized, with the failure status and available exit code; the receipt identifies retained build logs. Each parallel operation has its own preview. The active region is bounded by terminal height; excess activity is indicated explicitly. Long preview lines are clipped to terminal width, while retained output stays complete. This is a transient section of ordinary scrollback, with no alternate screen or keys. Redirected human output is bounded and append-only. Routine captured native lines are retained for verbose output, failure excerpts and evidence. Preparation subprocesses retain the same eight-line failure tail, including native causes without a recognized warning/error prefix; successful preparation clears its tail, and -v expands its captured output. JSON events and raw build task logs never collapse. A late parallel preparation event does not reset the Build heading. Installer worker stderr is followed into the same logging owner; its stdout remains the private worker protocol. Commands intentionally exposing a native pass-through payload retain that separate contract. Captured Rust compiler materialization also follows installer stderr through the invocation logger. Installer protocol stdout remains private; human views show bounded attention while JSON stderr and retained events preserve structured records instead of unframed rustup output. Native excerpts identify their task once and preserve source indentation and carets beneath that label. Decoded multiline Cargo diagnostics are written together under the invocation output lock; unstructured native output retains line-level ordering without guessing diagnostic boundaries. When a registered Cargo compiler warning arrives line by line, successful collapse preserves its first bounded context from that same stream, without repeating its already printed header. Other streams do not fill that context, and it shares the eight-line warning budget. Native status lines or a new diagnostic end that source context. Cargo packaging uses the same registration and warning facts; identical packaging warnings appear once per action at normal verbosity, while verbose output and raw evidence retain them. Consecutive warnings share an excerpt label; changing work restores its label. Routine preparation narration is live status or verbose detail, and slow project metadata completion says Ready without listing internal worker calls. Native process success is omitted because it precedes validation. Task completion and the final receipt retain their distinct meanings; failures include available exit codes. The linear view shows preparation and execution as named lifecycle records, then one receipt. At most four routine action starts and four slow completions appear by default; further work collapses into totals. Native warnings/errors retain bounded permanent context on both terminals and redirected streams. Warning and error budgets are separate so warnings cannot hide a later root failure, with omission notices and failure tails. -v expands captured output and successful preparation records. Context and command metadata remain in structured events and retained evidence. Every ten seconds it reports nonzero, disjoint action outcome counts, active work, dependency waits with causes/observed ages and elapsed time while execution remains unfinished. Graph growth updates known action totals without erasing existing outcomes. Action counts are never a time-remaining estimate; a liveness update is not progress. Cargo JSON compiler records are projected into concise compiled-target/status lines by the shared native projection, including native build-host workers; cached artifact records and build-script metadata are omitted from both human views. Registered go test -json streams show native output and failed test identities instead of JSON envelopes. Split records are assembled per scope and stream, bounded to one MiB per record; exceeding that display limit directs the reader to retained native logs. Compiler diagnostics and unknown output remain visible. Original output events, JSON mode, raw logs and artifact validation inputs are unchanged. Native processes retain their own buffering; Oyzu cannot show bytes before the process writes them. GitHub Actions keeps collapsible phase groups around the shared bounded view. The ordinary terminal shows reconciled scheduler counts beside its bounded live work, including short builds before the first heartbeat. Closing the dashboard with q preserves active scopes, elapsed age and native projection in the linear view. Automatic focus advances from completed setup to active work until the user pins a selection; subsequent workers and failures do not steal that selection. Native warnings are included in the receipt as NATIVE_WARNING diagnostics in JSON, and in the human Warnings section (the generic code is shown there only with -v). Cargo's typed warnings retain primary source locations when available; its repeated summary does not add another warning. Recognizable plain native warning markers, including Node runtime and npm warnings, are retained; unrelated JSON is not reinterpreted as a warning. This reports native diagnostic facts and never infers an action result from a warning or error string. Concurrent scopes share a synchronized sink so lines do not interleave at the byte level. Within-stream ordering is retained. Observation order between independent tasks or stdout/stderr is not a global causal order. Command-event argv is a redacted presentation value, not an authoritative command or portable shell script. Control characters are escaped. Text redirected to a file contains no dashboard cursor controls. Detected provider names include GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Azure Pipelines, Buildkite, Jenkins and TeamCity, with generic CI fallback. These are unverified presentation hints, never credentials or release authority. In GitHub Actions, preflight, dependency and planning phases use collapsible groups. Groups close before action execution; individual concurrent tasks do not open overlapping groups. On completion, Oyzu appends an HTML-escaped receipt to GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY if supplied. Failure to write the summary warns without changing build status. JSON mode still uses only JSON events on stderr, with no group commands. Local artifact paths are not presented as download links: artifact uploading, additional provider-native summaries and reliable source-location annotations are not implemented here.

A build stopped during preparation preserves its known selected target count and says Build failed during preparation and No build actions started. Prepared action records remain empty; they are not described as an empty target selection. Available target identity and the original preparation cause remain in diagnostics. Human diagnostic and recovery paragraphs wrap at word boundaries with a hanging indent (100 columns when the terminal width is unavailable). History summaries and bundle inspection retain that selected scope as well; the shared record summary owns the count rather than treating an empty prepared target array as no selected work. The completion summary of a successful build is the sectioned receipt described above: Outputs with project-relative paths and sizes (absolute with -v), Warnings, then the outcome line (Build succeeded, with warnings) with its target and non-zero action-outcome tally and elapsed wall time, and a Details line with the manifest path, event path and invocation id (or unavailable). Other outcomes keep the form below: the outcome and elapsed wall time first, then artifacts with target, bundle-relative path and recorded size, followed by actual manifest/event references or explicit unavailability. Multiple targets receive at most eight target rows with an omitted count; single-target builds omit that redundant table. Receipts distinguish selected targets from actions and reconcile disjoint action outcomes. A failed build ends with a Failure block per failed action (or one for preparation), Warnings, a summary that counts only non-zero outcomes (1 failed · 12 blocked · 130 succeeded) and Details; host failures add the note that existing local binaries were not updated. Interrupted builds keep the older form: failed and blocked actions with available exit codes/reasons. Empty artifact results say “No artifacts produced”; empty Reports sections are omitted. Fresh tests and reused test evidence have separate totals. Reuse identifies available producer provenance and never increments tests run now. A report with mixed or missing action ownership is labelled with unavailable origin. Coverage measurements remain visible when available. Missing reports do not imply zero failures or 100% coverage, and coverage is not averaged across unrelated metrics. Planned artifacts are labeled as planned. Diagnostic messages retain severity, code, affected action and available recovery. Success with warning diagnostics says so explicitly; warning detail remains visible. Default receipt sections are bounded to eight records and disclose omitted detail. -v (or a debug log level enabled for the command) additionally lists manifest and individual report paths; these files remain in the output bundle at normal verbosity. Human and structured views consume the same finalized facts; JSON retains the complete manifest. The summary uses semantic color on capable terminals and remains readable without color. Normal builds retain dist/logs/events.jsonl, numbered action stdout/stderr files, manifest.json and plan.json. Preparation output is included in events. Independent branches emit partial plan events as they become ready; later aggregate plan events preserve running/completed task states. Branch action logs are namespaced under logs/<target>/, and sealed plans are retained under plans/. Preflight records are temporarily spooled and replayed into the existing journal when the bundle becomes available, so collapsed installer output is retained on completed preflight flows. If setup fails before a bundle is created, a durable build journal is not published; terminal error details and JSON/redirected output remain available. The final console build outcome follows publication of the bundle; the journal is closed before publication. --plan uses a separate read-only preview receipt with stage selection, tool requirements and unresolved details; it runs no dependency preparation and creates no bundle. History follows the bundle lifecycle. Bundled development tasks (oyzu run test) also retain full stdout/stderr in their numbered log files in text and JSON modes. Text mode tees output live without duplicating it as console log events. The exception is a text-mode task explicitly marked interactive = true: it inherits terminal descriptors, which Oyzu cannot capture simultaneously without a pseudo-terminal. Its stdout/stderr files are empty; report collection still applies. See task stream behavior. Event records have schemaVersion, sequence, elapsedMs, scope, severity, target, invocationId, operationId, parentOperationId and a tagged event: diagnostic, heading, fact, inventory, preparation, progress, phase, plan, task, command, output or finished. Observed warnings/errors are retained independently of console filtering; disabled debug/trace messages are not constructed or persisted. Fact events carry explicit section/name/value presentation observations, without environment maps. Inventory contains selected target labels, platforms, check mode and color preference, without environment maps. Preparation/phase/task events carry lifecycle facts. The plan event contains only presentation inventory (target ID/builder, action ID/target/dependencies and artifact versions), never action environments. Output includes stream, text and continued; completion includes status, optional exit_code and optional duration_ms. Consumers should tolerate new event types. This experimental observation format remains separate from deterministic plan identity and release evidence. The logger adds no network calls. Environment maps are not dumped. Project commands/output can deliberately print sensitive values; arbitrary-output secret detection is not promised. Upstream broker credentials remain outside executor arguments/environment under the existing acquisition contract. Native raw-log size and process-time limits remain in force. Log sink failures do not override native process results; durable remote delivery is separate work.

tooling/test-build-logging.py --cli <compiled-cli> --evidence-dir <new-directory> runs two real Rust targets, verifies live parallel streams, four snapshot artifacts, report collection, JSON failure/blocked events and bundle inspection. The Rust image must already be provisioned. Add --linear to verify the linear view and human failure output instead of the GitHub grouped view. --image <reference> selects an explicit provisioned Cargo image containing the compiled worker and required quality tools. For real terminal acceptance, install tooling/terminal-requirements.txt, then run tooling/test-build-terminal.py --cli <compiled-cli> --evidence-dir <new-directory>. This uses ConPTY on Windows and a pseudo-terminal on Unix to exercise the actual CLI, independent active panels, navigation, resizing, failure focus, hide/restore behavior and resulting bundles. Screen transcripts and representative text frames are retained. Unit tests cover the event projection, full spool history, control escaping and evidence-based receipts. Registration is not passing evidence; see implementation status.

Builds use the global diagnostic controls. Routine lifecycle presentation is info; command observations are debug; failed completion is error and blocked tasks are warn. Native stdout/stderr events are always retained independently of threshold; a native stderr line is not an Oyzu error. Dashboard state and existing journal lifecycle facts continue to receive events even when console detail is filtered. Build journals retain observed diagnostic facts and the same correlation envelope as console JSON. They are observation evidence, not a complete execution audit; existing bundle retention remains in force; command argument redaction applies consistently to their presentation events as well.

A tool has one evolving terminal status followed by a final Ready result. Redirected output retains the initial check and final result, without repeating intermediate reuse/verification notices. Native output remains attributed to its operation. The human child-output projection removes SGR color/style escapes; other terminal controls remain escaped. Original child events and raw evidence retain their existing contracts. Failed operations retain their diagnostic tail. Executor capability results appear after the selected native environment has been checked, rather than as an additional speculative unchecked row.

Explicit installation and automatic build preparation send native installer stderr through the invocation-owned logger. JSON diagnostics stay on stderr; worker stdout remains its private protocol. Human output omits rustup's advice to add its temporary staging home to PATH, because Oyzu publishes and activates the verified installation itself. Native errors remain visible; raw events and JSON retain that advice. Redirected build progress emits changed task summaries once, with explicit omission notices when native previews are bounded. Multiline Oyzu diagnostics retain indented line boundaries while escaping terminal control sequences. Rust doctest compilation streams live output and retains bounded report diagnostics; see the Rust evidence contract. Native task heartbeats are visible in the linear view: while a subprocess is silent, its active terminal row updates elapsed time every ten seconds. Redirected output appends an elapsed-time update instead. These are liveness indicators, not percentages or proof that a native tool is advancing. Native output continues to stream as it arrives; Cargo may remain quiet during compilation or linking.
documents.s: Managed installation and long-running native output

documents.t: The first Ctrl+C (or SIGTERM, or SIGHUP when the terminal closes) asks the build to stop: schedulers stop starting work and running container steps are removed. A signal that was already ignored when the build started, such as SIGHUP under nohup, stays ignored and does not stop it. Steps blocked in a native or Docker call cannot observe the request, so the CLI prints Stopping build; waiting up to 10s for running steps. Press Ctrl-C again to force exit. A second Ctrl+C, or the end of the 10-second grace period, removes the containers this invocation started (named oyzu-* or the build worker names), ends the process tree and exits. On Windows the exit status of a forced exit is 1; on Unix it is 130. Unix forced exit does not yet kill native child processes in other process groups. Containers started before an earlier hard kill are not cleaned up by this mechanism.

Preparation is tracked as named steps. Fast routine success is collapsed by default; -v shows each successful step in completion order. A finished step has a mark, a name, a short result and its duration in a right-aligned column. A step of ten seconds or more remains visible; successful work retains its success marker. Durations read <0.1s, 5.9s, 149s and 10m 06s. ✓ Source captured 2781 files · sha256:668b3844b9d7 13.0s ✓ Rust compiler 1.95.0 · reused the packaged copy from an earlier build 0.8s ✓ Compiler in container restored into a read-only volume 19.5s ✓ Cargo crates 371 locked · all from the cache 5.6s ✓ Project metadata 8 container runs · slowest `cargo metadata` 9.0s 25.0s ✓ Build inputs ready compiler, crates and project metadata 60.8s In a terminal a running step shows in the live pane (› name detail); its tail collapses when it completes. Redirected output prints a step when it finishes, and a heartbeat line while a step is slow. With more than one target a step carries its target (Cargo crates · cli · linux/x86_64). Actions (prepare, build, archive, package) use the same column. While cargo compiles, the individual Compiling/Compiled lines are not printed: the running status shows the count and the latest crate (Running · 60s elapsed · 271 crates compiled · latest oxc_ast_visit), the completed line reports the total (Succeeded · 276 crates compiled), and warnings and errors still print in full. -v prints every crate line. With -v, the headline of a finished build is followed by where the time went (Preflight 71s · Build 174s · Collect 4s). What an isolated build's preflight does, per target: Rust compiler. The locked Rust installation is unpacked once per build, shared by all platforms, and packaged for the build container. The package is cached across builds under cache/rust-packaged in the Oyzu user-data directory, so a repeat build only reuses it. Compiler in container. The package is restored into a read-only Docker volume named oyzu-tools-<hash> (the hash covers the worker image, compiler archive digest and restoration format). The restored copy grants read/search access while preserving executable bits, so actions assigned the source owner's UID can use compilers installed privately with 0700 modes. The original installation and archive are unchanged. Older private-mode volumes are retained; the new restoration format uses a separate derived key. The volume persists across builds, so a repeat build reuses it in under a second instead of re-extracting the compiler (about 20 s). A second volume, oyzu-tools-<hash>-ok, is created only after extraction and accessibility normalization succeed; a volume without it is treated as unfinished and rebuilt. A lock file under cache/ in the Oyzu user-data directory serializes concurrent builds. Each compiler or worker-image change adds one volume (about a gigabyte). After a build restores or reuses its volume, it removes superseded oyzu-tools-<hash> and -ok pairs, keeping that volume and the three most recently created others; the same pass clears volumes leaked by earlier releases. Docker refuses to remove a volume a running container mounts, so concurrent builds are unaffected; failures are retried by the next build. Other Docker storage Oyzu creates is bounded by the Docker storage budget. Without the lock the volume is private to the build and removed afterwards. Cargo crates. Every crate in Cargo.lock is captured into a registry the container uses offline (the build container has no network). Archives are verified against the lock's checksums and cached across builds under cache/cargo-crates; registry index entries are cached for seven days. Project metadata. Several short container runs (cargo metadata, rustc -vV, lockfile generation) read facts about the project. They are one step that names the slowest run; every run is listed at debug verbosity (-v). Source snapshot and Dependency snapshot. Private, hashed copies the offline build uses. Version. The version stamped into the artifacts (see the facts block below). A native (non-isolated) build shows Source workspaces (a private copy of the sources) and one step per executor prerequisite (a small compile-and-link probe of the linker) in the same form. The live › Tools determining… line is a placeholder while any of this runs. Long lines wrap under a hanging indent aligned with the message column, and a generated platform id such as cli-platform-windows_x86_64-157f0d1f6adb is shown as cli · windows/x86_64. The same steps and durations are in the event journal (Step events with duration_ms).

The ordinary build transcript shows the shared Facts section before its plan and actions. -v adds full hashes and other context records; structured facts are also retained in plan events and the journal. The optional dashboard keeps its context inspection panel. Snapshot version facts do not confer release or publication authority. The final receipt leads with the outcome and elapsed time, then target/action counts and nonzero disjoint outcomes. Successful targets do not generate a second result table. Executed and reused tests stay separate; accepted test details collapse while reused evidence keeps its producing run/time and cache origin. Incomplete, rejected or unknown test evidence stays visible; -v includes accepted per-action details too. Root failures precede dependent impact, and error diagnostics precede warnings within bounded excerpts. Omitted actions, evidence and diagnostics have explicit counts and inspection routes. Artifact records give copyable paths under the published dist directory without padding to the longest path. Invocation identity, available manifest/event paths, missing evidence, cache fallback and failure recovery remain visible under quiet output. Help, shell code, selected-path and native pass-through contracts are unchanged. See executable selection when comparing installed and compiled output.

Waiting means a known dependency has not satisfied the action; ready means its dependencies are satisfied and it has not started. Neither means a process ran. Success/reuse/failure/blocking remain separate in the shared snapshot. Pending work prevented from launching by an interrupt is not-started, with a reason; the invocation is interrupted. Unix native tasks killed by the cooperative interrupt and reaped with SIGTERM/SIGKILL report confirmed cancelled; other platforms retain native outcome facts without inferring cancellation. Required checks, scheduling, permissions and exit semantics are unchanged. The dashboard keeps its selected task until the user changes it. New failures raise a notice; n selects the next failed task, arrows select tasks, and the existing log keys inspect complete retained view detail. Ctrl-C uses the same cooperative interruption path as plain output and restores terminal state. oyzu history <invocation-id> --json provides a bounded summary after a local bundle is published; oyzu inspect <bundle-directory> --json verifies the full bundle. See history scope and limits.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/build-tasks.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. For the in-development single inferred or declared Rust target, plain oyzu build now selects the native local path. Use oyzu build --isolated for the captured behavior described on this page. Other target shapes retain their current captured selection. Native self-bootstrap acceptance remains pending. oyzu build composes the selected builders' stages with discovered tasks, explicit replacements, prerequisites and hooks. It captures source and dependencies before executing the resulting graph in private target workspaces. Provision the CLI's native toolchain images and supported Docker executor first; see image provisioning and acceptance checks. This reference describes the current experimental executor, not native Windows/macOS target compilation. Builds now show live progress and multiplexed command output by default. Add --json when consuming the final manifest/plan programmatically. Captured builders that consume Oyzu-managed tool locks retain each participating oyzu.lock in the immutable source and tool evidence. Their native preparation and actions omit these exact control paths from private project views, so native license scans do not mistake engine metadata for upstream source. This role is the same for existing and automatically created locks. Unrelated nested fixture files remain visible. Paths covered by explicit target inputs, including a declared lock, are exempt from this control-file omission. Each builder's existing preparation source filtering otherwise remains unchanged. Authored hooks and replacement tasks keep their ordinary inputs, and Docker context membership retains its separate contract. Native actions carry the selected control paths in frozen configuration metadata; the action/cache identity covers the selection while source identity still covers the original lock bytes. This describes the captured executor, not host Maven development-task behavior.

A plain local oyzu build is a fast build: it runs the build and package stages and only the checks at level required, and skips the other test, lint and format-check stages (skip · fast local build in Plan). In the pr, ci and release build contexts, and with --full, the ci profile or --remote, every check that is not off runs. These are oyzu's defaults, expressed as per-context values of checks.run; a project changes them, and sets each check to off, advisory, enforce or required, in oyzu.toml (check levels): [checks] format = "off" # never run; rustfmt is not prepared for it lint = "advisory" # failures are warnings; the build still succeeds [context.release.checks] tests = "required" An off check is shown as off in Plan with where it was turned off, its stage never runs and the builder does not prepare its tools. An advisory check runs where checks run and reports a failure as a CHECK_ADVISORY warning. Required checks and report validation remain enforced for every stage that runs.
documents.s: Local fast builds and CI checks

documents.t: A local build that only writes its own dist/ uses each builder's development profile; a build whose artifacts are handed off (--slice), written to a shared remote cache, packaged by another selected target or published (the release context) is optimized. oyzu build --optimized and --no-optimized choose for one invocation, and build.optimized in a folder's oyzu.toml (optionally per context) chooses for the targets under it; policy constraints win. Rust builds cargo build --release when optimized and .NET uses --configuration Release; builders where optimization makes no difference stay development. Plan shows each target's profile and why (profile cli · optimized · --optimized), and Outputs labels each artifact. Optimized and development results never restore each other from the action cache, so for Rust and .NET a CI build that writes the remote cache (optimized) does not serve a local development build; build with --optimized to reuse those results. Builders where optimization makes no difference keep sharing. See optimized builds. For the supported single Rust target, plain oyzu build selects the current host and, unless the build is optimized, the development compilation profile, including when build.yaml declares a platform matrix. --platform <os/arch> (repeatable) selects other target platforms instead; Rust builds them natively with a cross toolchain where this host has one. --all-platforms requests the complete declared matrix through the existing captured executor and fails before running when a declared platform cannot be built here; --isolated explicitly selects captured execution and, like a plain build, keeps only the host platform from a declared platform matrix unless --all-platforms or --platform is also given. In a captured build a target that does not declare the host platform keeps its full matrix; a native build builds the one declared platform it can, or skips the target with the reason. See platforms and executors. The matrix backend currently requires Docker and provisioned worker images. Unsupported native relationships fail explicitly rather than ignoring them. Platform selection and isolation are distinct concepts; this implementation does not yet supply a host executor for every matrix variant. Plan records continue to report the actual scheduled stages and context without asserting production eligibility. See native local builds for caches, outputs and qualification limits. Tasks select user operations, and stages organize their work. The executable plan records the actions that implement them. An operation may contain internal actions without requiring extra task configuration. Native execution keeps its existing granularity: Maven's reactor still runs one build lifecycle, with module-specific artifacts and reports. Skipping a separate test stage does not disable tests that a native build command itself runs, such as Maven verify.

oyzu build oyzu build api oyzu build api web --plan No target arguments means all discovered targets. Positional arguments are exact target IDs, not task names, globs or paths. Repeated IDs are deduplicated; unknown IDs fail before image resolution or dependency acquisition. Use oyzu discover to inspect target IDs and oyzu run list for task names. Selection includes transitive depends_on and materialize.from producers, plus the owners of prerequisites and hooks reached from admitted builder stages. Each added target receives its complete applicable build/check/package sequence, not just the requested helper. Native preparation can reveal additional task contracts, so the engine expands selection until no new owner is needed; each target is prepared and planned once. An arbitrary custom task that is not reached from a build stage does not select its dependencies. Unrelated targets have no resolved toolchain, dependency acquisition, actions or artifacts in this invocation. Image overrides for a manager present elsewhere in the discovered workspace are accepted but are only resolved if that manager is selected. Selected targets retain their configuration and required checks; concurrency uses the smallest ceiling from root configuration and selected targets. Selection does not change task binding: an unqualified root hook or stage replacement belongs to every build it reaches whether or not that build is selected. Completed plans and their manifests record extensions["oyzu.dev/selection"]: sorted requested and selected IDs, mode (all, explicit or affected), and excluded targets with reason outside-selection. Excluded targets are not reported as successful. oyzu inspect dist rejects disagreement between the manifest's selection and its frozen plan. Older bundles with no selection extension in either record remain inspectable. A failure before planning can have no selection record. Discovery, configuration validation and source capture still cover the workspace. Malformed metadata in an unrelated project can therefore prevent a selected build; selection is not lazy discovery or a security boundary. The source digest remains repository-wide, while the plan digest binds selection. --plan instead performs a read-only preview, without source capture, image resolution or dependency preparation; native-derived details remain unresolved. Normal builds retain prior bundles under .oyzu/history as before. Finite Node runtime matrices expand logical selections to concrete variants; affected builds optionally select changed targets and their consumers from a local Git baseline. Native member-level impact and action-cache reuse remain unfinished. Discovery captures the bounded build.yaml contents and parsed target declarations once per invocation. Dependency selection, target ordering, platform constraints and materialization planning consume that same inventory. After source capture, the build checks that its inventory bytes match discovery before resolving toolchain images or preparing dependencies. Adding, removing or changing build.yaml during this interval fails with build.yaml changed between discovery and source capture; finish the edit and rerun. Byte identity includes comments and optional fields. Changes after capture do not modify the frozen inventory used by that invocation. This closes an inventory consistency gap; it does not imply that every native metadata race or full matrix expansion is implemented.

Ordinary projects need no task configuration. Builders supply applicable build, test, lint and read-only format-check operations. oyzu run list shows discovered tasks without running them. Mutating format tasks are for explicit development use and are rejected if included in a captured build. Explicit replacements retain the builder's mandatory report and policy obligations. A replacement runs in place of the operation's original actions. Analysis of the original native command does not describe an arbitrary replacement; its inputs remain unknown unless the final command has its own bound model. Its hooks and required reports still apply; Oyzu can add native reporting only to commands its builder recognizes. An arbitrary replacement must produce the required evidence at its bound report paths. It does not inherit precise input or write assumptions from the command it replaced. A qualified prerequisite uses the existing TOML task syntax: [tasks."api:pre_test"] argv = ["node", "scripts/check-api-inputs.mjs"] depends_on = ["schema:verify"] [tasks."schema:verify"] argv = ["node", "scripts/verify-schema.mjs"] Here api and schema are targets discovered or declared in build.yaml; their scripts are relative to their respective target roots. The example requires Node-compatible toolchains for both tasks. A custom command does not implicitly provision a new tool. Use the native ecosystem's command where appropriate; no new build-file task language is introduced. The schema:verify operation runs once per invocation even if several selected tasks require it. Its working directory, toolchain, resolved configuration, environment constraints and output/report paths belong to schema. Its dependencies and schema:pre_verify / schema:post_verify hooks run under the same ownership rules. api:pre_test waits for the prerequisite's post-hook and any deferred report validation before api:test can start. Hook names do not recursively acquire their own hooks. Builder stage order remains in force. A stage already selected as an earlier task's prerequisite is not executed again. Newly selected local prerequisites follow the previous local stage and retain their local dependency-list execution order, including sibling prerequisites. This ordering remains enforced while an earlier stage waits on foreign work; a later helper cannot run early simply because the target's worker is idle. Another target's prerequisites follow their own pipeline. Cycles involving task prerequisites, hooks, builder stage order, target dependencies or materialized artifacts fail before action execution. Error diagnostics currently identify an action cycle without providing its shortest path. Fix the ordering relationship and rebuild; rearranging YAML entries does not resolve a cycle. A root workspace task (a name that is neither a hook nor a builder stage, see below) reached through a qualified prerequisite inherits that prerequisite's target/toolchain context while retaining its declared root-relative working directory. In multiple-target builds, a root workspace task requested from more than one owner is rejected as ambiguous; qualify a shared task with its actual target. This prevents the first target visited from silently choosing its toolchain or private workspace. Task names and command bodies otherwise keep their existing configuration precedence.

Status: implemented (OEP-0022 OD3, D6). A task key in any oyzu.toml belongs to builds by these rules, checked when the configuration is read, before anything runs: Key Belongs to When it is wrong [tasks."api:pre_test"] (qualified) build api only, and it wins over an unqualified definition of the same name for api an unknown build (CONFIG_REFERENCE_UNKNOWN), a file outside api's folder chain (CONFIG_REFERENCE_MISPLACED), or a hook of a task api does not have (CONFIG_REFERENCE_UNKNOWN, with the nearest name) [tasks.post_build] (unqualified hook, pre_* or post_*) every build whose folder chain reads the file and that has the hooked task (package always counts); a root hook reaches every build, the root's own build included; at the root it is also the hook of a workspace task of that name a hook of a task none of those builds has (CONFIG_REFERENCE_UNKNOWN) [tasks.test] (unqualified, a builder stage) replaces that stage in every build its file reaches that runs it as a stage (a docker/image build without tests is not reached) reaching builds with different builders: CONFIG_TASK_AMBIGUOUS, naming them; qualify it per build [tasks.lint-docs] (any other unqualified name) a workspace task at the root (oyzu run lint-docs); in a sub-folder, a task of every build below that folder — "Reaches" follows ordinary configuration precedence: a nearer folder's definition, or a qualified key for the build, replaces a farther one for that build. A hook or stage replacement narrows further with when/unless (hooks only; a stage replacement takes no conditions). A bound task runs in its build's folder unless cwd says otherwise, relative to the file that declares it. Every depends_on entry must name an existing task, by id (schema:verify) or name (verify). # root oyzu.toml, with builds cli (rust/app), docs (node/app) and the root's own [tasks.post_build] # every build, the root's included argv = ["scripts/attest.sh", "{artifact.path}"] [tasks."docs:test"] # one build's stage: docs only argv = ["npm", "run", "test:ci"] [tasks.lint-docs] # a workspace task: oyzu run lint-docs argv = ["node", "tooling/check-docs.mjs"] Writing that docs:test replacement as [tasks.test] would reach cli too, a Rust build, and is refused: CONFIG_TASK_AMBIGUOUS: oyzu.toml:5:1: [tasks.test] replaces the test stage of builds with different builders: cli (rust/app), docs (node/app); one command cannot replace stages of different builders. Qualify it for each build instead, such as [tasks."cli:test"] Migration. Before this rule an unqualified root task replaced a stage only in a workspace with one build, and a qualified key naming no build, or written outside its build's folder chain, was silently ignored. A single-build project keeps writing [tasks.test]. A root stage replacement that now reaches builds with different builders must be qualified, and a misspelled or misplaced key is now an error naming its file and line. The task id of a root replacement in a one-build project is now the build's own (project:test, not test); oyzu run test still finds it. oyzu config validate checks task keys' build names and placement; hook targets and depends_on need the builds' discovered tasks, so oyzu build (including --plan), oyzu run and every other command that discovers the project check them. See names that cross files.
documents.s: Which build a task belongs to

documents.t: Status: implemented for build intent slice 8 (BIN-15..BIN-21). An authored task or hook in oyzu.toml can say when it applies (when, unless) and receive build values through {namespace.name} placeholders. Both are declarative data over a closed vocabulary; anything that needs logic belongs in the program argv runs. A runtime check of a shipped artifact is a post_build hook: [tasks."cli:post_build"] argv = ["{artifact.path}", "--version"] when = { optimized = true, platform = ["linux/x86_64"] } unless = { artifact = ["bin-oyzu-shim"] }

when and unless are tables over these facts, the one selector form that policy constraint selectors use: Fact Value Notes context local, pr, ci, release the context the build runs as (--context, OYZU_CONTEXT or detection); see the note below provider detected CI provider names (github-actions, gitlab, …) fork true, false false outside a detected pull request; inside one, read from GitHub Actions (the event payload's head and base repositories) and GitLab (CI_MERGE_REQUEST_SOURCE_PROJECT_ID); naming fork where the provider does not say is an error target target names matches the target's id and, for a matrix variant (cli-platform-linux-x86_64), the declared target it came from (cli); a name that is neither is a plan-time error listing the names platform os/arch[/abi] with the usual aliases the target's platform; a value without an ABI matches every ABI optimized true, false the target's build profile artifact logical artifact names (bin-oyzu, bin-oyzu-shim, as Outputs and the manifest name them, not file names) only on post_build and post_package hooks; a name the target does not build is a plan-time error listing its artifacts, except for a target that declares several platforms, where it may be built elsewhere (recorded as a note); a packaging-only name on post_build, which never sees it, is an error Every when key must match, and a list matches when any value does; one matching unless key excludes the task. A task without either always applies. Unknown keys, wrong value types, artifact on any other task, and conditions on a task that replaces a builder stage (put them on its pre_ or post_ hook) are configuration errors (CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE) when the configuration is read. Per-context declarations need no condition: a task under [context.release.tasks."cli:post_build"] already applies only in release. Conditions are not a security control. context is the context the build runs as. With only the generic CI hint (no vendor marker) a job can lower it (--context local), and policy has no hook setting: only tasks.* declares hooks. A context-gated hook selects behavior; it does not guarantee that a check ran. Use check levels and policy for checks that must run. Conditions are evaluated at plan time from frozen facts. A per-artifact hook is first checked on every key but artifact, so a hook excluded on its platform or profile is skipped before its artifacts matter. A task that does not apply is not scheduled, and whatever waited on it keeps its order. Plan says what runs and what was skipped, one task note per conditional task (a task that only uses placeholders gets no note; its resolved argv is in the records): task pre_build · skip · unless context = local post_build · run for bin-oyzu · unless artifact = bin-oyzu-shim The plan and manifest record each conditional task under the target extension oyzu.dev/task-conditions: the conditions as written, run or skip and why, each run's action id, artifact and resolved argv, and the artifacts a per-artifact hook skipped with the reason. oyzu build --plan shows the same Task: lines and taskConditions records; a hook that runs per artifact is once per matching artifact there, decided when preparation knows the artifacts.

A placeholder is {namespace.name}, replaced by plain text in one argv element at a time, and in the task's own env values. Nothing passes through a shell. Only {word.word…} is a placeholder. Everything else stays as written: {.Dir}, {a,b}, a lone brace and any doubled brace, so Go and Docker templates such as {{.Id}}, {{.Dir}} or {{json .}} pass through unchanged whether or not the task declares conditions. The one escape is a doubled name in a placeholder namespace (build, target, platform, artifact, env, tool): {{env.HOME}} writes the literal text {env.HOME}. Doubled braces in any other namespace are ordinary text, so Jinja, Mustache, Ansible and GitHub expressions such as {{item.name}}, msg={{ansible_facts.os}} and ${{github.sha}} pass through unchanged; a single-brace {item.name} is still PLACEHOLDER_UNKNOWN. An argv without a placeholder or that escape is never rewritten. A substituted value is never read again, and there are no functions, defaults or filters. Placeholder Value {build.context}, {build.provider}, {build.optimized}, {build.version} the context, comma-separated providers, true/false, the version this build gives the target (in oyzu run, the version the project declares; on the isolated path not available for builders that finalize versions after hooks, such as Node) {build.root} the build root, relative to the task's working directory {target.name}, {target.dir}, {target.builder} the task's target; dir relative to the working directory {platform.platform}, {platform.os}, {platform.arch}, {platform.abi} the target's platform (abi only when it names one) {artifact.path}, {artifact.name}, {artifact.kind}, {artifact.platform}, {artifact.os}, {artifact.arch} in a post_build/post_package hook: the artifact it runs for; path is the packaged file, relative to the working directory {env.NAME} a literal string declared in [env] of oyzu.toml; in argv only when it does not look sensitive (see below) {build.<target>.artifact.<field>} another target's artifact, only along a declared depends_on or materialize edge (a producer with several artifacts needs materialize.artifact) A hook that names the artifact fact or an {artifact.*} placeholder runs once per matching artifact, as actions cli:post_build[bin-oyzu] ordered one after another, each against the packaged file. post_build runs for the artifacts the build operation produced; post_package runs for every artifact the target packages into dist/. A target whose builder has no package stage in the build (such as a native Rust build, whose artifacts come from build) still runs a declared post_package hook: it follows every other action of the target, so it is never silently dropped. In both, {artifact.path} is the file or directory packaging copies to dist/. Just before a run, that file is copied to .oyzu/artifacts/<target>/<platform>/<file> in the target's private workspace, under its dist/ file name. A hook with no matching artifact is skipped with the reason. Every run executes even when an earlier one failed, so each artifact's result is reported; then any failure fails the build, like every hook. With no hook declared nothing runs. Oyzu never runs an artifact unless a project declares a hook that does. A per-artifact hook cannot declare outputs, which every run would share (CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE). Placeholders are resolved when the build is planned. These are errors, naming the task and argv element: an unknown name (PLACEHOLDER_UNKNOWN, with the valid names and the nearest one), an {env.NAME} not declared in [env] or an ambient variable (PLACEHOLDER_UNDECLARED), an [env] entry that is a secret reference, path list or table (PLACEHOLDER_UNAVAILABLE), another target's artifact without a declared edge (PLACEHOLDER_UNREACHABLE), and a value that does not exist where it is used, such as {artifact.path} outside a post_build/post_package hook (PLACEHOLDER_UNAVAILABLE). A run script cannot use placeholders, because it passes through a shell; use argv. argv is recorded unredacted in the plan, the manifest and the command log, while task env values are recorded as [REDACTED]. So an {env.NAME} whose name or value looks sensitive (names containing TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, API_KEY, CREDENTIAL, AUTH and the like, or a recognizable credential value) is refused in argv with PLACEHOLDER_SENSITIVE; pass it in the task's own env (TOKEN = "{env.API_TOKEN}") or through the tool's own credential mechanism. Other [env] values are recorded as written. Path values never expose the checkout path: they are relative to the task's working directory in its private workspace, in the platform's path form, and a path with no relative form is an error. The resolved argv is what the plan and manifest record and what the action cache keys bind, so identical builds on different machines resolve the same argv.

Path Conditions Placeholders oyzu build (native host) evaluated per target all, including per-artifact hooks oyzu build --isolated evaluated per target all but artifacts: a hook that reads artifacts is PLACEHOLDER_UNAVAILABLE there oyzu build --plan evaluated, per-artifact hooks pending rendered for the tasks it decides; {build.version} reads (resolved during the build), or is refused where the isolated build refuses it oyzu run evaluated with the host platform and the development profile a hook that reads artifacts is skipped (TASK_SKIPPED); a requested task that does not apply fails with TASK_NOT_APPLICABLE Known limits, with named follow-ups: {build.dist}, {artifact.digest} and {tool.NAME.*} are not available yet (PLACEHOLDER_UNAVAILABLE); placeholders in cwd are refused (a deliberate narrowing of the design); artifacts built by a captured image worker are not staged for hooks; per-artifact runs of one hook run one after another, not concurrently; when/unless on [context.*] setting tables is not implemented.

Captured builds inventory and freeze the admitted source once. Independent branches and aggregate execution use that inventory to materialize private, mutable target workspaces, instead of capturing the whole tree again for each branch. An existing planned source projection selects only its admitted entries; without a projection, the target still receives the full capture. There is no new option and no inferred narrowing of arbitrary task inputs. Final assembly of already completed branches does not materialize their workspaces again. Source selection applies case-sensitive in-tree .gitignore rules, including ancestor rules for a nested build root. Untracked nonignored files are included; tracked ignored files are excluded with SOURCE_TRACKED_IGNORED warnings when Git is available.
