Declare an ignored required path in the target's inputs to include it; this cannot admit Oyzu state, Git metadata or an opaque nested repository. Declaring a file permits traversal through its ignored parent directories, while unrelated ignored siblings remain excluded. Declaring a directory includes its ordinary descendants under the same mandatory state and repository boundaries. Global Git excludes and builder-specific ignore files do not define capture. The plan and manifest retain source.selection: effective rule bytes, the source prefix within its repository, authored inputs and encountered nested repository boundaries. This frozen selection lets consumers replay the same selection after relocation, including rules above a nested source root, without rereading mutable declarations or ignore rules. Host builds retain source.projections instead: each actual target capture's frozen rules and repository-relative target/input roots, plus the workspace prefix. Their source identity remains the existing aggregate of per-target digests. Replaying those projections selects current files under the recorded roots, so a newly added nonignored file changes identity while an unrelated sibling stays outside the target. A nested host replay requires its corresponding enclosing repository layout; metadata cannot authorize reads outside that boundary. Consumers must still compare the recaptured tree or aggregate digest with source.treeDigest; selection replay does not establish unchanged input bytes. The Windows host and Linux isolated Go artifact flows cover declared ignored inputs, ignored scratch data and changed-rule variants in the source qualification record. Native scanner replay and source-mismatch refusal have separate qualification evidence. These measured profiles do not establish support for every host or scanner. Materialization hashes each selected file while copying it and compares its size, digest and executable bit with the capture. Files are independent copies, never writable hard links to another target or the frozen source. Changed or missing captured entries, symlinks/reparse points, or copy failures abort materialization; resolve the filesystem problem and rerun the build for a fresh capture. Disposable target copies do not repeat capture's second hash pass or per-file sync. This is not a zero-copy implementation: selected bytes are still copied and verified per target, the full-copy fallback remains, and dependency preparation is still target-specific. Native host workspaces use their existing separate contract. No performance gain has yet been measured for this change; see verification status.

Docker preparation commands have fixed deadlines independent of action timeouts: Operation Deadline per command Image/platform inspection, daemon probes, tagging, worker control and volume operations 30 seconds Image pulls/exports, worker file copies and container tool restoration 30 minutes Failed restoration or running-worker forced removal 5 seconds These limits have no configuration override. Expiry fails the operation with an external-command deadline error and attempts to kill the local client; waiting for child output pipes cannot extend the deadline. Normal failed pulls and image operations preserve Docker's stderr in their error. Optional probes retain their existing fallback behavior. The limits apply per invocation, not to the whole preparation phase, and do not grant network access or supply missing images. Offline reuse still requires the previously provisioned inputs. Check daemon health, registry access and available disk space before retrying. Killing a Docker client does not prove daemon-side work stopped: failed tool restoration attempts a separate five-second removal, and cleanup is best effort. Inspect and remove leftover Oyzu containers after the daemon recovers. Build forced cancellation has a separate shared cleanup budget. These changes await runtime qualification on all three hosts.

Task prerequisites are ordering relationships. They do not transfer generated files between private target workspaces. Use declared artifacts and materialize when a consumer needs producer bytes; see directory artifacts. A prerequisite cannot read another target's mutated execution tree just because its task completed. Each action records its owner, tool identity, dependencies, environment and report obligations in dist/plan.json. The manifest records actual action results, retained reports and versioned artifacts. Bundle storage governs locking, replacement, history and recovery after finalization errors. Packaging waits for every selected task owned by that target, including custom tasks required by another target. A failed prerequisite, post-hook or required report blocks dependent actions and packaging; available evidence remains in the failure bundle. Independent targets may still finish successfully. oyzu inspect dist verifies recorded content integrity, not release eligibility. The executable plan also retains symbolic action/output inputs and native-unit attribution. A produced-input reference requires its producer; ordinary sequencing between selected stages does not turn skipped checks back on. Named outputs are declarations, not proof that bytes exist or that an action's filesystem effects are fully known. Collection and report validation still gate successful outputs; partial or failed results cannot satisfy downstream inputs. Result-cache publication retains its target-level success requirement. These internal records add no configuration option or broader platform/isolation guarantee. build.jobs bounds both independent dependency preparation and ready actions, using the smallest configured ceiling among the invocation and selected targets. Its default follows available CPU parallelism. Preparation uses private per-target destinations and container identities, and returns results in target order for planning. Builders declare preparation memory reservations, and worker-memory admission bounds every parallel phase by what fits in three quarters of the container engine's memory (docker info MemTotal), including default 2 GiB workers: a 16 GiB engine runs at most six at once, whatever the CPU count. Dependency-acquisition workers (brokered fetches, image capture, Python and Rust preparation) reserve 4 GiB each and may run for 30 minutes, since 2 GiB and 10 minutes failed mid-size npm, Python, Cargo, Maven and Gradle projects (#167). Measured with parallel fetches on the #160 corpus, the largest worker (uptime-kuma, 1,304 locked npm packages) peaked at 2.4 GiB of cgroup memory, about 1.0 GiB of it resident and the rest page cache and /tmp, and the slowest preparation took 2.2 minutes, so both limits keep at least 1.6 times headroom; see the throughput record. Without an engine to ask (the native host path), build.jobs alone applies. Each long-running isolated action receives an even share of the container engine's CPUs among the actions that may run at once, capped at one CPU per 512 MiB of its memory reservation and never below two. A single 8 GiB cross build on a 24-CPU engine therefore gets 16 CPUs instead of a fixed two; the chosen share is printed in the execution context. Cargo sizes itself from that allowance, so Oyzu no longer sets CARGO_BUILD_JOBS.

oyzu build --frozen replays the external-plugin selections pinned in oyzu.lock and fails with PLUGIN_LOCK_MISSING instead of resolving or rewriting the lock; --store selects the store that holds installed plugin packages. See plugin packages.

Set the ceiling for one invocation without editing configuration files. Remote and CI runners use this to fit a build inside a fixed memory allowance: oyzu build --jobs 4 # or -j 4 OYZU_BUILD_JOBS=4 oyzu build Precedence is --jobs, then OYZU_BUILD_JOBS, then build.jobs from configuration files and profiles, then the CPU-count default. Both invocation inputs replace every root and target build.jobs value, so the whole build shares one ceiling. Administrative constraints on build.jobs still apply on top, and worker-memory admission can still lower concurrency. --jobs accepts 1–65535; an OYZU_BUILD_JOBS value outside that range, or not an integer, fails before any work with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE, and an empty value is ignored. The build prints the resulting Shared budget or Preparation worker count in its context, the plan records it in oyzu.dev/execution.jobs, and oyzu config explain build.jobs names OYZU_BUILD_JOBS as the origin when the variable set it. oyzu run has no --jobs flag because development tasks already run one at a time; the ceiling does not limit threads a native compiler starts inside one action. Execution refills free slots as individual actions finish and their reports/artifacts are validated, without waiting for unrelated slower actions. The executor never runs two actions concurrently in one target's mutable workspace: the check stages of one target (test, lint, format-check) may overlap only when each runs confined in its own private view, and their changes reach the workspace in plan order (see checks that run at once). A failed check no longer blocks the next check; it still blocks packaging. When an action fails because its worker ran out of memory (exit 137, or ENOMEM, cannot allocate memory or a heap-limit message at the end of its output), the build adds the diagnostic worker-out-of-memory, which names the action, its memory reservation and how many actions could run at once, and points at build.jobs and the engine's memory setting. The diagnostic also records the reservation as memoryMiB and that concurrency as jobs. A dependency preparation worker that fails the same way (phase prepare) gets the same diagnostic, naming <target>:preflight and its 4 GiB reservation. Detection ignores case, so Go's cannot allocate memory counts. On Windows the message adds that Docker Desktop's file sharing can fail a large write into the build directory with the same error while the worker is well under its limit (#132), and that building from a checkout inside WSL avoids it. Oyzu does not retry it. On Windows, an action whose output ends with an I/O error (input/output error, or (I/O error) as hadolint prints it) gets the diagnostic worker-file-sharing-error: in #132 Docker Desktop's file sharing failed reads of Dockerfiles that were fine on disk. It names the action and suggests building from a checkout inside WSL. Other platforms do not get it, because there an I/O error usually means a disk fault. Failed prerequisites block dependent actions. Independent targets can now prepare, freeze their branch plan, execute and package while other targets are preparing. Preparation and execution share the configured job ceiling and 75% of worker memory; a ready branch can wait when its reservation would exceed that budget. Each branch plan is saved before execution in plans/, retained as bundle evidence and checked against the final aggregate plan by oyzu inspect. Cross-target dependencies, materialization, container composition and shared root tasks retain aggregate planning after preparation. Equivalent locked Rust compiler verification and archive extraction are shared within the build. Native target metadata and dependency preparation remain separate. Native compilers may also have their own thread limits. Execution uses captured offline inputs; task dependencies do not grant network, credential or host access. Development oyzu run uses the host environment. Integrated oyzu run test profiles produce test-only bundles that disclose host execution; they do not claim captured-build isolation.

Rust checks cover requested-target validation, transitive selection, root-task semantics, selection integrity, cross-target ownership, required report paths, post-hook collection boundaries, local sibling order and cycles visible only after combining build stages. The core captured-build suite exercises a shared custom prerequisite with two consumers, private workspace effects, successful snapshot packages and failure propagation from the producer post-hook. It also exercises explicit selection with an unprovisioned unrelated toolchain, deduplicated requests, exclusions and selected materialization producers. It tests local prerequisites while compilation waits on a foreign task, and a Node consumer requesting a Go-owned task through the materialization scenario. Its checks execute the compiled CLI with real native tools; suite registration alone is not acceptance. See implementation status for revision-specific local and CI evidence. This adds qualified task composition to the existing builders. It does not complete generated-output inference, task caching, matrix expansion, interactive services or tool installation. Use the authored scenarios and their acceptance criteria to track those remaining capabilities.

Host tasks receive the selected project's pinned tool directories on PATH, plus tool environment values such as GOROOT and JAVA_HOME. For example, argv = ["bash", "scripts/test-database.sh"] can invoke the pinned go by name. The tools must already be installed for the matching lock; oyzu run does not install them. Use oyzu install first (or install --frozen --offline with the required cached tools). Bare bash and sh use the shared host-shell lookup. On Windows, Oyzu skips System32 and WindowsApps WSL launchers, looks for a native shell on PATH, then derives Git for Windows' shell from git.exe on PATH, then checks standard Git install locations. A missing native shell fails with the search locations and an explicit-path remedy; it never silently enters WSL. Git Bash/MSYS converts the ordinary Windows PATH at startup, so pinned Windows tools remain available to the script without an Oyzu PATH conversion layer. Linux/macOS keep normal PATH lookup. Shell-string tasks with shell = "bash" or shell = "sh" use the same lookup. The default shell remains PowerShell on Windows and sh on Linux/macOS. Explicit shell executable paths remain caller-selected. This is host development execution; isolated builds use their executor's shell and tool environment.

oyzu run <task> reports configuration/discovery, selected task, pinned tool environment verification, and native execution as work begins. Preparation that has no native output emits a ten-second activity update; execution reports a heartbeat while its child is running. Required tool verification still completes before task launch and is not bypassed to shorten startup. Local tasks inherit stdin, including redirected pipes, in both text and JSON modes. Text-mode tasks without a bundle inherit stdout/stderr directly. Tasks recording a bundle (integrated oyzu run test, including its prerequisites and hooks) instead tee stdout/stderr to the caller's streams and retain the full output in the bundle's numbered dist/logs/*.stdout and *.stderr files. Output is forwarded without waiting for a newline and is not replayed on completion. -q suppresses routine Oyzu progress while preserving child output and logs. For a bundled task that needs real stdout/stderr terminal descriptors, set interactive = true: text mode then inherits those streams directly. Oyzu does not allocate a pseudo-terminal, so this interactive output cannot also be captured; that task's bundle stdout/stderr logs are empty. Ordinary tee capture preserves terminal stdin and live output, but the child's stdout/stderr are pipes, which can change native buffering, color and terminal detection. Required report files are collected in either mode. Use JSON capture when retained output matters more than terminal-dependent interaction. JSON mode keeps stdout as one final result with captured task output and streams structured diagnostics on stderr. Its child stdout/stderr are not terminals, so prompts on those streams are only visible after completion; use text mode for interactive prompting. Tasks with an empty-stdout validation contract also retain captured output so the check remains enforceable. Captured builds and internal probes continue to receive null stdin. PowerShell shell tasks need interactive = true to omit -NonInteractive; an explicit argv is passed as authored. Inherited native streams retain the child's own color and control-byte behavior, including its handling of NO_COLOR. For example, with a discoverable project and a provisioned POSIX shell, a task argv = ["sh", "-c", "read x; printf 'got:%s\\n' \"$x\""] can consume printf 'hello\n' | oyzu run ask -q and print got:hello. On Windows, use a provisioned native command or PowerShell task appropriate to that shell. An EOF or native input error remains the child's result; Oyzu does not synthesize input or restart the task. This stream change does not add remote terminal forwarding or service supervision. Host process completion wakes the coordinator through a waiter immediately; there is no mandatory 50 ms completion delay. The 50 ms maintenance wakeup remains for captured log following and cooperative cancellation, and heartbeats remain ten seconds. Wait/launch failures remain execution errors and trigger best-effort termination where a child exists. No task speedup numbers are available yet. Regressions cover piped input, live tee output, successful and failed bundle logs, the interactive capture exception and Unix terminal descriptors. See verification status and Windows lifecycle qualification for the platforms and stream scenarios actually checked. Native tools can still buffer their own output; Oyzu's heartbeat is not a claim that a silent tool is making measurable progress. Exit codes and task arguments remain unchanged by presentation.

Each local oyzu run <task> command, prerequisite and hook on Windows runs in a private, noninheritable kill-on-close job. The native task starts suspended, enters its job, then resumes its verified primary thread. Descendants inherit the job; breakaway is not enabled. Hard-killing the Oyzu controller closes its job handles and stops its task trees, releasing descendant-held ports. Ordinary task completion also terminates remaining descendants before joining output pipes. Tasks must not leave background services running after their command returns; run a service in the foreground for the intended lifetime. This applies to terminal, tee and JSON-captured local tasks. Native stdin, argument/batch handling, exit codes, console membership and Ctrl-C broadcast remain unchanged. The controller is not assigned to its own task job, and existing enclosing jobs remain in force. The job provides process lifetime containment, not filesystem/network isolation or permission to execute. Containment uses local OS APIs and needs no account or network access. Captured build processes, metadata probes and remote tasks retain their separate execution contracts; this repair does not change Unix behavior. Job creation/assignment and primary-thread lookup/resume failures abort launch and kill/reap the owned suspended child. Missing or multiple primary threads fail explicitly; there is no uncontained fallback. TASK_JOB_* and TASK_PRIMARY_THREAD_* diagnostics retain the launch failure details. An incompatible enclosing job or denied OS handle access must be corrected before retrying. Normal cleanup confirms job-wide exit within ten seconds; a failure is reported as TASK_JOB_CLEANUP_FAILED rather than successful completion. An externally killed controller cannot report cleanup evidence itself. The disposable compiled-CLI proof covers hard kill, normal exit and Ctrl-C in text and JSON modes, checking task/child/grandchild exits and loopback port release. See Windows lifecycle qualification for platform, commands and remaining verification limits.

Native builds use the shared logical task planner and bounded dependency scheduler. Independent targets may overlap up to build.jobs; declarations such as depends_on: [api] under builds.web delay web until API's selected stages finish successfully. Failed dependencies block consumers, not unrelated targets. Same-target stages and hooks remain ordered because they share native files. --plan exposes the logical edges without installation or execution; native preparation subsequently resolves exact commands and report contracts into the executable evidence plan. Artifact transfer through materialize is also supported in private host target workspaces, after producer actions and report obligations succeed. Ordering alone still transfers no files.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/build-verification.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The repository's captured-build harness executes the compiled Oyzu CLI against native project fixtures, inspects actual artifacts and reports, and checks expected failures. It covers the implemented profiles recorded in implementation status. A passing harness run does not establish acceptance of every case in the 58 authored design-contract scenarios.

Use Python 3.12 with tooling/design-requirements.txt installed to inspect the current groups without running builds: python tooling/test-build-scenarios.py --list-suites python tooling/check-build-suites.py The inventory check verifies unique registrations, conventional acceptance entry points, matching CI matrix coverage, compilation dependency and the aggregate gate. It neither provisions tools nor verifies native product behavior. The focused Node check-selection group covers fast omitted checks, full native zero-test JUnit, required tests in fast mode, missing-required-report failure and retained human/JSON selection agreement. Run it with --suite node --only check-selection. Its acceptance remains pending; the previously qualified 84-observation build-explanations group is unchanged. See the selection qualification. For real builds, supply a compiled CLI and provision the required toolchains. Captured-build acceptance currently runs on Linux with Docker and the toolchain definitions in tooling/images/. Node/core/Docker/dependencies checks also use host Node 22/npm; Java native adapter checks require host JDK 17. The provisioning script uses network access to obtain test tooling and images. Core/Go/Docker/Python/dependencies suites install the repository's explicit BuildKit AppArmor profile using sudo apparmor_parser; use a suitable Linux test machine. This is acceptance-fixture setup, not Oyzu's tool-installation feature or an implicit network fallback during a product build. From the repository on that Linux test machine: cargo build --locked bash tooling/build-scenario-tools.sh provision docker export OYZU_BUILDKIT_APPARMOR_PROFILE=oyzu-buildkit .ci-python/bin/python tooling/test-build-scenarios.py --suite docker --cli target/debug/oyzu --evidence-dir docker-evidence For suites with standalone native adapter probes, bash tooling/build-scenario-tools.sh native <suite> runs those additional checks. The Helm CLI probe expects the compiled binary at cli/oyzu, matching CI; copy your binary there before running that probe. The ordinary captured-build harness accepts any explicit --cli path. Native probes supplement captured builds; they cannot substitute for them. The Helm native phase also runs tooling/test-helm-direct.py against the downloaded CLI and provisioned Helm/plugin. This verifies the separate host oyzu run test to JUnit/manifest/inspection flow, including application and root library charts, unittest suites and hooks. It does not replace captured chart packaging checks. See Helm direct-report behavior and test-only bundles. Omitting --suite selects all and retains the original full-run ordering. Provisioning/native-probe scripts also accept all. A single-suite selection uses the same checks and assertions as the full run. Unknown suites and missing --cli arguments fail rather than selecting a fallback. When tools were provisioned into an explicit verified store, pass --store <absolute-tool-store> to tooling/test-build-scenarios.py. The harness forwards it to compiled-CLI build and exec invocations, including raw and background builds, so the independent consumer uses the same tool selection. It does not add the option to inspect or child arguments after --, and an explicit invocation-specific store takes precedence. The store must already exist; the harness does not provision it. Without this option the CLI retains its ordinary default-store behavior. Managed syntax and registration checks pass. The installer companion and native node-gyp producer/consumer exercised explicit store propagation; this does not qualify the full scenario catalog. The installer-recipe checks explicitly select each temporary fixture with --root <fixture> for builds and the independent consumer's exec. This bounds workspace discovery when the host's temporary directory has an ancestor Oyzu configuration. It preserves that configuration and the CLI's normal root-selection rules rather than scanning unrelated temporary projects. For a selected check that needs a distinct provisioned image, repeat harness --image <manager>=<image> as needed. These options reach only child build commands; a scenario's explicit image options take precedence. The harness does not pull, build or retag images. The node-gyp-recipe check needs an explicit Linux/amd64 npm image with compatible Python, make/compiler and the normal Node quality tools; it uses that image for both compilation and independent captured consumption. The default npm image does not provide that compiler environment. The bounded Linux/amd64 producer/consumer check passed with the explicitly provisioned task image: both native seven-action builds, three tests each, wrapper coverage, inspected archives and independent addon consumption. See installer recipe qualification for the exact image, artifact identities and platform limits. Maven and Gradle delivered-JAR consumers use the image digest recorded in that build's plan. Supply the actual candidate with --cli and retain its worker and component identities alongside the evidence. Their qualification summaries retain the actual consumer commands, exit codes and output streams. The maven check runs the nine reactor/report scenarios. The separate maven-managed-coverage check runs the mixed native-managed/fallback coverage reactor with the same full captured execution and artifact/report assertions. Run both named checks for the Maven scope; the complete java suite includes each once. Suite Included checks and toolchain dependencies core First the authored five-target mixed-monorepo build, then concurrency, explicit target selection and dependency closure, cross-target task prerequisites and hook failures, Go-to-Node materialization, baseline Node/Go/Python artifacts, repeatability and isolation; includes npm, Go, pip, uv, Poetry, Helm and Docker tooling node First the authored generated-source and test-owned service flows, then native overrides, dependency/preflight failures, npm/pnpm/Yarn, workspaces, lint/format, Jest, Vitest and Mocha python Test/report defaults, application archives, legacy packaging, quality selection and captured preparation inputs (dependency-group includes, editable project references, dynamic versions); includes native Python adapter probes go Libraries, workspace/cgo, registry modules and selected multi-binary image assembly; includes Docker tooling rust Native Cargo application/workspace/registry, packaging, tests and quality profiles java Ant, Maven and Gradle captured builds plus native metadata/reporting adapter probes dotnet .NET SDK selection, captured NuGet restore with lock replay and audit, offline build/test/pack, failing tests and SDK mismatch; includes the .NET SDK toolchain image helm Chart packaging, rendering, native suites and subchart variants plus native adapter probes dependencies Offline Docker dependency contexts for pip, uv, Poetry, npm, Yarn Classic, pnpm, Go and Cargo; includes their consumer runtimes and BuildKit, plus native store/export probes docker Dockerfile images, provisioned inputs, aliases, ARG defaults, quality, Go artifact assembly and Vite directory materialization; includes Go and npm/Node quality tooling The catalog is owned by tooling/test-build-scenarios.py; native assertions remain in tooling/build_scenarios/. New conventional verify(root, base, invoke, validate, source_files, verified) entry points must be registered. Keep helper assertions with their owning group and update provisioning when a composition check needs another builder's toolchain. No production builder rules belong in this harness. --suite go --only go-unavailable-version --cli <compiled-path> exercises the real preflight refusal for an explicit unpublished Go version. It requires ordinary catalog access but no working Docker daemon: selection must fail before worker startup. JSON and human output must name the tool and request, with no native actions, artifacts, reports or published lock and unchanged inputs. This negative does not qualify an isolated Go product or replace the other Go cases. Registrations that assert test, lint, format or coverage results must use the existing full_checks wrapper to select --full on their builds. Captured-only checks also use captured_checks (or their existing isolated-invocation wrapper) to select --isolated. These select separate behavior: isolation chooses the executor, while full checks choose the stages. Running with --isolated alone retains the fast build default. Neither wrapper provisions prerequisites or establishes that a native scenario passed. The core suite starts with mixed-monorepo, the first complete EX-030 demonstration. It copies the checked-in project without changing its five-target build.yaml, lists grouped tasks and invokes one oyzu build. Assertions require successful build/test/lint/read-only-format stages for every target, Python wheel/sdist/application outputs, a Node application directory, a Go binary embedded byte-for-byte in the OCI image, and a versioned Helm chart plus rendered deployment. The manifest must retain JUnit for every target and application coverage for Python/Node/Go, and oyzu inspect dist must verify the bundle. Provision core as above with Helm and Docker included. The real Linux build succeeded in job 110956041959 at aa1fa40, producing eight artifacts and all five targets' required stages/reports. That job then failed a harness assertion that incorrectly expected the Go producer's unexpanded target name. The corrected check resolves the actual Go target by its builder, source path and propagated Linux/amd64 platform. All corrected output assertions, schema/digest checks and the compiled CLI's inspect dist passed against the original retained bundle (artifact 11242079660). This establishes the first functional build and artifact proof; the original CI job remains failed and the corrected full suite still needs a rerun. EX-030's first proof is separate from its advanced negative cases, broader host qualification and proposed image-to-chart value binding. The current depends_on: [image] orders the chart after image packaging; it does not replace native chart values with the image digest. The check preserves that distinction and does not mark the entire authored scenario complete. The node suite also registers affected-targets against EX-033's declared-target variation. It executes no-change, API-only and shared-input builds, requires the correct dependency/consumer closure, snapshot packages, required stages/reports and inspected bundles. Captured acceptance remains pending. The separate tooling/test-affected-selection.py --cli <path> probe verifies no-change planning/building and inspection in a nested Git project without toolchain resolution; CI runs it after compiling the CLI on all three hosts. Windows passed locally; new cross-host results remain pending. These checks do not claim action-cache reuse: the harness runs every other build with --no-cache so native acceptance keeps executing real builds, and the node suite's action-cache and shared-source checks explicitly opt in to reuse (see local action cache). Run it alone with --only action-cache. Two bounded shared-source follow-ups are independently selectable with --only shared-source-denied-read and --only shared-source-external-input. The first requires a source file that succeeds in direct native execution, a recorded action view that excludes it, and the structured confined-read violation with reuse enabled and disabled. Unix views deny the read by hiding the file; this does not establish an operating-system EACCES enforcement mechanism. The second changes a real host file outside the captured source, verifies both values with the selected native Node, and requires captured execution and an independent fresh build to refuse the unavailable input without publishing an API artifact. Its computed read must retain the recorded uncertain boundary. Both use the existing numbered bundles, schema/digest validation and task-owned stores. Both finite groups passed with the qualified ac955ad28554 Linux CLI: external-input at harness e29a8fdd, and view refusal at corrected cd5fa13a. The original denial attempt lacked structured evidence and remains failed; its fixture correction retains all assertions. The earlier thirteen-build shared-source proof and exact limits are recorded separately in the qualification record. The node suite starts with two additional authored flows. generated-source runs EX-031 without a build file, requires a single native build stage, verifies both consumer tests and the generated module inside the snapshot package, then changes the schema and requires both tests to fail after regeneration. This proves the native generation-to-package flow when it passes; separate generator action identities and selective cache invalidation remain unfinished. service-test runs EX-044's real test-owned loopback HTTP server within the isolated test action, requires JUnit/coverage and the snapshot package, then closes the server before the request and requires a failed service test with no published artifacts. This is loopback within one action, not separately provisioned services or external network access. Service lifecycle descriptors and external-service reproducibility classification remain unfinished. Both new groups have pending captured Linux results. Their checked-in sources pass the compiled Windows CLI's native build/test/lint/format-check tasks with provisioned Node 24.14.1 and the shared quality toolchain. Linux CI provisions Node 22 and runs these groups after CLI compilation. Source formatting changes make the existing authored programs satisfy their native default formatter; neither project requires new Oyzu configuration. The dependencies suite separates package-store integration from the Docker platform-matrix checks. Run it explicitly when changing providers: bash tooling/build-scenario-tools.sh provision dependencies bash tooling/build-scenario-tools.sh native dependencies export OYZU_BUILDKIT_APPARMOR_PROFILE=oyzu-buildkit .ci-python/bin/python tooling/test-build-scenarios.py --suite dependencies --cli target/debug/oyzu --evidence-dir dependency-evidence Previously these five context groups ran inside --suite docker; that selection now runs image/platform and Node-application groups only. Use both suites or all to retain the previous coverage. The default all order and all existing assertions remain unchanged. Dependencies use native Linux consumer images and do not need the Docker suite's ARM emulation. Both suites remain required by the aggregate CI gate; this split lets package failures surface without first executing the long platform matrix. The Node build-explanations group reuses the conventional shared-source fixture below for invocation-bound explanation and history acceptance: python tooling/test-build-scenarios.py --cli <compiled-oyzu> --suite node --only build-explanations --evidence-dir <new-evidence-directory>. It preserves normal bundle rollover, compares human build --explain and history with recorded JSON, inspects the selected invocation after source/configuration changes and cache clearing, and checks real fresh/reused test evidence and failure propagation. It uses provisioned Node/Docker tools, including the native formatter; it installs no replacement quality commands. Linux-host confined views are required for the initial file-level/mixed-action acceptance. Windows runs retain independent observations but fail that required capability obligation. See the explanation qualification record. The separate Node shared-source group generates a conventional first-party repository with API/web imports of shared/greeting.mjs and an unrelated package, without authored dependency/input edges or a root workspace orchestrator. Run python tooling/test-build-scenarios.py --cli <compiled-oyzu> --suite node --only shared-source --evidence-dir <new-evidence-directory> with the same provisioned Node images. On Windows retain the compiled oyzu-shim.exe beside the CLI, because native package checks use locked oyzu exec. It explicitly seeds an isolated eligible cache, checks unchanged reuse and shared-source mutation, then builds the edited source in a separate workspace/output/result store with reuse disabled. It checks extracted native package imports and immutable tool/dependency identity, with separate correctness and efficiency verdicts. Nested invocation, API-only edits, literal optional-file creation/removal and required-source deletion are included. The group is registered but full native acceptance remains pending. The measured Windows-host/Linux-Docker baseline refreshes both consumers and agrees with an independent fresh build, but fails unrelated reuse on shared edits. See the qualification record for actual commands, platform limits and unproved variations. The existing action-cache group remains the separate declared-dependency regression.

The workflow builds the CLI on Linux, macOS and Windows first. Linux captured-build jobs download that run's compiled Linux binary, then run the ten suites with up to four concurrent jobs. Each job provisions only its required toolchain families. fail-fast: false allows unrelated suites to finish after one fails. The Captured build suite acceptance gate fails if any suite fails, is cancelled or is skipped. Three-host CLI/task checks and the separate isolated-worker job remain distinct checks with their own scope. Explicit Java quality, Hadolint and yamlfmt provisioning shares tooling/provisioning.py. Downloads make at most three attempts for transient transport failures and HTTP 429/500/502/503/504, with one- and two-second backoff, a 60-second socket timeout per attempt and the existing asset-specific byte limits. A truncated response with a declared content length is discarded before retrying. Authorization/not-found errors and oversized responses are terminal. Pinned SHA-256 verification remains mandatory in each owning provisioner; digest mismatches are not retried or accepted. The timeout is per socket operation, not a total invocation deadline. This supports CI/toolchain setup only and adds no product tool-installation or build-time internet access. The three-host task job exercises loopback retry/size/failure tests before provisioning. CI uploads each suite under oyzu-build-evidence-<suite> (including oyzu-build-evidence-dependencies for package contexts), replacing the former single oyzu-build-evidence artifact name. Evidence directories contain numbered build invocations, their available dist/ bundles, and a summary.json identifying the suite, selected groups, completed groups, verified assertions and success/failure. An exception preserves a failed summary with the active group; previously completed checks do not make an incomplete suite successful. Process termination can prevent final summary writing. The harness does not turn missing reports into passing evidence. An evidence directory must be new; choose a fresh path for reruns. Inspect the failing invocation and native logs, correct the underlying behavior or fixture, and rerun the affected suite. Do not weaken assertions or mark authored scenarios complete based on inventory checks. Retained artifacts contain build logs and sample outputs and are kept for 14 days in CI; fixtures must not contain real credentials. Local verification of this suite split includes inventory and shell/Python syntax checks, an AST comparison preserving existing baseline assertions and embedded source strings, retained provisioning/probe command checks, and failed-summary behavior after a missing executable. New Linux suite execution remains subject to the revision-specific CI evidence in implementation status. Windows/macOS execution of the full captured-build matrix and the remaining authored cases are still required work. The Docker captured suite now provisions ARM emulation explicitly through a pinned setup-qemu action before building Go and Node ARM images. The provisioner checks actual runtime architecture without network access. This is CI infrastructure, not product tool/emulator installation. Local execution of this suite needs equivalent pre-provisioned execution support. The two producer platform-matrix invocations allow up to 2,400 seconds in the test harness for emulated compilation; product acquisition/action limits remain unchanged. See toolchain platform verification. The isolated worker job additionally compiles and explicitly runs the Rust generated-definition conformance test after provisioning. It checks real reproducible OCI export, payload bytes/ownership and launch metadata with no source Dockerfile; it does not establish application packaging or smoke-test support. Its logs and archives are retained under worker-recipe-evidence in the worker artifact, alongside worker-evidence. Ordinary Rust tests compile this check but skip its Docker execution. The Python suite additionally provisions the shared BuildKit/converter image and runs the authored Python container variant. It checks exact archive materialization, default and custom provisioned bases, numeric user/workdir/argv overrides, OCI metadata and versioning, native reports/quality, repeated identities, failure blocking and incompatible runtime rejection. This group passed in Python job 110898263768 at 69b4d04. Worker-only conformance does not substitute for this application integration. The isolated worker job additionally runs the internal dependency-context conformance test after base provisioning. It exercises real RUN/COPY consumption, mount write rejection, exact subtree bytes, sibling exclusion and repeatable output. Evidence stays under worker-recipe-evidence/dependency-context. This is executor transport qualification; custom package-manager acquisition remains a separate acceptance requirement. The dependencies suite's docker-dependencies group checks public pip preparation in a provisioned Python 3.13 base. Separate docker-uv-context and docker-poetry-context groups check native lock export and offline installation in provisioned Python 3.12 manager images. Together they check real imports during RUN, package/runtime evidence, OCI/JUnit/quality output, repeated identities, implicit task discovery, explicit selection after ambiguity, rejected lock hashes, excluded development groups, and rejection of an attempted build-time internet download. They run after CLI compilation. The results and limitations below distinguish successful individual builds from full group acceptance; these checks do not claim private connector, secret-canary, other-ecosystem or full EX-058 acceptance. tooling/test-python-context.py --manager uv (or poetry) probes native runtime-only export, unchanged/stale locks, offline hashed installation/import and rejection of modified wheels. Provision Python 3.12, the corresponding manager and the Poetry export plugin before invoking it. Native fixture lock creation and wheel download use public network access; the export and install operations are offline. The dependencies suite runs these probes in its provisioned manager images before captured builds. They also passed independently on Windows with provisioned uv 0.12.21 and Poetry 2.5.1, but do not by themselves establish broker or container isolation. The dependencies suite also registers docker-npm-context, using the already-provisioned npm 11.11.0/Node 22 image. It requires locked broker acquisition in the consumer runtime, offline cache seeding and npm ci, exact runtime files with development packages omitted, captured package/runtime evidence, OCI/JUnit/quality, repeatability and rejected lock integrity. Native CI results are pending. tooling/test-npm-context.py separately exercises the acquisition adapter and tarball-only native replay; it passed on Windows with npm 11.11.0/Node 24.14.1. Dependencies-suite provisioning installs the pinned fixture npm from tooling/images/node-npm for this host probe, and the native phase selects that entrypoint explicitly. Fixture lock creation/downloads use the public registry; captured replay uses new empty caches offline. Neither fixture provisioning nor the spool test transport establishes private connector or full EX-058 acceptance. docker-yarn-context additionally provisions the Yarn Classic 1.22.22/Node 22 toolchain and requires native locked mirror preparation, offline installation/import, exact scoped/transitive image files, lifecycle suppression, snapshot OCI/JUnit/quality, repeatability and altered-lock rejection. Its native CI result is pending. The suite's native phase runs tooling/test-node-registry-acquisition.py --manager yarn --context --native-cli tooling/images/node-yarn/node_modules/yarn/bin/yarn.js, both normally and with --resolutions. Those probes passed on Windows with Node 24.14.1, including fresh-cache direct Yarn consumption, unchanged mirror/locks, native tests and corrupted mirror rejection. Existing acquisition/replay tests remain enabled; --context is a test harness option, not public CLI configuration. The first pip-context attempt at revision 5c8eaf6 failed in the harness before its image build: run list returned human-readable output to a JSON-only invocation helper. The pip and npm checks now explicitly request run list --json, matching existing suite conventions; both corrected task-list calls passed against the compiled CLI on Windows. The original failed job remains 110912572149. It verified preceding Docker groups but provides no package-context build acceptance. docker-pnpm-context provisions pnpm 10.11.0/Node 22 and requires ordinary and patched projects to consume the exported native store offline, retain exact image/patch evidence, remove temporary store files, produce snapshot OCI/JUnit/quality, repeat identities and reject altered lock integrity. Native CI results are pending. The dependencies native phase runs the registry probe with --manager pnpm --context, both normally and with --patches. Windows pnpm 10.11.0/Node 24.14.1 probes passed native store export/replay, empty graphs, tests after store removal, unchanged locks, stable repeated exports and corrupted-store rejection. Provisioning remains separate from Oyzu tool installation, and these host probes do not establish Docker isolation. node --test tooling/test-pnpm-store.mjs exercises the export boundary's rejection of unqualified versions, configuration files, side-effect indices and directory links/junctions into unrelated state. These three checks passed on Windows and run in the dependencies suite's native phase. They complement native pnpm replay rather than simulating package resolution or proving container output. docker-go-context uses the already-provisioned standard Go 1.24 image, without the modulezip adapter. It requires captured public module acquisition, read-only native cache compilation and execution in the build stage, an exact binary-only scratch image, versioned OCI/JUnit/quality, repeatability and rejected checksum before actions. Native container results are pending. The existing three-host tooling/test-go-metadata.py probe now additionally copies only the prepared module subtree into two independent stores, compiles/runs offline with fresh compiler caches, and checks identical binaries and unchanged source/store bytes. That extended probe passed on Windows with Go 1.24.13; it does not by itself establish a read-only container mount or final-image startup. docker-rust-context additionally provisions standard Rust 1.94.0 and Debian bookworm slim images. It requires actual native registry preparation without nextest/llvm-cov, unchanged native workspace versions, offline compilation and execution in the build stage, runtime-only image output, versioned OCI/JUnit/quality, repeatability and checksum rejection before actions. Its native container result remains pending. The Rust acquisition test, run during CLI verification on each host, now also compiles/runs against two detached registry copies with fresh native homes and checks unchanged locks/store bytes; that probe passed on Windows with Rust 1.94.0. It does not replace the captured-build check or claim final-container startup. The a653ea8 dependency job 110942213239 completed with failure after passing the pip context checks. Its two successful uv image builds had equal plan digests but different OCI digests. Inspection of the retained images found only uv_cache.json and its RECORD hash changed: native uv recorded a varying input-wheel modification timestamp. Original evidence remains retained under artifact 11240339977; this is not a successful dependency-suite run, and later groups were not reached. The executor now normalizes its private input copies before native execution. Its Rust test varies input times and verifies fixed file/directory times, unchanged content identity and unchanged originals, including a read-only Windows file. The Linux worker conformance test additionally records source/package/directory mtimes observed inside RUN and requires the fixed epoch plus repeated OCI identities after source times change. test-python-context.py --manager uv now supplements its existing pip replay checks with two real native uv installs against fixed-time copied stores; it checks equal installed bytes and retained native cache metadata. The Windows uv 0.12.21 probe passed. These host checks do not replace the pending corrected container build.

Captured-build jobs record native adapter conformance and end-to-end snapshot builds as separate step outcomes. When provisioning and inventory succeed, the compiled-CLI build step still runs after an earlier native conformance failure. The failed step remains failed, the job and aggregate gate remain red, and retained bundles show which actual build flows succeeded or failed. No assertion is disabled and no failure is converted to acceptance. This prevents a protocol/reproducibility check from hiding the functional result needed to guide implementation. Failed provisioning, invalid inventory or cancellation still prevent that dependent build step. Within a captured suite, each registered group runs independently. A failed group records its name, error and traceback in summary.json under failedChecks; subsequent groups still run. completedChecks contains only groups that returned successfully, and any group failure makes the command exit nonzero and the suite status failed. Exceptions within a group still stop that group's dependent steps, and interruption still stops the runner. Fixture directories remain owned by each group. This preserves failures while obtaining evidence for unrelated functional paths. Host task jobs also run tooling/test-node-framework-direct.py after CLI compilation and explicit native fixture provisioning. It proves implicit and npm-scripted Jest, Vitest and Mocha execution through test-only report bundles and inspection, including lifecycle/hooks and real failed assertions. Refer to direct test prerequisites for versions and current limits. The same host CI step runs tooling/test-npm-workspace-direct.py against EX-020 to check per-package direct JUnit/coverage bundles, real failures and sibling evidence. tooling/test-npm-workspace-tests.py retains native mixed-framework/nested-scope checks and now inspects the resulting test-only bundle. Marker-only overrides are verified as command execution with missing required evidence, not accepted as successful tests. The direct workspace probe now also accepts --manager pnpm and --manager yarn. It adapts EX-020's native workspace declarations, explicitly creates local native links offline, and checks a member script beside an inferred suite, failed/sibling reports, hooks, unchanged source/locks, root aggregation and inspection. CI runs all three managers after compiling the CLI and provisioning the pinned native packages. The npm mixed-framework probe checks the extracted shared scope/execution layer separately; pnpm/Yarn captured workspace artifacts and wider framework combinations are not implied by these direct tests. The Helm native-reporting probe checks chart source bytes separately from the intentionally generated direct-test dist/ and .oyzu/ outputs, and inspects each resulting CLI bundle. Preparation fixture copies omit those outputs. This corrects the old source-equality expectation after direct test bundle integration without dropping chart-preservation assertions. Host task jobs explicitly provision Rust 1.94.0 with LLVM tools, cargo-nextest 0.9.146 and cargo-llvm-cov 0.9.1, then run tooling/test-rust-direct.py using the compiled CLI. The reporting provisioner pins upstream release archive SHA-256 digests for Linux x64, Windows x64 and macOS Intel/ARM runners. These are CI prerequisites, not product tool installation. Windows uses MSVC; the locally available GNU compiler cannot execute coverage because it lacks profiler_builtins. The native direct-reporting step passed on all three hosts at bfa2b7c in run 37049720609. Those step results do not imply the entire workflow passed. Host task jobs also provision the pinned Ant/JaCoCo/JUnit fixtures and run tooling/test-ant-direct.py with JDK 17 after CLI compilation. The probe exercises both EX-025 project roots and native JUnit tests through direct report bundles, including hooks and actual failed assertions. It supplements the existing native Java-adapter and captured JAR checks. See Ant prerequisites and reporting scope; local and cross-platform results are tracked separately. tooling/test-maven-direct.py exercises the native reactor's direct JUnit/JaCoCo bundles, custom Surefire directories, reruns, hooks, failed assertions and inspection. CI supplies Maven 3.9.11 from a checksum-pinned distribution, then explicitly acquires fixture dependencies with --acquire before calling the compiled CLI. Product model/test invocations use offline Maven. This new host probe does not replace captured reactor artifact or Failsafe verification; see Maven direct testing. tooling/test-gradle-direct.py exercises EX-024 and an included-build test variation through the compiled CLI, with per-task JUnit/JaCoCo, a custom native report directory, source-free project omission, repeated runs, hooks, failed assertions and inspection. CI supplies checksum-pinned Gradle 8.14.3 and explicitly acquires fixture dependencies before offline product calls. Report injection is shared with captured builds; the native preparation probe still checks snapshot archives and offline repository replay separately. See Gradle builds and tests for prerequisites, evidence scope and remaining gaps. The Node suite registers yarn-workspaces for the checked-in EX-020 Classic variation: compiled-CLI discovery, captured offline build, two snapshot packages with matching local dependency versions, JUnit/LCOV, quality gates, source preservation and bundle inspection. Its failed-test and lint variations must block artifact collection. The suite already provisions the Yarn image. python tooling/test-native-workspace-build.py --manager yarn separately exercises the native capture/replay and packaging adapters after fixture dependencies are provisioned; CI also runs that probe in host task jobs. A passing native probe does not establish isolated CLI acceptance. The Node suite also registers pnpm-workspaces against the checked-in pnpm EX-020 variation, with the same functional package/report and failure obligations. python tooling/test-native-workspace-build.py --manager pnpm supplies the companion native capture/replay probe. CI runs both Yarn and pnpm native probes after provisioning their explicit fixture packages; the shared probe replaces test-yarn-workspace-build.py. Common package assertions live in tooling/build_scenarios/workspace_packages.py, with separate registered native-manager entry points.
documents.s: Independent functional evidence after native conformance

documents.t: With the Rust toolchain image already provisioned, run python tooling/test-build-logging.py --cli <compiled-cli> --evidence-dir <new-directory>. This executes parallel captured Rust builds and verifies live labeled streams, command records, final partial lines, snapshot artifacts, failure/blocked behavior, JSON mode and inspected retained bundles. CI runs it in the Rust suite after CLI compilation and explicit provisioning, retaining logging-evidence. It does not install tools or count as acceptance of every builder. The ordinary captured scenario harness now explicitly requests --json for builds because readable text is the default.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/cargo-sessions.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Oyzu supplies Cargo's native credential provider automatically for one admitted, named sparse registry. The helper is the compiled Oyzu executable, staged under cargo-credential-oyzu. Cargo receives a token in memory through its native process protocol; Oyzu does not run cargo login or write a credentials file. This is an opt-in local-agent prototype, not production platform authentication or captured oyzu build integration.

Set user or administrative configuration (the port is illustrative): [cargo] sessionEndpoint = "http://127.0.0.1:43199/session" The endpoint defaults to absent. The normal configuration cascade applies; project, local, invocation and profile configuration cannot select agent authority. User configuration remains excluded in CI under existing rules. Laboratory endpoints must use numeric-loopback HTTP without credentials, query or fragment. With Cargo provisioned, use its executable path or a declared managed command: oyzu exec -- /absolute/path/to/cargo build --locked eval "$(oyzu activate bash)" cargo fetch --locked Supported commands are build, check, test, fetch and generate-lockfile. Help/version bypass admission. Native publication is unsupported; publication belongs to oyzu publish. Command-line configuration, token, registry, manifest-path and directory overrides are rejected before admission. Subcommand passthrough after -- is not yet supported. The project declares its normal named-registry dependency: [dependencies] example = { version = "=0.1.0", registry = "internal" }

The launcher sends canonical working directory, tool cargo and arguments to the configured endpoint. A fixture response is: { "credentialEndpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:43199/credential", "name": "internal", "index": "sparse+https://packages.example.com/index/" } The registry name uses lowercase ASCII letters, digits, underscore or hyphen; crates-io is excluded. The index is credential-free HTTP(S), ending in a slash, without query or fragment. The launch sets the matching CARGO_REGISTRIES_INTERNAL_INDEX and CARGO_REGISTRIES_INTERNAL_CREDENTIAL_PROVIDER environment values and removes CARGO_REGISTRIES_INTERNAL_TOKEN. It preserves CARGO_HOME, caches and unrelated native configuration. It does not edit project manifests or lock files. The helper accepts Cargo's version-1 get request only for read and the exact admitted index. It forwards { "ecosystem": "cargo", "request": ... } to the credential endpoint, which supplies { "token": "..." }. The token is returned to Cargo with session caching and operation-independent caching disabled. Provider errors return a generic failure without exposing endpoint responses. This follows the upstream Cargo credential-provider protocol and registry configuration.

Every supported managed launch requires admission, including warm offline builds. Denial or agent outage fails the launch; help remains available. A native command failure retains its exit status. Human mode forwards native streams; --json captures them in the existing structured exec result. Temporary helper lifetime is bounded by the launch. Credentials necessarily enter Cargo's process memory; this is exposure reduction, not protection against a machine administrator. Read-only permissions must be enforced by the upstream identity. The first supported configuration is one named registry. This does not govern other registries, Git/path dependencies, crates.io replacement, custom aliases, source-replacement graphs or arbitrary child processes. Existing native provider configuration is preserved on disk but replaced for the admitted registry in the child environment. Do not infer universal source enforcement from that. Linux Cargo 1.95 and Bash are the qualification target; Windows/macOS and other shells remain unqualified. See the launch evidence.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/cli-help.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Run oyzu --help for a workflow-oriented overview: Develop & build, Project tools, Environment & configuration, Platform and Diagnostics. Common examples follow the options. Use oyzu <command> --help or oyzu help <command> for command-specific arguments and options, including nested commands such as oyzu config set --help. Help works offline without a project, installed tool selection or platform account. Hidden shell hooks stay out of the public command list. Help does not execute the examples, install tools or change project files. oyzu --help oyzu build --help oyzu help config oyzu config set --help oyzu --json --help Help uses cyan headings, green command/option names and yellow placeholders on color-capable terminals. Redirected help is plain text by default. Set NO_COLOR=1 to disable help color or CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 to request it explicitly (avoid setting both). These are clap's help-rendering controls; project ui.color does not apply because help runs before project configuration is loaded. With --json, successful help/version requests return unstyled text in output and exitCode: 0. The flag can precede the command or follow a command's --help. For oyzu help <command>, put --json before help. This presentation change does not alter other commands' result/error formats or exit codes. Human layout is not a stable machine-parsing contract. The layout and palette use the same CLI implementation on Windows, macOS and Linux. Windows tests cover root/nested help from an empty directory, complete public command grouping, redirected output, forced color, NO_COLOR and JSON help. See implementation status for evidence and platform limits. This design draws on GitHub CLI's command groups, uv's help navigation and the CLI Guidelines' restrained color guidance. No upstream source or new dependencies are included.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/cli-output.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Every public command defaults to readable text and accepts global --json for machine-readable output. DEC-033 and AGENTS.md record this product rule. Output selection never changes policy, configuration, lock contents or exit codes. The CLI design guide is the draft shared standard for mission, guardrails, state meanings, large-repository presentation and review criteria. This reference describes current interfaces, including bounded retained build history. Other target experiences in the guide require their own implementation evidence.

The help masthead uses the compact lowercase oyzu. wordmark. Terminals choose their own fonts; no Segoe UI or point-size claim is made for terminal output. Run oyzu or oyzu --help for the same workflow-oriented overview: Develop & build, Project tools, Environment & configuration, Platform and Diagnostics. The overview includes common examples; oyzu <command> --help or oyzu help <command> shows command-specific arguments and options, including nested commands such as oyzu config set --help. Help works offline without a project, installed tool selection or platform account. Hidden shell hooks stay out of the public command list. Bare oyzu exits successfully and uses the same stdout, color controls and static startup path as oyzu --help; neither opens project configuration or initializes a runtime. Use oyzu --json --help for the overview in a JSON envelope. oyzu reshim appears under Project tools and refreshes the fixed shim folder and existing activation launchers owned by this frontend. Human output reports the shims folder and recorded commands; --json returns directory and commands. See shim refresh for store selection, Windows prerequisites and recovery. shell groups startup profile install and remove; shim refresh has no nested spelling or alias. Help uses cyan headings, green command/option names and yellow placeholders on color-capable terminals. Redirected help is plain text by default. Set NO_COLOR=1 to disable help color or CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 to request it explicitly (avoid setting both). These are clap's help-rendering controls; project ui.color does not apply because help runs before project configuration is loaded. JSON help always contains unstyled text. The layout and palette use the same CLI implementation on Windows, macOS and Linux; native verification is recorded in the implementation status. This design draws on GitHub CLI's command groups, uv's help navigation and the CLI Guidelines' restrained color guidance. No upstream source or new dependencies are included.

oyzu --version identifies the compiled local build, for example: oyzu 0.1.0-local.8aee8560a0ca.dirty (debug; x86_64-pc-windows-gnu; build 1791211857) The suffix records the abbreviated source commit, whether the worktree was dirty when compilation captured its identity, Cargo profile, target triple and build Unix timestamp (seconds since the UTC epoch). SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH overrides that timestamp at compilation for reproducible inputs. Without Git metadata, source identity is explicitly unknown.source-unknown. This is diagnostic identity, not a release version, source attestation or production eligibility claim. All current builds are labelled local, including optimized release-profile builds (oyzu build --optimized); optimized never implies a release or publication eligibility. Identity is embedded at compile time. Version/help never opens project configuration, starts a worker, runs Git or contacts a service. --version --json uses the existing structured output/exit-code envelope.

A pull changes source; it does not replace an installed executable. oyzu --version reports the identity compiled into the selected executable. Use command -v oyzu in POSIX shells or Get-Command oyzu -All in PowerShell to inspect command routing. Compare it with the project-local binary directly: ./.oyzu/bin/oyzu --version ./.oyzu/bin/oyzu build --output plain On Windows use .\.oyzu\bin\oyzu.exe. oyzu build publishes collected artifacts under dist and promotes executable artifacts into the current project's .oyzu/bin only after a successful native build. Failed builds retain the previous binaries. A direct Cargo compilation through oyzu exec writes Cargo's target output and does not perform that promotion. Do not assume target/debug/oyzu identifies the executable selected by your shell. The repository bootstrap reuses an existing executable; it is not an update command. Activation can prepend the configured project-local .oyzu/bin to PATH; ordinary shell-wrapper commands select the application on PATH, while lifecycle hooks retain the bootstrap frontend. Preserve this architecture when updating: verify the successful build's artifact, promoted binary and selected version before changing any installation. No global bootstrap replacement is required for a project-local build. Native Windows routing qualification is recorded separately from cross-platform source/tests.

Ordinary builds show Facts after preparation and before Selection, Plan and the corresponding actions. No extra flag, builder setting, login or network access is needed. The shared view reads existing frozen plan records; it does not rerun discovery or query source-control APIs. Fact Meaning and limits Branch / Commit Local branch observation and commits recorded by version history/decisions; different target commits keep their attribution. They do not attest that Git HEAD equals the captured input tree. Git state Explicitly not verified. Existing source records use conservative dirty/commit placeholders; display does not interpret those as a clean/dirty Git observation. Source digest Content identity of admitted build inputs. Ordinary output abbreviates hashes; -v and structured evidence retain full values. Version / Basis Each target/package's planned version and recorded reason. Identical versions/bases within a target are grouped (package count normally, names with -v); differing package versions stay separate. Artifact intent versions are a fallback when decisions are absent, with the missing basis stated. Distinct native artifact coordinates remain visible in an Artifact row even when logical version decisions exist. Kind Recorded version intent, currently snapshots; a release context does not establish release classification. Context Effective local/PR/CI/release context with its detection or override source. Protection unknown · not queried; display adds no provider API discovery. Release Recorded production ineligibility and its target scope, or explicit unknown where decisions are missing. Version facts never authorize publication. Captured independent targets may execute while others are preparing. Each newly prepared plan shows new/changed facts before its actions; unchanged rows are not repeated. Hook-dependent versions say pending post-hook finalization; the existing post-hook event displays the final version under Build. Initial facts describe the initial plan; final bundle records describe produced artifacts. Quiet builds suppress this routine section. JSON contains no human heading: the allowlisted buildFacts field of each plan event carries structured inputs, alongside context fact events and bundle records. Environments, credentials and arbitrary extensions are excluded. Terminal controls are escaped; narrow text uses labelled records and hanging indents. Git/protection uncertainty does not change exit status, action/cache identity or release rules.

Default builds use compact linear progress, preceded by one plan table (targets by stages, or platforms by stages for a single target) shown before work starts; the dashboard remains an explicit option. The old linear preparation/context/stage tables and the per-stage Skipped lines are removed. Routine successes and accepted per-action test details collapse; -v, planning, inspection, history and JSON retain deeper detail. A build prints named sections in a fixed order and omits any that has nothing to say. The title line names the project and, right-aligned, the host platform, local or the CI provider, the build context value only (context pr, context local; the deciding signal or pin is shown in Facts and by config explain context, see Build context), and fast or full, followed by optimized or development when --optimized or --no-optimized asks for one. The CI provider label alone nearly fills 80 columns, so under a CI provider the subtitle may continue on the line below the project. A pin that a CI provider marker forbids lowering prints a CONTEXT_OVERRIDE_IGNORED warning. Every row, the title and the section rules share one width (80 columns, or less on a narrower terminal). ── Prepare ── lists every preparation step as a row (mark, name, detail, duration, and the warning count of the work that raised them). The Tools row summarizes the pinned tools (2 tools pinned · 0 installed now) and lists each beneath it with its version, already installed or installed now, and the detected requirement that needs it (or pinned in oyzu.toml), followed by detected toolchain components and host prerequisites of the selected targets. With several targets the block prints once, when Prepare closes, listing each tool once; a tool whose reason differs between targets shows each reason (detected from …; pinned in … · not detected for <target>). Best-effort detection adds attention rows (yellow !) beneath the tools: ! protoc needed by prost-build · no catalog entry; pin or provide it (an unknown tool; a detected tool that Oyzu can manage, pinned or not, is an ordinary detected from Cargo.lock row that resolves, locks and installs), ! protoc needed by prost-build in Cargo.lock · no usable checksum; pin it in oyzu.toml or silence it with tools.ignore (a detected tool that could not be resolved or installed; the build continues, only an explicit pin fails), host prerequisite … · not found on PATH, fetches <what> outside the lock (<file>) and detection failed: <reason> · nothing extra detected. They warn and never fail the build; tools.ignore silences a detection, visible only with -v. Rules and patterns: build tool scope. When another build holds the workspace, a Build lock row waits for it (waiting for pid N, started Ns ago) before any other preparation instead of failing; Ctrl-C stops the wait. Routine housekeeping that finishes after Prepare closes (end-of-build cache retention) is shown only when slow, failed or warned, or with -v. In an interactive terminal, work in progress shows under its section heading as one line per step or action with an animated spinner, redrawn several times a second; long status is shortened with … rather than wrapped. Redirected and CI output never redraws: each action prints a start and an end line prefixed with elapsed mm:ss, and the ten-second heartbeat names what is still running. ── Build ── has one row per finished action: mark, target, stage, the command shortened with … to fit the width, executed or reused, and its duration. ── Outputs ── lists artifacts as project-relative paths under dist/<target>/<platform>/ (any for a platform-independent target; see the bundle layout) with sizes and the build profile each was built with, development or optimized (cli dist/cli/windows/x86_64/oyzu.exe 64.1 MB development); -v and --json keep absolute paths, and the JSON artifact record carries the label as profile. ── Warnings (N) ── lists each distinct warning once, with its owner (for example docs · npm); it is not repeated inline during the run. The generic NATIVE_WARNING code is hidden in the default view and shown with -v and in JSON, while Oyzu-owned diagnostic codes are always shown. The summary line carries the outcome and counts only the outcomes that happened (2 targets · 1 executed · 1 reused · 235.3s), followed by a dim Details line with the manifest and event paths and the invocation id. The separate Action cache line, the "counts do not estimate time remaining" sentence and the "Check selection unavailable … retained evidence is incomplete" sentence are not part of the default build view; -v adds the Reuse and Cache facts, history keeps the selection caveat, and JSON is unchanged. ── Selection ── prints when a target is built by a plugin (its builder selection: the full record with remedies when the build adopted or installed one, otherwise one line per target; see plugin catalog) and when the build is not every declared target. For the latter: --affected shows what it was compared with (compared with origin/main at 0123456), the changed targets and changed paths, their dependents and the unaffected count; a conservative fallback shows ! Not narrowed with its reason, the recorded code and a fix only when one is known; an explicit request shows requested and required (prerequisites pulled in). ── Plan ── then prints once after it. Rows are targets; columns are the stages the builders declare, in the order format, lint, test, build, package and then any other stage. A cell is run (selected), skip (the builder has the stage but this build does not run it, for example a fast local build, or it is not available), off (a check level of off: never run and its tools not prepared) or - (the builder declares no such stage). Below the table, after a blank line, one dim line per distinct reason names the stages it covers: under an off label with where the check was turned off (format · disabled in oyzu.toml, test · disabled in oyzu.toml [context.pr]), under a skipped label (lint and test · fast local build), and under an advisory label for run stages whose failure is only a warning (lint · failures are warnings; the build still succeeds). One line per distinct build profile follows under a profile label, naming its targets with the profile and why (cli · optimized · --optimized, cli and docs · development · local dist only, cli · optimized · release builds are published). One line per distinct policy override follows under a policy label: the setting (a check reads as its name), the value policy made effective and why (format enforce · admin policy minimum in pr, release (project oyzu.toml sets off)), prefixed with the targets it applies to when not every target shares it. Overrides by the root oyzu.toml's project constraints follow in the same form under a project label (tests required · project constraint minimum in release (project app/oyzu.toml sets advisory)), and in a release build each check a nearer folder lowered below a farther [context.release] value under a lowered label (tests advisory · app/oyzu.toml:2 lowers required from oyzu.toml:5 [context.release]). One line per conditional task or hook follows under a task label, prefixed with its target when the plan has several: whether it runs (and for which artifacts) or why it was skipped (pre_build · skip · unless context = local, post_build · run for bin-oyzu · unless artifact = bin-oyzu-shim); a per-artifact run's Build row names its artifact (post_build[bin-oyzu]). oyzu build --plan prints the same lines as Task: lines under each target. Table notes follow under a note label, so none reads as a table row. A failed advisory check is shown once, as a warning: its Build row reads warn … failed · advisory, it gets no Failure block, Warnings holds one CHECK_ADVISORY entry with the action, exit code and native cause, and the summary counts it apart from failures (1 advisory failed); the build still succeeds. A single target built for several platforms (--all-platforms) pivots to one row per platform and says 1 target · N platforms. Above twelve rows, targets with identical stages share a counted row (29 targets) and a note line says so; a narrowed build's trailer reads N of M targets and an affected build adds a why column (changed, uses <target>); -v lists every target. When the table would not fit the terminal width each row becomes a record (cli build run · package -, then its skipped stages on the next line) so no value is lost. When a build routes a platform off the host, or a target declares platforms this run does not build, every row names its platform (hello · linux/arm64) and a built by column names the executor (host, cross toolchain (rust-lld)); when it does not fit, a built by footnote carries it instead.
