An other footnote lists declared platforms this machine could build with --platform and a not here footnote lists the rest with the reason (darwin/arm64 · needs a macOS runner (Apple SDK and linker)). A host-only build keeps the plain table. See platforms and executors. The table renders the planner's recorded stage, check-selection and platform routing facts and does not recompute them. The read-only --plan preview adds a Platforms · how each is built here table (target, platform, what builds it here, the CI runner it needs, and the reason). A failed action's Build row reads ✗ … failed <duration> (FAIL without color). After Build, a ── Failure: <target> · <stage> ── section shows the native cause (line breaks kept, terminal controls escaped, the first error context or the last lines written), the exit code, Log with the retained log path, and Next oyzu build <target> re-run only this target. Actions that did not run because a prerequisite failed are blocked (⊘), counted apart from failed; a blocked row says needs <target> · <stage>, only the first three get a row and the rest become + N more blocked · -v lists them. The summary counts only non-zero outcomes (✗ Build failed 1 failed · 12 blocked · 130 succeeded · 4m 02s) and is followed by Details and, for a host build, the note that local binaries were not updated. A preparation failure ends after Prepare with a ── Failure: preparation ── block and no Build section. In a build of more than twelve actions, clean successes fold into one ✓ 91 finished · 78 reused · 13 executed tally (-v lists every action); running, warned, waiting, blocked and failed actions keep their rows, and the Build heading says 143 actions. On a terminal the live pane shows ○ <target> · <stage> waits for <target> · <stage> for queued actions with unfinished prerequisites (at most three, then + N more waiting) and an N of M finished line. -q prints only Failure, Warnings and the summary line. Redirected output is rendered at 100 columns on every host; failure text wraps instead of exceeding it, Windows extended-length (\\?\) prefixes are not shown, and a long log path keeps its tail. Interrupted, --plan and --check builds keep their existing receipts. Redirected output and CI logs are appended, not redrawn: each action prints a .. target stage started line and an end line with its outcome and duration, both led by the elapsed mm:ss, and the ten-second heartbeat reads still running: api build 10s · auth-lib test 12s · 6 waiting. In a narrow terminal or without color every table falls back to records and nothing is dropped. When the selected targets live in more than one top-level directory below the project root (./ for targets at the root), the plan table groups its rows under a dim services/ heading, a prerequisite in another directory shows in a final needs column when it fits, Outputs are listed under their directory, and the summary gains one line per directory (services/ ✓ 2 targets 58.1s, where the time is the sum of that directory's action durations). Identical-stage grouping above twelve rows applies within each directory. A build in a single directory is unchanged. With color, state is a glyph (✓ ok, ↺ reused, ! warning, ✗ failed). Without color (NO_COLOR, TERM=dumb, redirected output) every mark becomes a padded word (ok, reused, warn, FAIL) and headings use -- Name ---, so no state depends on color. -q prints only warnings and the summary line (failures keep their existing receipt). The titles, rows and receipt are produced by the shared presentation and logging layer; JSON stdout, JSON events and exit status are unchanged. Build receipts include separate target/action totals and nonzero disjoint action outcomes, fresh tests, reused test evidence, warnings and available evidence references. Receipts distinguish captured checks selected (with their action outcomes) from checks not requested. Selection comes from the executed graph's retained target facts, including required checks in fast mode; a fast/full label or missing report never establishes that tests were not requested. A native report with an explicit zero total is labeled Native zero-test reports; native skips keep their own counts. Missing numeric facts display unavailable, not zero. Legacy records without captured selection say Check selection unavailable in history and failed receipts. Required report validation still fails the build, and a successful build does not itself establish release eligibility. Selected history uses the same labels. Successful target totals remain separate from actions labeled executed or reused. Expanded build --explain and selected history retain recorded selection and reuse decisions, source comparison context when available, native provenance and explicit uncertainty; they do not recompute causes from the current checkout. Ordinary misses remain ordinary execution, while material fallback warnings and required failures keep their existing visibility and exit semantics. Successful receipts say Build succeeded, including with warnings when warning diagnostics are present. Native warnings are listed once in the Warnings section, and both human views share compiler/test output projection; raw native records remain in JSON events and retained logs. Intentional stage skips use neutral grouped reasons; missing required work still receives attention. Lifecycle records use compact spacing and a simpler nested description at narrow widths; source excerpts preserve native indentation rather than repeated columns. invocationId correlates a build result with its live and retained events; runId remains the producing build identity. oyzu history lists up to twenty retained build summaries; oyzu history <invocation-or-run-id> --json is a bounded agent-readable result with causes and evidence availability. See retained invocation lookup for scope, limits, access and retention. This does not create an agent-only output mode or a general history service for every command. oyzu pin --dry-run oyzu pin --dry-run --json oyzu --json config show oyzu tools inspect-lock --json oyzu --json tools resolve --registry registry.yaml --tool hashicorp/terraform --version v1.16.5 oyzu exec --json -- ./my-program argument The flag works before or after the subcommand. Arguments after -- belong to the invoked task/program, so its own --json does not select Oyzu's output mode. Inspection, configuration and discovery use titled, indented human views; pin shows a concise requirement inventory. Builds retain their progress and receipt, task lists retain readable labels, and which prints the selected path. All human diagnostics use the shared status/subject/message renderer, including env -v, which -v and shell/payload commands. The old severity/target/timestamp logger envelope and separate build timeline renderer are removed. Verbosity expands observations within the same design. Multiline causes keep their line boundaries. Lookup and payload diagnostics are append-only and create no preparation spool, redraw worker or cursor controls; their stdout contracts (selected paths, environment data and shell code) are unchanged. Plain command views render events without a background redraw worker. Build views retain their ten-second progress heartbeat; interactive builds redraw at up to ten frames per second. Closing either timed build view wakes its wait immediately, so command completion does not wait for the next redraw or heartbeat. oyzu build --verify-contract adds a Contract check block after the Outputs of the final receipt: the outcome (passed, failed, nothing to verify), how many confined actions ran again with their whole target visible, how many matched, diverged or were not confined, and one Diverged row per mismatch naming the extra files and the declaration that fixes them. The same data is manifest.extensions["oyzu.dev/contract-verification"] in --json; a divergence is also an error diagnostic and a non-zero exit. A confined action's undeclared read is the diagnostic confined-read-outside-contract with the stage, path, missing fact and fix as indented lines (plain text; no color is needed to read it). See Local action cache.

This section is the normative style guide for every public command's human experience: startup, progress, subprocess output, results and failures. Command-specific presenters must follow it; a generic recursive data dump or raw diagnostic envelope is not a finished public interface. These are review requirements, not a claim that all existing commands have been audited. Lead with the outcome and relevant selection (such as the active profile). Use short, descriptive section headings and aligned columns for comparable records. Keep empty collections compact ([] for configuration values); omit empty diagnostic sections. Do not omit failures or unresolved requirements. Preserve identifiers exactly: env.CARGO_HOME, env._.path, checks.coverageMinimum and cargo-llvm-cov are copyable identifiers, not prose. Never title-case, split capitals, or replace their underscores and punctuation. Humanize only labels owned by the presenter. Group configuration settings by namespace, retaining full setting keys. Render booleans as true/false in configuration tables to match their authored types. Put long identities and low-priority metadata after the useful settings. Wrap long cells without losing characters; use labeled records on narrow terminals. Normalize Windows extended-path notation for human display, while preserving machine payloads. Use cyan headings, green success, yellow attention and red failures. Always include textual meaning; color cannot be the only signal. Preserve readable no-color output, escape terminal controls, and honor each command's redaction contract. Presentation must not recover upstream-redacted values. Verify the compiled command in human, no-color and JSON modes. Cover long identifiers and narrow layouts with focused rendering checks. JSON schemas and executable/native payloads are independent of presentation. Human output leads with the operation outcome, then groups details into named sections. Comparable records use aligned tables; nested or long records use labeled fields without dropping values. The shared renderer uses terminal width when available (100 columns otherwise), falling back to labeled records when a table would overflow. Color is supplementary: headings use cyan, success uses green and attention uses yellow; errors retain explicit severity labels. Shared result views enable color on terminals, omit it for redirected output or TERM=dumb, accept nonzero CLICOLOR_FORCE to force color, and let NO_COLOR override forcing. No project configuration is opened solely to style a result. JSON never gains ANSI sequences. Shell code, native streams and which path output retain their payload contracts. Untrusted control characters in shared human result values are escaped before styling. pin shows one compact setup table per target. For Rust it lists each compiler component and test/coverage helper separately, with a purpose column. Formatting, linting, testing and coverage tools are required when those checks are enabled by the build or policy; the labels do not make selected checks optional. Installation support is distinct from installed availability: pin does not probe or install tools. Sources, profiles, compatibility constraints, configured requests and discovery limitations remain in --json, rather than repeated human tables. Unknown requirements remain visible. Existing resolution-conflict diagnostics are unchanged. Preview/pinned outcomes distinguish completed and incomplete resolution. Incomplete resolution includes actionable diagnostics below the setup table. Environment inspection and shell-profile receipts also use the shared layout.

Command behavior Required human presentation Quick lookup (which, version) Preserve its concise documented payload; no artificial progress or decorative wrapper Inspection/listing (env, config, tools current/list/versions/info, tools resolve, tools evidence, task list, pin preview) Descriptive title, useful selection context, grouped tables or labeled records, actionable unresolved items Work (install, update, build, acquisition) Operation heading, named live steps, scoped subprocess output, final outcome/receipt Task/child execution (run, exec) Shared Oyzu preparation/progress; preserve the documented native stream/pass-through behavior Failure Failed operation and affected item, readable cause, recovery when known; preserve exit status and diagnostic code. A build summary shows each failed action's cause as an ERROR line even when the task never started (for example a rejected artifact handoff); text quoting native tools has its terminal controls escaped and its line breaks kept Shell code/private protocols Exact executable/protocol payload; never add human decoration Consistency means shared hierarchy, vocabulary and state semantics, not adding identical headings to payload commands. Select the pattern in the CLI presenter before starting effects. Application commands return outcomes and lifecycle facts; they do not select colors, terminal modes or human/JSON formatting.

Before potentially slow work, show the operation and what is currently being checked or performed. Do not delay all feedback until the final result. Immediate lookups need no synthetic progress. Name the item or step (rust, Dependencies, Source evidence), not an internal scope such as command or a repeated generic build label. Context statements belong in subtitles or explanatory text; do not make them look like work items. Use one shared state vocabulary: › running, ✓ completed/ready, ✗ failed, ! attention, and explicit Skipped, Blocked, or Unresolved labels. Starting verification is not completion. Mark ready only after the owning operation confirms its required checks. Close started steps on failure as well as success; never leave an apparently running step in a completed receipt. Use elapsed/still-working feedback for genuinely long operations. Use a percentage only when the operation supplies a meaningful total. Do not invent progress or claim stalled work is healthy merely because a heartbeat exists. Keep the default linear. Small redraws may update active rows and bounded subprocess tails on capable terminals; persistent panes, alternate screens and interactive input must not be prerequisites for ordinary use. Group concurrent work by stable target/task/tool identity. Indent and dim each captured subprocess tail beneath its owner, allowing about eight lines subject to the shared terminal budget. Collapse successful tails; retain relevant failure context. Never merge unattributed lines from parallel processes. Native pass-through commands retain their documented stream contract. Finish with a concise outcome and useful results, artifacts or recovery steps. Avoid repeating the complete progress history in the receipt. Partial success, failed verification and missing requirements must remain visible. Routine human progress must not default to envelopes such as [Info] [oyzu::commands] [00:00.045] [command]. Subsystem identifiers, timestamps and diagnostic metadata belong in explicitly requested diagnostic detail and structured logging. Warnings/errors still explain severity and retain useful codes; do not suppress them to make a display look clean. Illustrative shared lifecycle (values are examples, not measured output): Installing tools › rust Checking pinned installation… ✓ rust Ready · 1.95.0 · reused › cargo-nextest Installing… Downloading package… ✓ cargo-nextest Ready · installed Installation complete 2 tools verified · 1 installed · 1 reused The live terminal may replace the running rows; a redirected stream keeps a readable start/completion sequence. Both must communicate the same outcome.

Use the shared renderer's semantic palette and color controls above. Never add command-local ANSI strings or a second styling policy. Dim native previews, not essential status or recovery instructions. When terminal capabilities are absent, use append-only text with no cursor controls; disabling color alone must not remove information. Forced color may style redirected output without enabling redraws. Handle narrow widths without truncating copyable identifiers or paths. Keep progress/diagnostics on stderr and final results on stdout. Preserve the JSON, shell-payload and native-stream exceptions documented below. Quiet removes routine progress, not results or failures; verbosity adds diagnostics without changing execution. Preserve legitimate values under the owning sensitive-field policy: do not blanket-redact ordinary configuration, paths or version information, and never reveal protected values merely because verbose output is enabled.

For every new or changed public command: Identify its output pattern and reuse presentation result primitives plus the invocation-owned logging/linear view. Search existing renderers first; extend the shared owner when behavior is missing instead of building a local spinner, logger, color palette or table formatter. Exercise the real compiled entry point. Check startup feedback, one successful outcome and an applicable failure, including meaningful terminal step closure. A renderer unit test alone does not prove the command selected that renderer. Check ordinary human output, redirected/no-color output, JSON stdout/stderr separation and quiet behavior. Use focused rendering checks for narrow/long layouts and concurrent output when relevant; use a capable terminal for changed redraw behavior. State unavailable terminal/platform qualification explicitly. Confirm the payload exceptions, exit codes, sensitive-field handling and help/version fast path remain intact. Presentation must not change tool flags, plans, cache identity, evidence or policy. Update the owning reference and record actual verification. Fix inconsistencies in the changed command; record unrelated command-family gaps rather than claiming repository-wide compliance or launching an unbounded visual rewrite.

oyzu --help, oyzu help build, nested --help, --version and unknown-command diagnostics use the built-in command catalog. They work with an empty PATH, malformed project files and a nonexistent -C directory. They do not load project configuration, refresh enterprise policy, open tool stores, initialize backend workers or contact services. No installation or platform account is required. The operating system still loads the binary and Oyzu checks its executable identity to distinguish native tool shims. Actual run list/discover inspect a project; which validates the frozen tool selection. Those are explicit operations, not static command help, and retain their configuration and verification requirements. A native tool shim's help continues to invoke that selected tool. The public CLI and reusable application command layer share execution behavior; see the architecture boundary. Local run tasks retain stdin. In text mode, tasks recording a bundle tee full stdout/stderr to the caller and dist/logs, including in quiet mode, without replaying output at completion. Their output descriptors are pipes. Tasks marked interactive = true instead inherit terminal stdout/stderr; those streams cannot also be captured, so their bundle stdout/stderr files are empty. Non-bundled tasks also inherit output directly. JSON captures task output and keeps stdout as the final result. See task streams.

JSON stdout contains one result without Oyzu-added headings, ANSI styling or progress. Existing structured result shapes are retained where available. Oyzu diagnostics on stderr use JSON Lines, including non-build warnings. Read stdout for the command result. Native pass-through streams retain their documented behavior. Setup, operation and argument-parsing errors contain error and exitCode, with a nonzero process exit. JSON help/version return their text in output with exitCode: 0. exec --json captures child output in stdout and stderr strings and returns exitCode, also preserving that exit code in Oyzu. Input remains inherited; captured output appears when the child exits, not as a live terminal. The result's capture object discloses inherited stdin, piped stdout/stderr, no output TTY, non-streaming delivery and lossy UTF-8 decoding; invocationId correlates diagnostics. Non-UTF-8 bytes use replacement characters. JSON run outcome records disclose file-based stdout/stderr capture, inherited stdin, non-TTY/non-streaming output, lossy decoding and invocation correlation. Default execution remains pass-through.

activate, deactivate, environment hooks and env --shell SHELL emit executable shell code by default: headings would break evaluation. With --json, they return { "shell": "…", "script": "…" }. Evaluate raw code, never the JSON envelope. JSON mode retains the same activation/session-record effects. env inspection stays redacted; explicitly requested shell payloads contain actual assignments in both modes. oyzu config schema build.yaml and oyzu config schema oyzu.toml emit one JSON Schema document as their payload in human mode too, so the output can be redirected to a file; with --json they return the config-schema record that holds it under schema. oyzu config schema without a file is an ordinary listing. See editor schemas.

install SPEC, update and uninstall lead with the outcome (✓ Installed go 1.26.8), then indented facts: what was declared and where, the lock and its platforms, replaced requirements and notes about other scopes. --dry-run starts with Dry run · no files were changed. The inspection commands use an outcome line, an aligned table and an Attention section for unresolved rows; statuses are words (ok, not installed, blocked, deprecated, stale lock, ambiguous), never colour alone. All of them support --json. See tool commands.

tools resolve and tools evidence (see reference) use the inspection pattern: a title, an outcome line (✓ complete, ! attention), the snapshot, an aligned table of records (status words, never colour alone), then Unsupported platforms, Errors, Needs attention and Next steps sections. --json prints exactly one artifact-set document on stdout (the diagnostic lines of evidence, such as EVIDENCE_FETCH, go to stderr). Exit 3 means a complete document with undecided or unverified items. Recipe-supplied text is control-character escaped. Verified by the compiled-CLI tests in tests/integration/recipe_resolve.rs (human no-colour text, both JSON exit codes and error envelopes) and the proof runner; narrow-terminal wrapping reuses the shared table and was observed at 80 columns only.

oyzu discover answers "what does Oyzu see here?". It prints one block per target (the name oyzu build <target> accepts): builder, whether build.yaml or detection from native files chose it, package manager, version, location relative to the project root, which tasks are part of builds and which are development-only (with the reason when one is unavailable). It reads configuration and native files without running project code. The task catalogue and commands belong to oyzu run list; --json returns the complete discovery record. With no targets it explains what to add or where to run. See build tasks. With a build.yaml, a Not in build.yaml section lists every folder where discovery recognizes a build the file leaves out, as a Folder / Recognized by / Line to add table, and --json adds the inventory object. oyzu discover --check leads with Build inventory is current (exit 0) or error[INVENTORY_UNDECLARED] with the same table and a fix: line (exit 1); oyzu discover --write leads with what it declared (Declared 1 build in …, Created build.yaml with 2 builds, Nothing to write, or, in yellow, A choice is needed: …; nothing was written), a Build / Uses / Folder table, and a Needs a choice table (exit 1) for folders several builders recognize. A row for such a folder is marked example: with a <…> placeholder for uses. Folders a declared build's workspace manifest lists are counted, never tabled: Build inventory is current · 2 builds declared, 10 workspace members, (10 workspace members) after plain oyzu discover's all-declared line, and Covered as workspace members: cli 10 folders. below a table of undeclared folders. A workspace manifest that exists but cannot be read adds a yellow warning: build web: cannot read the workspace manifest package.json: … line, and its members stay in the table. Both print the build-inventory record with --json (workspaceMembers, warnings). See builds build.yaml leaves out.

oyzu tools list groups installations by tool (rust (core) · 12 installations · 17.0 GB), each with a Version / Platform / Size / Used by / ID table. ID is the start of the installation digest: it tells apart installs of one version that differ by recipe or platform ABI. --details adds location, tool identity and the full installation digest per row. The lead line totals installations, tools, unreferenced installs and disk use.

A bundle is the directory oyzu build writes (dist/ by default) or an exported OCI archive. oyzu inspect with no argument verifies the current project's dist/; a project root is accepted for its dist/. A missing bundle names where Oyzu looked and suggests oyzu build. On success the human view leads with ✓ Bundle contents verified · build succeeded|failed, then the run and source identity and tables of targets (builder, platform), actions (status, exit, gate), artifacts (path, size, platform, short digest), reports and diagnostics. It states that verification checks recorded digests, not who produced the build. An OCI archive shows kind, platforms, size and digests. --json keeps the full manifest. See build bundles.

oyzu.toml settings (including tools.* pins) inherit from the Git worktree root, while build.yaml does not inherit: the nearest ancestor build.yaml inventory selects the build (another tool's build.yaml never does). A project nested in a repository therefore sees the repository's tool pins. Pass --root . to fix both roots at the current directory and stop inheritance (see configuration).

Human failures from a command print ✗ <what failed and how to recover> with the diagnostic code underneath (for example COMMAND_FAILED), not a raw [Error] [oyzu::commands] envelope. A message that already leads with its own stable code (✗ CONFIG_SYNTAX: …, ✗ REMOTE_COMMIT_NOT_PUSHED: …) omits the generic code underneath; --json keeps its {"error", "exitCode"} object and -q keeps the plain error line. Internal pipeline scopes are shown as words (Setup, Preflight, Source, Plan); generated platform target ids are shown as target · os/arch. Running a task prints a heading, shared lifecycle rows and the task result, followed by the native tool output unchanged.

Diagnostic prose redacts only the credential-bearing part: a URL with userinfo becomes [sensitive diagnostic detail withheld], URL queries and fragments become ?[redacted], key=value / key: value forms for credential names keep the name and replace the value, and Authorization: or Bearer redact the rest of the line. Ordinary URLs and prose stay readable. Configuration display still hides any value that looks credential-bearing. Native child output is not rewritten.

Scripts parsing formerly JSON-only pin, discovery, bundle/tool inspection or configuration output must now pass --json. Human formatting is not a parsing contract. Result schemas remain command-specific; this does not change build evidence or introduce a universal result schema. CLI tests cover human defaults, both flag positions, structured errors, help/version, child execution and shell payloads. Measured results and outstanding checks are in implementation status. Windows verification does not qualify other hosts.

Global -v/--verbose enables debug, -vv enables trace, -q/--quiet selects warn, and --log-level error|warn|info|debug|trace selects an explicit threshold. Default is info. Options work on either side of a subcommand; arguments after -- belong to the child. More than two -v or one -q, or combining these controls, is an argument error before project loading. One explicit CLI control overrides all of OYZU_LOG. Otherwise this optional UTF-8 environment value accepts a level or comma-separated target=level directives, optionally preceded by a default level (info when omitted): $env:OYZU_LOG = 'warn,oyzu::executor=trace' oyzu run foo oyzu run foo --json -v Remove-Item Env:OYZU_LOG Targets are oyzu::commands, oyzu::config, oyzu::discovery, oyzu::tools, oyzu::acquisition, oyzu::executor, oyzu::builders and oyzu::reports. An exact target directive overrides the default. Unknown or duplicate targets, empty directives and invalid levels fail. Overridden environment filters are not read. Help/version ignore OYZU_LOG, including invalid values. These are invocation presentation options, not oyzu.toml settings. RUST_LOG does not control Oyzu diagnostics or enable dependency payload logging. Quiet hides routine Oyzu progress and the interactive dashboard. It preserves command results, warnings, errors and native child output. Verbosity does not change native flags/environment, plans, cache inputs, report gates or production eligibility. Logging is local, offline-capable and needs no account, service or new persistent sink. Human diagnostics identify severity and the affected work. Operational failures also identify the running executable/version, selected directory, host platform and observation identity when available. Help/version/syntax remain independent of runtime initialization. JSON diagnostic envelopes retain the existing event fields and add severity, target, invocationId, operationId and parentOperationId. Diagnostic events contain type, code and message, with numeric duration_ms for completed operations. Retained build journals now carry the same correlation fields and observed warning/error diagnostics, independently of console detail filtering. Filtered console projections may have sequence gaps. Sequence orders observations within an invocation; it does not establish causal ordering between native processes. Consumers must tolerate additive fields and event kinds. The existing unreleased manifest/envelope schemas gain optional invocationId in place; actions can carry namespaced log references and the explicit not-started outcome for interruption before launch. Reuse can identify the serving cache tier (local or remote), independently of its producer. All thresholds use the same field admission. No environment/header maps or unrestricted argument arrays are logged. Command events withhold arguments; credential-bearing parts of diagnostic prose are redacted (see Redaction). Arbitrary child output and explicitly requested shell payloads are not rewritten and may contain secrets. Trace is not an HTTP dump or a secret-inspection mode. Pin's human output includes a deduplicated execution-platform coverage section. It describes resolved metadata, not installed availability or platform execution qualification. JSON retains the full platform-specific compiler_metadata recipes.

Outside a project, oyzu run lists nearby projects by relative directory rather than importing their tasks under generated identifiers. The navigation lookup searches at most three directory levels, skips hidden/generated directories, stops below a project boundary and returns at most 32 projects. It reads no child configuration or native metadata and runs no tools. Change into a listed project or use oyzu -C <project> run. JSON returns status: "outside-project", directory, projects, searchDepth, limit and nextStep. An empty lookup fails with PROJECT_NOT_FOUND and the searched directory; requesting a task from the parent fails with TASK_PROJECT_REQUIRED before loading a child project. Explicit workspace roots remain workspaces and use the ordinary task listing. An unknown task returns TASK_NOT_FOUND, the selected project directory, available task names and a close spelling suggestion when one exists. It also points to oyzu run and oyzu -C <project> run <task> for recovery. No task-running preamble appears for this failure. Native execution is announced only after task selection and preparation; completed task rows include the exit code and duration, for example Failed (exit 7 after 0.20s). The process preserves the failed child's exit code; task JSON records retain exit_code and add duration_ms (execution time excluding discovery and tool preparation). oyzu run list opens with a count (Available tasks · 8 across 1 target), then shows one table: the Task / Source / Command header appears once and every group shares its column widths. Tasks are grouped by target (for example cli and docs), with ungrouped user tasks under Project; each group heading shows its builder and task count. Listing is a quick lookup, so it prints no progress or logger lines. Each row shows the qualified runnable name, source and effective command arguments. Builder-discovered tasks are labeled Inferred with their provider; TOML-defined tasks show the effective source file, relative to the project when possible. (override) indicates a replacement of an inferred task or an earlier configuration definition. Native package scripts discovered through a builder are also labeled inferred; this distinguishes discovery from an Oyzu TOML definition, not script authorship. Cyan headings separate groups, inferred sources are muted and authored sources are purple. ui.color, NO_COLOR and terminal detection control color; Explicit ui.color=always/never wins; in auto mode NO_COLOR disables color and CLICOLOR_FORCE=1 enables it when NO_COLOR is absent. Long rows use lossless labeled records on narrow terminals. Unavailable tasks retain their reason. Commands quote arguments descriptively; they are not a portable shell script. Dependencies and hooks may add execution beyond that row. Credential-like command previews are withheld and terminal controls escaped. Do not embed credentials in task command arguments; use the supported environment or secret mechanisms instead. Listing reads discovery and resolved configuration but executes no tasks or native tools. JSON retains the task map and adds each task's origin object: kind (inferred or user-defined), source (full configuration source or null) and override (boolean). Existing argv and redacted environment fields retain their contracts. No configuration or lock files are changed by listing.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/compliance.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The provisional repository guard runs independently of the Oyzu executable. It requires Git and Python 3.11+; it does not compile or run dependencies or require a platform account. Full rules, command options, outputs, review behavior and outstanding release obligations are maintained in the compliance guide. From the repository root, python tooling/compliance/check.py compares tracked dependency inputs and notices with the factual baseline. Exit 0 means the inventory matches, not that a license or distribution is approved. Exit 1 reports drift or invalid records. Investigate the change before using --write-baseline; new inputs must be tracked by Git. --report PATH writes the factual JSON report, and --base REF adds a change summary against that Git baseline. All these operations are local/offline. No file is changed without a write/report option. --release intentionally exits 2 after valid inventory checks because the actual target-specific audit and artifact/source-availability gate are not implemented. The checker does not certify existing development CI artifacts. It cannot identify arbitrary copied source, infer all manager graphs or satisfy attribution by itself. On 2026-10-03, the maintainer removed the mandatory current-head human-approval gate. Compliance CI now checks the factual inventory, preserved notices and provisional release restriction without calling the GitHub reviews API. No review token or approval event is required. CODEOWNERS may still route voluntary review; technical ownership and legal/distribution approval remain separate concerns. Nine regression tests exercise inventory drift, notice deletion/escape, duplicate records, unreviewed dependencies and provisional release failure. They run locally on Windows and in Ubuntu GitHub Actions. No production Rust capability changes with this tooling.
CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/configuration.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them.

publish.default selects a named OCI destination or publication set when oyzu publish has no --destination. publish.destinations is a typed map of names to registry, repository, and optional paired usernameEnv/passwordEnv credential references. publish.sets maps names to nonempty destination lists. Destination and set names must be distinct. Every selected destination is required. publish.requirements contains provenance (bundlePath, accepted Ed25519 publicKey, builderId) and signing (keyEnv, publicKey). Public keys are base64 raw 32-byte keys; keyEnv references a separately provisioned base64 32-byte signing seed. Never store secret values in project configuration. Evidence paths resolve relative to the source declaring effective requirements. Configured once, at the project root. publish.* follows the root-only scope rule (OEP-0022 OD7, the rule [constraints] follows too): only the project root folder's oyzu.toml and oyzu.local.toml may set it, in a base, [context.<name>] or profile table. A [publish] table anywhere else is a configuration error that names the file and line, for every command that reads the configuration: CONFIG_SCOPE: <root>/api/oyzu.toml:1:1: [publish] is allowed only in the root oyzu.toml (<root>/oyzu.toml); move it there: publishing is configured once, for the whole project Before this rule a sub-folder's [publish] was accepted and silently ignored, because oyzu publish reads the root; move any such table to the root. oyzu config explain publish.default reports resolution: projectRoot. Independently released packages still publish separately: destinations select artifacts by build. These settings use the ordinary cascade (user, root project and root local files), selected profiles and mandatory constraints. Each destinations map, sets map, and requirements object is atomic: a later source replaces the whole value instead of merging nested entries. The settings govern standalone safeguards; they cannot grant managed publication authority. The builds, outputs and platforms their selectors name are checked before any build action runs (see names that cross files). See publishing for the complete example, evidence profile, digest-only coordinates and current limits.

Status: implemented (OEP-0022 M9, D6). A name oyzu.toml uses for something build.yaml or a builder declares is checked by one validator against the frozen build inventory before any action runs. An unknown or misplaced name is an error (exit code 3, a build refused at Prepare included) that names the file, line and column, lists the valid names and suggests the nearest one: Name Example Checked by A task key's build [tasks."api:test"]: api exists, and the file is the root or in api's folder chain oyzu config validate and every command that opens the project (oyzu build, --plan, oyzu run…) A publish selector's or evidence key's build publish.destinations.<name>.artifacts, publish.requirements.provenance.byArtifact keys: cli in cli/bin-oyzu the same A selector's platform @linux/arm64 is one of the build's declared platforms (unchecked for a build that declares none) the same A bound chart's image (OD5) a publication that publishes a chart with bindings also pushes each bound image to its with.repository (CONFIG_BINDING_UNPUSHED); checked for publish.default and each publish.sets entry, and by oyzu publish for the destinations it selects (PUBLISH_BINDING_UNPUSHED) the same, and oyzu publish A hook's task and depends_on [tasks.post_biuld], depends_on = ["schema:verfy"] (see task binding) every command that discovers the project's tasks, not config validate A selector's output bin-oyzu in cli/bin-oyzu is an output of cli each build's Prepare, once native preparation knows the outputs of the builds it prepares, before their first action; oyzu publish keeps its final check against the bundle CONFIG_REFERENCE_UNKNOWN: oyzu.toml:13:13: publish.destinations.github.artifacts names "clii/bin-oyzu", but there is no build clii; builds: cli, docs; did you mean cli/bin-oyzu? CONFIG_REFERENCE_UNKNOWN: oyzu.toml:13:13: publish.destinations.github.artifacts names "cli/bin-oyz", but build cli has no output bin-oyz; outputs of cli: cli/bin-oyzu, cli/bin-oyzu-shim; did you mean cli/bin-oyzu? Limits: only files some build's (or the invocation folder's) chain reads are checked, so a stray oyzu.toml in a folder with no build below it is not read at all (a [publish] table there is still ignored; a follow-up will report it); a selector for a build this invocation does not prepare has its output checked by oyzu publish; [targets.<build>] tables (OD18) are not implemented. The configuration engine implements the public OEP-0002 draft in Rust. Its CLI and wire formats remain experimental; implementation authorization does not change the proposal's maintainer-review status. See the acceptance contract and measured implementation status. oyzu config show presents resolved status and profile first, followed by setting tables grouped by namespace and the computation digest. Keys retain their exact spelling; booleans use true/false and empty lists use []. Environment values and task bodies remain redacted under configuration inspection's contract; use oyzu env for environment inspection. --json retains the structured result. See the CLI style guide.

Oyzu captures caller environment hints once when opening the configuration session, before build workers set their own CI=true. Detection is offline and independent of terminals, hostnames, network access and operating system. This is unverified execution context, never runner authentication, authorization or release eligibility. The following nonempty markers identify providers. Empty values and the trimmed, case-insensitive values false, 0, no, and off disable that individual marker. Provider Marker GitHub Actions / Gitea Actions GITHUB_ACTIONS / GITEA_ACTIONS GitLab / Azure Pipelines GITLAB_CI / TF_BUILD Jenkins / TeamCity / Bamboo JENKINS_URL / TEAMCITY_VERSION / bamboo_planKey Buildkite / CircleCI / Travis / AppVeyor BUILDKITE / CIRCLECI / TRAVIS / APPVEYOR Bitbucket Pipelines / Bitrise BITBUCKET_BUILD_NUMBER / BITRISE_IO Google Cloud Build BUILDER_OUTPUT AWS CodeBuild / Harness CODEBUILD_BUILD_ARN / HARNESS_BUILD_ID Codefresh / GoCD / Prow CF_BUILD_ID / GO_PIPELINE_LABEL / PROW_JOB_ID Drone / Cirrus / Semaphore DRONE / CIRRUS_CI / SEMAPHORE Netlify / Vercel / Xcode Cloud NETLIFY / VERCEL / CI_XCODE_PROJECT TaskCluster requires both TASK_ID and RUN_ID to be nonempty (RUN_ID=0 is valid). Additionally, exact CI=woodpecker, CI_NAME=sourcehut, and CI_NAME=codeship identify those providers. Any enabled CI value selects CI behavior even when the provider is unknown. Multiple provider matches are retained in sorted order; CI=false disables only the generic hint, not an enabled vendor marker. With no matching signal the context is local. Unknown platforms without a recognized marker must supply the conventional CI=true; no detector can identify every future or privately hosted system without a signal. Generic variables such as BUILD_ID alone are deliberately insufficient. config explain exposes executionContext with ci, sorted providers, and matched variable names in signals. Values and private runner URLs are not recorded. Build plans retain the same context in oyzu.dev/execution-context. The detector follows the environment-marker approach used by ci-info; its implementation is first-party and adds no dependency or copied vendor dataset. Plain oyzu build defaults to artifact building and packaging locally, plus any check at level required. In the pr, ci and release contexts it also runs every builder check (test, lint, format-check) that is not off; see check levels. oyzu build --full runs every check that is not off regardless of context; it does not change context detection or profile selection. config explain includes the resolved fullBuild request (default false); build plans record fullRequested. oyzu --profile ci build also runs every check that is not off (oyzu's built-in ci profile sets checks.run = "all"). CI needs no extra flags. A different profile or --no-profile does not turn off the checks of a detected CI context; a project turns a check off, or narrows a context to required checks, in oyzu.toml. See build context behavior.

Status: implemented for detection, pinning, display, recording and explain (build intent slice 1, BIN-01, BIN-25 and the context part of BIN-22). The context selects per-context values, including oyzu's own check level defaults, and policy constraints can be limited to contexts with when/unless selectors (policy constraints and selectors, slice 7). Every build resolves one context: local, pr, ci or release. Detection is the default and needs no flags. With no signal the context is local; any CI marker is at least ci; a documented pull/merge request or tag signal of a matched provider raises it to pr or release. When signals conflict the more demanding wins (release over pr over ci). Detection never fails a build. Provider pr signal release signal Documentation GitHub Actions GITHUB_BASE_REF set (pull request events only) GITHUB_REF_TYPE=tag GitHub variables GitLab CI_MERGE_REQUEST_ID CI_COMMIT_TAG predefined variables Azure Pipelines BUILD_REASON=PullRequest BUILD_SOURCEBRANCH begins refs/tags/ build variables, environment naming CircleCI CIRCLE_PULL_REQUEST CIRCLE_TAG variables Buildkite BUILDKITE_PULL_REQUEST is not false BUILDKITE_TAG environment variables Travis CI TRAVIS_PULL_REQUEST is not false TRAVIS_TAG environment variables Bitbucket Pipelines BITBUCKET_PR_ID BITBUCKET_TAG variables Drone DRONE_BUILD_EVENT=pull_request DRONE_BUILD_EVENT=tag DRONE_BUILD_EVENT AppVeyor none verified APPVEYOR_REPO_TAG=true environment variables Jenkins CHANGE_ID none verified multibranch Every other provider, and a bare CI, resolve to ci; Gitea Actions is left at ci until its documentation is checked. Signals are read only from the matched provider, and only fixed literals (=tag) are ever recorded, never values. Overrides. oyzu build --context <name> or OYZU_CONTEXT=<name> pins the context (the flag wins). An unknown name is the only context error (CONTEXT_INVALID); because every command that opens a configuration session resolves the context, an invalid OYZU_CONTEXT fails install, exec and config get as well as build. The rule is one-directional: under a vendor CI marker a pin may raise the context but not lower it (the request is ignored and a CONTEXT_OVERRIDE_IGNORED warning names why); with only the generic CI hint, or no signal, a pin may also lower it. Use OYZU_CONTEXT=release once in a manually triggered release workflow, which carries no tag signal. Resolved fact. extensions["oyzu.dev/execution-context"].context carries detected and detectedSource, requested (value, source), effective and its source, policy (the stricter of detected and requested, which policy constraints will evaluate against) and note. The one-line title shows only the value (context pr, context local); the Build context fact in Prepare gives the full detected via … or requested by … source text; build plans (--plan, --plan --json) and manifests record the same object in extensions["oyzu.dev/execution-context"]. oyzu config explain context reports the value, source and deciding signal. Facts are unverified hints: they never grant publication, credentials or cache authority. The same record carries fork (beside context) for task conditions: false outside a detected pull request; inside one, whether it comes from a fork, read from the GitHub Actions event payload (GITHUB_EVENT_PATH: head versus base repository) or GitLab's CI_MERGE_REQUEST_SOURCE_PROJECT_ID and CI_MERGE_REQUEST_PROJECT_ID; absent when the provider does not say.

Status: implemented (build intent slice 2, BIN-02 and the settings-resolution part of BIN-20). This section covers ordinary values; policy constraints limited to contexts and folders are described in policy constraints and selectors (slice 7). Check levels (slice 3) use it for their context defaults. Any registered setting can take a value that applies only when a given context is the build's effective context, in the same oyzu.toml that holds its base value: [checks] coverageMinimum = 50 [context.release.checks] coverageMinimum = 90 [context.pr] checks.coverageMinimum = 70 The table name is [context.<name>] with <name> exactly local, pr, ci or release; below it, tables and dotted keys are written as they are for the base value. The tables are valid in every scope that holds the setting (user, project root, component folder, oyzu.local.toml) and follow its scope rules: a project file still cannot set cache.remote or trust.enabled under a context. Precedence. Within one file the order, lowest first, is: the base value; the ci profile when CI inference (not the user) selected it; the effective context's value; a profile the user chose (--profile, OYZU_PROFILE, a task's inherited profile or profile.default). So an inferred [profiles.ci] table loses to the same file's [context.ci.*] table, while --profile ci beats it. This is the maintainer's decision of 2026-10-18 (decisions). Between files, the nearer scope wins, as for every other setting: built-in defaults, then user, then the project root oyzu.toml, then each component folder's oyzu.toml (nearest last), then oyzu.local.toml, then invocation inputs. So a component folder's base value beats the root's [context.release] value; to vary a component by context, write a [context.release] table in that component's file. A context table never applies when its context is not the effective one, whatever the other tables say. A lowered release check is warned about (R6 of the configuration split decision): in a release build, when a nearer folder's value (a base or profile value, or oyzu.local.toml) leaves a check level (checks.tests, checks.coverage, checks.lint, checks.format) below what a farther folder's [context.release] table asked for, every command that resolves it reports a CONFIG_RELEASE_LOWERED warning naming both files and lines, relative to the farther file's folder (checks.tests = advisory from app/oyzu.toml:2 lowers required from oyzu.toml:5 [context.release] in this release build). Plan shows it as a lowered note, oyzu build --plan as a Lowered: line and --plan --json as releaseLowerings per target, and plan and manifest targets record it under extensions["oyzu.dev/release-lowerings"] (setting, value, source, releaseValue, releaseSource). Precedence does not change: the nearer value still wins. The nearer folder's own configured value is compared, never the resolved one, so a constraint that changes the level afterwards (a policy or project cap below the release value) neither blames the folder nor hides its lowering; value is that folder's value. A nearer folder's own [context.release] value is deliberate and never warns. To make lowering impossible, use a project constraint. Constraints always win. Project constraints and then administrative constraints are evaluated after every ordinary value, including context values and chosen profiles, exactly as for a base value: a required member is added to the set a context chose, and a lock or bound replaces a value outside it, visibly, as described in policy constraints and selectors. Per target or once per build. The registry declares how each setting resolves. A per-target setting (the default: checks, task and environment settings and most others) resolves from each target's folder chain exactly as tool pins do (build tool scope): a root value applies to every target, a value in docs-site/oyzu.toml to the targets under docs-site/, and targets sharing a folder share settings. There are no target-keyed sections and nothing in build.yaml. A once-per-build setting is one the build treats as a property of the whole run: the scheduling, presentation and selector settings (build.jobs, build.isolation, ui.color, profile.default, config.*) and the cache.* family. Its [context.<name>] values are accepted in the user file, the project root oyzu.toml and oyzu.local.toml, and a component folder's [context.<name>] table for it is a configuration error. Of that list, profile.default and the administrative config.* settings cannot vary by context at all, and cache.remote, cache.ciRemote and cache.dir are accepted only from user scope; the rest (build.jobs, build.isolation, ui.color and the other cache.* settings) can. scan.jobs is a per-target setting. A component folder's base value for a once-per-build setting is still read for its targets, and the build combines them: build.jobs is the minimum over the build root and every selected target. Explain therefore reports that minimum for build.jobs, with the folders that have their own value listed under targetValues and the rule under combine. A root-only setting (publish.*, resolution projectRoot) goes one step further: no file outside the project root folder may hold a value for it at all, base, context or profile table alike (see standalone publication settings); the root-only [constraints] table follows the same rule. Errors. An unknown context name ([context.relese]), a table that is not a table, an invalid value, a selector or trust setting that cannot vary by profile or context, compatibility/overrides inside a context, a once-per-build setting in a component folder, and tool pins ([context.<name>.tools], which are not supported yet) are configuration errors reported as CONFIG_CONTEXT_UNKNOWN or CONFIG_CONTEXT_INVALID with file:line:column and the table. A setting that a project or local file may never set (such as cache.remote or trust.enabled) keeps its typed CONFIG_SCOPE refusal, which now names the full key (context.release.cache.remote) and file:line:column. An unknown setting under a context table is, as in the base, an inert warning with its line. Explain. oyzu config explain <setting> [--context <name>] [--target <name>] resolves as that build context (default: the detected or pinned one) for the named build.yaml target (default: the current folder) and prints the value, every scope that set it with the table's context (origins[].context), the contextValues considered for the setting (applied says the table's context matched, effective says that value is the one that took effect, so a matching value that a nearer scope overrode is applied but not effective; the human view labels these applied, overridden and not this context), resolution (perTarget, perBuild or projectRoot) and the target. A once-per-build or root-only setting is read at the project root whatever --target names (target.resolvedAt is build root), combined with component values as described above. When a pin was ignored because a CI provider marker is present (--context local under GitHub Actions), the human view prints that note and explains as the context actually in effect. --context and --target cannot be combined with --global, --project or --local, which read one file without resolving. An unknown target fails with CONFIG_TARGET_UNKNOWN listing the declared targets. Recorded. oyzu build --plan --json (per target as contextValues) and the plan and manifest targets of a build bundle (extensions["oyzu.dev/context-values"]) list the settings whose effective value was written in a context table, with the setting, value, context, source file and scope, so a build can be reproduced under --context. The configuration digest already covers the resolved values. Settings that the base value or a nearer scope decided are not listed. Known gap: isolated docker/image container plan targets (built through build/containers.rs) do not record oyzu.dev/context-values yet. Not covered here: per-context tool pins (follow-up) and when/unless selectors on context tables (follow-up). Tasks and hooks take when/unless with the same selector form policy constraints use; see task and hook conditions.

Status: implemented (build intent slice 3, BIN-04, BIN-05 and BIN-06). Policy can set a minimum level, optionally only in some contexts or folders, through an ordered bound (policy constraints and selectors, slice 7). Each check a builder offers has one level. The registered checks are tests, coverage, lint and format; they replace the former checks.required set, which is no longer a setting (an old checks.required line is an unknown-setting warning and has no effect). [checks] format = "off" lint = "advisory" coverage = "required" [context.release.checks] tests = "required" Level Runs in A failure off never: the stage is not planned and its tools are not prepared (coverage: validation-only while tests run) — advisory builds that run every check a CHECK_ADVISORY warning; the build still succeeds enforce (default) builds that run every check fails the build required every build, including a fast local build fails the build Which builds run every check is the setting checks.run: required runs only required checks, all runs every check that is not off. Its oyzu defaults are per-context values at the lowest scope, shown by oyzu config explain checks.run with the source built-in: Context checks.run Checks that run local required (base default) required only (fast build) pr, ci, release all (built-in context values) every check that is not off any, with --full — every check that is not off A project can change them like any other value, per context and per folder, for example [context.ci.checks] run = "required" for pushes to a main branch, or [checks] run = "all" to run every check locally. --full and --profile ci (whose built-in value is checks.run = "all") run every check that is not off. No flag skips a check the project chose: turning a check off is a committed change in oyzu.toml. Each builder stage serves checks: the test stage serves tests and coverage (coverage is collected by the tests, so tests = "off" also turns coverage off), lint serves lint and format-check serves format. A stage runs when any check it serves runs; it is off when every check it serves is off. A test stage is advisory when tests is advisory. Each report is judged by its own check: a failing test report of an advisory test stage is a warning, while its coverage report follows checks.coverage, so required or enforced coverage (including a shortfall below checks.coverageMinimum) still fails the build; an advisory coverage shortfall is a warning. Coverage off is validation-only. Coverage is collected by each builder's test command (for example cargo llvm-cov with nextest for Rust, c8 for Node), and that command does not yet change with the coverage level: with checks.coverage = "off" and tests running, coverage is still collected and its tools are still prepared, but it is never judged (no minimum, its report is not required, a missing or invalid coverage report is a warning). Plan and --plan --json say Collected with test; not judged (checks.coverage = off). Running tests without coverage collection is a recorded follow-up. Levels resolve per target from the folder chain, like every per-target setting: the nearest folder wins, and a context value beats the base value in the same file. An administrative constraint still wins: a lock or a minimum level replaces a project value below it and Plan says so (format enforce · admin policy minimum in pr, release (project oyzu.toml sets off)); an allowed set such as ["enforce", "required"] refuses a project value outside it with CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED. See policy constraints and selectors. Errors. A level other than the four is CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. A positive checks.coverageMinimum with checks.coverage = "off" (or checks.tests = "off") is CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE naming both sources. A required check, or a positive coverage minimum, that the selected builder cannot run fails in Plan with CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED: <target> cannot satisfy required <check> check. A policy lock or minimum of enforce or above on a check that this build runs but the builder has no action for fails in Plan naming the constraint and its source: CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED: <target> has no format check, which admin policy minimum enforce in pr, release (local-administration) requires; its builder cannot run one. Narrow such a constraint with a path selector. An authored task that depends on the stage of an off check is CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE naming the action and where the check was turned off. A required test or coverage check also makes its report mandatory (report-missing when absent), as checks.required did. Shown and recorded. Plan shows an off cell with its source (format · disabled in oyzu.toml, test · disabled in oyzu.toml [context.pr]), a skip cell with its reason (fast local build, or only required checks run in ci (checks.run)), and an advisory note for advisory stages that run (build view). --plan --json reports stage status off with the same reason. Plan and manifest targets record extensions["oyzu.dev/build-checks"] with mode (fast or full), levels (each check's level) and off (each off stage and its source); each check action records extensions["oyzu.dev/check-levels"], and an advisory one has required: false (as do the report intents of advisory or off checks), so its failure is recorded with status failed, one CHECK_ADVISORY warning carries the native cause, the target's artifacts are still collected, the manifest status stays succeeded, the exit code is 0 and oyzu inspect dist accepts the bundle. This holds on the native host path and the isolated path alike. The plan policy's requiredChecks lists the checks at required. Tools follow checks. Builder tool requirements are derived from the stages that run, so a builder's own requirement for an off or skipped check is not prepared: with format = "off" the Rust builder no longer adds rustfmt. A component the project declares itself, such as components = ["rustfmt"] in rust-toolchain.toml, stays a declared requirement of the toolchain.

Slice 5 of the build intent draft (BIN-08 to BIN-11). Each target is built with the development profile (a fast edit-build loop) or the optimized profile. Optimization follows where the output goes: a target is optimized when this build sends its artifacts off the machine, and development otherwise. The build Optimized because is a slice (oyzu build --slice, with or without --handoff) artifacts are handed off (--slice) is configured to write results to a shared remote cache (a cache.remote or, in CI, cache.ciRemote with cache.write = true; not with --no-cache), for a target whose results can be cached remotely (not an external builder, a host image worker or a target with secret environment values) configured to write results to a shared remote cache (a remote that turns out unusable at open still counts) selects a target that packages this one: a materialize input with usage runtime or data, or the target's own container image artifacts are packaged by image runs in the release context (a tag, --context release, OYZU_CONTEXT=release) release builds are published does none of these development: local dist only build.optimized (boolean, unset by default) decides instead whenever it is set. It is an ordinary per-target setting: a folder's oyzu.toml sets it for the targets under that folder, optionally per context ([context.release.build] optimized = false), and policy can set or lock it. oyzu build --optimized and --no-optimized set it for one invocation, above every file; giving both is a usage error (CLI_USAGE, exit 2). Policy constraints still win: a locked build.optimized replaces a flag or file that contradicts it, and the override is shown, as for any constrained setting. A build.optimized in user configuration is ignored in CI, like every non-presentation user setting. # cli/oyzu.toml: the self-installed CLI is always fast [build] optimized = true # oyzu.toml: never optimize release builds of this folder [context.release.build] optimized = false What optimized means per builder. Each builder declares it: Builder Optimized Development rust/app (native and isolated) cargo build --release cargo build dotnet (isolated) --configuration Release for build, test and pack --configuration Debug go/app no difference: the Go compiler always optimizes and every build uses -trimpath Node, Python, Java (Gradle, Maven, Ant), Helm, Docker, external plugins no difference: no separate optimized build A builder with no difference applies development whatever was requested, so its artifacts are labeled development and its cache entries are shared. Test stages keep each builder's test mode (Cargo's test profile) in both profiles. The profile is resolved once per target before builder planning and recorded on the plan and manifest target as extensions["oyzu.dev/optimization"] (requested, applied, reason, builder); --plan prints it as Profile: optimized · --optimized (cargo build --release) and --plan --json reports it as each target's optimization with a summary. Each artifact's profile is optimized only when the builder's own optimizing commands produced it, so an authored replacement of the build stays development (build bundles). Optimized is not publishable. The profile never implies reproducible output or publication eligibility; native host output still confers none.

plugins.development maps a built-in builder id such as go/app to an absolute plugin executable path. It is accepted only from user, machine or administrative configuration and replaces that builder's native host operations for the invocation. See local development plugin bindings. plugins.packages maps such an id to { archive, sha256 } or { oci, identity?, trustedRoot? }: a verified, installed package whose selection oyzu.lock pins. Same scopes. See plugin packages. plugins.preview (boolean, default false) makes preview plugin releases from the catalog eligible. Same scopes, and never from a profile: a project file, oyzu.local.toml or profile that sets it fails with CONFIG_SCOPE. See plugin catalog.

engines.packages admits exact development engine archives; engines.development (boolean, default false) independently permits the explicit local build --engine-development invocation. Both are restricted to user, machine and administrative sources, never project/local files or profiles. Engine permission uses actual-root path constraints and the strictest caller context; CI/PR/release cannot use the development override. See engine staging for selection, evidence and errors. engines.requirePin is an administrative-only Boolean, default false. An applicable protected locked: true, value: true policy constraint requires an exact engine pin and complete build lock; a policy default alone does not. Ordinary machine/user/project/local/invocation settings and profiles cannot set it. See policy-required pins for the candidate behavior and qualification status. Project trust controls are trust.enabled (boolean, default true) and trust.parents (absolute folder paths, default []). They and platform.url, platform.account, platform.authentication.provider, cache.remote, cache.ciRemote are rejected in project/local scope, including profile overlays. Set them in user/global, machine or administrative configuration. Supported invocation environment sources are OYZU_PROJECT_TRUST, OYZU_PLATFORM_URL, OYZU_PLATFORM_ACCOUNT, OYZU_PLATFORM_AUTH_PROVIDER, OYZU_CACHE_REMOTE and OYZU_CACHE_CI_REMOTE; each overrides ordinary files while remaining subject to administrative constraints. OYZU_PROJECT_TRUST accepts true/false, on/off, yes/no or 1/0. See folder trust for the environment application boundary and native user-state records.

build.yaml accepts a builds mapping with uses, path, platforms, depends_on, inputs, materialize, bindings, fetches and with per entry; any other field fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE naming it. depends_on is an ordering-only list of producer build names; it does not transfer artifacts. inputs names extra source paths a build reads (declared inputs), fetches declares pinned downloads (declared fetches), and bindings writes a produced image's reference into a chart's values during the build (image bindings records its verification and limits). Configuration owns normalization and freezes all declared platforms; builders own validation of with. See the Rust build options for the implemented options and execution limits. This is a partial implementation of the proposed build model, not support for every future example. Tool requirements remain in TOML and lock identities remain in oyzu.lock. The root keys of an inventory are builds, members and exclude; any other root key fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE naming it. members (split inventories, OEP-0022 M18) is refused as not supported yet. exclude lists folders where discovery recognizes a build that is deliberately not one. In a build entry uses is optional (OEP-0022 OD13): web: {path: web} is a complete entry when exactly one builder recognizes web, and discovery freezes that builder into the inventory before planning. A folder no builder or several builders recognize fails naming the candidates and the line to write. Folders discovery recognizes that the inventory leaves out are listed by oyzu discover and oyzu build --plan, never built; oyzu discover --write declares them and oyzu discover --check fails on them in CI. A folder the native workspace manifest of a declared build lists as a member (Cargo members, go.work use, npm/Yarn/pnpm workspaces) is covered by that build and needs no entry (discovery decisions). oyzu config validate checks chart bindings (unknown producers, repository and values fields) without discovery. Checks that depend on an omitted uses (the with options of that build, bindings only on helm/chart builds, a docker/image producer) wait until discovery infers the builder, as oyzu discover and oyzu build --plan do. builds: is the only shape (OEP-0022 M1, step D5). The former flat shape, with build entries at the top level, is refused with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE; the message shows the file's own lines indented under builds:, which is the whole move: # Refused: builds at the top level cli: uses: rust/app # Accepted: the same entries, indented two spaces under builds: builds: cli: uses: rust/app Fields the flat shape once carried have their homes: matrix is refused (runtime versions are toolsets in oyzu.toml, see verification toolsets) with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE showing the toolset form. Artifact platforms are only platforms: [<os/arch[/abi]>, ...]: platform: <os/arch>, matrix.platform and the rust object are refused naming the replacement (platforms: [...]; Cargo features in with.features and cross-compilation targets as platforms entries). A build that declares one platform keeps its name; several platforms give each instance a platform-qualified ID (platform requirements). container is the python/app option with.container (Python application containers), dependencies is the docker/image option with.dependencies (Docker dependency contexts), and docker/image's former with.load is the docker.load setting; the old spellings fail with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE naming the new location. A builder checks its with options when the inventory is read, so oyzu config validate reports them. See the migration plan and the 2026-10-19 configuration split decision.

Other tools use the same file name: Dart's build_runner reads a build.yaml with targets:, builders: and global_options: in each package. A build.yaml is an Oyzu inventory only when its root has builds, members or exclude, or the refused flat shape (a top-level entry whose mapping has uses); a file that is not valid YAML also counts, so its syntax error is reported rather than the file skipped. A misspelled envelope counts too, so it fails naming the root keys (found build (did you mean builds:?)) instead of being skipped: a root key equal to builds, members or exclude ignoring case, the key build, or any root key with uses two levels below it (buildz: {web: {uses: node/app}}). A leading UTF-8 byte order mark is ignored. Any other build.yaml, including an empty one, belongs to another tool (OEP-0022 R7): it never makes its folder a build root, a project root or a configuration boundary; discovery and oyzu discover --check continue below its folder as if it were absent, so a Flutter package inside a monorepo no longer hides the builds under it; at the project root, zero-config discovery decides the builds, as without a build.yaml, and every discovering command (oyzu build, --plan, discover, run) warns CONFIG_BUILD_FILE_IGNORED: build.yaml: ignored, not an Oyzu inventory … naming its root keys (a JSON diagnostic event on stderr with --json); oyzu discover (and --check, --write) lists it under Skipped with its root keys; JSON records it in skipped_build_files (plain oyzu discover without an inventory) or skippedBuildFiles (the inventory record), each entry {path, keys}. oyzu discover --write never edits another tool's build.yaml at the project root: it fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE naming the file's root keys and leaves it unchanged. An Oyzu inventory cannot share that file, so such a folder can only use zero-config discovery (a known limitation of keeping the build.yaml name, OD2).

Every refusal of a build.yaml names the place to fix, as build.yaml:LINE:COLUMN: after the diagnostic code (OEP-0022 M22). This covers YAML syntax errors (CONFIG_SYNTAX), anchors, aliases, tags, merge keys and duplicate keys, which an inventory never uses (CONFIG_SYNTAX, CONFIG_DUPLICATE), the flat shape and wrong root keys, unknown, moved or retired build fields, uses, platforms, materialize, bindings and fetches values, unknown dependencies, a builder discovery cannot infer, and with options a builder refuses (at the option itself when the message names it, else at with). For example: ✗ CONFIG_SYNTAX: build.yaml:3:6: invalid YAML: while parsing a flow mapping, did not find expected ',' or '}' ✗ CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE: build.yaml:5:7: docker/image with.repository must be a repository name without scheme, tag or digest With --json the same text is the error record's error. Lines and columns start at 1. A leading UTF-8 byte order mark (written by some Windows editors and PowerShell 5) is ignored. The file is read by Oyzu's one YAML reader (crates/oyzu-yaml), which follows the YAML 1.2 core schema: true, ~, 12 and 1.5 are a boolean, null, integer and float, and yes, on or 1.2.3 stay strings.

Oyzu generates a JSON Schema for each of its two files, so an editor can complete keys and flag a value or a key in the wrong file while you type. The build.yaml schema comes from the build model (the root keys and every build field above); the oyzu.toml schema comes from the settings registry (every registered setting, nested by its dotted key) and the sections the reader accepts (profiles, context, toolsets, constraints, overrides, compatibility). Builder with options and settings a plugin registers are left open. A schema follows the reader, with two deliberate exceptions where it is stricter. In build.yaml it flags what the reader refuses: an unknown root key or build field, and a value of the wrong type or form. The exception: its path pattern (path, inputs, materialize to and into) refuses \ and : anywhere in a path, so a file stays portable across Windows, macOS and Linux, while the reader decides such a path where it is used. In oyzu.toml it flags a value of the wrong type for a registered setting and the wrong-file case: a build.yaml key such as [builds.web], exclude or a top-level uses is refused by the schema, while the reader only warns about it as an unknown section (CONFIG_UNKNOWN_OPTIONAL). Any other unknown key inside a section, or unknown section, stays open in the schema because the reader only warns about it and oyzu config validate --strict refuses it. The CLI's own checks stay the authority, including rules a schema cannot express (a value accepted only from user configuration, a root-only section, which ABIs an OS has). File Published at (every release, unversioned) build.yaml https://github.com/oyzuai/oyzu/releases/latest/download/build.yaml.schema.json oyzu.toml https://github.com/oyzuai/oyzu/releases/latest/download/oyzu.toml.schema.json The release workflow attaches both files to each release, so the URLs follow the latest release. The same schemas are committed as docs/contracts/v1alpha1/build.schema.json and oyzu-toml.schema.json; a test keeps them equal to what the CLI generates. oyzu config schema prints them, with no project, configuration session or network: oyzu config schema # both files, their URLs and how to print each oyzu config schema build.yaml > build.yaml.schema.json oyzu config schema oyzu.toml > oyzu.toml.schema.json oyzu --json config schema build.yaml # {"kind": "config-schema", "file", "asset", "url", "print", "schema"} With a file named, the schema itself is the output (a payload, like shell code), printed as JSON in both modes; --json wraps it in the record above. Without one, --json prints {"kind": "config-schemas", "schemas": [...]}. Use a saved copy on offline or air-gapped machines. To point an editor at them: build.yaml: the YAML language server (VS Code's YAML extension and others) reads a first-line comment # yaml-language-server: $schema=https://github.com/oyzuai/oyzu/releases/latest/download/build.yaml.schema.json. oyzu discover --write adds it when it creates or edits build.yaml and the file has no yaml-language-server: $schema= comment yet; add it by hand to a file you write yourself. build.yaml is not registered with SchemaStore, because SchemaStore already lists Dart's build configuration for that name. oyzu.toml: point Taplo or Even Better TOML at the URL (Taplo's [[schema]] setting, or a #:schema <URL> first line). Registration with SchemaStore, so editors find it by file name, is a maintainer action and is pending.

Configuration commands default to human-readable output. Pass global --json for structured results and errors; see CLI output. Use an Oyzu CLI built from this branch; these commands are not a promise about older releases. Standalone configuration inspection and editing require no platform account, Docker, native ecosystem toolchain or network service. The client has Windows, macOS and Linux implementations; platform qualification and measured checks are tracked in implementation status. Running tasks or builds additionally requires their explicitly provisioned native tools. In an otherwise empty directory named config-demo, save this as oyzu.toml: [build] jobs = 2 [profile] default = "dev" [profiles.dev.build] jobs = 3 [ui] color = "never" Run these commands from its parent directory. Expected values assume standalone operation with no administrative constraints, local overrides or OYZU_PROFILE selection: oyzu --root config-demo config get build.jobs oyzu --root config-demo --no-profile config get build.jobs oyzu --root config-demo config validate --strict --all-profiles oyzu --root config-demo --profile dev config set build.jobs 4 --project oyzu --root config-demo config get build.jobs oyzu --root config-demo --profile dev config unset build.jobs --project oyzu --root config-demo config get build.jobs The successive get results are 3, 2, 4, and 2.
