Validation reports success; with --json it returns valid: true. Removing the profile assignment exposes the base value; it does not restore the old value of 3. Set/unset return the destination path and updated key. No project task runs in this walkthrough.

oyzu --root path/to/project config show --json oyzu --root path/to/project config explain build.jobs --json oyzu --root path/to/project config profiles oyzu --root path/to/project config validate --strict --all-profiles oyzu --root path/to/project --profile integration run test oyzu --root path/to/project --no-profile run test --root explicitly fixes both build and configuration roots. Otherwise the nearest ancestor build.yaml inventory within the current Git worktree selects the build (another tool's build.yaml never does; see which build.yaml files are Oyzu's); configuration still inherits from the Git worktree root. Outside Git, the outermost ancestor with Oyzu configuration or a build declaration bounds inheritance, falling back to the invocation directory. With no build declaration, that boundary remains the conventional-discovery root. -C / --directory selects the invocation directory; --root alone also selects that directory. Git boundaries require recognizable repository metadata: HEAD plus the common objects and refs directories. A .git file must contain a gitdir: <path> pointer to that metadata; linked worktrees use its commondir pointer for the common directories. Relative pointers are resolved from their declaring directory. An unborn repository and packed refs remain valid boundaries; no commit or loose branch ref is required. Empty .git directories, malformed pointers and missing metadata do not define a workspace. They are left intact. Recognition reads bounded local metadata without running Git, executing configuration or establishing repository integrity. Conservative nested repository/submodule exclusions during target traversal remain in effect. Entering an independent nested example and running oyzu build --plan therefore selects the example without --root. Its oyzu.lock and build outputs belong to that selected root. Parent inventories are not merged, and automatic discovery skips nested build roots. An explicit parent target path remains authoritative. Configuration retains normal project/local precedence, relative paths retain their declaring-file origin, and machine/enterprise constraints remain enforced. A selected build root may declare its default profile; ordinary target subdirectories cannot. Explicit composition and shared-workspace lock ownership are not implemented. Relative task cwd values are now relative to the TOML file that declares them. For a root-file override of api:test, use cwd = "api/checks" to select that directory. Multiple targets cannot own the same native build unit; use distinct project paths or distinct builders where appropriate. Sources resolve in this order: built-ins, verified corporate defaults, protected local administrative defaults, machine configuration, user configuration, root-to-target oyzu.toml, eligible root-to-target oyzu.local.toml, and invocation compatibility inputs. Each source applies its base followed by the selected profile. Siblings receive separate snapshots. Arrays replace, tasks replace atomically, and [overrides].remove removes explicit environment/task entries. Environment removals also unset inherited variables during development task execution. A task environment can replace a global variable with the same spelling, but case aliases such as TOKEN and token are rejected across the combined environment on every host. Known tool aliases share that same precedence. For example, project node = "22" overrides global "oyzu:node" = "latest"; a selected toolset can override it through either spelling. Inspection retains the spellings with their effective value and winning provenance. Lock ownership follows the winning source. Declaring multiple aliases for one tool in the same overlay remains ambiguous. Administrative constraints bind the selected value regardless of its spelling. Profile selection uses explicit --profile or --no-profile, inherited task selection, OYZU_PROFILE, the eligible root/default selector, inferred CI's empty ci profile, then no profile. Names grant no authority. Inferred CI excludes user computation settings and local files; --local-overrides requests local files, subject to administrative restrictions. Excluded local files are not parsed.

A toolset is a named set of tool versions, for testing builds on other tools than the ones they ship with and for running commands with them (OD1, OD16). oyzu build adds a toolset's verification run for each build whose builder uses one of its tools: in every context but local unless the toolset lists contexts, and locally with oyzu build --verify-with NAME. A run repeats the build's build and test stages with the toolset's tools and never ships an artifact; verification toolsets describes runs, their evidence and CI fan-out. A profile cannot change tools: [profiles.<name>.tools] (or a tools key inside a profile table) is refused by oyzu config validate and by every command that reads the configuration, in every file, with CONFIG_PROFILE_TOOLS naming the file and line and showing the toolset that replaces it: CONFIG_PROFILE_TOOLS: oyzu.toml:4:1: [profiles.x.tools] is not allowed: a profile cannot change tools, so the tools a build uses never depend on the selected profile. Move the table to a toolset: [toolsets.x.tools] go = "1.24.13" and select it with `oyzu --toolset x exec -- …` (also run, env, activate, which, install, update and uninstall) Define a toolset in a project's oyzu.toml or oyzu.local.toml: [tools] rust = "1.99.1" [toolsets.go-test.tools] go = "1.24.13" [toolsets.node24] contexts = ["ci", "release"] # optional; default: every context but local platforms = ["linux/x86_64"] # optional; default: one run, on the build's first declared platform or the host tools.node = "24" and select it for one invocation with the global --toolset NAME option, written like --profile: oyzu --toolset go-test install --frozen oyzu --toolset go-test exec -- go version Commands. --toolset serves exec, run, env, activate (an activated shell keeps the toolset on every prompt), which, pin (locks only that toolset's tools), and the project-scoped install (without specs it installs, and locks when needed, the toolset's tools; with specs it declares them in [toolsets.NAME.tools]), update and uninstall (both act on that toolset's declarations and lock sets only). Every other command refuses it with TOOLSET_UNSUPPORTED, as do activate --shims and --global installs, updates and removals. oyzu build refuses it with TOOLSET_BUILD_REFUSED naming oyzu build --verify-with NAME: a build always uses the [tools] versions, so a toolset never changes what ships; --verify-with adds the toolset's verification run instead. Verification runs. contexts lists the contexts (local, pr, ci, release) whose builds run the toolset's verification runs; without it a toolset runs in pr, ci and release, never local, and contexts = [] turns it (or an inherited definition) off. platforms lists the os/arch[/abi] platforms to make one run each for; without it there is one run, assigned to the build's first declared platform (the host's when the build declares none), and a job builds the runs assigned to the platform it builds. A toolset applies only to builds whose builder uses one of its tools, so a Go toolset adds nothing to a Node build in the same folder. Precedence. The toolset's tool requests replace the cascade's, above every file (a nearer folder's [tools] value included) and below policy: administrative and project constraints still bind a toolset's tools, and a value outside a policy lock fails with CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED. Tools the toolset does not name keep their cascade value. A toolset is exempt from native pin agreement (OD10 rule 6): a toolset Go below the go.mod minimum is used as written, wherever the toolset is defined, never refused or replaced by the minimum. oyzu tools current --all lists toolset declarations with their toolset. Inheritance. One definition of a name applies, whole, as tasks do: the last one in the source order, which is every oyzu.toml from the root to the folder, then every included oyzu.local.toml from the root to the folder. So a nearer oyzu.toml replaces a farther one, and any included oyzu.local.toml that defines the name, even the root's, replaces every oyzu.toml, including a nested folder's. The folder the command runs from must have the name in its chain, or the command fails with CONFIG_TOOLSET_UNKNOWN, listing the toolsets defined there; a build target in another folder chain, which no file defining the toolset reaches, keeps its cascade tools. A build sees, per build, the toolsets its own folder chain defines, the nearest definition of each name applying whole. Nested folders lock nothing yet. The lock labels a toolset's sets by its name alone, so only a toolset whose applied definition is in the project root's oyzu.toml or oyzu.local.toml is locked. For one defined (or redefined) in a nested folder's file, --toolset NAME install, install SPEC, update, uninstall and pin, and any exec, run or verification run that would install or lock its tools, fail with TOOLSET_NESTED_LOCK, naming the file, and change nothing; exec, run, env and which with tools already locked still work. Plain oyzu pin and oyzu update (without --toolset) leave such a toolset out, name it under Toolsets not locked (toolsetsNotLocked in JSON) with the reason, and still succeed; so do they for a toolset whose tools policy refuses. A lock identity for nested-folder toolsets is a named follow-up. Nested commands. A task run with oyzu --toolset NAME run sets OYZU_INHERITED_TOOLSET (to @none when the task runs without one), so a nested oyzu exec, run, env, activate, which, install, update or uninstall keeps the task's toolset. Every other nested command, oyzu build included, removes the variable from its own environment before it starts anything, so neither it nor its native steps (and their nested oyzu exec) see a toolset its plan and cache keys do not record. Validation and additions. A toolset holds its tools table and optionally contexts and platforms. Unknown optional fields warn and are ignored, allowing a newer configuration to be read by an older CLI with this behavior. Unknown contexts, repeated or empty platform lists, and non-tool keys such as platforms or ignore under tools remain CONFIG_TOOLSET_INVALID errors. Toolsets are refused in user, machine and administrative configuration and inside [profiles.*] or [context.*] tables (CONFIG_SCOPE). Lock and caches. The tools a toolset supplies (declares itself) are locked in oyzu.lock as its own request sets, labelled toolset = "NAME", beside the [tools] sets, which carry no label; the tools it inherits from [tools] stay in the [tools] sets. A toolset install (or exec, run, update) first gives [tools] its own copy of any pin it requests that only the toolset's sets held (a tool moved from the toolset into [tools]), then drops the toolset's copies of tools it no longer supplies that another set still pins; a pin no other set holds is kept, since another toolset may rely on it. Tool identity, request digests and cache keys depend on the requests alone, never on the profile or the toolset name. A toolset's install, install --update, update, declaration (install SPEC), uninstall and the automatic installation of exec and run add or change only that toolset's sets: they never rewrite a [tools] request or another toolset's, and the [tools] commands never rewrite a toolset's. Without names, oyzu --toolset NAME update and install --update re-resolve only the tools the toolset declares, never the [tools] tools it leaves alone. One request string resolves to one version in the whole lock, so a request a toolset shares with [tools] (the same rust = "1.99.1") uses the same pin, and updating it updates it wherever it appears. A scope ([tools] or a toolset) that installs with a pin only another scope's set holds gets a labelled set of its own with that pin, and removing the tool from one scope gives every other scope that still declares it a set of its own first, so uninstall in one scope never takes away a pin another scope uses; it says where the tool is still declared. oyzu install --frozen writes nothing, so it adds no such set. oyzu install --frozen with or without a toolset replays the pins its requests need. oyzu pin covers every toolset: beside the [tools] sets it locks, for each build, the tools each toolset its folder sees supplies, in that toolset's labelled set, whatever the context and whether or not the build's builder uses them (a toolset can serve only oyzu --toolset NAME exec). oyzu --toolset NAME pin locks only that toolset's tools. Plain oyzu update re-resolves the [tools] tools and then each toolset's, each in its own sets, and its table names the set of each row; oyzu update TOOL updates the tool wherever [tools] or a toolset declares it. Locks written before D4a can hold a toolset's tools in an unlabelled set, which keeps working. This repository's opt-in Go adapter checks use the go-test toolset; see CONTRIBUTING.md. config show, get, explain, profiles, and validate do not execute project tasks. If resolution is blocked, show and explain return an explicit unresolved status without effective values; validate remains the failing validation command. The credential-origin and trust-control scope ban is an exception: platform.url, platform.account, cache.remote, cache.ciRemote, trust.enabled and trust.parents in project/local sources are hard errors even for show and explain, in human and JSON output and in CI when that source is included. The error names the key, source and user/global or administrative remedy. Configuration inspection displays ordinary environment settings and path arrays; credential-like environment names and recognizable sensitive values remain redacted, as do task bodies. Discovery/task listing also redacts environment values. Explain includes source histories, byte spans, exclusions, constraint source IDs and the effective computation digest. Warnings carry severity, source byte spans when available, target scope, and a remedy without including the configured value. Unknown optional settings warn and stay inert, including unknown sections, fields under [toolsets.<name>], controls under [env._], and unknown fields inside understood objects: tool requests, environment secret references and path controls, task report declarations, publication destinations and their evidence options, registry routes, and engine/plugin package source declarations. Known fields, including required identifiers and digests, still validate. Unknown enum values or destination kinds cannot be executed and remain errors. They are not exported to the environment or applied to effective configuration. Similarity to a known section name supplies a spelling hint, not a failure. This compatibility behavior applies to clients containing this fix; already installed older binaries retain their original parsing behavior. New functionality that is essential for correct execution must declare a required capability through [compatibility].requires rather than rely on an ignored setting. Constraint entries, policy rules, required publication evidence and selector expressions retain their documented validation; ignoring optional configuration does not authorize bypassing required controls. Known invalid values, unsupported required capabilities, duplicate keys and unsupported schema majors fail. --strict rejects optional warnings. --all-profiles validates inactive capability requirements and profile outcomes.

oyzu --root path/to/project config set build.jobs 8 --project oyzu --root path/to/project config set checks.tests required --local oyzu --root path/to/project --profile dev config set ui.color never --global oyzu --root path/to/project config unset build.jobs --project Exactly one of --global (the user configuration file), --project, or --local is required. --directory can select a contained nested project scope. unset removes an assignment in that file and exposes inherited values; it does not create a removal tombstone. Ordinary edits remain available to repair invalid values even when resolution is blocked; they do not activate values or alter protected records. Edits preserve unrelated comments and unknown syntax, validate known types/scopes, and compare the original bytes before atomic replacement. Concurrent changes produce CONFIG_EDIT_CONFLICT. A small .oyzu-config-edit.lock coordinates Oyzu writers and is excluded from source snapshots. Only an explicit --profile NAME directs an edit into that profile. An inferred/default profile does not change the write destination: an edit without --profile writes the base section. A profile cannot hold tools: config set tools.NAME VALUE --profile P fails with CONFIG_PROFILE_TOOLS; declare toolset tools with oyzu --toolset P install NAME@VERSION (see toolsets). Scalar booleans and numbers are parsed by type; strings are literal. Use --json-value for arrays or objects. The array example above uses shell quoting supported by PowerShell and POSIX shells. Edits cannot repair malformed TOML syntax; correct that syntax in an editor first. They cannot modify administrative or enrollment records.

All config commands default to human-readable output. Add global --json for structured results and errors. The JSON schema is experimental. Command Result and important behavior show Effective values, selected profile, digest, diagnostics and resolution status get KEY One effective value (a JSON value with --json); fails if the key has no effective value explain [KEY] Resolution evidence, optionally narrowed to a key; includes origins and constraints profiles Available profiles, selected profile and selection reason validate [--strict] [--all-profiles] valid: true on success; nonzero exit on validation failure status Standalone/enrolled state and managed cache health; does not refresh over the network refresh Explicit online policy acquisition; returns revision and offline deadline; requires protected enrollment set / unset Changes one ordinary file and reports its destination; does not establish that the edited value is effective show, get and explain accept mutually exclusive --global, --project and --local flags. These inspect only the selected file: the user configuration, oyzu.toml in the selected directory, or oyzu.local.toml there, respectively. For example, oyzu config get build.jobs --global reads the user declaration; oyzu -C packages/api config show --project shows that directory's declarations. Without a scope flag, the merged effective configuration remains the default. Scoped reads do not inject defaults, inspect other sources, contact policy services or execute tasks. They preserve the normal inspection redaction. An explicit --profile NAME overlays only that profile from the selected file; automatic/default profile selection does not apply to file inspection. show/explain report the source, scope and whether the file exists, with empty values when absent; get fails when the key is not declared there. These are declarations, not a claim that execution policy allows the requested values. TOML syntax failures identify file:line:column (one-based Unicode character coordinates) and the parser's reason, including during set/unset. Source snippets are omitted to keep configuration values out of diagnostics. Correct malformed syntax in an editor before retrying. Strict validation retains every warning's key, source, available line/column and byte span, message and remedy; human errors list them and JSON errors include a diagnostics array. Strict validation still fails instead of silently accepting the warnings. Human explain groups exact setting keys with effective values and their last source. Multiple origins appear as an ordered resolution history; the last source does not imply it supplied every element of a merged value. Only nonempty policy restrictions, exclusions and diagnostics are expanded. With no restrictions it prints one policy summary rather than an empty entry for every setting. Source paths omit Windows extended-path prefixes for display. Ordinary environment paths and compiler settings remain visible. Sensitive values stay redacted. explain <key> narrows the view; --json retains the complete metadata, including byte spans, constraint source IDs, context signals and digest. show and explain can exit successfully with status: "unresolved" and no effective values. status can likewise return an unhealthy managed state successfully. Automation must inspect these fields or use validate as its configuration gate. Execution errors are reported on stderr with a nonzero exit status. Inspection does not run tasks, but resolving an enrolled configuration can contact the policy endpoint and update its cache. Thus inspection is not necessarily network-free or free of persistent state changes.

Ordinary settings below can appear in machine, user, project or local configuration and in profiles, subject to eligibility and administrative constraints. An absent default means no value is contributed by the registry. Recognition of a setting does not imply that its downstream integration is available. Key Type and built-in default Current behavior scan.jobs Integer 1–65535; default 2 Bounds independent scan checks, including remote analysis waits; 1 serializes checks analysis.rules Table of rule id to off, advisory or enforce; no value (every rule advisory) Experimental (OEP-0020 S5). Unknown rule ids and levels are configuration errors that name the valid ids. The nearest scope that sets it replaces lower scopes as a whole; a managed constraint can pin the whole value. Consumed by oyzu build --check and oyzu build per target; never grants authority analysis.suppress Array of {rule, path?, reason} tables; none Experimental. reason is mandatory and non-empty, path is an optional project-relative glob over the finding's file. Suppressed findings do not fail and stay in --json; unmatched suppressions are reported as stale notes. Replaced as a whole by the nearest scope build.jobs Integer 1–65535; available logical parallelism, fallback 1 Bounds independent preparation and ready build actions; the smallest root/target ceiling and worker-memory admission apply. oyzu build --jobs N (-j N), then the OYZU_BUILD_JOBS environment variable, override every file for one invocation; see worker ceiling. Scheduling only: not part of the configuration digest, so a serial and a parallel build share cached results build.isolation auto, docker, crun; auto Which sandbox runs the isolated steps of Node targets on Linux: auto uses Docker when an engine answers and the daemonless sandbox (crun) otherwise; docker always uses Docker; crun uses crun even with Docker present. --no-docker and OYZU_NO_DOCKER=1 select crun. Scheduling only: not part of the configuration digest, so both backends share cached results build.optimized Boolean; no value Per target, per context allowed. Unset: optimization follows where the output goes; true/false selects the optimized or development profile. oyzu build --optimized/--no-optimized set it for one invocation; policy constraints win. Not part of the configuration digest: the profile a builder applies enters action keys instead, so builders that optimization does not change keep one entry build.executors Table of target platform (os/arch[/abi], aliases accepted and stored canonically) to host, cross-toolchain or container; no value Per target, per context allowed ([context.release.build.executors]). Declares the only executor that builds that platform; when it is unavailable the platform is not built here, with the reason, and an explicit request for it (--platform, --all-platforms, the host platform in release) fails with PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE. Nothing falls back to another executor. Undeclared platforms use the default route. See platforms and executors version.strategy auto, native, tags, conventional; auto Selects artifact version inference; computation setting consumed by each builder; never grants release authority checks.tests, checks.coverage, checks.lint, checks.format off, advisory, enforce, required; enforce Check levels: off never runs, advisory failures are warnings, enforce runs in builds that run every check, required runs in every build and makes its report mandatory checks.run required, all; required, with built-in context values all for pr, ci and release Whether a build runs every check that is not off (all) or only required ones; --full runs every check checks.coverageMinimum Integer 0–100; 0 Positive minimum requires coverage evidence when coverage runs; missing or zero-denominator coverage fails (a warning when checks.coverage is advisory); with coverage off it is a configuration error ui.color auto, always, never; auto Human task labels/status only; JSON stays unstyled profile.default Profile name; absent Default selector; cannot be declared inside a profile or nested project selector scope cache.remote OCI URL; absent Destination of the experimental remote OCI action cache (oci://host[:port]/repository/prefix; plain HTTP only for loopback hosts). Credentials, query and fragment are forbidden. A registry that asks for sign-in gets a token through its token endpoint; the credential is never a setting: it comes from OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN, or in a CI job from its ID tokens (OYZU_ID_TOKEN_URL) toolIndex.url HTTPS URL (HTTP only for a loopback host), or false; https://github.com/oyzuai/tool-index/releases/latest/download/ Base URL of the signed public tool index; by default the newest release of the public index. false: no index, so registry packages resolve from the pinned registry. No credentials, query or fragment toolIndex.trustedRoot Absolute path; absent (Sigstore's production trusted root: compiled in, or newer from oyzu tools trust refresh) A Sigstore trusted_root.json (Fulcio CA certificates, Rekor log keys and timestamp authorities) to verify the index's signature bundle against, for a private Sigstore deployment. User or machine scope only (CONFIG_SCOPE in a project file) toolIndex.identity https: URI; https://github.com/oyzuai/tool-index/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main The signing certificate identity (SAN URI) the index must be signed by, for a customer-signed index. The OIDC issuer (https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com) and runner environment (github-hosted) are fixed. User or machine scope only (CONFIG_SCOPE in a project file) toolCatalog.url HTTPS URL (HTTP only for a loopback host); absent Delivery edge of the organization tool catalog. Set: registry packages, all Oyzu archive providers and indexed Rust install only versions the organization approved, through the edge, with the token from OYZU_TOOL_CATALOG_TOKEN. Lock it in admin-settings.json to make it mandatory toolCatalog.adminUrl HTTPS URL (HTTP only for a loopback host); absent; env OYZU_TOOL_CATALOG_ADMIN_URL Base URL of the delivery admin API for oyzu tools request and --cancel (see tool catalog). User, machine or administrative scope only (CONFIG_SCOPE in a project file); lockable in admin-settings.json toolCatalog.keys Array of one to eight ed25519:<base64> public keys; absent The keys the edge's signed organization catalog must verify under. Required with toolCatalog.url; pin two while the edge rotates. User or machine scope only (CONFIG_SCOPE in a project file); lockable in admin-settings.json toolCatalog.maxOfflineAge 0, <n>h or <n>d (at most 366d); 7d How long after the edge built it the last good organization catalog may be used when the edge cannot be reached (network error or HTTP 5xx). 0 never uses it. User or machine scope only (CONFIG_SCOPE in a project file); lockable in admin-settings.json platform.url HTTPS URL (HTTP only for a loopback host); absent Platform for sign-in, remote runs and secrets; no credentials, query or fragment. The access token is never a setting: it comes from oyzu auth login or OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN platform.account Platform account identifier (lowercase letters, digits, hyphens); absent Account that sign-in validates, that remote runs are created in and whose secrets oyzu secrets manages platform.authentication.provider session, environment, workload, private-key, execution; absent Host-owned credential provider selection for platform commands; only session and environment are implemented. No credential value. Environment input OYZU_PLATFORM_AUTH_PROVIDER npm.sessionEndpoint Numeric-loopback HTTP URL; absent Opt-in experimental npm session; no credentials, query or fragment; requires a separately running laboratory agent nuget.sessionEndpoint Numeric-loopback HTTP URL; absent NuGet session prototype; user/admin authority only, no profile selection or implicit login python.sessionEndpoint Numeric-loopback HTTP URL; absent Python session prototype; user/admin authority only, no profile selection or implicit login cargo.sessionEndpoint Numeric-loopback HTTP URL; absent Cargo session prototype; user/admin authority only, one named sparse registry gradle.sessionEndpoint Numeric-loopback HTTP URL; absent Gradle session prototype; user/admin authority only, no profile selection or implicit login maven.sessionEndpoint Numeric-loopback HTTP URL; absent Maven session prototype; user/admin authority only, no profile selection or implicit login oci.sessionEndpoint Numeric-loopback HTTP URL; absent Isolated OCI session prototype; user/admin authority only, no implicit login or production agent cache.local Boolean; true Enables the local action cache (reuse of unchanged targets on the captured and native host paths). false runs every action, like oyzu build --no-cache, which bypasses it for one invocation cache.dir Absolute path; absent Replaces the default per-user action-cache store (Linux $XDG_CACHE_HOME/oyzu/actions, macOS ~/Library/Caches/Oyzu/actions, Windows %LocalAppData%\Oyzu\cache\actions). User or system scope only: a project oyzu.toml or oyzu.local.toml that sets it is rejected with CONFIG_SCOPE; not eligible for profiles; ignored with other user-scope settings in CI. Never part of an action key cache.ciRemote OCI URL; absent The CI repository: a CI build reads and writes only it; other builds read it first and never write it. Its trust comes from the registry refusing writes without the CI credential (OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN or the job's ID tokens from OYZU_ID_TOKEN_URL, environment variables, never a setting). Same URL rules as cache.remote cache.immutableTags Boolean; false Declares that every configured cache repository refuses to replace a tag, so pushes skip the racing-writer read and a refused tag write is a conflict. Never set it for a registry that replaces tags cache.read, cache.write Booleans; true, false Whether the remote OCI cache is consulted after a local miss and whether locally stored action results are pushed to it. No effect without cache.remote or with the local cache disabled. Transport preferences: not part of the configuration digest, so they never change an action key cache.nativeMaxMiB Integer 1–1048576; 8192 (8 GiB) Aggregate retained budget for the selected native Rust compiler caches; see retention. Independent of remote cache preferences. cache.dockerMaxMiB Integer 1–1048576; 20480 (20 GiB) Aggregate budget for Docker images Oyzu pulled; least recently used are evicted after isolated builds. See Docker storage budget. Not part of any action key tools.<name> Nonempty string; absent Explicit requests fail execution until a verified installation binding exists; no tool installation is performed tools.ignore Set of tool names; absent Folder-scoped: silences best-effort tool detection of the named tools (managed tools, host programs, fetching packages) for targets in that folder and below. Never removes a primary toolchain; an explicit [tools] pin still provides the tool. Ignored detections show in -v and --json as ignored by tools.ignore in <path> verification.<tool> Set of tool lines ("22", "3.12": one to three numbers), the tool named without a namespace; absent Per target. The lines of the tool a build needs passing verification evidence for before oyzu publish accepts it; policy and [constraints] require lines with required. A line no toolset covers adds a verification run, and a line outside the build's native range is recorded as not applicable. See required tool lines. Not part of the configuration digest env.<name> Literal string or { secret = "reference" }; absent Literal environment overlay; secret references require a future authorized consumer tasks.<name> Task record; absent Atomic task replacement; see syntax below docker.apparmorProfile Profile name; host-derived oyzu-buildkit when the detected Linux user-namespace restriction requires it, otherwise unconfined docker.frontends List of image references pinned by digest; empty # syntax= frontends a Dockerfile may request. A request matches an entry with the same repository and the same digest, or the same tag when the request has no digest. Oyzu's BuildKit frontend runs the approved frontend; any other request fails with FRONTEND_NOT_APPROVED naming the requested and approved references. See Docker frontends docker.load List of 0–8 distinct destinations, docker or k3d:<cluster>; absent Per target. Where oyzu run load puts a docker/image build's image (OD4): a team default in oyzu.toml, a personal cluster in oyzu.local.toml; [] in a nearer file turns a farther list off. Adds the load task; without the build's with.repository the task is unavailable with that reason. A destination, like publish.destinations: never part of an action key. See Loading the image locally Environment names use ASCII letters, digits and underscores, beginning with a letter or underscore; the OYZU_ prefix is reserved case-insensitively. Values are not expressions or interpolation programs. A literal [env] value is the only environment value a task placeholder can read ({env.NAME}); ambient variables and secret references never are. Inspection redaction does not make literal environment values a secret store: literals can participate in build inputs/evidence. Do not use a literal as a substitute for the deferred secret consumer. Task records select either run (a shell command) or argv (an argument array), and accept shell, cwd, env, depends_on, inputs, outputs, cache, interactive, reports, and the plan-time conditions when and unless; an argv task's elements and its own env values may use {namespace.name} placeholders. See task and hook conditions. cache = true with outputs makes an authored task cacheable by oyzu build (its inputs may only add paths inside its target); outputs on a hook lets the cache follow it; see authored tasks. Local oyzu run inherits stdin. Text-mode tasks recording a bundle tee stdout/stderr live and retain them in dist/logs; interactive = true instead preserves real output terminal descriptors, with no captured stdout/stderr logs. Tasks without a bundle inherit output directly. For PowerShell run scripts, interactive = true also omits -NonInteractive; it does not make captured builds interactive. JSON mode captures output while retaining stdin; see task streams and limits. Task env contains strings. Task execution also requires a discoverable native project. For example, with Node explicitly provisioned and a package.json containing {"name":"config-demo","version":"1.0.0"}, add this to oyzu.toml: [tasks.hello] argv = ["node", "-e", "console.log('hello')"] oyzu --root path/to/project run hello executes that command. A higher-priority task record replaces the entire record rather than merging its fields. To remove inherited environment/task entries, use dotted key strings in a removal list: Additional arguments after -- are appended to an argv task, including an argv that already contains -c or -Command (for example a Python expression). Tasks authored with run reject additional arguments; choose argv when a task needs parameters. This distinction follows the declared task form, not the spelling of arguments passed to the native executable. [overrides] remove = ["env.DEMO_MODE", "tasks.hello"] The following keys are administrative-only and cannot appear in ordinary files or profiles: Key Type and default Meaning config.localOverridesInCi Boolean; false Whether the local override request is eligible in CI config.allowedProfiles Set of names, including @none; absent Restricts selection when supplied tools.allowed Set of canonical tool IDs; absent Restricts tool eligibility tools.catalogs Ordered string array; ["public"] Catalog preference; unavailable protected bindings block execution registries.routes Route array; [] Each entry has protocol, scope, connectorId; protocols are npm, pypi, maven, cargo, go, oci, tools; standalone Node/Go installation supports explicit host tool bindings; real Node proxy acceptance passed, Go proxy acceptance remains pending; other connector execution remains deferred npm.sources Set of HTTPS URL prefixes ending in /; [] Extra locations an isolated npm build may download locked packages from, in addition to https://registry.npmjs.org/. For example, https://codeload.github.com/<owner>/<repo>/tar.gz/ admits a package that pins a public GitHub commit as a tarball. Declare it in package.json as that same HTTPS tarball URL and record the URL and its sha512 in the lockfile; a git+https or github: spec in package.json is refused, because native npm would refetch it as a git dependency instead of using the captured tarball. Each package still needs the lockfile's sha512 integrity, which is verified. Credentials, queries and fragments are refused. Applies to the npm builder only; git+https lock entries remain unsupported fetches.sources Set of HTTPS URL prefixes ending in /; absent Administrative allowlist for declared fetches. Absent, any HTTPS URL is admitted. Set, each fetch URL and every redirect must fall under a listed prefix, or the build fails with SOURCE_DENIED or REDIRECT_DENIED; an empty list admits none. Project configuration cannot set it. Credentials, queries and fragments are refused maven.snapshotRepositories Set of HTTPS repository base URLs ending in /; [] (off) Snapshot repositories that captured Maven acquisition may use for snapshot version paths only, each through its own broker source; every other path keeps the Maven Central or session-approved route. Credentials, queries, fragments and plain HTTP are refused. Snapshot inputs are inventoried in the dependency snapshot, and a build whose version intent is not a development snapshot fails rather than use one. See Maven snapshot repositories

Host Machine directory User configuration User state directory Windows ProgramData known folder + Oyzu RoamingAppData known folder + Oyzu/config.toml LocalAppData known folder + Oyzu/state macOS /Library/Application Support/Oyzu ~/Library/Application Support/Oyzu/config.toml ~/Library/Application Support/Oyzu/state Linux /etc/oyzu $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/oyzu/config.toml, fallback ~/.config/oyzu/config.toml $XDG_STATE_HOME/oyzu, fallback ~/.local/state/oyzu Windows paths come from native known-folder APIs. Relative XDG paths warn and use the home fallback. The machine directory contains ordinary config.toml, protected admin-settings.json, and protected enrollment management.json. Project/local files are named oyzu.toml and oyzu.local.toml; keep personal local overrides out of version control. Oyzu does not auto-enroll the machine. For persistent user data, including the tool store, an absolute Windows HOME that differs from the native profile selects <HOME>/AppData/Local/Oyzu. This lets disposable homes isolate tool caches and rollback records. With HOME unset or naming the normal profile, native LocalAppData redirection is preserved. A relative HOME fails with CONFIG_SCOPE; use an absolute path or unset it. This data override does not redirect the configuration and managed policy state locations in the table, or the separate action/image cache locations. Existing data is not moved or deleted when selecting another home. OYZU_USER_CONFIG optionally selects an absolute user configuration file, useful for disposable environments and testing user defaults without modifying a real profile. Relative paths are rejected. The file retains user-level precedence and authority; this setting cannot redirect machine policy, enrollment or state. Its sibling oyzu.lock owns user-default tool pins. Unset the variable to return to the native user configuration location. Help/version do not read this setting. Managed state includes signed policy entries under the user state directory and integrity pointers/high-water state in the native credential store. Ordinary configuration edits do not change that state. Source capture enforces size/complexity budgets, including a 1 MiB file limit, and detects concurrent source changes rather than mixing revisions. This configuration format has no include mechanism or executable configuration language.

Native locations follow OEP-0002: Windows known folders, macOS Application Support, and Linux /etc/oyzu plus absolute XDG user locations. Protected files require administrative ownership and permissions. Windows uses native ACL/handle checks; Unix checks root ownership and write permissions; macOS also examines extended ACL entries on the opened object and rejects non-root mutation grants using the native descriptor ACL API. An insecure, unreadable or malformed enrollment never becomes standalone mode. admin-settings.json uses the same typed constraint evaluator as corporate policy. Locks, allowed whole values, numeric and ordered bounds and required sets intersect independently of ordinary precedence. Required checks cannot be removed by empty ordinary arrays. The build planner requires configured checks to have actual actions/report contracts; report collection enforces the coverage minimum, including missing/zero-denominator failures.

Status: implemented (build intent slice 7, BIN-03 and the selector part of BIN-20). This section is the client contract: what a constraint can say and how a build applies it. How an organization authors, composes and delivers its policy is not described here. Central policy has two forms. A default ("default": …) is an ordinary inherited value at the policy's scope that a project can override. A constraint is a limit applied after every ordinary value (base, context and profile values, flags), which a project cannot go past: Constraint Applies to When the ordinary value is outside it "locked": true, "value": v any setting the lock replaces it; shown as an override "minimum" / "maximum" numbers (build.jobs, checks.coverageMinimum, cache sizes) and ordered levels (checks.tests, checks.coverage, checks.lint, checks.format: off < advisory < enforce < required) the bound replaces it; shown as an override "required": [...] sets the members are added; shown as an override "allowed": [...] any setting refused with CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED naming the setting and the policy source (the set names no single winner) Tools. A tool version request (tools.<name>) under a lock or allowed set is refused, not replaced, because a requested tool version is never silently substituted. A tool constraint binds every spelling of the tool: a lock on tools.rust also refuses [tools] "oyzu:rust" = "1.90" or "core:rust", and the reverse. An unconditional tool lock supplies the request. A tool lock limited by a selector supplies its version under the tool's id and short name and binds every target whose builder needs or detects the tool, exactly as an unconditional lock does, whether or not the project pins it (deleting [tools] rust cannot evade a release lock on Rust; if the locked version cannot be resolved the build fails). The version a target's builder needs (a pin, the builder's default such as lts, a detected tool's latest, or a toolset verification run's request) is also checked against every tool constraint wherever tools are prepared (build preflight and the isolated worker, oyzu run and oyzu install, scanner preparation): outside an allowed set or a lock it is refused naming the constraint (CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED: tools.node violates administrative constraints: 24 is outside allowed ["20","22"] in release (local-administration); pin an allowed version …; a tool a builder only detected can instead be silenced with tools.ignore). An allowed or locked version matches by version components: 22 admits 22, 22.14 and 22.14.0 (not 220.1); any other value (lts, latest) matches only itself. The version oyzu.lock resolves a request to is checked as well, before anything is installed or activated (oyzu install, --frozen included, exec, run, operation tools and the isolated worker), so a hand-built or stale lock that maps an allowed 22 to 26.1.0 is refused naming the constraint and the lock file. Write allowed sets as majors or exact versions: an allowed lts or latest admits the request but cannot vouch for the version it resolves to, so a locked version under such a set is refused. A tool constraint never affects a target whose builder does not use the tool, and a missing request alone is never a violation. A version a context-scoped lock supplies is locked per context: oyzu.lock keeps one entry per tool request, so a local build (rust = stable) and a release build (rust = 1.95.0 from the lock) need one entry each. The entries coexist and a later local build does not change the lock, but a build in a context whose entry is missing fails with TOOL_LOCK_STALE: oyzu:rust 1.95.0; it is locked by policy local-administration for this build and oyzu.lock has no entry for it; on a machine with the same policy, run OYZU_CONTEXT=release oyzu pin … (a build does not add it while other tools are already locked, and --frozen never does). Run oyzu pin and OYZU_CONTEXT=release oyzu pin once, on a machine where the same policy is installed, and commit the lock; frozen release builds and oyzu install --frozen then succeed. Setting the context does not reproduce other facts: for a lock limited by provider or path, pin from a build that has them (in that CI job, or in that folder). Not bound by tool constraints (known limits, follow-ups recorded): custom tasks that run tools by argv; plugin builders that run host tools without declaring them as requirements; oyzu exec, which activates only requested tools; a tool the isolated worker image supplies with no declared builder requirement (Helm, npm without packageManager, Yarn) or whose default request is missing from oyzu.lock, which runs the image's copy unchecked (a tools.helm allowed set with no pin is not enforced); and tool recipe artifacts (recipe:* entries in oyzu.lock), which oyzu install replays without tools.allowed or tool constraints. A project's configuration otherwise never breaks a build merely because policy tightened: policy wins and the CLI says so. Check levels. A policy lock or minimum of enforce or above on a check means the check runs wherever the constraint applies, whatever checks.run says: a project's [context.pr.checks] run = "required" does not skip a check policy requires in pr. The lift is recorded with the override (runs although checks.run = required) and changes the configuration digest. required additionally makes the check run in every build, including a fast local one, and makes its report mandatory. A minimum on checks.coverage also lifts checks.tests to at least the same level, because the tests collect coverage (coverage is collected by the tests), so tests = "off" cannot evade it. A policy minimum on checks.coverageMinimum lifts an off checks.tests or checks.coverage to enforce, or to advisory where a policy maximum or allowed set caps it there (a coverage minimum of 80 needs coverage) instead of the CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE a project's own minimum with coverage off gets; an advisory level is not lifted (it is judged, as a warning), so a policy coverage percentage with a policy lock of advisory works. A lift never overrides another policy constraint: a coverage percentage with a policy checks.coverage lock (or maximum, or allowed set) that keeps it off, or a coverage level with a lower tests lock, is CONFIG_POLICY_CONFLICT naming both, when the policy is read if both are unconditional, else when a build meets both. Selectors. A constraint can be limited with when and unless tables over the shared fact vocabulary: every key in when must match (a list matches when any listed value does), any matching key in unless excludes. The facts that have a value when policy is applied are context (local, pr, ci, release), provider (detected CI providers such as github-actions) and path (the target's folder, matched as a /-separated glob). A setting can carry one entry or a list of entries with different selectors: { "schemaVersion": 1, "kind": "local-admin-policy", "settings": { "checks.format": {"minimum": "enforce", "when": {"context": ["pr", "release"]}}, "checks.tests": [ {"minimum": "required", "when": {"path": "services/**"}, "unless": {"context": "local"}}, {"minimum": "enforce", "when": {"context": "release"}} ] }, "profiles": {}, "requiredCapabilities": [] } Contexts cannot be dodged. A build is taken as every context it detected, runs as or requested: the detected context, the effective one and the stricter of detected and requested (release over pr over ci over local). A when context matches when it names any of them, and an unless context excludes only when it names all of them. So neither lowering nor raising the context evades a constraint: a pull request job under GitHub Actions run with --context local (ignored) or --context release (honored for its values) still meets when context = pr, is not excluded by unless context = release, and a job with only the generic CI hint meets when context = ci with --context pr or --context local. explain reports these facts as policyFacts (contexts, providers, path). Folders. path is the target's folder relative to the repository boundary: the nearest Git boundary above the build root, climbing from a submodule (a .git file whose gitdir lies under <superproject>/.git/modules/) to its superproject. A linked worktree, a nested clone (its own .git folder) and any other repository are their own root, and the boundary is never the user's home folder or above it (a home under Git is ignored). Without Git it is the nearest folder holding oyzu.toml, oyzu.local.toml or build.yaml, else the build root. --root, a nested build.yaml and the current folder never move it, so building the submodule services/pay on its own still sees services/pay. A submodule of a linked worktree climbs to that worktree. A target folder outside the boundary (reached through a link) is a CONFIG_SCOPE error, never the root. Path selectors are not containment. They select by repository layout: a git init (or a nested clone) in a subfolder makes it its own root, and a when path services/** constraint then no longer matches it. Write rules that must hold everywhere as unconditional constraints (or limit them by context or provider), not by path. Patterns are normalised (./services/ is services) and compared without case. services/** matches services and every folder below it; * matches one folder level. The repository root itself (.) is matched only by . and **, so a pattern for subfolders never reaches it. Conflicts. Constraints on one setting that can apply to the same folder in the same context are compared when the policy is read: an unconditional lock off with minimum required when context = release, or two constraints scoped to a shared context that cannot both hold, fail the policy with POLICY_INVALID naming both entries. Constraints for different contexts load (lock off when local with minimum required when release); when one build is taken as several contexts and they cannot all hold, the constraints of the strictest context (local < ci < pr < release) win: its lock, minimum or maximum, and the intersection of its allowed sets. The rank is the context's, not the value's: a local build raised with --context release gets the release constraint even when it is looser than the local one. Constraints whose when.path patterns lead to different folders (services/**, docs/**) never meet. Allowed sets that agree pairwise but share no value when one build meets all of them fail closed at resolution with CONFIG_POLICY_CONFLICT. Errors. An unknown fact, a fact without a value at this point (fork is not detected yet; target, platform, artifact and optimized are decided after settings), an unknown context, a non-string value, an empty table, an absolute, .., .-segment or // path pattern, an unknown entry field (wehn, named in the message) and when/unless on a default are POLICY_INVALID naming the setting. A bound that is not a valid value of the setting (a level that is not one of its levels) is CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. A minimum or maximum on a setting that is neither a number nor an ordered level, a non-integer numeric bound, reversed bounds, and unconditional constraints that cannot hold together are CONFIG_POLICY_CONFLICT. Like every policy error these stop the session before a build starts. Shown and recorded. When a constraint replaces the value configuration chose: oyzu config explain <setting> lists it under Policy overrides (checks.format enforce admin policy minimum in pr, release (project oyzu.toml sets off)), adds a policy-<kind> step to the resolution history, and marks each constraint with applies; --json has policyOverrides (setting, value, kind, bound, source, selector, the replaced value and its origin, and its label) and policyFacts. org policy labels enrolled (corporate) policy, admin policy the machine's admin-settings.json. Plan prints one policy note per distinct override (see the build view); oyzu build --plan prints Policy: lines (Constraint: for a project constraint) per target and --plan --json has policyOverrides per target. Plan and manifest targets record extensions["oyzu.dev/policy-overrides"]: the setting, value, constraint (source, label, kind, bound, selector), replaced (value, source relative to the project root, scope) and the note. The configuration digest covers the resolved value as before. Every command that resolved an overridden setting (exec, run, scan, env, build, config …) reports a CONFIG_POLICY_OVERRIDE warning once per override, naming the setting, the policy source and the value that lost (checks.format = enforce by admin policy minimum in pr (local-administration) instead of off from oyzu.toml), shown in human output by default and in the configuration result's diagnostics. The shell prompt hook does not repeat it. config validate --strict reports it without failing. A value a task passes on as written (a task's own env) is still checked without replacement, so a locked environment value a task contradicts is refused with CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED. A policy lock or minimum of enforce or above on a check the builder cannot run fails in Plan naming the constraint (see check levels). Signed, cached corporate policy carries the same entries and keeps working offline within its expiry. Verification. Unit and library-level tests cover selectors, ordered bounds, overrides, the context rules, repository-relative folders, load-time conflicts, the check lifts, explain, Plan notes and the Plan failure. The compiled-CLI proof with a root-owned policy file is recorded in the status entry. config status reports enrollment and cached-policy status. config refresh performs a headless request to the enrolled platform's public configuration-context endpoint. Signed responses use pinned Ed25519 keys, canonical JSON, identity/context binding, monotonic sequences, expiry and explicit offline permissions. Cache entries are content-addressed and flushed before an OS credential-store pointer commits them. A corrupt entry can only be repaired from a newly verified online response. Windows Credential Manager, macOS Keychain and Linux Secret Service hold integrity state. If that service is unavailable, managed execution fails; standalone use does not need it. Transport backoff never extends signed deadlines. Server denial cannot become offline permission.

Status: implemented (configuration split step D9, migration item M20, OD17; status entry). A project without central policy can make a rule hold in every folder with a [constraints] table in its root oyzu.toml. It uses the policy constraint and selector vocabulary and is applied after every ordinary value and before central policy, so a component folder cannot undercut it: # root oyzu.toml only [constraints."checks.tests"] minimum = "required" when = { context = ["release"] } With services/oyzu.toml setting [checks] tests = "advisory", a release build of services runs its tests as required, and a local build keeps advisory. Vocabulary. Each entry is a table, or a list of tables ([[constraints."checks.tests"]]), with the policy fields locked = true with value, minimum, maximum, allowed, required, when and unless; they mean exactly what they mean in policy, including ordered check levels, tool version matching and the "tools are refused, not replaced" rule. Name the setting by its whole path in quotes ([constraints."checks.tests"]). A default is refused: a project default is an ordinary value, written in the setting's own table. Only settings a project file can set may be constrained, and not env.* or tasks.*; credential destinations, trust controls and administrative settings are refused naming the setting. Selectors. context and provider behave as in policy. path is the target's folder relative to the root oyzu.toml's folder (the configuration root: the Git top level, else the outermost folder with oyzu.toml, oyzu.local.toml or build.yaml, or --root), not the repository boundary policy paths use, so a project's own rules keep matching when it moves or sits inside a larger repository. explain --json reports it as policyFacts.projectPath. Only the root file. A [constraints] table in any other file is an error naming the file: a component folder's oyzu.toml (CONFIG_SCOPE: app/oyzu.toml:1:1: [constraints] is allowed only in the root oyzu.toml, with the full paths), oyzu.local.toml, user or machine configuration, and a [context.<name>] or [profiles.<name>] table. Unknown optional sections are ignored with a warning, including names close to known sections ([Constraints], [constraint], [constriants], [check]). These warnings suggest the intended section; config validate --strict rejects such warnings when checking for spelling mistakes. An invalid entry is CONFIG_CONSTRAINT_INVALID naming the file, line and setting; entries that cannot hold together in one context fail as policy entries do. Policy always wins. Project constraints are the inner layer, and a project can never loosen policy. A project constraint that cannot hold together with the policy constraints that apply to a build is set aside for that build: a floor or ceiling of an ordered or numeric setting is clamped to what policy allows: a project minimum = "required" under a policy maximum = "enforce" becomes minimum = "enforce" and still raises a lower folder value to enforce, recorded as a project constraint override; a project maximum = "off" under a policy minimum = "enforce" becomes maximum = "enforce", and policy raises the value; a lock, an allowed set or a required set policy rejects, or any project constraint where policy limits the setting with an allowed set, is dropped; a coverage floor that would lift another check level across layers is resolved the same way: a policy coverage percentage lifts tests over a project lock of off (the project lock is dropped), and a project coverage floor that needs tests above a policy cap is dropped and lifts nothing. Every command reports each one as a CONFIG_PROJECT_CONSTRAINT_SET_ASIDE warning naming the project constraint, the policy constraint and the value the build uses (checks.tests: project constraint minimum required in release (oyzu.toml [constraints]) is clamped to minimum enforce by admin policy maximum enforce (local-administration); checks.tests = enforce), so a project floor never disappears silently. When both layers apply and hold together, the project constraint replaces the folder value first and policy then replaces the project's value; each step is recorded. Shown and recorded as policy overrides are, labelled project constraint instead of admin policy or org policy, with source oyzu.toml [constraints]: oyzu config explain lists it under Constraint overrides (checks.tests required project constraint minimum in release (project services/oyzu.toml sets advisory)) with a project-<kind> step in the resolution history and label in --json; Plan prints a project note; oyzu build --plan prints a Constraint: line; plan and manifest targets record it in extensions["oyzu.dev/policy-overrides"] with constraint.label; every command reports a CONFIG_CONSTRAINT_OVERRIDE warning (checks.tests = required by project constraint minimum in release (oyzu.toml [constraints]) instead of advisory from oyzu.toml). A project minimum of enforce or above on a check makes it run whatever checks.run says, as a policy one does. oyzu config validate --strict does not fail on CONFIG_CONSTRAINT_OVERRIDE or CONFIG_PROJECT_CONSTRAINT_SET_ASIDE (a constraint tightening a folder value is not a configuration error), but does fail on CONFIG_RELEASE_LOWERED, which asks for a deliberate [context.release] value or a fix. Limits. --root selects the configuration root: oyzu --root app build reads app/oyzu.toml as the root file, and the repository root's [constraints] does not apply to that build. This is an accepted, known limit. The registered-section rule covers constraints and toolsets; targets joins it when that section is implemented (OD18).

Rust targets take Cargo features from with.features and cross-compilation targets from platforms entries, built by the native cross toolchain or the executor build.executors declares (Rust platforms). The former rust object (features and a targets list of Cargo triples that generated build-<triple> tasks) is refused naming that replacement. build.yaml describes target intent separately from the TOML cascade. The python/app builder's optional with.container option is a boolean or a finite object with base, user, workdir and entrypoint; see Python application containers for types, defaults and current runtime support. The builder validates it when the inventory is read, and it is frozen with the target inventory. config validate rejects malformed option values without resolving images or executing a build. The object introduces no task language or additional precedence layer. Administrative execution checks and resolved owner settings still apply to generated image actions.

The Docker adapter registers docker.apparmorProfile, docker.frontends and docker.load. A builder applies a registered setting that adds a task (such as docker.load) from the target's resolved snapshot during discovery, never by reading files itself. docker.apparmorProfile replaces direct adapter reads of OYZU_BUILDKIT_APPARMOR_PROFILE; the legacy environment variable remains a diagnosed invocation input and faces the same policy constraints. The default still detects the host's AppArmor user-namespace restriction. Builder namespaces stay behind the crate-private Builder contract. A frozen build configuration contributes its digest to target/action records. Formatting, profile names and presentation preferences do not affect that configuration digest. Policy revision and online/offline context remain separate evidence. No policy snapshot grants signing, publishing or credential issuance. Build preparation and planning require the resolved invocation snapshot and every selected target's snapshot, including inferred targets without configuration files. Missing internal snapshots fail with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE; they never disable policy checks or cause adapters to recalculate defaults. Library callers must use discovery to obtain this state; serialized discovery JSON is an inspection result, not a resumable workspace. Rediscover the workspace if that state is missing. Docker reads its execution profile from the admitted snapshot before preparation starts. Later edits to live configuration files do not change an already frozen plan; start a new invocation to resolve them. The current native tool-store, authenticated platform-session, connector-binding and shell-secret-consumer implementations are not completed by this configuration change; the remote action cache is an experimental development-scope implementation that signs in only with a token from OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN or a CI job's ID tokens (see the action cache). Explicit tool requests that cannot be bound to a verified installation are rejected before builds. Enforced routes/catalogs requiring unavailable bindings fail before public acquisition. Managed builders that still require public dependency preparation are blocked; offline-capable local Docker and Helm preparation remains separate from those network paths. Development secret references require an authorized consumer and are not substituted into build literals. build.jobs bounds concurrent ready actions. The invocation uses the smallest admitted root/target ceiling; each target retains serial mutation and hook order. Targets have private workspaces and output roots. Dependency or deferred-report failure blocks consumers while independent targets can finish. ui.color controls human-readable task labels and outcome statuses: always emits ANSI color, never disables it, and auto enables it only when the relevant output stream is a terminal. Task-specific resolved preferences apply to that task; root tasks use root preferences. JSON output remains unstyled. Cache preferences do not grant cache credentials or trust: a remote hit is a development result. These boundaries are deliberate failures rather than claims that all OEP-0002 ecosystem and platform integration acceptance cases pass. Three-host ACL/keychain qualification, signed server interoperability, authenticated logout/account-switch flows, complete connector routing and tool-store integration remain release gates. Development execution checks tool eligibility, explicit tool requests and protected routing/catalog requirements before any prerequisite or hook runs. Managed host tasks remain blocked until approved development execution and connector bindings exist; the host runner cannot claim to enforce managed network routing. Task-specific and native-adapter environment additions must satisfy administrative environment restrictions. Each build's own task cascade determines whether a root hook or stage replacement reaches it, is replaced by a nearer or qualified definition, or is removed, consistently with inspection and build planning (task binding).

Diagnostic or symptom Recovery CONFIG_SYNTAX, duplicate keys Correct the source file's syntax/duplicate declaration, then validate CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE, CONFIG_SCOPE Use the registered type and permitted scope; ordinary set/unset can repair invalid values CONFIG_PROFILE_UNKNOWN Inspect profile declarations and select an existing name; use --no-profile only if policy permits CONFIG_PROFILE_TOOLS Move [profiles.NAME.tools] to [toolsets.NAME.tools] and select it with --toolset NAME; see toolsets CONFIG_TOOLSET_UNKNOWN, CONFIG_TOOLSET_INVALID Define the toolset in a project oyzu.toml or oyzu.local.toml in this folder chain, holding only a tools table of tool versions TOOLSET_BUILD_REFUSED, TOOLSET_UNSUPPORTED Use --toolset only with exec, run, env, activate, which, or the project-scoped install, update or uninstall; build with the [tools] versions TOOLSET_NESTED_LOCK The toolset is defined (or redefined) in a nested folder's file; define it in the project root's oyzu.toml or oyzu.local.toml to lock it, or use it with tools already locked Optional-setting warning / strict failure Correct the spelling or remove inert optional settings; ordinary validation does not execute unknown syntax Unsupported schema major or required capability Use a compatible client; do not remove a requirement unless the project no longer needs it CONFIG_POLICY_CONFLICT, CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED Reconcile conflicting administrative constraints or choose an allowed value; unavailable execution bindings require their implementation/provisioning CONFIG_EDIT_CONFLICT Re-read the file and retry the intended edit; do not overwrite another writer's changes CONFIG_LIMIT Reduce file size, nesting or configuration entries, including inactive profile data POLICY_INVALID Inspect enrollment protection and policy/cache validity; an administrator may need to repair bootstrap permissions or signing configuration POLICY_EXPIRED, POLICY_UNAVAILABLE Restore endpoint/native credential-store availability and run config refresh; failure never converts an enrolled machine to standalone POLICY_CLOCK_UNCERTAIN Correct clock problems and reconcile online; do not erase rollback-protection state to bypass the error Offline execution requires explicit signed permission and remains bounded by both signed expiry and maximum offline age (at most 24 hours). CI requires online policy. Transport retry/backoff preserves these deadlines; denial and malformed responses do not authorize offline fallback. Explicit refresh can fail while an older valid cache remains stored. A corrupt cache entry requires a newly verified online response; damaged integrity-store state can require administrator intervention. Refresh rechecks time after I/O, so a request that finishes after a deadline does not extend authorization. Changing protected bootstrap pins invalidates the previous cache binding. Recovery requires an online response verified against the current pins with a strictly newer policy sequence; existing high-water state remains in force. Do not delete credential-store state as a key-rotation procedure. Cache commit ordering preserves the old committed pointer until the new entry has been flushed; full crash/reboot qualification remains a release gate. Platform sign-in is the separate oyzu auth; there are no enrollment commands in this delivery. Revisit session-to-policy identity binding, account/organization switching, logout invalidation, credential lifecycle, authenticated refresh and CI identity, plus end-to-end server interoperability. Configuration policy is not a login session and does not grant publishing/signing authority. Connector credentials, shell secrets, verified tool installation and remote action caching also remain separate integrations.

The implementation status records tested revisions and host coverage. The current contracts have focused coverage in resolution and editing tests, CLI tests, execution enforcement tests, and signed managed-policy tests. Agent transition tests beside the policy agent cover key rotation, elapsed deadlines and denial/clock behavior. These tests do not establish interoperability with a production authenticated service. Documentation structure is checked with node tooling/check-docs.mjs; that check does not validate product behavior. The quick-start command sequence and the provisioned-Node task example were separately exercised against the compiled CLI on Windows during this documentation update.

The shell activation reference documents env._.path, its atomic replacement and file-relative paths. The optional compatibility capability is config.env-path/v1. This metadata is not exported into task/build environments.

Global verbosity and OYZU_LOG are typed invocation-only presentation inputs, resolved before any project session. They are not project keys and never enter effective execution snapshots or configuration digests. Explicit CLI controls override the complete environment filter. Help/version do not resolve it. See CLI diagnostic controls for grammar and errors.

[tools] declarations can also be written, replaced and removed with oyzu install SPEC, oyzu uninstall and -g/--local, and in a toolset with oyzu --toolset NAME install SPEC, which keep comments and lock the result; see tool commands. A declaration is a version string, or mise's option-table form with only a version key (node = { version = "22" }), which validation normalizes to that string so every consumer sees one form. Edits change only the table's version. Unknown option keys warn and are ignored; they do not install hooks, select platforms or change acquisition. A table without a valid version string still fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE; see option tables. tools.platforms is an optional project string set (never a profile value) consumed through the normal configuration cascade. It restricts Rust lock metadata coverage, not the artifact matrix or installation authority. When absent, pin uses the finite default metadata platforms. An empty or unsupported selection fails pin. Values are exact OS/architecture/ABI tuples; this setting is not a tool version request. No schema version changes.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/declared-fetches.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. A declared fetch names one file by HTTPS URL and SHA-256 digest in build.yaml. Captured preparation downloads it, verifies it and delivers it to the build. The build itself then runs offline, so a RUN curl or a script download can be replaced with a pinned input. Status: experimental. This first slice follows the draft declared fetches design; field names and messages may still change. It has unit tests but has not been qualified end to end yet (see verification).

builds: image: uses: docker/image fetches: - name: migrate url: https://github.com/golang-migrate/migrate/releases/download/v4.18.1/migrate.linux-amd64.tar.gz sha256: <64 lowercase hex characters> unpack: tar Field Required Meaning name yes Target-unique name: a letter, then up to 63 letters, digits, _ or - url yes An https:// URL without user information, query or fragment sha256 yes Expected digest of the downloaded bytes, 64 lowercase hex characters unpack no tar (plain or gzip, detected from the bytes) or zip. Without it the file is delivered as is A target can declare at most 64 fetches. Two names that give the same environment variable, such as migrate-cli and migrate_cli, are refused. An invalid declaration fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE when build.yaml is read, before any preparation. Without unpack, the file keeps the last segment of its URL as its name. That segment may contain only letters, digits, ., _, + and -.

In a Dockerfile, copy from the named context oyzu-fetch-<name>: COPY --from=oyzu-fetch-migrate migrate /usr/local/bin/migrate The context holds the unpacked tree, or the single downloaded file. A Dockerfile that reads oyzu-fetch-<name> without a matching declaration fails during preparation. These context names are reserved and are never treated as images. Command actions (prepare, task and package commands) get OYZU_FETCH_<NAME>, the name upper-cased with - replaced by _. It points to the file, such as /dependencies/fetches/migrate-cli/migrate, or to the unpacked directory, such as /dependencies/fetches/migrate. Content is read-only. Declared fetches are delivered only on captured worker paths: oyzu build --isolated and builders whose host build runs a captured worker, such as Docker images. A native host build of a target with fetches fails and asks you to run oyzu build --isolated. A builder that captures no dependency inputs cannot receive fetches and fails with a message naming the target.

Standalone, any HTTPS URL is admitted, and HTTPS redirects are followed. The broker forwards no credentials, and every hop must still be HTTPS. An administrator can restrict fetches with fetches.sources, a list of HTTPS URL prefixes ending in / (see configuration). Then: A URL outside every prefix fails with SOURCE_DENIED before anything is downloaded. The prefix is matched by path segment, so /tools/ does not admit /toolsets/. Every redirect must stay inside the listed prefixes, or the fetch fails with REDIRECT_DENIED. Project configuration cannot set fetches.sources, so a project cannot widen it. Setting it there fails with CONFIG_SCOPE.

Verified bytes are stored by digest under <user data>/cache/fetches/sha256-<hex>. Bytes are checked before they are stored or unpacked. A mismatch stores nothing, and a damaged store entry is replaced rather than trusted. A later build reuses the stored file without downloading. With --offline, a fetch that is not stored fails with DEPENDENCY_INPUT_MISSING. Run one online build to capture it. Archives are unpacked with the tool store's defenses: path traversal, links that leave the tree and oversized expansion are refused.

Each fetch becomes a package in the target's dependency snapshot: Field Value id fetch:<target>/<name> version, digest sha256:<hex> sourceId fetch:<host> standalone, or fetches.sources/<index> under an allowlist size Downloaded size in bytes purpose build verification digest-only: the digest matched, but no publisher signature was checked The snapshot extension oyzu.dev/fetches records each fetch's environment variable, path, context and tree digest. Both are part of the snapshot digest, so the plan and its evidence bind the fetched content. A second build of the same declaration records the same package identity.

Each message starts with its code and names <target>: declared fetch <name>. Code Cause Recovery CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE Missing digest, non-HTTPS URL, or a URL with user information, a query or a fragment Fix the declaration INTEGRITY_MISMATCH The downloaded bytes do not match sha256. The message shows both digests Check the URL and the upstream release before updating the digest. The observed digest has not been independently verified SOURCE_DENIED The URL is outside fetches.sources Use an admitted source, or ask an administrator to admit it REDIRECT_DENIED A redirect left the admitted sources Pin the final URL, or ask an administrator to admit its source SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE The server answered with a status other than 200 Check the URL DEPENDENCY_INPUT_MISSING An offline build needs a fetch that is not stored Run one online build

Only SHA-256 digests are accepted. sha512 and Subresource Integrity strings and a helper that prints a URL's digest are open decisions in the design. Builder recipes for common downloads, such as Puppeteer's browsers, reuse this engine; see installer-asset recipes. Credentialed sources are not supported. Dockerfile ADD <url> with --checksum is still refused. Use a declared fetch and COPY --from=oyzu-fetch-<name>. Native host builds do not receive fetches. docker/image targets cannot build with --offline, because the Docker builder does not support offline preparation yet. Their fetches are still stored and reused by later online or --isolated builds without downloading again. Only tar (plain or gzip) and zip can be unpacked. An offline RUN curl still fails at execution. The failure does not yet suggest a declared fetch. A captured npm install whose lifecycle script tries the network does: see downloads without a recipe.

Unit tests cover declaration validation, admission and the allowlist, digest mismatch with an empty store, offline reuse with the same package identity, tar unpacking, broker download and redirect denial, Docker named contexts and worker context capture. An integration test covers validation when build.yaml is read. These map to acceptance FETCH-02 to FETCH-05 and part of FETCH-01.
