Not yet demonstrated: a Docker image built with oyzu build and with oyzu build --isolated that copies a fetched file, its evidence, and Windows and macOS behavior.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/direct-tests.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu run test produces a test-only dist/ bundle for single-package Node projects and native npm/pnpm/Yarn workspaces using node:test, Jest, Vitest or Mocha, Python projects using pytest through pip, uv or Poetry, Go modules/workspaces using native testing, Helm charts using local validation and optional helm-unittest suites, Rust apps/workspaces using nextest and Cargo doctests, supported Ant assertion/JUnit targets, native Maven reactors, and Gradle multi-project/composite builds. Native dependencies and any required reporters must already be installed. Node itself is resolved during oyzu build preflight when the project has no pin (see below); oyzu run uses an existing selection. There is no Docker, desktop, sign-in or tool-installation prerequisite for this host workflow. See Python test reporting, Go testing and Helm testing for native prerequisites and coverage scope; the examples below use Node. oyzu run list oyzu run test oyzu inspect dist oyzu run test -- --test-name-pattern=greeting The builder recognizes the conventional runner or a supported exact test command and supplies native JUnit and applicable application coverage reporting. Helm records coverage as inapplicable, with one local-validation report and a separate native unittest report when detected. Host Helm tests require prepared chart dependencies, a provisioned Helm executable and the helm-unittest plugin when suites are selected. Their orchestration is compiled into Oyzu and requires no Python interpreter; they do not install tools or download dependencies. Existing npm pretest/posttest lifecycle behavior stays native. Qualified names such as api:test use that target's configuration and working directory; Oyzu pre_/post_ hooks and declared prerequisites follow the task engine's ordering. Forwarded arguments apply only to the requested task.

With the development node/app binding, the native npm checks slice supports single-package node --test reporting and opaque authored report commands. Required test and coverage obligations remain present for both. The built-in Jest/Vitest/Mocha and workspace integrations described below do not transfer automatically to that plugin. Its report-integration label is currently absent; command/report/acceptance evidence remains recorded. See Node plugin behavior and qualification.

The invocation uses the same report binding, validation, collection and bundle transaction as captured builds. dist/manifest.json links current JUnit and coverage reports (LCOV for Node, Cobertura for Python, native statement profiles for Go), their summaries, the recorded plan, execution envelope and logs. It records no newly built application artifacts and does not run packaging, lint or formatting just because tests were requested. Use oyzu build for builder stages and snapshot artifacts. Local text-mode tasks inherit stdin and tee stdout/stderr live to the caller and the bundle's numbered log files, including on native failure. The child's output streams are pipes. An explicitly interactive = true task instead inherits real stdout/stderr descriptors in text mode; its output cannot also be retained and its bundle stdout/stderr logs are empty. JSON mode captures both streams even for interactive tasks, without terminal output descriptors. Native report files and their validation remain required independently of stream capture. See development task streams for empty-stdout checks, quiet mode, completion waiting and current verification limits. Native test failures, missing required reports, malformed reports and an unmet configured coverage minimum fail the command. Valid failed-test reports and bounded malformed report bytes are retained when available. Collection waits for the post-hook so that a report-transforming hook can finish. A failing pre-hook blocks its test; a failing test skips its success-only post-hook; a failing post-hook retains the test's available reports. A launch failure produces failed action evidence rather than success. Unexecuted actions are marked blocked. Default reports use a fresh private directory for every invocation. Custom commands are not parsed as arbitrary shell programs or replaced with guessed native commands. Hooks and commands receive OYZU_TEST_REPORT and OYZU_COVERAGE_REPORT for concrete assigned paths.

oyzu build and oyzu run <target>:test resolve the same task: an explicit Oyzu task, else the project's native package.json test script, else the builder default. Discovering a script does not by itself add it to the build lifecycle. The resolved task has one of three integration modes, shown in the human summary and in extensions."oyzu.dev/report-integration": builder-default: no native test override; the builder runs node --test with JUnit and lcov reporters, and the Node runner and coverage need no extra packages. native-runner: a package.json script that is exactly node --test followed only by plain --flag options. The script still runs through npm, so project config and pretest/posttest lifecycle behavior stay native and tests run once; reporter and coverage options are appended after --. Scripts that name paths, their own reporters, coverage or watch options are not instrumented, because flags after paths are silently ignored by Node. opaque: any other command is preserved verbatim, with nothing appended or guessed. Supported reports are collected only if the command writes them to the assigned OYZU_TEST_REPORT / OYZU_COVERAGE_REPORT locations (or a declared reports path) during this execution. Absent reports are recorded as status: missing. Each test action also produces a test-evidence record (manifest.extensions."oyzu.dev/test-evidence", the Test evidence block in human output and evidence in oyzu run --json outcomes) with separate command, test-results and coverage status, and an acceptance verdict: Case Outcome Builder default, reports collected accepted Native override, reports collected accepted Opaque command passed, reports absent, not required incomplete: "command passed; test results missing; coverage missing"; the build still succeeds Test command failed (any mode) command fails; partial reports are retained; rejected Report missing and required (checks.tests = "required" or checks.coverage = "required", checks.coverageMinimum, or an explicit task reports entry) report-missing error diagnostic; command fails; rejected Builder default but a report is missing fails Only reports produced by the current execution can satisfy a requirement; stale files are rejected. Oyzu does not edit package.json or checked-in configuration. A literal declaration can also redirect a supported exact command: [tasks."project:test"] argv = ["node", "--test"] reports = [{ kind = "test", format = "junit", path = "reports/junit.xml" }] The path is relative to the task's working directory. Oyzu creates missing parent directories for literal paths. A report declaration does not remove the other required report kinds. Explicit report paths or globs must have no existing matching output before the invocation; preserve or remove earlier files before rerunning. Oyzu fails rather than treating stale evidence as current. For a glob, the command remains responsible for producing matching files and directories; no single output path environment variable is inferred for multiple files.

Host tasks often build into dist/ before running tests. Direct tests preserve those files alongside their new evidence, recording paths, sizes and digests under extensions.oyzu.dev/host-outputs. Previous artifact bytes are preserved as ordinary host output; they are not listed as artifacts produced by this test invocation. Inspection verifies the preserved inventory. Earlier Oyzu reports, evidence and logs stay in history rather than becoming current test results. The previous directory moves to .oyzu/history/<new-run-id> through the shared transaction. Native output must use portable regular files/directories; links, reparse points and collisions with new evidence fail. manifest.json, plan.json, envelope.json and logs are reserved bundle paths. An application-owned manifest or other reserved-path collision needs to be preserved or relocated before this workflow can finalize. Failures during preflight or output preservation can leave the earlier bundle in place; check the command outcome and run identity instead of assuming any existing dist belongs to the latest attempt. See bundle retention and recovery.

The plan, envelope and manifest disclose oyzu.dev/invocation with kind: test, execution: host, isolation: none, source: observed-before-run and toolIdentity: unverified. Source identity is observed before executing against the live checkout; dependencies, ambient tools and subsequent source mutations are not captured. Actions declare network: host, are not cacheable, and disclose that sandbox resource limits are not enforced. Environment values in plan records are redacted. Native output/logs remain the output of the invoked programs; they are not a general secret-redaction service. CI detection gives ci-unverified, not a trusted producer identity. Effective configuration identity and available management metadata are recorded, but this test invocation does not satisfy unrelated full-build checks or grant publication/signing authority. Inspection checks integrity and agreement of invocation records, not authenticity. This is local development evidence, not hermetic or production provenance. Integrated profiles are single-package Node tests and npm workspaces (node:test, Jest, Vitest and Mocha), Python's pytest default, native Go module/workspace tests and Helm charts. Rust app/workspace native acceptance passed on all three CI hosts as described below. Ant tests and Maven reactor tests connect their native test and JaCoCo adapters to this collector. Gradle composite tests also supply named native reports. pnpm/Yarn workspace tests now use native membership with the shared package collector. Docker still lacks this test-only bundle integration. A supported test depending on an unsupported test profile fails before execution rather than claiming complete evidence for both. These are implementation gaps; the intended common builder reporting contract remains broader. The native probe is python tooling/test-direct-test-bundles.py --cli <compiled-oyzu-path>, with dependencies from tooling/design-requirements.txt. It checks real native tests, application coverage, lifecycle behavior, hooks, failed/missing/malformed evidence, redirected/stale reports, launch failures, native output preservation, history and inspection tampering. CI runs it after CLI compilation on Windows, macOS and Linux. Revision-specific results and remaining gaps are recorded in implementation status; CI wiring alone does not prove all hosts passed. python tooling/test-helm-direct.py --cli <compiled-oyzu-path> --helm <helm-path> exercises application and root library charts, qualified targets/hooks, native unittest, failed reports, coverage inapplicability and bundle inspection. The probe requires Helm 3.22.0, helm-unittest 1.2.0 and Python 3.11+; Python runs this repository's verification harness, not the product's Helm orchestration. The shared TaskPlan carries coverage applicability into target records, including after post-hooks; a positive coverage minimum cannot be satisfied by a chart without a coverage report. The Linux Helm suite runs this probe after downloading the compiled CLI. Windows native results and pending Linux execution are recorded in implementation status; macOS native execution is not yet qualified.

Jest 29.7.0, Vitest 5.0.3 with matching @vitest/coverage-v8 5.0.3, and Mocha 11.8.0 with c8 10.1.3 are exercised by the direct framework probe. Provision project dependencies before oyzu run test. Mocha requires project-installed c8 10.x or explicitly provisioned fallback tools via OYZU_NODE_REPORTING_HOME; see Mocha reporting. Tests do not install missing reporters. Vitest's declared coverage provider must match its version; other framework major versions are not qualified by these checks. No test section is needed. Detection selects the implicit runner; exact native scripts (jest, jest --ci, vitest, vitest run, mocha) keep npm pretest/posttest behavior while the existing framework adapter adds JUnit and LCOV. Native configuration remains authoritative for test selection, reporters and coverage scope. Both implicit and scripted tests use the common bundle collector, with native failures retained in the manifest. Recognized command overrides retain report obligations; arbitrary script bodies must supply their assigned reports themselves. The framework wrappers resolve npm to its provisioned JavaScript entrypoint, preserving argument arrays and avoiding shell-dependent .cmd invocation on Windows. They retain native npm configuration. The three-platform CI probe covers implicit runners and npm scripts; pnpm/Yarn scripted host combinations are not yet qualified by this probe. Host tests retain ambient network access as disclosed in the invocation; they do not establish hermetic build evidence. Run python tooling/test-node-framework-direct.py --cli <compiled-path> after npm ci in tooling/fixtures/jest, tooling/fixtures/vitest, tooling/fixtures/mocha and tooling/images/node-quality, with tooling/design-requirements.txt installed. It invokes the real CLI and native frameworks, validates JUnit/LCOV bundles, checks native/Oyzu hook ordering and failed assertions, and calls oyzu inspect dist. Fixture copies preserve npm's executable symlinks: dereferencing Unix .bin entries breaks Vitest's relative imports before the native test command can run. The initial Linux/macOS probe exposed that harness error. The corrected probe passed on all three hosts at bfa2b7c in run 37049720609. npm workspace report ownership and native prerequisites are described in npm workspaces; pnpm/Yarn direct workspace integration is described in native workspace tests; Yarn and pnpm captured workspace builds are now implemented with isolated CLI acceptance pending. Rust app/workspace direct tests use the same collector with nextest JUnit, Cobertura and doctest invocation reports. The direct reporting step passed on Windows MSVC, Linux and macOS at bfa2b7c. The local Windows GNU toolchain lacks the required profiler runtime. See Rust prerequisites and current verification for measured scope and unsupported combinations. Workspace bundle publication holds an invocation lock through finalization and rollback. Completing or abandoning the transaction explicitly unlocks it so a transient inherited Unix file description cannot keep the next invocation locked out. Concurrent active invocations still fail with the workspace-lock diagnostic; this does not permit concurrent writes to one bundle.

With no configuration pin, oyzu build preflight requests lts whether or not engines.node is present: it selects the greatest release whose Node index lts field is a non-empty string and that satisfies every engine constraint. If no LTS release satisfies them, it falls back to the greatest stable release satisfying them; the requirement reason in the plan explains this fallback rule. With 24.x marked LTS and 26.x Current, >=22 selects 24.x and >=26 selects 26.x. Configuration pins, including latest, 26, exact versions and lts/<name>, keep their existing behavior and must satisfy engines. Preflight writes oyzu.lock and installs the selection before any action runs; it prepares tools only and never runs tests. See Node selection. oyzu build --connector-bindings <file> supplies host bindings for administrator-routed tool sources. .nvmrc/.node-version are not read yet. python tooling/test-node-test-reporting.py --cli <compiled-oyzu-path> [--store <dir>] [--lock <oyzu.lock>] creates temporary Git fixtures and runs oyzu build --full and oyzu run site:test for: builder default, native node --test --test-concurrency=1 with pretest/posttest (each runs once per invocation), opaque wrapper, a cooperative wrapper, failing default and native tests, and an opaque wrapper with checks.tests = "required". It asserts the integration mode, per-capability statuses, acceptance verdict, retained partial reports and the report-missing diagnostic. Qualification limits are recorded in implementation status.
documents.s: Node selection and the Node task probe

documents.t: CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/directory-artifacts.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The experimental build engine can collect, inspect and materialize a declared directory artifact. The Node application adapter declares directory outputs for conventional Vite builds and explicit node/app custom builds using the dist/ convention. Platform matrices expand matching producer/consumer variants and select matching provisioned toolchains. Platform independence and the remaining negative cases still require work before the full directory-materialization example can pass. This does not infer directory outputs for arbitrary unclassified build scripts.

A directory artifact retains the normal artifact identity, target, producing action, version and relative bundle path. Its kind is directory. In addition: entries is a complete sorted inventory of every contained file and directory, including hidden files and empty directories. Paths are relative to the artifact root; the root itself is omitted. Every entry has path, kind, size and executable. Files additionally carry their SHA-256 digest. Directories have zero size, false executable intent and no file digest. Artifact size is the sum of file bytes. Its digest is SHA-256 over oyzu.tree.v1alpha1, one NUL byte, then the JCS-encoded entries array. It is a logical tree identity, not an archive checksum. This uses the engine's existing tree encoding and includes directory entries explicitly, including nonempty directories. Relative paths determine order; timestamps, absolute checkout paths and user/group IDs do not enter the hash. Collection uses the complete tree rather than source exclusions: names such as dist, target and .hidden remain artifact content. The manifest schema requires the inventory for directories and rejects it on other artifact kinds.

oyzu inspect <bundle> reads the actual directory without changing it and compares its inventory, total size and tree digest to the manifest. Changed bytes, extra or missing entries, missing empty directories, mismatched inventory metadata and invalid contained paths fail inspection. No tools, project scripts or network services run during inspection. Integrity verification does not authenticate a producer or establish release eligibility. When a directory output is selected by materialize, its contents appear immediately beneath the configured destination. An artifact containing index.html copied to site becomes site/index.html, without an extra output-directory layer. The producer must have succeeded. The engine verifies its recorded content before copying and verifies the new copy afterward. Each consumer gets independent bytes; editing them cannot alter the producer bundle. Existing destinations, overlapping mappings and collisions with captured source fail. Producer test/coverage references retain their original scope. Directory handling does not establish platform independence. Compatibility requires matching producer and consumer artifact target OS/architecture, independently of their worker platforms. Consumer requirements propagate backward through materialization to matching producer variants, as described in matrix selection. Cross-platform reuse requires additional builder facts and selection rules; arbitrary JavaScript-generated files do not receive that classification automatically. See Docker target selection for the current distinction and limits.

Traversal rejects symlinks, nonregular file types, nonportable names and case-colliding paths. It is bounded to 100000 entries and 10 GiB of file contents per tree. File changes detected during inventory/copy fail the operation. Failed capture can leave partial unrecorded output; that output is not a valid artifact and must not be reused as successful evidence. Restore an intact bundle or rerun the producer after resolving the underlying error. Unix executable bits participate in inventory and copying. Windows currently captures files with executable: false; transferring Unix executable directory trees to Windows without preserving their mode intent is not supported by this implementation. Static data directories with no executable files avoid that mismatch. General portable executable metadata remains required work. Rust tests exercise complete capture, stable identities, hidden/output-named content, empty directories, changed/added/missing content, inventory tampering, independent flattened copies, failed producers and overwrite rejection. Unix CI additionally checks links and executable-bit changes. Public build::inspect and compiled-CLI integration tests verify directory bundles without going through private adapter APIs. Windows checks passed locally; all three CLI jobs at ea204c8 passed, with Linux job 110779088872 explicitly recording the directory integrity, executable/link and public-inspection checks. Schema fixtures cover required inventories, duplicate entries and missing file digests. These checks do not prove a native builder emits directory artifacts or that EX-050's two-platform Docker build works; native output acceptance is tracked separately in Node applications. Native host producer/consumer directory handoff is covered by tooling/test-host-workspaces.py; see host workspace behavior. This does not qualify the separate Docker/platform-matrix scenario above.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/discovery-selection.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Experimental. Static discovery decides each exclusive role of a Node or Python target, such as its package manager or formatter, from native project files. It reads bounded metadata, never runs a tool, script or configuration file, and never breaks a tie silently. When native evidence settles a role, no Oyzu configuration is needed. When it does not, discovery fails and names both the conflicting inputs and the build.yaml declaration that settles the role. oyzu build --plan shows every decision with its reason.

With a build.yaml, its builds are the inventory and discovery only supplies an omitted uses and reports folders the file leaves out (builds build.yaml leaves out). Without build.yaml, discovery selects a native project at the root or searches below that root for targets. The inventory walk stops descending as soon as it finds a target; the selected native builder owns discovery within that target. Nested Git repositories and directories with their own build.yaml inventory also stop the walk. A build.yaml that belongs to another tool (its root has none of builds, members and exclude, such as Dart build_runner's targets: file) does not: the walk continues below it, and oyzu discover lists it under Skipped with its root keys (which build.yaml files are Oyzu's). With such a file at the root, discovery runs as if there were no build.yaml. Existing generated/dependency directory exclusions, the depth limit of 32 and the limit of 1,024 targets still apply. Ordinary files below an already selected target do not add inventory traversal work. These rules apply equally to human and JSON discovery output. The invocation's configuration boundary also bounds conventional target discovery. An empty or malformed ancestor .git marker does not select that ancestor as a workspace: for standalone sibling projects with no enclosing Oyzu configuration, oyzu -C first run list discovers only first's tasks. In a real Git workspace, discovery still includes its conventional targets, and an unqualified task exposed by several targets remains ambiguous. Use the target-qualified task named by the error, or --root first when deliberately selecting a narrower root. Gitdir-pointer repositories and linked worktrees follow the same boundary rules. Each detector reports a candidate with evidence of one strength. The strongest evidence wins: Strength Examples declared a test script that runs exactly one recognized test runner native a lockfile, package.json packageManager, a framework configuration file, a pyproject.toml tool table conventional a declared dependency, a settings-only pnpm-workspace.yaml, a uv.lock that locks no packages default the documented default when nothing else applies, such as npm, ESLint, Prettier, pip or Ruff Two different candidates with the strongest evidence are a conflict. A candidate the builder has no adapter for, such as packageManager: nub@0.8.3, is unsupported. Both fail discovery; neither registration order nor file order picks a winner. Native rules that settle a role without configuration: Lockfiles beat a settings-only pnpm-workspace.yaml. pnpm reads settings from pnpm-workspace.yaml and can write the file on its own; only its packages list declares a workspace (the pnpm adapter already treats a settings-only file as no workspace). A file without packages is conventional pnpm evidence, so package-lock.json (npm) outranks it, while with no lockfile it still selects pnpm over the npm default. A file with packages, or one that is not a YAML mapping, stays native and conflicts with another manager's lockfile. The runner a compound test script names. When the test script is not exactly a recognized command (jest, vitest run, mocha, ...) but its &&, ||, ; and | segments name exactly one of jest, vitest, mocha or node --test, that runner is declared evidence. Segments such as pnpm lint, npm run unit or yarn unit are followed into the referenced package script. Leading NAME=value assignments, cross-env, npx and <manager> exec are skipped. A script with quotes, $, backticks, parentheses, redirection or manager flags such as --filter is not read; its framework is then decided by the remaining evidence. The script itself still runs natively, without report instrumentation unless it is an exact recognized command. A uv.lock that locks no packages. uv records the project itself in uv.lock, so a lock without any [[package]] cannot belong to this project's manager. It is conventional evidence and yields to poetry.lock or [tool.poetry]. A uv.lock that does lock packages stays native.

When discovery fails, declare the target and add the selector the error names under with: builds: pytest: uses: python/package with: formatter: ruff If native files identify more than one builder, select uses first. For example, the pinned Mermaid root contains both package.json and Dockerfile; its build.yaml needs builds: {mermaid: {uses: node/app}} before the Node test-runner decision can be made. That choice does not require a with.test-framework selector: pnpm lint && vitest run selects Vitest from the native test script. Builder with key Values node/app, node/package package-manager npm, pnpm, yarn test-framework node-test, jest, vitest, mocha, custom linter eslint, biome formatter prettier, biome python/app, python/package, python/library package-manager pip, uv, poetry linter ruff, flake8 formatter ruff, black The keys match the role names in --plan and in the target's oyzu.dev/discovery plan extension. A selection wins over every observation; discovery still records the observations, and the selected value must be one of the listed values. Any other value, a non-string value or any other with key fails. A selection applies to the declared target's own root only; it does not change the decisions of packages inside a Node workspace. Tool versions are not selected here: they belong in oyzu.toml. Example errors: conflicting Python formatter candidates black, ruff: black via pyproject.toml tool.black; ruff via pyproject.toml tool.ruff; declare the intended one for this target in build.yaml with `with: {formatter: black}` or `with: {formatter: ruff}` conflicting Node package manager candidates nub, pnpm (nub unsupported): nub via package.json /packageManager; pnpm via pnpm-lock.yaml lockfile; declare the intended one for this target in build.yaml with `with: {package-manager: pnpm}` The suggestions list the supported candidates that were observed; when none was, they list every supported value. Selecting a manager or runner the project does not natively use can still fail later, in that tool's own preparation or test run.

oyzu build --plan shows a Discovered table per target with each role, the selected candidate and the reason. With --json, each entry of targets has a discovery object mapping the role to selected and reason. For example: package-manager npm native package-lock.json lockfile; outranks pnpm (conventional pnpm-workspace.yaml settings without packages) formatter ruff build.yaml with.formatter; discovery also observed black A reason names the strength and evidence of the winner and every candidate it outranked with non-default evidence. Executed builds keep the complete observations, detector registry and any selector in the plan's oyzu.dev/discovery extension.

The Rust builder reads rust-toolchain.toml and rust-toolchain in every form rustup accepts: the legacy rust-toolchain file holding only a toolchain name, such as nightly-2020-07-10, stable or 1.95.0; the TOML [toolchain] table, in either file, with channel (stable, beta, nightly, <major.minor>, <major.minor.patch>, optionally dated or with a host triple), components, targets and profile; a table without channel, which rustup resolves to the default toolchain: Oyzu then uses its own default (the [tools] rust selection in oyzu.toml, otherwise the adapter baseline) and keeps the declared components, targets and profile; path, a local toolchain directory. Oyzu cannot provision it, so oyzu pin and build tool resolution fail with toolchain.path names the local toolchain ...; select a Rust release in oyzu.toml with [tools] rust = "<version>". An explicit [tools] rust overrides it. An empty [toolchain] table, channel together with path, or an empty or whitespace-containing channel fails. Both files together still fail with both rust-toolchain.toml and rust-toolchain exist, although rustup itself prefers rust-toolchain. Reading a channel is not resolving it: the Rust tool backend currently resolves exact three-part stable versions, and other channels report that backend version selection is needed.

With a build.yaml, only its builds exist: discovery never adds one (OEP-0022 OD13). It does two things for the inventory instead. It supplies uses. A named build may omit uses. When exactly one builder, built in or from a catalog detection, recognizes the build's folder, discovery uses it, freezes it into the inventory before planning, and oyzu discover shows the build as chosen by build.yaml; builder detected from project files (builder_selection: inferred in --json). Builds that name uses stay explicit. builds: web: {path: web} # discovery supplies uses: node/app cli: uses: rust/app # written out: review sees exactly what was chosen platforms: [linux/x86_64, linux/arm64] exclude: [tools/scratch, tooling/**] A folder no builder recognizes, or several do, fails discovery, planning and builds with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE naming the candidates and the entry to write: build both: both is recognized by docker/image and node/app, so discovery cannot choose; write the one you want in build.yaml, for example both: {uses: docker/image, path: both} It reports undeclared folders. A folder where a builder recognizes a project that no entry covers is listed, never built: oyzu discover lists every such folder with the builders that recognize it and the shortest line to add (web: {path: web} with one builder). A folder several builders recognize gets an example marked example: with a placeholder to replace, both: {uses: <docker/image or node/app>, path: both}, never one candidate presented as the choice. --json adds an inventory object with tracked, undeclared and excluded lists; a failure to list them is reported there as inventory.error and never fails discovery. oyzu build --plan names at most five of them under Not in build.yaml, then the count of the rest and oyzu discover for the full list. Plan JSON has undeclared: {total, folders, tracked} (or {error}). Only the plan lists them: a real build, including its --no-docker and sandbox guards, neither walks the tree for them nor fails because of them. oyzu discover --check writes nothing and exits 1 while a folder holds a build that build.yaml neither declares nor excludes, printing error[INVENTORY_UNDECLARED], a table of folders and the fix. Without a build.yaml, every discovered build is undeclared. It exits 0 with Build inventory is current otherwise. Add it to CI to catch a new folder that would silently not build. oyzu discover --write declares every undeclared folder one builder recognizes, each as one line with uses written out (web: {uses: node/app, path: web}), appended to the builds: block so comments, order and hand-written entries (including ones without uses) stay as they were. It creates build.yaml when there is none, and refuses one whose builds: is not a block mapping at the start of a line. A folder several builders recognize is not written: it is listed under Needs a choice and the command exits 1 (outcome incomplete); when nothing else was written, the first line says A choice is needed: …; nothing was written. The result is parsed as an inventory before it replaces the file; a symlinked build.yaml or one changed meanwhile is refused, and so is another tool's build.yaml at the root, which is left unchanged. When it writes, it also adds the first line # yaml-language-server: $schema=https://github.com/oyzuai/oyzu/releases/latest/download/build.yaml.schema.json unless the file already has a yaml-language-server: $schema= comment, so editors validate and complete the file (editor schemas); a byte order mark stays first. --write and --check print the build-inventory record with --json (mode, outcome = current, undeclared, written or incomplete, path, tracked, undeclared/added/needsChoice and excluded; each folder has path, builders, name, entry and, when excluded, glob). --check and the inventory object of oyzu discover --json also list workspaceMembers, the folders covered as workspace members, each with path, builders and the owning build (named apart from the planned build.yaml root key members). --check, --write and, when there are any, the inventory object list warnings for workspace manifests that cannot be read. --check and --write list skippedBuildFiles, the inventory object lists it when there are any, and plain oyzu discover --json without an inventory lists skipped_build_files: other tools' build.yaml files the walk passed over, each with its root-relative path and its root keys. The two options cannot be combined. Workspace members. A folder that the native workspace manifest in a declared build's folder lists as a member is covered by that build: it is never reported undeclared and --write never declares it. Ownership comes from the manifest, not from where the folder sits: Builder Manifest in the build's folder Members rust/* Cargo.toml [workspace] members paths and globs (*, ?, […]), minus each exclude path and its subtree; a member listed as a literal path stays a member even below an excluded path, as in Cargo go/* go.work each use folder, one module each; a use never covers modules in its subfolders node/* package.json workspaces (npm, Yarn; an array or {packages: [...]}) and pnpm-workspace.yaml packages the folder globs, minus those written with a leading ! A crate below crates/ that members does not list is not a member (Cargo would not build it as part of the workspace), so it is still reported. The build's own builder answers: a docker/image build at the root does not own a Cargo workspace there. A build that omits uses asks every built-in builder recognizing its folder. A member covers only its own folder, so the walk continues below it, and a declared folder, a separate repository or a nested build.yaml keeps its own rules. A manifest that exists but cannot be read or parsed owns nothing and never fails the check, the plan or a build: its members stay reported as undeclared, and oyzu discover, --check and --write print warning: build web: cannot read the workspace manifest package.json: … (fix the file, then run the check again). Human output counts the members (Build inventory is current · 2 builds declared, 10 workspace members, or Covered as workspace members: cli 10 folders. below the table of undeclared folders). The walk follows zero-config discovery: it starts at the build root, skips the dependency and output folders listed above, nested Git repositories and folders with their own build.yaml inventory (another tool's build.yaml is listed as skipped and the walk continues), and stops below a folder a builder recognizes, which owns its subtree. A declared folder below the root owns its subtree too, whether or not a builder recognizes it (a development plugin may build it) and whether or not Git tracks a file directly in it. The build root never owns the tree while a build.yaml exists: a build declared at the root (path omitted or .) covers the root only, and every folder below it is still checked; the members its workspace manifest lists are covered (above), and any other project below it is listed until it is declared or excluded. Without a build.yaml a recognized root is the only build zero-config discovery has, so --write declares just that. An excluded folder is deliberately not a build, so the walk continues below it. Names: without a build.yaml the folders already are builds, so --write keeps their zero-config names (project at the root, project-<path> below it, for example project-web); writing the inventory never renames a build, its dist/ paths or its cache identity. With a build.yaml, an undeclared folder is not a build yet and is named after the folder, then its path joined with -, then a numbered variant. exclude: holds folder globs relative to the build root, written with / on every platform and matched case-sensitively as Git matches paths: * stays within one folder, tooling/** covers the whole subtree below tooling, and . is the build root itself. Absolute paths, .., backslashes and drive letters are refused. The key is exclude, not ignore, so it is not confused with tools.ignore. It only silences the listing and the check; it never changes which builds exist. Git. Inside a Git work tree only tracked files count, so a file a CI job creates cannot fail the check: a folder is considered when Git tracks a file directly in it (read from the index with git ls-files, no network and no index writes). Outside Git, or without a git executable, every file counts and the output says so (tracked: all-files).

Selections are read once, at discovery, from the frozen build.yaml inventory. Captured workspace planning reuses the target's decisions for its root. The host development composition of npm workspace tests and quality checks re-detects each package, including the root, without them, so a root that needed a selection fails there. Node output profiles and the Python test framework have no selector. The six discovery stops in the feasibility corpus are covered by fixtures in tests/integration/discovery.rs; the shared resolver by discovery::detectors unit tests; Rust toolchain forms by builders::rust::requirement_evidence unit tests. The pinned-corpus qualification records a compiled-CLI Windows plan against all six real source commits, including required selector reruns and its limits. It does not qualify builds or other host platforms. Undeclared-folder detection approximates "tracked" by folder: an untracked manifest beside tracked files still counts. The Plan and oyzu discover open a second configuration session to list folders, and the catalog detection budget of zero-config discovery applies to the whole walk; exceeding it fails --check and --write (with a remedy) and is reported, not fatal, in the plan. Workspace members are read from the manifests alone: Cargo's automatic membership of path dependencies inside the workspace folder, Maven modules, Gradle include, .NET solutions and uv workspaces are not read yet, so such members are still reported until declared or excluded. npm documents globs in workspaces but not !; Oyzu reads a leading ! there as pnpm defines it. One-line entries, the inventory commands and the Plan listing are covered by the compiled-CLI tests in tests/integration/build_inventory.rs (human, NO_COLOR and --json output, exit codes, Git tracking, --write text preservation, a Cargo workspace's members), the walk, naming and the Cargo, Go, npm and pnpm member rules by discovery::coverage unit tests, each manifest reader by its builder's workspace unit tests, the text edit by config::build_write unit tests and the root keys by config::build_model unit tests. Verified on Windows; the walk uses no platform-specific paths.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/docker-frontend.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. docker/image builds run every Dockerfile through oyzu-buildkit-frontend, a BuildKit gateway frontend shipped in the Docker toolchain image (oyzu-toolchain/docker:buildkit0.25.0). It runs BuildKit v0.25.0's stock Dockerfile frontend unchanged and adds two things around it: build-time injection into RUN steps, and an approved list for Dockerfiles that request their own frontend with # syntax=. Generated image recipes (Python containers and similar) still use BuildKit's built-in dockerfile.v0. The frontend is loaded from an OCI layout inside the toolchain image (/usr/share/oyzu/buildkit-frontend), never from a registry. Preparation records the layout's manifest digest under extensions.oyzu.dev/docker.frontend.manifest in the dependency record, and the build action pins it, so a changed toolchain image changes the plan.

When a plan carries injection material, the frontend gives every RUN step: a read-only bind mount of that material at /oyzu-inject, and APT_CONFIG and/or SSL_CERT_FILE pointing at the named files inside it. A RUN's own value for either variable is replaced. The mount and variables are set on each RUN operation, not on the image. They exist only while that step executes: no layer, image configuration entry or history line carries them, and the base image keeps its original digest. The Dockerfile is not edited. A RUN that mounts something at /oyzu-inject itself fails, because the path is reserved. The material is a directory captured under the prepared dependencies (inject/...), copied into the worker's private storage, checked against its planned tree digest and passed to BuildKit as the oyzu-inject local source. This is the delivery path the OS package lock proposal uses for replay apt configuration and the broker CA. Nothing in Oyzu produces injection material yet; until OS package locks or broker trust supply it, builds run with no injection and the frontend changes nothing about RUN.

A Dockerfile whose first line is # syntax=<reference> builds only when that reference is on the docker.frontends list (see configuration). Every entry must be pinned by digest: # oyzu.toml, user or managed configuration [docker] frontends = ["docker/dockerfile:1.17@sha256:<index digest>"] A request matches an entry with the same repository (after Docker's normalization, so docker/dockerfile and docker.io/docker/dockerfile are equal) and either the same digest, or the same tag when the request names no digest (an untagged request means latest). The approved frontend image is captured from the local Docker engine like a base image, for the worker's platform, and loaded by digest; the tag is never resolved again. Oyzu's frontend runs it and applies the same injection to the build graph it returns. Anything else fails during preparation, before a worker starts: FRONTEND_NOT_APPROVED: Dockerfile requests frontend docker/dockerfile:1, which is not on the approved list; approved: docker/dockerfile:1.17@sha256:... An entry without a digest fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. Oyzu never ignores the line or substitutes its own default. The frontend applies the same rule again inside BuildKit. The Dockerfile is still parsed by the pinned BuildKit v0.25.0 parser during preparation, so syntax that parser does not understand fails admission even when the requested frontend would accept it.

Injection reaches only RUN steps. A requested frontend's own intermediate evaluations (for example, reading a file from a stage while it plans) run before Oyzu rewrites its graph and do not see the mount. The frontend tracks BuildKit v0.25.0's Dockerfile frontend; updating it means updating the toolchain image. How injected options appear in provenance is not decided (open in the OS package lock proposal). The published toolchain image pin must be refreshed after the image is republished; an older toolchain image lacks the frontend and fails preparation reading its digest.

Measured on 2026-10-10 on Windows 11 with Docker Desktop's Linux engine 29.8.1, using the branch CLI and a locally built toolchain image (frontend manifest sha256:4a98e4e120fa405ef0b51fe4072005afb577cc8ef98b00f50bd2ec8a1ada2e56); commands are in the pull request. oyzu build of a FROM alpine:3.22 + RUN project succeeds, and BuildKit's log shows oyzu.dev/buildkit-frontend@sha256:4a98e4e1… loaded from the client's OCI layout. A # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.17 project fails with FRONTEND_NOT_APPROVED (exit 2) while docker.frontends is empty, and builds once docker/dockerfile:1.17@sha256:38387523… is approved; the frontend loads from the captured store and the RUN completes. Not yet run natively: a FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM cross build. Go unit tests (src/builders/docker/runtime/frontend, run while building the toolchain image): every RUN gains the read-only mount and environment with the graph still connected, graphs without RUN are untouched, the reserved path is refused, option file names are contained, approval matches by tag or digest and refusals name both references, and the layout is deterministic. Rust unit tests: build-action arguments, admission and planning agreement, captured syntax frontend binding, and the injection store's exact copy. Ignored native tests in src/executor/worker/native_frontend.rs build through the real toolchain image: RUN reads the injected files and variables, the read-only mount refuses writes, and the exported image contains neither the files nor the variables, with and without an approved # syntax= frontend.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/docker-images.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The experimental Docker builder supports scratch, internal stages and image references already provisioned in the executor's Docker image store, including bases selected through global ARG defaults. The same path captures external COPY --from and literal image-backed mount references reported by the native Dockerfile parser. No extra project configuration is needed: FROM alpine:3.22 COPY greeting.txt /greeting.txt RUN test -f /etc/alpine-release
documents.s: Docker image inputs and offline builds

documents.t: A Dockerfile whose final stage only adds files to one base and edits image settings is built without Docker, BuildKit or any container engine. Earlier stages may contain RUN when the final stage is clearly independent; those earlier stages are not executed or included in the image. Oyzu fetches the final base from its registry, writes each COPY as a new layer and edits the image configuration itself. This is the same approach as ko, Jib and crane append. No configuration selects it; the Dockerfile's content does: FROM gcr.io/distroless/base-debian12:nonroot@sha256:7f0c72cd138b442ae0deeb69c08b1acf5525439ba251a49ad93c320a061567e5 COPY bin/server /server USER 65532:65532 EXPOSE 8080 ENTRYPOINT ["/server"]

Instruction Supported form FROM The final base is scratch or a reference pinned by @sha256: digest (a tag may also be present), optional AS name. No --platform. Earlier stages must also use literal scratch or digest bases. COPY Context sources (files or directories, no wildcards), shell or JSON form, --chown=user[:group] (names or ids) and --chmod=<octal>. Relative destinations resolve against WORKDIR. WORKDIR, USER, STOPSIGNAL One literal value. ENV, LABEL key=value pairs with shell quoting; legacy ENV KEY value without quotes. EXPOSE Ports with optional /tcp, /udp or /sctp; no ranges. CMD, ENTRYPOINT JSON (exec) form or shell form, which becomes /bin/sh -c. The independent-stage case uses the same recognized instruction grammar in earlier stages, except that their RUN instructions are skipped. For example, FROM scratch AS unused, RUN exit 99, FROM scratch, COPY greeting.txt /greeting.txt assembles only the final COPY. A final-stage RUN, stage references such as FROM unused or COPY --from=unused, ADD, ARG, HEALTHCHECK, VOLUME, SHELL, ONBUILD, unsupported COPY flags, heredocs, variable expansion, a # syntax= or non-default # escape= directive, a base pinned only by tag, and a .dockerignore or Dockerfile.dockerignore file keep the BuildKit worker. The choice is made per target; a project can mix both paths.

Oyzu first checks whether the exact digest-pinned reference is provisioned in the local Docker image store. An available OCI index or manifest is exported and admitted by immutable identity: the index must uniquely bind the requested platform, and the manifest, configuration and every layer must verify. A present image with an identity, platform or export error fails; it does not select a different registry image. Classic Docker stores exposing only a configuration ID cannot supply this native local capture. Missing Docker, an unavailable daemon, --no-docker, or a genuinely absent local image preserves registry acquisition. Registry acquisition uses the OCI Distribution API by digest, so a moved tag can never select different content. For an index, the entry for the target platform (linux/amd64 or linux/arm64) is used. Verified content is retained in the native user image cache (%LocalAppData%\Oyzu\cache\images on Windows, ~/Library/Caches/Oyzu/images on macOS, $XDG_CACHE_HOME/oyzu/images or ~/.cache/oyzu/images on Linux). Project cache.dir cannot relocate image admission records. Later builds trust admitted content; offline registry builds require retained content, while provisioned local images can be admitted without network. Builds under managed configuration never contact a public registry. Only anonymous pulls are supported: a registry's bearer-token challenge is answered without credentials, which covers public images on Docker Hub, gcr.io, ghcr.io and similar registries. A private base fails preparation with an explanation; it does not fall back to BuildKit. HTTPS_PROXY, NO_PROXY and SSL_CERT_FILE apply as for other Oyzu downloads. A loopback registry (localhost:5000/...) is contacted over plain HTTP. A base with ONBUILD triggers, zstd or foreign layers, or a platform other than the target fails explicitly.

Base layers are copied byte for byte. Docker schema 2 bases are written with the equivalent OCI media types. Each COPY is one gzip layer, and so is a WORKDIR that creates a directory. Entries are sorted, timestamped with the export epoch (1980-01-01 UTC) and carry numeric ownership with no user or group names. Files are 0644, or 0755 when they are executable on a Unix host or start with an ELF header or #!. Directories are 0755. --chmod overrides both. New files and any directories COPY creates are owned by --chown, or root. Names resolve against the base image's /etc/passwd and /etc/group; an unknown name fails the build. Without a group, the user id is also the group id, as in Docker. Directories that already exist in the base keep their ownership. The configuration is the base's, with Env, Labels, User, WorkingDir, ExposedPorts, Cmd, Entrypoint and StopSignal edited as in Docker. An ENTRYPOINT discards an inherited CMD unless the Dockerfile sets one. An image without PATH gets Docker's default. created and the appended history entries use the export epoch. COPY reads the same inputs BuildKit would: the files under each COPY source in the target directory, plus explicitly materialized artifacts. Nothing else in the workspace is visible. The output is the same <target>-<version>.oci.tar layout with the same name annotations, the same integrity and platform validation and the same evidence. Rebuilding unchanged inputs produces the same image digest on every host. It is not byte-identical to an image BuildKit would build from the same Dockerfile.

The target's dependency record (dist/dependencies/<target>.json) names the adapter docker/oci-assembly, records imageSource: registry or provisioned-local, the typed recipe under extensions.oyzu.dev/docker.assembly, the base's requested reference, manifest digest, configuration digest and store-tree digest under images, the selected context files and the Dockerfile digest. The executor checks the Dockerfile and base store against those identities before writing anything. The build action records the oci-assembly execution mode and its enforced properties (no-container-engine, no-project-code-execution). Local capture uses the daemon only to export already provisioned content; assembly itself remains in-process.

When Docker cannot provide the oyzu-toolchain/docker image, for example on a host or pod with no Docker engine, an admitted target still builds: its worker identity becomes Oyzu's own executable (oyzu-builtin/in-process), whose platform is the Linux platform of the host's architecture. oyzu build --isolated --no-docker admits this target when its selected work is the native build and packaging path; the plan reports needsDaemon: false and isolation: in-process. In-process preparation and actions do not probe Docker's memory, and do not require crun or user namespaces. Other targets retain their worker-capacity checks. Tasks that need the toolchain image remain required: --full selects Dockerfile lint (hadolint) and format checks (dockerfmt), so the no-Docker guard stops with NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON before preparation. Unsupported Dockerfiles also retain that refusal. A digest-pinned base with ONBUILD triggers fails explicitly during assembly without running those triggers or falling back to BuildKit. Measured commands and limits cover the Windows qualification.

The execution image dogfood recipe connects an ordinary Rust producer to RUN-free image assembly through a runtime artifact materialization edge. It stages exact source and notices as inputs, builds the Linux CLI, then copies only the accepted producer artifact into the replacement's default CLI and compiled-worker paths. Required producer reports, Dockerfile quality checks and OCI validation remain gates. Use independently available, compatible execution seeds. In particular, the Rust seed's compiled reporting adapter must implement the current required report contract; compiling newer source does not update the adapter executing that build. Native concurrency can be set through ordinary resolved [env] configuration without raising isolation limits. The recipe documents the exact inputs and commands. Its complete seed-to-replacement runtime qualification is in progress; a compiled binary alone is not acceptance. The initial runtime base is a local development asset, not a publicly distributed bootstrap or an official release.

Provision Docker with a Linux image store and the selected BuildKit user-namespace/AppArmor profile. The builder image (oyzu-toolchain/docker:buildkit0.25.0, built from tooling/images/docker-metadata.Dockerfile) includes BuildKit 0.25.0, native metadata/image adapters and the quality tools; Oyzu pulls it itself when it is missing (see Published toolchain images). For Dockerfiles that use the BuildKit worker, provision the declared base images separately using your organization's approved mechanism; Oyzu does not pull missing base images or read registry credentials in that profile. Daemonless assembly needs none of this. After a successful BuildKit action, Oyzu waits up to 30 seconds for Docker to confirm removal of its isolated worker before accepting the exported image. If Docker does not confirm cleanup within that bound, the build fails and the output is not accepted; check Docker daemon health and retry the build. oyzu run list oyzu build --plan oyzu build oyzu inspect dist Planning includes input preparation and therefore requires the provisioned images. oyzu run build remains a native development command; it does not provide this captured-build boundary. Windows and macOS hosts require a suitable Linux Docker environment; native Windows images and emulation remain unfinished. Some Docker Desktop Linux daemons report an empty AppArmor profile after starting an explicitly unconfined worker. Oyzu accepts this representation only when the container's security options retain apparmor=unconfined and an independent daemon capability query confirms that AppArmor is absent. Named profiles still require an exact observed match. Missing or contradictory evidence fails startup; network isolation, unprivileged execution and the process sandbox remain required. The daemon query is docker info --format '{{json .SecurityOptions}}'. Docker Desktop 29.8.1 on Windows 11 answers with a list such as ["name=seccomp,profile=builtin","name=cgroupns"], which satisfies the check. A running Linux engine always lists some security options, so an answer that is not a list of strings (for example null) is missing evidence, not an empty list. The build then stops with cannot verify the BuildKit worker's AppArmor boundary, naming the name=apparmor requirement and what Docker reported. Retry once the Docker engine is fully running; an engine that keeps answering this way cannot run isolated BuildKit builds with an unconfined worker.

An explicit target can differ from the BuildKit worker for image assembly that does not execute target code: builds: image: uses: docker/image platforms: [linux/arm64] With a Dockerfile containing only FROM scratch and COPY operations, a provisioned amd64 worker can assemble this arm64 image. Supported explicit Docker targets are currently linux/x86_64 and linux/arm64 (linux/amd64 and linux/aarch64 are accepted aliases; an ABI is refused). Omitted platforms retains the selected worker's platform; this increment does not introduce a new global default. Architecture-variant suffixes and unsupported OS/architectures fail admission. No image or emulator is installed automatically. Preparation records the toolchain platform under manager.platform and the artifact target under targetPlatform. Plans retain tool/worker identity separately from target identity, pass the artifact target to BuildKit, and check that captured facts match the request and resolved toolchain. Base image inputs must match the platform of the stage that uses them: the artifact target, or the worker for a FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM stage. A locally provisioned base with the wrong architecture fails before export; a matching tag alone is insufficient. Materialized producers must also have the same artifact OS/architecture as their consumer. Explicit consumer platforms propagate to producer variants through materialization; this does not establish platform independence or a capable executor. The native parser records required targetExecution evidence for any RUN, including commands in intermediate stages. Until suitable native/emulated executor admission is implemented, a Dockerfile with RUN requires matching worker and target platforms. A foreign-platform RUN fails preparation before application actions, even if the host happens to have an emulator. OCI integrity/platform assertions verify bytes and metadata; they do not execute the image or replace required application tests. Every OCI image is checked against its artifact target during default testing, collection and bundle inspection. A valid image for the wrong architecture cannot be retained as a successful output merely because its archive hash is valid. Snapshot artifacts, JUnit and lint/read-only-format gates otherwise retain their existing behavior. List several platforms, platforms: [linux/x86_64, linux/arm64], to expand separate image builds. Each produces its own versioned OCI archive and reports. Complete selected image families additionally produce an OCI index; see matrix builds for selection, producer propagation and compatibility details.

When a build needs one of Oyzu's own oyzu-toolchain/* images that the local Docker engine does not have, Oyzu pulls it from ghcr.io/oyzuai and tags it with the name the builder expects. The packages are public, so no registry login or credentials are involved. The pull is by digest, using the pins committed in src/executor/published_images.json, so the registry verifies the content and a moved tag cannot substitute another image. A fresh machine therefore needs only Docker: oyzu build # first run: "Pulling toolchain image oyzu-toolchain/helm:3.22.0 from ghcr.io/oyzuai/..." Published today: builder-worker:v1, docker:buildkit0.25.0, go:1.24-mod0.25.0, helm:3.22.0 and node:npm11.11.0-node22, all linux/amd64. Every other image, including base images and the remaining toolchain images, is still provisioned by hand from tooling/images and never pulled. An image already present locally is used as is and never replaced, so locally built images keep working. Set OYZU_NO_TOOLCHAIN_PULL=1 to forbid pulling (for example on an offline or air-gapped host); a missing image then fails with the existing provisioning message. Limits: the pinned digests are not yet recorded in oyzu.lock, a pulled image is trusted by its pin and not re-verified on later runs, and routing pulls through the tool broker or a private mirror is not implemented. The Helm and worker images embed a compiled Oyzu worker, so their pins move when a CLI release republishes them.

Isolated builds add Docker resources, so Oyzu bounds the ones it creates. It never touches anything it did not create: a resource is Oyzu's only when it carries the label dev.oyzu.owner=oyzu or is recorded in the per-user ledger docker-storage.json (in the cache directory of the Oyzu user-data directory). Containers and volumes are labelled when created. Docker cannot label an image after a pull, so images are recorded instead: one pulled from the published toolchain namespace ghcr.io/oyzuai/oyzu-toolchain/ (including those pulled by earlier releases, which are adopted on the first pass) or a container tool Oyzu installed. Locally built oyzu-toolchain/* images, base images and everything you pulled yourself are neither listed, measured nor removed. After an isolated build that used a Docker image, under a lock shared by builds: Images. Recorded images that lost their tag to a newer pinned image, and those unused for 60 days, are removed. Beyond that, the least recently used are removed until the recorded images total at most cache.dockerMaxMiB (default 20 GiB). Images used by the finishing build are never selected, and Docker refuses to remove an image a container uses. Containers and anonymous volumes. Labelled containers that exited over an hour ago are removed with their anonymous volumes. This includes the BuildKit worker's private store, which is where BuildKit's build cache lives, so that cache cannot outlive its worker. Volumes. Unused labelled volumes are removed. Persistent oyzu-tools-* volumes keep their own retention (see build logging). The pass is best effort: a failure leaves the work to the next isolated build and never changes a build's result. Host builds add no Docker resources and run no pass. Set cache.dockerMaxMiB (1–1048576 MiB; it is not part of any action key) in the ordinary configuration cascade to change the image budget; the 60-day and one-hour ages are fixed. oyzu cache status reports the recorded image count, size and budget on its Docker line and under docker in --json; it is omitted when Oyzu has recorded no image or Docker cannot be queried. oyzu cache clear empties the action cache only.

The native parser identifies image requirements without executing Dockerfile commands. Global ARG defaults resolve base/platform selections through BuildKit's expansion library. Unsupported dynamic mount references, remote ADD, secret/SSH mounts and host networking fail admission. A # syntax= frontend builds only when it is on the digest-pinned docker.frontends list; see Oyzu's BuildKit frontend, which runs every Dockerfile build. To bring in a pinned download instead of remote ADD or RUN curl, declare a fetch and copy from the reserved named context oyzu-fetch-<name>; such references are never treated as images. The host executor inspects each provisioned image and exports its immutable config identity, so a tag change between inspection and export cannot substitute another image. It never starts that image or gives project code the host Docker socket. An offline Go adapter uses go-containerregistry 0.20.6 to read the native transport archive, verify image integrity/platform and write an OCI content store. It preserves native config/layer content and media types. Images containing ONBUILD instructions fail because their hidden inputs are not yet part of discovery. Preparation freezes the store. Plans record the requested reference, normalized native context name, config digest, manifest digest and store-tree digest. Before worker startup, the executor copies each store into private storage and verifies its planned tree identity. BuildKit receives native OCI named contexts through its client session. The worker and Dockerfile RUN processes remain offline. Image stores are read-only worker inputs, not arbitrary host mounts or mounts inside RUN containers. No shared result cache is imported. Inputs are recorded under extensions.oyzu.dev/docker.images in the target's dist/dependencies/<target>.json; imageSource identifies the current provisioned-daemon source. These identities also affect the dependency and build plan digests. The OCI manifest digest may differ from a registry's original manifest identity because a Docker save transport does not preserve every registry representation. The config identity and captured content are verified; no original registry provenance is invented. The same extension's metadata.selection records targetPlatform and sourceDateEpoch. Preparation supplies these facts to the native adapter, and planning rejects facts that differ from the selected artifact target or export epoch. The export epoch has one owner in the executor contract and is used both during selection and native export; it is currently 315532800 (1980-01-01 UTC). Before worker startup, Oyzu also sets the private source, Dockerfile, materialized-artifact and prepared-context copies' file/directory access and modification times to that same epoch. Original source and prepared stores are unchanged. Content identity excludes acquisition/copy times, so exposing them to RUN would make identical inputs behave differently. On Unix, the existing private-copy mode normalization still preserves executable intent while removing host umask/setuid differences. Timestamp updates are required; an unsupported file type or failed metadata update stops worker startup rather than silently using host timestamps. This does not freeze application clocks, process randomness or every filesystem metadata field. This corrects a native uv repeatability failure: uv embedded the input wheel's varying copy-time mtime in uv_cache.json and changed its RECORD hash. OCI export-time normalization alone could not repair those file contents. Installers keep their normal metadata; no Dockerfile change or metadata-deletion option is required. Regenerate affected images with the updated executor. The existing plan's content identities do not authorize reuse of an output produced by the older executor. Successful builds retain the versioned <target>-<snapshot-version>.oci.tar artifact and its OCI digest in dist/manifest.json, plus default integrity/platform JUnit and native quality results. Container integrity checks do not measure application code coverage; materialized producers retain their own test/coverage evidence. Version inference supplies a tag-derived base when available and a source-derived snapshot suffix. The exported OCI reference uses that same version. Changed base-image inputs change the plan/content digests even if that version string is unchanged.

with.repository declares the image's approved registry repository (a name without scheme, tag or digest, for example registry.example.com/team/app). Building never publishes or contacts it. A helm/chart image binding reads it to name the image it consumes. docker/image accepts two with options: repository and dependencies. oyzu config validate and every command that reads the build inventory check them; any other key is refused. Where the built image is loaded locally is not a with option but the docker.load setting.

The docker.load setting lists where oyzu run load puts an image you have already built, so a local cluster can run it with no custom docker load step. Which cluster is personal, so the list lives in the configuration cascade, not in build.yaml (OEP-0022 OD4): a team default in oyzu.toml, your own cluster in oyzu.local.toml, or user configuration. Like any per-target setting it applies to the docker/image builds in its folder and below, the nearest file wins, and [context.<name>] and profile tables can vary it. The image is named by the build's with.repository: # build.yaml builds: image: uses: docker/image with: repository: registry.example.com/team/app # names the loaded image # oyzu.local.toml (Git-ignored), or oyzu.toml for a team default [docker] load = ["docker", "k3d:dev"] oyzu build oyzu run load # or: oyzu run image:load when several targets exist oyzu config explain docker.load --target image # where the list came from A list holds zero to eight distinct destinations; an empty list (load = []) in a nearer file turns a farther default off. When docker.load reaches a build without with.repository, the load task is listed as unavailable with that reason instead of failing other commands. An unknown or repeated destination is refused as the value is read, naming docker.load, so oyzu config validate reports it and every command that reads that configuration fails. The setting never changes an action key, so changing it does not rebuild anything. The earlier with.load key is refused with a message pointing at this setting. oyzu.local.toml is ignored in CI unless --local-overrides is given (inspection and selection). The task never builds, never pushes and never contacts a registry. It reads the latest dist/manifest.json (the build must have succeeded and the archive must still match its recorded digest), selects the single OCI archive produced by this target, and makes the image resolvable as <repository>@<manifest digest>, the reference a bound chart uses, so a deploy pulls nothing. Destination What happens Requires docker docker load of the archive, docker tag as <repository>:<version>, then docker image inspect <repository>@<digest> must succeed. Docker Desktop Kubernetes shares this engine. docker on PATH; Docker's containerd image store, which keeps OCI manifest digests. Another store fails the inspect with an explanation. k3d:<cluster> k3d image import of the archive, then on every server and agent node ctr -n k8s.io images tag names the image <repository>@<digest> and <repository>:<version>. docker and k3d on PATH (pin k3d with oyzu install k3d) and a running cluster. A platform matrix with several image variants is refused for now; loading a chosen variant is not implemented. Registry publication is not part of loading: publishing belongs to oyzu publish. Verified on Windows 11 with Docker Desktop (containerd image store) and k3d 5.7.4 on 2026-10-09: oyzu run load loaded the EX-029 image into Docker and a k3d cluster; the manifest rendered from the bound chart (kubectl apply) started its pod with the kubelet reporting the image "already present on machine" and no pull. python tooling/test-build-scenarios.py --suite docker --only image-load covers the Docker destination and the refusals. Docker Desktop's own Kubernetes was not enabled or exercised; k3d was run by hand, not by the harness; Linux and macOS hosts were not run. That run used the earlier with.load key; after the move to docker.load the same scenario passed on Windows 11 with Docker Desktop on 2026-10-19, reading the list from oyzu.toml (status); k3d was not rerun.

Image selection can use conventional Dockerfile defaults without an Oyzu configuration file: ARG REGISTRY=docker.io/library ARG VERSION=3.22 ARG BASE=${REGISTRY}/alpine:${VERSION} FROM ${BASE} RUN test -f /etc/alpine-release Only global declarations before the first FROM participate in base/platform selection. Defaults expand in declaration order using BuildKit's native quoting, escape and parameter-expansion rules. Later declarations with values replace earlier ones; declarations without a value retain an existing default. A missing value can use a native expression such as ${BASE:-alpine:3.22}. An empty resolved base or explicit platform fails preparation. Stage-local arguments do not become global defaults, and host environment variables are never consulted. Captured metadata records resolved stage bases/platforms and image requirements; source identity still binds the original Dockerfile. An argument resolving to scratch or a prior stage does not create an external image dependency. A resolved stage platform must be the selected artifact target or the worker's own platform (FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM); any other platform fails admission. A base for a worker-platform stage is captured for the worker's platform and bound as the BuildKit context <name>::<platform>, so the same reference can serve both a build stage and the target stage. Automatic TARGETPLATFORM, TARGETOS, TARGETOSVERSION, TARGETARCH and TARGETVARIANT use the captured target platform, parsed by the same pinned containerd platform library used by BuildKit. TARGETSTAGE names the final stage, or default when it is unnamed. Global declarations retain native scope and can replace these defaults. For example, ARG BASE=registry.example/runtime:${TARGETARCH} selects a provisioned architecture-specific image without reading the host architecture. The executor supplies SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH as a build argument. A global declaration makes that value available to image selection and overrides any Dockerfile default for it. Without a global declaration, it is not part of global selection scope. A stage-local declaration can expose it to native RUN commands independently. These facts do not establish target execution capability; RUN still requires matching target and worker platforms. Native lint/format policy continues to apply, including Hadolint's checks on explicit FROM --platform flags. Automatic worker arguments (BUILDPLATFORM, BUILDOS, BUILDOSVERSION, BUILDARCH, BUILDVARIANT) use the Docker toolchain worker's platform, recorded as metadata.selection.buildPlatform and checked against the worker during planning; the target platform is never assumed to describe the worker. RUN in a stage pinned to the worker's platform is not target execution, so the common cross-compile pattern (FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM golang AS build, then COPY --from=build into a target-platform stage without RUN) builds an arm64 image on an amd64 worker. RUN in a target-platform stage of a cross build still fails before any action runs. Public build-argument overrides and stage-local mount expansion remain unfinished.

A missing image fails preparation with a provisioning diagnostic; there is no automatic internet fallback. Platform mismatch, malformed transport, config mismatch, hidden ONBUILD, mutated frozen stores or native worker failures block artifacts. Correct the input or provisioned toolchain, then create a new plan. Native lint/format failures retain their existing gates; adding a usable base does not waive them. There are at most 64 distinct image references, a 10 GiB transport/captured-tree limit and 100,000 transport entries per image. Transport inspection rejects traversal, duplicate member names and transport links without extracting layer files on the host. The offline adapter is also constrained by executor resource/time limits. Images using unsupported transport forms fail explicitly. Equivalent references such as alpine:3.22 and docker.io/library/alpine:3.22 share one BuildKit context when their captured manifest, config and store-tree identities agree. Both requested references remain in the evidence. Conflicting identities fail planning; reference order never chooses between different images. Rebuild custom Docker toolchain images for the current metadata adapter, which requires explicit target-platform, epoch and build-platform arguments, for oyzu-docker-images, and for oyzu-buildkit-frontend. Metadata without selection.buildPlatform and records without the frontend identity fail rather than assuming defaults; regenerate them. Prepared dependency layout version 5 requires targetExecution metadata and distinguishes tool execution from artifact target facts. Older metadata without that field fails rather than assuming no target execution. Regenerate captures/plans made by older adapters; missing or mismatched selection facts cannot silently acquire new defaults. Scratch-only plans still work with an empty image list and explicit selection facts. No project-file migration is required. This is an explicitly provisioned image-input profile. Registry acquisition through approved connectors, managed source authorization, additional package-manager integrations, secret brokerage, additional Dockerfile-free application profiles, caching and full platform matrices remain required work. The existence of an image in a local daemon is not an enterprise trust or release-eligibility assertion.

The new platform unit checks exercise arm64 image planning with an amd64 worker, mismatched capture rejection, native-only builder admission, materialization mismatch, and OCI inspection against target identity. The native parser checks target execution requirements without running project code. The Linux captured Docker suite now also requires actual arm64 OCI assembly from the EX-026 scratch fixture on an amd64 worker, JUnit/quality gates, unchanged sources, repeatable snapshot archives, and pre-action foreign RUN rejection. These cross-target checks passed in Docker job 110868387899 at revision ad6cbf1; that job also verified the EX-027 and EX-050 matching-platform producer graphs described in toolchain platforms. Native image-adapter tests run from src/dependencies/runtime/images with provisioned Go 1.24.13 and its checked-in module/checksum locks: go test -mod=readonly ./... They generate Docker transports with the native SDK and verify OCI config/layers, repeated identities, normalization, unchanged inputs, mismatched config/platform, hidden ONBUILD and unsafe transport rejection.
