Run the same command in src/builders/docker/runtime/metadata for native parsing, argument expansion, ignore rules and source-boundary checks. Argument tests cover composed/quoted/redeclared defaults, missing values, target architecture/variant/stage facts, epoch override/scope, host-environment independence and rejection of uncaptured worker facts. Rust checks cover selection/execution agreement, required bindings, offline arguments, contained store copies and post-plan tampering. Parsing an ARM platform in a unit test does not establish ARM execution support. These native/unit checks do not prove Docker worker integration. CI runs native metadata/conversion checks on Windows/macOS/Linux after compiling the CLI. The separate Linux worker job builds an ARG-selected provisioned-base image through the compiled CLI with a process/network/mount canary and requires repeated OCI identities. The broader captured suite exercises the checked-in EX-026 variants, reports, input evidence, aliases, global defaults and missing-base/default failures. These captured checks passed Docker job 110767008269 at revision 8dbf1b4 in run 36983990838, which also passed the three-host task jobs and isolated worker job. See implementation status for the exact scope and remaining work. Native API references: BuildKit OCI named contexts, go-containerregistry layouts and Docker archive support. The toolchain preserves dependency licenses/notices alongside the compiled adapter.

Provisioned image capture is shared through dependencies/images; Dockerfile parsing still determines Docker's required references. The capture path preserves existing immutable config/platform checks and OCI-store evidence. This internal relocation adds no registry fallback or configuration precedence rule. Within one oyzu build, each distinct base is exported with docker image save and converted once. Other targets that need the same base, matched by reference, the daemon's immutable image ID, the target platform and the converter image, wait for that capture and receive a verified copy of its store; the copy must have the same tree digest. Before this, several targets on one large base (for example three Liquibase migration images) each exported and converted it at the same time, holding several copies in the Docker engine's memory at once; on a 16 GB Docker Desktop those builds failed reading the base with cannot allocate memory. Evidence and plan digests are unchanged, since every target still records the same identities. The kept stores live in the system temporary directory and are deleted when the build finishes. A failed capture is not reused; the next target tries again. Separate oyzu build processes do not share captures. The isolated BuildKit worker receives each captured base store as a private copy made with docker cp before the worker starts, not as a host bind mount. BuildKit reads a base's layers more than once (unpacking it, then again for COPY). On Docker Desktop for Windows, those large reads through a host bind mount failed with cannot allocate memory under VM memory pressure. The copy has the verified tree digest, is owned by root inside the worker, and is removed with the worker. The source context, definition and output directories are still bind-mounted. The first application container: true integration is Python application packaging, whose default and override profiles passed Linux CI. It uses the internal typed assembly boundary and shared captured-base acquisition. Additional runtime profiles, application-container matrices and startup smoke tests remain unfinished. Existing Dockerfile builds continue to use their captured source definition. The worker verifies the bytes actually staged for BuildKit against the planned digest, so a definition changed during copying is rejected rather than executed. The executor's prepared dependency-context transport has native conformance verified in Linux CI. The Docker package-manager integrations are the experimental Python, Node-manager, Go-module and Cargo profiles below. The pip context passed its captured checks in the dependency job linked below; the complete suite remains unverified. Other ecosystems, private sources and full EX-058 credential-policy acceptance remain unfinished.

For a Docker target, an external context named dependencies requests a prepared package store. With a single Python ecosystem and requirements.txt, no dependency selector is needed. Select the Docker builder explicitly when the project also looks like an application: builds: image: uses: docker/image FROM python:3.13-slim-bookworm WORKDIR /app COPY requirements.txt . RUN --mount=type=bind,from=dependencies,target=/dependencies \ pip install --no-index --no-cache-dir --no-compile --find-links=/dependencies -r requirements.txt COPY app.py . CMD ["python", "app.py"] Supply application files with the Dockerfile's ordinary COPY instructions. --no-compile avoids installation-time bytecode timestamps in this example; use python -B for build-time import checks to avoid creating timestamped bytecode afterward. Arbitrary Dockerfile commands are not automatically made reproducible. A requirements entry such as six==1.17.0 is resolved by pip inside the exact provisioned base image, using that image's Python, pip, ABI and platform. Preparation downloads binary wheels through Oyzu's scoped public-PyPI broker. It does not add application-build, test or quality tools to this runtime store. No project code or source build runs during resolution. The subsequent Docker build remains offline and installs from the captured store; Oyzu does not rewrite RUN commands. When other ecosystem manifests make automatic selection ambiguous, the docker/image builder's with.dependencies option names the provider: builds: image: uses: docker/image with: dependencies: python/pip This option is frozen build inventory, not an additional TOML precedence layer: choosing among the native facts the tree already shows is the same for everyone (OEP-0022). The value must be one provider name; oyzu config validate refuses anything else. The earlier top-level dependencies: build field is refused with a message naming with.dependencies. The implemented Python providers are: Provider Required native inputs Tools already required in the consumer image python/pip requirements.txt Python and pip python/uv pyproject.toml and uv.lock Python, pip and uv python/poetry pyproject.toml and poetry.lock Python, pip, Poetry and its export plugin One matching provider can be inferred; multiple matching managers require an explicit with.dependencies, even within Python. Unknown providers and missing native manifests fail explicitly. A with.dependencies without an external dependencies reference also fails. A Dockerfile stage actually named dependencies remains a native stage, not a package-store request. Other external names retain image-reference behavior. uv uses its native locked, offline exporter with --no-default-groups; Poetry uses its native export plugin restricted to the main group, with project plugins disabled. Runtime stores exclude development/default groups and optional extras. Stale locks and lock hash mismatches fail. The same native lock/source restrictions as Python preparation apply; local/path/VCS dependencies and arbitrary extra indices are not implemented by this profile. An explicit locked provider consumes its own lock, not a neighboring requirements file. All three providers include a generated requirements.txt beside the resolved wheels. It pins the complete selected closure with SHA-256 hashes. This is a projection of the already-resolved native inputs; it does not replace the source lock or perform another dependency resolution. For a uv/Poetry project, an offline Dockerfile step can consume it without copying or exporting the project lock itself: RUN --mount=type=bind,from=dependencies,target=/dependencies \ pip install --no-index --no-deps --require-hashes --no-cache-dir --no-compile --find-links=/dependencies -r /dependencies/requirements.txt uv's native uv pip install can consume the same hashed requirements. This is not transparent support for arbitrary uv sync or poetry install commands/cache layouts. Missing native tools in the base fail preparation; Oyzu never installs them. Native tests currently provision uv 0.12.21 with Python 3.12, and Poetry 2.5.1/export 1.10.1 with Python 3.12. Other tool versions require qualification. The base image must already exist locally and provide Python 3.11 or later with pip; the first native fixture uses Python 3.13. The worker and artifact platform must match for package preparation, even for a Dockerfile that only copies store files. Consumers using earlier named stages resolve to their original base. Multiple distinct consuming bases, scratch consumers and incompatible platforms fail rather than sharing an unchecked closure. Preparation resolves the already-captured immutable base config, not a tag that may have moved. Commands that subsequently change the interpreter or libraries in a stage remain the Dockerfile author's responsibility; the initial runtime binding does not prove compatibility after arbitrary stage mutations. The prepared dependency record retains wheel identities, digests, source/lock identities, actual interpreter and manager versions, immutable runtime config and a separate store-tree digest. Only the wheel subtree and generated hashed requirements enter BuildKit's private named context; broker/control state stays outside it. The context is read-only by default for the shown native bind mount. Build output remains the normal versioned OCI archive with integrity/platform JUnit and Docker quality gates. Integrity evidence is not a release authorization or proof that a package's contents are trustworthy. The initial profile uses the existing public PyPI and Python-hosted-files routes. Direct URL requirements, alternate-index directives and source distributions are rejected. Native requirement constraints/hashes retain their existing pip validation. This preparation needs upstream availability; there is no persistent offline acquisition cache yet. Managed acquisition and enforced connector routes fail closed until approved connector bindings exist. No registry token is supplied to the image, build arguments or Dockerfile. This does not yet implement the private-registry canary and all-manager credential requirements of EX-058. Remote syntax frontends and secret mounts remain unsupported by the captured Docker profile. On failure, inspect the retained diagnostic and native logs, correct the manifest/provider or provisioned runtime, and start a new build. Preparation failures produce no action artifacts; failed offline RUN commands block packaging. The Linux dependencies CI suite provisions the three Python profiles and exercises native resolution/install/import, exact package/runtime evidence, versioned output, repeatability, implicit tasks, ambiguity/explicit selection, excluded development groups, lock-hash rejection and forbidden build-time network fetching. Dependency job 110942213239 at a653ea8 passed the pip checks, then failed uv's repeated-image identity assertion. Both uv builds succeeded with the same plan, but the retained images differed in uv_cache.json and RECORD because wheel input mtimes varied. The fixed worker-input timestamp behavior above addresses this cause; its container acceptance is pending. Poetry and later context groups did not run in that attempt. Package-context groups run separately from the Docker platform matrix; see suite selection and retained evidence. Provisioned Windows uv/Poetry probes have verified native export, unchanged locks, hashed offline installation/import, wheel-tamper rejection and stale-lock rejection; these narrower probes do not establish Docker isolation or container output.

node/npm exports verified registry tarballs using the Node builder's existing native locked acquisition. A Docker target with package.json and a v2/v3 package-lock.json or npm-shrinkwrap.json can infer this provider. Shrinkwrap takes precedence, as it does in npm. Multiple ecosystems require with.dependencies: node/npm in the build declaration. The shared runtime, platform, policy and context rules above also apply; the captured consumer base must already contain Node and npm. A declared packageManager must match that provisioned npm version, and native npm validates engine constraints. The tested profile uses npm 11.11.0 with Node 22 in CI fixtures and Node 24.14.1 in a Windows native probe. A package that npm records as bundled by its parent (inBundle, nested under the parent's node_modules, with no resolved URL or integrity of its own, such as the optional @emnapi/* packages under Tailwind 4's @tailwindcss/oxide-wasm32-wasi) is not acquired separately: it ships inside the parent's tarball, whose integrity is verified. Any other inBundle entry is refused with a message naming the package. Packages outside the public registry, such as a source-only package pinned to a public GitHub commit tarball (declared as that HTTPS tarball URL in package.json and recorded in the lockfile; a git spec is refused), are acquired only from locations the project declares in npm.sources; their locked integrity is still verified. For the provisioned CI image, a complete Dockerfile example is: FROM oyzu-toolchain/node:npm11.11.0-node22 WORKDIR /app COPY package.json package-lock.json ./ RUN --mount=type=bind,from=dependencies,target=/dependencies \ for archive in /dependencies/*.tgz; do npm cache add "$archive" --offline --cache /tmp/npm-cache --ignore-scripts; done \ && npm ci --offline --cache /tmp/npm-cache --ignore-scripts --omit=dev --no-audit --no-fund \ && rm -rf /tmp/npm-cache COPY app.js . CMD ["node", "app.js"] Use your already-provisioned compatible base instead of the CI image as appropriate. Copy all required workspace manifests/sources for a workspace install, and copy npm-shrinkwrap.json instead when using shrinkwrap. The shown glob expects at least one captured registry package; dependency-free projects can run native offline npm without seeding a store. No generated Dockerfile or automatic rewrite of RUN commands is involved. The store contains only <sha256>.tgz files. Preparation fetches all locked registry tarballs through the scoped public npm broker, validates SHA-512 lock integrity, and invokes native npm offline with lifecycle scripts disabled to reject stale locks and incompatible installations. Local workspace links stay in the source graph; native npm owns dependency resolution and installation layout. Development and optional packages are captured too, with their existing evidence purposes; this is an all-lock store rather than a runtime-only pruning resolver. The shown consumer decides to omit development installation through native --omit=dev. Acquisition does not execute project lifecycle scripts; the example also disables them during the offline build. Packages requiring lifecycle compilation need an explicitly provisioned compiler and a deliberate offline Dockerfile command. Only tarballs enter the named context. npm's temporary cache, logs, user/global configuration, acquisition workspace and broker state are not exported. The consumer seeds its own disposable cache and removes it in the same RUN instruction, avoiding both cache log timestamps and an extra cache layer. Native npm verifies the lock again during installation. Package names, versions, purposes, content hashes, lock/source identity, observed Node/npm versions and immutable base identity remain in dist/dependencies/<target>.json; the normal versioned OCI artifact, JUnit and Docker quality checks remain mandatory. This does not promise reproducibility for arbitrary lifecycle scripts or other Dockerfile commands. Missing/stale locks, unsupported lock versions, integrity failures, incompatible engines or a mismatched declared package manager fail preparation. Correct the native inputs or provisioned base and rebuild; preparation failures emit no actions/artifacts. The current public route is https://registry.npmjs.org/; private registries, VCS/direct non-registry sources, managed connector authorization and npm-specific credential canaries are not implemented. There is no persistent acquisition cache or internet fallback during execution. tooling/test-npm-context.py passed on Windows with actual npm 11.11.0/Node 24.14.1. It checks broker-transported product acquisition, script suppression, tarball-only export, two fresh offline cache/install operations, transitive runtime packages, omitted development installation, unchanged locks/store and rejected integrity. Its fixture transport does not prove the production broker's network isolation. The registered Linux docker-npm-context group additionally requires compiled-CLI preparation, actual offline RUN/import, exact resulting image files, package/runtime evidence, implicit tasks, OCI/JUnit/quality output, repeated identities and integrity rejection before actions. Its native result is pending; this is not full EX-058 acceptance.

node/yarn exports a native offline mirror after the existing Yarn acquisition adapter validates the frozen dependency graph. With package.json and yarn.lock, it is inferred for a Docker target when there is no competing manager/ecosystem. Multiple native locks require an explicit with.dependencies: node/yarn. A modern Yarn lock is not silently treated as Classic. The consumer image must already contain Node, Yarn Classic 1.22.22 and the adapter's @yarnpkg/lockfile 1.1.0 parser at /opt/oyzu-yarn/node_modules/@yarnpkg/lockfile (as in the provided toolchain image). The native adapter also accepts its existing OYZU_YARN_LOCKFILE image-provisioning path. Oyzu installs none of these tools during preparation. For the provisioned CI image: FROM oyzu-toolchain/node:yarn1.22.22-node22 WORKDIR /app COPY package.json yarn.lock ./ RUN --mount=type=bind,from=dependencies,target=/dependencies \ printf 'yarn-offline-mirror "/dependencies"\ndisable-self-update-check true\n' >/tmp/oyzu.yarnrc \ && yarn install --offline --non-interactive --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts --use-yarnrc /tmp/oyzu.yarnrc --cache-folder /tmp/yarn-cache \ && yarn cache clean --offline --non-interactive --cache-folder /tmp/yarn-cache \ && rm -rf /tmp/yarn-cache /tmp/oyzu.yarnrc COPY app.js . CMD ["node", "app.js"] Only the verified mirror archives enter dependencies; temporary Yarn caches, configuration, broker state and inventory files do not. The ephemeral consumer configuration points at that read-only context, and cleanup occurs in the same RUN instruction. Preparation uses the consumer's exact immutable Node/Yarn runtime, validates native package-manager/engine constraints, and keeps lifecycle scripts disabled. Native Yarn performs dependency selection, including supported registry-only resolutions; the adapter rejects a changed native graph before exporting the mirror. Source locks remain unchanged. Like its application-build adapter, Yarn captures all locked inputs and conservatively records their purpose as build, without claiming a resolved runtime-only inventory. The admitted profile supports a single project, Classic v1 locks, SHA-512 or legacy SHA-1 lock integrity, transitive and scoped registry packages, registry version-range resolutions and the root .yarnrc/.npmrc settings listed in Yarn project settings. Copy those files into the consumer stage too if native Yarn should apply them there. Acquisition uses the existing public npm/Yarn routes. Workspaces, other .yarnrc/.npmrc settings, .yarnrc.yml, path/VCS dependencies, modern Yarn, private registries and managed connector authorization remain unsupported. The shown configuration is generated inside the private RUN filesystem, not checked into the source project. Missing tools, unsupported input profiles, stale locks, altered integrity or changed runtime identity fail before artifacts; correct the inputs/provisioned base and rebuild. Offline execution cannot fill a missing store from the internet, and there is no persistent acquisition cache yet. The mirror digest, observed manager/runtime, original source/lock identities and verified package identities remain in the Docker dependency evidence; ordinary snapshot OCI output, required JUnit and quality gates are unchanged. Windows native checks using Yarn 1.22.22/Node 24.14.1 passed ordinary and selective-resolution profiles, stable repeated captures, scoped/transitive mirror export, fresh-cache offline installation/tests, lifecycle suppression, unchanged locks/mirrors and corrupt mirror rejection. Existing pnpm patch capture/replay also passed after the shared lifecycle change. These checks use a fixture spool and do not establish Docker isolation. The registered Linux docker-yarn-context group requires real compiled-CLI preparation, offline install/import, exact image contents, evidence, repeatability and altered-lock rejection; its native result remains pending.

node/pnpm prepares a native pnpm store in the immutable consumer image, using the Node adapter's existing brokered registry archives and frozen-lock validation. package.json and a single-project v9 pnpm-lock.yaml select it when unambiguous; otherwise use with.dependencies: node/pnpm. The image must already provide Node, pnpm 10.11.0 and yaml 2.8.1 at /opt/oyzu-pnpm/node_modules/yaml, as in the provisioned toolchain. The adapter's existing OYZU_PNPM_YAML image-provisioning path is also accepted. The exported store format is deliberately qualified against this exact pnpm version; other versions fail context export pending qualification rather than borrowing cache semantics silently. FROM oyzu-toolchain/node:pnpm10.11.0-node22 WORKDIR /app COPY package.json pnpm-lock.yaml ./ RUN --mount=type=bind,from=dependencies,target=/dependencies \ cp -r /dependencies /tmp/pnpm-store \ && pnpm --config.manage-package-manager-versions=false install --offline --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts --ignore-pnpmfile --config.verify-store-integrity=true --config.side-effects-cache=false --store-dir /tmp/pnpm-store \ && rm -rf /tmp/pnpm-store COPY app.js . CMD ["node", "app.js"] The named context stays read-only. Copying its store gives pnpm a private writable location for its native verification metadata; remove it in the same RUN instruction. Native package imports remain usable after that store is removed. This uses pnpm's offline installation semantics, not an Oyzu resolver or a renamed-tarball cache. Adding local tarballs with pnpm store add does not create the registry identities needed by this qualified frozen-install profile. Only the native v10/files content and v10/index records are exported. The adapter resets each index file's checkedAt verification hint to zero and serializes index keys deterministically. Package bytes, native integrity values, modes, sizes and package identity remain unchanged; zero prevents relying on acquisition-time freshness shortcuts after copying. The pinned native consumer rechecks the copied content with store-integrity verification enabled. The exporter rejects links, special files, unknown store paths/index fields and side-effect caches, with the existing 100,000-file/10-GiB capture limits and a 16-MiB per-index limit. Empty locked graphs can export an empty store. User configuration, native log/cache state outside this content store, temporary paths and broker state are not included. The profile retains existing single-project registry and source-patch support. For a patched project, copy pnpm-workspace.yaml and patches/ before installation, or use the supported package.json patch declaration. The native frozen install applies and verifies patches; dependency evidence retains original package integrity and source-patch digests. Acquisition has lifecycle scripts and side-effect caching disabled. All locked registry inputs are captured and conservatively classified as build inputs, without claiming runtime-only pruning. Workspaces, .npmrc, .pnpmfile.cjs, unsupported native overrides, direct/path/VCS dependencies, other pnpm versions and managed/private connectors remain explicit gaps. Stale locks, altered archive integrity, missing native tools or unqualified store metadata fail preparation and produce no action artifacts. Correct the inputs or provisioned toolchain and rebuild. Build actions have no registry access: an incomplete/corrupt offline store fails instead of being replenished from the internet. Existing context/base identity checks, versioned OCI artifacts, JUnit and quality gates apply. No credential is placed in the store by Oyzu; package content integrity is not provenance or release authorization. Windows native checks using pnpm 10.11.0/Node 24.14.1 passed ordinary, patched and empty-graph preparation, repeated export identities, fresh offline consumption, tests after temporary-store removal, unchanged source locks and rejection of tampered store content. A Yarn selective-resolution mirror check also passed after the shared export-callback update. Both generated pnpm Dockerfiles passed native Hadolint and read-only dockerfmt checks. The registered Linux docker-pnpm-context group requires actual compiled-CLI capture/builds for ordinary and patched projects, exact image files/patch evidence, offline imports, snapshot OCI/JUnit/quality, repeatability and pre-action lock-integrity rejection. Those container results remain pending; the host probes use a fixture spool and do not qualify the production broker or full EX-058.

go/modules exposes the Go builder's native, checksum-verified module cache through dependencies. A Docker target containing go.mod or go.work can infer this provider; mixed ecosystems require with.dependencies: go/modules. Native metadata resolves contained workspace members, local replacements and test imports using the original source/checksum files. The existing public Go proxy broker obtains required module inputs, and native Go verifies go.sum. Preparation must leave manifests and checksum files unchanged. The consumer base must already contain Go and a POSIX shell; projects using cgo also require the configured C compiler. The CI profile uses the standard golang:1.24-bookworm image. Context preparation compiles the owned metadata helper with that provisioned Go compiler using only the standard library. It does not require oyzu-go-modulezip, project snapshot version projection or module artifact packaging. Those remain responsibilities of ordinary go/app/go/library builds. Toolchain auto-download, VCS access and user Go configuration are disabled during preparation. For a pure-Go command with a complete go.sum: FROM golang:1.24-bookworm AS build WORKDIR /src COPY . . RUN --mount=type=bind,from=dependencies,target=/dependencies \ GOMODCACHE=/tmp/gomodcache GOPROXY=file:///dependencies/cache/download GOSUMDB=off GOTOOLCHAIN=local CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -mod=readonly -trimpath -buildvcs=false -o /app . FROM scratch COPY --from=build /app /app ENTRYPOINT ["/app"] The prepared module subtree is Go's download cache (module zips with their .mod and .info files), mounted read-only. The build reads it as a native file proxy and extracts the modules it needs into its own writable GOMODCACHE; native Go verifies each zip against go.sum, and no registry is reachable. Extracted module trees are not stored, because writing their many small files through a Docker Desktop bind mount was slow; it does not receive a broker, credentials or Go acquisition metadata as files. Native metadata, observed Go version/platform, lock/source digests and used module archive identities remain in the dependency evidence. The context's module-artifact list is empty because dependency preparation does not publish the project's own module. Compiler output/cache stays in the private build stage, and the final scratch stage contains only the copied binary. Use a suitable runtime instead of scratch for cgo or other runtime-library requirements; arbitrary Dockerfile commands remain responsible for compatible compilation and reproducibility. Missing checksums, stale manifests, escaping workspace/replacement paths, failed native metadata or incompatible tools fail preparation before action artifacts. Update and commit native metadata or provision the correct image, then rebuild. The shared provider policy/platform rules still apply, including managed acquisition rejection until approved connector bindings exist. Private module routes, direct VCS sources, checksum-database service integration and persistent acquisition caches remain unfinished. Current verification uses committed go.sum; it does not claim independent checksum-database attestation or production release authority. Windows Go 1.24.13 native checks passed existing workspace/cgo and checksum cases, plus two detached module-store copies compiled offline into identical binaries that both ran with expected output. Source and store bytes remained unchanged, and no extra fixture broker requests occurred during replay. The exact Dockerfile passed native Hadolint/read-only dockerfmt. The Linux docker-go-context group requires real compiled-CLI preparation in a standard Go image, read-only cache compilation and execution in the build stage, exact final binary contents, snapshot OCI/JUnit/quality, repeatability and checksum rejection. Container results remain pending. Docker integrity JUnit does not replace source tests or coverage; use a separately built Go producer when those language-builder reports are required. The check does not claim it starts the final image.

rust/cargo exposes the existing Rust acquisition adapter's native local registry. A Docker target with Cargo.toml and a checked-in Cargo.lock can infer it when there is no other ecosystem; use with.dependencies: rust/cargo for explicit selection. The lock is mandatory even for a local-only workspace. The current consumer profile requires provisioned Rust/Cargo 1.94.0, a POSIX shell and the native compiler/linker required by the project. CI uses rust:1.94.0-slim-bookworm. Context preparation does not require Python, nextest, llvm-cov or the ordinary Rust artifact/reporting adapters. For the checked-in Rust registry example, after provisioning both referenced images: FROM rust:1.94.0-slim-bookworm AS build WORKDIR /src COPY . . RUN --mount=type=bind,from=dependencies,target=/dependencies \ CARGO_HOME=/tmp/cargo-home CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/cargo-target CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0 cargo \ --config 'source.crates-io.replace-with="oyzu-captured"' \ --config 'source.oyzu-captured.local-registry="/dependencies"' \ build --release --locked --offline \ && cp /tmp/cargo-target/release/oyzu-registry-example /app RUN test "$(/app)" = "Answer: 42" FROM debian:bookworm-slim COPY --from=build /app /app ENTRYPOINT ["/app"] The original complete lock is admitted before acquisition. Only crates.io registry sources with matching native index/archive SHA-256 checksums are currently supported. Public requests use the existing shared host transport and its source/redirect/size limits. Cargo then validates the original workspace and lock offline inside the exact captured consumer image. It does not run project build scripts during preparation, project snapshot versions, rewrite the source lock or produce the workspace's crate artifacts. Ordinary Rust builds retain those artifact-generation responsibilities. Only *.crate archives and their captured native index/ entries enter the read-only context. This uses Cargo's documented local-registry source replacement, preserving native resolution, extraction and checksum validation. Acquisition configuration, Cargo home, unpacked cache, temporary workspace and credentials are excluded. The example's command-line source configuration points directly at /dependencies; Cargo unpacks into a fresh private home. Its final stage copies the executable and uses a provisioned Debian runtime for the standard compiler's dynamic-library requirements. A dependency-free workspace needs no source replacement. Contained local workspace packages remain source inputs rather than registry entries. The dependency record retains original Cargo metadata, compiler/manager and immutable consumer identity, source/lock digests and verified registry packages. It deliberately contains no projected workspace metadata or nextest/coverage-tool evidence. The image has the normal snapshot version, OCI artifact, required integrity JUnit and Docker quality gates. Docker integrity testing does not measure Rust test execution or coverage; use a Rust producer target when those reports are required. Arbitrary Dockerfile build scripts still need their own declared inputs and deterministic behavior. Missing/stale locks, mismatched checksums, unsupported Git/alternate registry sources, escaping local paths or missing native tools fail before action artifacts. Fix the native inputs or provision the image and rebuild; offline actions never replenish missing dependencies. Managed/private connector authorization, persistent acquisition reuse and other Rust versions/platforms remain unfinished. Neither content verification nor a snapshot version authorizes release publication. The Rust native acquisition test passed on Windows with Cargo 1.94.0: two detached registry copies and fresh native homes/compiler caches produced executables that ran with the expected output, while lock/store bytes stayed unchanged. Existing native tests, Clippy, verified packaging and altered-archive rejection also passed. This uses fixture acquisition bytes and does not prove a read-only container mount. The exact Dockerfile passed native Hadolint and read-only dockerfmt with the builder's trailing-newline convention. The registered dependencies suite's docker-rust-context group requires actual compiled-CLI preparation, offline compilation/run, no reporting-tool requirement, unchanged native versions, runtime image output, OCI/JUnit/quality, repeatability and pre-action checksum rejection. Container execution remains pending; final-image startup and full EX-058 acceptance are separate unfinished obligations.

For an external dependencies context, Oyzu verifies that the provisioned runtime still has the captured OCI config digest, then executes its immutable Docker image ID. These identities can differ with Docker's containerd image store, where the image ID of a single-platform image is its manifest digest: Oyzu then exports the image, verifies the manifest bytes against that ID and reads the config digest from it. Classic storage reports the config digest as the ID directly. A changed base reference fails before dependency execution; Oyzu never silently substitutes a newer base. Version-1 dependency-context evidence records runtime_config separately from runtime.digest (the execution ID).

The Python (python/pip, python/uv, python/poetry) and Cargo (rust/cargo) providers orchestrate preparation with Oyzu's compiled Linux worker running inside the consumer image, so that the image's own interpreter or compiler resolves the packages. A Dockerfile base such as python:3.13-slim-bookworm does not contain that worker, and Oyzu never rebuilds or modifies it. Before preparation, Oyzu copies the worker executable out of the provisioned oyzu-toolchain/builder-worker:v1 image (pulled by its published digest when it is absent and pulling is allowed) into a Docker volume private to the build, and mounts that volume read-only at /usr/local/libexec/oyzu for the preparation containers only. An idle holder container (oyzu-worker-<pid>-<n>-hold, no network, read-only, no capabilities) keeps the volume in use throughout preparation, so another build's storage cleanup on the same Docker engine cannot remove it. Holder and volume are removed when preparation ends, including when an interrupted build unwinds; the offline Dockerfile build never sees them. A forced exit (second Ctrl-C) removes the holder like other tracked containers. If the process dies without cleanup, the holder (labelled dev.oyzu.owner=oyzu, started with --rm) exits by itself after 6 hours, and the then-unused volume is removed by the storage cleanup after the next isolated build. Before preparation, Oyzu starts the worker once in the consumer image (--version) to check that it can run there. The worker image's identity is recorded as worker in the captured context (extensions.oyzu.dev/docker.dependencyContext of dist/dependencies/<target>.json), so a different worker changes the dependency and plan identities. Go and Node providers run native tools only and receive no worker. Requirements and failures: The worker image must be available: provisioned locally (see Prerequisites and commands) or pullable from the published toolchain images. Otherwise preparation fails with the usual missing-toolchain-image message. Its platform must equal the consumer runtime's platform. The published image is linux/amd64; any other runtime platform fails with the compiled Oyzu worker image ... is linux/amd64, but runtime image ... is ... until a matching worker image is provisioned. The worker is a glibc executable built on Debian bookworm. The consumer base must provide a compatible glibc (bookworm or newer, and other glibc distributions of similar age). A musl base such as Alpine cannot run it: the start check fails with the compiled Oyzu worker cannot start in runtime image ..., naming the glibc requirement. Supplying the worker needs the Docker executor; the daemonless sandbox refuses it. The worker executable is the one built into the provisioned image, not the running CLI, as for every other toolchain image. Rebuild oyzu-toolchain/builder-worker:v1 from the same source when developing the worker protocol. Provisioned image capture also supports attestation-bearing OCI indexes by selecting and exporting the runnable manifest for the requested platform. Oyzu verifies its digest and captured config while retaining the immutable index identity for execution. This requires Docker image inspection/export support for --platform; Docker 29.8 was verified. It does not verify signatures or establish trust in attestations. Unsupported selection/export fails rather than substituting an image. A Windows-coordinated compiled-CLI proof acquired pip dependencies and consumed them offline in the actual indexed Linux image, verified six 1.17.0 in the final image, and passed bundle inspection. Other Docker versions remain unqualified.
documents.s: Compiled worker in the consumer runtime

documents.t: CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/docker-quality.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Dockerfile discovery now exposes native lint, read-only format checks and explicit formatting without an Oyzu configuration file. The defaults are Hadolint 2.15.1 and dockerfmt 0.5.4. They complement the existing isolated image build and OCI validation; neither tool builds or runs the application.

oyzu run list oyzu run lint oyzu run format-check oyzu run format oyzu build lint runs hadolint --no-color Dockerfile. Native rules, severities, configuration and inline suppressions determine its exit status. format-check runs dockerfmt with --check and does not change source. Only the explicitly requested format task uses --write; it is marked mutating and is not a build stage. With no target-local .editorconfig, Oyzu adds --newline so its default formatting retains a final newline. With that file present, native dockerfmt configuration and defaults determine formatting, including the EOF convention. These tasks appear even when tools have not yet been provisioned. Static discovery records native configuration evidence or a fallback selection without executing tools. Missing binaries fail execution with installation guidance; they are not downloaded or silently skipped. Task overrides and pre/post hooks use the existing shared task engine. A replacement task owns its behavior and is not automatically another native checker. Hadolint interprets target-local .hadolint.yaml/.hadolint.yml, including ignored rules and severity settings. Dockerfmt interprets target-local .editorconfig. Oyzu does not parse either into a new configuration language. Invalid native configuration remains a native failure. Development execution can also observe ambient native configuration; captured execution has no host configuration mounts. Parent configuration outside the captured target is not currently imported, so keep required configuration inside the target for matching captured behavior. When validating a standalone example, copy it outside the repository's parent configuration before checking native defaults. Dockerfmt defaults to four-space continuation indentation, while this repository's EditorConfig uses two spaces. The native quality probe checks the provisioned-base, argument-base and image-alias fixtures in a private standalone directory through the compiled CLI, preserving all source bytes during checks. In a captured build, lint and format-check are required gates before final artifact collection. Failure retains native action diagnostics and blocks the snapshot OCI artifact. The captured source and live checkout are unchanged by those checks. Repair lint failures, run explicit formatting where appropriate, and rerun the build. Lint diagnostics are not counted as application tests or coverage; existing OCI assertions supply the image's JUnit and its packaging-only coverage applicability remains explicit. .dockerignore controls the image context, not whether native checkers can see their configuration. The planner preserves .hadolint.yaml, .hadolint.yml and .editorconfig in the private checking workspace even when native Docker ignore rules exclude them from COPY. Their bytes remain part of captured input identity. The BuildKit context retains its separately verified native file list.

Host development tasks need provisioned hadolint and dockerfmt on PATH. The CI native probe supports Windows x86_64, Linux x86_64 and macOS x86_64/arm64. The current captured BuildKit profile remains Linux amd64 and requires the existing explicitly provisioned rootless worker/AppArmor capabilities. This change does not expand captured executor platforms. Rebuild the default toolchain image to include the new tools: docker build -f tooling/images/docker-metadata.Dockerfile -t oyzu-toolchain/docker:buildkit0.25.0 . Image provisioning downloads checksum-pinned Hadolint assets and builds dockerfmt from its Go module/checksum lock using the Go 1.24 tool dependency mechanism. Each downloaded asset is limited to 128 MiB and must match its pinned SHA-256 before being installed; oversize and checksum errors are reported separately. Downloads happen during explicit provisioning, not project build execution. The image preserves upstream licenses/notices and records its immutable identity in build evidence. Native preparation checks tool availability and retains their reported versions in the Docker dependency record. The formatter's development-build version string does not replace its pinned source version and image identity. Custom --image docker=<image> profiles now need both quality executables as well as BuildKit and the native metadata adapter. Older images fail preparation until rebuilt. This is an intentional change from the previous profile, which advertised lint/format checks as unavailable. A native lint or formatting violation can now make an otherwise buildable image fail its build gates. For explicit local test provisioning, use python tooling/provision-hadolint.py --destination <tools-directory> and build the tracked dockerfmt tool from tooling/images/docker-quality with a provisioned Go 1.24.1+ compiler. The CI workflow shows the exact native download, verification and build commands. These repository scripts are not a tool-installation feature of the Oyzu CLI.

python tooling/test-docker-quality.py --cli <compiled-oyzu> --tools <provisioned-tools-directory> The native probe tests task listing without tools, actual lint failures and native suppression, malformed configuration, read-only format failures, explicit writes, EditorConfig overrides, missing tools and task replacement. Windows native checks passed; cross-host CI confirmation is tracked in implementation status. The compiled-CLI Linux suite additionally requires successful quality gates for the snapshot image, each quality failure blocking artifacts, unchanged source and checker configuration remaining available while absent from image layers. These assertions passed job 110767008269 at revision 8dbf1b4 in run 36983990838; this is isolated Linux evidence, not a claim of captured execution on every host. Hadolint is a static linter, not a container vulnerability scanner or proof of policy compliance. Native suppressions can change its result. Dockerfmt has documented syntax limitations, including escape directives and some shell grouping forms; support for every Dockerfile dialect is not claimed. Native configuration/tool behavior is described by Hadolint and dockerfmt. Unsupported forms and broader scanner integrations remain part of the build-system work. Literal bases can now use captured provisioned images. Dockerfile-free packaging, registry image/dependency acquisition, platform matrices and Helm image bindings remain unfinished. Quality checks do not make those scenarios implemented.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/dotnet.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Status: bounded Linux captured fixture verified. The dotnet/sdk builder's full restore/build/test/pack flow, independent consumption of its delivered NuGet package and finite failure/report scenarios passed on Linux amd64 with SDK 10.0.401. Native selection/evidence also passed the finite SDK 400/401 and 301/401 matrix. Broader corpus and host qualification remain pending; see verification for the exact evidence boundary. A directory with a solution (.sln, .slnx) or an SDK-style project (.csproj, .fsproj, .vbproj) needs no Oyzu configuration: oyzu run list oyzu build --plan oyzu build oyzu inspect dist Plain oyzu build selects the fast build/package path. Use oyzu build --isolated --full to request the captured build and native test checks described below. Selecting isolation alone does not select tests. This builder has no host build adapter; it currently uses the captured executor even without an explicit --isolated flag.

Captured builds use the explicitly provisioned image oyzu-toolchain/dotnet:10.0.401. It is built from the pinned definition, a digest-pinned mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:10.0.401-noble-aot base plus the compiled Oyzu worker: docker build -f tooling/images/builder-worker.Dockerfile -t oyzu-toolchain/builder-worker:v1 . docker build -f tooling/images/dotnet.Dockerfile -t oyzu-toolchain/dotnet:10.0.401 . The -aot variant adds clang and zlib, so NativeAOT projects have their native linker prerequisites. The image is not published by the toolchain-image workflow and is never downloaded automatically. Select a different SDK image with --image dotnet=<image>. Linux amd64 is the only provisioned platform.

A directory is claimed when it directly contains a solution or a project whose root element names an MSBuild SDK (Sdk="...", an <Sdk> element or an SDK import). Legacy non-SDK projects are not claimed. Discovery adds install, build and test tasks that run dotnet restore, dotnet build and dotnet test. A literal SemVer Version or VersionPrefix in the entry project or root Directory.Build.props becomes the native version; computed values stay native. Every native command receives one entry file: a single solution, otherwise a single SDK-style project. More than one candidate fails and names them. Select one explicitly: builds: app: uses: dotnet/sdk with: project: src/App.slnx with.project must be a relative solution or project file in the target. Other with keys are rejected.

global.json in the target root selects the SDK as the native host does: sdk.version, sdk.rollForward (default patch with a version, latestMajor without one) and sdk.allowPrerelease (default true). Native preference matters: patch can retain an exact installed SDK even when a newer admitted patch is available; latestPatch chooses the latest admitted patch. The adapter observes dotnet --version in the unchanged target directory instead of predicting a maximum version. Without global.json the native host chooses the image's SDK. oyzu build --plan shows the request and the default image SDK in its tool requirements, for example dotnet-sdk 10.0.300 rollForward latestFeature; default image SDK 10.0.401, or image default 10.0.401 (no global.json). The discovery record keeps the same choice under sdk. The preparation container lists its installed SDKs from /, then observes native selection in the target directory. Both probes use the shared bounded native process runner with a 30-second timeout. It fails before restore when none is admitted, naming the request, the provided SDKs and --image dotnet=<image>. The observed version must be installed and admitted by the strict request. Dependency manager and .NET SDK evidence record that native version. Offline restore observes selection again and requires agreement with preparation. Native probe failures, timeouts and invalid observations fail preparation rather than producing package evidence. global.json must be strict JSON; comments are rejected rather than guessed. Custom native SDK search-root provenance, including sdk.paths, remains unqualified: installed-version membership does not attest which filesystem SDK root supplied that version. The bounded multi-SDK qualification records actual policies, versions and measured limits.

Preparation runs dotnet restore <entry> once, with network denied, through a loopback mirror that forwards only the NuGet V3 flat container and vulnerability data of https://api.nuget.org/ to the scoped acquisition broker. Restore reads only a generated NuGet.Config (--configfile), and project-declared RestoreSources, additional sources and fallback folders are cleared. Repository and user feeds, package source mappings and credentials are therefore not used. When any packages.lock.json exists in the target, restore runs with --locked-mode. NuGet enforces each lock for its own project; projects without a lock restore normally. Lock files are recorded in lockDigests. Restored packages are stored as a NuGet global packages folder in the prepared tree. Each package's .nupkg digest and size is recorded in the dependency record. The recorded package source is normalized to the public index so the prepared tree does not depend on the mirror's port.

Preparation restores with NuGetAudit=true and keeps NU1900–NU1905 as warnings, even under TreatWarningsAsErrors or WarningsAsErrors. Findings come from NuGet's own project.assets.json logs and are: summarized as a NuGet audit preflight step, for example known vulnerabilities: 1 high; logged per finding as NUGET_AUDIT warnings; recorded under oyzu.dev/nuget-audit in the dependency record, with complete: false when NuGet could not read vulnerability data. Audit findings never fail preparation. Build actions restore with NuGetAudit=false, so audit warnings cannot become later compile errors.

Captured build actions run with network denied and these steps: A prepare action restores offline from the prepared packages into /workspace/.oyzu-dotnet/packages, which is also NUGET_PACKAGES. It keeps --locked-mode when preparation used it. build runs dotnet build <entry> --configuration Release --no-restore --disable-build-servers -p:Version=<version>. When selected (for example by --full), test runs dotnet test --no-build --no-restore with TRX results: VSTest uses --logger trx; Microsoft.Testing.Platform uses --report-trx and --solution/--project. This mode is selected when global.json sets test.runner: Microsoft.Testing.Platform. All TRX files are converted into one JUnit report, keeping class names, failures and skipped tests. A passing run without TRX results fails rather than reporting an empty suite. A custom native test task retains the shared required-JUnit obligation; a zero exit without that report fails the action and blocks package output. The package step runs dotnet pack --no-build --no-restore into one directory artifact, nuget-packages-<version>. It fails when no project is packable. The version is the shared version inference result over the native version and Git history. It is passed to restore, build and pack as -p:Version. CI is removed from the action environment, because ContinuousIntegrationBuild source mapping needs a .git directory that captured source excludes. Telemetry, first-run output, workload notices, MSBuild node reuse and online certificate revocation checks are disabled. Actions reserve 4096 MiB and time out after 30 minutes.

SDKs supplied by NuGet, such as Aspire.AppHost.Sdk or Microsoft.Build.NoTargets, are named by Sdk="Id/Version" on a project or import, an <Sdk Name Version> element, or msbuild-sdks in the root global.json. MSBuild's SDK resolver restores them while it evaluates a project, ignoring the generated NuGet configuration, so a network-denied evaluation failed and restore skipped the project (NU1503). Preparation scans the root global.json and every project, props and targets file for literal versions and restores each SDK package through the broker into the prepared packages before restoring the entry. The ids and versions are recorded under msbuildSdks in oyzu.dev/dotnet, and the package appears in the dependency record. The offline build restores them from the prepared packages before the entry, so the resolver finds each SDK in the global packages folder. SDKs bundled with the .NET SDK (Microsoft.NET.Sdk*) are never restored. A version written as a property, range or wildcard is not seeded and fails in MSBuild as before.

These choices are provisional pending maintainer review: the builder id dotnet/sdk; the default SDK and image; audit is reported but never enforced; CI is removed; the action memory and timeout limits; packing every packable project into one directory artifact; failing on ambiguous entries, unsatisfiable SDK requests and missing TRX results. Not yet supported: private feeds, credentials, package source mapping and nuget.sessionEndpoint in captured builds; workloads, and MSBuild project SDKs whose versions MSBuild computes or a range names (see below); global.json and Directory.Build.* files above the target directory, which are outside the captured source; coverage, lint and format integrations; per-package file artifacts, dotnet publish outputs and NativeAOT publishing as a build stage; Windows and macOS images; multi-project repositories without a root solution, unless with.project selects one. Restores are bounded by the shared broker: 1 GiB and 4096 requests per session, and 256 MiB per response. The prepared tree is bounded at 100,000 entries and 10 GiB. NuGet's HTTP cache and extraction scratch use /scratch/nuget, whose engine tmpfs size ceiling follows the action's 4 GiB memory reservation, not the 512 MiB /tmp mount, so large packages such as Microsoft.Playwright fit. This does not raise the action's memory reservation; where cgroups are available, their limit covers process and tmpfs use together. Managed NuGet launch sessions for oyzu exec remain separate; see NuGet sessions.

Unit tests cover SDK roll-forward admission, entry selection, lock discovery, TRX to JUnit conversion, audit collection, mirror routing and plan shape. The dotnet suite in tooling/build_scenarios/dotnet.py exercises tooling/fixtures/dotnet-app through the compiled CLI: SDK display in --plan; full captured restore/build/test/pack, including recorded SDK/lock/package evidence and real test results with a skip; independent offline restore, compilation and execution of a consumer using only the delivered versioned NuGet package and the recorded SDK image; repeatability and source preservation; a real failing test that retains JUnit and blocks package export; a real passing native test override without required report evidence that fails its action and blocks package export; native rejection of changed dependencies against the existing lock; a reported audit finding retained in dependency evidence; an unsatisfiable SDK request. Run the bounded suite with a provisioned CLI and its matching worker image: python tooling/test-build-scenarios.py --cli <compiled-oyzu> --suite dotnet --only dotnet --evidence-dir <new-evidence-directory> The selected suite passed on Linux amd64 on 2026-10-16 at combined candidate 2986aa4a19ff25a29a830e3a87c98655281aa97c, tree a01a60ee0dad1d85a73fe821bb12fff4532a8654, with the compiled CLI and matching worker source. Its seven builds include expected failures, with no failed acceptance assertions. The normal fixture produced JUnit 3 total, 2 passed, 1 skipped, and the independent offline consumer printed Hello, Oyzu!. The completion record records exact source, binary/image identities, commands, outputs and failure gates. That historical run proves its single-SDK fixture and selected scenarios. A later native correction at a640740520e0f982e2d2063983656fcf762df209 made recorded SDK evidence agree with native preference in complete SDK 400/401 and 301/401 images. Its 24 expected build outcomes and three real offline package consumers passed, including exact/default/latest/fallback policies and required refusals. The multi-SDK record owns exact source, images, commands, reports, consumers and measured limits. These bounded fixtures do not resolve #181's eight-repository corpus. Windows/macOS, Microsoft.Testing.Platform, NativeAOT and other native inventories remain outside the measured scope. Broader support belongs in implementation status.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/engine-staging.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Experimental implementation for the native-engine program (#703, deliveries #704, #705 and #706). This page describes the development archive route. It does not establish an official release channel, production distribution availability, or native sandboxing. The Windows x64/MSVC real Go flow has verified cold staging and independent selections and override with explicitly admitted development binaries. The later Windows lifecycle qualification covers native preparation, offline use, retained-input replay and cancellation.

The draft isolated Go execution-assets slice also requires the coordinator to be the admitted host member of its exact archive, even when the running identity already equals the pin. Its Linux semantic workers use the Linux member of that archive and check compiled identity, platform and entrypoint before running. A missing or incompatible member fails without falling back to the environment's baked engine. Native-only builds retain the behavior below. The first mounted Windows-to-Linux Go flow and its offline replay have passed, as have the independent A/P1, B/P1, B/P2, warm A/P1 series and same-constituent preassembled reuse. Whole-build default B and exact A6 handoff also passed through the same image's actual default CLI. Candidate C also passed cold and frozen/offline replay with byte-identical complete placement/dependency evidence, using mounted C and the same image-installed P1/Go. Supported local repository gates and the corrected full-build reporting proof also passed; the qualification record retains unavailable validation prerequisites and wider qualification limits. An optional [engine].identity in oyzu.lock selects an exact engine build. Captured builds with that pin require an explicitly admitted archive, including graphs containing only built-in builders and invocations whose current identity already matches. The coordinator and semantic workers use members of that same archive. A missing runtime member refuses before builder preparation; the image's baked worker is never the fallback. Native-only builds retain direct continuation when the active identity matches. Unpinned built-in builds retain their provisioned worker route. This also applies when an explicit --image or built-in native-routing metadata selects a captured worker without --isolated. Bootstrap uses the declared producer closure for requested logical target names, so an unrelated unselected captured target does not change a simple native build. Affected selections, concrete variant IDs not yet expanded, and materialized relationships are classified conservatively before full discovery: they can require the admitted archive even when later routing can execute natively. Full target selection still owns validation and execution; bootstrap never invokes an external plugin's admission role to decide this requirement. Common captured target and dependency evidence records the selected member's identity, archive digest, platform and executable digest separately from the observed baked worker and asset placement. Dependency preparation inside a consumer image uses this selected member too, rather than acquiring the legacy builder-worker image. Exact assets still require the container process executor; unsupported executor controls refuse. This does not extend execution-image replay to built-in builders. Daemonless in-process image assembly records its admitted coordinator member, without inventing an OCI image, Linux worker member or baked-engine observation. Preparation and action reuse keys bind the selected archive/member identity; placement and baked observations do not grant reuse authority. An explicitly permitted --engine-development invocation remains a non-exact local override, and evidence does not claim correspondence to a pinned archive. The existing CLI restrictions against combining it with --isolated, explicit images or remote execution remain binding. External captured builders still require admitted engine assets and refuse that override. The built-in integration status records the current verification boundary. A tiny Linux x86-64 Rust build has verified exact selected-engine execution over a different baked worker, required test/coverage/doctest reports, a runnable delivered binary and unchanged locks. Other built-in families share the selection contract but are not newly runtime qualified by that Rust proof. Without a pin, the active executable remains the engine. A different pin requires an explicitly admitted archive; Oyzu installs that engine beside the frontend and hands the build invocation to it before execution preflight, discovery, plugin roles or planning. The frontend and project lock remain unchanged. build --plan and plugins update use the same bootstrap; updater preflight therefore runs under the selected engine's actual capabilities before adopting any plugin. A compatible engine change does not update plugin or tool selections. A deliberate plugin update retains the engine pin and native tool selections. Help, version and invalid command syntax finish before opening configuration.

The required-pin implementation for issue #792 is under qualification. A protected administrative policy can require a complete build lock with an exact engine pin using engines.requirePin. This Boolean is administrative-only, defaults to false, and is unavailable in ordinary machine, user, project, local, invocation or profile settings. A nonbinding policy default alone does not require the pin. For example, a protected policy's settings can contain: { "engines.requirePin": { "locked": true, "value": true, "when": { "context": ["ci", "pr", "release"] } } } Use the existing administrative policy file and selectors; do not copy this into oyzu.toml. The actual build root and the stricter detected/requested context determine applicability. A weaker --context, profile or ordinary override cannot waive the mandate. Enrollment, CI hints and the mere presence of administrative settings do not require a pin. Standalone CI, release and local builds remain optionally pinned without an applicable mandate. A required build refuses a missing [engine].identity before discovery, plugin roles or preparation, and cannot use --engine-development to bypass the pin. It replays existing plugin selections and refuses unpinned local development plugin bindings. Before tool preparation, it checks that selected tool requests have portable lock entries; execution owners retain the applicable platform, component and recipe checks. No missing plugin or tool selection is implicitly adopted or written. Deliberately prepare the complete lock before running the governed build; removing --frozen does not remove a policy requirement. For a missing plugin selection, restore a complete approved lock or deliberately adopt the bound package with oyzu build in an approved context where policy permits adoption. If none is available, ask the policy administrator for a lock-preparation context. oyzu plugins update replaces existing selections; it does not adopt a missing first selection. Tool pin/install commands do not repair a missing plugin selection. An engine handoff retains the required-lock state; an older receiver that does not understand that private handoff marker refuses it. The qualification record records Windows native application proofs, focused policy/complete-lock checks, compiled handoff refusals, and Linux protected-policy application/refusal proofs. The Linux evidence uses an explicitly attributed combined development candidate. Protected Windows CLI qualification is unavailable with the current non-elevated token; this is not a claim of complete platform qualification.

For a captured external-builder build, --image go=<provisioned-reference> selects the Go execution image independently of the engine, plugin and tool pins. Resolution captures its immutable digest and platform once. Preparation metadata, including the image's PATH, and accepted actions use that frozen identity. Changing a tag affects a new invocation; it does not redirect active work. This is the existing explicit image mapping, not a new configuration catalog or a deployment environment. Retain the successful build bundle outside the application's captured source. To request its exact images again, use: oyzu build app --isolated --platform linux/amd64 --full --frozen \ --execution-images-from /retained/build-a This performs execution image replay, not arbitrary historical-plan execution. Oyzu verifies bundle integrity (not producer authentication), compares the captured source, target/variant/builder selection, exact lock bytes and admitted engine selection, then runs ordinary current preparation and planning. Saved commands, environment variables, mount paths and image-placement receipts never grant execution authority. The new plan records the originating plan, envelope and image-selection digests separately from its current actual choices. Current policy, required checks and executor controls still apply; the entire old configuration is not restored. The option requires --isolated --frozen. It cannot be combined with --image, remote execution, previews, affected selection, slices, handoff, --engine-development or contract verification. This initial slice supports captured external builders with an admitted multi-platform engine archive; built-in and derived application-container replay are explicitly unsupported. Bundles without the required comparison facts are also unsupported. Existing bundles remain inspectable. EXECUTION_IMAGES_SOURCE_CHANGED or EXECUTION_IMAGES_SELECTION_CHANGED requires restoring the recorded source/pins or making a new ordinary build. EXECUTION_IMAGE_UNAVAILABLE names the target, exact recorded digest and platform when it is unavailable or refused by the current executor. Provision that exact image under the existing image admission rules and retry; Oyzu does not substitute the current tag or default. --offline retains ordinary offline acquisition rules and never authorizes missing tools or dependencies. The Windows-to-Linux Go qualification demonstrates a new invocation selecting B after the tag changes, an active accepted A plan continuing on A, and historical image replay selecting A. Source/pins remain unchanged; incomplete pins, changed source, unavailable recorded images and a disabled current executor refuse before actions. The full candidate build, workspace tests, Clippy, formatting and nine compiled CLI task scenarios passed. The qualification retains an existing, separately owned Go feature-conformance failure and unavailable validation prerequisites; it does not claim complete plugin qualification. Other platforms and automatic replacement-image production are not qualified by this slice. On Windows, the waiting frontend preserves console cancellation until the staged engine finishes its cleanup and returns its exit status. The staged engine owns interruption diagnostics and the failed build bundle; the frontend does not run a second cancellation watchdog. This does not add native process isolation. For supported setup commands, install --store <directory> and exec --store <directory> -- <command> use that same store when discovering requirements from an already installed, locked external builder. Neither command adopts a missing plugin: first prepare it through the admitted build path. On Windows, install oyzu.exe and oyzu-shim.exe together. Setup publishes native shims through the shared shim owner, including when an ordinary store path makes the internal digest-named image exceed the legacy Windows path limit. Updater handoff requires both frontend and receiver to implement that operation. The historical #704 qualification engine supports build handoff only and refuses an updater handoff with ENGINE_HANDOFF_INVALID. Invoke that engine directly for its updater or select an admitted receiver implementing update handoff; no fallback changes the pin or package selection. The admission belongs in user or system configuration, never in a project file, local override, or profile. Mandatory constraints and normal CI source rules apply: user configuration is excluded in CI. No project setting can authorize its own engine executable. Example values below are illustrative: [engines.packages] "0.1.0-local.0123456789ab" = { archive = "E:/qualification/engine.tar.gz", sha256 = "sha256:<64 lowercase hex>" } The map contains at most 64 exact build identities. Each binding contains exactly an absolute archive path and its sha256 digest. There is no default source, tag lookup, newest-cache selection, or network fallback. Configuration edits use the shared config set --global --json-value and config unset commands, including individual quoted map entries. The build's --store selects the existing tool store; engines occupy engines/<archive-sha256-hex>/.

To test a project-built CLI while retaining the shared pin, first allow the override in user configuration (or ask the administrator to permit it): oyzu config set --global engines.development true Then invoke that compiled executable explicitly, or select it through your existing PATH/activation, with build --engine-development. For example: ./dist/cli/artifacts/oyzu.exe -C E:/projects/app build app --engine-development The boolean permission defaults to false, is forbidden in project/local files and profiles, and remains subject to administrative constraints evaluated against the actual build root. Permission does not activate an override: the flag is required for each invocation. Overrides are restricted to local development; detected CI and requested CI, PR or release contexts refuse them, including a weaker --context local on detected CI. Remote, isolated, image, all-platform and slice invocations reject the flag. Removing the permission with oyzu config unset --global engines.development restores the default denial. The flag retains the executable already running. It does not search for a different executable, stage the pinned engine, rewrite the pin, or change PATH, activation or the installed backstop. A staged private handoff cannot become a development override. An unreadable lock still fails before work. Bootstrap hashes the active executable once, only for this explicit mode. Build inventory and local preview JSON record developmentOverride: true, pinned: false, actual identity, executableDigest, requestedPin, identityLabelComparison and pinnedContentComparison: "unknown". The human Context facts identify the override, its digest and the bypassed pin. Even an equal dirty version label does not establish equal pinned content. This evidence identifies development bytes; it is not a publisher attestation. Ordinary installed package payloads retain install-time verification and trust.

A gzip tar or ZIP contains engine.json at its root and each platform executable at its declared relative entrypoint. One admitted archive binds all members of the engine build. The manifest has exactly these fields: { "contract": "oyzu.engine.v1alpha1", "identity": "0.1.0-local.0123456789ab", "runtimes": [{ "platform": { "os": "windows", "arch": "x86_64", "abi": "msvc" }, "entrypoint": "bin/windows/oyzu.exe", "executableDigest": "sha256:<64 lowercase hex>" }] } The configured digest authenticates the entire archive, including every manifest field. Every declared executable must be a regular file whose digest matches the manifest, verified at installation. A manifest has 1–16 unique platform members and distinct entrypoints. The unreleased single-member fields have been replaced in place: regenerate development packages; old installations are not new proof. Platform OS, architecture and compilation ABI must match the current engine's platform exactly; this lane does not infer ABI compatibility. The receiving engine also compares its independently compiled identity and its executable location with the admitted installed entrypoint. A manifest cannot relabel a different compiled engine and trigger another handoff. An engine identity is the first version token printed by oyzu --version. It omits compilation profile, target and timestamp; different dirty builds can share that token. The archive and executable digests identify the actual admitted content. Explicit local digest admission is not publisher signature verification or official provenance. Release infrastructure and public publication retain their separate owners and gates. The store verifies the archive before extraction, uses bounded no-follow extraction, checks the manifest and executable, then atomically publishes one installation under a per-digest transaction lock. Shared leases retain it while the frontend waits and the selected engine runs. Installed payloads are trusted after installation and are not rehashed on each command. Warm reuse still requires current admission; cached bytes alone never authorize an engine.

The child receives the original operating-system arguments and cwd, with inherited stdin/stdout/stderr. -C, --root, human/JSON mode and exit status retain their public meaning. Private handoff arguments carry only loop and correlation data: the child independently reads configuration and lock facts, checks current admission and refuses a second handoff. They do not propagate as an inherited environment variable to native build commands. Every build retains the actual engine identity and pin state in its inventory. For a currently admitted staged executable, that inventory also records the archive release digest, executable digest, compilation platform and explicit-local-development admission. Plugin and tool identities remain under their existing report owners. Native execution supplies no filesystem/network isolation guarantee.

Diagnostic Meaning and recovery ENGINE_PIN_MISMATCH No currently admitted source supplies the different pin. Run the pinned engine or admit its exact development archive in an allowed scope. ENGINE_DEVELOPMENT_DENIED The explicit override lacks trusted-scope permission or is outside local context. Remove the flag or obtain applicable local permission. ENGINE_DEVELOPMENT_UNAVAILABLE The active development executable could not be read for content evidence. Restore/read the compiled executable and retry. CONFIG_SCOPE A project/local/profile source attempted engine admission. Move admission to the user or responsible administrator. ENGINE_PACKAGE_UNAVAILABLE Required archive bytes are missing. Restore the admitted archive. ENGINE_PACKAGE_DIGEST Archive bytes differ from the admitted digest. Obtain the expected archive; do not blindly update the digest. ENGINE_INCOMPATIBLE Manifest bootstrap contract or platform is unsupported. Supply a matching build. ENGINE_IDENTITY_MISMATCH / ENGINE_HANDOFF_MISMATCH Manifest or running build does not establish the requested identity/entrypoint. Correct the package. No second handoff occurs. ENGINE_HANDOFF_CHANGED Pin or admitted release changed across handoff. Retry with consistent selections. ENGINE_START_FAILED The verified executable could not start. Check genuine host prerequisites and the package layout. Bootstrap failure precedes build effects and does not adopt plugins or tools or rewrite selections. Complete verified engine installations may remain reusable. The selected project's lock must be readable even for build --plan: bootstrap cannot determine its engine from a malformed lock. An independent nested build uses its own lock; a malformed parent lock does not replace that selection. The local archive route itself needs no network. Prepared native offline use and replay are described below. Independent engine and plugin selection and the explicit development override belong to #705. Container and cross-platform semantic workers, release channels, broader host qualification, stress tests and automatic upgrades are outside this slice.

The repository-owned verification harness tooling/test-native-engine-staging.py uses the real Go fixture in tooling/fixtures/go-registry: its go.mod and go.sum lock github.com/google/uuid 1.6.0. It creates a separate Git project, pins Go 1.24.13 through the supplied CLI, packages the actual engine/plugin executables, and admits their archive digests in a task-owned user config. It never implements a substitute engine or downloads a compiler itself. Supply a bootstrap-capable development seed and a separately compiled engine with a different actual version identity. Build the selected engine with oyzu build and the plugin with oyzu exec -- cargo build --locked -p oyzu-plugin-go --features plugin. Wait for build completion before accessing its output. Then, from the repository: oyzu exec -- python tooling/test-native-engine-staging.py ` --seed E:/qualification/seed/oyzu.exe ` --engine dist/cli/artifacts/oyzu.exe ` --plugin target/debug/oyzu-plugin-go.exe ` --source-revision <declared-plugin-source-reference> ` --destination .oyzu/native-engine-program/proof The destination must be new. The harness retains exact inputs, source commit, lock, archive/payload hashes, host facts, commands and output logs. Its cold build app --no-docker must install into an absent engine/plugin/tool store, produce the executable plus JUnit and Go coverage reports, and run the artifact to print 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000. It checks unchanged seed and lock bytes and removes engine admission to verify both cold and warm refusal. It then runs the same project without an engine pin and checks that the active seed owns the JSON-mode build, before restoring the original pinned lock. --source-revision is a caller-declared source reference, not proof of the compiler invocation.
