Record the actual compile base, dirty state and any source-identical Cargo cache reuse separately, as the linked qualification does. These local development archives carry no official signing claim. Network access is required for initial tool and Go module acquisition.

The experimental isolated external Go path can admit exact selected assets already installed in an immutable Linux image. The measured Windows-to-Linux proof establishes mounted composition, retained-input offline replay and the same selected B/P1/Go constituents in a locally assembled immutable image. Five fresh actions, required reports and the actual application run passed with all three assets image-installed and no asset overlays or tool restoration volume. This is a development Go application slice, not general image or platform qualification. Selection still comes from the admitted engine archive, plugin lock/package and locked tool distribution. Image labels and PATH do not select versions. During package installation, the store retains verified contents in a store-owned package-contents sidecar outside the package payload. It binds the package kind, release, verified tree and full-archive or selected-platform payload basis. Older installs without these optional facts retain mounted placement; damaged optional metadata also leaves ordinary package use available. Installed files are never rehashed to manufacture a missing sidecar. Reinstalling a removed package renews its optional sidecar from the newly verified archive or platform member under the installation lock. A retained sidecar does not block reinstallation or stand in for the new member's facts. If publication is interrupted while those optional facts are absent, placement remains mounted. The package payload itself still uses atomic no-replace publication. The executor compares these facts, or the verified tool archive, against the immutable image's merged filesystem once. It checks the complete selected tree, regular executable entrypoints and directory ancestors. The current supported content trees contain regular files and directories; unsupported member kinds, including links, remain mounted rather than receiving image placement. Windows file-mode observations are not treated as Linux executable-mode facts. The resulting native user image-cache receipt binds image/index, selected manifest/configuration, platform, constituent identity, layout and installation path. Project action or preparation records contain evidence references only; they cannot grant image placement authority or choose receipt paths. An admitted image-installed constituent uses its baked path without the corresponding mount or archive restoration. Tool admission occurs before volume lookup, creation or retention. Otherwise placement remains mounted. Docker declared volumes, scratch paths and explicit overlays cannot hide admitted assets. A conflicting overlay fails with ENGINE_CONTROL_CONFLICT. Required source/output scratch and execution controls remain enforced. Warm receipts are trusted without repeated installed-payload hashing; removing the trusted image cache requires fresh image admission, not a changed package selection. Reused dependency preparation still admits the current locked tool/archive placement before freezing asset evidence. Reusing captured dependency bytes does not skip placement registration or grant authority from cached records. Captured execution-asset evidence records bakedEngine separately from the selected archive/member. A lazy image-owned observation records the immutable image, manifest, configuration, platform and the regular-file digest at Oyzu's known semantic-worker path, /usr/local/libexec/oyzu/oyzu. Directory ancestors must be valid. Missing, unsupported or unavailable observations are explicit; no readable build identity or source provenance is inferred from bytes or labels. The baked executable is never launched for this observation. The native user image cache retains the observation, so warm builds do not rehash or reprobe it. It provides evidence only and never changes engine selection. When an outside launcher starts a whole build inside a container, that launcher must pair its immutable-image evidence with the inner CLI's selected-engine evidence; the inner CLI does not automatically discover a trusted outer-container identity. After a successful build has installed the exact engine, plugin and tools and populated the selected ecosystem's dependency cache, the qualified Windows Go flow supports these commands with the same project, store and admission: oyzu -C <project> install --frozen --offline --store <store> oyzu -C <project> exec --offline --store <store> -- go mod download oyzu -C <project> build app --frozen --offline --no-docker --no-cache --store <store> Preserve the explicit GOMODCACHE, GOCACHE and GOPATH used for preparation. The qualification sets GOENV=off, GOWORK=off, GOTOOLCHAIN=local, GOPROXY=off, GOSUMDB=off, and GOVCS=*:off; it also uses unavailable loopback HTTP proxies with empty proxy bypass lists. These are client and native tool controls, not OS network isolation. --offline alone does not establish that an arbitrary project command cannot contact the network. Missing engine or plugin installations can still be restored from their exact admitted local archives. A cached tool archive can likewise supply an absent installation. If neither eligible installation nor required archive is present, the command refuses the missing package; a missing Go module reports module lookup disabled by GOPROXY=off. Restore the exact content through the approved online preparation path, then retry. Do not change the lock to whatever happens to be cached. Setup discovers an already installed plugin and does not provide independent plugin acquisition. Replay here means executing the recorded command again with the same executable, arguments, working directory, source/lock, package selections and relevant environment/host facts. There is no new history-execution command or automatic historical environment restoration. Current admission still applies; removing engine admission refuses even retained bytes with ENGINE_PIN_MISMATCH. Incompatible platforms and unavailable required native prerequisites remain explicit errors. Matching evidence is not a byte-reproducibility guarantee. The pure-Go fixture has no C compiler or SDK requirement. The qualified Rust companion uses the existing MSVC compile/link probe before project consumers; an unavailable selected linker produces EXECUTOR_PREREQUISITE_UNAVAILABLE with provisioning guidance. Discovery does not install host SDKs or elevate. On cancellation, the staged engine records interrupted, emits BUILD_INTERRUPTED, accepts no successful artifact and returns exit 130 through the frontend. The representative concurrent proof preserves the peer's active lease and shared installed content, then lets that peer finish successfully. See the linked qualification for reusable harness commands, exact identities, failures discovered during implementation and the limits of Windows coverage.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/example-collection.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The public Oyzu examples repository owns self-contained native project candidates, canonical recipe instructions, four learning paths and a coverage inventory. Standalone examples need no platform account. Each entry states whether it is executable, blocked or planned; the collection does not imply that every registered adapter or provider is qualified. Each recipe separates the copied project/ from metadata and verification expectations. Use instructions and project files from the same exact commit. Native manifests and oyzu.toml own tool requirements, oyzu.lock owns resolved identities, and build.yaml declares only necessary build intent/relationships. The website imports selected recipes and actual source excerpts at an immutable commit, identified by its source links. Product support, example maturity and measured verification are independent. An executable recipe is not necessarily verified on your host/executor; old results apply only to their recorded subject. Unsupported capabilities remain explicit gaps with a next proof. The collection includes basic adapter/manager projects, package consumers, workspaces, generated sources, task hooks, affected selection, cache reuse, artifact materialization, local serving and file publication. Captured execution requires the named compatible executor; a controller's host is distinct from the artifact target. Follow the recipe's prerequisite and profile instructions. Recorded baseline consumers cover all ten existing builder families. That does not qualify every package manager, runtime, platform or provider. Yarn Classic is supplied by its captured executor. uv and Poetry examples use native Python manifests and provided runtimes; explicit Python tool-lock handoff is not proved. The complete Rust platform matrix remains a documented gap. The Windows pnpm workspace record requires the separately identified CLI correction and verifies both delivered archives through an independent offline consumer. Offline replay needs the selected sources and normal cached prerequisites. Publication/deployment additionally need scoped destinations and credentials. A successful build is not publication or observed deployment and cannot waive required evidence or organizational controls. The maintainer selected Apache-2.0 for first-party examples on 2026-10-17. Retain copied project licenses and applicable third-party notices. See the repository's contribution guidance and integration operations for selection, preparation, failures, release retention and verification limits.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/go.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The experimental Go builder discovers go.mod and go.work without Oyzu configuration. A workspace owns its declared modules. Static task listing does not run Go; explicit development execution and captured preparation use native metadata to select package patterns. Native preparation determines whether the project has main packages. A project with no main package now produces module artifacts instead of failing as an unsupported library. An explicit uses: go/library selects module packaging even when commands are present.

oyzu run list oyzu run test oyzu run lint oyzu run format-check oyzu build --plan oyzu build oyzu inspect dist An experimental external build of the same host lane can be selected with a local development plugin binding; without one the built-in builder described here is used. Development tasks use provisioned go and gofmt. The implicit tasks include dependency installation, compile, test, vet, formatting and formatting checks. oyzu run format modifies source; builds use format-check, whose native gofmt -l output must be empty. Native go.work members supply the package patterns for development build/test/vet commands. Direct tests produce the test-only evidence described below; other development tasks do not produce a collected build bundle. Captured builds require Docker and a Linux toolchain image. Oyzu can acquire the default amd64 Go image from the published toolchain image set; offline hosts and custom profiles need the image already provisioned. To build the default CI image locally: docker build -f tooling/images/go.Dockerfile -t oyzu-toolchain/go:1.24-mod0.25.0 . The current recipe extends golang:1.27-bookworm with the owned module packaging adapter linked against checksum-locked golang.org/x/mod 0.25.0. Dependency downloads occur in this provisioning step, not in project build execution. The image retains the upstream BSD license notice. Its bootstrap compiler is separate from the admitted, locked compiler selected for the project. Rebuild the embedded worker from the same candidate as the CLI and verify it executes inside the image; an existing image tag does not establish worker freshness. Native local checks use Go 1.24.13 on Windows; new cross-host module packaging checks and isolated library builds are wired into CI but still require revision-specific confirmation.

Oyzu runs Go with GOTOOLCHAIN=local, so Go never switches or downloads a toolchain itself; Oyzu selects the Go from the project's own files instead (OD10 rule 9). The Go minimum is the newer of the go and toolchain lines in the build folder's go.work when it has one, and in its go.mod otherwise. Go orders versions as 1.24 < 1.24rc1 < 1.24.0 < 1.24.5. A toolchain line is always honored. A suffixed name is read as Go reads it (go1.24.3-bigcorp and go1.24.3+auto as 1.24.3); toolchain default and toolchain local are ignored; any other value that is not a Go release name is refused with a remedy. A go line from Go 1.21 on is a toolchain minimum. Before Go 1.21 it was a language level, so a go 1.16 line only constrains the selection: with no toolchain line and no [tools] go, the newest stable Go is used, and a configured value below the line fails resolution. In a workspace, the go.work lines decide; a go.mod beside the go.work keeps its go line as a constraint and its toolchain line is ignored, as Go ignores it. Modules in subfolders are not read: Go itself refuses a workspace whose go line is older than a module's. Project Go selected toolchain go1.24.5 (or go 1.24.5), no [tools] go exactly 1.24.5 go 1.24 with no patch, or toolchain go1.25rc1 the newest stable release of that line (1.24.x, 1.25.x): Oyzu acquires stable releases only, so a line with only a release candidate fails resolution [tools] go at or above the minimum, in any folder that value (1.25, 1.24 for a 1.24.5 minimum, latest); the minimum still binds its resolution [tools] go below the minimum in a folder above the module (the project root, or user configuration), in oyzu.toml or oyzu.local.toml the minimum: the farther value loses, and the Tools row shows overrides 1.23.4 from oyzu.toml [tools] go below the minimum in the module's folder or below it, in oyzu.toml or oyzu.local.toml refused before any work with TOOL_NATIVE_MINIMUM_CONFLICT, naming both files a command-line or environment value, or a policy value below the minimum (a toolset value is exempt) refused with TOOL_NATIVE_MINIMUM_CONFLICT, naming its source and the native file; a policy value cannot be changed in the project, so the remedy is to ask the policy owner or lower the minimum For example, with toolchain go1.24.5 in app/go.mod, a root [tools] go = "1.25" and [tools] go = "1.24.0" in app/oyzu.toml, oyzu build stops after loading the configuration with exit status 3: ✗ TOOL_NATIVE_MINIMUM_CONFLICT: hello: [tools] go = "1.24.0" in app/oyzu.toml is below the go minimum 1.24.5 that app/go.mod declares (toolchain line); set [tools] go to 1.24.5 or later in app/oyzu.toml, or remove it so the native file decides Next: Make the configured tool version reach the native minimum, or change the native file, then retry. With only a root [tools] go = "1.23.4", the build uses the minimum and says so in the Tools block: ✓ Tools 1 tool pinned · 0 installed now 1.9s go 1.24.5 already installed detected from go.mod · overrides 1.23.4 from oyzu.toml Only plain releases and lines (1.23.4, 1.23) are compared with the minimum where they are written; another request form (a range) is resolved against the minimum and fails resolution when nothing satisfies it. Tool policy (a tools.go lock or allowed set) applies to the selected version whichever file requested it, the minimum included; when policy refuses the minimum itself, TOOL_NATIVE_MINIMUM_CONFLICT names the policy source and says it cannot be changed in the project. In a workspace, which builds in the isolated executor, the same refusal is reported as the build's preparation failure (exit status 1) with nothing run. oyzu config explain tools.go still shows the configured value; the override is shown only in the Tools block. The selection is locked in oyzu.lock like any request, with the minimum recorded as the native constraint go-minimum:>=1.24.5. Changing [tools] go needs oyzu pin before the next build, as for any explicit request. So does a changed minimum: go get and go mod tidy rewrite the go and toolchain lines, and the next build stops with the cause named: ✗ TOOL_LOCK_STALE: oyzu:go 1.24.5; app/go.mod declares go 1.24.5 (toolchain line) but oyzu.lock pins 1.27.2; run oyzu pin Run oyzu pin and commit oyzu.lock. An oyzu.lock written before the Go minimum was read holds the request * and needs the same step once. A project that pins Go ([tools] go = "1.23", locked with oyzu install go@1.23) builds with that exact Go in the captured worker, not the image's copy. Preparation reads the Linux (linux/amd64/gnu) archive recorded for the pinned version in oyzu.lock, downloads it through the tool broker unless a copy cached under the user data directory still matches the locked SHA-256, verifies the bytes against the locked digest, restores them read-only in the worker at /scratch/gotool and puts that go first on PATH (GOROOT is set to it) for preparation and every build action. The plan records the archive digest under oyzu.dev/locked-tool, so a different pin or archive changes the action identity. Without a pin, the Go that build preflight locked from the Go minimum is used the same way, so the selected compiler can satisfy a newer native minimum independently of the image's bootstrap compiler. A project whose existing oyzu.lock has no Go entry, a managed build or a non-Linux worker uses the image's Go. A tampered lock is rejected by the lock's own identity check, and a corrupted cached archive is replaced by a verified download. This changes the default Go image from the base Go distribution. Custom --image go=<image> profiles must now include oyzu-go-modulezip as well as the existing compiler/native tools and require explicit provisioning. Oyzu does not install a missing adapter into an image. Image content identity enters the build evidence. A missing executable fails preparation; it does not disable library packaging silently. Docker consumers can separately request the experimental Go module dependency context. It reuses native metadata/acquisition but only exports the captured module cache; the consumer's standard Go image does not need the module packaging helper. This exception applies to dependency preparation, not ordinary Go artifact builds or their report obligations.

oyzu run test instruments the implicit go test ./... command with -json, a fresh -coverprofile destination and -count=1. Native Go owns test discovery and compilation. Oyzu converts its JSON events to JUnit and retains the native coverage profile under dist/, with digests and summaries in the manifest. Statement coverage does not claim branch or line coverage. Packages with no tests retain an honest zero-test summary; native Go may succeed in that case. Missing/malformed reports and configured coverage thresholds can still fail the invocation. For a go.work root, native workspace metadata selects contained member package patterns and the invocation combines their actual test events and coverage. Members outside the task root fail. Forward selectors through oyzu run test -- -run TestGreeting; forwarded arguments go only to the requested task. The default disables reuse of Go's cached test results, while Go may still reuse its native compilation cache. The shared collector normalizes JUnit before post_test, exposing OYZU_TEST_REPORT and OYZU_COVERAGE_REPORT to hooks. Final validation and capture follow the hook, so report transformations are retained. Invalid native event streams or preexisting normalized outputs remain failures even if a hook subsequently writes valid XML. A failed test skips its success-only post hook and retains available evidence. Exact argv = ["go", "test", "./..."] and run = "go test ./..." overrides receive the same instrumentation. Other custom bodies remain unchanged and must write their required JUnit and Go coverage reports. An explicit coverage declaration can redirect the native profile; an explicit JUnit declaration selects file-based reporting and requires the custom task or hook to produce that XML. The default Go command itself emits JSON, not JUnit. Declared paths must be fresh; see direct report binding. This workflow needs a provisioned Go compiler and available dependencies, without Docker or a platform account. Host execution retains native environment/network behavior; use existing dependencies and native GOPROXY=off, GOSUMDB=off, GOTOOLCHAIN=local settings when verifying an offline fixture. It is not an isolated build, does not produce application artifacts and confers no publishing authority. Direct test evidence describes host provenance, output preservation, errors and recovery. python tooling/test-go-direct.py --cli <compiled-oyzu-path> --go <native-go-path> exercises real modules and workspaces, report inspection, test selection, failures, skips, empty suites, hooks, thresholds and custom-command obligations. CI runs it with provisioned Go 1.24.13 after compiling the CLI on each host. Current local and cross-host results are recorded separately in implementation status.

Native Go commands own manifest parsing, workspace membership, main package discovery, dependency selection and cgo detection. Captured inputs must contain local modules and replacement paths; escapes and missing inputs fail. Public module acquisition uses the existing scoped Go proxy broker and go.sum verification; the proxy's redirect of a large module zip to its own storage bucket is followed as a redirect-only route (acquisition transport). Private source routing and direct VCS acquisition remain unfinished. The compiler/ABI is recorded for cgo, and execution cannot turn off required cgo support through an environment override. Preparation captures the native dependency cache and module artifact candidates. Go works in a module cache on an engine tmpfs (/scratch/gomodcache), and the prepared store keeps only its download cache: module zips with their .mod, .info and .ziphash files. Each build action serves that store to Go as a file:// module proxy and extracts the modules it needs into its own tmpfs module cache, where go.sum verifies every zip. Extracted modules are many small files, and writing them through a Docker Desktop bind mount of a Windows path made preparation of a mid-size backend take about fifteen minutes. Library candidates come from captured source before build outputs or private compiler caches exist. The build then runs compile, native tests, vet and read-only formatting checks with denied networking and the prepared module cache. Final artifact collection occurs only after required gates pass. Prepared candidates are not successful build artifacts by themselves.

Root-owned captured pure-Go application targets describe each main-package build and each selected real package test as separate native actions. Production inputs come from fresh native package/import/file/embed metadata; synthetic Go test variants do not become binary inputs or extra test actions. Newly selected source and embed files change the captured read set. Native observation happens during admitted preparation, never static discovery or pure planning. Binary compilation writes private bytes without consuming the injected snapshot version. Export applies the current versioned filename after required build and report gates, including when compilation restores earlier bytes. Explicit native or user environment values remain real inputs. The new path fixes the native context used for metadata selection; a conflicting task environment fails validation before reuse. It does not silently reinterpret a changed build flag. Package tests use go test -json -count=1 with distinct package-attributed JUnit and native statement-coverage reports. Each test receives the entire original captured workspace and its own initially empty output and scratch directories. It cannot consume another action's reports or workspace mutations. Declared prepared proxy resources and the selected tool/image/environment remain bound; the compiler cache lives in scratch, outside retained binary-result changes. Restored reports retain their producing-run evidence and pass current report gates. These isolation bindings also apply with --no-cache. This path requires the compiled private Oyzu worker in the Go executor image; a missing worker fails the action. Libraries, cgo, nested targets, native workers, targets with materialized inputs and configurations with any authored tasks or hooks retain the existing coarse plan. This preserves their actual command and hook lifecycle, including generated inputs and post-test report transformations. The decision uses the resolved preparation configuration. Tests requiring generated or materialized workspace state need an actual supported input binding; the private-source path must not silently discard those inputs. The measured candidate passes a Linux-host/Docker shared-production edit with unrelated compilation reuse, an independent fresh oracle, test-only reuse and source-only second-checkout restoration with original producers. Its agreed finite cases also pass, including source/embed membership, runtime data, changed image identity, required failure/report gates and coarse hook/cgo boundaries. An original hook fixture failure remains retained separately from its corrected supplemental result. Existing library, workspace/cgo, multi-binary materialization, immutable dependency capture and locked-Go regressions also pass. The original stale proxy assertion remains visible separately from its corrected registry supplement; see the qualification record. On Windows, a public single-module fixture embedding seed/hello.sql through //go:embed completed oyzu build --isolated --full with the provisioned Go image: the embedded-byte test passed, JUnit and Go coverage were collected, and the resulting Linux/amd64 binary printed the SQL text. The compiled CLI was built at 25939715; its Go preparation, builder and snapshot sources match origin/main at d5b77871, while its Windows Go ZIP bound differs. This confirms that captured preparation includes that input in this flow; other embed patterns and platforms have not been qualified by this fixture. Direct oyzu exec -- gofmt uses the selected Go installation's bundled formatter after its layout has been admitted; see Go installation. Each engine-owned scratch tmpfs keeps a 2 GiB minimum size ceiling and grows to match its action's memory reservation when that is larger. This does not raise the action's memory reservation; where cgroups are available, the limit covers combined process and tmpfs use. Go build actions reserve at least 4 GiB, so /scratch/gotmp can hold larger compiler and test-linker intermediates than the separate 512 MiB /tmp mount. The Docker and daemonless execution paths use the same ceiling. Application builds retain their existing single primary binary or named multiple binaries, using -trimpath and disabled ambient VCS stamping. Libraries compile package patterns without fabricating an executable. Native test JSON becomes JUnit, and native Go coverage retains its statement denominator. Shared collection stores these under dist/, with paths, digests and summaries in dist/manifest.json. Failed tests, vet, formatting, missing reports or compilation prevent final artifact collection. Source files remain unchanged during captured execution; inspect task logs and reports to repair the failing native input.

When the Go client cannot publish or consume an acquisition spool request, its local proxy returns HTTP 502 with a fixed category, for example module acquisition failed: BROKER_RESPONSE_BODY (broker HTTP 200). The received broker status is retained for body-read/size failures; it describes the broker response, not a successful module download. Diagnostics exclude raw filesystem/JSON errors, spool paths, credentials and redirect URLs. Category Meaning and recovery BROKER_REQUEST_ID Request ID generation failed; inspect the worker's runtime availability. BROKER_REQUEST_WRITE, BROKER_REQUEST_PUBLISH The worker could not write/publish its request; inspect the engine-owned spool mount and permissions. BROKER_RESPONSE_READ, BROKER_RESPONSE_METADATA The worker could not read/decode response metadata; inspect broker delivery and the spool mount. BROKER_RESPONSE_BODY, BROKER_RESPONSE_LIMIT The response body was unreadable or exceeded the existing 256 MiB client limit; inspect broker delivery or module size. BROKER_TIMEOUT The broker did not answer within the existing 55-second client wait; inspect host broker execution. Upstream HTTP statuses and the broker's sanitized source/authorization failure messages continue to pass through unchanged. These categories do not identify an upstream root cause by themselves or change retries, deadlines, size limits, offline behavior or source authorization. The opt-in contributor check is oyzu --toolset go-test exec -- node tooling/test-go-acquisition.mjs; it exercises the actual proxy handler/client against a local test spool with network access disabled. See contributor tool setup.

Each library/workspace module produces three independently identified files: Artifact Contents module-<index>-<version>.zip Native Go module archive with the <module>@<version>/ prefix module-<index>-<version>.mod The exact projected go.mod included in that archive module-<index>-<version>.info Native proxy version metadata; no invented release timestamp Indices follow the captured, sorted module directory order. Manifest artifact names are module-<index>-zip, module-<index>-mod and module-<index>-info. Each artifact records its native module snapshot version. dist/dependencies/<target>.json records module paths/directories, filenames, versions and native h1: zip/go.mod checksums in oyzu.dev/go-module-artifacts, allowing later publication code to map files to registry identities. Publishing itself is not implemented by this increment. Versions use shared version inference with a tag-derived base when available and the build's source-derived -dev.g... suffix. Without applicable tags, the logical base is 0.0.0; native module packaging maps that fallback to the module path's major where required, for example v2.0.0-dev.g... for /v2. An explicitly inferred/tagged version must satisfy native module path rules: v3.0.0 for an unchanged /v2 module fails instead of silently changing the selected version. These are snapshot prereleases, not Go VCS pseudo-versions or release authorization. Exact RC tags preserve their qualifier, for example v2.6.0-rc.2.dev.g.... Application binary filenames and manifest coordinates use their owning module's inferred version; Oyzu does not inject application version variables. An upstream Conventional Commit can declare a breaking tool-minimum change without changing the Go module path. Under the default auto strategy that still infers a major bump, and native packaging refuses an incompatible module coordinate. Projects whose released tags define their desired development line can explicitly select the existing tag strategy. That choice is recorded in configuration and version evidence; native path-major validation, tool selection and required build/report checks still apply. The original Gin default refusal and separately configured proof are recorded in toolchain selection qualification. Go preparation now captures module directory/path identities and native local import and test-import edges before version resolution. Each module receives its own transitive input scope and decision. Directory-scoped tags such as math/v2.4.2 and api/v1.4.2 supply independent workspace baselines. Root tags are admitted for a module at the Git root; a workspace root tag does not coordinate its children. The root module's decision subject is the Oyzu target name; other subjects are their target-relative module directories. Paths outside module directories are conservative shared inputs. Custom namespaces and special major-directory layouts require further integration. The host freezes a native-path-keyed version-plan.json; the native module adapter uses each selected version when creating zip/mod/info candidates and rewriting local requirements. Captured dependency extensions retain oyzu.dev/go-module-versions and oyzu.dev/go-metadata.modulePaths, while ordinary version decisions retain baseline tags, commits and input scopes. Native archive versions, including any path-major fallback mapping, are recorded in oyzu.dev/go-module-artifacts. Dependency layout version 4 and the new version-plan argument require rebuilding the provisioned Go image and recreating older captures. Dependency-context-only preparation still requires neither the module adapter nor artifact version inference. The adapter uses Go's native module zip library for allowed files, nested-module/vendor exclusions, case collisions and archive limits. It uses native module/manifest APIs for identity and projection, and native dirhash for checksums. It does not reimplement zip rules or infer source files from extensions. Workspace dependencies are projected to their matching snapshot module versions. Native package imports, including test imports, supply local dependency edges even when a workspace member has no explicit require entry yet. Contained local replacements to a captured workspace module with the same module identity are removed from published go.mod files. The source manifests remain unchanged. These files use the Go module proxy protocol; independent consumer checks provision them into a local file proxy and compile a separate project with a fresh module cache.

The #477 candidate retains separate native production/test package graphs, selected file/embed facts and native context during preparation. Pure-Go application plans describe one native build per main package and one fresh go test -json -count=1 invocation per selected real package, with separate JUnit/statement-coverage reports. Synthetic test variants remain metadata. Compiled Rust exports private binary outputs under the current module version after required checks. Library and cgo paths retain their existing coarse flow. This action decomposition is experimental. Linux/amd64 with selected Go 1.27.2 passes the agreed incremental and finite native proof, including usable binary stdout, fresh/restored report attribution and a second absolute checkout using an explicit shared local result store. The original full-group hook-authoring failure remains visible; its corrected qualified-hook and cgo supplemental checks pass. Existing Go regressions also pass, including current-version module artifacts, workspace/cgo, digest-preserving multi-binary OCI assembly, immutable dependency capture and captured Go 1.23.12 selection/lock refusal. The earlier Windows controller's unrelated-reuse failure remains unwaived; Linux results do not qualify every host or native mode. See the bounded qualification record. Pinned Go in the captured worker was verified on Windows 11 with Docker Desktop: with go = "1.23" locked (1.23.12) and the worker image carrying Go 1.24.13, a Go binary built for a linux/amd64 image embeds go1.23.12; a second build reused the cached archive; a corrupted cached archive was re-downloaded and verified; a lock with a changed digest was refused. Only linux/amd64 workers were exercised, and only the Go archive layout (go/ prefix, tar.gz) is admitted. The Go module dependency context and native-path builds are unchanged. Offline builds need the archive already cached (TOOL_OFFLINE otherwise). The checked-in library variant has no Oyzu configuration. The native probe is: python tooling/test-go-modulezip.py --adapter <provisioned-modulezip> --go <provisioned-go> python tooling/test-go-metadata.py --go <provisioned-go> --cli <compiled-oyzu> The module probe checks single-module and workspace consumption, major-version identity, matching go.mod bytes, native checksums, repeatable bytes, unchanged inputs, projected implicit dependencies and invalid local replacement rejection. Rust checks cover inferred/explicit library planning and artifact path admission. CI additionally requires measured test/coverage evidence and snapshot artifacts from an actual captured library build, repeats it for byte identity, then verifies a real failed test blocks collection. tooling/test-go-workspace-version-inference.py --cli <compiled-cli> --evidence-dir <new-directory> creates scoped tags for a three-module workspace. It exercises independent library archive versions and local requirements, two binaries owned by different modules, RC snapshots and a native major-path conflict. The probe checks actual outputs, reports, bundle inspection and unchanged original source files. It requires a provisioned gofmt (or --gofmt <path>) for fixture setup and the current Go build image. Measured results are recorded in implementation status; registration alone does not prove acceptance. Registry replacements that require different publication semantics, local replacement modules outside the selected workspace, private/VCS routing, cross compilation and module publication remain unfinished. Standalone direct test bundles are implemented for modules and contained workspaces; their host provenance is separate from captured-build evidence. Unsupported replacement projection fails preparation rather than producing a module known to depend on an unreproducible local path. Native source archives do not claim a compiled ABI or production provenance. Full cgo/sysroot portability and all authored scenario acceptance remain part of the active goal; see implementation status. Platform matrices can select matching provisioned Go toolchains through platform selection. Preparation verifies actual Go OS/architecture, and tests execute in each selected runtime. The authored Go-to-container matrix is now required by Linux CI; its new ARM execution result is pending. General cross-compilation, ABI admission and all EX-027 cases are not established by this selection capability.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/gradle.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Status: experimental. Oyzu detects build.gradle or build.gradle.kts without a build YAML file. A native multi-project or composite build is one Oyzu target: Gradle owns project membership, included builds, task dependencies and native output paths. Oyzu uses that model to plan artifacts and collect reports. The EX-024 project demonstrates an application, library and included support build.

oyzu run list oyzu run test oyzu inspect dist oyzu build Static task discovery does not execute Gradle. It exposes native build and test tasks and the shared Java lint/format tasks. Native build already includes tests, so captured builds do not repeat a separate test stage. Qualified task names and TOML replacements follow the common task engine. No test/report configuration is needed for the default Java test tasks. Plain oyzu build uses the supported host Gradle path. Its native build lifecycle can run tests even under Oyzu's fast selection; --full additionally selects Oyzu's separate quality operations. Use --isolated --full to request the captured path with full checks. A custom native JUnit directory does not change the independently observed JaCoCo destination: both remain required host build evidence, and missing coverage blocks successful artifact export. This report-binding correction and missing-coverage export gate passed the Linux native host regression. Direct tests require provisioned Gradle 8.14.3, JDK 17 and native project/test dependencies, including JaCoCo 0.8.13. Set GRADLE_HOME or put Gradle on PATH, and configure JAVA_HOME for the JDK. The native Gradle user home and project repositories remain authoritative. An existing wrapper is used when discovered; its distribution must already be provisioned. Direct-test invocation uses these provisioned tools. Host oyzu build separately uses shared tool preparation and records its selected versions in oyzu.lock; a tool on PATH alone does not pin that build's identities. Product model/test commands pass --offline and disable automatic Java toolchain downloads. Missing cached dependencies fail explicitly; offline dependency resolution does not sandbox arbitrary native build logic or prevent a wrapper from trying to provision itself. Captured builds additionally require Docker and the provisioned toolchain image: docker build -f tooling/images/gradle.Dockerfile -t oyzu-toolchain/gradle:8.14.3-jdk17 . oyzu -C examples/builds/java-gradle-multi-project/project build --isolated --full

A JDK the project selects, by [tools] java or native requirements, is locked by build preflight and restored read-only in the worker at /scratch/jdktool from the verified Temurin archive in oyzu.lock, as for Maven. An explicit toolchainVersion in gradle/gradle-daemon-jvm.properties selects and constrains the daemon JDK's feature release. For example, toolchainVersion=25 normally selects a stable Java 25 release; an explicit [tools] java override must satisfy the same native constraint. The declared vendor remains binding at native launch. The existing provider supplies Temurin; explicit vendors other than ADOPTIUM/Eclipse Adoptium and native-image-capable daemon requirements are refused before acquisition with the source path and field. Literal generated property names and integer feature releases are supported; malformed or escaped criteria require correction or a matching provisioned native runtime. When daemon criteria are absent, existing inference uses the highest literal Java level in root/first-level build scripts (JavaLanguageVersion.of(21), sourceCompatibility) as a compiler floor, or Java 21 when none is declared. With explicit daemon criteria, compilation and optional toolchain declarations remain unchanged for Gradle to enforce; they do not replace the daemon runtime. The worker restores one selected JDK. Builds requiring another JDK for a task can still fail natively with automatic downloads disabled; this is not multi-JDK provisioning. The selected installation is always offered through -Dorg.gradle.java.installations.paths, including before Gradle's daemon JVM selection; automatic toolchain downloads stay disabled. The standard image's Gradle 8.14.3 runs on the selected JDK when it is release 24 or older. For a newer JDK the launcher retains the image's bootstrap JDK while offering the selected installation to native Gradle. A suitably provisioned newer Gradle can use that installation for its declared daemon criterion; Gradle 8.14.3 compatibility remains a native limit. A project's own wrapper version is not yet provisioned in the captured worker. A selected JDK older than 17 is refused with TOOL_UNSUPPORTED_VERSION. The CLI does not pull a missing image. Captured acceptance runs on Linux; portable host tasks do not establish isolated executor support on every platform.
documents.s: Locked JDK in the captured worker

documents.t: After common task admission, the builder evaluates native models for the root and included builds. The observation command requests only Oyzu's metadata tasks; it does not deliberately execute project lifecycle tests or compilation. Gradle configuration, plugins and native build logic still execute normally. This is explicit host execution, not static discovery or a security boundary. The model identifies enabled test tasks with attributable source files, their native JUnit destinations and injected JaCoCo destinations. Projects without test sources do not create test obligations. Builds with no discovered tests fail rather than manufacturing a passing suite. The exact implicit command is instrumented to run the discovered tests across the composite, respecting native dependencies. Custom command bodies remain unchanged and must fulfill the required reports; forwarded extra arguments are not yet supported by the default reporting adapter. Before each run, the adapter removes previous XML from the selected native test directories and their selected coverage XML. Native rerun semantics produce current evidence. JaCoCo finalizers generate coverage, including after failed assertions. Native suites are combined per test task without replacing their test cases, and fresh private JUnit/JaCoCo files enter the shared collector. dist/manifest.json links each report and its summary, plan and logs. Native output remains in project build directories; source files and versions are unchanged. Direct tests create no application artifact records and do not run packaging, lint or formatting. Common pre/post hooks apply; a failed test blocks its success-only post hook. Failed assertions, missing or malformed reports and unmet configured coverage thresholds fail the command while retaining available evidence. oyzu inspect dist verifies the resulting bundle. See direct test reports for output preservation, history, report overrides and host provenance limits. Direct execution is not hermetic, and a local passing test grants no publication or signing authority.

Preparation evaluates native models and acquires Maven-layout dependencies through the scoped public repository adapter. Build execution uses the captured repository offline. Private/custom repository connectors are not yet supported. Gradle plugins come from the admitted plugin portal. Version inference resolves native versions, scoped tags and commit impacts before projecting source snapshots in the private build. Gradle archive tasks supply filenames and archive versions; supported file kinds include JAR/WAR/EAR, ZIP, TAR and gzip archives. The bundle records their planned versions and digests. The first native model pass retains original versions. The host freezes a version-plan.json keyed by project directories across the composite, then native preparation validates original versions and applies each decision. Offline execution uses that same projection. Unique native project names supply scoped tag subjects; repeated names use directory paths. An unspecified native version can use a tag baseline without inventing a native declaration. Captured native resolution supplies local project dependencies with full build-tree identities, including substituted projects in included builds. Project identities come from Gradle's public Project.buildTreePath; selected dependency edges retain Gradle's resolved ProjectComponentIdentifier.buildTreePath. Detached configuration roots are not used as project identities. The shared resolver computes transitive version impacts; unrelated project directories retain independent bases. Missing or unresolved graph facts fail preparation. Host metadata-only queries do not resolve this graph. Prepared layout version 3 adds these facts; recreate older captures. JAR manifest attributes remain native build behavior rather than being rewritten to add implementation-version metadata. Native Java tests supply JUnit and JaCoCo, with source-free projects omitted. Shared Java quality gates run before successful artifact publication into dist. Report injection is shared with direct testing; repository routing, snapshot projection and isolation belong to the captured path. Missing archives, unresolved dependencies and required stage/report failures remain build failures.

Captured acquisition admits two public sources: Maven Central and the Gradle plugin portal (https://plugins.gradle.org/m2/). The broker also admits the portal's artifact host, https://plugins-artifacts.gradle.org/, so that portal redirects for plugin JARs stay authorized; redirects to Maven Central use the Central source. Plugins applied in settings.gradle or a project plugins {} block, and gradlePluginPortal() declared in pluginManagement, buildscript or project repositories, resolve through the broker during preparation: // settings.gradle plugins { id 'com.gradle.develocity' version '4.2' } The init script adds an Oyzu Central entry and an Oyzu portal entry to pluginManagement, which takes the place of Gradle's implicit portal default, and routes each recognized repository to its own loopback broker path. Any other repository URL still fails preparation with Gradle repository requires an approved source adapter. Captured files from both sources land in one Maven-layout repository that the offline build reads. The prepared tree records the serving source of each file in repository-sources.json, and the dependency snapshot attributes every inventoried package to maven-central, gradle-plugin-portal or gradle-plugin-artifacts accordingly. A redirect to any other host fails with a source denial rather than widening admission. Settings plugins are resolved while Gradle evaluates the settings script, before Oyzu can reroute repositories the script itself declares; Oyzu's own entries come first, so a plugin they serve is found there. Plugin behavior that downloads at run time (for example Gradle toolchain provisioning) is outside this admission. The native probe python tooling/test-gradle-preparation.py --gradle-home <gradle-home> --java-home <jdk-home> includes a portal settings-plugin case. The positive portal/JMH composite supplement now passes a captured/full build, required reports and fresh delivered-JAR consumers at source 47363a03; original corpus failures retain their separate scope in the JVM qualification.

python tooling/test-gradle-metadata.py --gradle-home <gradle-home> --java-home <jdk-home> checks metadata-only host observation and an offline captured-graph fixture with duplicate project paths across an included build. It requires native project identities and the actual substituted local edges without external dependencies. The Gradle 9.8.0/Java 26.0.2.1 diagnosis confirmed that an empty detached configuration has a separate non-project root while public project build-tree paths retain the composite identities. The corrected adapter and regression passed native metadata qualification on Gradle 9.8.0/Java 26.0.2.1 and Gradle 8.14.6/Java 17. At source 47363a03, the seven registered captured cases also pass, including usable delivered App/Support JARs and required failure gates. The host direct report/coverage probe passes separately. The original RxJava :bundle failure and Mockito/Pioneer/SpotBugs preparation failures remain recorded separately; these bounded results do not complete the JVM corpus. python tooling/test-gradle-direct.py --cli <compiled-path> --gradle-home <gradle-home> --user-home <native-cache> exercises EX-024 and an included-build test variation with custom JUnit paths, repeated runs, hooks, actual failed assertions, source preservation and bundle inspection. Install tooling/design-requirements.txt for the harness. Its optional --acquire explicitly provisions fixture dependencies before offline product invocation. CI provisions a checksum-pinned Gradle distribution and runs the probe on Windows, macOS and Linux after compiling the CLI. Both native direct variations passed locally on Windows with Gradle 8.14.3/JDK 17.0.20.1; the direct probe also passed on Linux and macOS at c15008b in run 37054773923 (jobs 110998609377 and 110998609418). The Windows CI step remains pending. Current results are recorded in implementation status; CI registration alone is not acceptance. tooling/test-gradle-preparation.py separately exercises native repository capture, a fresh offline Gradle home, snapshot archives and report generation. It passed on Windows after the shared reporting extraction, including successful and failed-test reports. It uses an explicit fixture download proxy, not the product executor. The captured Java suite passed at revision 039f83a in job 110970888463, before the direct-reporting extraction. The bounded normalized composite qualification adds root/included-build report ownership, custom native JUnit destinations, per-module JaCoCo classes, usable delivered JARs and failed-check blocking to the existing Gradle group. The direct probe additionally checks a plain host build with custom JUnit output and a zero-exit native run that omits required coverage. On 2026-10-16, the first normalized captured flow passed on Linux, including actual delivered App/Support execution, attributed native reports and bundle inspection. The complete direct probe and both independent host cases also passed. The full registered Gradle group passed repeatability, native lint/format/test failure gates, custom/included paired JUnit/JaCoCo ownership and included-test failure export blocking. See the qualification record for exact runtime identities and the distinction between provisioned direct tools and managed host tools. This qualifies the bounded Linux fixture, not the complete authored Gradle scenario catalog. Broader Gradle versions, non-Java languages, custom coverage plugins/source ownership, generated test sources and all plugin/composite configurations are not qualified by these fixtures. Native disabled tests and source-free tasks are omitted; unknown test source ownership fails explicitly. Release authorization, private connectors and full authored-scenario coverage remain separate implementation work. The compiled Oyzu worker owns process sequencing and native report composition. Native Java integrations remain embedded assets; Python is not required to execute these builder operations. Rebuild captured images after updating the worker. The observed daemon-JVM selection gap and pending native proof are recorded in Gradle daemon JVM qualification.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/gradle-sessions.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. This opt-in client adapter prepares native Gradle invocations through oyzu exec and bare gradle in activated Bash. It does not implement platform login or change the isolated oyzu build dependency acquisition path. A local agent supplies admission and repository sessions; the proof uses a disposable simulator.

Configure the local agent in existing user or administrative Oyzu configuration: [gradle] sessionEndpoint = "http://127.0.0.1:43199/session" The port is illustrative. Numeric-loopback HTTP is required, without userinfo, query or fragment. Project/local/invocation endpoint overrides are rejected; profiles cannot choose this setting. It is absent by default. Removing it restores standalone behavior. User configuration is excluded in CI under existing rules; this prototype does not establish CI identity. With Gradle and JDK provisioned on the native PATH: oyzu exec -- /opt/gradle-8.14.3/bin/gradle build # Or, with the native installation on PATH: eval "$(oyzu activate bash)" gradle build Use the native gradle executable. Wrapper commands are not integrated. The proof scope is Linux, Gradle 8.14.3 and JDK 17; no blanket Windows/macOS compatibility claim is made. Windows managed-session shell shims are not implemented.

The agent selects one Maven-layout source for the invocation. Oyzu's bundled initializer maps plugin-management, settings dependency, project buildscript and project dependency repositories to that source and installs authentication through Gradle's native APIs. Existing Maven-layout repository declarations are redirected; non-Maven repository types fail explicitly. This includes redirecting native local Maven repository declarations: managed mode does not treat them as independent approved sources. Unrelated project options and native lock files remain owned by Gradle and are not rewritten. The adapter adds a default repository where needed. It does not resolve arbitrary conflicts between project repositories and settings repository modes, merge several connector identities, or govern arbitrary plugin HTTP calls. Custom init scripts are outside the supported invocation shape. Projects that deliberately mutate repositories later are not a hostile-code containment boundary.

The compiled launcher requests admission before starting native work, even with a warm dependency cache. It stages the owned initializer plus temporary JSON holding only the selected URL, username and credential endpoint, then supplies its path to the child. The initializer fetches the password into memory on every invocation; it must not keep credentials in static state across daemon reuse. Artifact downloads go directly from Gradle to the selected repository. Passwords are not written into project configuration, command arguments or launcher environment variables. Native Gradle code and plugins can access credentials in process memory. The session endpoint itself is access-sensitive and is not a production authenticated IPC implementation. Upstream identity permissions enforce read-only access; publication remains an oyzu publish responsibility. The launcher disables Gradle configuration-cache use. Explicit configuration-cache requests are rejected until credential persistence in serialized configuration is qualified. Native dependency caches and daemon reuse remain enabled. Temporary session files are removed on ordinary completion/failure; caches and daemon state retain their native lifecycle. Crash cleanup is deferred.

Native streams/exit codes and global JSON follow the existing exec contract. Agent denial/outage fails before native launch without fallback or an offline grant. Public help and native help/version/daemon-status/stop requests do not contact the agent. NATIVE_SESSION_* identifies shared authority/transport failures; GRADLE_SESSION_INVALID identifies invalid response/arguments; GRADLE_SESSION_CONFLICT rejects unsupported overrides, configuration caching or publication-shaped requests. Correct configuration or agent authorization rather than bypassing the managed launch. Native argument checks are intentionally bounded, not a complete Gradle grammar. Production agent bootstrap, CI identity, arbitrary custom native settings, configuration cache, hostile-code isolation and cross-platform qualification remain separate work. No Oyzu schema version is introduced. See the integration proof for reproduction, observed native behavior and exact verification scope.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/helm.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The experimental helm/chart builder discovers an application or library chart at Chart.yaml or chart/Chart.yaml. A basic chart needs no Oyzu configuration. If both locations exist, choose explicit target paths in build.yaml; ambiguous discovery fails. The chart example includes a contained local library dependency and optional native assertion suites. Vendored children under charts/ must also be declared in the parent's native Chart.yaml dependencies for strict lint. For a contained child, declare its name/version and omit the repository URL. Passing child assertions does not waive this native metadata requirement. If lint reports missing dependencies, correct the parent declaration; Oyzu does not silently add native dependencies or disable the lint gate.
documents.s: Helm charts and native chart tests

documents.t: Development commands use an already provisioned Helm executable. Direct test/report orchestration is compiled into Oyzu; native assertion suites require the helm-unittest plugin in Helm's configured plugin directory. Oyzu does not install these tools. Local verification used Helm 3.22.0 and helm-unittest 1.2.0 on Windows; Linux native checks are wired into CI. This is not a claim of verified plugin execution on all three hosts. oyzu run list oyzu run test oyzu run lint oyzu run format-check oyzu run format oyzu build --plan oyzu build oyzu inspect dist oyzu run list discovers tasks without launching Helm or interpreting assertion YAML. The initial group is project; explicit targets use their own names. Native development tasks are install (helm dependency build), build (helm package), lint (helm lint) and test. These development commands have native effects: install may acquire dependencies and update locks, and package writes a chart archive. Direct test now writes a test-only dist/ bundle with native validation JUnit, an additional independent unittest JUnit report when suites are detected, logs and a manifest. It records coverage as inapplicable, produces no chart artifact and uses the shared hook/report/bundle workflow. Both default validation and unittest run against private chart copies that exclude .oyzu, .git and existing dist output; root charts therefore do not expose the live bundle lease to Helm. Native dependencies must already be prepared (for example with oyzu run install); testing does not acquire them. Run oyzu inspect dist to inspect the retained evidence. The default adapter accepts no extra native flags; use an explicit task replacement and report declarations for customized arguments. See direct test reports. Captured builds require Docker and an explicitly provisioned toolchain image: docker build -f tooling/images/builder-worker.Dockerfile -t oyzu-toolchain/builder-worker:v1 . docker build -f tooling/images/helm.Dockerfile -t oyzu-toolchain/helm:3.22.0 . This repository provisioning step downloads checksum-pinned Helm, unittest and yamlfmt distributions. The CLI does not download toolchain images or plugins during a build. The current image is Linux amd64 and includes the compiled Oyzu worker and yamlfmt 0.21.0, with no Python runtime prerequisite. Its plugin directory is /opt/oyzu-helm-plugins; the build plan fixes HELM_PLUGINS to that toolchain-owned location so a task environment override cannot redirect it to project code. Custom images must provide the compatible executables and directory layout. Image identity is captured in build evidence.

A project that pins helm ([tools] helm = "4.3.0", locked with oyzu install helm@4.3.0; helm takes only an exact version and oyzu pin does not resolve it) builds its charts with that exact helm instead of the image's copy. Preparation reads the Linux (linux/amd64/gnu) archive recorded for the pinned version in oyzu.lock, downloads it through the tool broker unless a copy cached under the user data directory still matches the locked SHA-256, verifies the bytes against the locked digest, restores them read-only in the worker at /scratch/helmtool and puts that directory ahead of the image's /usr/local/bin on PATH for preparation and every build action. The dependency record carries the pinned version as the manager version and the archive evidence under oyzu.dev/locked-tool, so a different pin or archive changes the action identity. The image still supplies the worker, yamlfmt and the helm-unittest plugin; a pinned helm must be able to run that plugin. A project with no helm pin uses the image's helm as before, a tampered lock is refused, and offline builds need the archive already cached (TOOL_OFFLINE otherwise). Before this, any helm pin failed every helm/chart target with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. Not yet verified end to end in a Docker worker; python tooling/test-build-scenarios.py --suite helm --only locked-helm is the check.
documents.s: Pinned helm in the captured worker

documents.t: A chart can consume the identity of an image built in the same oyzu build, so a deploy needs no --set image.digest=...: builds: image: uses: docker/image with: repository: registry.example.com/team/greeting # the approved eventual repository chart: uses: helm/chart path: chart bindings: - from: image artifact: image type: image-reference repository: /image/repository digest: /image/digest from and artifact select the producer's output, as in materialize; type: image-reference is the only type. Name either one reference destination (it receives repository@sha256:...) or the repository and digest pair; mixing them, naming neither, or binding the same values field twice fails during configuration. Destinations are JSON Pointers into the chart's values.yaml, and each must already name a string there (an empty digest: "" is the usual shape). Nothing is created, templated or evaluated. The image must declare with.repository, a repository name without scheme, tag or digest. Building does not publish: the bound reference names the intended destination and the actual OCI manifest digest of the local archive, and the chart does not become deployable until the image is pushed there. Retargeting the repository means rebuilding the chart. How it runs: a binding implies the dependency on the image (like materialize) and a data-only copy of the image's OCI archive in the chart target (.oyzu-bindings/<n>.oci.tar, recorded in dist/inputs/<chart>.json). After the chart is copied into its private workspace and before it is packaged, linted or rendered, the compiled bind action reads the archive's single manifest digest and rewrites the destinations in that private copy's values.yaml. The packaged archive's default values and rendered.yaml therefore carry the produced reference, and the checked-in chart is never edited. The rewrite re-serializes values.yaml in the private copy, so YAML comments in the packaged defaults are not preserved. A changed image (a different manifest digest) reruns the chart's actions; an unchanged one reuses them. A failed or blocked image blocks every chart action. A multi-platform image layout (more than one manifest) is refused for now; binding a complete OCI index is not implemented. Verified on Windows 11 with Docker Desktop on 2026-10-09 through python tooling/test-build-scenarios.py --suite helm --only chart-bindings: a Go binary, a scratch image and a chart (the EX-029 fixture); an umbrella chart with two service subcharts bound to two images (one by the repository/digest pair, one by reference); a Dockerfile-only change rebinding the chart; and the failed-image, missing-destination, missing-repository and conflicting-form cases. Not verified: Linux or macOS hosts, bindings through a platform matrix with several variants, publishing, and a deployed cluster.

Discovery supplies a read-only format-check build stage and an explicit, source-mutating format development task. Both use native yamlfmt through compiled Oyzu orchestration. Development execution requires yamlfmt on PATH; verification uses yamlfmt 0.21.0. Missing tools fail with process diagnostics. The repository's python tooling/provision-yamlfmt.py --destination <directory> is an explicit maintainer/CI provisioning step that verifies pinned release digests and retains the upstream license. It is not invoked by the CLI. Put that directory on PATH before running development formatting. The adapter selects .yaml/.yml files immediately inside chart roots identified by Chart.yaml, plus YAML below their tests/ and crds/ directories. It includes unpacked subcharts and contained sibling charts within the target root. Go templates under templates/, native __snapshot__ baselines, packaged chart archives, Chart.lock, generated output and hidden directories are excluded. Formatting does not edit or repack dependency archives. Template formatting remains unfinished; a passing YAML check makes no claim about Go-template style. An explicit private yamlfmt configuration fixes LF line endings and a final newline while retaining native basic-formatter defaults. Parent/home formatter configuration is ignored. Target-local .yamlfmt, .yamlfmt.yaml, .yamlfmt.yml, yamlfmt.yaml or yamlfmt.yml currently fails the implicit operation with guidance to override the affected tasks; native custom formatter configuration support remains unfinished. Use existing TOML task overrides when customization is necessary, without adding a build-file formatting DSL. format-check lists differing paths and exits unsuccessfully without changing files. Invalid YAML also fails with the native diagnostic. Run oyzu run format, review the changes and retry the check/build. Explicit formatting writes changed files as it proceeds; if a later file fails, earlier formatting edits remain. Neither command downloads dependencies or contacts a cluster. Selection rejects links/reparse points and nonregular YAML inputs, with limits of 100000 traversed entries, 4 MiB per selected file and 64 MiB total. Native formatter invocations each have a 30-second timeout. Host tasks are not a security sandbox; captured builds use the executor's isolation. Verified on Windows 11 with Docker Desktop on 2026-10-09: plain oyzu build of a Go binary, a scratch image and a chart built all three targets and wrote the chart archive and rendered.yaml. Before this change the same build failed in chart:package with cp: cannot stat '.oyzu-build/rendered.yaml', because only the unselected test stage wrote that file. The worker inside the Helm toolchain image carries this adapter, so rebuild that image after updating Oyzu.

Declare unpacked subcharts in the parent's native Chart.yaml dependencies. An empty repository selects the already-present charts/<name> directory. Suite discovery does not repair missing dependency declarations; native strict lint rejects inconsistent chart metadata even when the child assertions pass. Without native suites, the implicit test validates local rendering and values schemas for an application chart. A library chart uses strict native lint with subcharts, because it cannot be rendered as an installable application. Captured application rendering uses helm template --dry-run=client, an empty kubeconfig and no cluster access. This is chart validation, not a claim that a deployed application works. An immediate tests/*_test.yaml file under the selected chart or an unpacked subchart in charts/<name>/ activates helm-unittest automatically. Nested unpacked subcharts and suites inside local charts/*.tgz archives are included even when the parent has no suite. Archive evidence binds the original archive digest and a tar: member location (nested archive boundaries use !/). Each traversed subchart must have a regular Chart.yaml; dot/underscore-prefixed chart directories are ignored. Discovery records the selected framework and suite evidence; Helm unittest owns YAML parsing, assertions, test selection and native results. Malformed YAML remains a native test failure, rather than being interpreted by a new Oyzu test language. Detection permits up to 128 suite files and 4096 inspected test/subchart-directory entries across the selected chart tree, at most 16 subchart levels, with bounded source reads. Nonportable paths, symlinked suites/directories and invalid source types fail discovery. For example, chart/tests/deployment_test.yaml can contain: suite: deployment contract templates: - templates/deployment.yaml tests: - it: uses one replica asserts: - equal: path: spec.replicas value: 1 Archive inspection is static and never extracts into the checkout. Archive inputs share the 4 MiB metadata-file bound; expanded archive bytes across one discovery scope are bounded to 64 MiB and 4096 entries, with 16 levels of archive nesting and 128 total suites. One chart root with Chart.yaml is required. Nonregular entries, links, duplicate/case-alias paths, nonportable paths and mixed roots fail. These constraints admit native Helm-generated archives, not arbitrary tar layouts. No test section is added to build.yaml. oyzu run test displays the logical helm unittest --strict <chart> task; its adapter expands packaged subcharts in a private copy before invoking the native plugin. Captured builds run both the independent render/schema validation and native unittest, requesting the plugin's JUnit output. Native subchart behavior remains enabled when the plugin is selected. Test suites remain source inputs; use native .helmignore with tests/ if they should be excluded from the published chart archive. Oyzu does not silently rewrite the chart's packaging rules. Helm can interpret non-chart files beneath charts/ as dependencies. Keep checksum metadata outside that directory or exclude sidecars using native .helmignore, such as charts/*.tgz.sha256. The packaged-only example retains its fixture checksum in source and excludes it from native chart loading/packaging. Its host probe now exercises the exact checked-in chart through lint, rendering, assertions and private dependency preparation, including the sidecar.

Preparation expands contained prepackaged subcharts in its private workspace and captures the chart's contained local file:// dependency closure, rejects cycles/escapes and runs native dependency preparation offline. Existing locks are honored; stale locks fail. Generated lock timestamps and chart archive metadata are normalized. Expansion never overwrites an existing chart directory; ambiguous packed/unpacked copies fail. Prepared layout version 2 records this behavior; regenerate older prepared dependencies. Each source archive remains unchanged in the checkout. The root chart version uses shared version inference over its native version and applicable Git history, with a source-derived snapshot suffix; native appVersion and dependency versions retain their own meanings. The build packages the chart, runs testing, strict lint and read-only YAML formatting, then collects successful outputs. Applications produce a snapshot .tgz and rendered.yaml; libraries produce the snapshot .tgz only. The packaging step renders an application chart itself (helm template --dry-run=client on the packaged chart copy, no cluster), so a build that does not select the test stage, such as plain oyzu build, still writes rendered.yaml; when the test stage runs it rewrites the same file. A failing check prevents final artifact collection. Build-time rendering, generated files and snapshot projection take place in private captured workspaces, leaving the checkout unchanged. Formatting checks the captured source YAML, not the regenerated dependency chart or its projected version. This adds a default gate: previously accepted charts with formatting differences now need explicit formatting or a task override. Shared bundle collection retains reports beneath dist/, and dist/manifest.json records their paths, content digests and parsed summaries: junit.xml records one native render/schema or library-validation check. unittest.xml is required when native suites are selected and retains native test cases, failures and skips. It is independent of the render result. The target's coverage applicability is explicitly inapplicable: chart assertions have no application-source coverage denominator. No synthetic coverage percentage or application coverage file is produced. The manifest also records framework discovery, action outcomes and successful artifact identities. Render success cannot override assertion failure. Missing/invalid required reports, plugin launch failure, native failure and timeout fail testing. Selected unittest execution must produce at least one native test case; a zero-test success is rejected. Stale report files are removed before invocation; prior success cannot satisfy a failed launch. Native validation and unittest each have a 120-second adapter timeout, in addition to executor lifecycle controls. Inspect retained task diagnostics and reports, correct the native suite/toolchain/values or lock input, and rebuild. Shared TOML task replacement and hooks still apply. Replacing a test command does not remove its required report obligations. A replacement that returns zero without producing the required reports fails collection. Inspecting bundle integrity does not certify release eligibility or production trust.

Helm unittest can create missing matchSnapshot baselines even without --update-snapshot. Oyzu unittest execution compares the path/content identities of files under native __snapshot__ directories before and after unittest. Creating, changing or deleting a baseline fails the task and prevents artifact collection. The original native JUnit is retained: it may show a passing assertion while the action fails the baseline-integrity check. Read both action status and reports. Generate or update baselines deliberately using native Helm unittest outside the captured build, review the resulting files and commit them with the suite. Then a matching baseline passes, while a changed rendered value fails normally. Direct oyzu run test now uses the same private-copy baseline check and also rejects creation or alteration. Update baselines deliberately with the native Helm command, not this read-only Oyzu operation. This is a compatibility change from earlier direct task execution; development results still are not captured build evidence. The private test copy is bounded to 100000 entries and 64 MiB of files, excludes .git, .oyzu and dist directories, and rejects links/reparse points. The copy includes the chart tree only; relative references to external files are not transported. Development execution remains a host process, not a filesystem or network sandbox. Captured builds retain the executor's isolation. Archive expansion uses the same 4 MiB compressed/64 MiB expanded bounds and refuses collisions. The baseline inventory rejects symbolic links, unreadable traversal and nonregular baseline files, and bounds scanning to 100000 chart entries, 16 MiB per baseline file and 64 MiB total baseline contents. Exceeding these limits fails the task. This checks persistent baseline changes; it is not a general filesystem write monitor.

python tooling/test-helm-reporting.py --helm <provisioned-helm> --cli <compiled-oyzu> python tooling/test-helm-archive.py python tooling/test-helm-quality.py --cli <compiled-oyzu> --yamlfmt <provisioned-yamlfmt> The native reporting probe exercises static CLI listing with an empty PATH, successful and failed native assertions (including subchart-only suites), malformed suites, independent render/schema results, library validation, missing-tool stale-output rejection, missing snapshot creation, matching reviewed baselines and native snapshot mismatches. Packaged-only native probes passed real assertions and failures, unchanged source archives, declared local archive dependencies, empty-suite rejection and read-only baseline handling on Windows. Static archive tests cover nested evidence and rejected unsafe/oversized inputs; these new captured scenarios await Linux CI. Rust tests cover discovery, dependency containment, planning, required report declarations and fixed plugin location. CI captured-build cases additionally require snapshot chart/rendered artifacts, manifest evidence, unchanged source and artifact rejection after assertion or baseline-integrity failure; root-suite/baseline cases passed run 36967080170 at 51464a9; the newer subchart-only assertions still require CI confirmation. See implementation status for revision-specific results. The compiled-CLI quality probe checks implicit task metadata, native read-only checks, explicit formatting, unchanged templates/baselines, invalid YAML, ambient configuration isolation, custom-config rejection and task overrides against authored charts. It is wired into the three-host task jobs. The captured Helm suite additionally requires a successful format action and proves unformatted values block artifact collection without changing source; this new gate awaits Linux CI evidence. The earlier chart/assertion scenarios, including packaged subcharts, passed Linux job 110767008279 in run 36983990838, resolving the earlier pending subchart acceptance above. Automatic discovery of custom suite globs, templated test charts and suites in unprepared sibling file:// dependencies remains unfinished.
