Static discovery follows unpacked chart directories and inspects local chart archives already present under the selected chart; it does not extract archives or acquire dependencies. Image bindings support single-manifest OCI archives with the Windows qualification recorded above; multi-platform OCI index binding is unsupported, and Linux/macOS host and multi-variant matrix qualification remain unverified. Other plugins, remote/OCI chart dependency acquisition, Go-template formatting, native formatter customization, publishing/signing and broader platform execution remain required work. These limitations do not change the full builder/scenario objective.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/installer-recipes.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Some packages download extra files while they install or run: Puppeteer downloads a browser, node-gyp downloads Node.js headers. A captured build runs without network, so those downloads fail. For a package Oyzu recognises, the builder downloads the matching file during preparation and points the tool at it through the tool's own settings. The project declares nothing. Status: experimental and provisional. This answers the "known recipes" open decision of the declared fetches design for the Node builder. The choices marked provisional below need maintainer review. Recipes have unit tests and a registered compiled-CLI check, which have not been run yet (see verification).

A recipe is a table owned by the builder: a recognised package, the asset URL for its locked version, a SHA-256 pinned in the repository, and the settings and cache layout the tool reads. Recipes reuse the declared fetches engine, with no second download path: After the package manager's captured preparation, the Node builder reads the locked packages, the verified registry archives and the captured Node version. For each recognised package it looks up the pinned asset. A version or platform without a pinned asset is reported (below) and nothing is guessed. Each asset is admitted against fetches.sources, downloaded through the broker, verified against the pinned digest, stored by digest under <user data>/cache/fetches/ and unpacked under recipes/<recipe>/ in the prepared tree, in the tool's own layout. Execution sees the prepared tree read-only at /dependencies. Every command action (install, tasks and package) gets the recipe's settings, so the install script skips its download and the tool finds the asset at run time. Recipes apply to captured Node builds, which is oyzu build --isolated. A native host build runs with network and downloads as the package intends.

Recognised Every locked version of the registry package puppeteer, in npm, pnpm or Yarn locks Assets Chrome for Testing chrome and chrome-headless-shell for linux64, at the build Puppeteer pins for that release URL https://storage.googleapis.com/chrome-for-testing-public/<build>/linux64/<browser>-linux64.zip Layout recipes/puppeteer/<browser>/linux-<build>/<browser>-linux64/, Puppeteer's cache layout Settings PUPPETEER_CACHE_DIR=/dependencies/recipes/puppeteer, PUPPETEER_SKIP_DOWNLOAD=true Pinned Puppeteer releases 24.0.0 to 25.13.0, in puppeteer.tsv Puppeteer's install script reads PUPPETEER_SKIP_DOWNLOAD and does not try the network. puppeteer.launch() and puppeteer.executablePath() read PUPPETEER_CACHE_DIR and resolve the browser for their own pinned build, so the project needs no change. Both browsers are delivered because Puppeteer's install script downloads both by default. Firefox is skipped by Puppeteer by default and has no recipe. Limits: Only linux/amd64 workers are pinned. Chrome for Testing has no Linux arm64 build before Chrome 153, and on other platforms the log reports that the browser is not pinned. A Puppeteer configuration file or variable that selects another browser build (PUPPETEER_CHROME_VERSION, chrome.version in .puppeteerrc) or another cache directory overrides the recipe for that setting, and the install fails offline. The toolchain image omits the system libraries Chrome needs to start (libnss3 and others). The recipe delivers the browser; a build that launches it needs an image that has them.

Recognised A locked registry package whose archive has a top-level binding.gyp, or a binding.gyp in the project root. Native install compiles these with node-gyp Asset node-v<version>-headers.tar.gz for the captured Node version URL https://nodejs.org/dist/v<version>/node-v<version>-headers.tar.gz Layout recipes/node-gyp/<version>/node-v<version>/include/node/ Settings npm_config_nodedir=/dependencies/recipes/node-gyp/<version>/node-v<version> Pinned Node.js 18.0.0 to 26.11.1, in node-headers.tsv node-gyp reads npm_config_nodedir and uses those headers instead of downloading them. The scripts npm, pnpm and Yarn run inherit the variable. The headers are not enough on their own: compiling an addon also needs Python, make and a C++ compiler in the image, and the default toolchain image has none. Addons that download a prebuilt binary first (prebuild-install, node-pre-gyp) still fail offline unless they fall back to compiling. The authored npm-node-gyp-consumer fixture prepares a root Node-API addon with no package dependencies. Its native tests and standalone exported-addon consumer are written, not executed. Qualification must use a separately provisioned compiler/Python image through the existing build --image npm=<image> override, retaining the normal header recipe, network-denied execution and report gates. A Linux addon must be consumed in a matching Linux runtime; a Windows host Node process cannot establish that proof. The install analyzer now records the root binding.gyp probe and retains the existing unbounded lifecycle scope when npm implicitly runs node-gyp rebuild; see builder-owned stages. Its focused regressions and native proof remain unrun. This preserves native installation semantics without adding an explicit install script to the fixture. The registered node-gyp-recipe acceptance check supplies the original fixture's exact Node request and tool lock, without a handcrafted dependency lock. It requires a real compiled addon and three native tests with JUnit/coverage, then extracts only the inspected archive's regular addon/wrapper/results files into a separate dependency-free consumer project. A second captured build executes that consumer in the selected Linux image, runs three additional native tests and packages its actual consumed.json. Both builds retain full quality gates, source/tool-lock equality and bundle inspection. Each temporary project selects its explicit fixture root, avoiding unrelated ancestor configuration. This flow remains unrun: oyzu exec --store <verified-tool-store> -- python tooling/test-build-scenarios.py --suite node --only node-gyp-recipe --store <verified-tool-store> --image npm=<provisioned-native-image> --cli <compiled-oyzu-path> --evidence-dir <task-evidence-directory>

Preparation continues and the build log shows one fact per recipe, for example: Recipe puppeteer puppeteer@25.14.0 has no pinned Chrome for Testing build in this Oyzu release; its install script will try to download one Preparation does not fail, because the project may already avoid the download with the tool's own settings. Otherwise the install then fails as described next.
documents.s: When a package is recognised but not pinned

documents.t: When a captured npm install fails because a lifecycle script could not reach the network, the error names the package, the URL and the remedy, where npm's output shows them: DEPENDENCY_INPUT_MISSING: the install script of cypress@13.6.0 tried to download https://download.cypress.io/desktop.json, and captured execution has no network. Oyzu has no recipe for this asset. Declare it as a pinned fetch in build.yaml (name, url, sha256) and point the package at OYZU_FETCH_<NAME> through its own setting; see the declared fetches reference. The original npm output follows the message. The package comes from npm's npm error path line and the URL from the script's output on the host named by its network error (getaddrinfo EAI_AGAIN, ENOTFOUND, connect ENETUNREACH, EHOSTUNREACH, ECONNREFUSED or Could not resolve host). Without a URL the host is named; without a network error the npm failure is reported unchanged. This diagnosis covers npm installs; pnpm and Yarn report their native error. For the root package, npm reports the effective build version applied by version inference, which may differ from the source manifest's version. The acceptance check compares that exact published identity alongside the URL and declared-fetch remedy. To supply such an asset yourself, add a declared fetch and set the tool's own variable to its path in the target environment. For Puppeteer on an unpinned release, for example, fetch the Chrome for Testing zip with unpack: zip and set PUPPETEER_SKIP_DOWNLOAD=true and PUPPETEER_EXECUTABLE_PATH=/dependencies/fetches/<name>/chrome-linux64/chrome.

Spotless steps backed by Eclipse formatters (<eclipse>, <greclipse>, <eclipseWtp> and <eclipseCdt> in the Maven plugin, and their Gradle equivalents) provision Eclipse P2 bundles from download.eclipse.org at run time, into Spotless's own P2 cache rather than a file path. There is no JVM recipe, and a declared fetch cannot be pointed at that cache. In a captured Maven build spotless-maven-plugin:check fails during preparation with java.net.UnknownHostException: download.eclipse.org (observed for assertj/assertj in the captured-feasibility corpus). Recovery: run that Spotless check outside the captured build, or keep the Eclipse step out of the captured lifecycle, for example with a Maven profile that sets spotless.check.skip=true.

Every recipe asset has a SHA-256 in an in-repo table. A download whose bytes do not match fails with INTEGRITY_MISMATCH and stores nothing. Oyzu never takes a digest from the network at build time (no trust on first use). Chrome for Testing publishes no checksums. Each digest was computed from the downloaded zip after its bytes matched the MD5 that Google Cloud Storage reports for the object (x-goog-hash), and its size matched. The build list comes from PUPPETEER_REVISIONS in each puppeteer-core release. Node.js headers digests come from each release's SHASUMS256.txt and were checked against the downloaded bytes. The signature of SHASUMS256.txt was not checked when the table was written. The snapshot records each asset as a package with verification: digest-only: the bytes match the pinned digest, but no publisher signature was checked. tooling/refresh-node-recipes.py regenerates both tables with the same checks; review the diff before committing.

Each asset becomes a package in the target's dependency snapshot: Field Value id recipe:<target>/<recipe>/<asset>/<version>, for example recipe:web/puppeteer/chrome/136.0.7103.94 name, version The asset name (chrome, chrome-headless-shell, node-headers) and its upstream version sourceId fetch:<host> standalone, or fetches.sources/<index> under an allowlist digest, size The verified bytes purpose, verification build, digest-only The extension oyzu.dev/recipes lists each applied recipe with the packages it serves, its settings and each asset's path and tree digest. Both are part of the snapshot digest, so the plan binds the delivered assets.

Recipe assets use the declared fetch errors. The label names the recipe, the asset and the package, for example web: puppeteer recipe asset chrome 136.0.7103.94 for puppeteer@24.9.0. Code Cause Recovery SOURCE_DENIED An administrative fetches.sources does not admit the asset's host Ask an administrator to admit it, such as https://storage.googleapis.com/chrome-for-testing-public/ INTEGRITY_MISMATCH The upstream bytes differ from the pinned digest Report it; do not edit the table without checking the upstream release DEPENDENCY_INPUT_MISSING An offline build needs an asset that is not stored, or an install script without a recipe tried the network Run one online build, or declare the asset as above

These need maintainer review: Recipes apply automatically to every captured Node build that locks a recognised package. There is no setting to turn one off yet. The digest tables live in the repository and cover a fixed range of releases. A newer release needs a table update and an Oyzu release. A recognised package without a pinned asset is a build-log fact, not a preparation failure. Recipe settings override the same variable from the builder plan, and a variable delivered twice (for example by a recipe and a declared fetch) fails. fetches.sources governs recipes as well as declared fetches.

The first functional proof combines the compiled CLI's ordinary captured build of the unchanged npm installer fixture with a separate native companion project, preserving each project's source and lock bytes during execution. Preparation must acquire and verify both pinned Puppeteer browsers through the existing broker; the network-denied install and build must produce an inspected, independently usable artifact. Dependency evidence must identify the two browser assets and their effective cache settings. An expected unsupported refusal alone does not establish this successful flow. A second required flow compiles and consumes a native node-gyp addon using the captured headers and an explicitly identified compiler/Python runtime. This establishes recipe reuse beyond browser delivery. Browser startup remains a separate functional obligation when a browser-executing project is selected; the existing missing-system-library limitation is not silently waived. Keep additional hosts and architecture qualification separate from these bounded Linux/amd64 flows. Unit tests cover the pinned tables, Puppeteer and node-gyp recognition from captured facts, unpinned versions and platforms, recipe capture, offline reuse, digest mismatch and allowlist denial (dependencies::fetches and builders::node::recipes), and the install diagnosis (node --test tooling/test-install-diagnosis.mjs). The installer-recipes check in the node suite builds tooling/fixtures/npm-installer-recipes (puppeteer 24.9.0, esbuild and sharp) with oyzu build --isolated, checks source and tool-lock preservation and inspects the bundle. It retains the diagnosis for an unrecognised download. Its native npm exclusion and build-only scripts remain unchanged; this baseline alone cannot establish artifact/report acceptance. The separately selectable installer-recipes-consumer check uses npm-installer-consumer sources. Before the source snapshot, the harness derives its package manifest from the original and adds only ordinary native packaging/build/test declarations. It copies the original exact dependency/tool locks, tool request and ignore file. Its name, version and dependencies match the lock's root; no lock regeneration or second tracked dependency declaration is needed. Native files: ["dist"] declares packaging intent. Native esbuild compiles a TypeScript module and sharp generates a PNG; Node's three tests consume those outputs and check both prepared browser executables. The existing full_checks wrapper selects real test/lint/format stages and required JUnit/coverage collection. Acceptance requires the inspected npm archive to deliver the module, PNG and dist/results.json. The standalone consume.mjs executable runs in a separate Node process selected through oyzu exec and imports the exported module, reads the PNG signature/dimensions and checks the four successful recipe results, without project dependencies or the private build workspace. Reports must come from the actual native tests; no XML is fabricated. Neither check starts a browser or proves node-gyp compilation. The separately selected puppeteer-startup follow-up adds a real native Node test that calls Puppeteer's prepared headless-shell executable, evaluates a local page to 42, captures a 64-by-32 PNG and waits for the browser to exit. It requests Puppeteer's default sandbox, checks that neither --no-sandbox nor --disable-setuid-sandbox was supplied, and fails rather than skips when native libraries or sandbox prerequisites are missing. Absence of bypass flags is not a general browser-confinement qualification. This check derives its native manifest from the same original installer fixture, reuses its exact dependency/tool locks and copies the completed companion's build/tests without changing those originals. Existing full_checks plus the isolated invocation select genuine native JUnit/coverage and quality gates. All four tests must pass, including the actual browser test, before packaging. The exported npm archive must contain the rendered HTML, screenshot and receipt in addition to the companion's original module/PNG/results. Independent built-in-only Node consumers check only files extracted from that final archive; they do not launch a host browser. Browser execution belongs to the captured producer, not these output-consumption checks. The focused invocation is: oyzu exec --store <verified-tool-store> -- python tooling/test-build-scenarios.py --suite node --only puppeteer-startup --store <verified-tool-store> --image npm=<qualified-browser-image> --cli <compiled-oyzu-path> --evidence-dir <new-evidence-directory> Supply an explicitly qualified Linux/amd64 image with a matching compiled worker, the existing Node quality tooling, Chrome's native libraries and working default browser sandbox support under the ordinary executor. No image is provisioned or security setting changed by this check. The standard missing-library boundary above remains; this authored check has not yet established a passing browser startup. See the startup qualification checkpoint. With managed Python, harness requirements and the Linux Docker worker available, the focused command from the repository root is: oyzu exec --store <verified-tool-store> -- python tooling/test-build-scenarios.py --suite node --only installer-recipes-consumer --store <verified-tool-store> --cli <compiled-oyzu-path> --evidence-dir <task-evidence-directory> The bounded Windows-controller/Linux-amd64 flows are now demonstrated. The unchanged original fixture passed its four build-only actions and inspection; the genuine unknown download produced the package, effective version, URL and pinned-fetch remedy. The separate companion passed all seven native actions, three tests, coverage, full quality gates and inspection, and an independent Oyzu-managed Node process consumed its delivered module, PNG and results. All source inputs and locks remained unchanged. Earlier failed registered summaries remain failed; detailed corrections are in qualification. The registered node-gyp-recipe also passed end to end with a verified compiler/Python task image. It compiled the addon offline using captured Node 22.23.3 headers, packaged the regular ELF addon and transferred only the exported payload to a second Linux captured project. Both builds passed seven native actions, three genuine tests each, wrapper LCOV, full quality gates, packaging and inspection. The independent consumer loaded the addon and packaged its consumption result. All nine original inputs and the tool lock stayed unchanged in each project. Node LCOV covers the JavaScript wrapper; C is not instrumented. With the same prerequisites, select that check and explicit provisioned image: oyzu exec --store <verified-tool-store> -- python tooling/test-build-scenarios.py --suite node --only node-gyp-recipe --store <verified-tool-store> --image npm=<linux-amd64-image-IID> --cli <compiled-oyzu-path> --evidence-dir <task-evidence-directory> Rust formatting, managed Python/JavaScript syntax, registration, tool-contract shape/schema and documentation checks pass. The isolated full workspace Rust rerun passed with 1,819 tests passed, zero failed and 37 ignored, including all 17 previously failing tests. The original failure and its test-only/launcher corrections remain recorded in qualification. Strict workspace/all-target Clippy also passes with warnings treated as errors. All nine reported real CLI development-task behaviors pass against the paired candidate, including Windows native launchers. The fresh-checkout proof is unavailable on this Windows host because its explicit platform guard supports Linux/macOS only. Unix host confinement, browser startup and wider platforms remain unproved. A Windows controller does not qualify Windows workers; macOS workers are not covered. Native candidate records do not establish exact Git-to-compiler byte binding or release provenance. See the qualification record for the actual commands, image and artifact identities, preserved failures and verification limits.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/java-quality.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Maven, Gradle and Ant targets expose lint, format-check and format without project configuration. These experimental defaults use native Checkstyle 10.21.4 and google-java-format 1.28.0. The shared Java adapter owns file selection and native invocation; the existing task engine owns overrides, hooks, ordering and failure propagation. oyzu run list oyzu run lint oyzu run format-check oyzu run format oyzu build Use target-qualified names such as api:lint in a multi-target workspace. Static discovery requires no Java tools and records the selected fallback linter/formatter. Execution requires provisioned tools. lint and format-check are implicit build stages; format is explicitly mutating and is never automatically added to the build. Failed quality gates block final artifact collection. Available native test and coverage evidence remains in dist/manifest.json; quality diagnostics live in action logs rather than fabricated JUnit or coverage reports.

Tool installation remains outside the implemented CLI scope. For development, provision a JDK 17 or newer and the quality tools explicitly: python tooling/provision-java-quality.py --destination /absolute/path/java-quality Oyzu does not provision these tools itself yet, so oyzu build --full on a fresh checkout stops at lint and format-check with a message that names Checkstyle, google-java-format, the provisioning command and the alternatives (replace the task in oyzu.toml, or build without --full); the build artifacts are withheld, as for any failed quality gate. The provisioner owns the exact versions and checksums. The JDK itself is prepared automatically (Java installation). Native provisioning of the quality tools is deferred: it needs a non-archive tool kind and review of Checkstyle's LGPL terms. Set OYZU_JAVA_QUALITY_HOME to that absolute directory and put the JDK's java executable on PATH. In PowerShell, use $env:OYZU_JAVA_QUALITY_HOME = 'E:\tools\java-quality'; in POSIX shells, use export OYZU_JAVA_QUALITY_HOME=/absolute/path/java-quality. The provisioner downloads checksum-pinned upstream JARs and copies the owned Java launcher and lint defaults. It retains complete upstream archives with their embedded licenses/notices and records source URLs. Python is needed for provisioning and verification, but development quality tasks themselves require only the JDK and provisioned files. Missing or relative tool homes, missing tools, invalid Java, tool failures and extra forwarded arguments fail explicitly. Correct the prerequisite or source and rerun; the checks never repair source automatically. The Maven, Gradle and Ant Dockerfiles provision the same tools at /opt/oyzu-java-quality. Build all three images from the repository root, including Ant and Gradle whose build context previously used tooling/images: docker build -f tooling/images/builder-worker.Dockerfile -t oyzu-toolchain/builder-worker:v1 . docker build -f tooling/images/maven.Dockerfile -t oyzu-toolchain/maven:3.9.11-jdk17 . docker build -f tooling/images/gradle.Dockerfile -t oyzu-toolchain/gradle:8.14.3-jdk17 . docker build -f tooling/images/ant.Dockerfile -t oyzu-toolchain/ant:1.10.18-jdk17 . Rebuild older images with these tags. Custom images must supply the matching JDK, JARs and checks.xml at the fixed tool home. Captured builds use the adapter embedded in the CLI, and the planner protects this tool-home setting from task environment replacement. Development tasks use the adapter copied during explicit provisioning; reprovision after adapter updates. Build execution does not download these tools or consult user-home caches. Image provisioning is an explicit online preparation step; quality actions run inside the existing network-disabled build sandbox. Host oyzu run tasks are ordinary development execution, not a claim of isolation. The previous google-java-format 1.24.0 profile fails on JDK 25 with NoSuchMethodError for Log$DeferredDiagnosticHandler.getDiagnostics. Version 1.28.0 includes upstream handling for the changed javac diagnostics API. Reprovision development tools and rebuild the affected Maven, Gradle and Ant images to replace the old JAR; changing the CLI alone does not replace provisioned tools. The updated profile passed the Linux host quality probe for all three builders on native JDK 17.0.20.1 and 25.0.4.1, plus a captured Maven reactor's full quality gates; exact source/runtime attribution and limits are recorded separately. Genuine lint or formatting findings still fail their quality gates and block artifacts.

The lint defaults check unused imports, redundant imports, empty statements and equals/hashCode consistency. Checkstyle owns parsing and rule evaluation. google-java-format owns formatting and import normalization. format-check invokes its native dry-run and nonzero-on-change flags; format invokes native replacement. See the upstream formatter CLI and Checkstyle CLI for their native behavior. Each task selects .java files recursively beneath its target, including custom source roots, reactor modules and included builds within that tree. It skips directories named .git, .oyzu, .oyzu-build, .oyzu-maven, .gradle, .idea, target, build, dist, out, node_modules and .venv. These exclusions apply at every depth. The adapter does not guess arbitrary native output directories or distinguish generated files outside these exclusions. Projects that put authored source in an excluded directory, require narrower scopes or own a different formatting style should define explicit native task replacements. Inventory is sorted, bounded to 200,000 visited entries and 16 MiB per Java file, and does not follow symbolic links. Encountering a link outside excluded names fails instead of silently reading outside the target. Native invocations are batched within a 16,000-character argument allowance; any failed batch fails the operation. No candidate files produces an explicit not-applicable diagnostic, not invented source evidence. Build checks operate on the private workspace and do not modify the checkout. Explicit development formatting changes selected files in place and is not transactional: a later malformed file can leave earlier files formatted.

Native Ant lint, format-check and format targets take precedence over corresponding defaults. Existing TOML task replacements and pre/post hooks work through the shared task system. For example, a project that already owns Gradle quality tasks can replace the defaults: [tasks.lint] argv = ["gradle", "--no-daemon", "checkstyleMain", "checkstyleTest"] [tasks.format-check] argv = ["gradle", "--no-daemon", "spotlessCheck"] [tasks.format] argv = ["gradle", "--no-daemon", "spotlessApply"] Those task names and plugins must actually exist in the project; these examples do not provision them. Use ./gradlew or gradlew.bat if the project uses its native wrapper. Replacement tasks must remain compatible with the captured offline toolchain when used in builds. The default launcher rejects extra arguments, including attempts to pass --replace to format-check; put native flags in an explicit replacement instead. This increment does not yet infer Maven quality-plugin bindings, Gradle quality tasks, arbitrary Checkstyle XML/suppression files, Kotlin/Groovy quality tools or per-module formatter differences. Configured checks still run through their native build lifecycle, and can coexist with the defaults; use replacements when their rules differ. It is not a claim of full Java scenario acceptance or all Java language versions.

python tooling/test-java-quality.py --cli <compiled-oyzu> --tools <quality-home> exercises real native tools through the CLI without Maven, Gradle or Ant execution. Earlier Windows/JDK 17 verification with google-java-format 1.24.0 passed task discovery without tools, native lint and formatting failures, unchanged source during checks, explicit formatting, custom source directories, output exclusions, missing prerequisites and task replacements. These historical results do not qualify the updated formatter. CI runs this probe on Windows, macOS and Linux after compiling the CLI. For the updated 1.28.0 profile, the same host probe passed on Linux for Maven, Gradle and Ant targets with --java-version 17 (native 17.0.20.1) and --java-version 25.0.4 (native 25.0.4.1). It verifies the actual runtime satisfies the managed release/feature request. Positive checks, deliberate native lint/format failures, explicit formatting, task replacements, source boundaries and missing-prerequisite checks all passed. This is quality-task execution, not execution of each builder's native lifecycle. A separate captured Maven reactor with selected locked Java 25.0.4 and formatter 1.28.0 passed all five full-profile actions, two native JUnit tests and per-module JaCoCo reporting, producing five exports without changing its eight tracked files. Compiled inspection passed, and a fresh offline consumer mounted only its two delivered JARs and printed Hello, Oyzu!. The original JUnit4 corpus full build remains failed; its separate successful default build and delivered-JAR consumer retain their original attribution. The broader captured suite's lint/format negative cases and Gradle/Ant captured profiles remain separate qualification; host checks do not establish them. Track results in implementation status.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/local-builds.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The current implementation connects host-native Cargo, Go applications, npm dist applications and pip wheel builds to the local development proposal. Qualification is recorded by scenario in the tool user-flow record. Do not interpret the commands below as completed qualification of every platform or build mode. The host coordinator also admits existing captured docker/image workers, with per-target placement shown by --plan. See image workers and qualification limits. Host processes remain unrestricted; worker enforcement does not extend to the entire graph. BuildKit actions supervise both the docker exec client and the worker. A nonzero client exit reports BUILDKIT_BUILDCTL_FAILED; a stopped, OOM-killed or unreachable worker reports BUILDKIT_WORKER_UNAVAILABLE. Container state and daemon probes run every five seconds with individual two-second deadlines; the final check runs immediately when the client exits. An observed stopped or OOM-killed container fails immediately. Failed inspection or daemon probes need three consecutive failures; a successful check resets the count. A dead daemon therefore does not wait for the action timeout. Diagnostics retain the buildctl exit code/signal when available, container exit and memory limit. State.OOMKilled confirms OOM; exit 137 alone is reported as possible OOM or external SIGKILL. If the Docker client is still stuck, its exit is explicitly unavailable. Cleanup has a separate five-second bound. Retry after restoring the worker or providing enough memory; failed actions do not publish artifacts.

oyzu pin --dry-run previews requirements and lock changes without installing native tools or changing project files. For a new project or a version-1 resolution lock it resolves compiler metadata; --offline requires matching cached metadata. oyzu pin publishes complete resolutions, with conflicts and incomplete inputs reported as failures. See tool planning. All project locks use one version-1 contract. pin resolves requirements whether or not installation records already exist, and preserves those records when publishing resolutions. Incomplete resolution leaves the lock unchanged. Build preflight installs missing supported pinned tools; native host prerequisites still require external provisioning. Pinning itself does not install tools. When a selected builder admits automatic tool resolution and the project has no oyzu.lock, native build preflight resolves its requirements and publishes the lock without editing authored TOML. It captures the published lock before installing and activating the exact selection for native actions. This uses the normal acquisition verification and installation leases; an ambient compiler is not required for supported managed tool requirements. Existing locks remain frozen: incompatible or missing selections require an explicit pin update rather than silently resolving during execution. Captured build --offline never automatically resolves tool metadata or publishes pins, including when an existing lock has no tool records. It retains the selected targets and reports the applicable preparation failure without rewriting that lock. Offline preparation requires the existing metadata, archive or installation needed by the selected provider. The empty-store qualification and current platform limits are recorded in the fresh-checkout record. The initial adapter covers Rust: rust-toolchain.toml or the legacy rust-toolchain file, Cargo package/workspace rust-version minimums, declared components/targets/profile, and the tools/components required by the existing native build/test/lint/format stages. Every toolchain-file form rustup accepts is read; see Rust toolchain files. A file without channel keeps its components and uses the configured or default Rust; a local path toolchain fails resolution unless oyzu.toml selects a release. Both toolchain filenames together are an error. In the discovery inventory, no toolchain declaration means Rust is reported without a selected version; a build then locks the greatest stable release (pinning is optional). That inventory reports effective Oyzu tool settings separately without claiming resolution. The resolver resolves those inputs through the tool-planning contract described above. Each fact includes its source; repeated facts retain their sources. System linker/SDK requirements are explicit. Windows discovery uses the declared toolchain channel: windows-gnullvm identifies LLVM-MinGW UCRT, Clang linking and a Rust profiler runtime; windows-msvc identifies Microsoft Build Tools and the Windows SDK. A windows-gnu declaration explicitly calls for a coverage-capable alternative. An unqualified channel such as 1.95.0 lists GNU/LLVM and supported MSVC as alternatives, rather than assuming the user's rustup default. This static discovery does not run rustup, inspect PATH or install Windows components. Dependency build-script requirements, compiler/profile compatibility and inherited parent-directory toolchain files are not inferred in this slice. Node requirements are also resolved through the shared tool contract. For the native pip wheel path, CPython is resolved from requires-python or .python-version and installed from Python Build Standalone (details); uv, Poetry and legacy Python tools are not provisioned. Other unsupported requirements remain explicit. The command works offline in standalone mode; existing configuration loading and managed policy rules still apply. Pinning currently requires the workspace root. On 2026-10-03 the compiled discovery implementation inspected this checkout's requirements with PATH empty. Two integration tests passed for toolchain-free inspection, unchanged lock bytes and conflicting manifest rejection. Other hosts are unverified. Discovery evidence is available in pin JSON alongside the resolution preview. It is not installed-tool evidence. Unsupported prerelease lock versions are rejected; no legacy decoder or automatic migration is provided. Existing tool stores are left intact. See the lock contract.

Native Rust compilation retains compiler state under the original project's .oyzu/native/rust/<host>/, while source compilation runs in a private target projection. The Rust builder explicitly identifies its absolute cache and inventory arguments as host paths, including the separate test cache when quality stages are selected. These exact arguments retain their host locations even when a project is rooted under /workspace/, /out/ or /oyzu/. Captured workspace, output and runtime paths still translate into the source projection, report output and engine runtime. Path declarations do not relax native cache, binary inventory or artifact containment checks. Isolated execution reuses completed read-only tool restorations (Docker volumes or daemonless directories) under the existing restoration locks. A completed restoration is trusted as an installed tool, so reuse does not hash its source archive again. A new restoration verifies the archive before worker launch/extraction; incomplete restoration is never a hit. This does not change archive acquisition checks or current tool/catalog admission. Native Rust builds infer snapshot artifact versions through the same resolver as captured builds. Each member keeps its package scope and tag baseline, augmented by the declared target prerequisite closure. For local fast builds in the development profile, with no output distribution, Cargo retains declared package versions so a source edit does not invalidate every workspace member's incremental compiler identity. CARGO_PKG_VERSION is the declared version in this mode; each version decision records it as compiledVersion, alongside the source-specific inferred artifact version. Artifact metadata and action keys remain source-specific. Action keys also bind the actual compiled package versions, so a local result cannot satisfy a version-stamped build with the same source and selected stages. Applications must not assume the local development compiled version equals the artifact coordinate; use build evidence for it. Full/CI, explicit tags/conventional version strategies, optimized, handed-off, remotely cached, packaged and release builds continue projecting inferred versions into private manifests: their compiled CARGO_PKG_VERSION matches the inferred artifact version. --no-optimized does not disable stamping for distributed outputs. Cargo reconciles the private lock offline and preserves locked external packages. Executable filenames retain their native names. The original manifests and Cargo/tool locks remain unchanged. Conflicts and missing offline dependencies fail preparation with recovery guidance. This new Rust projection passes the Windows three-application pair with and without a declared producer edge, including native reports and independent compiled-version execution. This does not qualify other hosts or all native profiles; see version inference. This fixes issue #384, where an absolute host cache was mistaken for a captured /workspace/ mount and compilation failed with COMMAND_FAILED: No such file or directory after successful preparation. Retry the same native build with the corrected CLI; no project configuration or cache migration is required. python tooling/test-native-host-paths.py --cli <compiled-oyzu> --parent <writable-directory> checks two native binaries, repeat compilation, bundle inspection and unchanged source/configuration files. Use a parent under /workspace/ to exercise the original collision; --full additionally checks native quality-stage cache paths with provisioned test/coverage tools. This does not qualify captured builds or other operating systems.
documents.s: Host cache paths and source projections

documents.t: Native Rust builds now check the selected environment with a temporary, dependency-free Cargo compile-and-link probe before compiling project code. The probe honors Cargo linker configuration and Rust flags; selected test stages also request coverage instrumentation. Success verifies this basic capability, not every library needed by dependency build scripts. Temporary probe files are removed after success or failure. No OS components are installed. oyzu run performs the same probe before starting a Rust task that compiles or links (cargo build, test, install, check, clippy, doc, run, rustc), once per target and after tool preparation. Tasks that compile nothing, such as cargo fetch, skip it. Without a linker the task fails in under a second with the guidance below instead of a raw compiler error; a windows-gnullvm toolchain is told to put LLVM-MinGW's bin directory on PATH. Oyzu does not install LLVM-MinGW. A failure reports EXECUTOR_PREREQUISITE_UNAVAILABLE with the native cause and external provisioning guidance. Correct the selected toolchain/linker/SDK and rerun. Discovery and pinning remain static and report availability as not checked; only actual preflight executes the probe. Managed tools and executor prerequisites are separate categories in the inventory. Compile-only inventory omits automatic quality-stage helpers; explicitly declared components remain requirements. This check currently covers native Rust execution. It does not introduce remote executor probes, arbitrary system-package detection or OS provisioning. A ready host capability is not a claim of hermeticity or publication eligibility. Plain oyzu build selects native development execution when every selected target is native-eligible (Rust, Go, Gradle, Maven, npm node/app and pip Python, plus admitted image workers). Other builder/workspace shapes retain their existing captured behavior. oyzu build --isolated explicitly uses the existing captured container executor; --image also retains that path. --affected computes its selection first and then follows the same native-eligibility rules as a plain build, falling back to the captured path only where a plain build would. A failed native or isolated build never retries through another executor. CI detection does not change this selection. Plain local builds need pinned Rust/Cargo and provisioned native compilation prerequisites. Preflight verifies or installs the pinned tools before native dependency preparation. Declared platform relationships and target selection are validated before automatic pinning acquires tool metadata or publishes a lock. Invalid or ambiguous matrix relationships therefore fail without starting tool provisioning. Quality stages additionally need their tools: rustfmt for formatting, Clippy for linting, and nextest, cargo-llvm-cov and the compiler's LLVM tools/profiler runtime for tests with coverage. The Rust test prerequisites describe report tooling. Native dependency preparation first checks the Cargo cache and acquires missing locked inputs when online, as described below. The existing historical Windows coverage qualification includes the MSVC toolchain/linker/SDK. The locally provisioned windows-gnu 1.95 compiler failed a coverage probe with missing profiler_builtins on 2026-10-03. A separate Rust 1.95 x86_64-pc-windows-gnullvm experiment on 2026-10-04 passed two tiny-project tests through cargo-llvm-cov 0.9.1 and nextest 0.9.146, producing a Cobertura report with five of six lines covered using LLVM-MinGW UCRT 20260616 and Clang linking. The compiled CLI also passed oyzu run test on that probe; oyzu inspect dist confirmed both tests and the same collected coverage counts. This required no Microsoft Build Tools installation. It proves direct test and coverage execution, not the complete Oyzu self-build or automatic tool provisioning. The full Oyzu checkout also passed cargo check --locked --offline --bin oyzu with GNU/LLVM, Clang and native CMake/Ninja; final executable linking was not tested by that check. Coverage remains required when the test/coverage stage is selected; plain local compilation does not select it automatically. The native path builds development-profile binaries unless the build is optimized: oyzu build --optimized, build.optimized = true, or a build whose artifacts leave the machine (a slice, a shared remote cache write, a packaging target, the release context) runs cargo build --release instead; see optimized builds. Tests keep Cargo's test profile. Plain local oyzu build automatically schedules compilation and any check at level required. oyzu build --full, the pr, ci and release contexts or the CI profile also schedule test/JUnit/coverage/doctest integration, Clippy and read-only formatting checks, except those whose check level is off. Required checks, hooks and task prerequisites remain enforced in fast mode. Binaries are collected only after the selected stages succeed. oyzu run test, oyzu run lint and oyzu run format-check remain explicit task entry points. Native build overrides are currently rejected with an explicit diagnostic. Ordinary hooks and task prerequisites use the shared task graph. Required configuration checks remain enforced; unsupported managed host execution fails before native preparation. This repository sets Cargo's development and test profiles to debug = 0, omitting generated debug information while retaining debug assertions. The development profile optimizes the direct SHA-256 dependency (sha2 0.10.9) at level 3; the test profile inherits that package override. Oyzu's own code and other dependencies retain their existing optimization settings. This reduces the CPU cost of full tool-payload and evidence hashing without caching or skipping verification. Dependency upgrades must keep this version-specific override aligned with the direct sha2 dependency. Release settings are unchanged. Windows worker tests relaunch their own test executable; embedded debug information previously grew that executable beyond the worker's 512 MiB image limit and caused TOOL_WORKER_IMAGE_INVALID before launch. Source-level debugger information is unavailable in these default builds. Profile overrides that restore debug information can reintroduce this failure; rebuild with the repository defaults to recover. The image limit, integrity checks, test/report gates and scenario timeouts remain unchanged. Other projects retain their own native Cargo profile settings. --all-platforms requests the declared matrix through the existing captured executor; it requires its provisioned Docker environment. Native execution cross-compiles only where a builder has a native cross toolchain (see platforms and executors) and never confers production publication eligibility. Native development output is a runnable binary, not a versioned source distribution; use the isolated path for the existing packaging contract. Its manifest record still carries the bundle's required version: the builder's own artifact version where it has one, otherwise the target's resolved version. A consumer that declares a platform other than the host, such as a docker/image with platforms: [linux/x86_64] that materializes a Go binary on a Windows host, does not use the native path, because native producers are built for the host only. Plain oyzu build (and --plan) then selects the captured executor, which builds each producer for the platform its consumer requires, so the binary is a Linux executable. When the consumer's platform is the host's, the native path is unchanged. A pinned Go, Node or helm is restored from the lock in that captured worker (see Go, Node and Helm); any other pinned tool the worker cannot yet take from the lock is still refused there.

Two terms stay distinct. The target platform is what an artifact is built for; the executor is where its build actions run: this host for its own platform, a native cross toolchain on this host, the container executor (--isolated, --all-platforms), or a remote pool (--remote, reported only). The executor is part of the build's identity: the manifest and plan record it on each target (oyzu.dev/platforms), and action keys bind every executor other than the host, so a cross-compiled or container result never satisfies a host build of the same platform or the reverse.

Every platform is written os/arch[/abi]: linux/x86_64, linux/arm64, darwin/arm64, windows/x86_64, windows/x86_64/msvc. Input also accepts the aliases amd64 (for x86_64) and aarch64 (for arm64), in build.yaml platforms, --platform and --allow-incomplete; output, records, variant IDs and dist/ directories always use the canonical form. The ABI is optional and only meaningful where an OS has several: gnu or musl on Linux, msvc, gnu or gnullvm on Windows. Without one, the builder chooses its default (see Rust). Container engines and registries keep their own spelling (linux/amd64) at that boundary only. The ABI a build resolves (Rust: musl for a Linux cross build, msvc on Windows, gnu on a Linux host) is recorded in the target's platform and its artifacts' compatibility. Published names (dist/ directories, asset names, selectors) carry an ABI only when it differs from the OS's naming default (GNU on Linux, MSVC on Windows); see release asset names. The musl default for Linux cross builds is a risk for glibc-dependent code (dlopen, NSS name lookup); declare linux/<arch>/gnu where it matters.

Invocation Platforms built oyzu build The host platform, leniently. A target that declares no platforms builds for the host. A target that declares platforms but not the host builds the one declared platform this machine can build; with several it stops and asks for --platform; with none it is skipped with the reason. oyzu build --platform

(repeatable) Exactly those. A target that does not declare a named platform is skipped for it with the reason; so is a target that declares no platforms and cannot build it here. A declared platform that cannot be built here fails the build before anything runs (PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE), as does a run in which no selected target builds anything. A requested ABI narrows a declaration without one (--platform linux/arm64/gnu for a declared linux/arm64); a different declared ABI is not the requested platform. The native executors build one platform per target in a run; build each with its own --platform (one CI matrix job each) or add --isolated. oyzu build --all-platforms Every declared platform through the container executor, strictly: one the container executor cannot build here fails the build before it runs. --platform and --all-platforms exclude each other and --remote. An invalid name is a usage error (exit status 2). A platform-independent target (a static site, dist//any/) is built once whatever platforms are selected. Plan shows what builds each platform. When a build routes a platform off the host, or a target declares platforms this run does not build, every row names its platform and a built by column (or footnote, on a narrow terminal) names the executor; other lists declared platforms this machine could build with --platform, and not here lists the rest with the reason: ── Plan ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── format lint test build package hello · linux/arm64 skip skip skip run skip other windows/x86_64 · host with --platform linux/x86_64 · cross toolchain (rust-lld) with --platform not here windows/arm64 · missing MSVC arm64 build tools (Visual Studio VC/Tools/MSVC//lib/arm64); --isolated builds it with the container executor darwin/arm64 · needs a macOS runner (Apple SDK and linker); --isolated builds it with the container executor built by hello · linux/arm64 · cross toolchain (rust-lld) A builder without a native cross toolchain builds only its host's machine natively; other platforms report the runner they need (needs a Linux runner) and, when the container executor can build them, that --isolated would. Go, Node, Python, Java, .NET and Helm have no native cross toolchain yet. Native output confers no publication eligibility.

Without a declaration a platform takes the default route: the host for its own machine, otherwise a native cross toolchain when the builder has one (or the container executor under --isolated). A project can instead declare the executor of a platform in oyzu.toml, per target folder and, like other per-target settings, per context: [build.executors] "linux/arm64" = "cross-toolchain" # always cross-compiled, never built on an arm64 host "darwin/arm64" = "host" # only on a macOS arm64 runner [context.release.build.executors] "linux/x86_64" = "container" # releases build it in the container executor A declared executor is the only one used for that platform, in every context: when it is unavailable here (no cross linker, the wrong host, container without --isolated, host or cross-toolchain under --isolated), the platform is not built here and Plan says why; an explicit request for it fails with PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE before anything runs. Nothing falls back to another executor. In the release context the host platform the default selects is such a request too: a release build fails clearly instead of skipping it. So a release builds each platform exactly as its plan says, and the executor stays part of the build's identity (oyzu.dev/platforms and the action key). Plan, the preview rows (declaredExecutor) and the CI matrix entries (executor) show the declaration.

oyzu build --plan --json reports, for each selected target, a platforms record (target, the logical target; declared; declaredExecutors; one row per declared or requested platform with selected, executor, declaredExecutor, reason, refused and runner; and the platform and executor this run would use), and at the top level a matrix: one include entry per declared platform of every selected target with the runner (os as CI providers name it: linux, windows, macos; and arch) that builds it on its own host, the declared executor (else host) and the targets that declare it. The matrix does not depend on what the planning machine can build: a target declaring only darwin/arm64, planned on Linux, still gets its entry. unconstrained lists selected targets that declare no platforms. With --affected <ref> the selection, and so the matrix, holds only the affected targets and their platforms. A workflow can feed it to a matrix strategy: jobs: plan: runs-on: ubuntu-latest outputs: matrix: ${{ steps.plan.outputs.matrix }} steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - id: plan run: echo "matrix=$(oyzu build --plan --json --affected origin/main | jq -c .matrix)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT" build: needs: plan strategy: matrix: ${{ fromJSON(needs.plan.outputs.matrix) }} runs-on: ${{ matrix.runner.os == 'macos' && 'macos-15' || matrix.runner.os == 'windows' && 'windows-2025' || 'ubuntu-24.04' }} steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: oyzu build ${{ join(matrix.targets, ' ') }} --platform ${{ matrix.platform }} Mapping runner to a provider's runner label (and choosing an arm64 runner) stays with the workflow. Publication then checks the declared platform set: see incomplete platform sets. The .matrix holds platform builds only. Toolset verification runs are listed under a separate .verify key, each with its runner and command; a platform job builds the runs assigned to its platform, or the workflow passes --skip-verification to the platform jobs and runs each .verify command (oyzu build app --verify-only node24) in its own job, whose bundle oyzu publish takes as evidence beside the platform bundles. See verification toolsets.
documents.s: A CI matrix from the plan

documents.t: oyzu build --plan previews the same execution-path selection as a build: local host when supported, otherwise the captured executor. --isolated, --all-platforms, named targets, profiles and --full keep their normal selection meaning. The preview itself needs neither Cargo nor Docker installed. The preview reads configuration and native manifests, applies the shared target, matrix and task-selection rules, and shows each target's discovery decisions with their reasons, selected/skipped stages, declared task ordering and consolidated tool requirements. See discovery decisions and selectors. It does not install tools, fetch packages, execute build tools or project scripts, create a lock, open a tool store, write a source snapshot, or create/replace a build bundle. Application dependencies are acquired only by an actual build's preparation. --affected additionally hashes local source and reads the local Git baseline using Git; its existing conservative fallback rules still apply, with no network or checkout writes. A preview is deliberately incomplete: installed-tool availability, executor capabilities, dependency cache readiness, exact commands, native-generated stages, artifact names and report bindings remain unresolved. A selected stage means configuration requests it, not that its prerequisites have passed. Dynamic target relationships may add work during real preparation. Success means the static preview was produced; it does not certify build success or publication eligibility. Live build output shows one plan table once, before work starts: targets by stages with run, skip or - cells and one footnote per skip reason. A single target built for several platforms pivots to one row per platform; above twelve rows targets with identical stages share a counted row (-v lists every target). See Result output. Matrix expansion (--all-platforms, --isolated) can yield targets that differ only by platform. In the live build output a single target built for several platforms is one plan table with a row per platform; the requirements table shows "all N targets" when every target shares a requirement. --json still reports every target individually. Targets whose plans differ keep their own sections. Human output uses stage/requirement tables with semantic color on capable terminals (or CLICOLOR_FORCE=1); NO_COLOR preserves plain text. Owned styling is emitted once, after escaping project-controlled values. --json returns a version-1 build-preview record with resolved: false, selection, targets (each with a discovery map of role to selected and reason), tasks, requirements, unresolved details, effect flags and timings. It is not the executable build-plan retained by actual builds in dist/plan.json. The former captured --plan behavior that acquired dependencies is superseded; use an actual build and its retained plan for execution-level evidence. No schema version was bumped. timings reports where the preview spent its wall-clock time, in milliseconds: totalMs and phases, in order discovery (configuration and target discovery), selection (selection, variants, task graph and requirements), source (inventorying the working tree for analysis from file metadata; no file is read until analysis asks for it), analysis (with targets, one entry per analyzed target, then finishMs for merging facts and rulesMs for the diagnostic rules) and planning (stage and task listing). source and analysis are absent when analysis is disabled or fails. Timings describe one run only and are never part of the analysis record, which stays identical between runs.

oyzu build --remote --plan previews what oyzu build --remote would run on a platform pool, without contacting the platform or needing its settings or token. It is the same read-only preview with the pool's selection: isolated execution, full checks, and the ordinary isolated platform selection. --remote does not imply --all-platforms or introduce additional platform variants. Named targets and --affected <base> select as the remote run does; --affected compares with the merge base of <base> and HEAD. The record's execution is remote. The platform's planner runs this command with the project's pinned Oyzu on a checkout of the exact commit to learn each job's requirements before it is queued. The preview reads the working tree, so local uncommitted changes are included even though a remote run never sends them. --isolated, --all-platforms, --image, --check and --download are refused with --remote. Every preview target carries these placement facts: Field Meaning platform The artifact platform. From the target's variant when it declares one; otherwise the executor's own platform decides, shown as unresolved until executor selection. platformSource variant, executor or host (a development-mode host target). executionPlatform The platform an executor must run on, or null when any executor works. A Rust cross-compile in the container executor runs on linux/x86_64 whatever it targets. A Docker image needs its own platform when its reachable final stage has RUN; a clearly independent final stage ignores RUN in unused earlier stages. Ambiguous stage relationships retain the conservative whole-file requirement. needsDaemon, daemonReason Whether the selected work needs a Docker engine on the executor, and why. false for development-mode host targets, Node targets that can use the daemonless sandbox, and admitted image assembly with only its native build task selected. Selected quality tasks or hooks can make an image target require Docker. isolation What the executor must provide to run the target: host (development mode), crun (Linux with unprivileged user namespaces, or a Docker engine), in-process (Oyzu's native OCI assembly and output copy), or docker (a Docker engine). id, logicalTarget, variant Concrete target ID, its original logical name, and its expanded axes. IDs may be normalized and hashed; clients must use the returned ID rather than construct one. A logical dependency waits for every selected variant; a concrete dependency names that variant only. dependsOnTargets Concrete declared ordering and artifact-input dependencies. Cross-target tasks[].dependsOn edges also contribute to the graph. sliceable Whether the static preview finds no reason this target cannot be reused by another slice. false means include it in the consumer's slice, not a separate handoff producer. Runtime preparation, invalid output writes or storage failures can still prevent reuse. sliceReason, sliceDetail Stable refusal code and human explanation when sliceable is false; otherwise null. Codes: ALWAYS_RUN_HOOK, UNCACHED_TASK, UNSCOPED_INPUTS, UNBOUNDED_OUTPUTS, SECRET_ENVIRONMENT, CACHE_DISABLED, SOURCE_PROJECTION. | platforms | How each declared or requested platform is built here; see a CI matrix from the plan. | Platforms are written in the canonical form (linux/x86_64, darwin/arm64); a development-mode host target reports its routed platform (the host, or a native cross build's) that way too. The top-level matrix lists every declared platform of the selected targets with the runner that builds it. OYZU_NO_DOCKER=1 does not alter preview selection or placement facts. Plan-only requests never enable the execution guard. Remote planning needs no credentials. Hooks always run, including hooks declaring outputs. Authored tasks need both cache = true and valid declared outputs; inputs outside their target cannot be cache scoped. Static analysis can identify native stages with unbounded outputs (omitted with --no-analysis). Secret environments and disabled local caching prevent storage. Image builders currently use source projections the action cache declines to store. sliceable describes upstream reuse, not whether a target may execute as a slice. Failed builds and runtime output-contract violations are not predictable by this read-only preview and still fail downstream reuse safely. The top-level placement object names which facts are final and which can grow. Each target's platform, executionPlatform and needsDaemon are final, as are the tool requirements of targets whose requirement status is discovered. The selected targets, the task graph, each target's stages and the requirements of unsupported targets can grow: dynamic target relationships found during preparation can add targets, and each added target brings its own facts. The Dockerfile analysis uses the Docker builder's native assembly grammar to identify a clearly independent final stage. Unsupported syntax, stage references and ambiguous dependencies fall back to a whole-file RUN check, which can over-require but never under-require native execution.

oyzu build --no-docker, or OYZU_NO_DOCKER=1 in the environment, is for executors that have no Docker engine, such as a container or Kubernetes pool. In this mode Oyzu runs no Docker command at all. Before anything is prepared or run it works out the same preview as --plan for the build's selection; if any selected target has needsDaemon: true, the build stops with exit status 3 and nothing runs. Any other value of the variable than empty or 0 enables the mode. oyzu build --isolated --no-docker --json {"error":"NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON: cli need a Docker engine, which this executor does not provide (--no-docker); nothing was run","reason":"NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON","targets":["cli"],"exitCode":3} Exit status 3 signals a placement mismatch, so a runner can tell it from a failed build (1) or a refused invocation (2) and requeue the job on a pool that has Docker. Placement normally comes from --remote --plan; this is the guard for when that plan was wrong. Node targets run in the daemonless sandbox in this mode. An admitted RUN-free Dockerfile with FROM scratch or a digest-pinned base can build in process with --isolated --no-docker; it needs no crun or user namespaces. A final stage independent of an unused earlier RUN stage can also use this path; see Docker image assembly. --full selects Dockerfile lint and format checks that still need the Docker worker, so the guard refuses that selection rather than skipping checks. Unsupported Dockerfile work such as RUN also requires Docker. Development builds of host targets run. --no-docker cannot be combined with --remote.

Unchanged captured npm builds can reuse verified script-free dependency acquisition before action lookup. Current tool admission and the offline install, lifecycle scripts, hooks and report gates keep their existing rules. See acquisition reuse for invalidation, offline behavior and cache controls. On Linux, the isolated steps of a Node target (npm, pnpm or Yarn) can run under crun, a rootless OCI runtime, instead of docker run. The step gets the same sandbox: no network, a read-only image root, no capabilities, no-new-privileges, a seccomp filter, Docker's masked and read-only /proc paths, the same mounts and the same tmpfs sizes, inside a user namespace that maps the workspace owner to itself. The image's root filesystem is unpacked once per image digest under the image cache and shared by every build on the host. The backend is not part of the action key: both backends produce the same keys and outputs, so a result cached by one serves the other. The build.isolation setting selects the backend: auto (default) uses Docker when an engine answers and crun otherwise, docker always uses Docker, and crun uses crun for Node targets even with Docker present. --no-docker and OYZU_NO_DOCKER=1 select crun for Node targets whatever the setting says. oyzu install downloads a pinned crun release (1.24), checks its SHA-256 and keeps it in the user data directory; OYZU_CRUN names a crun the executor already provides instead. Images come from their published, digest-pinned source, or from a local Docker engine's copy when one is running; a tag-only local image with no engine has no source and the build fails before running anything. Before running anything, a build that selected crun checks that crun runs and that the host lets an unprivileged process create user, mount, network and PID namespaces. When it cannot, the build stops with NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES, exit status 3 like NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON, naming what failed (for example kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=1, a seccomp profile that blocks unshare, or cgroups mounted in hybrid mode). Oyzu never runs the step without the sandbox. {"code":"NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES","error":"NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES: the daemonless sandbox (crun) cannot run on this host: cgroups are mounted in hybrid mode, which crun does not support; nothing was run","exitCode":3,"nextStep":"Run on a Linux executor that allows unprivileged user namespaces and has crun, or on one with a Docker daemon.","reason":"NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES"} crun runs without a cgroup of its own, so the executor pool's limits bound the step rather than per-step memory and CPU limits. Each action in the build manifest records how it was sandboxed in sandbox: backend (docker or crun), the crun runtime version, and resourceLimits (cgroup or pool).

A build can be split into jobs queued along the target graph, each reusing the results its predecessors built. Each job runs a slice: a build of the named targets in which every other target the build needs may only be reused, never built. The pinned worker's private admitted preparation and execution operations use the same executor preflight as ordinary builds: no-Docker refusal, resolved build.isolation selection, then the required sandbox probe before native preparation. They honor the existing OYZU_NO_DOCKER control. A read-only public preview still performs no executor preparation. Private assigned execution emits its completed manifest even when the build fails, then returns the ordinary failure status: 1 for failed/interrupted work, 4 for unavailable upstream reuse or 5 for failed handoff publication. A failed manifest cannot appear to the worker as successful execution. Native admission still requires exact selected records; mismatch diagnostics name the record and changed field names without printing command/environment values. oyzu build --slice --handoff oci://registry.oyzu.dev/acme/web/ci web Input Meaning Target arguments One or several logical target names or concrete preview targets[].id values. A logical name uses the same variant selection as a whole isolated build: runtime variants remain selected, while declared platforms use the normal host filter unless --all-platforms is given. A concrete ID builds exactly that variant, including a non-host platform. Upstream dependencies remain reuse-only unless explicitly named too. --slice-plan <target-id> Requires --slice; repeat once per concrete ID in the original preview, including folded upstreams and unrelated jobs. This is the client contract for inPlan; pass the complete original set unchanged to every slice and retry. Without it, inPlan uses this invocation's selection before preparation and cannot detect growth since an earlier preview. --slice Build only the named targets (at least one is required). Every action of any other target the selection needs (the named targets' depends_on, materialize and task prerequisites, transitively) is looked up in the local cache and the remote tiers; one that is missing fails with UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED instead of running. A slice runs the captured (isolated) path, as pool jobs do. With --plan it prints the isolated preview of that selection, with the same needsDaemon and isolation as --remote --plan. With --no-docker (or OYZU_NO_DOCKER=1) it is judged as an isolated build: a Node target runs in the daemonless sandbox, and any other target stops it with NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON (exit 3) before anything runs, so a pool without Docker requeues it rather than failing it. It cannot be combined with --remote, --affected, --check, --no-cache or --verify-contract, and it needs an active action cache when any selected upstream is unnamed. With cache.local = false, naming the entire selection permits a folded slice to run without reuse or handoff writes; an unexpectedly unavailable cache still fails admission. --handoff <oci-url> Requires --slice. The OCI repository (oci://host/path, the same form as cache.remote) read first for upstream results, before cache.ciRemote and cache.remote, and written with every result this slice produces whatever cache.read and cache.write say. The registry decides whether the job may write there, with the credential an ordinary remote uses (OYZU_CACHE_TOKEN or the job's ID token). A URL this client cannot use is refused (exit 2) before anything runs. None of these inputs changes a key: a slice derives every upstream key exactly as a whole build does, from the outputs it restores, so per-target slices of a commit produce the same action keys and artifact digests as one whole build. A producer that built something else than this checkout expects therefore shows up as a miss, never as a wrong reuse. The entries are the frozen OEP-0011 entries every remote tier holds; a handoff hit is verified and materialized like any remote hit. Reason codes, each with its own exit status so an executor can act without parsing text: Reason Exit Raised when UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED 4 An action of a target the slice does not build was not restored from any cache. It is recorded as failed, everything that needs its output is blocked, and nothing of it runs. HANDOFF_PUSH_FAILED 5 A result of a named target could not be written to the handoff repository (refused, unavailable, or the repository was switched off after an earlier failure). The build is failed even when every action succeeded, because the jobs after it would miss. Exit status 1 stays a failed build and 2 a refused invocation; 3 is NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON or NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES. When both happen, UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED wins. A failed slice prints one JSON line last on stderr, in human and --json mode alike, so an executor that forwards only the tail of the output can act without --json. It has the shape of NEEDS_DOCKER_DAEMON's error plus the failure's fields (below): {"action":"app:package","error":"UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED: app:package of upstream target app (key sha256:…) is not in the local cache or oci://registry.oyzu.dev/acme/web/ci; a slice reuses upstream targets and never builds them","exitCode":4,"inPlan":true,"key":"sha256:…","reason":"UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED","repositories":[{"location":"oci://registry.oyzu.dev/acme/web/ci","status":"active"}],"target":"app","why":null} The build record (dist/manifest.json, printed by --json) carries an oyzu.dev/slice extension: Field Meaning targets The concrete targets this slice built (requested targets and their variants). upstream The other targets it reused. handoff The --handoff location, or null. written One entry per result of a built target that is in the handoff repository: target, action, key and outcome (pushed, converged when an identical entry was already there, conflicts when a different one held the key and was kept). The runs service keeps these on the job, so a later miss can tell a producer that wrote a different key from one that wrote none. misses Every upstream action that was not restored: target, action, key, repositories (each remote asked, with status active or unavailable and why), inPlan, and why when the action was never looked up (for example an authored task without declared outputs, which is never cached). notWritten Every result of a built target that did not reach the handoff repository: target, action, key, repository and status (the registry's answer). failure null, or the first miss (reason: UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED, exitCode: 4) or else the first unwritten result (reason: HANDOFF_PUSH_FAILED, exitCode: 5), with that entry's fields. inPlan tests membership in the original set passed with --slice-plan. false means a missing producer was absent from that preview, including a dependency added between preview and execution. That is an explicit plan mismatch; it does not authorize a whole-build replay or repetition of effects that may have occurred. true means an expected producer did not leave a reusable result. Both exit 4; neither permits the slice to execute an unnamed producer. The action cache's summary gains a handoff section beside ciRemote and remote, with the same fields. A result restored from the handoff repository is not a CI result: a later CI build that finds it in its local store looks it up again, as it does for a development remote's. An upstream marked sliceable: false must be named alongside its consumer, for example oyzu build --slice --handoff oci://localhost:5000/demo/ci generate web. If several consumers require its live state or its effects are not known safe to repeat, keep the coupled work in one engine invocation. Transferability and repeatability are separate facts; cache ineligibility does not authorize one execution per consumer. An unnamed unreusable upstream still fails with UPSTREAM_NOT_CACHED and its why. Every upstream target is prepared (its dependencies acquired) because its keys include the prepared dependency identity. Verified with the slice-handoff build scenario against zot on Linux (OYZU_ZOT_BINARY=<zot> python tooling/test-build-scenarios.py --cli <oyzu> --suite node --only slice-handoff): per-target slices of a two-target project match one whole build key for key and digest for digest with no upstream action run, a deleted upstream entry exits 4, and refused handoff writes exit 5; see implementation status. The expanded scenario adds concrete matrix IDs, folded hooks and graph growth. --suite rust --only slice-corpus adds the pinned serde and regex workspaces, three declared crate targets each, checking every action key and cached output tree digest plus artifact digests from fresh local stores. A slice hands its results off and so builds the optimized profile; slices and the reference whole build are compared at the same profile, so the reference runs with --optimized. These additions await execution with Docker; the earlier two-target proof does not qualify them. Invalid configuration, unknown targets and statically invalid relationships fail normally. Configuration is opened offline to preserve the no-network contract; managed configuration that cannot resolve offline fails closed rather than bypassing policy. Correct the reported configuration or run a normal build to perform the preparation needed to resolve remaining details. Native macOS runtime qualification remains pending.
documents.s: Building a slice of a split run

documents.t: Successful binaries are collected in dist/<target>/<platform>/ (the host platform, such as dist/cli/windows/x86_64/; see the bundle layout) with their normal native names, then exposed at .oyzu/bin/<name>[.exe]. Outputs labels each one with the profile it was built with, development or, for an optimized build, optimized; each binary is statically verified as an executable for the host before it is collected (executable verification). The shared bundle store retains manifest, plan, envelope, reports and action logs. These disclose host execution, observed source and unverified tool identity; they do not confer production eligibility or assert enforced isolation. Rust state lives under .oyzu/native/rust/<compiler-host>/: target holds native compilation state and tests holds separate instrumented/test state. Cargo owns native invalidation. Prepared package bytes remain in the already provisioned native package cache; this slice does not implement an acquisition proxy, import unmanaged caches as trusted evidence or add a shared artifact cache.

After tool admission, the Rust builder tries locked offline Cargo metadata. If the cache is sufficient, it proceeds without fetching. Otherwise an online build runs cargo fetch --locked through the host executor with live, labeled preflight output, then resolves metadata offline again. Cargo owns registry/Git downloads, checksums and its cache; Oyzu does not rewrite Cargo.lock. Compilation remains offline. oyzu build --offline never takes the fetch path and reports missing inputs with guidance to run an online build or correct the manifest/lock.
