This is the standalone native path: Cargo uses its configured repositories, credentials and network settings. It is not a broker-controlled acquisition or network isolation guarantee. Managed host tool admission remains unavailable; this does not enable it or change captured-build acquisition. Native preparation failures retain a safe category and recovery guidance even when credential-bearing native details are withheld. Warm-cache qualification alone does not prove cold repository self-building; see the recorded qualification results. Previous claimed artifacts move to bundle history on either successful or failed native builds; unrelated dist files stay protected. See bundle finalization and recovery. Failure returns a nonzero exit and leaves .oyzu/bin at the last successful generation. Treat it as stale relative to the failed attempt. Promotion renames the previous image before replacing the stable name, avoiding direct overwrite of a running Windows image. An image that cannot yet be deleted may remain as a hidden previous generation; repeated Windows self-rebuilds still require proof.

Build the initial executable with cargo build --locked --release --bins, then copy target/release/oyzu[.exe] and target/release/oyzu-shim[.exe] together to a dedicated user PATH directory outside the checkout, preserving any existing installation. This independent fallback must not point back into the compiler output or .oyzu/bin. Check the build exit status before copying, verify the copied binary, and retain a rollback copy. Release builds avoid installing the much larger development/debug executable; the initial release build can be substantially slower than an incremental local build. On Windows, saving a directory in the user PATH does not update an already-open terminal or its parent application. Update the current PowerShell session explicitly, substituting your fallback installation directory: $fallbackBin = 'C:\path\to\oyzu-bootstrap\bin' $env:Path = "$fallbackBin;$env:Path" oyzu --version New terminals inherit PATH from their parent process, so opening another tab in an already-running terminal application may still inherit the older value. The repository configuration contains: [env] _.path = ["./.oyzu/bin"] Activate the shell through the fallback as described in shell activation. For PowerShell 7.5+, use oyzu activate pwsh | Out-String | Invoke-Expression. Run oyzu build, then _oyzu_hook if an explicit refresh is needed. Get-Command oyzu -CommandType Application (PowerShell), type -P oyzu (Bash), or whence -p oyzu (Zsh) should resolve to the project output. Ordinary oyzu invocations use the activation wrapper, which dispatches to that application; an unqualified command lookup can show the wrapper function instead of its destination. Leaving the project restores the baseline PATH. Merely writing TOML does not activate an existing terminal. Oyzu's repository configures +crt-static for x86_64-pc-windows-gnullvm in .cargo/config.toml. This links the compiler's unwind runtime into the Oyzu executables so workers can start without LLVM-MinGW's libunwind.dll on PATH. It does not install an OS component or relax the worker's explicit environment. Other targets retain their native defaults. Compiler flags supplied explicitly through Cargo's environment can override this repository configuration; preserve the static-runtime setting when building this target.

Fresh-store installation and a small native Rust build --full have passed on Windows GNU/LLVM, including automatic helper installation, JUnit and coverage collection, formatting and linting, followed by offline reuse. Use oyzu build --store <path> to select the same store as oyzu install --store <path>. The default remains the shared user store. Relative overrides resolve against the invocation directory (or global --root), before workspace-root discovery. The selected store is used for native installation and verification and captured-build tool preparation; it never changes pins, tool identities, checks or image policy. A missing or invalid installation in that store does not fall back to another store. --offline requires its cached inputs; use the same override on install, build and tool-inspection commands. Repository test fixtures explicitly select their intended profile, and doctest compilation no longer has a private two-minute timeout. Git and Windows PowerShell must be available for the repository's own tests. See commands, measurements and qualification limits. Native execution inherits host capabilities. Cargo's offline mode is not network denial for arbitrary build scripts. New process/network isolation and approved broker routes remain future work. An installed fallback, local successful build or local isolation flag cannot grant production publication authority. Current implementation verification and missing end-to-end evidence are recorded in implementation status. The intended host matrix is Windows/macOS/Linux, but no new host is qualified by this document.

Rust discovers an explicit install task; no custom bootstrap task is needed. See Rust executable installation. With the required tools available, run from this checkout: oyzu run install -- --bins --force --root "$env:LOCALAPPDATA/Oyzu/bootstrap" The destination is machine-local, not committed task configuration. Windows self-installation stages the Cargo result before replacing the running bootstrap. This invokes Cargo installation, not the full Oyzu build quality gates. Cargo uses release compilation by default; add --debug after -- for a development installation. These profiles use different compiler caches. Run oyzu install first to materialize the pinned native toolchain and its verified installation receipt. An outdated bootstrap can initially be replaced by invoking Cargo directly with the provisioned toolchain: cargo install --path . --bins --locked --force --root "$env:LOCALAPPDATA/Oyzu/bootstrap" oyzu run fetch prepares Cargo dependencies; oyzu run install installs project executables; oyzu install provisions development tools. They remain distinct.
documents.s: Updating this repository's bootstrap with Cargo

documents.t: The Windows task flow uses a pinned MSVC installation, which needs Visual Studio Build Tools (C++ workload, no IDE) installed first: oyzu pin, oyzu install, then oyzu run install. A checkout whose oyzu.lock was installed with the earlier GNU/LLVM default holds a stale Rust-only installation record that conflicts with the new selection (TOOL_LOCK_AMBIGUOUS); delete that oyzu.lock and rerun oyzu pin and oyzu install. Ordinary tool installation does not provision Docker or a Linux worker. Keep machine-specific linker/CMake paths and Cargo cache locations in ignored oyzu.local.toml, using [env] and _.path. Cargo's CARGO_INSTALL_ROOT selects the bootstrap prefix (the binary goes under its bin directory); this setting also applies to oyzu run install. The selected verified Cargo/compiler remain owned by Oyzu, while LLVM/MinGW, CMake and dependency-specific native prerequisites are provisioned separately. Do not commit one developer's absolute machine paths. See native Rust task execution. The Oyzu executable explicitly links its existing unwinder statically on Windows GNU/LLVM. Rust 1.95 otherwise emits a libunwind.dll import, causing startup to fail before CLI code runs when LLVM is absent from PATH. See the upstream Rust explanation. This binary-only link declaration does not change downstream project profiles or install a compiler runtime globally. The local bootstrap retains the provisioned LLVM license next to its installation; packaging remains subject to the existing third-party distribution review, not cleared by this development proof. On Windows, the inferred Oyzu Cargo install task stages installation under the explicit destination root (CARGO_INSTALL_ROOT or forwarded --root). Cargo compiles and installs into staging while the existing bootstrap remains callable. Only after Cargo succeeds does execution publish binaries with Windows file replacement, retaining one .NAME.previous backup per replaced file. Cargo's installation bookkeeping is staged and published too. Cancelling compilation or a native install failure leaves the installed bootstrap unchanged. A forcibly terminated process may leave its private .oyzu-install-* staging directory; do not remove one belonging to an active installation. Publication is per file, not an atomic transaction across the CLI, shim and Cargo metadata. On a publication error, inspect the named file and adjacent backup; close processes still holding an older backup before retrying. Concurrent Oyzu installs to this root serialize; a simultaneous direct Cargo install is outside that coordination. Other packages and non-Windows installs retain native Cargo behavior. Without an explicit root, Oyzu leaves Cargo's destination selection alone and does not move the running executable out of the way. Native builds acquire the same verified configured tools as tasks before invoking builder metadata. Leases are retained and reused by all stages with the same frozen target configuration. No tool verification gate is bypassed. Repeated successful native builds replace artifacts recorded by the prior bundle at the newly collected artifact paths. Test-only runs continue preserving those files without claiming them as new build artifacts. Unclaimed native files still cause a collision rather than being overwritten; prior bundles remain in history. Build output starts with Building <directory name> (or Planning for --plan), followed by host platform or the requested matrix, local/isolated execution, and the requested fast/full mode. Relative . paths resolve to the actual directory name. This initial summary does not override configuration or policy; preflight establishes the selected targets and required checks. JSON emits a structured heading event on stderr; quiet mode suppresses it and stdout remains unchanged. Build output follows Preflight → Build → completion summary. Preflight includes configuration, target discovery, pinned tool preparation, native dependency metadata and planning. These internal steps are not competing top-level phases. The default view shows tool, requested version and observed installation status on the same row. Missing tools report acquisition/installation, followed by verification; reused tools report verification before receiving a success mark. The Rust component installer currently reports downloading and installing as a combined step; it does not invent byte percentages. A success mark requires the existing installation verification to finish. Errors stop preflight and remain visible. External SDK/linker prerequisites explicitly remain unchecked until the native tools run; discovering them does not establish availability. Optional formatting, linting, testing and coverage tools are omitted from the fast-build summary unless quality stages are selected. The full declared inventory remains in detailed logs; this presentation does not change pins, installation recipes, enabled stages or enforcement. Additional environment, execution and source context is available with p, rather than repeating it in the default view. Native execution does not imply isolation or verified commit identity. Auto and plain modes use a linear, scrollback-preserving build flow. They do not open an alternate screen or maintain panes. Color is independent of interaction: ui.color=auto colors terminal output unless NO_COLOR is set to a non-empty value; always also colors redirected text and never disables color. A terminal is capable when TERM is not dumb and, on Windows, when the console accepts virtual terminal processing, which the CLI switches on for its own stdout and stderr; a console that refuses gets plain text and no line clears. Active tools and build subprocesses show eight dimmed output lines beneath their headers on capable terminals. Success collapses those lines; failure retains them. Redirected output appends each update. --output interactive retains the old dashboard as an explicit opt-in. JSON remains structured and unstyled; raw child output and retained evidence are unchanged. See build logging. Native builds automatically install missing configured and builder-required tools from existing pins using the shared user store, then verify the selected environment before compiling. Builds never update pinned versions or write a new lock: run oyzu pin for missing or stale resolutions. --offline forbids acquisition and requires the installer's cached inputs. Small terminals retain detailed logs (d) for values outside the visible area. Automatic installation uses the same acquisition, checksum, installation lease and policy checks as oyzu install, consuming the configuration snapshot selected for the build target. Installation errors stop execution before native metadata or compilation. A denied or corrupted selection is not replaced by an unverified PATH tool. This applies to the supported native build path; isolated builds retain their provisioned image contract. Provisioned builds without a portable pin retain their existing behavior. With a portable pin, selected tests include the pinned nextest and cargo-llvm-cov helpers automatically; ordinary fast builds omit them. System linkers and SDKs remain external prerequisites. See helper installation. Native Rust preflight names linker/runtime prerequisites from the selected compiler's reported host (GNU/LLVM, MSVC, MinGW, Apple, or Linux). The actual prepared Cargo environment performs the compile/link probe, including inherited linker configuration and coverage instrumentation when selected. Ready means that probe succeeded using executor-provided facilities; it does not claim that Oyzu installed an OS SDK or independently identified every library's version. Pin's executor table omits tool-version and installation-backend columns because those prerequisites are externally provided and are not probed by pin.

Native host execution records an observed source identity. It validates and hashes source files using the captured-source exclusions, path/type rules and change detection, but does not write an unused temporary source copy. The native compiler still reads the checkout; this does not provide a frozen filesystem or isolation. Captured/container execution still creates its required input copy. Preflight names output-bundle opening, compiler-cache retention, source hashing, CLI identity hashing and report preparation. Each running operation has an explicit completion or failure; report contracts and binding readiness share one completion row. Source and CLI identity completion include measured durations. Slow operations retain named activity updates. See linear logging. The 2026-10-06 provider-identity refresh passed the actual Windows repository bootstrap → pin/install → fast build → local-CLI self-install loop, plus a fresh Linux fixture's install/build/offline/activation flow. See the commands, fixture corrections and limits. Subsequent qualification passed the Windows repository build --full, the Linux repository host build inside Docker, and a deliberate failed-test fixture with retained reports and no published artifacts. See the measured results and cache baseline.
documents.s: Local source evidence and startup progress

documents.t: Rust source refresh and version projection preserve the modification times of final Cargo.toml files and Cargo.lock when their newly reconciled bytes are identical to the previous projection. This keeps Cargo and its build scripts from treating unchanged versions as changed source. Each current file is hashed before its time can be retained; changed bytes keep their fresh time. Expendable digest/time hints live in manifest-projection.json beside the native compiler cache. Missing, damaged or unwritable hints fall back to ordinary Cargo fingerprinting. Source admission, Cargo resolution/version decisions and action keys still run. This also applies with --no-cache, which disables Oyzu action reuse while retaining native compiler caches. Oyzu's own build script watches existing Git metadata and the current loose ref or its existing parent. An absent optional path such as packed-refs no longer forces a build-script run on every invocation; unborn and packed branches still refresh the compiled identity when commits change. Native Rust oyzu build retains at most cache.nativeMaxMiB MiB across its selected host's declared compiler caches after normal completion. The default is 8192 MiB (8 GiB). Configure it through the ordinary configuration cascade: [cache] nativeMaxMiB = 8192 When the budget is exceeded, Oyzu first runs Cargo's clean --workspace --offline --target-dir <validated-directory> across the selected native caches, retaining registry dependency compiler products when workspace cleanup makes them fit. Only if the aggregate is still above budget does it evict whole roots with Cargo's own clean. Oyzu first marks each declared cache directory with the standard CACHEDIR.TAG, because current Cargo refuses to clean a target directory without one; a cache created before the tag existed would otherwise fail every build once the budget was exceeded. The setting accepts 1–1048576 MiB, supports ordinary policy numeric constraints, and applies identically online and offline. It is separate from remote result cache preferences. Progress reports the measured size and any reclaimed roots; JSON builds keep those diagnostics on stderr and the result on stdout. The build holds the workspace transaction lock while checking the budget before execution and after collecting artifacts and reports. If over budget, execution runs the selected Cargo's clean --offline --target-dir <validated-directory>. Cargo retains ownership of compiler-file cleanup and its own cache locking. After the workspace-only pass, whole roots are evicted in this order until under budget: the obsolete separate doctest target, coverage target, ordinary build target. Under budget, no native cleanup runs. Doctests now reuse the ordinary build target; instrumentation keeps coverage in a separate target. A budget below the working set trades incremental reuse for space and can cause a cold compile on every invocation. This is a retained-size policy, not a peak disk quota: compilation can temporarily exceed it, and a crash or full disk before collection may leave oversized state until the next invocation. End-of-build cleanup failure emits NATIVE_CACHE_RETENTION_FAILED without discarding build evidence or changing its result; the next pre-build check retries, and a failure there stops execution. Root/entry symlinks and Windows reparse points are rejected rather than followed. Use a normal directory or remove the redirection before retrying. No claim is made of protection against a hostile concurrent filesystem writer. Only builder-declared roots under the selected target's .oyzu/native are eligible. Installed tools, downloads, .oyzu/bin, dist, history/recovery, proof files, other platform roots, direct Cargo's project target, and arbitrary oyzu run tasks are outside this policy. No schema changed and no legacy data was relabeled. The regression entry point is python tooling/test-native-cache-budget.py --cli <compiled-oyzu> with this checkout's pinned Rust/check tools and native linker prerequisites. It proves small-budget rebuilds, retained warm state, doctests, report inspection and failed-build preservation through the compiled CLI.

Run oyzu build or oyzu build --plan from a nested project containing its own build.yaml; no --root is required. Source subdirectories select their nearest ancestor declaration. Repository configuration continues to inherit, while the selected build owns its lockfile and outputs. Parent builds do not automatically include nested build inventories. See configuration boundaries for the configuration contract.

A project whose selected profile has a native host build runs on the machine without Docker: Oyzu resolves missing tools, installs them into the shared store, then invokes the ecosystem's own tools. Other profiles use the isolated executor and fail with a message naming that requirement when Docker is unavailable. Profile Host build Unpinned tool selection Rust (Cargo) Yes Automatic (greatest stable release; must satisfy Cargo rust-version; a rust-toolchain.toml channel or explicit pin wins; see Rust installation) Node node/app with npm and a dist/ output Yes Automatic (greatest LTS satisfying every engines.node constraint; greatest matching stable release if no LTS matches; selection) Go go/app: one module, no go.work, exactly one package main Yes Automatic (exactly the Go minimum from the go.mod go and toolchain lines; see Go version selection) Python pip with pyproject.toml Yes (wheel) Automatic (greatest stable CPython satisfying requires-python; see Python installation) Java Maven reactor (readable jar names; a committed mvnw is run) Yes (jars; tests run in verify) Automatic (JDK from the declared level, Maven 3.9 unless a wrapper supplies it; see Java installation) Java Gradle build (a committed gradlew is run; jars from Gradle's model; tests run in build) Yes Automatic (JDK from the declared level, Gradle 8 or 9) Go libraries, workspaces, several binaries; Ant and other Java; uv/Poetry/requirements-only Python; other Node profiles No: isolated executor Not applicable Package tools that a builder detects (for example protoc for a Rust project whose Cargo.lock has prost-build) follow the same rule without a pin: the version is the folder pin, else the detection's version hint, else the latest stable catalog release; preflight locks it with the other requirements and installs it, and oyzu pin records the same selection. A tool with no catalog entry, no usable checksum, or that cannot be resolved or installed is left as an attention row and the build continues (tools.ignore silences it); only a tool you pinned in oyzu.toml fails the build when it cannot be verified or installed. Verified on Windows: a Rust project whose Cargo.lock lists prost-build resolved protoc 36.2, locked it for every platform and installed it on the first oyzu build; the second showed it already installed. oyzu pin is optional for Rust, Go and Node. With no oyzu.lock, preflight resolves the requirement, writes oyzu.lock and installs from it; commit that file to make later builds reproducible, or delete it to re-resolve. An explicit [tools] go = "1.24" takes precedence when it reaches the Go minimum; a module-folder value below it is refused. The Go build runs go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false -o <private output> with GOTOOLCHAIN=local, so only the locked toolchain compiles and none is downloaded mid-build, and GOPROXY=off under --offline. Compiler diagnostics are shown with their file and line, the exit status is preserved and no previous binary is republished. The artifact is the executable <target>-<version>; --full adds go test -json with coverage, go vet and gofmt -l. Dependencies use Go's module cache in the user's Go environment (not isolated per project). Evidence: fresh-checkout qualification.

The host coordinator selects declared targets and their dependency closure, prepares verified configured tools, asks each builder for its native build contract, and executes one shared task graph into one evidence bundle. Before preparation, host execution and --plan share logical selection, prerequisite/hook expansion and cycle validation. The executable host plan retains those dependency edges; the shared scheduler runs independent targets concurrently up to the resolved build.jobs ceiling. Build YAML depends_on gates consumers on the producer's selected stages. A failed dependency blocks its consumers while unrelated targets may finish. Stages within one target remain ordered to protect their shared native workspace. It does not claim process/network isolation or production eligibility. Explicit --isolated retains the isolated path and its existing tool-identity admission limits. Native and captured builds use the same executable-action description and shared operation/hook/report composition. Native artifact locations remain machine-local collection bindings to the plan's logical outputs. This changes no executor selection or fast/full default: native build commands retain their own lifecycle, including Maven tests within verify. Internal action boundaries do not imply a separate native invocation for each module or more precise cache inputs. Required reports and successful collection still gate artifacts; private workspaces alone do not establish enforcement. See task composition. Native support includes Cargo, Maven reactors producing jars, single-binary Go applications, explicit npm dist applications, and pip pyproject wheel distributions. Other Node/Python profiles retain the existing isolated path and its admission limits. npm uses npm ci for declared dependencies and requires a lockfile. Installation is the native target's prepare action: it runs before pre_build hooks on a cache miss, and an unchanged whole-target cache hit reuses it with the build. A failed installation blocks hooks/build and publishes no artifacts. --no-cache runs installation again. npm lifecycle scripts and offline behavior stay native; no node_modules directory is retained in the source projection. pip uses its native PEP 517 wheel builder, including build-backend acquisition. Offline adds npm offline/pip no-index behavior and may fail when native prerequisites are unavailable. CPython is provisioned as a managed tool (Python installation); pip is the one bundled with it. pip performs build-backend acquisition during its wheel command; this is visible native preparation output, not a separate Oyzu dependency graph. Host wheels are distribution artifacts, not a bundled runnable Python application. The build performance assessment records the reviewed paths, measured repeated-build timings and remaining preparation costs. Reproduce its bounded npm checks with python tooling/test-build-performance.py --cli <compiled-oyzu>; both modes require the pinned Node and the provisioned npm worker image. Use --mode native for host checks alone. The probe checks reuse, source edits, fresh-output equivalence, native hook ordering and install failure propagation; timings are observations, not portable pass/fail thresholds. First functional proof: run oyzu build from examples/tasks/grouped-targets/project without root overrides, produce the Python wheel and Node dist directory in one dist/manifest.json, then validate the bundle with oyzu inspect dist. Target selection, failure handling and a repeated invocation close the remaining functional checks. Broader native profiles remain separate follow-ups. Native builds now use private target workspaces and explicit artifact transfer. An ordering edge alone does not copy files. Additional shared-source inputs currently require the native host path. Windows verification: the grouped API/web build and oyzu inspect dist succeeded with both artifacts. python tooling/test-native-multi-build.py --cli <compiled-oyzu> verifies real npm multi-target builds, a selected target, repeated publication, missing-fresh-output rejection and a native child failure that blocks dependent tasks. The concurrency proof uses a two-process rendezvous, and the dependency proof checks producer completion before consumer execution. Native executable filename collisions are rejected before build actions. These checks do not qualify full-quality dependency availability for every ecosystem.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/maven.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Status: experimental. Oyzu detects a pom.xml without a build YAML file and treats a native Maven reactor as one target. Maven owns inheritance, active profiles, module order, dependency resolution and lifecycle execution; Oyzu captures inputs, projects snapshot versions, enforces isolated execution and collects evidence. The reactor example includes unit/integration reporting variations.

Development tasks use provisioned Maven or the native Maven wrapper. Static oyzu run list does not execute Maven. Implicit install runs dependency preparation, build runs mvn -B verify, and test runs mvn -B test. The explicit test task is not separately repeated during the build lifecycle. Checks already bound to verify run under Maven. Shared Java quality defaults add native lint and read-only formatting gates, with explicit task replacements available. Captured builds require Docker and the explicitly provisioned Maven 3.9.11/JDK 17 image: docker build -f tooling/images/builder-worker.Dockerfile -t oyzu-toolchain/builder-worker:v1 . docker build -f tooling/images/maven.Dockerfile -t oyzu-toolchain/maven:3.9.11-jdk17 . oyzu -C examples/builds/java-maven-reactor/project run list oyzu -C examples/builds/java-maven-reactor/project build

The image's JDK 17 is used only when nothing selects another. A JDK chosen by the project, either by [tools] java or by the root POM's declared level (see how versions are chosen), is locked by build preflight and restored in the worker: preparation reads the Linux (linux/amd64/gnu) Temurin archive recorded in oyzu.lock, downloads it through the tool broker unless a copy cached under the user data directory still matches the locked SHA-256, verifies it and restores it read-only at /scratch/jdktool. JAVA_HOME and the front of PATH point at it for preparation and every build action, so Maven and the compiler run on it. The plan records the archive under oyzu.dev/locked-tool, so a different JDK changes the action identity. A selected JDK older than 17 is refused with TOOL_UNSUPPORTED_VERSION, because Maven and Oyzu's Java integration in the worker need JDK 17; JDK 17 and newer compile older levels with --release. An existing oyzu.lock without a JDK entry keeps the image's JDK. Rebuild this image for the native test-plan extension; an older image with the same tag cannot produce the required metadata. Oyzu does not pull a missing image or install Maven. Custom --image maven=<image> toolchains need the matching extension, native tools and the matching compiled Oyzu worker at /usr/local/libexec/oyzu/oyzu. Windows native metadata/lifecycle probes and Linux captured builds are separate verification scopes; a portable CLI does not establish a native isolated executor on every host.
documents.s: Locked JDK in the captured worker

documents.t: Preparation captures native POMs and evaluates the reactor inside the constrained toolchain. Version inference combines native versions with scoped Git tags and relevant commit impacts, then the native versions plugin projects each selected version and local reactor references into private POMs. The checkout stays unchanged. Supported artifact packaging is pom, jar and war; other packaging types fail explicitly. Outputs retain native final names and carry planned snapshot versions in the bundle. The native model is captured before projection. The host resolves per-module decisions and freezes version-plan.json, then preparation continues in the same private workspace. The final native coordinates must agree with those decisions; changed native facts or failed projection stop the build. Native version expressions are evaluated by Maven, never by a host-side POM expression interpreter. Scoped tags use the module's artifact ID when unique. Root tags do not automatically coordinate a reactor. The native reactor graph supplies local upstream projects, including reactor parents, to the shared transitive version-impact resolver. A library change therefore affects its consumers without automatically advancing an unrelated module. Shared root inputs conservatively affect all modules. Prepared layout version 4 requires these graph facts; regenerate older captures and reprovision the toolchain image with the current metadata extension. Snapshot intent does not authorize publishing. For modules without their own version element, private preparation first uses Maven's raw model writer to make the originally resolved version explicit. The versions plugin can then project that module independently of its parent. This serialization may normalize private POM formatting; the checked-in POM is never rewritten. The final native reactor must match all selected coordinates before dependency acquisition continues. Host metadata observation disables this mutation. The standalone source profile routes Maven through a loopback mirror backed by Oyzu's scoped Maven Central broker. Upstream requests occur during acquisition; the captured repository is then copied into a private workspace for offline execution. Custom/private repositories, corporate connector credentials and complete dependency-edge evidence are not implemented by this profile; administratively admitted snapshot repositories are the only additional public source. Maven has no general lockfile here: the prepared repository identity records the actual captured inputs and is not a claim that independent future acquisition resolves identically. Project dependency acquisition uses Maven's effective project resolver after private version projection. Maven applies parent dependency management, imported BOMs and transitive conflict mediation before it acquires the external graph. Exact reactor group/artifact/version identities are excluded from artifact resolution, so preparation does not require prebuilt local JARs or execute compilation/tests. Unused dependency-management entries are not fetched merely because they are declared. The private prepared project-dependencies.xml retains the acquired external coordinates alongside native reactor metadata. Existing go-offline and plugin/provider acquisition remain; their additional versions can coexist in the captured repository. This is not a globally minimal repository or complete dependency-edge report. Missing required external bytes fail preparation before an executable plan is frozen. An older provisioned metadata JAR that does not acknowledge project dependency acquisition also fails preparation; reprovision the Maven metadata extension rather than reuse an incomplete capture. Every expected projected reactor coordinate must be present, including an explicit empty acquisition record for dependency-free projects. The managed-transitive qualification records the observed gap and current verification status. The shared acquisition transport applies bounded retries to eligible transient failures without treating transport errors as permission denials. Maven runs with native error traces (-e) so nested plugin/dependency-resolution causes can appear in the retained failure diagnostic; debug logging is not enabled. An exhausted or terminal acquisition failure blocks planning and requires successful preparation before any build artifact can be collected. One offline lifecycle runs native verify and JaCoCo reporting. The effective project's JaCoCo version and existing prepare-agent execution own native preparation, including inherited configuration, phase, skip controls and property names. Oyzu adds an initialize preparation only where no such execution is declared. Activation preserves effective inherited pluginManagement version, configuration and executions; JaCoCo 0.8.13 is the fallback when no managed version supplies one. Captured preparation observes this same effective plugin model. Preparation explicitly prefetches every effective JaCoCo plugin version through the existing broker-routed transitive dependency:get, alongside its declared dependencies. Native go-offline alone can leave a different module's plugin dependency closure incomplete in a mixed-version reactor; the selected plugin JAR and POM alone do not establish offline usability. Explicitly disabled native preparation is preserved and does not receive a replacement agent. Reporting uses the same effective native plugin version, rather than a competing version. No source POM is rewritten. A failed lifecycle attempts coverage reporting without rerunning tests and preserves failure. Required reports, logs, artifacts and their digests are recorded under dist/ and in dist/manifest.json. Any failed gate or invalid/missing required report prevents final artifact collection. oyzu inspect dist verifies bundle integrity, not release eligibility. Publishing, signing and production promotion are outside this builder increment.

After acquisition, the extension asks Maven for the effective verify execution plan. It records report directories for bound Surefire test and Failsafe integration-test goals using Maven's plugin configuration and expression evaluator. Defaults, inherited configuration, execution-specific settings and paths with spaces remain native Maven behavior. The directory plan is frozen in prepared metadata; shared planning does not parse POM expressions or guess test-class filename patterns. For captured builds and direct tests, the native extension prefixes an explicitly configured literal Surefire/Failsafe argLine with @{argLine} in the private effective model. This lets the selected JaCoCo prepare-agent supply its default agent while preserving the project's JVM flags and execution-specific overrides; the source POM is unchanged. Where a bridge is added, a missing default property retains the native user/system value or is initialized empty so the late token remains resolvable; existing project values are never replaced. Existing property expressions, custom JaCoCo property names and nonforking test configuration retain native Maven behavior; this literal bridge does not establish their coverage outcome. Absent coverage still fails the required report gate. Before execution, the adapter removes old TEST-*.xml outputs from those declared directories in the private workspace. After the lifecycle it copies produced XML unchanged into .oyzu-maven/reports/<reactor-index>/, using source-path hashes to avoid filename collisions. The shared report collector validates every retained XML file and records its actual results. Duplicate native directories are collected once. Individual Surefire/Failsafe directories may be empty: a module with only integration tests does not need fabricated unit-test XML. Modules with captured test sources require at least one native JUnit file across the combined group, plus their JaCoCo report. If every engine leaves no XML, disabled reporting or skipped tests fail that obligation; malformed XML also fails. The combined group records available native files and does not prove per-engine completeness when a custom reporter suppresses some outputs. No passing report is synthesized. Report paths must remain inside the captured workspace, outside reserved .oyzu-maven state, without redirected directories. Different modules must use distinct native report directories; shared paths fail planning rather than attributing the same tests to multiple modules. Each XML file is bounded to 16 MiB and each module's group to 64 MiB. Native test failures retain XML and available coverage while blocking artifacts. Fix the test, native report configuration or missing evidence and rebuild; prior successful bundles remain history rather than satisfying the current invocation. Native goals within one module may rewrite a shared report filename; Oyzu retains the final native files, not invented per-execution copies. Prepared layout version 2 requires the frozen directory plan; regenerate older prepared inputs and rebuild the toolchain image. Retained test-report paths change because collection now combines native engines. Consumers should follow manifest report records rather than assume Surefire-specific paths. JaCoCo remains at the module's conventional target/site/jacoco/jacoco.xml beneath its effective build directory; custom coverage destinations, aggregate reactor coverage and test source roots added only during later lifecycle execution need further integration.

oyzu run test now produces a test-only dist/ bundle for a native Maven reactor. Each module with discovered test sources receives named JUnit and JaCoCo reports; oyzu inspect dist validates the result. The exact implicit mvn -B test command (or the discovered wrapper equivalent) receives automatic reporting without project configuration. Qualified tasks and hooks retain their shared task-engine behavior. Arbitrary task replacements keep their command bodies and required report obligations. Additional forwarded arguments and alternate lifecycle selections are not yet integrated into this direct adapter. Provision Maven 3.9.11, JDK 17 with java, javac and jar, and the project's plugins/test dependencies, including JaCoCo 0.8.13. Set MAVEN_HOME to the installed Maven distribution and JAVA_HOME to the JDK, or put the JDK executables on PATH. Wrappers require an already provisioned distribution; Oyzu does not implement wrapper installation. Native Maven settings and environment remain in effect. The product passes Maven's offline flag for model observation and execution; an unavailable plugin or dependency fails instead of falling back to online resolution. After shared task admission, a temporary compiled extension reads the effective reactor and the native test execution plan. It exits its dedicated Maven process after writing the model, before validate bindings or default lifecycle tasks run. Native Maven model evaluation can load extensions; this is explicit host execution, not static discovery or sandboxing. run list remains static and does not invoke Maven. Captured builds continue to observe the broader verify plan, which includes bound Failsafe integration tests. The direct action clears prior XML in its declared native test directories and prior conventional JaCoCo execution/XML files, then runs prepare-agent, test, and report. On test failure it attempts report generation without rerunning tests. The adapter wraps native XML suites unchanged in meaning into one JUnit document per module and copies JaCoCo XML to fresh private output paths. The shared collector validates the reports and finalizes the bundle after post hooks. No successful reports are invented for empty suites or missing outputs. Native compilation output remains in the project; POMs and versions are not rewritten, and native module build files are not claimed as newly published artifacts. Direct tests do not invoke verify, package snapshots, run quality gates, or include integration-only Failsafe suites. Use oyzu build for that full captured flow. Missing tests/reports, failed native tests or unmet coverage constraints fail the command and retain available current evidence. See direct test boundaries for host output preservation and provenance. Custom JaCoCo destinations and aggregate reactor coverage retain the limitations above. The real Windows probe passed with Maven 3.9.11/JDK 17.0.20.1: the authored reactor, a custom Surefire directory, per-module reports, repeated tests without stale evidence, hooks, a failed assertion, unchanged POMs and inspection. Run python tooling/test-maven-direct.py --cli <compiled-path> --maven-home <maven-home> --repository <native-repository> with tooling/design-requirements.txt installed. Its optional --acquire explicitly provisions fixture dependencies before product execution. CI provisions a pinned Maven distribution with tooling/provision-maven.py and runs this probe on all three hosts after CLI compilation; the direct step passed on all three hosts at 343c682 in run 37052623343 (Linux job 110991301336, macOS 110991301392, Windows 110991301544). These step outcomes do not establish whole-workflow success.

The native extension can be exercised with provisioned Maven/JDK tools: python tooling/test-maven-metadata.py --maven-home <maven-home> --java-home <jdk-home> python tooling/test-maven-metadata.py --maven-home <maven-home> --java-home <jdk-home> --test-lifecycle --repository <prepared-native-repository> The default check needs no downloaded plugins. The lifecycle variant needs its pinned fixture plugins/dependencies in that native repository; adding --acquire explicitly permits a native online clean verify fixture run to provision them before the offline checks. That test setup is distinct from Oyzu's captured acquisition protocol. The lifecycle probe reads effective Surefire/Failsafe directories and checks native XML after offline clean verify: successful tests, a failed integration test and an integration-only module. Native clean removes prior XML and compiled test classes; source preservation, disabled executions and directory containment are also checked. Its coverage cases run forked tests that count actual JaCoCo agents, preserve literal JVM flags and inherited properties, and check paired module coverage with fallback 0.8.13 and inherited active or managed-only native 0.8.15. Native disabled preparation and skip controls remain disabled, without fabricated coverage. This probe does not invoke the compiled report collector or prove normalized bundle reports. Use tooling/test-maven-direct.py with a compiled CLI for direct report collection and the captured Maven acceptance suite for the complete build/report/artifact flow. Historical Windows testing passed the native custom-directory and lifecycle cases. The later captured/full reactor qualification at source 99096a93 passed all nine authored cases through the compiled worker, including normalized reports, coverage ownership, failure gates, source preservation and delivered-JAR consumption. That result is distinct from this native model/XML probe and does not qualify subsequent source changes. Java quality defaults are documented in the shared Java quality reference. Remaining work includes broader test providers, custom/aggregate coverage, generated test roots, private repositories, release policy and complete corpus qualification. The compiled Oyzu worker owns process sequencing and native report composition. Native Java integrations remain embedded assets; Python is not required to execute these builder operations. Rebuild captured images after updating the worker.

Captured preparation explicitly fetches dependencies declared on build plugins from Maven's effective model, in addition to dependency:go-offline. The native metadata extension supplies coordinates using Maven's artifact type/classifier mapping; Rust sequences dependency:get through the acquisition broker. The plugin's build goal is not run to discover those dependencies. Reprovision Maven images with the current metadata extension and CLI together; older metadata without plugin dependency facts fails with a reprovision message. System-scoped plugin dependencies are unsupported by this acquisition path. A dependency selected only by executing plugin code remains undiscovered and can fail the offline build. No online retry is introduced. Spotless's Eclipse-backed formatter steps are one such case: they provision Eclipse P2 bundles from download.eclipse.org and fail with java.net.UnknownHostException. They are unsupported; see Spotless Eclipse P2 artifacts. Private source selection uses the optional Maven session endpoint; without it, standalone Central acquisition remains unchanged. The qualification covers ordinary JAR plugin dependencies. Per-coordinate transitive prefetch can acquire a superset of a plugin's overridden/excluded graph; those configurations and reactor-produced plugin dependencies remain unqualified. See the measured proof.

Some plugins resolve an artifact named in their own configuration while they run, not through declared plugin dependencies. Oyzu prefetches these for a small owned table of known plugin parameters, read from Maven's effective model after native interpolation. The table currently covers: Plugin Parameter Requested type org.codehaus.mojo:animal-sniffer-maven-plugin signature signature com.github.siom79.japicmp:japicmp-maven-plugin oldVersion/dependency Configured type, default jar Both plugin-level and execution-level configuration are read after native inheritance and property expansion. Animal Sniffer accepts the structured form and the groupId:artifactId:version[:classifier] shorthand: <plugin> <groupId>org.codehaus.mojo</groupId> <artifactId>animal-sniffer-maven-plugin</artifactId> <executions> <execution> <goals><goal>check</goal></goals> <configuration> <signature> <groupId>org.codehaus.mojo.signature</groupId> <artifactId>java15</artifactId> <version>1.0</version> </signature> </configuration> </execution> </executions> </plugin> For japicmp, the supported form is an explicit old-version dependency: <oldVersion> <dependency> <groupId>org.jsoup</groupId> <artifactId>jsoup</artifactId> <version>1.23.2</version> <type>jar</type> </dependency> </oldVersion> Place this inside the plugin or execution's <configuration>. Optional classifier and native artifact type are preserved; omitted type means jar. Maven's artifact handler supplies an omitted classifier (test-jar maps to jar:tests); an explicit classifier takes precedence. Acquisition captures the old artifact before offline execution so the native comparator can actually compare it with the new artifact. A successful build alone does not prove comparison: retain japicmp's native output and check that it resolved the configured old version rather than warning that it was unavailable. File-based versions, newVersion, version ranges and versions computed by japicmp are outside this bounded support. The extension reports org.codehaus.mojo.signature:java15:1.0:signature, with the extension from Maven's type mapping, and acquisition fetches it with the same broker-routed dependency:get as declared plugin dependencies. The signature file, or japicmp's old-version JAR, is listed in the dependency snapshot's package inventory. A configured coordinate with a missing field or an expression Maven did not resolve fails preparation and names the plugin; fix the POM or its properties and rebuild. Plugins outside the table, and parameters supplied only on the command line or computed by plugin code, are not discovered and can still fail the offline build. Reprovision the Maven image with the current metadata extension together with the CLI. Run python tooling/test-maven-metadata.py --maven-home <maven-home> --java-home <jdk-home> for the native extension check. The unchanged pinned JUnit4 corpus now has a captured offline build and delivered-JAR consumer proof: the configured signature was prefetched and consumed offline, with native test and coverage reports. Its separate full build failed the native quality gates and exported no artifacts; this is not a full-check or general plugin-closure qualification.

Both behaviors follow the decisions of 2026-10-10. Captured Jsoup execution has measured target-derived OS properties and a usable JDK 17 product. Jackson's protected administrative configuration, snapshot-parent/BOM acquisition and default captured offline product/report/consumer flow pass at source 9ec5efb2 after the native coverage ownership repair. Earlier agent-collision and resource failures remain in the corpus qualification, with exact revisions and limits. These bounded results do not establish full-quality checks, all platform properties or other JDKs.

Some projects inherit a parent that exists only as a snapshot, for example jackson-core, whose jackson-base -SNAPSHOT parent is published to the Sonatype Central Portal snapshot repository and declared in the project's own <repositories>. Captured acquisition routes every repository through one native mirror (mirrorOf *) to Maven Central, which serves no snapshots, so such a build fails preparation by default. An administrator can admit snapshot repositories with the administrative maven.snapshotRepositories setting. It is a set of HTTPS repository base URLs ending in / and is empty, meaning off, by default. Only corporate policy or the protected local admin-settings.json can supply it; project, local, user, machine and invocation configuration cannot enable or widen it, and a project file that names it fails with CONFIG_SCOPE. For example, inside the settings object of admin-settings.json: "maven.snapshotRepositories": { "locked": true, "value": ["https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots/"] } When the set is non-empty: Each URL becomes its own broker source, maven-snapshots-<n> in sorted URL order. URLs with credentials, a query or a fragment, plain HTTP and URLs without a trailing / fail preparation. Admitted repositories cannot carry credentials. The native mirror and its repository identity stay unchanged, so the offline build reads snapshots from the captured repository exactly as it reads releases. The compiled adapter sends only snapshot version paths (group/.../artifact/<version>-SNAPSHOT/...) to the admitted repositories, trying them in order until one returns the file; every other path keeps the Central (or session-approved) route. The admitted repositories, not the URLs the project declares, serve every snapshot the build requests. Maven only requests snapshots when some declared repository enables them, so the project still declares its snapshot repository, as jackson-core does; the mirror replaces its URL. Snapshot inputs are recorded in the dependency snapshot like any other input: each captured .pom, .jar, .module or .signature file beneath a snapshot version directory is listed in the package inventory with the maven-snapshots-<n> source that served it. The admitted repositories are listed under extensions."oyzu.dev/maven".snapshotRepositories. Preparation fails with MAVEN_SNAPSHOT_REPOSITORY, naming the file, when a captured snapshot package was not served by an admitted repository, and acquisition fails when one snapshot directory was served by two repositories. This applies whether or not the setting is on, so a snapshot that a session-approved repository serves on the ordinary route is refused too. Release builds never use snapshot inputs. Preparation checks every module's version decision: if any snapshot input was captured and any decision's intent is not a development snapshot or is production eligible, preparation fails with MAVEN_SNAPSHOT_RELEASE, even when the setting is on. Oyzu has no release-build operation yet, so every captured build is a development snapshot build today; this check fails closed for the release intent that OEP-0013 will add. A build without snapshot inputs is unaffected by the setting. Recovery: without the setting, a snapshot parent or dependency fails native acquisition with Maven's "could not find artifact" error naming the snapshot. Ask an administrator to admit its repository, or depend on a released version.

POMs that use os-maven-plugin properties, such as Netty's parent with <tcnative.classifier>${os.detected.classifier}</tcnative.classifier>, select platform-specific artifacts. A project such as jsoup that imports Netty's dependencies does not run the extension itself, so the expression is never resolved. Where the extension does run, it detects the machine Maven runs on. Captured preparation and execution therefore pass fixed Maven user properties derived from the job's target platform, not the host or toolchain image: Property linux/amd64 linux/arm64 darwin/arm64 windows/amd64 os.detected.name linux linux osx windows os.detected.arch x86_64 aarch_64 aarch_64 x86_64 os.detected.bitness 64 64 64 64 os.detected.classifier linux-x86_64 linux-aarch_64 osx-aarch_64 windows-x86_64 Names follow the plugin's own normalization (kr.motd.maven.os.Detector); other platforms the plugin names, such as linux/ppc64le (ppcle_64) and linux/s390x (s390_64), map the same way, and a target the plugin cannot name fails preparation. The classifier has no Linux distribution suffix (os.detection.classifierWithLikes). The distribution-derived os.detected.release* and kernel os.detected.version* properties are not supplied, because a target platform names neither; a POM that needs them keeps Maven's native behavior. Maven user properties take precedence over the extension's detected values in model interpolation, profile activation and plugin parameters, so ${os.detected.classifier} resolves the same way in every run, including in dependency POMs. A project that declares the extension still runs its host detection; only the four properties above are fixed. The properties are frozen in the prepared tree (properties.json) and listed in the dependency snapshot under extensions."oyzu.dev/maven".userProperties. Artifacts that a plugin downloads from such a property while it runs, outside declared dependencies, are still not prefetched. Direct host tests (oyzu run test) keep native detection. Run python tooling/test-maven-metadata.py --maven-home <maven-home> --java-home <jdk-home> for the native interpolation check of a plugin dependency classifier.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/maven-sessions.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. This client prototype prepares an admitted Maven invocation through oyzu exec and bare mvn in an Oyzu-activated Bash shell. The same endpoint selects the approved source for captured oyzu build dependency acquisition. It requires a separately provisioned local agent; the qualification uses a disposable simulator, not platform login or policy.

Provision Maven 3.9.11 and a JDK with java, javac and jar on the selected launch PATH. Set the endpoint once in user or administrative Oyzu configuration: [maven] sessionEndpoint = "http://127.0.0.1:43199/session" The port is illustrative. The endpoint must be numeric-loopback HTTP without userinfo, query or fragment. Project, local and invocation overrides fail the resolved-authority check. The setting is absent by default, cannot be selected through a profile, and removing it restores ordinary standalone execution. Existing configuration rules exclude user configuration in CI; this proof does not establish CI authentication. No new schema version is introduced. oyzu exec -- /opt/maven/bin/mvn verify # With that native Maven on PATH: eval "$(oyzu activate bash)" mvn verify These examples show the entry points. The settings-composition fixture binds a purpose-built plugin to package; it does not qualify the full default lifecycle. No project authentication files or extension copies are required. Only the installation's mvn executable is supported, not mvnw or arbitrary launch wrappers. Linux with Maven 3.9.11 and JDK 17 is the qualification target. Windows/macOS native execution and Windows session shell shims remain unqualified; the latter are not implemented.

Resolve current Oyzu configuration and native executable. Ask the agent to admit the directory, tool and arguments before preparing or launching Maven, including when the native dependency cache is warm. Receive an ordered set of admitted native mirror mappings. The directory is a context hint, never verified source provenance. Compile/package Oyzu's bundled minimal Java extension against that Maven's libraries. Write a temporary credential-free admission projection. Maven reads its normal user/global settings, including explicit -s/-gs selections. The native execution-request hook compares existing mirrors with admission, preserves blocking mirrors, and installs admitted mirrors plus a blocked catch-all. It retrieves credentials into native memory and supplies Resolver authentication for the admitted mirror ID and exact endpoint. Profiles and properties retain Maven's native merge behavior; Oyzu does not merge policy in the client. Remove temporary source, classes, JAR and admission projection after success or ordinary failure. Native caches and project outputs remain native-owned. The experimental native-launch response is: { "sources": [ { "id": "approved-libraries", "mirrorOf": "company-libraries", "access": { "repository": "https://packages.example.com/maven/", "username": "reader", "credentialEndpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:43199/credential/session" } } ] } Use mirrorOf: "*" for one aggregate repository, or separate mappings for central, company-libraries and company-plugins. Maven matches repository IDs, not artifact group names. The ordered mappings use native mirror precedence; exact matches precede wildcard patterns. IDs and selector strings must be unique, with 1-64 mappings. The reserved oyzu-source-denied ID cannot be supplied. An unmatched repository is blocked, including repositories discovered from POMs. Existing nonblocking mirrors must match an admitted URL, selector and layout; otherwise the invocation fails with settings-file paths. Matching mirrors can have a different local ID; admission owns the effective ID and authentication. Ambient server credentials are not used as a fallback. Native profiles, properties, proxies and JVM configuration remain native-owned; proxy authentication and custom TLS settings are not separately qualified by this proof. Admission uses POST JSON; the extension retrieves a bounded UTF-8 password via GET. This evolves the unreleased prototype response in place: native-launch agent simulators must return sources. Captured acquisition and Gradle retain their existing single-repository response. This is not authenticated IPC or a frozen platform API. Temporary credential locators are access-sensitive even though upstream passwords are absent from those files. Artifact traffic goes directly from Maven to the selected repository. Oyzu is not a package data proxy. Passwords are not placed in settings, arguments or launcher environment variables; Maven and its plugins share a process that can access them. Upstream credentials enforce read-only permission. No hostile-code containment or inability to bypass the managed path is claimed.

Agent denial or unavailability fails before native launch, without a direct fallback or offline grant. Public CLI help and Maven --help/--version do not contact the agent. Native output/exit status follow the existing exec contract; --json returns its captured-child representation. NATIVE_SESSION_CONFIG, NATIVE_SESSION_DENIED, NATIVE_SESSION_UNAVAILABLE and NATIVE_SESSION_INVALID identify configuration/admission transport failures. Correct authorized configuration, restore the agent or resolve its denial. MAVEN_SESSION_INVALID identifies malformed Maven response data; MAVEN_SESSION_PREPARE requires a usable JDK/Maven installation. MAVEN_SESSION_UNSUPPORTED rejects installations without the expected lib directory. MAVEN_SESSION_CONFLICT identifies incompatible mirrors, conflicting mapping identities/selectors, extension overrides or deployment-shaped arguments. Correct the reported settings or admission mapping; publishing belongs to oyzu publish. MAVEN_ARGS and MAVEN_OPTS remain available. Oyzu rejects extension-path replacement through arguments or JVM options and project .mvn/extensions.xml, whose bootstrap downloads can precede the lifecycle hook. Existing .mvn argument files are checked for conflicting extension/deploy options. This is bounded compatibility checking, not a hostile-code sandbox or complete Maven grammar. Arbitrary plugin networking is outside Resolver admission. Wrappers, additional Maven versions, concurrent credential rotation, abrupt termination cleanup and adapter compilation caching remain unqualified/deferred. See settings composition qualification and the historical initial integration proof.

With the endpoint configured at user/admin scope, oyzu build admits a Maven acquisition session before preparation. The experimental request uses tool mvn and arguments ["oyzu-build-acquire"]; this is a purpose marker, not an actual native command. The host retrieves the read credential into memory and supplies Basic authentication to the existing acquisition broker for the selected source. This path requires a credential-free repository base URL ending in /. The preparation worker gets only the repository URL and existing filesystem broker transport. It remains --network=none, as does subsequent execution. The broker mediates acquisition; execution consumes the resulting captured Maven repository offline. Unlike the native-launch path, Maven does not receive the upstream credential. With no endpoint configured, the standalone Maven Central source remains available. Configured denial or failure never falls back to it. Snapshot versions are admitted only from administratively listed snapshot repositories; a snapshot the approved repository serves fails preparation. Preparation is not proof that arbitrary Maven plugins have disclosed every input. A plugin resolving an undeclared coordinate during execution can fail offline. Declare the dependency through the plugin's supported Maven configuration where possible, then build again. Oyzu does not rerun the build online automatically. Publishing remains a separate operation; these sessions do not enable native Maven deploy. This prototype does not establish real-platform authorization, credential rotation, CI provisioning or general dynamic-dependency support. See the captured-flow qualification for the actual build proof and its limits.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/mise-maintenance.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Oyzu owns its tool-provider contract and does not depend on the mise application, maintain a runtime fork pin, or run scheduled fork observation/qualification. The unreleased version-1 identity is defined in src/tools/identity.rs. Source revisions in extracted crate notices are attribution, not runtime inputs. Old development locks must be refreshed with oyzu pin --refresh, followed by oyzu install. Existing installations are retained but never silently assigned the new provider identity. There is no legacy identity fallback or migration layer. Preserve notices and adaptation provenance in oyzu-shell and oyzu-tool-metadata. The historical record preserves previous experiments and decisions. Their runner scripts, nested Cargo project, and fork-observation workflows have been retired; results and notices remain. Standalone metadata-capture and notice-verification utilities remain available for source review, independently of any production mise dependency.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/mocha.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The experimental Node builder detects Mocha from an exact mocha test script, native .mocharc configuration, a mocha section in package.json, or a declared dependency. Configuration files are observed without executing them during discovery. Declared commands, including a compound test script that names only Mocha, have stronger evidence than configuration or dependencies; equally strong conflicting framework evidence fails selection and names the with: {test-framework: <name>} selector. See discovery decisions and selectors.

Keep the existing project and native configuration. No Oyzu test/report section is required: { "scripts": {"test": "mocha"}, "devDependencies": {"mocha": "11.8.0"} } With no test script, a detected Mocha project exposes node node_modules/mocha/bin/mocha.js as its implicit test task. oyzu run list shows it and oyzu run test executes the native development task. Single-package and npm workspace direct tests also collect JUnit and LCOV in a test-only dist/ bundle; see direct test evidence and workspace report ownership. Captured builds require a declared, captured Mocha dependency. Mocha 11 is the qualified API family, tested at 11.8.0. The common Node toolchain includes c8 10.1.3 for coverage. A project-installed c8 takes precedence and must be version 10.x; a declared but missing c8 fails instead of silently using the fallback. Rebuild tooling/images/node-quality and its npm/pnpm/Yarn descendant images after updating the toolchain lockfile. No build action downloads reporting tools. Host adapter probes and direct tests use OYZU_NODE_REPORTING_HOME to locate explicitly provisioned fallback tooling when the project does not supply c8. This is a prerequisite for automatic direct coverage; a missing reporter fails explicitly.

Captured actions and direct tests run the native test command under c8. Recognized scripts retain their package manager's lifecycle behavior. Mocha loads native test configuration and plugins in the test action. The reporter adapter composes the configured native reporter with Mocha's own XUnit reporter, preserving native reporter options without implementing an XML serializer or test counters. This qualified adapter uses Mocha 11's native option loader to recover reporter selection; configuration evaluation and lifecycle counts have regression checks. c8 retains native include/exclude scope, source-map handling and thresholds from package metadata or configuration files. It writes required LCOV into a fresh private directory; configured alternate coverage formats are not additionally exported. Without a native all setting, c8's default denominator covers loaded source files, not necessarily every repository file. Configure broader scope natively when needed. See c8's options and Mocha's XUnit reporter. The engine collects JUnit and LCOV under dist/<target>/<platform>/reports/ and records paths, digests and summaries in the manifest. Failed assertions retain available reports and block packaging. A failed native coverage threshold also fails the action even when all tests passed. Configuration/startup failures cannot reuse an earlier invocation's reports. Correct the native failure and rerun; action logs and diagnostics explain missing evidence. Successful builds retain the ordinary versioned Node package artifact. Build, test, lint and read-only formatting remain ordinary builder stages. ESLint fallback rules recognize Mocha globals in conventional test directories and test/spec files; native lint configuration remains authoritative.

Automatic captured adaptation recognizes bare mocha, its known direct Node entrypoint and equivalent exact task overrides. Arbitrary shell programs and scripts with additional flags retain their bodies and must satisfy their report contract without guessed rewriting. Native configuration is the supported customization path for recognized invocations. Watch mode is disabled. Parallel Mocha reporting requires further integration and fails explicitly where detected. Browser runners and every custom reporter form are not qualified by this initial profile. npm workspaces compose implicit and recognized scripted Mocha suites using the same reporting adapter. Each member resolves its native runner, configuration and c8 coverage scope from its own directory, including hoisted installations. A publishable root without a test script has a separate implicit suite that excludes workspace members and engine state through native Mocha --ignore options. Existing native exclusions remain in force. Explicit scripts retain their native selection, including --file entries that Mocha does not filter through --ignore. An explicit root test script owns a single aggregate report pair. Otherwise each package receives its own JUnit/LCOV pair; assertion failures retain sibling results and block artifact collection. See npm workspace ownership and Mocha 11 file selection. Native configuration is executable project code. Development tasks run on the host; captured tests use the prepared offline sandbox. Reporting receives no upstream credential or acquisition channel. Report integrity does not establish release eligibility. tooling/test-mocha-reporting.py --cli <compiled-path> explicitly provisions fixture dependencies and checks discovery, no-script tasks, reporter preservation, configuration/lifecycle counts, escaped/skipped/failed tests, LCOV, coverage thresholds and startup failure. It also exercises the workspace fixture through compiled development tasks and the native reporting adapter, including package scope and root-script precedence. CI runs it after CLI compilation on Windows, macOS and Linux. The Node captured-build suite separately builds the single-package and workspace fixtures, verifies snapshot package versions/reports, and rejects assertion/threshold failures. Consult implementation status for completed checks; registration is not proof of passing execution.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/node-applications.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The experimental node/app builder declares a versioned directory artifact for a recognized Vite build or an explicitly selected application with a custom native build script. No output section or new Oyzu setting is required. This supports standalone package roots, including native Vite 8 configurations and the conventional dist/ contract below; native workspace application outputs and automatic custom-script output inference remain unfinished. Platform matrices can select matching provisioned Node images through toolchain selection; the Docker suite has verified the authored EX-050 graph with amd64 and ARM execution.

For a project whose native script writes dist/, application intent is sufficient: builds: frontend: uses: node/app path: frontend The authored directory example uses "build": "node build.mjs". Oyzu runs the native script through its selected manager, then stages the contents of frontend/dist/ as the primary directory artifact application-<snapshot-version>. A consumer using materialize: [{from: frontend, to: site}] receives site/index.html, without a nested dist directory. This is a documented convention selected by explicit application intent, not static interpretation of arbitrary JavaScript. Custom scripts retain native lifecycle semantics and can use compound commands supported by their manager. The output must be a freshly produced contained directory. Missing output, a file in place of the directory, linked entries or special files fail packaging; previous bundle contents cannot satisfy the new build. Build/test/lint/read-only format gates still apply, and the default quality checks exclude the generated dist. Browser globals are not inferred merely from the application selection. Static content alone does not prove platform independence: the current artifact retains its execution platform, and multi-platform reuse remains unimplemented. The npm builder's own fixed dist collector has a native read contract for that tree and stages its artifact under the engine-owned output mount. On supported hosts it can run confined; a project command, another manager or a different output directory cannot borrow that model. Distributed safe repetition still requires every executed action's admitted facts, rather than inferring it from directory output or a successful cache lookup. Discovery exposes builder_selection: explicit and the dist-application output profile. A recognized framework such as Vite has stronger output evidence and keeps its native adapter and validation. Explicit node/package retains native archive packaging. For compatibility, an automatically inferred Node target with an unknown custom script still uses native package output; add uses: node/app only when the script follows this directory convention. A custom non-dist output requires further native output integration; no new general-purpose output configuration is introduced here. Node workspaces continue to use native workspace package planning rather than this single-root application profile.
documents.s: Custom build scripts and the dist convention

documents.t: A package with a captured vite dependency and "scripts": {"build": "vite build"} uses Vite's native dist output. Ordinary package discovery selects node/app, so a standalone project needs no build.yaml. The authored frontend/image variant demonstrates a grouped consumer: builds: frontend: uses: node/app path: frontend image: uses: docker/image path: image materialize: - from: frontend to: site The image's Dockerfile can use COPY site/ /site/. It receives site/index.html and the generated assets, with no extra dist layer. The consumer uses the producer's recorded artifact identity and matching execution platform. The executor assembles the private BuildKit context from selected source files plus explicit materializations. Directory inputs retain all artifact descendants, including empty directories and names such as dist that source capture normally excludes. It rejects linked inputs, collisions and paths outside the image target; combined inputs are bounded to 100,000 selected entries and 10 GiB of file bytes. Directory copying uses the shared snapshot traversal and verifies that its content identity did not change during the copy. Native source ignore rules do not filter explicit artifact inputs. For a different directory, use the native script vite build --outDir public-site. The currently recognized grammar is exactly vite build with an optional literal --outDir <path>. Paths must be contained, portable and use ASCII letters/digits, slash, underscore, hyphen or dot; parent/dot segments, absolute paths, shell expansion, quoting and compound commands are not interpreted. Vite defines the native default and outDir option; Oyzu does not assume that every Node build script follows that convention. Static discovery records the output profile and configuration-file evidence without executing project code. Unsupported Vite flags still fail captured planning with an explicit diagnostic. Unknown custom scripts follow the intent/convention rules above, and explicit node/package retains a package archive even with a Vite script. These are compatibility limits, not complete application packaging support.

Existing vite.config.js, .ts, .mjs, .mts, .cjs and .cts files use Vite's own loader. For example, the configuration overlay selects web/production from the native mode and emits an extra asset through a Vite plugin. Neither discovery nor dependency acquisition evaluates that configuration. After dependency installation in the private offline workspace, preparation replaces the private package's build script with an Oyzu wrapper. The native manager still invokes its prebuild/build/postbuild lifecycle. The wrapper calls Vite 8's native builder API and observes its resolved configuration and written output. The original checkout is unchanged. A literal --outDir retains native precedence over the configuration's output directory. Package-manager behavior still determines which lifecycle hooks run. The plan names application-<snapshot-version> before execution. Native configuration determines an intermediate output location during execution; after a successful build, packaging copies that directory into the planned artifact. The second artifact, build-metadata, is vite-output-<snapshot-version>.json with media type application/vnd.oyzu.vite-output.v1+json. Its bounded record includes schema version, kind, Vite version, snapshot version, native root, output directory and mode. Both artifacts participate in bundle integrity checks. Consumers that omit an artifact name still select primary. The current adapter requires one finite client environment and directory output. Native root/output must remain within the captured target without linked parents. Library/SSR builds, multiple environments, watch mode and write: false fail explicitly. Bundler output options must agree with the resolved directory; the adapter checks before writing and again when observing written output. Native plugins remain executable project code subject to the sandbox, not trusted release evidence. A failed build does not produce a successful output record.
