Missing, malformed or version-mismatched metadata fails packaging; correct the native configuration or failed operation and rerun the build. Vite versions outside major 8 require another qualified API adapter.

oyzu run list exposes native build and test scripts, inferred lint/read-only format checks and explicit mutating formatting. oyzu build retains the existing dependency preparation, native build, test, lint and format-check gates before packaging. For recognized Vite projects, fallback ESLint includes browser globals alongside Node globals. The selected native output directory is excluded from implicit quality traversal; supplied native scripts/configurations remain authoritative. After a captured build, implicit quality tasks use its recorded output. Before that record exists, explicit quality execution resolves native configuration in production build mode; this can execute configuration code on the host for development tasks, or inside the sandbox for captured tasks. Listing tasks remains non-executing. See Node quality. Native Node tests produce JUnit and LCOV through the existing reporting adapter. The versioned primary artifact appears beneath dist/<target>/<platform>/application-<snapshot-version> in the build bundle, for the platform the target was built for (see the bundle layout); consult its manifest path rather than constructing this path in consumers. Only the selected native output tree is staged. Source, dependencies and tests are not automatically copied into that artifact. Failed tests or quality checks block artifact publication to the bundle; collected failure reports remain available. The manifest records kind: directory, version, producing action, complete inventory and logical tree digest. Collection and oyzu inspect dist use the shared directory integrity contract. Missing output, links, special file types and oversized staging fail packaging. A failed operation can leave partial unrecorded output; it is not a valid artifact. materialize copies verified content into a fresh consumer context and retains producer evidence references. This does not prove platform independence or production release eligibility.

Oyzu can resolve and install Node and supported npm/pnpm releases through shared tool management. Automatic native build preflight is currently limited to npm node/app targets with the conventional dist-application profile; other application profiles retain the captured path. Development tasks require an existing compatible tool selection, native project dependencies and quality tooling. Installing Node does not install every project's test or quality dependencies. See native local builds for selection, offline behavior and admission limits, and fresh-checkout qualification for measured empty-store results. The authored variant pins Vite 8.3.2 and npm 11.11.0, with Node >=22.12. Captured acceptance uses the provisioned Node 22/npm image, the quality image, Docker metadata tooling and the isolated BuildKit worker described in builder verification. CI provisions those tools explicitly before invoking the already compiled CLI; automatic acquisition covers only the published toolchain images. Dependencies are acquired through the selected native manager's existing broker/capture flow before isolated execution. Build actions replay prepared dependencies offline; this output integration introduces no new download route or credential channel. Native project build scripts remain executable project code and receive the existing sandbox restrictions. Vite SSR/library modes and compound Vite-command recognition, native workspace application output and cross-platform directory reuse need further integration. Windows transfer of Unix executable directory metadata retains the shared directory limitation. python tooling/test-node-conventional-application.py --cli <compiled-oyzu-path> exercises the custom script's actual native build/test/quality tasks and directory staging on the host, including missing/wrong-kind output failures. The captured Node suite also builds the authored frontend target, then a single-platform consumer variant, checks versioned directory and OCI contents, repeatability and missing-output failure. These are separate scopes: host staging does not prove isolated execution, and the single-platform variant does not establish full EX-050 matrix acceptance. See implementation status for revision-specific results. Rust checks cover non-executing discovery, literal output arguments, package/application distinction and configured output declarations. tooling/test-node-application.py --cli <compiled-path> executes native Vite development tasks and staging, including browser lint, native configuration/plugin assets, npm lifecycle hooks, output overrides, quality exclusions and rejected failures. CI runs that probe on Windows, macOS and Linux. The Docker acceptance suite builds the plain and configured variants, verifies actual image bytes against the directory manifest, JUnit/coverage, repeatability, custom outDir, metadata, tampering and failed-producer rejection. The configured native probe uses Vite 8.3.2 with an ESM config; every supported native loader form and package manager still needs equivalent qualification. See implementation status for checks actually completed; test registration alone does not establish acceptance. The original custom script's two-platform execution is covered separately below. The Docker suite additionally runs the original EX-050 two-platform configuration with matching provisioned amd64/ARM Node images. It requires independently executed tests/coverage and quality, two directory snapshots, exact Docker copies, a complete OCI index and repeatability. These checks passed at revision ad6cbf1 in Docker job 110868387899. This does not establish platform-independent directory reuse or complete every authored negative case.

A project that pins Node ([tools] node = "22.12", locked with oyzu install node@22.12) runs on that exact Node in the captured worker, not the image's copy. Preparation reads the Linux (linux/amd64/gnu) archive recorded for the pinned version in oyzu.lock, downloads it through the tool broker unless a copy cached under the user data directory still matches the locked SHA-256, verifies the bytes against the locked digest and restores them read-only at /scratch/nodetool. The directory is added to PATH just before the image's system directories, so the package manager the image provisions (its pinned npm, pnpm or Yarn, found earlier on PATH) keeps running and only the runtime changes; the same environment applies to preparation and every build action. The plan records the archive under oyzu.dev/locked-tool, so a different pin or archive changes the action identity. Without a pin, the Node that build preflight locks using the LTS preference and engine constraints described below is used the same way; an engine range with no matching LTS release can select a newer stable runtime even though the image carries Node 22. A project whose existing oyzu.lock has no Node entry, a managed build or a non-Linux worker uses the image's Node. Other Node versions are tested with verification toolsets, which run natively and never in the captured worker. Oyzu's own test reporting passes Node 22 flags (--test-coverage-exclude), so a pin older than Node 22 builds but its native test stage fails with bad option. Pin Node 22 or later when tests run. Verified on Windows 11 with Docker Desktop and the npm image (Node 22.23.3, npm 11.11.0): with node = "22.12" locked, preparation observed Node 22.12.0 under npm 11.11.0 and the native test stage ran on it (a test asserting v22.12. passed and one asserting the image's v22.23. failed); with no pin the image's Node was observed; a changed lock digest was refused; the cached archive was reused. Only the npm image was exercised: the pnpm and Yarn images are not provisioned on that machine, so their PATH handling is untested. Only linux/amd64 workers are admitted, and offline builds need the archive already cached. Without a configuration pin, the default request is lts whether or not engines.node is present. It selects the greatest stable release with a non-empty string in Node's index.json lts field that satisfies every engine constraint. If no LTS release satisfies them, it falls back to the greatest stable release satisfying them. For example, with 24.x marked LTS and 26.x Current, >=22 selects 24.x and >=26 falls back to 26.x. The preference follows publisher data without a compiled-in major. node = "latest", node = "26", exact pins and lts/<name> retain their existing selection behavior and must satisfy engines. .nvmrc and .node-version are not read yet. build --plan explains the LTS default and fallback rule in the requirement source; pin previews and locks retain the lts request. A matching lock keeps its exact version, including a stable fallback, without consulting today's LTS metadata; engine constraints still validate offline. A previous default * request does not match the new lts default; preflight must resolve the new request online before an offline build can use it. Standalone indexed resolution uses the same publisher selection, then looks for that exact release in the signed index. Under an organization catalog the signed index currently has no LTS markers: use an approved exact version or named line such as lts/krypton; the moving alias fails with TOOL_LTS_METADATA_UNAVAILABLE without contacting a publisher outside the catalog. All repository Node image definitions (quality, npm, pnpm and Yarn) and the builder-worker image install Debian libatomic1, needed by newer Node binaries. Rebuild provisioned images to pick this up; existing tags and published digest pins do not change when a Dockerfile changes. Node 26 execution and worker-death qualification remain pending for the #289/#290 fix; see the qualification record.
documents.s: Pinned Node in the captured worker

documents.t: A locked npm or pnpm release, selected under [tools] or by an exact packageManager, runs in the captured worker in place of the image's manager, on the same Node the section above selects. It is restored read-only beside Node and recorded under oyzu.dev/locked-manager. See npm and pnpm installation for the paths and limits.
documents.s: Pinned npm and pnpm in the captured worker

documents.t: See native local builds for the bounded host profiles, prerequisites, artifact differences and multi-target evidence behavior. This is separate from the isolated packaging contracts above.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/node-quality.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Node builders expose implicit lint, format-check and explicitly mutating format tasks. This experimental integration serves single packages using npm, pnpm or Yarn and npm workspace composition. It does not make all package-manager workspace forms supported. Native scripts and TOML task replacements retain precedence; no additional Oyzu quality section is required.

Separate static detectors select the linter and formatter. ESLint and Prettier are defaults; their native configuration provides stronger evidence. A biome.json or biome.jsonc selects Biome for both roles. Conflicting native evidence for the same role fails discovery rather than choosing by registration order. Discovery reads configuration evidence without executing JavaScript configuration or launching tools. From the package or npm workspace root: oyzu run list oyzu run lint oyzu run format-check oyzu run format An explicit format:check script retains that task name. Build planning treats it as the read-only formatting operation. Implicit checks reject extra arguments before executing a checker; use a native package script or explicit argv task for custom flags. This prevents forwarded arguments from changing a lint/check request into a formatting write. Custom scripts have their own effects; Oyzu does not infer that an arbitrary script is read-only from its name. oyzu build includes lint and read-only formatting as gates before final artifact collection. A native failure remains a failed action and blocks collected artifacts. format is never automatically selected as a build stage. Explicit formatting can leave partial changes when a later file or package fails; it is not a transactional operation.

Integration Provisioned default Current adapter behavior ESLint 10.11.0, with pinned recommended JS/TS support Native configuration when present; recommended JS/TS rules otherwise; no automatic fixes Prettier 3.9.9 Native configuration, EditorConfig and ignore files; check or explicit formatting Biome 2.5.15 Biome 2 native lint and format commands; native configuration and ignores; only explicit format adds --write Project-installed packages take precedence, including native hoisted resolution. A tool declared in the current package but missing from its installed dependencies fails instead of silently using a fallback version. Other unavailable tools can use an explicitly provisioned directory identified by OYZU_NODE_QUALITY_HOME. That directory must contain the toolchain package.json and installed node_modules; Oyzu does not download checkers during a build or development task. The authoritative default versions and native dependency lock are in the quality toolchain. To provision the development defaults yourself: npm ci --ignore-scripts --no-audit --no-fund --prefix tooling/images/node-quality Set OYZU_NODE_QUALITY_HOME to that directory's absolute path when invoking development tasks outside the repository. For captured builds, first build the common image with docker build -t oyzu-toolchain/node:quality tooling/images/node-quality, then the relevant npm/pnpm/Yarn image as described in the CLI reference. The image identity binds the provisioned defaults. Biome's optional platform binary packages must be present; missing binaries fail without an installation fallback. Its upstream wrapper selects the native binary; Oyzu does not copy that platform-selection implementation. Local verification uses Windows with provisioned Node 24/npm 11; CI uses Node 22 and runs CLI/native task checks on Windows, macOS and Linux. Captured build scenarios run separately on Linux. The listed defaults are exact tested versions, not proof that every version in their major range works. Legacy ESLint configuration needs an installed compatible ESLint 8/9 or migration to flat configuration. The Biome adapter rejects non-2.x packages; other 2.x versions still require native compatibility verification.

Implicit quality checks currently select JS/JSX/TS/TSX and their CommonJS/ESM extensions. They do not format JSON, CSS or other non-code files, even where the native tool supports them. Captured builds project versions into package metadata, so original-metadata formatting needs a distinct source-validation contract; it is not silently inferred from rewritten build inputs. Broader formatting is available through an explicitly authored native script, and automatic non-code coverage remains work. Source traversal excludes dependency directories, .git, .oyzu, .oyzu-build, dist, build and coverage output, and never follows source symlinks. It is bounded to 100,000 source candidates. npm workspace root defaults exclude member roots, and member defaults exclude nested members; scripts retain their own scope. See npm workspaces for composition and failure behavior. Detected Mocha projects receive Mocha globals in fallback ESLint rules for conventional test/tests directories and test/spec files. Custom test locations can declare native lint configuration. The common toolchain also provisions c8 for captured Mocha coverage; that integration belongs to the reporting adapter and does not run during lint or formatting. ESLint preserves native configuration and uses Node globals for fallback rules, plus Jest globals for inferred test files. Recognized Vite applications also receive browser globals, and their inferred native output directory is excluded from implicit checks. Prettier respects native options and ignores. Biome receives explicit file arguments and applies its native configuration/ignore rules; it does not use stdin mode, which has different ignore semantics. Biome invocations are split into bounded argument batches for host compatibility, retaining failure if any batch fails. Unsupported/ignored files can yield no applicable check; native output and actual exit status are retained, not synthesized lint results. Native configurations and plugins can execute their own code where the native tool supports that. Development tasks execute on the host with the task environment. Captured actions use the prepared offline execution environment, and these quality adapters do not introduce network acquisition or credential delivery. Global inherited configuration, every plugin form and complete cross-manager configuration inheritance still require further qualification. For configured Vite applications, implicit checks exclude the output location recorded by the captured native build. When that record does not yet exist, the explicit quality task resolves Vite configuration in production build mode to obtain the exclusion, preserving a recognized native --outDir override. That resolution may execute native configuration code, just as native checker configurations can; it never happens during discovery or task listing. Invalid output metadata or an uncontained configured output fails the check instead of silently expanding the source scope.

Oyzu enables native coverage collection for the required report. Vitest may scan source files that no test imports, so its test action retains the complete target source view through the existing target-directory fallback. This applies even when the project omits coverage.enabled or sets it to false. Test discovery facts remain available, but they do not narrow away files needed by native coverage. The project's include/exclude rules, reporters and thresholds still belong to Vitest; Oyzu does not reinterpret or waive their result. Other stages retain their own input contracts. The Node Vitest reporting adapter caps the selected native suite at one worker. This is a global concurrency setting for suites using this adapter; it does not change test selection, the TypeScript prelude, project test-timeout settings (including Hono's unchanged 5,000 ms limit), configuration, coverage, JUnit/LCOV reporting, or failure and publication gates. Serializing workers may make some suites slower under the unchanged 600-second action deadline. The Hono qualification record includes a passing ordinary product and later passing two-product proof, as well as an intervening failed attempt under this cap. These observations do not establish the timeout's underlying cause or a general timing guarantee. python tooling/test-node-quality.py --cli target/debug/oyzu python tooling/test-biome-quality.py --cli target/debug/oyzu python tooling/test-npm-workspace-tasks.py --cli target/debug/oyzu Use target/debug/oyzu.exe on Windows. The Biome probe checks native JSONC configuration, real lint/format failures, unchanged input bytes during checks, explicit formatting, native ignores, private-state exclusions, argument guards, batched failure retention and installed-tool precedence. Workspace checks mix inferred tools with scripts. Native probe success alone does not establish sandbox execution; the separate CI build cases verify snapshot packages, reports and failed gates through the compiled CLI. For a missing declared tool, install the project's native dependencies and retry. For a missing default, provision the toolchain explicitly. For conflicting evidence, resolve the competing native configurations or select the tool in build.yaml with with: {linter: <name>} or with: {formatter: <name>}, as the error states; task overrides do not bypass ambiguous static discovery. See discovery selectors. Native diagnostics remain authoritative for invalid configuration and failed rules. Revision-specific results and remaining gaps are recorded in implementation status. Native integration reference: Biome CLI.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/node-static-analysis.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Status: experimental, OEP-0020 slices S1 to S4 and S5 step C. The design lives in OEP-0020; this page describes only what is implemented and measured. Nothing here is a stable contract, and the analysis does not yet change caching, selection or sandboxing. S1 added the fact model, manifest/tsconfig/import-graph analysis and the plan view. S2 added framework profiles, the constant evaluator, environment-file rules and per-stage narrowing for test. S3 added the script graph and exact TypeScript input sets. S4 added advisory diagnostic rules. S5 step C added rule levels, suppressions and oyzu build --check.
documents.s: Node static analysis in oyzu build --plan

documents.t: oyzu build --plan now ends each Node target with a Static analysis section: for each stage it lists the files the stage is predicted to read, the paths it writes, the environment variables it reads, the workspace targets it depends on, the tools it needs and anything the analysis could not bound. Every line carries its confidence and source (file:line). The analysis reads and parses files. It never runs project code, scripts, package managers or the network, and it is read-only. Confidence Meaning exact Proven from literal text (for example copyFileSync("../shared/src/greeting.mjs", ...)). over-approximate A superset that contains the truth (a glob, several resolution candidates, a bounded dynamic import). unknown Not pinned down (computed require, computed file path, a command the analyzer does not model). unknown only ever widens; it never removes another fact. An unknown with a bound (a missing relative import, an unexpanded test pattern, a command with no tool profile) widens a confined stage only by that bound (rung widened); one without a bound widens the stage to the whole target scope. See bounded unknowns.

oyzu build --plan api # analysis for every stage of the target oyzu build --plan api --stage build # one stage oyzu build --plan api --why ../shared/src/greeting.mjs oyzu build --plan api --unknown # only unknown and over-approximate facts oyzu build --plan api --facts # raw facts, one table row per fact oyzu build --plan api --no-analysis # skip analysis; whole-target scope oyzu build --plan api --json # everything, including the full analysis record All five flags require --plan and are read-only. --why accepts a path relative to the target (../shared/src/x.mjs) or to the repository root. Its answer per stage is input (facts name it), not-an-input, covered-by-bound (no fact names it but the bound of an unknown fact covers it), or covered-only-by-fallback (no fact names it but an unbounded unknown fact widens the stage to the whole target). Example (EX-033, examples/builds/affected-graph/variants/targets): api:build · confidence: over-approximate · scope: predicted 10 exact, 1 over-approximate, 0 unknown Reads Path or name Confidence Source Why package.json exact api/package.json manifest ../shared/src/greeting exact api/build.mjs:3 file-read · copyFileSync · outside the target directory .mjs build.mjs exact api/package.json:7 script-entry ! ../shared/src/greeting.mjs is outside api/. Declare it as a source input or a dependency, ... The api target never declares ../shared, yet its build script copies it; the analysis reports it as an exact read with the script line that does it.

A normal oyzu build analyzes the captured snapshot after capture and before planning, silently. In S1 it only reports: unknown facts and analysis failures are logged at debug level (--log-level debug) with the file, line, construct and what widens. A build is never failed or changed by the analysis. build --plan does not capture source, so it analyzes the working tree through the same bounded reader and says so ("analyzed from the working tree"). The preview inventories the tree from metadata alone (paths, kinds and sizes, with capture's exclusions and path checks) and opens only the files analysis reads, so planning a large checkout costs a directory walk, not a read of every file. The reader checks each file it reads against the inventoried size. The preview and a captured snapshot of an unchanged tree yield identical facts and diagnostics; this is checked by the preview_and_captured_snapshot_yield_identical_facts test. Only the record's snapshotDigest differs: for the working tree it is the inventory digest (domain oyzu.tree-inventory.v1alpha1, over paths, kinds and sizes), never a captured tree's digest, and it does not change when a file's bytes change at the same size.

Layer Facts package.json, lockfiles, rc files manifest and ancestor manifests, lockfiles, engines/packageManager tools, main/module/types/bin/exports entry points, files as outputs, workspace:/file:/workspace-name dependencies (depends-on-target) Workspace graph workspaces globs and pnpm-workspace.yaml members; bare imports of members resolve to their exports/main (every condition) Scripts build, test, lint (plus pre/post hooks) read with the closed script grammar tsconfig extends chain, include/exclude/files expansion against the snapshot, paths aliases, references, outDir/tsBuildInfoFile outputs Import graph static import, export … from, require, literal import(), import x = require(); relative, alias and workspace specifiers; every resolution candidate is kept (all extensions, TypeScript .js→.ts mapping, index files) Literal file access fs read/write/copy/stat/readdir calls with constant paths ("…", path.join(__dirname, …), import.meta.dirname, new URL(…, import.meta.url), process.cwd()); computed paths are unknown Environment process.env.X, process.env["X"], import.meta.env.X, destructuring; computed keys and whole-object use are unknown Dynamic access require(expr)/import(expr): a template with a literal directory prefix is bounded to that directory (over-approximate), anything else is unknown; child_process calls are unknown Paths in facts are snapshot-relative POSIX paths, so facts are identical across checkout paths and hosts. Only the build, test and lint script stages are modeled.

Human output follows the shared presentation standard: outcome first, aligned lossless tables, labelled confidence, readable without color. --json adds an analysis object to the build-preview document: analyzedFrom (working-tree or captured-snapshot), snapshotDigest, per-target stage views with confidence, fallback (predicted or target-directory) and counts, the query, diagnostics and record, the complete analysis record. The record follows the draft analysis schema (v1alpha1, evolved in place; no version was introduced). Real output was validated against that schema during S1.

Rules read the facts and report problems that are only visible across files and targets. They are advisory by default: a finding never fails oyzu build --plan, and fails oyzu build --check or oyzu build only when you set its rule to enforce (rule levels). Findings are the record's diagnostics (rule, severity, message, facts), so they appear with the existing view and in --json: Warning (phantom-dependency): app:build imports `left-pad` at packages/app/build.mjs:2, but packages/app/package.json does not declare it; it resolves today only because package.json declares it and the package manager hoists it. Fix: add `left-pad` to the dependencies of packages/app/package.json. facts lists the ids of the facts behind the finding, so --json consumers can walk from a finding to its evidence. Variable names appear in messages, never values. Rule Reports Evidence phantom-dependency A bare package import the importing file's own package.json does not declare (dependencies, devDependencies, peerDependencies, optionalDependencies, bundled, its own name, or the matching @types package). The message names the ancestor manifest that declares it when the import works only through hoisting diagnostic-evidence from the Node import graph escaping-reference An import, import glob, CSS reference or literal file read that leaves the target's directory when the target has no workspace dependency (workspace:, file: or a matching version) on the package that holds the path reads-path/reads-glob marked outside the target, depends-on-target undeclared-env A literal process.env.X/import.meta.env.X read in project source for a name that no task environment of that stage sets and no environment file the stage reads defines. NODE_ENV, MODE, BASE_URL, DEV, PROD, SSR and CI are never reported. A computed name is a note: "could not verify" reads-env, environment-file facts, task environment names public-env-secret-name A variable inlined into browser output (VITE_, NEXT_PUBLIC_, PUBLIC_, NUXT_PUBLIC_) whose name has a SECRET, TOKEN, PASSWORD or PRIVATE segment. A bare KEY is not reported, so publishable keys are left alone reads-env with a public prefix exports-target-missing A main, module, types, bin or exports path that is neither in the source nor under anything the build is known to write. When the build's outputs are not known the finding is a note that says it could not be verified entry-point, writes-path output-outside-declared A build-stage script or source write (writeFileSync, mkdirSync, ...) to a path outside every output location the build is known to use: a compiler outDir, a framework output or generated directory, warm state. A target with no known output location is not judged writes-path (file-write) against the target's other writes-path and warm-state facts config-unreadable A configuration file (framework config, tsconfig, manifest, environment file, test-runner config such as next/jest) the analysis could not read statically. Always a note: the stage falls back to the whole target dynamic-access unknown script-wrapper-opaque A script step the closed shell grammar cannot resolve (for example a redirection). Always a note dynamic-access unknown (script-command, script-graph) lockfile-manifest-drift The nearest lockfile no longer follows from the target's package.json: a declared range differs from, or is missing in, what the lockfile recorded, or the recorded range matches but the locked version does not satisfy it. Read: npm-shrinkwrap.json/package-lock.json (version 2 or 3; all four dependency sections), pnpm-lock.yaml (version 5 to 9; the importer's specifiers), yarn berry yarn.lock (the workspace entry, with regular, dev and optional dependencies merged as berry records them, plus peers) and yarn classic yarn.lock (each declared name@range must be an entry). The fix names the manager's command (npm install --package-lock-only, pnpm install --lockfile-only, yarn install, yarn install --mode=update-lockfile). What cannot be judged is never reported: the version check skips non-semver specs (tags, git, URLs, file:, link:, workspace:, catalog:, npm: aliases), prerelease locked versions and packages under npm overrides, yarn resolutions or pnpm overrides; the range comparison skips workspace members and links in a classic lock and unquoted YAML specs that parse as numbers (cypress: 4); npm lockfile version 1, pnpm lockfiles outside version 5 to 9, a berry lock without the target's workspace entry and lockfiles that do not parse yield nothing diagnostic-evidence from manifest and lockfile redundant-declaration A build.yaml inputs entry that lies inside the target's own directory, which is always captured. An input outside the directory is never reported (capture needs it). Exact reads the analysis already found under the input are cited authored inputs, target directory, reads-path Severity is warning for a violation and note when the rule could not decide. A finding resting on an over-approximate fact says so in its message. Tool-owned reads (BROWSERSLIST, manifests, configuration) are not source reads and are never reported by these rules. Enforcement gate (NSA-09). Only a warning from an enforced rule whose cited facts are all exact may block a build (rules::blocking, called by the check step). Every catalogued rule is implemented except where noted per row. Limits: phantom-dependency compares manifests only, because installed node_modules are not in the snapshot, so it cannot confirm that the import resolves through hoisting today; a package imported from a file whose nearest package.json is not the one you expected (nested packages) is judged against that nearest manifest. escaping-reference ignores authored inputs (they are accepted but not consumed until S5), so a path you already list there is still reported. exports-target-missing does not expand exports patterns containing *.

Experimental. Policy about rules is configuration, so it lives in the oyzu.toml cascade (see configuration); the names follow the design. [analysis.rules] phantom-dependency = "enforce" # off | advisory (default) | enforce [[analysis.suppress]] rule = "escaping-reference" path = "legacy/**" # optional glob over the finding's file reason = "vendored fork, tracked in the migration plan" # required Level Meaning off The rule's findings are dropped from --check and from build logs advisory Reported, never fails anything (the default for every rule) enforce A blocking finding fails oyzu build --check and oyzu build A finding is blocking only if its rule is enforce, it is a warning (never a note), and every fact it cites is exact. An enforced finding that rests on an over-approximate or unknown fact is reported as not blocking with its confidence and never fails a build; --check counts those so enforcement is never silently weaker than it looks. A suppression needs a rule and a non-empty reason; path is a project-relative glob (* stays within a directory, ** crosses directories) over the file the finding cites first, and omitting it covers every file. A suppressed finding does not fail and is listed under Suppressed (with its reason in --json as suppressedBy). A suppression that matches no finding is reported as a stale note and never fails a build. Suppression changes reporting only; it never changes a stage input or cache key. oyzu build --check # analyze and apply the rules; runs nothing oyzu --json build --check # the build --plan --json document plus a `check` object oyzu build --check is static analysis only: it prepares, installs, downloads and executes nothing. Selection follows build --plan (targets, --affected); it cannot be combined with --plan or the analysis view flags. Exit status is 0 unless at least one finding is blocking (1); usage errors keep their exit status 2, and help, version and syntax errors finish before any project is opened. If analysis cannot complete, --check fails with that error rather than reporting a pass. ✗ Check failed: 1 blocking finding in enforced rules phantom-dependency · enforce Blocking packages/app/build.mjs:2 app:build imports `left-pad` at packages/app/build.mjs:2, but ... Fix: add `left-pad` to the dependencies of packages/app/package.json. The check object in --json has outcome (passed or failed), counts (blocking, advisory, nonBlocking, suppressed, staleSuppressions), findings (rule, level, severity, status, target, path, line, message, fix, confidence, and suppressedBy when suppressed) and staleSuppressions. A normal oyzu build applies the same levels, through the same function, to the snapshot it captured (or, for native host builds that capture nothing, to the working tree it observes) before any action runs. A blocking finding stops the build with the same file, line and fix and the failed bundle records it. Advisory findings stay in the debug log. A native host build that enforces no rule skips this analysis. Limits: Only the ten implemented rules can be named; an unknown id, a level other than the three, an empty reason, an unknown suppression field or an invalid glob is a configuration error naming the valid ids. analysis.rules and analysis.suppress are whole-value settings: the nearest scope that sets one replaces the lower ones rather than merging per rule. Managed policy can pin a value through the existing constraint mechanism; per-rule "cannot loosen" semantics and platform-managed pinning belong to the platform and are not implemented here. build --plan still lists every finding and ignores levels and suppressions. Per-rule severity overrides, expiring suppressions and authored inputs semantics are deferred. lockfile-manifest-drift uses the lockfile nearest the target (a directory with several uses the one packageManager names, else the order shrinkwrap, package-lock.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, yarn.lock). It does not check transitive entries, pnpm catalogs' resolved ranges or .pnpmfile.cjs/yarn plugin rewrites. Verified on Linux. Windows and macOS were not run.
documents.s: Rule levels, suppressions and build --check (S5 step C)

documents.t: Each stage script (build, test, lint, with pre<name> and post<name>) is read with a closed shell grammar and resolved into a command graph whose leaves are tool invocations. Scripts are read, never run. Every visited script is a stage-script fact (exact, sourced at the script's line in package.json) that records its command, its leaves (tools and unknown constructs), the scripts it calls, its depth and, below the root, the via chain (build > build:compile > compile), the hook (pre or post) and the workspace member it belongs to. Construct Handling &&, ||, ;, newline, | every segment is analyzed (a superset of what runs); # comments, quotes and \ escapes are honored $VAR, ${VAR} reads-env fact, except inside single quotes or after \$ NAME=value cmd, cross-env, env [-i] [-u N], npx/pnpx, time, command stripped; the real program is classified. Unknown flags of these wrappers are an unknown leaf dotenv [-e file] -- cmd the env files are exact reads (default .env); -c cascades are unknown cd dir later commands in the same script use that directory npm run <s>, npm test/start/stop/restart, pnpm run <s>, pnpm <s>, yarn <s>, node --run <s> delegation to the script of the same package, with pre/post hooks; --prefix/-C/--dir/--cwd select another package; --if-present tolerates a missing script. A missing script is an unknown leaf -- and trailing arguments appended to the last command of the delegated script (npm run c -- -p x.json reaches tsc); for pnpm/yarn, arguments after the script name pass through npm run s -w <name|dir>, --workspaces/-ws, pnpm -r/--recursive, pnpm --filter/-F <sel>, yarn workspace <n> s, yarn workspaces run s, yarn workspaces foreach … run s fan out to workspace members that define the script. -r and foreach exclude the root; pnpm selectors accept names, globs, ./path, !negation; a dependency or git-range selector (name..., [ref]) selects every member (a superset); a selector that matches nothing is an unknown leaf npm-run-all, npm-run-all2, run-s, run-p script names and name:* patterns (* stays within one : group, ** crosses groups), per-pattern arguments, -- shared arguments; a pattern that matches nothing is an unknown leaf node, tsc entry files, --require/--import/--env-file preloads, --test, directories and extensionless names resolved like node (package.json main, index.*); tsc -p/-b, project lists, files on the command line, --outDir/--declarationDir/--tsBuildInfoFile/--outFile as writes. node -e/-p, --watch and tsc --watch are unknown leaves rimraf, del, del-cli, rm, rmdir; mkdir, mkdirp, touch; cp, copyfiles, cpy, cpx, ncp, mv; cat; echo, sleep, true, … data in profiles.rs (UTILITIES): script-delete/script-create/script-copy writes (over-approximate), script-read reads (globs become reads-glob), no effect for echo-like commands. A glob or computed target of a write is unknown tools with a framework profile run through the profile when the command runs in the analyzed target's directory; in another workspace member it is an unknown leaf ./script.sh, `bash sh redirections (>, >>, <) the command is still analyzed; each non-/dev/null target is an unknown leaf (2>&1 names no file) subshells, $(…), backticks, &, unterminated quotes, eval, other programs, unknown wrappers unknown leaf that widens the stage Bounds: delegation deeper than 8 levels or more than 256 script instances in a stage stops with one unknown fact naming the chain; a cycle (a > b > a) is an unknown fact naming the cycle. unknown leaves widen only their own stage. The generated npm, pnpm and Yarn workspace build command can run native member builds, check their declared public entries and pack their packages as one operation. Script facts alone do not describe every read made by that compound operation: native packing can also read a package's files selection, ignore rules and lifecycle inputs. For this generated build runner, analysis records an unbounded read of the target source and uses the target-directory fallback for confinement and cache inputs. This does not change which member producers are selected or turn a script-graph superset into proof that a member build ran. An authored root build script without the generated workspace runner keeps its own analyzed bounds. See the action-cache fallback for the effect of unknown reads on reuse. Example (tooling/fixtures/node-analysis/script-graph, oyzu build --plan --stage build): Entry points, scripts and frameworks Path or name Confidence Source Why prebuild exact package.json:7 npm run clean build exact package.json:8 run-s build:* build:assets exact package.json:9 build > build:assets · cross-env NODE_ENV=production node scripts/assets.mjs --minify build:compile exact package.json:10 build > build:compile · npm run compile -- --pretty false compile exact package.json:11 build > build:compile > compile · node scripts/stamp.mjs && tsc -p tsconfig.build.json postbuild exact package.json:12 node scripts/report.mjs clean exact package.json:13 prebuild > clean · rimraf dist and the entries they reach (scripts/assets.mjs at package.json:9, scripts/stamp.mjs at :11, scripts/report.mjs at :12). In the same project --stage lint lists redirection to or from "lint.log" is not analyzed as an unknown fact at package.json:17; the build stage has none.

tsc -p, tsc -b, project lists and a bare tsc (which searches upward for tsconfig.json; tsc -b looks only in its directory) predict the compiler's own file list: the extends closure (including extends of a workspace-member package, read from the snapshot through the member's package.json tsconfig field or subpath; any other package stays unknown), files/include/exclude (the default exclude applies only when none is set), allowJs and the extension priority between a.ts, a.d.ts and a.js, references (each referenced project's own set), composite/incremental build-info files as warm state (at the compiler's default path: beside the config, under outDir, or with rootDir also set at the config's path relative to rootDir resolved from outDir), and the imports reached from those files. The compiler also reads the package.json of every directory above each program file (module format) and of every workspace member an import resolves to (exports/types/main); both are exact reads (package-scope, package-resolution). The measurement harness checks the prediction against the compiler itself: tsc -p <project> --listFilesOnly in the prepared copy, restricted to files in the copy outside node_modules. This is test tooling; the product has no probe action and runs no native tool during analysis.

A profile is a versioned row of data (src/builders/node/analysis/profiles.rs) that the analyzer interprets: the commands that run the tool, the configuration file names, the configuration keys that refine the convention, conventional reads, outputs, warm state and environment-file rules. A profile only refines: a value found in the configuration beats the convention (an explicit Next.js distDir or Vite build.outDir replaces .next/dist), and a value the evaluator cannot read makes only the facts derived from it unknown. The table has no hand-maintained version number. Its identity is a digest of its content: the first 16 hex characters of a SHA-256 over a fixed JSON serialization of every framework table in profiles.rs (profile rows, the SvelteKit layer, entries, templates and adapters, the Astro vocabularies, integrations, conventional modules and shipped tsconfig bases, the React Router, Angular and Nest tables, PostCSS/Tailwind CSS companions, Browserslist, Vitest/Jest match defaults and Next.js route roots). The serialization keeps declaration order and holds only strings, booleans and sequences, so the same table gives the same digest on every host and run, and editing any row changes it. The digest is part of the node-framework analyzer version in the record's analyzers list (4+profiles-<digest>, for example 4+profiles-0123456789abcdef), so a record says which rules produced it without anyone bumping a number. The script analyzer's utility table, also in profiles.rs, is not part of it. A profile applies when a stage's script runs its command (vite build, vitest [run], next build, jest, eslint, nest build, ...), and each run emits a framework fact for that stage: framework, profile, profileVersion, tableDigest (the same digest as in the analyzer version), engine, mode and evidence. Because fact ids are content hashes, a profile table edit also changes every framework fact's id, while facts the table does not shape keep theirs. Profile Command Reads Writes / warm state Notes Vite vite build [--mode m] [--config f] config and what it imports, index.html (or build.rollupOptions.input / build.lib.entry), then the module graph from its scripts, stylesheets and assets, public/, tsconfig, PostCSS/Tailwind build.outDir (default dist); node_modules/.vite resolve.alias, import.meta.glob, CSS @import/url() and new URL(…, import.meta.url) are followed; plugins other than the React plugins make the stage unknown Vitest vitest [run] config (vitest.config.*, else vite.config.*), files matching test.include minus test.exclude (defaults per Vitest), setupFiles, globalSetup, their imports, .env for mode test; with sveltekit() in the config, the SvelteKit layer's reads too (no adapter) warm node_modules/.vite; with sveltekit(), .svelte-kit test.workspace/projects/includeSource/typecheck, coverage and a workspace file are unknown Next.js next build config, route files of app/ (page, layout, route, … and metadata files) and every source file of pages/, src/ variants, root middleware/proxy/instrumentation, public/, and the TypeScript compiler's file set from tsconfig (the type check) distDir (default .next), out/ for output: "export", <distDir>/cache, generated next-env.d.ts webpack, turbopack, experimental.turbo/swcPlugins, images.loaderFile and cacheHandler make the stage unknown. PostCSS and Tailwind CSS v3 configuration is predicted as for Vite (below). In an app-router route.* file, environment reads inside the POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE and OPTIONS method exports are request-time: not reads-env facts, recorded as diagnostic-evidence request-time-env-read with provenance and a reason. GET/HEAD reads are request-time too when the file exports dynamic = "force-dynamic" (reason force-dynamic), or when the build uses Next 15 or later and the file does not opt into static generation (reason next-15-default; see Next route-handler GET default). Page and component functions, module scope, handlers re-exported from another module and static-capable GET/HEAD handlers stay exact SvelteKit (tier 4, layered on Vite) vite build whose Vite config lists sveltekit() from @sveltejs/kit/vite svelte.config.js/.ts and what it imports, route files (+page, +layout, +server, +error, in .svelte/.js/.ts) under kit.files.routes and the whole routes directory as a bounded glob, kit.files.assets (static/), kit.files.params matchers, hooks.client/hooks.server/hooks (universal), service-worker and instrumentation.server as <base>.js|ts or <base>/index.js|ts, app.html, error.html, tsconfig.json and jsconfig.json, .env* from kit.env.dir (PUBLIC_ or kit.env.publicPrefix names), the $lib alias, kit.alias and the module graph through every component's <script> and <style> .svelte-kit (or kit.outDir) instead of dist; Next 15.0.0 changed app-router GET route handlers from static to dynamic by default (Next 15 release notes, "GET Route Handlers are no longer cached by default"; the route.js version history lists it under v15.0.0-RC). next build then calls a GET handler only when Next's isStaticGenEnabled holds for the module or the route is a metadata route (checked against Next's source at v15.0.0, v15.5.0 and v16.0.0, where it is identical, and present from v15.0.0-canary.0). The Next profile applies this per build (framework/next_routes.rs) and per route file (source.rs): Input Effect Next version The exact version the nearest lockfile (the one lockfile-manifest-drift reads: npm package-lock.json/npm-shrinkwrap.json version 2 or 3 by Node resolution, pnpm-lock.yaml version 5 to 9 from the target's importer, yarn berry yarn.lock from the workspace entry and yarn classic yarn.lock from the declared next@<range> entry) installs for the target, else the lowest major the declared dependencies/devDependencies range admits (15.1.0, ^15, ~15.2, 15.x, >=15, || alternatives). A lockfile without a record for next, or whose record is a link or another protocol, falls back to the declared range. Tags (latest, canary), *, upper bounds alone and non-registry specs resolve nothing Major below 15, or unresolved Next 14 default: GET/HEAD reads are build inputs unless the file exports dynamic = "force-dynamic" next.config.* not statically readable, output: "export", or cacheComponents, experimental.cacheComponents or experimental.dynamicIO set or not readable Next 14 default (these prerender handlers, or cannot be ruled out) Otherwise (Next 15 or later) Dynamic default for route files under app/ (or src/app/): GET/HEAD reads are request-time unless the file opts in Per-file opt-in (Next 15 or later) An exported dynamic other than "auto"/"force-dynamic" ("force-static", "error", or a value not read as a literal), revalidate other than 0 (false, a positive number, or any other expression), generateStaticParams, any of these three names re-exported (export { dynamic } from), or export * from: the file's GET/HEAD reads stay build inputs Metadata routes Route paths Next treats as metadata routes (normalized path starting with /robots or /manifest, equal to /favicon.ico, or containing /sitemap, /icon, /apple-icon, /opengraph-image or /twitter-image; route groups and @slot segments removed) stay static by default Each next build records the decision as one diagnostic-evidence fact next-get-handler-default with default (static or dynamic) and a detail naming the version, its source and any configuration reason. Handlers defined in another module and re-exported (export { GET } from "./get") or exported through a local specifier (export { POST }) are not recognized as handlers, so their reads stay exact (conservative). A route with a dynamic segment and no generateStaticParams, and a route file that also exports POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE or OPTIONS (Next raises a dynamic-usage error before calling GET during prerendering, in Next 14 and 15 alike), are not prerendered either, but their GET reads still count as build inputs (over-reporting, not a soundness gap). Partial prerendering (experimental.ppr) is not modeled.

SvelteKit is not a command of its own: vite build plus sveltekit() in the Vite configuration is a SvelteKit build, so the vite profile detects the plugin and applies the SvelteKit layer (framework/sveltekit.rs, data in profiles.rs) in place of the index.html entry, the public/ directory and the dist output. The layer emits its own framework fact (sveltekit, layeredOn: vite) next to the Vite one. Everything is read statically; no project code runs. The same layer applies to Vitest when its configuration (vitest.config.*, else vite.config.*) lists sveltekit(): the plugin loads svelte.config.*, syncs .svelte-kit (it scans the routes, params, hooks and templates and writes generated types), loads .env* for mode test from kit.env.dir and resolves $lib, $env/* and kit.alias for the tests. The framework fact then says layeredOn: vitest and engine: Vitest. No adapter runs under Vitest, so a modeled adapter adds only the environment variables its module reads when the configuration imports it; an unmodeled adapter stays unknown, since importing its module can read files. The prediction is an over-approximation for tests: route modules and what they import are predicted although Vitest only lists them. Components. The import graph reads a .svelte file through its <script> blocks (instance and module, lang="ts" honored) and <style> blocks (@import and url()), by blanking everything else, so facts carry the file's own line numbers. Markup is never guessed: import( or import.meta in markup is unknown, and so is a <style lang="scss">-style preprocessor. Routes. Only +-prefixed files in the routes directory are graph entries (the rest of the directory is covered by its glob and by import edges). Generated base configuration. tsconfig.json normally extends the tsconfig.json SvelteKit writes into kit.outDir. The layer registers that path as generated, so the extends is not unknown; without the layer the same extends stays unknown (the framework, not the tsconfig analyzer, models it). Generated route types. import type { PageData } from './$types' in a route file names a module SvelteKit writes under <outDir>/types and maps beside the route through rootDirs. The layer registers <dir>/$types for every routes directory holding a + file, so the import is neither read nor unknown; the bundler erases it. A $types import elsewhere stays an unresolved import. Adapters are modeled from the published source of adapter-static 3.0.10, adapter-node 5.5.7, adapter-vercel 6.3.2 and adapter-netlify 6.0.4 (the SvelteKit 2 line; 7.x requires SvelteKit 3); the table is data in profiles.rs. Other versions are not qualified. adapter-netlify publishes to netlify.toml build.publish (read with a TOML parser; absent or empty means build), writes its functions (lambda, split or edge) under .netlify and its temporary edge bundle under kit.outDir, copies _headers and _redirects from the working directory when they exist, and reads NETLIFY_SVELTEKIT_USE_EDGE. adapter-cloudflare is modeled from the published source of 7.2.9 with Wrangler 4.149.0 (unstable_readConfig, which does not follow a .wrangler/deploy/config.json redirect). The Wrangler file is the config option's path, else the first wrangler.json, then wrangler.jsonc, then wrangler.toml found by searching the working directory and each ancestor up to the source root, one name at a time (an ancestor's wrangler.json wins over a local wrangler.toml). Every candidate probed is an input, found or not. The file is parsed as JSONC or TOML, and main, assets.directory and pages_build_output_dir, at the top level and in every env section, are outputs relative to the file. The union means neither CF_PAGES (Pages mode) nor CLOUDFLARE_ENV (the section) can move an output outside the prediction; both are reads-env facts. The adapter also writes <outDir>/cloudflare and <outDir>/cloudflare-tmp, copies _headers and _redirects from the working directory, and rejects a _routes.json there. Options other than config, fallback, routes and platformProxy, a file that does not parse, a path value that is not a string or leaves the source, and any route option module (+page, +layout, +server, with .server variants, .js/.ts) that names prerender or re-exports a whole module are unknown. Prerendering starts Wrangler's platform proxy (Miniflare), which is not modeled. adapter-auto is modeled from 7.0.1. It loads the adapter of the first environment whose variable is set: VERCEL, CF_PAGES, NETLIFY, GITHUB_ACTION_REPOSITORY (Azure), SST and GCP_BUILDPACKS (adapter-node). With none set, it only warns. A captured action sees only the variables its task sets (oyzu.toml env and task environments), never the caller's environment. The analyzer therefore reads the build task's variable names (names only, never values). With none of the six set, the adapter adds nothing but the six reads-env facts. For each one that is set, the selected adapter's model applies with default options. A set variable whose adapter is not declared in package.json is unknown, because adapter-auto installs it at build time. So is one whose adapter is not modeled (Azure, SST). Since a set variable may be empty, every set candidate is applied, not only the first. Absent inputs. Missing hook, service-worker and instrumentation modules are recorded as one candidate glob each, since creating one changes the build. Not modeled (their reads are not predicted): code that runs at prerender time beyond literal file access the import graph already sees, svelte-kit sync/svelte-check as separate script commands, Tailwind CSS v4, @sveltejs/enhanced-img, adapter environment variable names other than adapter-vercel's two, adapter-netlify's one, adapter-cloudflare's two and adapter-auto's six (Wrangler's own logging variables are not listed), Wrangler's log files under the home directory (outside the source), kit.paths/CSP/version options (they read no files), and Svelte 4 only syntax beyond what the script parser accepts. Components. A <script> or <style> tag inside an HTML comment in a component's markup is markup, not a block. Build identifier. SvelteKit stamps the build time into client chunks unless kit.version.name is fixed, so their content and content-hashed names change on every build. The confinement gate compares such files by name shape (below); the sveltekit-app fixture fixes the version, sveltekit-netlify does not.

astro build is its own engine (AstroBuild, framework/astro.rs, data in profiles.rs). It was modeled from Astro 7.3.8's published source (resolveConfigPath, createFileBasedRoutes, the content and actions file searches, env/env-loader.js) and checked against real astro build traces. Everything is read statically; no project or Astro code runs. Static output by default. The default output: "static" (and "server") is modeled; outputs are outDir and .astro, warm state is cacheDir (the content data store and image and font caches). Configuration. astro.config.* is evaluated with the constant evaluator and checked against a closed vocabulary (ASTRO_CONFIG_KEYS and the vite, markdown and image sub-vocabularies in profiles.rs). Keys that change no file access (site, base, trailingSlash, build, server, redirects, i18n, security, ...) are accepted; any other key is unknown. Integrations and adapters. @astrojs/sitemap (3.7.4, any options: it reads no project file and writes into outDir) and @astrojs/mdx (8.0.3, without options: adds .mdx routes and entries) are modeled. Every adapter (@astrojs/node, -vercel, -netlify, -cloudflare) and every other integration (UI frameworks such as @astrojs/react, @astrojs/markdoc, Starlight, Tailwind) is unknown. Environment. Files load the Vite way from vite.envDir (default the root); names with PUBLIC_ (or vite.envPrefix) are reported from the files, every import.meta.env.NAME read in frontmatter, scripts or markup is reported from the graph (server-side private names are inlined at build time too), and every env.schema key is an exact reads-env fact (role: env-schema), since the build validates them. astro:env/* imports are virtual. Virtual modules. Specifiers starting with astro: (astro:content, astro:assets, astro:env/client) are neither files nor packages: the graph skips them and the phantom-dependency rule does not see them. Components.
