nuxt build and nuxt generate (from nuxt or @nuxt/cli, also run as nuxi) have their own profile (framework/nuxt.rs, data in profiles.rs). It was written against the source of Nuxt 4.5.2, @nuxt/cli 3.37.0 and Nitro 2.13.4 and checked with real builds of those versions; Nuxt 3 defaults come from @nuxt/schema 3.21.11 and were not built. Nothing of the project runs. Configuration. The script forms of nuxt.config are read by the constant evaluator, with defineNuxtConfig (a global in Nuxt) as an identity wrapper. The other forms c12 accepts (JSON, YAML, TOML, nuxt.config/index.*, .config/nuxt.*) and Nitro's own nitro.config.*/.nitrorc make the stage unknown; one candidate glob records that creating any of them changes the build. A .nuxtrc in the project is unknown (the user's ~/.nuxtrc is outside the snapshot and not modeled), and so are the $production block (or the block --envName names) and $env, which c12 merges over the configuration. Version and srcDir. The major version of the declared nuxt dependency picks the defaults. Nuxt 4 uses app/ unless that directory is absent, or holds only router.options.* and spa-loading-template.html while the root has app.vue or a pages-style directory; Nuxt 3 uses the root unless future.compatibilityVersion is 4. In Nuxt 3 server/ and public/ follow srcDir; in Nuxt 4 they stay at the root. Scanned directories. Nuxt imports by scanning, not only by import edges, so each scanned directory is a bounded glob, present or absent, and every .vue, .js or .ts file in it is also a graph entry. server/, shared/ and public/ are globs too. Components. .vue files are read like .svelte files (<script> with lang="ts"/tsx, <style> @import and url()), and the template's static asset URLs are followed as Vue compiles them (img/source src and srcset, video src/poster, image/use href; ~/x drops the tilde). A template in another language (lang="pug") or file (src=), a <script src> or <style src>, and an asset that does not resolve are unknown. An import of a .vue file without its extension does not resolve and is unknown. Environment. Nuxt's own loader reads the root .env (not mode files); Vite runs with srcDir as its root, so its .env, .env.local, .env.production and .env.production.local are read from srcDir (VITE_ names are inlined). NITRO_PRESET, SERVER_PRESET, the compatibility-date variables and NUXT_APP_BASE_URL, NUXT_APP_BUILD_ASSETS_DIR and NUXT_APP_CDN_URL are build inputs. runtimeConfig overrides (NUXT_API_SECRET, NUXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE, with NITRO_ as the second prefix) are read by the server at run time, so a plain nuxt build does not depend on them; a real build confirmed that a NUXT_PUBLIC_ value does not reach .output. When routes are prerendered (nuxt generate, --prerender, routeRules, nitro.prerender, nitro.static), the prerenderer runs the server and the value is baked into the HTML (also confirmed), so every key path of runtimeConfig becomes a reads-env fact under both prefixes (NUXT_PUBLIC_* with publicPrefix: true), plus NITRO_ENV_PREFIX and NITRO_ENV_EXPANSION. A runtimeConfig the evaluator cannot read is unknown in that case. Presets and outputs. The build writes .nuxt and .output. Nitro picks the preset from --preset, NITRO_PRESET/SERVER_PRESET, nitro.preset, then the deployment provider it detects; without a configured preset the output layout depends on where the build runs, so the stage is unknown and the detail says to set nitro.preset or pass --preset. node-server (and its aliases) and node-cluster write .output; static, nuxt generate and prerendering also create the dist link to .output/public. A preset variable set in the environment is a recorded input, but the predicted writes follow the configured preset. Unknown options. modules, extends/theme, rootDir, hooks, builder (webpack and Rspack), components, serverHandlers, spaLoadingTemplate, build.templates, build.transpile, typescript.typeCheck, vite.plugins, vite.resolve, vite.css, vite.root, vite.vue, vite.build, vue.transformAssetUrls, the Nitro options that add code or directories (plugins, handlers, publicAssets, serverAssets, srcDir, scanDirs, modules, hooks, rollupConfig, output.publicDir/serverDir), postcss.config, PostCSS plugins other than the inert ones, and local layers/ and modules/ directories make the stage unknown. Not modeled (their reads are not predicted): what a module reads (the realism ui/tailwindcss project's tailwind.config.js is covered only by the stage's unknown), presets other than the five names above, the webpack and Rspack builders, nuxi typecheck/prepare/analyze as script commands, Nuxt Content and other module conventions, Sass/Less, and Nuxt 3 behavior beyond the directory defaults. Fixture determinism. Nuxt writes a random build identifier and absolute paths into its output, and the order of .nuxt/dist/server/styles.mjs changes from run to run. The fixtures fix buildId, turn off features.inlineStyles, and the confinement gate runs each copy at one fixed path (below).

Remix's successor is React Router's framework mode (@react-router/dev); Remix v2 (@remix-run/dev, remix vite:build) is in maintenance and has a profile of its own (Remix v2, below). react-router build has its own engine (ReactRouterBuild, framework/react_router.rs, data in profiles.rs), written against the published source of @react-router/dev 8.4.0 and @react-router/fs-routes 8.4.0 (the current release when it was written) and checked against straced builds with Vite 8.3.4. React Router 7 projects run the same command; their reads were not traced. Nothing of the project runs. Configuration. react-router build hands Vite no config path, so Vite's own vite.config.* search applies; that file is read with the constant evaluator and its plugins must be reactRouter() and optionally vite-tsconfig-paths (below; any other plugin is unknown, as for vite build). Vite root, environments and builder are unknown; Vite's build.outDir and build.rollupOptions.input are replaced by the plugin's own. react-router.config.* (the first of .js, .jsx, .ts, .tsx, .mjs, .mts in the root) is read the same way. Its modeled keys are appDirectory, buildDirectory, ssr, prerender (a boolean, a list of paths or { paths }), and keys that read no files (basename, future, routeDiscovery, serverBuildFile, serverModuleFormat, splitRouteModules, subResourceIntegrity, allowedActionOrigins). buildEnd, presets, serverBundles and a prerender function run project code at build time and are unknown. App modules and routes. Under appDirectory the root route, the optional entry.client and entry.server modules and the route configuration routes.* are found the way the plugin finds them; the absent candidates before the first match are inputs too. The route configuration is evaluated: index(file), route(path, file, options?, children?), layout(file, options?, children?) and prefix(path, routes) from @react-router/dev/routes, plain route objects ({ file, children }) and await are understood, and every named module becomes a graph entry (relative to appDirectory). A spread such as ...prefix() hides its routes from the evaluator and is unknown (pass prefix() as a children argument instead); relative() and other packages' helpers are unknown. flatRoutes() from @react-router/fs-routes (optionally with rootDirectory) reads its directory: every file in it and the route.*/index.* module of each folder are entries, dot entries excepted; ignoredRouteFiles only removes routes and is not applied. Default entries. Without app/entry.server.* the package's default is used, but only if package.json dependencies has isbot; otherwise the build adds it to package.json and runs an install, which is unknown. Generated types. Route modules import ./+types/<route> (generated into .react-router/types and resolved through rootDirs). Such an import that does not resolve in the source names a generated file and is not unknown. Environment. The plugin loads loadEnv(mode, envDir ?? root, "") into process.env, so the .env, .env.local, .env.<mode> and .env.<mode>.local files of envDir are inputs; VITE_ (or envPrefix) names are inlined into client output. REACT_ROUTER_ROOT moves the project root and is a build input. Server code's process.env reads are graph facts as usual. Preview pass. With prerender set or ssr: false, the build starts a Vite preview server whose plugin runs in serve mode: it renders the prerendered paths (and the SPA fallback) by running route loaders, generates route types into .react-router/ and starts a file watcher. Measured, the watcher stats every file below the project root, not only the root's entries and the app directory, so the stage reads the whole project as one bounded glob (node_modules and .git excluded) and its key is the target scope in effect. A plain SSR build has no preview pass and is precise. Outputs. buildDirectory (default build, with client/ and server/), .react-router with the preview pass; warm state node_modules/.vite (Vite's cacheDir) and node_modules/.vite-child-compiler (the plugin's route-export compiler). Not modeled (unknown or not predicted): react-router dev, typegen, routes and reveal as build commands (only build is a modeled subcommand), a project directory argument, --config (it also moves the root), --profile, --sourcemapClient/--sourcemapServer, React Server Components (@vitejs/plugin-rsc, unstable_reactRouterRSC()), presets such as @vercel/react-router, serverBundles, the Cloudflare and other Vite plugins (@tailwindcss/vite), what a loader reads with a non-constant path during prerendering.

vite-tsconfig-paths (framework/tsconfig_paths.rs, written against 4.3.2 and 6.1.1) resolves bare specifiers through tsconfig paths and baseUrl. With no projects option it finds every tsconfig.json and jsconfig.json (or the configNames) under the root, skipping node_modules and .git, and parses each with its extends chain. The stage reads **/tsconfig.json and **/jsconfig.json as bounded globs, so adding one is seen; every file found, or named in projects, is read and joins the tsconfig closure. Their paths become aliases of the import graph, and their baseUrl a fallback alias tried after paths and before packages, so import x from "app/lib/x" under baseUrl: "." is followed. The graph applies aliases to every importer, while the plugin applies each file's only to the files it includes, so two files that set different paths or baseUrl are unknown. loose, parseNative, ignoreConfigErrors, projectDiscovery and logFile read nothing else; any other option (root, skip, importerFilter, a non-constant list) is unknown. Only the React Router and Remix profiles model the plugin; for vite build and Vitest it stays unknown.

remix vite:build has its own engine (RemixBuild, framework/remix.rs, data in profiles.rs REMIX), written against the published source of @remix-run/dev 2.17.5 (the last 2.x release) and checked against straced builds with 2.17.5 and Vite 6.4.1. It reuses the React Router engine's route helpers. Nothing of the project runs. Configuration. The Vite configuration is found as for vite build and read with the constant evaluator. Its plugins must be vitePlugin() from @remix-run/dev (usually imported as remix), cloudflareDevProxyVitePlugin() (dev only) and optionally vite-tsconfig-paths (above); any other plugin is unknown. A configuration without vitePlugin() is unknown. Vite root, environments and builder are unknown. The plugin's first argument holds the Remix options: appDirectory, buildDirectory, future and keys that read no files (basename, ignoredRouteFiles, which only removes routes, manifest, serverBuildFile, serverModuleFormat) are modeled. routes (a function), presets, buildEnd and serverBundles run project code and are unknown, as is SPA mode (ssr: false), which renders the root route at build time. App modules and routes. Under appDirectory (default app) the root route and the optional entry.client and entry.server modules are found the way the plugin's findEntry does (.js, .jsx, .ts, .tsx), absent candidates included. Routes come from the built-in flat-routes convention over <appDirectory>/routes: every file directly in it and the route.*/index.* module of each folder (.js, .jsx, .ts, .tsx, .md, .mdx) are graph entries, dot entries excepted. With future.v3_routeConfig the routes.* route configuration replaces the directory and is evaluated as for React Router, with the helpers of @remix-run/route-config and flatRoutes() from @remix-run/fs-routes. Default entries. Without entry.server the package's default is used; with no isbot in package.json dependencies the build adds it and runs an install, which is unknown. Environment. .env* of envDir by mode, VITE_ (or envPrefix) names, and REMIX_ROOT, which moves the project root. Outputs. buildDirectory (default build, with client/ and server/; emptied first); warm state node_modules/.vite (cacheDir, shared by the plugin's child compiler). Not modeled (unknown or not predicted): remix build (the classic esbuild compiler), remix dev and the other subcommands, a project directory argument, --config, --profile, the source-map flags, SPA mode, presets (Vercel and others), serverBundles, a routes function (remix-flat-routes and similar) and Vite plugins other than the ones above (MDX, vanilla-extract, Sentry).

ng build has its own engine (AngularBuild, framework/angular.rs, data in profiles.rs ANGULAR). It was written against the published source of @angular/cli and @angular/build 21.2.26 and checked against straced builds with 21.2.26 and 20.3.39; the webpack browser builder against @angular-devkit/build-angular 21.2.26 and traced with 21.2.26 and 15.2.3. Angular 22.2.2 (the current release) has the same application builder option schema and conventions, but it needs Node 22.22.3 or later and was not built (the measuring host has Node 22.22.0). Nothing of the project runs. Workspace and target. angular.json (then .angular.json) must be in the target directory; one found only above it is unknown. The project is the one named on the command line, else the one whose root is the workspace root, else the only project. Its architect.build (or targets.build) target must use @angular/build:application or @angular-devkit/build-angular:application, which that package's builders.json maps to the same implementation, or the webpack @angular-devkit/build-angular:browser (below). Every other builder, including browser-esbuild and the other webpack builders, is unknown. The target's options are merged with each configuration of -c/--configuration (comma separated, in order) or with defaultConfiguration; a configuration the target does not define is unknown. Options. Paths are relative to the workspace root. tsConfig (required), browser (default <sourceRoot>/main.ts, sourceRoot defaulting to <root>/src), index (a path, { input } or false; default <sourceRoot>/index.html), polyfills (a file in the source is a graph entry, any other name a package, and the candidate path is an input either way), styles (CSS files go through the stylesheet scan, so @import and url() are followed; Sass, Less and Stylus are unknown), scripts (read as text), assets (a path is a file or a whole directory; { glob, input, ignore } is a bounded glob under input with ignore excluded), fileReplacements (both files are inputs and with is a graph entry), outputPath and inlineStyleLanguage (css only) are read. Options that read nothing else (aot, optimization, outputHashing, sourceMap, budgets, baseHref, extractLicenses, define, loader and the rest listed in ANGULAR) are accepted. SSR (ssr, server, outputMode: "server"), prerender, appShell, serviceWorker, localize, watch, poll, webWorkerTsConfig and stylePreprocessorOptions are accepted only when absent or falsy; any other key is unknown. Program and component resources. tsConfig is a compiler program like a tsc run (its include/exclude/files set, extends and paths), followed through the import graph from the browser entry. The Angular compiler's file system stats every entry of each directory TypeScript's include walk visits, so the stage also reads, as bounded globs, the entries directly in the tsconfig's directory and everything below each include pattern's literal base directory, excluded files and non-TypeScript files included. In every source file the graph parses, including files the compiler only type-checks, @Component({...}) metadata is read: templateUrl, styleUrl and styleUrls are inputs relative to the component (their stylesheets scanned for @import and url()), and inline styles strings are scanned the same way. A spread, a computed key or a non-literal resource is unknown, as is a Sass, Less or Stylus component stylesheet. Webpack browser builder. @angular-devkit/build-angular:browser reads the same workspace, configurations, program, component resources, styles, assets, replacements, CSS tooling, Browserslist and cache as the application builder, with its own option vocabulary (ANGULAR.webpack_*): main is the required entry (a missing one is unknown) and browser is not an option, outputPath is a required string written as is, and webpack-only options that read nothing (buildOptimizer, vendorChunk, commonChunk, namedChunks, resourcesOutputPath and the rest) and their flags are accepted; ngswConfigPath and the other disabled options must be absent or falsy, and application-only options such as ssr or outputMode are unknown. Webpack's resolve.modules is [baseUrl || projectRoot, "node_modules"], so a bare specifier such as src/app/x resolves under the tsconfig's baseUrl (else the project root) before node_modules: that directory is a fallback alias of the import graph. Its description-file lookup reads package.json in every directory from a module up to the project root, so the stage reads <sourceRoot>/**/package.json as a bounded glob and each directory between sourceRoot and the project root exactly. Babel runs with babelrc and configFile off, so no Babel configuration is read. CSS tooling and targets. The builder looks for postcss.config.json, .postcssrc.json and tailwind.config.{js,cjs,mjs,ts} in the project root and the workspace root: every candidate is an input and a present one is unknown (Tailwind CSS through Angular is not modeled). Browserslist files (.browserslistrc, browserslist) and package.json from the project root up, and BROWSERSLIST, BROWSERSLIST_CONFIG, BROWSERSLIST_ENV, are inputs. Environment. Angular loads no .env files. The CLI and builder read CI (which turns the disk cache off with the default cli.cache.environment), NG_BUILD_MANGLE, NG_BUILD_OPTIMIZE_CHUNKS, NG_BUILD_TYPE_CHECK and the other variables in ANGULAR.build_env; they are build inputs. Flags. -c/--configuration and a project name are modeled. Flags that only change output bytes (--base-href, --output-hashing, --source-map, --optimization, --aot, --progress, --verbose and the others in ANGULAR.build_flags, in kebab or camelCase, with --no- or =value) are accepted. Every other flag is unknown, including --watch, --localize, --ssr and builder option overrides that move reads or outputs, such as --output-path, --browser or --ts-config. Outputs. outputPath ({ base } or a string; default dist/<project>, with browser/ inside) and warm state .angular/cache (cli.cache.path) unless cli.cache.enabled is false. The tsconfig outDir is reported as for any tsconfig even though the Angular build does not write it. Not modeled (unknown or not predicted): SSR, prerendering and app shell, service workers, i18n (localize, i18n in the project), web workers, Sass, Less and Stylus, Tailwind CSS and PostCSS configurations, the webpack builders other than browser (server, karma, dev-server), a custom webpack configuration, custom builders (@angular-builders/*, Nx executors), library builds (ng-packagr), ng test, ng serve and ng run, the global CLI configuration (~/.angular-config.json), a workspace above the target directory and a project root other than the workspace root when several projects exist.

nest build from @nestjs/cli has its own engine (NestBuild, framework/nest.rs, data in profiles.rs), written against the published source of @nestjs/cli 12.0.8 (the current release when it was written) and checked against 11.0.24, the last 11.x release, which behaves the same in everything modeled here apart from the swc differences noted below. The installed @nestjs/cli major is read from the lockfile, else from the declared range; anything other than 11 or 12 (or no version) is unknown. The default tsc builder and the swc builder (framework/nest_swc.rs) are modeled. Nothing of the project runs. Configuration. nest-cli.json, else .nest-cli.json, in the working directory, or the -c/--config file, is read as JSON; without one the CLI's defaults apply. Modeled top-level keys are sourceRoot and compilerOptions; $schema, collection, entryFile, exec, generateOptions, language, monorepo, projects and root read no project files for a build that names no application. In compilerOptions, tsConfigPath, builder, webpack, deleteOutDir, assets, and for swc typeCheck and emitDeclarations are read, and allowOutsidePaths, manualRestart, watchAssets and webpackConfigPath change no read. typeCheck and emitDeclarations do nothing under tsc. Any other key is unknown. Builder. --tsc turns compilerOptions.webpack off; otherwise compilerOptions.webpack: true selects webpack. Then -b/--builder, then compilerOptions.builder (a name or { type, options }), then tsc. webpack and rspack are unknown: they load project configuration code. Compiler program. The tsconfig is -p/--path, else compilerOptions.tsConfigPath, else the tsc builder's options.configPath, else tsconfig.build.json if it exists and tsconfig.json otherwise, relative to the working directory. Its program is predicted exactly as for tsc -p (see TypeScript input sets); the harness compares it with tsc --listFilesOnly. Nest emits through a transform that rewrites paths aliases; the files it resolves are the compiler's own. Assets. Each compilerOptions.assets entry, a glob string or { include, exclude?, outDir?, watchAssets?, ... }, is joined under sourceRoot and read as a bounded glob with its exclude; a match that is a directory is copied whole, so <glob>/** is read too. Nest matches with minimatch: a pattern with an extglob (+(a|b)), a leading !, a .. segment or an absolute path is unknown. An entry without a string include is unknown (Nest fails on it). swc builder. Nest still parses the selected tsconfig (its extends chain is read and its options become swc's: paths, baseUrl, outDir, sourceMap), then reads the .swcrc (builder.options.swcrcPath, else .swcrc in the working directory; absent is fine) and runs @swc/cli over sourceRoot. Every file below sourceRoot with a builder.options.extensions extension (default .js and .ts) whose path below the root has no dot-named segment is compiled; CLI 12 passes the tsconfig exclude patterns as swc's ignore (CLI 11 does not, so it compiles spec files too), and a builder.options.ignore replaces them, which the engine models by dropping the exclusions. Each compiled file is a graph entry that is compiled but never run: its imports are followed (swc stats the files a relative or paths import names), and its run-time reads and environment variables are not facts. A glob per extension covers files added later. For every compiled file @swc/core looks up .swcrc in its directory and each one up to the working directory, the nearest package.json and a sibling .map, so <sourceRoot>/**/.swcrc, <sourceRoot>/**/package.json and <sourceRoot>/**/*.map are read globs and the same names in the directories between are read paths. The .swcrc is one JSON-with-comments object; its keys $schema, exclude, inlineSourcesContent, isModule, jsc, minify, module, sourceMaps, swcrc and test are modeled, every jsc.paths target is a read glob (* widened to **), and jsc.experimental may hold only keepImportAttributes, emitAssertForImportAttributes, emitIsolatedDts and an empty plugins list. builder.options may hold swcrcPath, outDir (another write), extensions and ignore, the read-free deleteDirOnStart, logWatchCompilation, only, outFileExtension, quiet, stripLeadingPaths, sync, watch and workers, and copyFiles, includeDotfiles and onlyChanged only when false. With typeCheck (or --type-check; --no-type-check wins over the configuration) the compiler program of the tsconfig is predicted as for the tsc builder, and compiler plugins are then unknown (their metadata generator runs package code); without a type check the swc builder never loads them. emitDeclarations (or --emit-declarations, CLI 12) runs tsc --emitDeclarationOnly over the same program. Outputs. The tsconfig's outDir, or dist when it sets none (Nest deletes it first with deleteOutDir and copies assets into it), and each asset's own outDir. Incremental build info is the compiler's warm state: the starter layout (rootDir: "./src", outDir: "./dist") puts tsconfig.build.tsbuildinfo beside the config, as the compiler derives it. Not modeled (unknown): the webpack and rspack builders, compiler plugins (for example @nestjs/swagger, which runs inside the compiler) under tsc or an swc type check, the swc options and .swcrc keys listed above as unknown (env reads Browserslist, configFile names another file), includeLibraryAssets, application names and --all/--parallel (monorepo projects), -w/--watch and --watchAssets. Not predicted: the paths transform also probes <baseUrl or working directory>/<specifier> for each bare import before asking Node for the package; a project file at such a path would be stat-ed. The transform emits the same specifier either way when the package resolves. swc makes the same probes under jsc.baseUrl (which Nest sets to the tsconfig directory when paths is set without baseUrl), also unpredicted.

Script configs (.js, .mjs, .cjs, .ts, .mts, .cts) are parsed to an AST and evaluated by a closed interpreter (consteval.rs), never eval, never the project's code. It understands object and array literals, string and template concatenation, path.resolve/join/dirname/normalize/basename, __dirname, import.meta.dirname/filename/url, fileURLToPath, new URL(x, import.meta.url), spread, await (of a constant or a package call), conditionals and logical operators with constant operands, top-level const bindings, defineConfig(x)/defineConfig(() => ({…})) wrappers (and Nuxt's global defineNuxtConfig), and relative imports of other config files and JSON. Everything else — any other call, a loop, a function parameter, process.env.X (recorded as a reads-env fact from the import graph, value unknown), a binding mutated after its declaration — evaluates to unknown for that value only. Budgets: 50,000 evaluation steps, 10,000 items per array or object, 64 KiB per string, six levels of config imports, 200 levels of expression nesting and 400 bracket depth; hitting one makes the value unknown and names the limit.

For the mode of the command (production for vite build and next build, test for Vitest, or the value of --mode), the profile's load order lists the candidate files as inputs — present or absent, because creating one changes the build: Framework Files read (load order, lowest precedence first) Vite, Vitest .env, .env.local, .env.<mode>, .env.<mode>.local in envDir (default: the project root) Next.js .env, .env.<mode>, .env.local, .env.<mode>.local (.env.local is skipped in mode test) Nuxt .env at the root (Nuxt's loader), then Vite's .env, .env.local, .env.production, .env.production.local in srcDir Each file fact lists the variable names it defines; values never enter facts. Names with a framework-inlined prefix (VITE_* or the configured envPrefix; NEXT_PUBLIC_*) become reads-env facts with publicPrefix: true and the file and line that defines them, in addition to the facts from source that reads them (import.meta.env.VITE_X, process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_X). A mode that is not a constant name (for example --mode $MODE) is unknown.

Facts belong to the stage that needs them, so the test stage lists the runner's test files and setup files and the build stage does not. A test-only edit (a new test file, a new helper imported by tests, an edited setup file) therefore leaves every build fact unchanged and changes the test facts: oyzu build --plan --why tests/extra.test.ts --stage build # not-an-input oyzu build --plan --why tests/extra.test.ts --stage test # input When the runner's configuration is not statically readable (a computed test.include, a config built by next/jest), only the test stage falls back: it gets an unknown fact, fallback: target-directory, and --why can no longer claim a path is not an input. The build stage does not depend on test discovery and stays bounded. Vitest's test action also retains this complete target view when discovery is bounded: Oyzu's reporting adapter always enables native coverage, which can read unimported source files. The Node profile therefore records coverage reads as unknown whether authored coverage.enabled is absent, false or true. The final test action is target-directory and not confined to its predicted import graph; other stages keep their existing contracts. Native coverage configuration and thresholds remain effective over the supplied files. This conservative scope avoids incorrectly reporting full coverage after omitting an unimported source. The vitest-coverage fact identifies the owned reporting effect; unreadable project configuration retains its separate config-unreadable diagnostic.

Five stages of a Node package run commands the builder chooses rather than a project script: the version stamp (version), the npm install (prepare), npm pack (package), and, for a package without a lint or format-check script, the default ESLint and Prettier checks (node-quality.mjs). Their reads follow from the command, so analysis/owned.rs models them and --plan lists them under those stages (oyzu build --plan --stage package). Each such fact names its command in runner (node-version-stamp, npm-install, npm-pack, node-quality-eslint, node-quality-prettier); the builder tags the same command with the same runner, and a stage contract uses the facts only for an action that runs it. The full table of reads and of what is unknown is in the stage/action contract. Absent files are reads. A tool that looks for a file reads its absence: the version stamp probes npm-shrinkwrap.json, npm .npmrc and .npmignore, ESLint every eslint.config.* and .eslintrc* in and above the target, Prettier every configuration name and .editorconfig in and above it. Creating one changes the stage's key. Whole-package reads. npm pack without files (or with a glob in it) reads the whole package directory; the quality checks read every JavaScript and TypeScript file below the target. Implicit native installation. npm's install probes binding.gyp, including its absence. If it exists, gypfile is not false, and there is no nonempty install or preinstall script, npm defaults to node-gyp rebuild. The analyzer marks that implicit lifecycle as unbounded unknown, just like an authored install script, so preparation retains the target-directory scope instead of hiding native sources in a predicted confined view. A postinstall script does not suppress the native default. This does not parse gyp actions or bypass the existing confinement contract. Formatting and the captured native addon/independent-consumer flow pass with a Windows controller and Linux/amd64 worker. Focused Rust regressions, the full workspace suite and strict all-target Clippy pass. Unix host confinement qualification remains pending; container execution does not qualify that host source-view path. Not modeled. Workspace roots and members, pnpm and Yarn installs and packs, application package commands, Biome, legacy ESLint configuration, Prettier script configurations and plugins, install lifecycle scripts, unreviewed dependency install scripts and local, Git or URL dependencies. Each is unknown for its stage only (or, for another command, simply not joined), so that stage keeps the target-scope key and the others stay confined.

Advisory except for one consumer: on the captured executor path the analysis keys and confines the actions of an analyzed package whose command it models: build and test (slice S5 step B) and the builder-owned stages (see Confined actions). --affected and the native host path still ignore it (slice S5). Rule findings never fail a build; build --check, rule enforcement controls, suppression and --trace-inputs are not implemented (see diagnostic rules). Profiles cover Vite, Vitest, Next.js, Jest, ESLint, PostCSS/Tailwind v3, SvelteKit, Astro, Nuxt, React Router framework mode (Remix's successor), Remix v2 (remix vite:build), the Angular CLI (ng build with the esbuild application builder or the webpack browser builder) and Nest (nest build with the tsc and swc builders); SvelteKit is a layer over the Vite profile, and Astro, Nuxt, React Router, Remix v2 (remix vite:build), Angular and Nest have engines of their own (tier 4, above). Remix's classic remix build, Angular's other webpack builders and Nest's webpack and rspack builders are not modeled; their commands or builders are unknown. Script graph limits (S3): no if/for/while/case, functions, aliases, here-documents, glob expansion of shell arguments (an argument glob is unknown except for cp-like reads), concurrently, turbo, nx, lerna, bun, or yarn plug-and-play specifics. Framework tools run from another workspace member's script are unknown rather than analyzed there. Passing arguments to a hook script and npm config in .npmrc that changes scripts (for example script-shell, ignore-scripts) are not modeled. tsc: extends of an installed package, types/typeRoots, lib files and anything under node_modules are outside the snapshot and not predicted; command-line compiler options other than -p/-b, the output flags and files are not applied to the file set. The compiler comparison needs the harness; the product runs no tsc --listFilesOnly probe (OEP-0020 open decision 7). Configuration functions that frameworks call at build time (Next.js rewrites(), redirects(), headers(), generateBuildId) are not executed or analyzed; if one reads a file, that read is not predicted. Sass/Less @import, +()/*() extglob repetition (approximated by one occurrence) and negated extglobs are not modeled; inline <script type="module"> in HTML is unknown. Real third-party projects are measured report-only; see implementation status. package.json exports conditions, node_modules packages, .d.ts lookups in @types and tool installations are not analyzed; bare imports of installed packages yield no read facts (only the phantom-dependency evidence). Hostile-input bounds: a per-file size/read budget (1 MiB per file, 256 MiB and 20,000 files per snapshot), a lexical depth guard before every parse (400 open brackets, or an estimated 1,000 levels counting chains that nest without brackets, such as ?:, prefix operators, arrows and else if), a tree-depth bound in the source walk, a 5,000-file import graph budget, symlink and containment checks, and non-UTF-8 as opaque. Each limit widens the affected stage to unknown with a named construct rather than truncating it; the NSA-11 cases are unit-tested (stress_tests.rs). The guard over-estimates (it does not skip strings or comments), so an unusually deep but legitimate file can lose precision. The parser is oxc_parser; see the dependency assessment. Trace measurement covers the corpus on Linux; on Windows the ETW prototype has run on the tier 0 to 2 corpus (Tier 0 to 2 on Windows). The code normalizes paths for Windows and macOS. The Windows run of --rules and --determinism (facts and rules, no tracing) passed; see Windows qualification. macOS was not run.

python tooling/measure-node-analysis.py --cli <oyzu> compares predictions with straced reads of real npm run build, test and lint stages on the tier 0, tier 1 and tier 2 corpus (tooling/fixtures/node-analysis: Vite SPA, Vite + Tailwind, Next.js app and pages routers, a SvelteKit app, an Astro site, two Nuxt apps, two React Router apps, an Angular app and two Nest apps (tsc and swc builders; tier 4), Jest + ESLint library, and for S3 a script-heavy project, a tsc --build project-references repo and a pnpm workspaces monorepo), compares every listed tsc project with tsc --listFilesOnly (--self-check proves both comparisons can fail), and checks determinism across checkout paths. A call strace logs in two halves because another thread interrupted it (<unfinished ...> and <... resumed>) is joined before it is compared. --realism DIR fetches the pinned third-party projects of tooling/node-analysis-realism.json into DIR (outside the repository) and reports them without gating (--only TEXT fetches, measures and checks determinism of just the matching projects); results are recorded in implementation status. Every measured project also reports its plan time: the build --plan --json wall time, the number of JavaScript and TypeScript sources in the copy and the per-phase timings the plan reported (see local builds). A realism entry may add files to the unmodified checkout, such as a build.yaml that selects the builder. --rules checks the rule findings alone (no strace needed) against tooling/node-analysis-expected-findings.json: each tier 3 seeded-defect project (tooling/fixtures/node-analysis/defects) must report exactly its seeded finding, and tiers 0 to 2 only the findings reviewed there. --determinism plans the same projects from checkouts at two paths, a CRLF copy and a byte-order-mark copy and compares the whole record (see Windows qualification). Both modes need only Python and the compiled CLI. Unit tests live beside the analyzers and the rule engine; tests/integration/node_analysis.rs drives the compiled CLI in JSON, human and no-color forms.

python tooling/measure-node-analysis.py --cli <oyzu> --confinement (no strace; it runs the real native stages, so it needs the project toolchains: npm, and pnpm for ts-monorepo). For every stage of every authored project whose analysis has no unbounded unknown fact it runs the stage twice from the same prepared copy: once with the whole project visible and once with every file the stage's predicted reads and bounds do not cover removed, the stage contract's projection. It compares the exit code and every file the stage created or changed. A second whole-project run finds output that differs run to run on its own (Next.js writes a random build identifier); that output is excluded and counted in the noise column. A directory or file named by such an identifier (Nuxt's builds/meta/<uuid>.json) is compared under one placeholder name, so a third value in the confined run is not a difference. A build that stamps its time into its output (SvelteKit's default kit.version.name) also renames every content-hashed chunk that embeds it (start.BXjHf8fU.js, 6hRs4Xk-.js): a hashed name that differs between the two whole-project runs is compared by its shape (start.*.js) and count, not by its name or bytes, and counted in the renamed column; the confined run must produce the same number of files of each such shape. A shape whose count differs between the two whole-project runs is noise. Stages with an unbounded unknown fact are reported as not confined; a bounded one keeps its bound visible (bounded unknowns). A negative control removes shared/src/greeting.mjs from the EX-033 api prediction and requires the gate to report the stage as diverged. Every run of a stage (whole, repeated and confined) happens at one fixed path, because Nuxt embeds absolute paths in its output and content-hashed chunk names would otherwise differ between copies. The gate also runs each builder-owned stage the analysis models for a target, natively and the way the captured executor runs it: the version stamp, npm ci (or npm install without a lockfile) offline, npm pack after the target's build, and quality.mjs lint and format-check with a provisioned node-quality home. For a check the verdict (exit code and report) is compared, so a check that fails must fail the same way confined. Result (2026-10-10, Linux, Node 22): 107 equal, 0 diverged, 21 not confined or not measured, the control caught; see the implementation status. Result (2026-10-08, Linux, Node 22, npm and pnpm from the sandbox): 18 equal, 0 diverged, 2 not confined (script-graph lint and next-pages test each have an unknown fact); the control was caught. Status: passed on one Windows host, 2026-10-08 (--rules and --determinism, exit code 0). Reported by the run session on a maintainer-owned machine; not independently verified by the PR author. Environment: Windows 10.0.26200.9550, x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, rustc 1.95.0 (59807616e 2026-04-14), Python 3.12.10, core.autocrlf true, oyzu 0.1.0-local.a5ef2d3a8ae9 (debug) built from main a5ef2d3a8ae9 with a clean worktree. Result: 16 --rules projects ok (tier 3 seeded defects each reported once) and 16 --determinism projects ok. The full evidence is in PR #82. macOS is not covered. strace is Linux-only and is not needed: the two modes below need only Python 3.11+ and a built oyzu.exe, no Node, npm or network, and they plan the authored corpus without running any native stage. Prerequisites: Rust (stable, as for any Oyzu build), Python 3.11+ on PATH, and a Git checkout of this repository. Check out with the default core.autocrlf=true so the fixtures arrive with CRLF line endings, as a Windows user's would; the harness also makes its own CRLF copy, so the result does not depend on that setting. From the repository root in PowerShell: cargo build --locked python tooling/measure-node-analysis.py --cli target\debug\oyzu.exe --rules python tooling/measure-node-analysis.py --cli target\debug\oyzu.exe --determinism Expected on success: --rules ends with RULES RESULT: every seeded defect reported; no unreviewed findings on tiers 0 to 2, and --determinism ends with DETERMINISM RESULT: records byte-identical across checkout paths; equal for CRLF line endings and byte order marks .... Each exits 0. Both can be given in one invocation. A failure prints the project and the difference. What the modes check: --rules: every project in tooling/node-analysis-expected-findings.json (EX-033, the tier 0 to 2 fixtures and the tier 3 seeded defects) is copied to a scratch checkout and planned; the reported rule findings must equal the reviewed list exactly (rule, severity, target, stage, file and line). --determinism: the same projects are planned from four copies: a checkout path, a different deeper path, a copy with every text file converted to CRLF, and a copy with a UTF-8 byte order mark on package.json and the other files the analysis reads (lock files and Oyzu YAML/TOML stay unmarked). The whole analysis record must be byte-identical between the two paths. The CRLF and byte-order-mark copies must produce the same record apart from the byte offsets in spans, the fact ids derived from them (and the fact order that follows the ids) and the snapshot digest, all of which legitimately depend on file bytes. No string in any record may contain the checkout path, a drive letter (C:\ or C:/) or a backslash. Recording the result: do not edit this section to say "passed" from memory. Paste the complete console output of both commands, the output of oyzu --version, python --version, the Windows version and whether core.autocrlf was on, into the pull request that records the run, and add one dated line to implementation status and to the cross-platform item of the verification plan naming that PR. A failing project is a finding to report, not something to exclude. Not covered by this run: trace soundness on Windows (an ETW tracer has since been run on the tier 0 to 2 corpus; see Tier 0 to 2 on Windows), macOS, case-insensitive resolution (implemented later on Linux, below), and Windows confinement views (not supported, so Windows keeps target-scope keys). The run was a single debug build on one machine.

Status: prototype; probe and the tier 0 to 2 corpus passed on one Windows host, 2026-10-10, with zero soundness failures (see Tier 0 to 2 on Windows). tooling/node_analysis_etw.py gives the harness a Windows tracer with the same contract as the Linux strace one: it runs a native stage, fails if the stage fails, and returns the checkout-relative files (outside node_modules, .git and .oyzu) that the stage or any process it started opened or queried. On Windows the traced measurement (--cli <oyzu> with no mode flag) uses it in place of strace; nothing else in the harness changes. How it works: an ETW session started with the in-box logman records the Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-File Create events (every open, including the opens behind attribute queries) and the Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-Process start and stop events to an .etl file while the stage runs. tracerpt decodes it to XML. The session is system-wide, so the tracer follows the stage's process tree the way strace -f follows forks and drops every other process. It keeps opens of existing files only (the FILE_OPEN disposition, not directories), maps NT device names (\Device\HarddiskVolume3) to drive letters, and matches paths case-insensitively against the checkout, reporting each file with its on-disk spelling. A trace whose header reports lost events, or no lost-event count at all, is rejected, because a lost Create event would hide a read. Prerequisites: Windows, an elevated prompt or membership in Performance Log Users (kernel providers need one of them; a new group membership applies after signing in again), logman and tracerpt (both in-box), Python 3.11+, and for the measurement itself Node, npm and pnpm as on Linux. Check the tracer before trusting a measurement: python tooling/measure-node-analysis.py --trace-probe python tooling/measure-node-analysis.py --cli target\debug\oyzu.exe --only vite-spa --trace-probe needs no CLI. It runs a small Python program (and a Node one when node is on PATH) that reads a file, stats one, queries one with GetFileAttributesW, opens one with the wrong case, starts a child that reads a file, writes and appends to files, and reads one in node_modules and one outside the checkout. The tracer must report exactly the reads, stats and the child's read. It prints TRACE PROBE RESULT: tracer saw exactly the probe's reads and exits 0, or names each missed or extra file. It runs on Linux too, against strace, where it passes (2026-10-10, Node 22); a tracer that drops a read makes it fail. The ETW decoding is unit-tested on any host (python tooling/test-node-analysis-etw.py: event order, the lost-event header, tracerpt's RenderingInfo block, the process tree with a reused process id, the disposition and directory filters, device-name mapping and checkout matching). Windows run (2026-10-10, Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26200.9550, Python 3.12.10, oyzu 0.1.0-local.9200779469c1 built from this branch, elevated; reported by the run session on a maintainer-owned machine, recorded in PR #172). The first probe missed every read: tracerpt writes a second, GUID-less <Provider> inside each event's RenderingInfo block, which overwrote the provider GUID. The decoder now reads only the System and EventData blocks. The harness's setup and untraced stage commands also failed to start npm, a .cmd shim, and now resolve it on PATH as the tracer does. The real trace confirmed the other assumptions: EventsLost 0 in the header, CreateOptions in hex, FileName as \Device\HarddiskVolumeN\..., decimal process ids. With both fixes: --trace-probe passed (Node probe included, so GetFileAttributesW, fs.statSync and fs.existsSync do produce Create events), and --cli target\debug\oyzu.exe --only vite-spa exited 0 with zero soundness failures: vite-spa project build traced 17 predicted 18 precision 0.944 unknown 0.0 unsound 0 vite-spa project test traced 10 predicted 11 precision 0.909 unknown 0.0 unsound 0 The one predicted file not traced in either stage is package-lock.json. Tier 0 to 2 on Windows​ Run 2026-10-10 16:42 to 17:06 UTC on the same host (Windows 10.0.26200.9550, Python 3.12.10, Node v24.14.1, npm 11.11.0, pnpm 10.0.0, TypeScript 6.0.2 on PATH, oyzu built from PR #254 at 456018a, elevated; reported by the run session on a maintainer-owned machine). --trace-probe exited 0, and --cli target\debug\oyzu.exe --max-tier 2 --rules --determinism exited 0 with zero soundness failures. Every tsc --listFilesOnly comparison matched (tsc-library 3/3, tsc-references 5/5, ts-monorepo 2/2, script-graph build 2/2 and test 3/3). Determinism was identical, and --rules reported every seeded defect with no unreviewed findings. Project Stage Traced Predicted Precision Unknown Unsound EX-033 (each of 3 targets) build 3 4 0.75 0 0 tsc-library build 6 6 1.0 0 0 npm-workspace build 7 11 0.636 0 0 tsc-references build 10 11 0.909 0 0 script-graph build 10 11 0.909 0 0 script-graph test 6 8 0.75 0 0 script-graph lint 2 5 0.4 0.143 0 vite-spa build 17 18 0.944 0 0 vite-spa test 10 11 0.909 0 0 ts-monorepo build 10 11 0.909 0 0 vite-tailwind build 11 12 0.917 0 0 vite-tailwind test 6 7 0.857 0 0 jest-eslint-lib lint 6 7 0.857 0 0 jest-eslint-lib test 6 7 0.857 0 0 next-app build 13 14 0.929 0 0 next-app test 8 9 0.889 0 0 next-pages build 11 12 0.917 0 0 next-pages test 14 14 1.0 0.1 0 In the first run, two stages had no numbers. The ts-monorepo build failed with TS2307 because the harness's stage copy followed the workspace junctions (fixed below), and the vite-tailwind test hit vitest's "Timeout starting forks runner" on a loaded machine. A --resume rerun of those two projects (2026-10-11 03:11 to 03:13 UTC, oyzu built at d9fe556, same host and tools) measured both, and their rows above come from it. The probe and the measurement exited 0, with zero soundness failures and the ts-monorepo tsc list equal (2/2). The rerun also re-checked rules and determinism over all 11 projects, and both passed again. Harness changes this run needed (PR #254): tsc_listing resolves the compiler with PATHEXT (tsc.cmd) and keeps any absolute listing line, including E:/... paths; the parser is unit-tested on any host. pnpm and npm workspace links on Windows are absolute junctions, which shutil.copytree follows. Stage and confinement copies now skip junctions and recreate them, retargeting links inside the project into the copy. --max-tier N limits a run to tiers 0..N, --resume DIR saves each project's result and skips projects already saved, and progress lines ([mm:ss] ..., one per project and stage) go to stderr (OYZU_MEASURE_QUIET=1 turns them off). The ETW decoder streams the tracerpt XML and keeps only the events it uses, and the .etl and .xml are deleted after parsing (OYZU_MEASURE_KEEP_TRACES=1 keeps them). The first full run crashed the host under heavy disk I/O (a storage driver bugcheck, not memory pressure). A full tier 0 to 2 run still writes about 3 GB of decoded XML, so filtering events before decoding is the next speedup. Still to run on Windows: the realism set (tiers 3 and up). Record further runs the same way: complete output, oyzu --version, python --version and the Windows version in the pull request, and one dated line in implementation status. Known limits of the prototype: an open of an existing file for writing only is counted as a read, because the Create event carries no access mask (this can report a false soundness failure, never hide one); failed opens of existing files are counted too; a build that outlives a large system-wide burst of file activity may lose events, which is reported as a failure, not as a pass. The session buffer sizes are untuned.

The analysis code was reviewed for Windows path risks. This is what was found: Fixed: a leading UTF-8 byte order mark (written by Notepad and Windows PowerShell 5) was kept in the text offered to the parsers, which dropped facts (a .env file whose first variable is hidden by the mark, a tsconfig or manifest that failed to parse) and could raise a false undeclared-env finding. SnapshotReader now drops one leading mark; provenance byte offsets index the text after it. Unit test: leading_byte_order_mark_is_not_part_of_the_text. Verified correct, test added: line and column numbers are computed from \n only, so a CRLF file reports the same lines and columns as the LF file (crlf_text_has_the_same_lines_and_columns_as_lf_text); the harness checks the same for every corpus project. Already handled by the snapshot, unchanged: the inventory converts \ to /, rejects non-portable names and case-colliding paths, and refuses symlinks and reparse points; analysis paths are POSIX relative strings and the code in src/analysis and src/builders/node/analysis never formats a host path (the harness checks the records for leaks). Not changed, limitation: join rejects a relative specifier containing \ or :. It is not exercised by the corpus. Fixed later (2026-10-10), case-insensitive resolution: the resolver matched specifiers case-sensitively, whereas Windows and default macOS open a file whose name differs only by case. A mismatched import became unknown (sound but imprecise), and one case was unsound: with A.js and a.ts beside each other, ./a.js was predicted to read only a.ts (TypeScript's mapping), while Node on Windows opens A.js. Each resolver probe (relative and alias specifiers, member entries, directory index and package.json lookups) now also matches the one inventoried path that differs only by ASCII case and records it under its real spelling, so the prediction is the superset on every host and facts stay host-independent. Capture already rejects case-colliding paths, so the match is unique; if a snapshot ever held two, the probe matches neither and the import stays unknown. A path with non-ASCII characters is matched exactly, because NTFS (upcase table) and APFS (normalization) fold those differently. Every other exact-name lookup the analyzers make (a framework config, a tsconfig.json, a directory convention) is not changed one by one: the snapshot reader remembers each lookup that missed only by case, and the analysis adds a target-wide case-variant-path unknown naming the asked and found paths, so a Vite.config.ts where Vite asks for vite.config.ts widens the target instead of being predicted absent. Tests: case_insensitive_lookups_name_the_inventoried_entry_and_remember_near_misses, imports_differing_only_by_case_resolve_to_the_inventoried_file and non_ascii_case_variants_and_exact_name_lookups_widen_to_unknown. Plans of every authored corpus project and all 27 pinned real projects are byte-identical before and after the change on Linux (none has a case mismatch). Not run on Windows or macOS. The residual gap for Unicode normalization was closed the same day (below). Fixed later (2026-10-10), Unicode normalization: APFS and HFS+ open a name in either normalization form (NFC é or NFD e plus a combining accent), and a Mac can commit either, while Linux and Windows treat them as different names. Before, an import spelled in one form of a file inventoried in the other stayed an unresolved unknown (sound but imprecise), and an exact-name analyzer lookup that missed only by normalization was predicted absent without widening. A probe for a non-ASCII path now also matches the one inventoried entry with the same NFC spelling and records it under its real spelling, which is again the superset on every host. When several entries share that spelling and none is the asked one, nothing matches and the target widens; a miss by case and normalization together widens too, since non-ASCII case folding differs between hosts. The snapshot reader's near-miss key is now the lowercased NFC spelling, so exact-name analyzer lookups that miss only by normalization also add the case-variant-path unknown, whose detail now says "differs only by case or Unicode normalization". Capture still rejects only case collisions; a tree holding both forms of a name is kept. NFC comes from icu_normalizer, already compiled in through reqwest's url/idna. Tests: normalization_insensitive_lookups_need_one_spelling and imports_differing_only_by_unicode_normalization_match_one_file_or_widen. Not run on macOS. Fixed later (2026-10-10): a package.json that starts with a byte order mark was rejected by Node target discovery (src/builders/node, outside the analysis), so oyzu discover and oyzu build --plan failed on such a project. The Node builder's Rust-side manifest reads now drop one leading mark with the same helper the snapshot reader uses. Tests: byte_order_marked_package_json_is_discovered_like_an_unmarked_one and compiled_build_plan_reads_a_byte_order_marked_package_json. The Node runtime adapters used in isolated builds read package.json through the shared runtime/manifest.mjs, which drops the mark the same way. quality.mjs and version-stamp.cjs run as node -e, so they drop it inline. Proof: node --test tooling/test-node-manifest.mjs. A real isolated build of a marked project has not been run (the worker image pull returned 403 where this was checked).

documents.t: CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/node-workspace-tests.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Status: experimental. oyzu run test collects package-owned JUnit and LCOV for npm, pnpm 10 and Yarn Classic workspaces. Native managers determine workspace membership; Oyzu infers each package's test runner and uses the shared report collector. This direct host flow requires no build YAML or reporting section. oyzu run list oyzu run test oyzu inspect dist

Install the project's dependencies and provision Node and its native package manager before running tests. Oyzu does not acquire tools or dependencies during this operation. Measured local versions are Node 24.14.1, npm 11.11.0, pnpm 10.11.0 and Yarn 1.22.22 on Windows. CI provisions Node 22 and those manager versions after compiling the CLI. New pnpm/Yarn cross-platform acceptance remains pending. Static listing reads native markers and scripts without executing a package manager. package.json workspaces identify npm/Yarn workspaces; pnpm-workspace.yaml identifies pnpm even before a lock exists. Native lockfiles and packageManager declarations still participate in the normal manager conflict rules. Actual membership is observed only after an explicit admitted test request: npm uses its installed graph adapter, pnpm uses its native recursive JSON list, and Yarn Classic uses its native workspace-info output. Oyzu does not implement a competing workspace glob parser. See pnpm list and Yarn Classic workspace commands. pnpm/Yarn must expose their provisioned JavaScript entrypoint on PATH through a normal package installation or native executable link. This supports package-local .bin directories and ordinary global installations on Windows and Unix without spawning a .cmd shim through a shell. Corepack-based acquisition and standalone bundled pnpm executables are not used by this adapter. pnpm automatic manager-version management is disabled; Yarn uses offline mode and ignores yarn-path redirection. Other native project settings still apply. Missing prerequisites or an unsupported manager major version fail explicitly.

Without a root test script, listing shows the native recursive test command for the selected manager. At execution, Oyzu observes membership, freezes package scopes and report obligations, then runs each member's native script or inferred Node/Jest/Vitest/Mocha suite. An explicit root test script instead owns one aggregate report pair and runs once. A publishable root without a script also owns an implicit suite where the native manager permits that root layout. Yarn Classic requires a private workspace root. Native package scripts keep their manager's argument and lifecycle behavior. Inferred suites exclude nested members; explicit scripts retain their own selection semantics. Framework dependencies and reporters must already be installed; see native reporting prerequisites. pnpm/Yarn native Node suites and root aggregation are verified locally; their broader mixed-framework combinations remain to be qualified. The existing npm mixed-framework probe exercises the shared execution layer separately. Each package's current JUnit and LCOV files enter a test-only dist/ bundle with plan, logs and manifest summaries. Package names provide stable report identities. A failing assertion fails the command while allowing later suites to run and retaining available reports. Missing native tools, malformed metadata or unresolved framework selection may stop execution before any suite starts. Missing or invalid required reports remain errors, including under task overrides. No success is manufactured for a command that emits no evidence. Oyzu pre/post hooks use the common task engine. A failed test blocks its success-only post hook. Exact implicit commands receive report instrumentation; arbitrary TOML replacements retain their bodies and must fulfill the required report contract. Member commands receive OYZU_TEST_REPORT and OYZU_COVERAGE_REPORT. Replacing a whole workspace task must supply its named obligations or explicit report collection paths. Forwarded arguments reach each selected native test command; a root script receives them once.

Direct tests do not rewrite package versions or locks, build snapshot archives, or run unrelated quality gates. Native test scripts may write host files and access the host environment/network. Offline manager flags restrict native acquisition behavior, not arbitrary script effects. Installed dependencies are consumed as they exist; this is not frozen dependency provenance or publication authority. See direct test evidence for history, existing output preservation and failed-bundle inspection. npm has captured workspace packaging and implicit member build/quality composition. Yarn Classic now also implements captured workspace packaging and quality/report composition, with isolated CLI acceptance pending. pnpm now uses the same captured workspace planner with native member/importer facts and packing; isolated CLI acceptance remains pending. pnpm/Yarn direct host member build/quality defaults are still incomplete. A pnpm YAML packages declaration selects workspace planning, while patch-only configuration retains the single-project path. Yarn modern releases and all workspace configurations are not covered by this increment. npm workspace builds documents the separately implemented captured path. Run the compiled-CLI probe after provisioning native fixture packages in tooling/images/node-pnpm and tooling/images/node-yarn, plus tooling/design-requirements.txt: python tooling/test-npm-workspace-direct.py --cli <compiled-path> --manager npm python tooling/test-npm-workspace-direct.py --cli <compiled-path> --manager pnpm python tooling/test-npm-workspace-direct.py --cli <compiled-path> --manager yarn The probe adapts EX-020's native manifests for each manager and explicitly provisions its local workspace links before product execution. It verifies inferred and scripted member tests, hooks, failed/sibling evidence, source/lock preservation, root aggregation and inspection. CI runs all three after CLI compilation. Implementation status records revision-specific results without treating a host test bundle as captured artifact acceptance.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/npm-workspaces.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. This experimental integration uses npm's native workspace membership and installed dependency graph. It supports private aggregation roots and publishable root packages, with independent snapshot packages and test reports. It does not yet complete every EX-020 requirement; affected selection, member task groups and duplicate target selection remain unfinished.
documents.s: npm workspace builds and development tasks

documents.t: Captured builds resolve artifact versions per native member using scoped Git baselines and the transitive local dependency graph. Unrelated member changes do not advance a package's base; shared root inputs conservatively affect all members. Packaged local references use each dependency's selected version. Provide Node/npm and install the project's native dependencies yourself. Oyzu does not install tools. Native development verification uses Node 24/npm 11 on Windows; CI provisions Node 22/npm 11 on Windows, macOS and Linux. These measured versions do not establish compatibility with every older version. From a conventional npm workspace root containing package.json and its native lock: oyzu run list oyzu run build oyzu run test oyzu run lint oyzu run format-check oyzu run format No Oyzu configuration is required. run list is static and does not invoke Node/npm or project scripts. Explicit execution resolves installed workspace facts with npm's bundled membership library and Arborist. Missing dependencies or native tools can therefore allow listing but prevent execution. Provision dependencies with the project's normal npm workflow, then retry. Installed workspace links must resolve to their declared member directories. Identity comparison uses native canonical paths so directory aliases do not change ownership. A link to a different directory or a copied package in place of a workspace link fails before member commands run; repair the native installation and retry. A root package's declared workspace dependency is validated against its actual version/specification using npm's native validator. Arborist's synthetic membership edge describes a local path and is not a substitute for that dependency constraint. Invalid required declarations fail before member execution even when a workspace link exists; optional dependency handling retains native edge semantics. Default quality tasks additionally require the selected ESLint/Prettier or Biome tools and their supporting packages. Installed project packages take precedence; a declared but missing tool fails. For a project without those tools, supply the provisioned defaults described in the Node quality reference, using OYZU_NODE_QUALITY_HOME for development. That directory contains the quality toolchain's package.json and node_modules. Oyzu does not fetch missing checkers.

Operation Explicit root script Without an explicit root script build Run it once with native npm lifecycle hooks Run member build scripts in dependency order; report members without scripts as not requesting compilation test Run it once with native npm pretest/posttest hooks Run each member's test script or detected Node/Jest/Vitest/Mocha runner; a publishable root also runs its own implicit suite lint Run it once Check root-owned source; use each member's lint script or selected ESLint/Biome format-check Run format-check or format:check once Check root-owned source; use each member's corresponding script or selected Prettier/Biome check format Run it once on explicit request Format root-owned source; use each member's format script or selected Prettier/Biome formatting Native script names remain visible in task listing, including a root format:check alias. When that alias owns the operation, use oyzu run format:check; Oyzu does not add a duplicate format-check task. Existing TOML task replacements take precedence over inferred tasks. See configuration for settings, profiles and task override behavior. For a coarse native root build, the shared captured workspace runtime checks concrete public JavaScript entries selected by Node's import and require conditions before packaging. It also checks concrete declaration files selected by Node's types condition and literal legacy declaration paths; file presence does not establish TypeScript validity. A missing selected regular file fails the build, while null exclusions and conditional alternatives remain native Node decisions. This prepack check does not certify that npm included those files in its archive, nor does it validate browser/custom conditions or every wildcard path. See the pnpm qualification record for the bounded native omission evidence; it is a shared workspace check, not pnpm-specific packaging behavior. Workspace tests resolve each member's installed framework, including hoisted dependencies. Native Jest/Vitest/Mocha entrypoints come from their package bin declarations. Implicit Node suites use native test filename patterns; implicit parent suites exclude nested members and engine state. Explicit scripts keep their own selection semantics, so a script can deliberately aggregate other packages. A private root without a test script is an aggregation container and has no additional implicit root suite. Native assertion failures fail the aggregate while allowing later suites to run; discovery, missing-runner or selection errors can stop the operation before later suites start. Missing Node tests currently fail explicitly instead of producing an empty successful suite. The bounded Node selection allows at most 4,096 files and 24,000 path characters. Development test commands preserve native console output and script argument forwarding and export the test-only bundle described below. Use oyzu build for captured execution and snapshot artifacts. Native scripts and framework configuration execute on the host during run test; only static listing is nonexecuting. Default root checks exclude workspace members. Default member checks exclude nested members, so a parent default cannot bypass a child's explicit script ownership. The current quality file scope is JavaScript/TypeScript and their supported JSX, CommonJS and ESM extensions. Dependency directories, engine state, build output and coverage are excluded; source symlinks are not followed. Native ESLint configuration and Prettier configuration/ignores are respected. This is not yet a general formatter for all repository file types. Default checks are read-only. format writes files and is never selected as an implicit build check. A user-authored script can perform its own effects; its name does not establish that it is read-only. A failed member build stops dependent compilation. Quality failures continue through the other members to collect diagnostics, then fail the aggregate. Already executed script effects or explicit formatting writes are not rolled back. Native scripts receive forwarded arguments through npm. A composed operation containing any default quality checker rejects extra arguments before invoking member operations; define a native script or explicit argv task for custom checker options. Native Biome configuration can select Biome instead of the ESLint/Prettier defaults for a member; see Node quality for supported versions and scope. Cyclic workspace build dependencies currently fail before member build execution. Large development plans exceeding the current 20,000-byte encoded plan bound fail with a host argument-limit error.

oyzu run test now writes a test-only dist/ bundle with JUnit and LCOV for each package. No reporting section is needed. An explicit root test script owns one aggregate report pair; otherwise each member has a pair, plus an implicit root suite when the root is publishable. Named report IDs use the same native package identity as captured builds. A failing assertion fails the command but retains available sibling reports; Oyzu's success-only post hook is blocked. Run oyzu inspect dist to check the bundle. See direct test evidence for history, preserved host output and host-isolation disclosures. This workflow uses already installed native dependencies. Native membership and installed link identities are observed only after an explicit, admitted test request; run list still executes no native code. The frozen report contract is built before hooks or prerequisites execute, so install the workspace dependencies before invoking tests. This does not acquire dependencies, update package versions or rewrite the lockfile. Ordinary host network access and native npm configuration remain in effect. The same package test adapter now serves captured and host execution. Implicit suites exclude nested members, and Jest/Vitest/Mocha resolve configuration from the package being tested, including native scripted members. Native scripts retain their npm lifecycle and forwarded arguments. Framework/reporting prerequisites match the single-package profiles; notably Vitest needs its matching coverage provider and Mocha needs native c8. Custom commands keep their body but must supply required reports. They receive per-package OYZU_TEST_REPORT and OYZU_COVERAGE_REPORT paths when invoked by the native workspace composition. Replacing the entire workspace task must fulfill its package report obligations or declare explicit report collection paths through the shared task contract. A marker-only command that previously returned success now fails for missing evidence; no successful test report is invented for it. Root aggregate report declarations can redirect the single pair of native destinations. Individually redirecting every native member report through configuration is not implemented. python tooling/test-npm-workspace-direct.py --cli <compiled-path> copies EX-020, provisions its native local npm links, and proves direct tests, separate member reports, hooks, failed/sibling evidence, unchanged metadata and bundle inspection. The mixed-framework probe below also checks a publishable root and nested members through report bundles. CI runs these only after the CLI is compiled. Measured host results and pending CI results are recorded in implementation status.

oyzu build requires Docker and a provisioned npm toolchain image; see CLI image provisioning. It captures source and locked dependencies, resolves the native graph, and prepares snapshot versions in a private execution copy. Execution replays prepared dependencies offline. Acquisition can access configured sources; the build does not authorize arbitrary new downloads. Development run tasks use the host environment and normal npm configuration, so they do not provide this isolation guarantee. oyzu build oyzu inspect dist Each member declares its own npm archive with a version containing the captured source identity. A root without private: true additionally produces a root package; a private aggregation root does not. Local dependency references are projected to the member snapshot versions. Native npm selects package contents. Engine state is excluded; root staging rejects symlinks, inconsistent inventories and selections above 100,000 files or 1 GiB. The repository's manifests and lock are not version-edited in place. Creating an artifact, including one for a private member, does not authorize publication. Members that share a package name, or are versioned latest, fail before acquisition; see member names. Acquisition requires a lock record for every native member whose recorded name, if present, matches the member. A member's own version in the lock is left to native npm ci, which reconciles it with that member's package.json; planning reads versions from package.json and projects them into the private copy's lock. A lock that is stale in a way npm itself rejects, such as a member version that no longer satisfies a sibling's dependency, still fails during acquisition with npm's own error. file: dependencies on local folders are admitted, in workspaces and single projects alike. npm records each one as a link ("link": true) plus a lock record for the folder, for example "@oyzu-example/fixture-helper": "file:tools/fixture-helper" in the EX-020 npm-file-link variation. The folder must be a relative path inside the captured source, outside node_modules, with its own lock record and package.json, and no symbolic link on the way. Native npm links it during installation; the folder is captured as source, never acquired. Registry packages that npm locks beneath the folder (tools/fixture-helper/node_modules/...) are captured like a member's. A link to anything else fails acquisition with npm link is not a captured native workspace or local folder. The folder is not a workspace member, so it gets no artifact, tests or version projection of its own; root quality checks cover its source as root-owned files. An explicit root test script owns one aggregate invocation. Otherwise member suites run individually and a publishable root also requires its own tests. Supported native Node/Jest/Vitest/Mocha integrations produce JUnit and coverage; arbitrary custom commands must satisfy their report obligations. A publishable root with no discoverable Node tests currently fails. Root framework filtering excludes members and engine state while retaining native project exclusions; Jest filtering handles canonical and aliased root paths. Implicit member tests in captured builds use the same package-owned scope selection as development tests. Planned exclusions prevent a parent implicit suite from rediscovering its nested members; explicit scripts retain native selection. The resulting dist/manifest.json records retained artifacts, reports and status alongside the plan, envelope and logs. Test and quality failures block final artifact collection. Native package receipts detect archive changes between packaging and collection. Missing or invalid required reports remain failures, including under task overrides. inspect checks bundle integrity, not production trust or release eligibility. Earlier bundles are preserved under .oyzu/history.

The native probes exercise real npm packaging, snapshot dependency references, relocated archive reproducibility, root/member reports, failures and quality ownership: python tooling/test-npm-workspace-build.py python tooling/test-npm-workspace-tasks.py --cli target/debug/oyzu python tooling/test-npm-workspace-tests.py --cli target/debug/oyzu node --test tooling/test-node-lock.mjs covers file: link admission and member-version ownership without npm; python tooling/test-npm-workspaces.py acquires and replays the npm-file-link variation with native npm, and the compiled-CLI node-workspaces group builds it. Those native and compiled-CLI runs have not yet been recorded for this change; see implementation status. Use target/debug/oyzu.exe on Windows and provision native quality tools first. The workspace test probe also needs the native dependencies from tooling/fixtures/jest and tooling/fixtures/vitest; override their locations with --jest-modules and --vitest-modules. It verifies native Node, Jest 29 and Vitest 5, not arbitrary framework versions. The Jest reporter probe additionally needs --jest-cli pointing to an installed native Jest entrypoint. CI builds the CLI before these host checks and runs separate compiled-CLI captured-build scenarios on Linux. Native probes do not by themselves prove sandbox behavior. Revision-specific results and outstanding cross-host verification are recorded in implementation status. Mocha 11 workspace reporting additionally uses native c8 10, preserves package-local reporters and produces per-package evidence for implicit and recognized scripted suites. python tooling/test-mocha-reporting.py --cli target/debug/oyzu provisions and exercises its native workspace fixture; the captured Node suite independently checks versioned package outputs and failed-member gating. Implicit Mocha suites use native --ignore options for member/engine-state exclusions; explicit native scripts retain their selection scope. Additional test frameworks, complete framework configuration inheritance, cyclic graphs, affected selection, caching and publication remain separate work. Native workspace test bundles now also support pnpm/Yarn direct execution. Direct test bundles contain host test evidence, not the captured build's versioned artifacts. This reference describes the npm integration, not a claim of complete builder or scenario support.
