On the native host lane, retirement never moves anything and previous is always false: the target directory is a private projection that core rebuilds from the frozen source selection before each build, so anything already at the path would be source, which the overlap rule refuses first. What keeps an earlier output from being republished here is that rebuild; retirement is kept so the guarantee does not depend on it. The record is not part of action cache keys. Captured planning checks the frozen source selection without changing it. The frozen plan retires output in the mutable private execution workspace before dependency setup and authored operations, then exports the fresh artifact through the common containment and no-link checks. It never retires files in the original project or the read-only planning mount. To recover from a refusal, have the plugin name a project output that is not source, not core or version-control state and not dependency trees, and remove any link at that location. Each operation runs one fresh plugin process through core's plugin process host: no arguments, a minimal environment, a fresh scratch working directory and a 60-second deadline, after which the whole process tree is terminated. Bound targets are reused from the local action cache like built-in ones: the action key binds the plugin's executable digest and runtime, so rebuilding the plugin re-runs its targets. Bind the plugin executable itself: a binding to a wrapper script is never reused, because the digest covers only the script and not the program it starts (see external builder targets). An unchanged one-module repeat build launches the plugin 5 times: tasks, requirements (asked once per distinct request and stage set and reused for the invocation), native-admission, native-build and one task-command per frozen command (two when it asks for an observation). Core asks task-command for every command, including the ones the plugin produced, because the plugin may expand them (the Go plugin expands its own instrumented test command under a go.work). Launch counts scale with the number of bound targets.

oyzu-plugin-node serves node/app only, for the lane the built-in Node builder already runs natively: manager npm, the target declared uses: node/app, no workspaces, and a non-empty scripts.build that does not start with vite build. Any other node/app target is refused with the plugin's reason (admission reasons); while the binding exists such a target cannot build at all, because a bound id has no fallback to the built-in builder. node/package stays built in. For non-workspace npm targets, oyzu run test instruments a default node --test or the existing recognized flag-only npm test script with native JUnit and lcov reporters. Opaque commands keep their exact argv and may write reports to OYZU_TEST_REPORT and OYZU_COVERAGE_REPORT or declared report paths. Missing optional reports produce incomplete evidence; required missing reports, malformed present reports and native failures fail the command. Other managers and workspace tests fail explicitly with node.test-lane. Direct tasks require already prepared native dependencies and a selected Node runtime. An admitted application build offers these ordered actions. The shared check levels decide which checks run; --full selects every check that is not off. Action Command When <target>:install npm ci, plus --offline when requested Nonempty dependencies, devDependencies or optionalDependencies <target>:build Selected authored build task, normally npm run build Always <target>:test Authored test script or detected default Tests selected <target>:lint Authored lint script or native ESLint/Biome adapter Lint selected <target>:format-check or <target>:format:check Authored check script or native Prettier/Biome adapter Format selected; mutating format is never selected Default quality commands reuse the built-in native API adapter. Install the project's selected ESLint/Prettier/Biome dependencies first; an explicitly provisioned OYZU_NODE_QUALITY_HOME may supply undeclared fallback packages. Declared-but-uninstalled packages fail rather than falling back. Native config and ignores remain authoritative; generated output and symlinks are excluded by the existing adapter. oyzu run format mutates source; format-check does not. Authored scripts win over defaults. format:check, build:prod and other portable colon names are retained; unsupported names fail discovery explicitly. Use oyzu run app:format:check or [tasks."app:format:check"] when qualifying a name. Native task environment defaults enter the ordinary configuration and policy pipeline; reserved OYZU_* names remain unavailable to authored config. Recognized-runner qualification in this slice is Node's built-in runner only. Jest/Vitest/Mocha detection and default commands are available, but their native report adapters are not exported by this plugin: they behave as opaque commands and must produce authored reports to satisfy required gates. No framework, pnpm/yarn or workspace support is implied. See the native checks qualification and the separate captured npm proof. The plugin echoes the build task's argv in its build operation because the host requires a command for build ("native build invocation missing" otherwise). This contradicts the wire contract, which says an operation without command runs the target's own task; the mismatch is tracked as a follow-up issue. The artifact is the dist directory the build script writes (origin: target, subject to fresh-output checks), named application-<version> from the version core resolved. Dependencies without package-lock.json fail at plan time, before any action, with PLUGIN_OPERATION_FAILED: … (NativeBuild): node.lock-file: host npm dependency preparation requires package-lock.json; create it with npm before building (an npm-shrinkwrap.json alone is not enough, as for the built-in). A failed npm ci blocks the build action and collects nothing. Differences from the built-in builder for the same project: The artifact name uses core's resolved version (for an unversioned checkout 0.0.0-dev.g<source hash>), not package.json's version. The directory inventory and content digests are the same. The install action is <target>:install, the target's install task (npm ci with a lock file), where the built-in runs an internal <target>:prepare action: core runs a plugin operation only when the target has a task of that name. Its environment is the install task's admitted environment, where the built-in gives npm ci the build task's; they are the same unless the two tasks' environments differ. Because it is a task, an authored install task in oyzu.toml replaces npm ci, and disabling the install stage drops it; the built-in's prepare can be neither replaced nor disabled. Core runs an authored task on its host path with the ambient environment, not the pinned tool environment the plugin's install operation gets, so an authored npm ci can fail where the plugin's own install works (on Linux without a global npm: cannot execute npm: No such file or directory). Report integration labels and framework adapters. The plugin supplies command/report intent but not the built-in's integration-mode metadata or Jest/Vitest/Mocha adapters. Core still records command, report and acceptance evidence independently. Each bound target launches a plugin process for its discovery/planning operations and command adaptation. Earlier N1 timings remain historical measurements; this checks slice does not claim new performance results. The complete list, with the differential test that holds it, is in known differences.

Error Cause Recovery CONFIG_SCOPE: plugins.development is not permitted in this scope The setting is in a project file or profile Move it to user or machine configuration PLUGIN_BINDING_INVALID: … cannot read plugin executable The path is missing or not a regular file Build the plugin or correct the path PLUGIN_BINDING_INVALID: … is not a builder id a built-in builder serves The id is unknown Use an id such as go/app PLUGIN_OPERATION_FAILED: <id> plugin <path> (<operation>) The plugin failed, answered unsupported, broke the protocol, exited nonzero, wrote no result or exceeded its deadline; the cause follows, with the plugin's warning and error diagnostics Fix the plugin; the cause names the rule broken PLUGIN_ISOLATED_UNSUPPORTED / ENGINE_ASSET_UNAVAILABLE Captured execution lacks an admitted package capability, platform member, supported profile or exact engine assets. When the plugin also declined the target for the native host lane in native-admission, the message ends with one clause per such selected target, ; target <id> was not admitted to the native host lane: <reason> (for example ENGINE_ASSET_UNAVAILABLE: no admitted execution assets selected; target hello was not admitted to the native host lane: host Go builds require exactly one main package). If native-admission itself failed, it ends with ; target <id>: its plugin failed native-admission: <cause> Fix what the reason names so the plugin admits the target for the native host lane, or supply the documented captured package and engine prerequisites plugin … sets command env, which the native host lane does not carry yet A build operation or test command carried env Use native-build output env; per-command env is a Milestone A limit PLUGIN_ARTIFACT_REFUSED: artifact … names … An origin: target artifact overlaps the frozen source selection, passes through a link or reparse point, or lies below a file; or core could not move a previous output aside Name a project output that is not source and has no link in its path (project-written outputs) A failed operation fails the build or task like any preparation failure; no partial plugin result is used.

A plain oyzu build routes a bound target to the native host lane first. When the plugin declines it, the build cannot continue on the captured path without execution assets, so it fails during preparation, before any plugin build action or tool installation, with the code above and the plugin's reason appended. The message names every selected bound target the plugin kept off the native host lane, one clause each, not only the first target that failed: with an admitted api and a refused tools, it ends ; target tools was not admitted to the native host lane: <reason>. A plugin that fails native-admission is named the same way. The human and --json outputs carry the same message (in JSON, the failed result's diagnostic message). oyzu build --plan does not fail: its "Unresolved until preparation" list (unresolved in JSON) adds the same clause for each such target (Target <id> was not admitted to the native host lane: <reason>). A refused target that captured planning would admit still gets its clause when a different target is the one that fails; the remedy in the table applies to the refused targets named, not to the one that happened to fail first. The clauses are asked of the plugins only after a failure. A target that captured planning takes is planned exactly as before, and a build in which every bound target is admitted launches nothing extra. The answers are the ones native selection already cached for this invocation; a target native selection never reached (it stops at the first refusal) costs one native-admission launch. With --isolated or --all-platforms, engine selection runs first and does not launch plugins, so the engine's own refusal (ENGINE_PIN_MISMATCH when no matching engine archive is admitted) is what you see until the engine is admitted. Once it is, a target that cannot be planned on the captured path fails with its PLUGIN_ISOLATED_UNSUPPORTED message and the same appended clauses. That failure now launches each selected bound target's plugin on the host for native-admission if the answer is not cached, once per target; a failing or hanging plugin can add up to its 60-second deadline per target. A target the plugin admitted natively gets no clause. The reason is only ever added to a failure: a target that captured planning admits proceeds to captured planning exactly as before.

A binding runs the named executable with your user's permissions whenever Oyzu discovers a workspace. Only bind executables you built or trust. The digest records which content ran; it is not a signature and grants nothing. The plugin receives no credentials and no inherited environment.

Go go/app with one module and one package main is the only admitted Go host build, as for the built-in host path. go/library and workspaces keep task execution through the plugin but are not admitted to native builds, so oyzu build refuses them while bound. Node: npm node/app applications only, including native check/report intent (the Node plugin). The captured npm extension in #789 has a passing local Linux proof. pnpm, yarn, workspaces and frameworks are not served by that extension; remove the binding to build such projects with the built-in builder (a bound id has no fallback). Per-command env in native-build operations and the native-test command is refused (see above). Observation commands are matched by tool short name (go for oyzu:go) on the task PATH; core does not yet verify the resolved file belongs to the locked tool. Ctrl-C (or SIGTERM/SIGHUP on Unix) terminates a running plugin and its descendants on every command. oyzu build reports a cancelled build. On Unix, commands without build interrupt handling (oyzu run, oyzu build --plan) stop the plugin first and then end with the signal as before. A plugin that fails native-admission fails oyzu build --plan as it fails the build. If oyzu run or oyzu build --plan ends from a signal, the private copy of the bound executable (an oyzu-plugin-* temporary directory) is not removed. Successful operations' diagnostics are not shown.

Milestone A was demonstrated on Linux x86_64 with the compiled debug CLI and examples/builds/go-app/project: the bound and unbound builds produced the same artifact name and byte-identical content, the same test and coverage reports, and the bound build recorded the plugin path and digest. A two-module Go workspace exercised task-command with one observation round through oyzu run build and oyzu run test. Commands and results are in the wire contract's verification section and in implementation status. Windows and macOS were not exercised. Project-written outputs (issue #746) were demonstrated through the compiled CLI on Windows (Linux pending) with the reference plugin bound to node/app (its project-output target runs the project's own script and names the dist it writes): oyzu exec -- cargo test --locked --test integration plugin_artifact_origin. See the qualification record. The Node plugin's npm application build (issue #772) was demonstrated through the compiled CLI on Windows and Linux (WSL): the bound and built-in builds of the same project produced the same directory digest, npm ci ran as the install action, and the preparation-boundary cases above pass: oyzu exec -- cargo test --locked -p oyzu-plugin-node --features plugin. See the qualification record.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/plugin-inspection.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Experimental. oyzu plugins shows which plugins the catalogs offer, which are installed, and which one each target of a project uses and why, without installing or launching anything. The design is the draft discovery proposal; this page records what is implemented (issue #586, tracking #578). Catalogs, detection and the build's Selection section are in plugin catalog; the store and oyzu.lock records are in plugin packages; changing a locked selection is oyzu plugins update.

Command Shows oyzu plugins search [QUERY] [--type build] The uses references the effective catalogs offer, with their package, registered capability, description, newest stable version, the version oyzu build would select, and status oyzu plugins versions REFERENCE Every known release of a reference, labelled, with why each can or cannot be selected here oyzu plugins info REFERENCE[@VERSION] One release: package, publisher, contracts, profiles, platforms and payload digests, acquisition routes, qualification, what is verified oyzu plugins list The plugin releases installed in the plugin store, side by side, with the references that name them; a stored release a consulted catalog withdrew or revoked is marked (withdrawn) or (revoked) (JSON catalogStatus) oyzu plugins current This project's locked selections: installed or not, still eligible or not, the update candidate, and a line per plugin-backed target oyzu plugins explain [TARGET] Why each target uses its plugin: the build's Selection record, with the ways to change it Every command takes the global --json (before or after the subcommand), --store DIR (the plugin store, as oyzu build --store), --refresh and --offline (--refresh conflicts with --offline). --type accepts build, the only capability the preview registers; it filters by core-registered role, never by author-defined category. The commands work in any directory. Without a project, search, versions, info and list need nothing else, and current and explain find no target. None of them installs a package, launches a plugin, runs a project tool, adopts a selection, or writes oyzu.lock, configuration or any project file. --help and syntax errors finish before a project, configuration, the store or the network is opened (checked by the startup tests).

search, versions and info read the same snapshots the build resolves with (see the catalog snapshot): the verified published official catalog, or an organization catalog, which is exclusive. Release eligibility is the build's own rule (Context::refusals), so a version shown as selectable is the one a build can select. Default: the cached snapshot. Nothing is fetched. --refresh: update the verified catalog cache from the permitted sources first, bounded to the catalog document. It never downloads a plugin. (An official catalog is fetched only with plugins.preview, as for builds.) --offline: never touch the network. Metadata that is not cached is reported as unavailable, with the reason, rather than guessed. An expired authentic snapshot is shown as history only: rows and versions say so, release eligibility is reported as snapshot expired, and current reports eligibility as unknown. Its withdrawals still apply, as for builds. A snapshot that was refused (failed trust, rolled back) is not shown; the view says no catalog is usable and why. Search covers the effective official and organization catalogs only. It does not crawl OCI registries. A plugin referenced explicitly (uses: or plugins.packages) can be usable without being listed. Under an organization catalog the official catalog is not consulted, so a company replacement shows as its own canonical package (acme/go for go/app) and the official package does not appear beside it.

Label Meaning latest-stable Newest non-prerelease, non-withdrawn release in the displayed snapshot. It can be incompatible or outside the adopted major. latest-compatible Newest stable release whose contract generation, builder profile, support status and platform payload fit this engine and host. update-candidate The newest selectable release inside the project's adopted major (the project locks this reference). adoption-candidate What oyzu build would adopt now (the project does not lock this reference). locked The release oyzu.lock holds for this reference. A contract-compatible major 3 is latest-stable and latest-compatible for a project that adopted major 1, and shows outside the adopted major 1; it is never the update candidate. A prerelease shows preview only unless plugins.preview is on, and never becomes a default. Reason strings (stable, in --json reasons): withdrawn, revoked, preview only, stable releases come from the official catalog, unsupported, no supported protocol generation, no such builder profile, no payload for this platform, outside the adopted major N, snapshot expired. Compatibility is judged for the actual running engine, its supported required role features, the v1alpha1 contract and the host platform only. The requested [engine] identity is shown separately as requestedPin in JSON and Engine pin in human output; inspection does not stage that engine or infer its capabilities from its label. A remote worker's platform is not evaluated and the view says so.

explain computes the same record oyzu build prints in its Selection section and records as extensions["oyzu.dev/plugin-selection"]: the typed Explanation built by the same resolver (Context::decide), the same lock and store replay and the same renderer. Human output is the build's section with every plugin-backed target in full, followed by what it was evaluated against. --json is { "kind": "plugin-explain", "target", "evaluation", "coverage", "lock", "selection": <Explanation> }. coverage.choice says why the snapshot is the one it is, or is absent: published (the official catalog), organization (the organization's catalog, exclusive), no-index (toolIndex.url = false: there is no catalog) and official-unavailable (the official catalog was never obtained, or is refused or expired; coverage.unavailable gives the reason). The value in selection.catalogChoice is the same. With plugins.preview on and no catalog, the notes say so and that running online is the remedy. Two states exist only here, because a build would adopt or install and inspection must not: state Meaning not-adopted The catalog or a binding selects a release but oyzu.lock has no entry. The next oyzu build records it. not-installed oyzu.lock selects a release the plugin store does not hold, and a binding or its current verified catalog entry supplies a source for that exact digest. The next online, non-frozen oyzu build installs it without changing the lock. For a catalog route, the JSON route names the route that would be used, and explain shows it in its human view (the compact current table shows only the state); inspection does not contact it. A real build never shows this state, since it installs the release. For the lock and binding state, inspection does not show as installable what a build refuses. Where the build would fail on that state, explain and current fail with the same error: a locked release missing from the store with neither a binding nor a current catalog listing is PLUGIN_LOCK_UNUSABLE; a binding that names another release is PLUGIN_LOCK_MISMATCH; a catalog release that is not in the store and has no OCI route is PLUGIN_ROUTE_UNAVAILABLE; one with an OCI route is not-adopted (inspection never downloads). (not-adopted states that a bound source or an installed copy exists for the release the build would adopt.) Withdrawals, revocations and organization rebinding (including an authentic expired copy) are the build's same refusals. A Refused catalog remains PLUGIN_CATALOG_UNAVAILABLE; Absent and Expired snapshots never offer routes. build --plan never downloads, because its preview pass runs offline: with a clean store it stops with PLUGIN_ROUTE_UNAVAILABLE and installs nothing. That message names --offline even though the flag was not passed, a known wording limit that it shares with first adoption. Known gap: inspection does not run the host-platform and archive or manifest checks a build runs when it acquires a package (launch_target, check_manifest). A catalog release already in the store that this host cannot run shows as not-adopted, where the build fails with PLUGIN_PLATFORM_UNSUPPORTED; a bound source that has not been installed is likewise not opened or verified. Recorded on #601. For a selection you dispute, the same copyable remedies appear as in the build: declare the targets in build.yaml (or an explicit uses:), bind another package for the reference, undo an adoption, and pin a tool in oyzu.toml. Ambiguous evidence (two catalog detections, or a catalog detection and a built-in one) is the build's focused conflict, printed with the smallest build.yaml selector; explain fails with it and installs nothing. Native tool requirements come from the plugin's requirements operation, which runs the plugin. Inspection never does, so tools is absent from the record, the human view says deferred, and a generic tool-version remedy (oyzu pin <tool>@<version>) stands in; oyzu build lists the tools. current returns { "kind": "plugin-current", "evaluation", "coverage", "lock": { path, exists, selections, enginePin }, "locked": [...], "selection": <Explanation> }. Each locked entry carries the reference, package, major, version, release, installed, eligible (null when no usable catalog lists the release), reasons, latestStable, latestCompatible and updateCandidate. A newer release cached in the store does not change what oyzu.lock selects: list shows both immutable packages, current shows the locked one.

Lists <store>/plugins/* read-only: package, version, release digest, profiles, platforms, the references a consulted catalog or this project's lock names for it, and whether this project locks it. It cannot know other projects' selections: the store keeps no inventory of the projects that use it, and the view says so.

Human output leads with the outcome, uses aligned tables, wraps without loss at narrow widths, escapes untrusted terminal controls and uses color only for emphasis; meaning never depends on color alone (the Selection marks are words without color). --json prints one typed object per command on stdout and errors in the usual error shape. Both are serialized from the same value (plugins::inspect results and resolve::Explanation); the human renderer (src/presentation/output/plugins.rs) recomputes nothing and the Selection text is rendered by logging::plugin_selection_section, the build's own view. Errors: PLUGIN_REFERENCE_UNKNOWN (no consulted catalog lists it; names what is listed), PLUGIN_VERSION_UNKNOWN (no release matches the selector), PLUGIN_TARGET_UNKNOWN (no plugin-backed target of that name or path), plus the build's own resolution errors (PLUGIN_DETECTION_CONFLICT, PLUGIN_CATALOG_UNAVAILABLE, PLUGIN_RELEASE_REVOKED, ...), unchanged.

tests/integration/plugin_inspection.rs drives the compiled CLI against a signed, served organization catalog and a shell plugin: Scenario Test PLG-DISC-09 browse with no installed plugin; nothing downloaded or written search_browses_the_catalog_without_downloading_or_changing_anything PLG-DISC-10 one package, several profiles same test PLG-DISC-11 major 3 latest while major 1 adopted versions_distinguish_latest_stable_compatible_candidate_and_locked PLG-DISC-12 newer package cached, older locked a_cached_newer_plugin_does_not_change_the_locked_selection PLG-DISC-13 offline, snapshot age, expired history offline_inspection_reports_snapshot_age_and_never_claims_eligibility_from_expired_metadata PLG-DISC-14 company replacement visible search_browses_the_catalog_... (canonical acme/go, company-binding) PLG-DISC-15 one typed result in human and JSON human_and_json_views_serialize_the_same_typed_result explain/current states, remedies, store and lock untouched, field-for-field agreement with the discovery record the build uses explain_and_current_show_the_build_selection_without_adopting_or_installing Conflict named with its selector explain_names_a_detection_conflict_and_its_selector Same refusals as the build (PLUGIN_ROUTE_UNAVAILABLE for a lock the catalog lists with no route, PLUGIN_LOCK_MISMATCH; the unlisted PLUGIN_LOCK_UNUSABLE case is in the plugin_oci row below) explain_and_current_refuse_what_a_build_refuses Clean-store locked route, read-only human/JSON agreement, and catalog refusals plugin_oci::catalog_routes::clean_store_inspection_and_plan_report_the_route_without_acquiring, clean_store_replay_refuses_denied_unlisted_and_unavailable_catalogs_before_routing (Linux; results in the lock replay record) The agreement test compares explain's selection with Workspace.plugin_selection from oyzu discover --json on an adopted project, ignoring tools and the generic tool-version remedy. That is the value oyzu build renders and records; the stand-in plugin cannot run a full build.

Host platform only; remote workers are not qualified. Tools of a target are deferred (see above); no plugin is launched. --type has one value, build; publish and deploy are not registered roles yet. No policy admission view: organization policy beyond the catalog's own withdrawals is not modelled by the client yet. The official catalog is refreshed only with plugins.preview, as for builds, because it lists nothing else yet. Windows and macOS behavior is untested here (the new tests are Unix-only, as the catalog tests are).

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/plugin-packages.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Experimental. Selects an external builder from a verified, installed package instead of a raw executable path, pins that selection in oyzu.lock, and records the engine identity of every build. The design is the draft external plugin proposal; this page records what is implemented. A package comes from a local archive or an OCI registry named in configuration. The plugin catalog can select a release; its bytes come from such a binding, from the store, or, with no binding, from the OCI route in the verified catalog entry (catalog), through the same installer as an OCI binding. How first-party releases reach GHCR is plugin releases.
documents.s: Plugin packages, the plugin store and lock selections

documents.t: A package is a .tar.gz or .zip archive holding the plugins-v1alpha1 manifest as plugin.json at its root, and the platform payloads the manifest's runtimes name by entrypoint. tooling/package-plugin.py builds one for the host platform from a built executable: oyzu exec -- cargo build --locked -p oyzu-plugin-go --features plugin python3 tooling/package-plugin.py --executable target/debug/oyzu-plugin-go --out go.tar.gz # prints sha256:<archive digest> Installation refuses a package that: hashes to a different digest than the one configured (before any extraction); exceeds the archive bounds (512 MiB archive; at most 4096 entries, 1 GiB extracted, 512 MiB per file, depth 16, expansion ratio 100), or contains traversal, absolute paths, hard links, symbolic links whose target leaves the payload, or non-portable names (the shared archive extractor). Relative symbolic links that stay inside the payload are admitted, as for tool archives; an entrypoint must still be a regular file; has no valid plugin.json, or one with unknown fields. Fields naming another plugin (dependencies, preferences, successors) are unknown fields, so peer plugin dependencies are refused; names an entrypoint missing from the archive, not a regular file, or whose SHA-256 differs from the manifest's runtimes[].digest; is not the package the bound reference names (go/app needs package name go with builder profile app) or supports no protocol generation v1alpha1. Nothing in a package runs during installation: there are no install hooks.

User or machine configuration (never project files or profiles; CONFIG_SCOPE, like plugins.development) binds a builder id to an archive and its expected digest, or to an OCI release: [plugins.packages] "go/app" = { archive = "/home/me/plugins/go-0.1.0.tar.gz", sha256 = "sha256:…" } # or "go/app" = { oci = "ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/go:0.1.0" } A binding is a user-level default, so it applies only where it is used: only the references this project's targets actually use (explicit uses, or what detection finds) are resolved, adopted or required. A Go binding never touches a Python or Rust project: its discover, run and build neither fail nor write a lock entry for it. Keys are short references without a major selector; archive is absolute; sha256 is sha256: plus 64 lowercase hex digits. The OCI form is described below. At most 64 entries. A reference may be bound by this setting or by plugins.development, not both (PLUGIN_BINDING_INVALID). Something outside the project must name the implementation (a project cannot choose code to run), and the digest is the only identity available for local bytes. When the digest is the release digest of the release the catalog selects for the reference, the binding is that release's local archive route and the package must also be the catalog's package and version; any other digest is a local package binding, the explicit-source form. Neither form can bypass a catalog's withdrawal or revocation: a binding of a release a consulted catalog (the last verified copy, an expired one included) withdrew or revoked is refused with PLUGIN_RELEASE_WITHDRAWN or PLUGIN_RELEASE_REVOKED before it is recorded or launched (see plugin catalog).

A binding can name a release in an OCI 1.1 registry whose token endpoint (if it has one) is on its own origin, such as GHCR, the distribution registry or Harbor, laid out as the Oyzu OCI package contract defines: an immutable release root (an image index) binding the plugin manifest and one manifest per platform payload, with a detached Sigstore signature attached as a referrer of the root. [plugins.packages] # Official first-party release by tag: signed by oyzuai/oyzu's plugin-release.yml. "go/app" = { oci = "ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/go:0.1.0" } # Another registry by tag: say whose signature to require. "go/app" = { oci = "registry.example.com/team/go:1.2.0", identity = "https://github.com/acme/plugins/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main" } # By digest: the digest is the trust, as for an archive (no signature checked # unless identity is set or the reference is in the official namespace). "go/app" = { oci = "registry.example.com/team/go@sha256:…" } Field Value Meaning oci registry/repository:tag or registry/repository@sha256:<hex>, no scheme The release root. A tag and a digest together are refused identity https:// certificate identity (SAN URI) The signer the root signature must come from: a GitHub Actions workflow identity on a GitHub-hosted runner, exactly as toolIndex.identity. Required for a tag outside ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/; refused for an official reference trustedRoot Absolute path A Sigstore trusted_root.json replacing the production root (a private Sigstore deployment or a test instance). Needs a signer; refused for an official reference A reference under ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/ (also spelled ghcr.io:443/…) is official: it must be signed by exactly https://github.com/oyzuai/oyzu/.github/workflows/plugin-release.yml@refs/heads/main, issued by GitHub Actions OIDC on a GitHub-hosted runner and verified against Sigstore's production trusted root, the same pinning as the tool index. A copy of the workflow on another branch signs as @refs/heads/<branch> and is refused. An official binding with identity or trustedRoot is CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE: configuration cannot replace the official signer or let a private CA vouch for it. Any other tag without identity is CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE at configuration load. These binding rules decide by the reference's namespace and are unchanged. A release acquired from a verified catalog's route, with no binding, is decided by the package's identity instead (decision of 2026-10-20): a package of the official publisher oyzu requires the same official signer and production trusted root on every route, a company mirror included, and a package of any other publisher is trusted by the digest the signed catalog lists. See route trust. On a glibc Linux host, when a release has no payload without an ABI or for gnu, oyzu uses its musl payload for that architecture: the contract requires musl payloads to be statically linked, and the official releases ship only musl Linux payloads. A musl entrypoint with an ELF PT_INTERP header (dynamically linked) is refused on a glibc host with PLUGIN_PLATFORM_UNSUPPORTED naming the loader it needs, before it is run. The host's runtime is validated on the extracted candidate before the release is published into the store (a runtime for this host, an executable entrypoint, the static-linking check), so a package this host cannot run is refused without leaving an installed release. An already installed release is not scanned again beyond the checks a launch makes. Acquisition runs only where an archive would be read (a real oyzu build adopting a selection, or installing a locked release missing from the store). It needs no Docker, ORAS, crane or container daemon and no login: oyzu speaks the OCI Distribution API itself, anonymously, following a registry's Bearer challenge to its token endpoint without credentials, as public GHCR packages allow. A loopback registry (localhost, 127.0.0.1, ::1) is reached over plain HTTP; every other registry over HTTPS through the configured proxy and certificate trust. It fetches, in order: the release root: by the locked digest, by the binding's digest, or, only at first selection, by tag. The release digest is the SHA-256 of the bytes received, never a registry header; the signature (when a signer is required): referrers of the root through the referrers API, and the sha256-<hex> referrers tag for registries without it; each Sigstore bundle is verified against the root digest, the signer and the trusted root until one verifies; the metadata manifest and the plugin manifest blob, checked against the bound reference as for an archive; this platform's manifest and payload archive only. Other platforms' payloads are never downloaded. Every object is fetched by digest and must hash to its descriptor (and size) before use; the root must carry the release artifact type, the payload descriptors must match the plugin manifest's runtimes one to one, and the extracted entrypoint must match its manifest digest. Only then is the release published into the store. A tag is resolved once: the lock records the root digest, and later builds, --frozen replays and reinstalls into an empty store fetch that digest, never the tag, so moving the tag changes nothing. An OCI release in the store holds plugin.json and the payload of the platform that installed it. Bindings by archive and by OCI can name the same release only if their digests agree, which they never do (an archive digest and a root digest differ), so switching a binding's source is an explicit re-adoption (PLUGIN_LOCK_MISMATCH for a digest binding; a tag binding replays the lock). Not implemented: registries that send clients to a token endpoint on another host (Docker Hub's auth.docker.io): the token realm must be on the registry's own origin, as for every Oyzu registry client; credentials for private registries (anonymous only; a private package fails with PLUGIN_PACKAGE_UNAVAILABLE naming the refusal), organization route configuration (a mirror is listed as a catalog route instead), a tool that populates a mirror, HTTPS layout-archive routes, offline exports, and streaming of very large payloads (a payload is held in memory, at most 512 MiB). A catalog's OCI route is acquired from, including an organization catalog's mirror of an official package; its HTTPS layout-archive route is not.

Packages live in the tool store (--store, default the shared user store) under plugins/<hex>/, where <hex> is the release digest (the archive digest, or the OCI release root digest). Releases sit side by side; a platform payload is selected from the manifest at launch. Installation takes a per-digest lock, so concurrent first builds extract once and the others reuse the published release; the release is published by an atomic no-replace rename, so readers never see a partial extraction. A shared lease on the release is held for the whole invocation to protect running executables (relevant on Windows). An installed release is trusted: later builds do not hash it again, and only a missing release needs the archive.

First resolution writes the selection to oyzu.lock in the project root under the lock-edit transaction. The selection is appended to the file's existing bytes, so other records, comments and ordering are untouched: [[plugin]] reference = "go/app" profile = "app" package = "oyzu/go" major = 0 version = "0.1.0" release = "sha256:…" [[plugin.payloads]] os = "linux" arch = "amd64" digest = "sha256:…" Field Meaning reference, profile The logical reference and its profile package Canonical publisher/name major Manifest version major, established at first resolution version Exact release version release Archive digest, or the OCI release root digest (the catalog's root_digest) payloads Executable digest per platform runtime, from the plugin manifest (for an OCI release, every platform the root binds; the root digest binds the platform manifests themselves) Machine-local paths, acquisition times and the platform an invocation used are not recorded. The schema is the in-place plugin and engine additions to tool-lock.schema.json; there is no new lock version. A lock keeps its [[plugin]] entries through oyzu pin and other tool operations. Only a real oyzu build (not --plan or --check) may install a bound package and record a new selection, and only oyzu plugins update may install a release to replace a selection already locked. Every other command that discovers the project (build --plan, build --check, run, discover, lock --check, …) replays the lock and the store and writes nothing. Situation Behavior Bound, no locked selection, oyzu build Install the bound package, record the selection, build Bound, no locked selection, any other command PLUGIN_NOT_ADOPTED: nothing installed or written; run oyzu build Locked selection, release installed Reuse it; the archive is not read Locked selection, release missing, binding present oyzu build installs it from the bound source (an archive, or an OCI reference fetched by the locked digest), only if a binding that names a release names the locked one; other commands report PLUGIN_NOT_INSTALLED Locked selection, no binding configured Reuse the installed digest. If missing, an online, non-frozen oyzu build acquires that exact release from its current verified catalog entry's OCI route, without changing the lock. An unlisted release or absent/expired catalog supplies no route (PLUGIN_LOCK_UNUSABLE); a refused catalog is PLUGIN_CATALOG_UNAVAILABLE; a listed release with no OCI route is PLUGIN_ROUTE_UNAVAILABLE. A plugins.development binding for the same reference still replaces the locked package Binding names a different release than the lock PLUGIN_LOCK_MISMATCH: builds never change a selection; adopting another release is explicit: oyzu plugins update <reference> Installed release differs from the lock PLUGIN_LOCK_UNUSABLE oyzu build --frozen, selection missing PLUGIN_LOCK_MISSING; nothing resolved, installed or written. Restore a complete approved lock, or deliberately adopt through oyzu build in an approved context where policy permits it; removing --frozen never waives policy. Ask the policy administrator if no preparation context is available. plugins update only replaces an existing selection oyzu build --frozen, selection present Replay it; missing content may still be installed from a bound local archive, never fetched from an OCI binding or catalog route Two builds of one project at once One build per workspace runs at a time: the other is refused with the existing "another oyzu build is using this workspace" error. Recording is still safe under the lock-edit transaction: an identical selection is a no-op, a different one for the reference is PLUGIN_LOCK_MISMATCH Lock this oyzu cannot parse, no binding, [[plugin]] visible in it Discovery refuses with the lock error rather than listing built-in tasks for a project whose builder it cannot know; a lock without [[plugin]] is left to the commands that need it Lock with sections or fields this oyzu does not know Refused before anything is modified ("use the oyzu release that wrote it") A lock that holds only a plugin selection does not count as pinned tools: a fresh project's first oyzu build still resolves and pins the tools its builders need (for example oyzu:go). Builds of different projects sharing a store converge: a build whose tool pinning loses a race on the lock reuses the pins the other build published (or retries for up to 30 s) instead of failing with PIN_EDIT_CONFLICT. Two builds of the same workspace are not allowed at all; the second is refused cleanly. Limits: @vN major selectors in bindings and revocation are not implemented. Locked selections are updated with oyzu plugins update.

Every build records the actual engine (Context Engine fact and the retained inventory {"engine":{"identity","pinned"}}). The identity is the version token of oyzu --version (for example 0.1.0-local.36bdcec27267.dirty, without the profile, target and timestamp). An optional exact pin is written by hand: [engine] identity = "0.1.0-local.36bdcec27267" An applicable protected administrative policy can require this pin and a complete lock. The policy-required pin contract describes its candidate enforcement and qualification status. CI or release context alone leaves the pin optional. A different pin uses exact native engine staging before semantic discovery or plugin resolution when an allowed user/system source explicitly admits its development archive. Missing admission fails with ENGINE_PIN_MISMATCH. Staging preserves the installed frontend and project lock. An explicit development override retains the invoked executable when independently permitted, recording actual content and the bypassed pin without changing shared selections. Package role features are requirements on the running engine. The preview builder supports go-test-events; unknown required features or unsupported role contracts fail with PLUGIN_ENGINE_REQUIREMENT before plugin operations, on first acquisition and warm replay. The message names required capabilities and the actual engine, and directs selection of a supporting admitted engine or a compatible plugin. No guessed minimum version or stable compatibility promise is inferred from development version labels. Catalog eligibility applies the same supported-feature rule.

A package's entrypoint is launched in place: it is the immutable store file whose digest was verified at installation. A plugins.development executable is copied to a private per-invocation file and hashed while it is copied, so the digest recorded is the digest of the bound file as launched (for a wrapper script, the script only: what it starts is not covered, so its targets are never reused from the action cache); replacing the source afterwards changes nothing in the invocation, and a second workspace discovery in the same invocation reuses the copy without hashing the source again. The copy is disposable, so it is not flushed to disk. The private copy is removed when the command finishes. Action keys bind the plugin identity (reference, package release and version, executable digest and runtime) recorded on each plugin-built target as extensions["oyzu.dev/builder-plugin"]; see external builder targets. Every plan, execution envelope and manifest of a build or oyzu run carries extensions["oyzu.dev/plugins"] when an external builder is bound (the plan digest therefore covers it), so plugin-built output is distinguishable from built-in output: {"reference":"go/app","source":"package","package":"oyzu/go","version":"0.1.0", "release":"sha256:…","executableDigest":"sha256:…","selection":"adopted"} {"reference":"go/app","source":"local-development", "executableName":"plugin","executableDigest":"sha256:…"} A development record keeps only the executable's file name, never the user's absolute path; executableDigest is the identity. Nothing refuses to publish plugin-built output; the record only makes it visible. oyzu inspect requires the records to be identical in the plan, manifest and envelope (see build bundles). oyzu run --store DIR, oyzu scan --store DIR and oyzu lock --store DIR move the plugin store with the tool store, as oyzu build --store DIR does. Known limit: the private copy of a development executable is removed when the command finishes normally; if the process dies from a signal it stays in the temporary directory as oyzu-plugin-*, to be deleted by hand. The invocation's bindings are fixed by the first discovery. A later discovery in the same process that asks for a different set (another executable, changed bytes, another reference) fails with PLUGIN_BINDING_CONFLICT instead of silently replacing the builders already handed out. The set is still a process-wide lookup, which is service-locator debt this page does not hide. The sites that read it directly are: Site Use src/builders/mod.rs get (external::bound) Every builders::get(id) caller: 61 of them — src/build 48, src/tools 4, src/tasks 3, src/executor 1, src/discovery 1, src/builders and tests src/builders/mod.rs development_command (external::bound) Task command observation for an externally bound target src/build/mod.rs (external::bound) Selecting admitted captured planning or refusing unsupported bindings before isolated execution src/build/native.rs (external::bindings, external::bound) Recording bindings in the context facts and marking bound targets uncached src/discovery.rs (external::records) Freezing the records onto Workspace.plugins None of the get callers takes a workspace. Raw development executable bindings are refused for isolated execution; admitted packages can use the bounded captured Go and npm paths below. Remote execution is not qualified by those paths. Moving the lookup onto the workspace is left for when a second binding source per process exists.
documents.s: Which bytes run, and how output records them

documents.t: Code Cause Recovery PLUGIN_PACKAGE_DIGEST Archive bytes differ from the configured digest, or an OCI object differs from its descriptor Fix the digest or the archive; for OCI, the registry or mirror serves wrong bytes PLUGIN_PACKAGE_INVALID Manifest, entrypoint or archive rule broken Rebuild the package PLUGIN_PACKAGE_MISMATCH Package does not provide the bound reference Bind the right package PLUGIN_PACKAGE_UNAVAILABLE Archive missing and release not installed; an OCI object (root, manifest, payload) missing, or the registry refused anonymous access or is unreachable. The missing object's digest is named Restore the archive; complete the mirror; make the package public PLUGIN_SIGNATURE_MISSING No Sigstore bundle referrer for the OCI release root. For an official (oyzu/*) package on a catalog's mirror route, the message says the root must carry the official signer's signature and the mirror must serve the signature referrers Binding: publish the release's signature, or bind by digest outside the official namespace. Catalog mirror of an official package: copy the release's signature referrers (the sha256-<hex> referrers tag or referrers API entries, with the signature manifest and bundle) into the mirror unchanged; the catalog cannot waive the signature PLUGIN_SIGNATURE_INVALID No attached bundle verifies for the root digest, signer and trusted root Binding: check identity and trustedRoot; the release was not signed by that signer. Catalog mirror of an official package: the mirror must serve the official release and its original signature; a build or signature of the company's own cannot stand in for oyzu/* (list it as the company's own package instead) PLUGIN_PLATFORM_UNSUPPORTED No runtime for this OS/architecture/ABI (the message names the host and what the package provides) Use a package that has one PLUGIN_LOCK_MISSING / _MISMATCH / _UNUSABLE, PLUGIN_NOT_ADOPTED, PLUGIN_NOT_INSTALLED See the lock table PLUGIN_BINDING_CONFLICT A second discovery asked for different plugin bindings Bindings are per invocation ENGINE_PIN_MISMATCH Running engine is not the pinned one Run the pinned oyzu

Issue #730 adds captured-plan to the existing plugin protocol. This path is under qualification; the published preview is not claimed to provide it. A locally admitted development package must declare the capability and contain both the host and selected Linux execution payloads. The host runs discovery roles; the Linux member runs captured-plan on read-only source, supplying build, artifact and test-report intent. Core supplies version, output paths, exact locked tools, immutable dependency inputs and execution controls. The plugin cannot use observations or acquire dependencies in this role. The bounded implementation supports a single conventional Go application module with one main package, a matching Linux artifact/execution platform and the process container executor. It requires an admitted multi-platform engine archive, a usable immutable Linux environment, and a locked Go tool for that platform. Use oyzu build app --isolated --platform linux/amd64 --full with the Linux platform declared in build.yaml. Local native defaults are unchanged. Raw executable development bindings, Go libraries, workspaces, missing capabilities and unsupported execution controls fail explicitly. The existing Go preparation provider owns native checksum validation, broker acquisition and the local module proxy. Its retained native metadata adapter remains existing implementation debt; the new planner and export orchestration are compiled Rust. Warm/offline preparation requires every exact input to be retained; a missing input fails without networking. The frozen dependency record binds engine archive/member, host and execution plugin members, environment, tool archives and the accepted plan. Required JUnit and Go coverage reports remain gates. A changed package control or missing engine never selects a baked fallback. See the first-proof contract for remaining functional qualification and explicit exclusions.

The implementation in issue #789 extends the same package and engine contracts to npm node/app applications. The local Linux proof passed; this is not a capability claim for the published preview package. The matching development package must declare captured-plan and supply the selected Linux member. Core prepares the locked Node/npm archives and dependency inputs, then performs the required offline install before the plugin's build and check operations. The plugin supplies intent; it does not acquire dependencies during planning. Required JUnit and LCOV reports pass through the common report gates, and project-written dist is retired only in the private execution workspace and exported with the common artifact containment checks. The bounded command is oyzu build app --isolated --platform linux/amd64 --full --frozen --image npm=<admitted-node-seed>, with tools selected in oyzu.toml and resolved in oyzu.lock. It requires the same admitted engine assets and immutable Linux image as captured Go. Missing package capabilities, required reports, locked inputs or compatible assets fail explicitly. pnpm, Yarn, workspaces and frameworks are outside this extension. See the captured npm proof and scope.

Store, lock and schema behavior has unit tests (src/tools/store/plugin.rs, src/tools/lock/tests.rs, src/tools/plugin_package/oci.rs), compiled-CLI tests (tests/integration/plugin_packages.rs, plugin_oci.rs, tool_lock.rs) and the shape check python3 tooling/check-tool-contracts.py. plugin_oci.rs runs the CLI against an in-process loopback registry that demands the anonymous token flow, with signatures from a test-only Sigstore instance. Acceptance held: PLG-PKG-02 (substituted bytes rejected before launch, archive and OCI), PLG-PKG-03 (a new platform payload is a new root; the old lock is never satisfied by it), PLG-PKG-04 (concurrent first installs publish once), PLG-PKG-08 (native package acquired from OCI without Docker or login), PLG-PKG-09 (missing payload or signature, or no payload for this platform, fails naming it, with no fallback), PLG-COMPAT-03, 04, 05, 10 and 11. The recorded end-to-end run on examples/builds/go-app/project is in implementation status.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/plugin-preview.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Experimental. The commitments for the first public plugin: the builder for Go projects, oyzu/go, published as an Oyzu OCI package on GHCR. It states how a preview is selected, which combinations are supported, how long releases are supported and retained, how each release status affects selection, adoption and replay, and what to do when a release or the catalog goes wrong. The design is authoring and publication and preview and stable contracts (PLG-COMPAT-01); tracking is #589. Published. oyzu/go 0.1.0-preview.1 is on ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/go and listed by the official catalog from serial 21. The maintainer agreed the terms below on 2026-10-19 (relayed by the coordinator session); they are collected in Decisions. Everything else describes behavior the compiled CLI has today.
documents.s: Go builder preview: terms, support and recovery

documents.t: oyzu/go 0.1.0-preview.1 (agreed version; a version is never reused) extracts the existing Go builder into a plugin that runs as a separate process. A preview promises: Immutable releases. A published version never changes. A fix, a changed payload or an added platform is a new version and a new release root. Verified bytes. The CLI accepts the release only when it is signed by plugin-release.yml on refs/heads/main from a GitHub-hosted runner, and checks every object by digest (plugin releases). No surprises. A lock never silently changes the implementation. A newer release, a newer preview and a new catalog serial change nothing until you run oyzu plugins update. Visible and reversible selection. The build shows which builder each target got and prints the line that undoes it (plugin catalog). A preview does not promise the plugin interface (v1alpha1) is stable (it is edited in place until a second ecosystem validates it), that a later preview behaves like this one, that every platform in the package is qualified, or that a preview is supported after a newer release supersedes it. It is excluded from ordinary stable resolution and updates.

Selection is deliberate and user-scoped; a project file cannot select a preview (CONFIG_SCOPE), because the release is code that runs. In user, machine or administrative configuration: [plugins] preview = true # makes preview releases eligible That is all. The build acquires the release from the route in the verified official catalog (ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/go@sha256:25f830bd…f9bf; see the catalog) and shows the source as official default. Optionally a plugins.packages binding supplies the bytes instead and keeps precedence: [plugins.packages] "go/app" = { oci = "ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/go:0.1.0-preview.1" } A tag binding has these consequences: The tag can move. GHCR tags are mutable and plugin-oci.py push has an --allow-retag option for dry runs. The tag is resolved once, at first selection, so an unlocked project (a fresh checkout without a committed oyzu.lock) can resolve different roots at different times. The lock is what pins the release: oyzu.lock records the root digest, and later builds, --frozen replays and fresh stores fetch that digest, never the tag. Commit oyzu.lock, or bind by digest (ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/go@sha256:<root>). It is a local package binding. A tag is never the catalog's route, so the catalog's supported, deprecated and unsupported statuses and its qualification do not apply to it when it supplies the release, and a withdrawal or revocation can refuse it only once #662 is on main. The preview flag still applies to oyzu plugins update, which never selects a preview it was not asked for by name (the binding path below). A digest binding equal to the release the catalog would select is that release's route and is shown as the official default. CI. oyzu ignores the whole user scope when any CI marker is set (CI, GITHUB_ACTIONS and the other variables DETECTION_VARIABLES in src/config/context.rs lists; pinning OYZU_CONTEXT=local does not help), and a project file cannot select a preview or a binding, so the two lines above have no effect in a CI job and the build silently uses the built-in Go builder. Machine scope is not excluded, so the maintainer decided on 2026-10-19 (#670) that a CI job selects the preview through it: the job writes the same [plugins] settings to the root-owned machine configuration before it builds. On a GitHub-hosted Linux runner: - name: Select the Go preview run: | sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/oyzu sudo tee /etc/oyzu/config.toml > /dev/null <<'TOML' [plugins] preview = true TOML - run: oyzu build Keep the file owned by root and not writable by group or others. Oyzu does not check the ownership or mode of the machine config.toml (it does for the administrative policy file), so this is advice, not enforcement. The recipe replaces any machine configuration the runner already has, so use it on ephemeral runners. A project file cannot select the preview or a binding; the workflow that writes this file is reviewed like any other workflow change. It has run in a hosted workflow: a manual-only proof, plugin-preview-ci-proof.yml (script tooling/plugin-preview-ci-proof.sh), ran this recipe twice on GitHub-hosted ubuntu-24.04 runners on 2026-10-19 (15:53 and 15:54 US Eastern, EDT), both successful: run 39314759614 and run 39314889946, on main at 4a1635c. Each built the pinned oyzu from source, checked that the same settings in user scope are ignored (and are read outside CI), and, with the recipe's machine file, asserted the official-default Selection source, the release and oyzu.lock root sha256:25f830bd…f9bf, the artifact output Hello, Oyzu!, build --frozen replay (locked) and official default in plugins info. Details and limits are in the status entry. The Selection section of the build shows oyzu/go 0.1.0-preview.1 when it took effect. No new channel, setting or flag is added; accepting a preview opt-in from a CI-honored project or environment source is not part of this decision and would be a separate design. Earlier verified on Linux (2026-10-19) in a mount namespace with a scratch /etc, before the hosted runs above: a build with CI=true GITHUB_ACTIONS=true and that file selected the plugin and wrote its [[plugin]] lock entry, and the unit test plugin_preview_settings_survive_ci_from_machine_scope_but_not_user_scope keeps the scope rule. macOS (/Library/Application Support/Oyzu/config.toml) and Windows (%ProgramData%\Oyzu\config.toml) use the same rule but are untested. Acquiring from the catalog's own routes (#664) does not remove the need for the opt-in, which is also user, machine or administrative scope only. oyzu build needs no account and no login, and no Docker. Undo with the line the build prints: rm oyzu.lock, then oyzu config unset --global 'plugins.packages."go/app"' and oyzu config set --global plugins.preview false. With plugins.preview off, a build never refreshes the official catalog and a Go project uses the built-in builder as before. oyzu plugins update never moves a selection to a preview unless you name it (go/app@0.1.0-preview.2, which needs the opt-in); a routine update stays inside the adopted major and skips previews (updating plugins).

The statements below are for oyzu/go 0.1.0-preview.1; they change only with a new release or a new catalog qualification entry, never with a new core release. Dimension Supported Not supported or unqualified Plugin interface Protocol generation v1alpha1 (the only one); builder role with the go-test-events feature; profiles go/app and go/library. Checked against the signed manifest before launch Any other generation or required feature fails before role work Core The oyzu release that first carries this preview and later ones that still speak v1alpha1 (agreed: tested core 0.1.0). A newer core is not promised compatible until a release says so; the catalog can name incompatibility Older cores have no plugin host Platforms in the package linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 (static musl, used on glibc and musl hosts), darwin/arm64, darwin/amd64, windows/amd64 (msvc), all built by plugin-release.yml A host with none of these fails with PLUGIN_PLATFORM_UNSUPPORTED naming what the package provides; the CLI never substitutes another payload Platforms qualified linux/amd64 only (agreed catalog qualification.tested): the Go example builds end to end on it linux/arm64, darwin and windows payloads are listed and verified but have not run a build; treat them as untested. Isolated (container) execution is refused for plugin builders Native tools The Go toolchain the project's go.mod requires, acquired through the tool index (the recorded end-to-end run used the default selection and a pinned 1.24.5; see plugin catalog verification) Other native tools, other Go versions and cgo toolchains are not separately qualified

Agreed terms (nothing here is enforced by the client except where a status is described under Lifecycle statuses): Support. Only the newest preview is supported. When a newer preview or a stable release supersedes it, the catalog marks it deprecated with an end of at least 30 days and a message naming the successor, then unsupported at the end. Fixes ship as a new preview; there are no backports. Withdrawal. A defective release is withdrawn at once, without waiting for the deprecation period (runbook). Retention of contents. Release roots, platform payloads and their signature referrers stay in GHCR for at least 12 months after the release is superseded, and are never removed by cache or Actions-artifact cleanup. The payload-* workflow artifacts are build intermediates with Actions retention and are not part of the release. A withdrawn or revoked release's bytes and evidence are kept as long as its withdrawal is listed. Retention of catalog entries. The catalog lists supported releases within their retention; withdrawals are kept for good. A release pruned from the catalog is unlisted, not withdrawn: new resolution no longer offers it, but a lock that names it still replays while its bytes remain in the store or GHCR. Transparency log. Each signature is a public Sigstore (Rekor) entry and cannot be deleted; withdrawing a release does not remove its entry. Freshness. The catalog is re-signed daily and never valid more than 31 days; a client with the preview opt-in refreshes it at most hourly. Support expiry, deprecation, unavailable bytes and denied execution stay distinct: a deprecated or unsupported release still replays; missing bytes fail with PLUGIN_PACKAGE_UNAVAILABLE; denial is PLUGIN_RELEASE_WITHDRAWN or PLUGIN_RELEASE_REVOKED.

How each catalog status affects the three operations when the catalog selects the release (the route path), as exercised by the compiled CLI against a signed organization catalog (tests/integration/plugin_lifecycle.rs; the official catalog uses the same code path with a different signer). This is the documented path: the release is acquired from the catalog's own route. A plugins.packages binding is optional and is described after the table. Status New selection (unlocked build) Adoption (oyzu plugins update) Replay of an existing lock supported Offered A candidate Replays; an online, non-frozen build with an empty plugin store re-acquires the exact locked digest from its current verified catalog entry's OCI route without rewriting the lock deprecated (even past its ends) Offered; no warning in the build. oyzu plugins info shows the status and message, and --json also the ends date (the human view omits it) A candidate Replays unsupported Not offered; the built-in builder serves go/app instead. An explicit plugins.packages digest binding still installs it Not a candidate ("up to date"); an explicit binding of the release still adopts it Replays preview, without plugins.preview Not offered Never selected by a routine update; PLUGIN_PREVIEW_NOT_SELECTED Replays preview, with plugins.preview Offered Only when named exactly (go/app@<version>) Replays unlisted (pruned after retention) Not offered (not separately exercised: it is absence, as for a withdrawn release) Not a candidate (not separately exercised) Replays from the store; a fresh store still needs a binding of the locked digest, else PLUGIN_LOCK_UNUSABLE. Catalog-route replay cannot recover an unlisted release withdrawn Not offered; a plugins.packages binding of it is refused (PLUGIN_RELEASE_WITHDRAWN) before it is recorded or run (needs the resolver change in #662; before it, such a binding was adopted and only the next build refused it) Refused by name or binding Refused on every command, including --plan and --frozen, naming the lock entry; the lock is never rewritten revoked As withdrawn, with PLUGIN_RELEASE_REVOKED ("it will not run") As withdrawn As withdrawn

For a plugins.packages binding (an optional override that takes precedence over the catalog's route) the catalog is consulted for withdrawals only: Binding New selection (oyzu build) Update (oyzu plugins update) Replay of the lock Withdrawn or revoked Tag (oci = "…/go:<version>") Support and qualification not applied (a local package binding); preview flag not separately exercised. The tag is resolved once and the lock pins the digest Preview releases are never adopted by a routine update, whatever supplies them (PLUGIN_PREVIEW_NOT_SELECTED; exercised with a digest binding) Replays by the locked digest Refused once the installer has the release (before it is recorded or run) and on replay, with #662; before it, adopted on first use and refused by the next build Digest (oci = "…@sha256:…", archive with sha256) unsupported installs (exercised); preview flag not separately exercised unsupported is adopted through the binding (exercised); a preview is refused as above Replays Refused before install, with #662 Locked, no binding n/a n/a Replays Refused on every command Support is advice and withdrawal is authority: unsupported and deprecated never stop a lock, while withdrawn and revoked always do. Known limits, recorded rather than fixed here: a passed ends date does not change the status by itself (agreed: the catalog is re-published as unsupported), the build shows no deprecation warning, and revocation cannot reach a machine that never verified a catalog (#601) or stop an installed copy that is not replayed through a lock.

Owner (agreed): the release owner, Micah Martin (no second owner), who holds the right to merge oyzuai/tool-index changes and to run plugin-release.yml. The catalog source is config/plugins.toml in oyzuai/tool-index; every change there needs a person (code owner). A catalog change reaches clients as the next release serial of the tool index (the release workflow runs when config/plugins.toml changes and re-signs daily); clients with the opt-in pick it up at their next refresh, at most an hour later, and apply its withdrawals on every command. Incident Action What users see and do A release is defective Add a withdrawals entry (kind = "withdrawn", package, version, root digest, reason, optional replacement) and remove the release from the list. Publish a fixed version as a new release Builds and --plan fail with PLUGIN_RELEASE_WITHDRAWN naming the catalog serial and the lock entry. Run oyzu plugins update go/app (needs a binding for the replacement, as above); oyzu plugins versions go/app shows why a release is excluded Content or the signing path is compromised Withdraw with kind = "revoked". If the signer identity itself is compromised, a new CLI release must change the pinned identity: tell users to upgrade; revoke each affected release by digest PLUGIN_RELEASE_REVOKED ("it will not run") on every command; recover as above. Installed copies outside a lock are not removed The catalog is wrong or must be rolled back A serial never goes backwards: clients refuse a lower serial, the same serial with other bytes and a higher serial generated earlier. Fix forward with the next serial A rolled-back or stale copy is ignored and the last verified copy stays in force with its withdrawals The catalog is tampered with, or its signature fails The client refuses it and keeps its last verified copy. Restore the correct release assets and investigate the workflow Unlocked references: PLUGIN_CATALOG_UNAVAILABLE. A lock replays only against a verified copy. Offline or with an expired copy, withdrawals still apply and a PLUGIN_CATALOG_EXPIRED warning is shown. A user can bind a package explicitly to continue without the catalog GHCR is unreachable or the package is private No change to releases. If the package was made private by mistake, restore public visibility (organization owner) PLUGIN_PACKAGE_UNAVAILABLE naming the missing object or "refused anonymous access". A release already in the store keeps working: builds that find it installed need no network A release cannot be published Hosted runners are required: the build matrix uses macOS and Windows runners, and clients accept only a signature from a GitHub-hosted runner on main. Check the dry run before publishing Nothing changes for users; the catalog lists only what is available A signed release must be removed There is no deletion: the Rekor entry is permanent and the bytes stay for retention. Withdraw it As a defective release Order matters in both directions: publish bytes and signature first, the catalog entry last (a catalog never lists bytes that are not there); withdraw in the catalog first, then deal with bytes.

Agreed by the maintainer on 2026-10-19. Decision Value First version 0.1.0-preview.1 Tested core in the catalog qualification 0.1.0, platform linux/amd64 (musl) only Support model Newest preview supported; superseded preview deprecated for at least 30 days, then unsupported; no backports Retention of release contents and evidence At least 12 months after supersession; withdrawn and revoked releases kept while listed Whether a passed ends date makes a release unsupported The catalog is re-published as unsupported; the client does not compute it Release owner and incident contact Micah Martin, the oyzuai organization maintainer; no second owner Selecting the preview in a CI job Machine-scope configuration written by the job (the recipe in Selecting the preview); no new channel (#670) Selection contract plugins.preview = true; the release is acquired from the catalog's own OCI route (#664); a plugins.packages binding is optional and takes precedence Where the release is built and signed GitHub-hosted runners (enabled for the organization on 2026-10-19); the client keeps accepting only a github-hosted signer. The self-hosted alternative in #663 is not accepted

Compiled-CLI tests in tests/integration/plugin_lifecycle.rs (a signed organization catalog, a stand-in plugin so selection and lock behavior is measured, not the Go build): new_selection_offers_only_eligible_releases, adoption_offers_only_eligible_releases and replay_follows_the_lock_until_the_release_is_withdrawn_or_revoked (including recovery by update). They found one defect: a plugins.packages binding of a digest the catalog had withdrawn or revoked was adopted and launched on first use. It is fixed, with its own tests, in #662, which this page's withdrawn and revoked rows assume is on main. The real Go plugin under the real official catalog and GHCR is the publication proof in plugin releases. Route proof, no binding (2026-10-19, linux/amd64): see the status entry: only plugins.preview = true, the Selection source reads official default and the package line names the catalog route. Native Windows run (2026-10-19 21:30 US Eastern, MICAH-DESKTOP, Windows 10.0.26200 x86_64, main at 67a28f0): the same user-scope-only selection built the example, ran the windows/amd64 payload and printed Hello, Oyzu!; the CI control ignored the user scope. A frozen replay with the plugin store removed fails with PLUGIN_LOCK_UNUSABLE (the documented binding-only re-acquisition gap) and the machine-scope recipe was not run; see the status entry. Earlier published proof, with a binding (2026-10-19, linux/amd64): from a clean store, anonymously and with only the official catalog (serial 21) and GHCR, oyzu build detected go/app, acquired and signature-verified oyzu/go 0.1.0-preview.1 (sha256:25f830bd740620e6a54a5eac922d1a9505e12f1e1db732f8538152447ba1f9bf), recorded exactly that release in oyzu.lock and produced a running artifact; oyzu build --frozen replayed it. The package was acquired through a user plugins.packages OCI binding (the Selection source read local package binding), before route acquisition (#664); the catalog supplied the detection, the reference and the preview listing. The binary was built against the Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock of 1febd94, because main did not build with --locked at the time. Exact commands, captured output and the time (about 09:40 US Eastern) are in the status entry. Other platforms are listed in the catalog but not proved end to end.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/plugin-releases.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Experimental. How a first-party plugin becomes an Oyzu OCI package in GHCR that any oyzu can acquire without Docker or an account. The package layout is the Oyzu OCI package contract; how the CLI acquires and verifies it is plugin packages; the design is plugin authoring and publication. No release has been published. The GHCR package ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/go does not exist yet; publishing waits on the organization-owner checklist on issue #619, on GitHub-hosted runners (see Limitations) and on maintainer authorization. The terms the first release carries are in Go builder preview.

Piece Role tooling/plugin-oci.py Release tooling, Python standard library only: assemble builds the release root as an OCI image layout directory from one executable per platform and prints the root digest; push copies it to a registry under a tag (refusing to move an existing tag to a different root); assemble-downloaded does the same from the workflow's downloaded payload artifacts; attach attaches a Sigstore bundle as a referrer of the root and in the sha256-<hex> referrers tag; catalog-entry prints the oyzuai/tool-index config/plugins.toml release entry from an assembled layout (every field the catalog schema requires; tested = [] unless --tested CORE=os/arch[/abi],... names platforms of the release; bad input exits nonzero with a message), checked by python3 tooling/test-plugin-oci-catalog-entry.py, which validates the entry against catalog.schema.json. The CLI never runs it .github/workflows/plugin-release.yml Manual (workflow_dispatch) workflow: validates the inputs (semantic version, package name), builds oyzu-plugin-<package> for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 (static musl), darwin/arm64, darwin/amd64 and windows/amd64 (msvc), assembles the root, then runs either the dry-run job (read-only token) or the publish job (packages: write, id-token: write, main only)

oyzu exec -- cargo build --locked -p oyzu-plugin-go --features plugin python3 tooling/plugin-oci.py assemble --out layout --version 0.1.0 \ --revision "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" \ --executable linux/amd64=target/debug/oyzu-plugin-go # prints sha256:<root digest> python3 tooling/plugin-oci.py push --layout layout --to localhost:5000/oyzuai/plugins/go:0.1.0 --executable takes os/arch[/abi]=PATH (OCI spelling: linux, darwin, windows; amd64, arm64; gnu, musl, msvc) once per platform. The plugin manifest comes from docs/contracts/plugins-v1alpha1/examples/manifest.go.json (--manifest to change it) with the version, revision and one runtime per executable filled in; each payload archive holds the executable at bin/<file name>.
