Archives and manifests are reproducible (fixed times, sorted keys), so the same executables give the same root. Any OCI 1.1 registry whose token endpoint is on its own origin works as a target. Without Docker, the distribution registry binary serves one on loopback: registry serve config.yml with http: {addr: 127.0.0.1:5000} and a filesystem storage directory. A user binds the pushed release by digest (no signature needed outside the official namespace) and builds: [plugins.packages] "go/app" = { oci = "localhost:5000/oyzuai/plugins/go@sha256:<root digest>" }

gh workflow run plugin-release.yml -f version=0.1.0 (dry run, the default): builds the payloads, assembles the root, starts the distribution registry binary on the runner (checksum-verified, no Docker), pushes to it, bootstraps the oyzu of this commit and builds examples/builds/go-app/project with the release bound by digest, checking that oyzu.lock records the root and that --frozen replays. Nothing leaves the runner and nothing is signed (a dry run writes no public transparency-log entries). -f publish=true, from main only: pushes the release to ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/<package>:<version> with the workflow's GITHUB_TOKEN (packages: write); signs the root keylessly: tooling/plugin-oci.py statement writes an in-toto statement (predicate https://sigstore.dev/cosign/sign/v1) naming the root digest, and cosign attest-blob --statement --bundle (cosign v3.0.2, checksum-verified) signs it with the workflow's OIDC identity (id-token: write), giving a Sigstore bundle v0.3 with a DSSE envelope from a Fulcio certificate for https://github.com/oyzuai/oyzu/.github/workflows/plugin-release.yml@refs/heads/main, logged in Rekor. This is the tool index's signing path. cosign sign-blob is not used: it writes a message-signature bundle, which the client does not accept; attaches the bundle as a referrer of the root. The signature is detached: it never changes the root. Clients require it for ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/* and verify it against exactly that identity, on a GitHub-hosted runner, before installing. Two separate checks apply. The certificate's identity is pinned to the workflow at @refs/heads/main: a branch that edits the workflow signs as @refs/heads/<branch> and is refused, and the publish job also runs only on main. And the certificate must record a github-hosted runner environment, refusing a self-hosted or an unrecorded one. Neither check protects against someone who can merge to main (their workflow is the pinned one) or against a compromised GitHub-hosted runner; hosted runners are ephemeral, which limits the second. The workflow uses ubuntu-24.04, macos-15 and windows-2025 (the organization enabled hosted runners on 2026-10-19; hosted minutes are reserved for releases). A self-hosted signer was merged in #663 and reverted before any release was signed; see the decision. This signing path differs from the CLI's GitHub release workflow (PR #617), which signs build provenance with a self-managed witness key: plugin packages use portable keyless Sigstore as the design requires, the same trust model as the public tool index.

The ordered sequence for PLG-AUTHOR-04 (private source, public binary, catalog last). Every step after 2 has outward effects that cannot be undone: a package in GHCR, a permanent public Sigstore (Rekor) entry, a public package and an advertised catalog entry. Run it only with the maintainer's authorization of the exact version. Commands assume gh authenticated as an organization member and a checkout of main. VERSION=0.1.0-preview.1 is the agreed version (decisions); a version is never reused. Preconditions. GitHub-hosted runners are available to the organization (enabled by the maintainer on 2026-10-19) and a dry run on main is green on them. The workflow uses hosted runners for the five builds and the signing, and the client accepts only a certificate whose runner environment is github-hosted, which the maintainer kept. Before that, with the repository private and hosted runners off, every job failed within seconds with no runner (the 2026-10-18 dry run, run 39173379822). The self-hosted signer merged in #663 was reverted before any release was signed. The #619 checklist: public packages allowed for the organization (done); the workflow may write plugins/go (item 2, below). #662 (a bound withdrawn or revoked release is refused before install) and this documentation pull request are merged, so main carries the workflow, the refusal and catalog-entry. oyzuai/tool-index can advertise a release whose evidence is under the referrers tag: its .github/scripts/plugin-availability.sh must fall back from the referrers API to the sha256-<hex> tag, because ghcr.io answers the API with 404 (checked 2026-10-19 against an image that has tag-schema referrers). Without that change the catalog silently omits the release. That change is oyzuai/tool-index#39 (under review, not merged when this was written); it is a dependency of step 5, and plugins.json must be checked to list the release (below). Dry run (read-only, nothing leaves the runner, nothing signed). The helper dispatches the workflow and selects the run it created: newer than the dispatch, on the head of main, and named for the package and version (the workflow's run-name), so two dispatches at the same moment are told apart: dispatch() { # dispatch VERSION [publish]; sets RUN to the new run's id local t sha; t=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ); sha=$(git rev-parse origin/main) gh workflow run plugin-release.yml --ref main -f package=go -f version="$1" ${2:+-f publish=true} RUN= for _ in $(seq 30); do RUN=$(gh run list --workflow plugin-release.yml --event workflow_dispatch --json databaseId,createdAt,headSha,displayTitle --limit 10 \ -q "[.[] | select(.createdAt >= "$t" and .headSha == "$sha" and (.displayTitle == "Plugin release go $1" or .displayTitle == "Plugin release go $1 (publish)"))][0].databaseId // empty") [ -n "$RUN" ] && break; sleep 5 done [ -n "$RUN" ] || { echo "no run found for the dispatch" >&2; return 1; } gh run watch "$RUN" --exit-status } git fetch origin main && dispatch 0.0.0-dryrun.1 gh run download "$RUN" -n catalog-entry -D dry-run-entry && grep -c '^\[\[packages.releases.platforms\]\]' dry-run-entry/catalog-entry.toml # 5 Hosted runner minutes are reserved for this workflow, so this is the one pre-release dry run: it must be on the final workflow, with the proof fix, on main. Run 39191353142 proved the five hosted build legs and the steps through the bootstrap only, and a workflow that differs from the one that ran it by more than runner labels or run-name needs the maintainer's word before another dry run. Expect validate, the five Build jobs and Dry run green and five platforms in the entry. Fix any failure before going on; a dry-run version may be reused. Publish (from main only, the signer identity requires it): git fetch origin main && dispatch 0.1.0-preview.1 publish ROOT=$(gh run view "$RUN" --log | grep -o 'ROOT=sha256:[0-9a-f]\{64\}' | tail -1 | cut -d= -f2) && echo "$ROOT" gh run download "$RUN" -n catalog-entry -D release-entry # the tool index entry, tested = [] The Publish job pushes ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/go:0.1.0-preview.1, signs the root keylessly and attaches the bundle. ROOT is also in the job summary line Published …; step 4 checks that the lock records exactly it. If the push is refused with a permission error, the package does not yet grant this workflow write access: an organization owner opens github.com/orgs/oyzuai/packages → plugins/go → Package settings → Manage Actions access → add oyzuai/oyzu with role Write (item 2 of #619; the first publish creates the package, so this can only be done now), then re-run the failed job. If the push succeeded but a later step failed, a re-run is only safe when it produces the same root; a rebuild that yields a different root makes push refuse the tag, and the version is spent: publish 0.1.0-preview.2 instead. Make the package public (an organization owner, GitHub UI): plugins/go → Package settings → Danger Zone → Change visibility → Public. Visibility is per package and does not expose the repository. This is reversible (set it back to private if step 4 fails), but the bytes were public meanwhile. Anonymous pull and signature proof with the CLI's own verifier, from a clean state, no Docker and no credentials, in an ordinary shell (not a CI job: user-scope settings are ignored in a CI context): S=$(mktemp -d) && mkdir "$S/home" && cp -r examples/builds/go-app/project "$S/project" printf '[plugins]
preview = true
[plugins.packages]
"go/app" = { oci = "ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins/go:0.1.0-preview.1" }
' > "$S/user.toml" run() { env -u GITHUB_TOKEN -u GH_TOKEN HOME="$S/home" XDG_DATA_HOME="$S/xdg" OYZU_USER_CONFIG="$S/user.toml" OYZU_PROJECT_TRUST=off oyzu -C "$S/project" "$@" --store "$S/store"; } run build # acquires, verifies the signature, installs, builds grep -F "release = "$ROOT"" "$S/project/oyzu.lock" run build --frozen # replays by digest Success is a build whose Selection section names oyzu/go 0.1.0-preview.1 as a local package binding, the lock recording ROOT, and the artifact running. PLUGIN_PACKAGE_UNAVAILABLE … refused anonymous access means step 3 is not effective; PLUGIN_SIGNATURE_* means the release must not be listed. Catalog entry last. On merge the tool-index release workflow checks the root and evidence anonymously and signs plugins.json; verify the new release lists the package, not just that the asset exists (a release whose catalog step failed or left the package out still has the tools assets): D=$(mktemp -d) && gh release download --repo oyzuai/tool-index --pattern 'plugins.json*' --dir "$D" jq -e --arg root "$ROOT" '.content.packages[] | select(.publisher == "oyzu" and .name == "go") | .releases[] | select(.version == "0.1.0-preview.1" and .root_digest == $root)' "$D/plugins.json" jq -e exits nonzero when no release matches. The CLI verifies the bundle in step 7. Remove the bundled preview source (separate pull request, merged only after step 5 is verified live): the compiled-in catalog, its generator and the "temporary" notes are gone, so the published catalog is the only source. The bundled catalog's archive digest stood in for a root that was never published; leaving it would list a second 0.1.0-preview.1 with different bytes. Final proof from a clean store, with only the official catalog and GHCR: the step-4 commands again, now with plugins.preview = true and the binding only (no archive, no local bytes), then oyzu plugins info go/app showing the release from official catalog serial N. A version is published once. push refuses to move a tag to a different root; a fix, a changed payload or an added platform is a new version and a new root. Releases and their signature referrers are retained; no cleanup policy applies to ghcr.io/oyzuai/plugins. A lock cannot recreate deleted bytes.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/plugin-updates.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Experimental. oyzu plugins update replaces plugin selections that oyzu.lock already holds: a routine update within the adopted major, an explicit new major, or one exact version or release (an exact release root is how an update is undone). A standard GitHub workflow runs it on a schedule and opens a pull request. The design is the draft compatibility and updates proposal; this page records what is implemented (issue #587, tracking #578). How a selection is first adopted is in plugin catalog; the [[plugin]] lock record is in plugin packages; read-only views are in inspecting plugins.

oyzu plugins update # every locked selection, each within its adopted major oyzu plugins update go/app # only go/app oyzu plugins update go/app@v2 # adopt major 2 of go/app explicitly oyzu plugins update go/app@1.0.0 # exactly version 1.0.0 of go/app's package oyzu plugins update go/app@sha256:… # exactly this release root: the printed undo oyzu plugins update --dry-run # preflight and show the change; oyzu.lock is not written Options: --dry-run, --offline (update from the cached catalog only), --store DIR (the plugin store, as oyzu build --store) and the global --json. It works without an account. --help and syntax errors finish before a project, configuration, store or network is opened. Publishing or caching a newer release never changes a lock: builds replay it (PLG-COMPAT-05). Only this command, or deleting the entry, changes it.

Before catalog or candidate evaluation, an exact engine pin uses the shared engine bootstrap. A mismatching active frontend must have an admitted source for that engine. The selected engine evaluates its own supported role features, including on warm package reuse; unsupported required capabilities fail before adoption or plugin roles. A compatible update changes only the requested plugin entries and retains engine and native-tool pins. Metadata-only inspection continues to use the running engine without staging. Refresh the catalog. Unless --offline, the verified catalog cache is refreshed from the permitted sources first, as a real build does. A refused catalog (failed trust, rollback, a verified copy gone missing) or an expired one refuses the whole update with PLUGIN_CATALOG_UNAVAILABLE: an update never adopts a release without a current verified catalog. This includes a refresh that obtained a newer copy and refused it while an older verified copy is cached: a build goes on with that copy, an update does not. With --offline, the cached copy is used as asked. Choose each candidate with the build's resolver and eligibility rule, within a selector: Written Selector Candidate go/app (or nothing: every locked reference) the adopted major the newest eligible release in that major; never an older one while the locked release may still be used go/app@v2 or go/app@2 major 2, explicitly the newest eligible release of major 2 go/app@1.4.2 exactly version 1.4.2 of the package the catalog binds that release, newer or older go/app@sha256:… exactly this release root, which also names its package that release; the printed undo uses this form Routine and @v<major> updates never select a preview release, whatever supplies it, catalog or plugins.packages binding (ordinary updates exclude previews, PLG-COMPAT-01): PLUGIN_PREVIEW_NOT_SELECTED. A release is a preview when its version is a prerelease or when the catalogs list it (by root digest, or by package and version) as one. A listing by root digest decides before one by package and version. An exact @<version> or @sha256:… can select a preview, and only with plugins.preview. A routine update never changes the canonical package either: when an organization catalog rebinds the reference (or a binding supplies another package) it fails with PLUGIN_PACKAGE_CHANGE, and the change is adopted only with an explicit selector such as @v1. Eligible means what it means for a build: listed by the consulted catalog, not withdrawn or revoked (by package and version or root digest, in any consulted snapshot), not a preview without plugins.preview, supported, on the v1alpha1 contract, with the builder profile and a payload for this host. A plugins.packages binding for the reference supplies the package instead, as it does for a build; it must still fit the selector and replay under the lock rules below. Preflight. Each new release is installed into the plugin store from its route (already in the store, the plugins.packages binding that names its digest, or, with no binding, the OCI route in its verified catalog entry, as a build acquires it) and checked exactly as a first adoption is: archive or OCI digest, the catalog's package and version, the builder profile, the protocol generation, and an executable payload this host runs. The proposed selection must then pass the build's own lock rules (Context::check_locked): not withdrawn, not revoked, not rebound by an organization catalog. Write once. Only when every requested reference passes is oyzu.lock rewritten, in one lock-edit transaction that replaces exactly those [[plugin]] entries in place (comments above an entry are kept). Unrelated selections, tool records, the engine pin and the lock format are untouched. If another process changed one of those entries meanwhile, nothing is written (PLUGIN_LOCK_CHANGED). Any refusal leaves the lock byte for byte as it was. An update never launches a plugin, edits configuration, or touches another project file. Releases it installed stay in the store (content-addressed and immutable), also after a refused or --dry-run update.

Updated 1 plugin selection in oyzu.lock Changes Reference Before After Change Why go/app acme/go 1.0.0 acme/go 1.0.1 patch the plugins.packages binding supplies this release go/library acme/go 1.0.0 — unchanged newest eligible release in major 1 Releases go/app sha256:a9713fde…7583 → sha256:d660c518…06ca · installed now from /home/me/acme-go-1.0.1.tar.gz Undo oyzu plugins update go/app@sha256:a9713fde547a6353975dd14aad1c837a4c70b475961ec37563ae320fb32d7583 Restores the earlier releases while they remain eligible; reverting the oyzu.lock change does the same. Lock ./oyzu.lock (updated) Evaluated against Engine 0.1.0 (running engine) … Review and commit oyzu.lock to share the update. Nothing was launched and no configuration changed. Change is patch, minor, major (an explicit new major), rollback (an older release, by @<version> or because the locked one may no longer be used), package (another canonical package now serves the reference, adopted with an explicit selector) or unchanged. --dry-run heads the view with Would update … and labels the undo Undo (once adopted). Notes report, for example, a binding that pins the locked release while a newer one is eligible. --json prints one object, the value the human view is laid out from: {"kind":"plugin-update","dryRun":false,"wrote":true,"lock":"/work/app/oyzu.lock", "changes":[{"reference":"go/app","selector":null, "from":{"package":"acme/go","major":1,"version":"1.0.0","release":"sha256:…"}, "to":{"package":"acme/go","major":1,"version":"1.0.1","release":"sha256:…"}, "level":"patch","reason":"…","installedNow":true,"route":"/home/me/acme-go-1.0.1.tar.gz"}], "undo":"oyzu plugins update go/app@sha256:…","notes":[], "evaluation":{"engine":"…","engineSource":"running engine","platforms":["linux/amd64"],"…":"…"}, "coverage":{"choice":"organization","snapshots":[{"label":"acme catalog serial 2","…":"…"}],"…":"…"}} evaluation and coverage are the records the inspection commands print.

The undo line selects each changed reference's earlier release root exactly (@sha256:…), so it names the package as well as the version: after a package change, two packages can share a version number. It goes through the same checks, so it succeeds only while that release remains available and authorized: a release the catalog has since withdrawn or revoked is refused (PLUGIN_UPDATE_UNAVAILABLE, naming the withdrawal), and so is the earlier package while a catalog binds the reference to another one. That refusal states only what is known: which package and version the release belongs to, which package the catalog holding the binding (named or primary) binds the reference to, that under an organization catalog a lock of the other package, such as a reverted oyzu.lock, is refused by builds too (PLUGIN_BINDING_CHANGED), and the two ways forward: ask the catalog's owner to bind that package, or update the bound one with an explicit selector. It does not claim the reference ever used the other package. Reverting the oyzu.lock change in version control restores the same records; the next build then replays them under the same rules. If a plugins.packages binding supplied the new release, the undo also needs that binding to name the earlier release again or be unset; the update says so in its notes, and an undo against such a binding fails with PLUGIN_UPDATE_CONFLICT and the oyzu config unset line.

Code Meaning and recovery PLUGIN_CATALOG_UNAVAILABLE No current verified catalog (refused, expired, or none usable). Restore access and run again PLUGIN_UPDATE_NOT_LOCKED The reference has no selection in oyzu.lock; run oyzu build to adopt one first PLUGIN_SELECTOR_INVALID The selector is not v<major>, an exact version or a sha256: release digest, or a reference is named twice PLUGIN_UPDATE_UNAVAILABLE No eligible release fits the selector (with the reasons, such as outside the adopted major 1, no payload for this platform, or the withdrawal). A routine update whose locked release still replays reports unchanged instead PLUGIN_MAJOR_CHANGE A binding supplies a release outside the adopted major; run the printed @v<major> update to adopt it explicitly PLUGIN_UPDATE_CONFLICT A plugins.packages binding supplies another release than the requested @<version> or @sha256:… PLUGIN_PREVIEW_NOT_SELECTED The release that would be adopted is a preview: routine and @v<major> updates never select one; an exact selector needs plugins.preview PLUGIN_PACKAGE_CHANGE A routine update would change the canonical package (an organization rebinding, or a binding to another package); adopt it with the printed explicit selector PLUGIN_UPDATE_REFUSED The proposed selection fails the build's lock rules (wrapping PLUGIN_RELEASE_WITHDRAWN, PLUGIN_RELEASE_REVOKED or PLUGIN_BINDING_CHANGED), for example a binding to a withdrawn release's archive PLUGIN_ROUTE_UNAVAILABLE The candidate is not in the store, no binding supplies it and its catalog entry has no OCI route (or --offline forbids using it); the message prints the plugins.packages line to bind its archive PLUGIN_ROUTE_FAILED The candidate's catalog route could not be reached or does not hold the release, or lists an unusable address; nothing was installed or recorded. A signature, digest or package failure on the route keeps its own code PLUGIN_PLATFORM_UNSUPPORTED, PLUGIN_PACKAGE_MISMATCH, PLUGIN_PACKAGE_INVALID, archive digest errors Preflight of the installed package failed; no other release is chosen instead PLUGIN_LOCK_CHANGED oyzu.lock changed while the update ran; run it again Each refusal says oyzu.lock was not changed. The build's remedies now point here: PLUGIN_RELEASE_WITHDRAWN, PLUGIN_RELEASE_REVOKED, PLUGIN_BINDING_CHANGED and PLUGIN_LOCK_MISMATCH end with oyzu plugins update <reference>, as does the Selection section's other-implementation remedy for a selection locked earlier.

workflows/oyzu-plugin-update.yml is the standard workflow. Copy it to .github/workflows/ in a repository whose oyzu.lock selects plugins. Weekly and on demand it runs three jobs, so that nothing an unreviewed plugin does can change what is proposed: update runs only oyzu plugins update --json, which launches no plugin (it invokes the oyzu updater directly; no other dependency bot needs to understand oyzu.lock). It stops if oyzu.lock did not change; otherwise it uploads the proposed oyzu.lock, the JSON report, the change levels and the pull request body as one artifact and passes on its id. verify downloads that artifact by id, writes its oyzu.lock into a fresh checkout and runs BUILD_COMMAND (default oyzu build --frozen), which launches the newly adopted plugin. It has no write credential (the checkout keeps none and no token is in the job) and uploads nothing: it is a pass/fail gate only, and nothing it writes reaches the propose job. See the limitation below on what the plugin can still reach in this job. propose runs only if both passed. In a fresh checkout without persisted credentials it downloads the update job's artifact by id, refuses it unless it holds exactly body.md, levels, oyzu.lock and report.json as regular files, writes only oyzu.lock into the tree, commits it to the oyzu/plugin-update branch, force-pushes it, and opens a pull request, or refreshes the open one, whose body lists each change, its level, why, notes and the undo line. The token is in this last step only. With AUTO_MERGE_PATCH: 'true' and only patch changes, it enables GitHub auto-merge, which merges only after the repository's branch protection and required checks pass. When it refreshes an open pull request with anything else, it turns auto-merge off (gh pr merge --disable-auto) and confirms it is off before it pushes the new lock, so a request made for an earlier all-patch proposal never applies to the new one. Every gh call before the push fails closed: a failed pull request lookup (which counts only this repository's pull request, not a fork's with the same branch name), a failed --disable-auto, or auto-merge still requested afterwards stops the job with nothing pushed. It never merges directly. It needs a secret OYZU_UPDATE_TOKEN (a GitHub App or fine-grained token with contents and pull-requests write access), used by the propose job only: pull requests opened with the default GITHUB_TOKEN do not start the repository's workflows, so required checks would never report. The Install oyzu steps are placeholders to replace with a pinned, checksummed installation: no oyzu release is published yet. The update job needs jq, which GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runners include.

an exact selector needs plugins.preview a_binding_never_brings_in_a_preview_without_an_exact_selector_and_the_opt_in A release the catalog marks preview with a plain version (1.1.0) is treated as one a_release_the_catalog_marks_preview_is_one_whatever_its_version A preview matched by root digest alone; --offline uses the cached copy a_refused_refresh_stops_the_update_even_with_a_verified_copy_cached A refused refresh stays a refusal behind the cached copy that stands in unit catalog::tests::a_refused_refresh_stays_a_refusal_behind_the_cached_copy Human, no-color and --json agree; typed JSON errors; only oyzu.lock and the store change update_output_agrees_in_human_and_json_and_writes_nothing_else PLG-COMPAT-06 the shipped workflow's three jobs, each in a fresh clone of a local bare remote with its own runner directory and a snapshot of the update job's artifact, with the compiled CLI and a recording gh that remembers the open pull request. A failing build proposes nothing. An artifact with an extra file is refused before any push. The build stand-in sees no token (environment or .git/config), then rewrites the tree's oyzu.lock and its copy of the lock, levels and body: none of it reaches the push or the pull request. A passing run pushes only oyzu.lock and opens the pull request with the change table and undo, requesting patch auto-merge. With auto-merge requested and a minor release, a failed lookup, a failed --disable-auto and auto-merge still requested afterwards each stop the job with the branch untouched; the next run turns auto-merge off before the push (the stub records the branch head at each call), then refreshes the same pull request from main (gh pr edit) without requesting auto-merge. After merge, a run proposes nothing the_standard_workflow_proposes_a_built_lock_change_as_a_pull_request The stand-in plugin cannot run a full build, so the tests replay the updated lock with oyzu build --frozen up to the plugin launch, and the workflow test's build command checks that no credential is visible and runs oyzu plugins explain.

Only the host platform is evaluated for payloads; other required execution platforms (a declared matrix, remote workers) are not preflighted. Only a catalog's OCI route is acquired from (as in a build); a candidate whose entry lists only an HTTPS layout-archive route needs a plugins.packages binding. @vN in uses: references is not implemented; the selector exists only on this command. The verify job runs the newly adopted, unreviewed plugin on the default branch, in scheduled runs and in runs started with workflow_dispatch. It holds no write token for the repository, but on a GitHub-hosted runner the plugin runs as the job's user (with passwordless sudo), so it can read the job's ACTIONS_RUNTIME_TOKEN, and with that write Actions caches scoped to the default branch, which other workflows restore, or upload artifacts of its own. The propose job is protected (it reads only the update job's artifact, by id, and checks it), but other workflows that restore default-branch caches are not. Today the workflow does nothing about this beyond running verify in its own job with no repository credential. Setting permissions: {} on the job would not prevent it either: that limits GITHUB_TOKEN, not the runtime token the Actions cache and artifact services use. Where possible, run the verify job on an ephemeral, isolated runner and keep workflows that matter from restoring caches the verify job could write (for example, key their caches so this workflow cannot produce them). The workflow has been run locally against a bare remote with a stub gh, not yet on GitHub-hosted runners against a real plugin project; it has no oyzu installation step until a release exists. Windows and macOS are untested.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/pnpm.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Oyzu recognizes a conventional Node project using pnpm and its pnpm-lock.yaml. Single projects and conventional native workspaces need no Oyzu build configuration. The experimental adapter captures public-registry dependency archives, verifies their SHA-512 lockfile integrity, and uses native pnpm for frozen-lock validation and installation. Native pnpm retains responsibility for dependency layout and peer resolution.

The current provisioned profile is pnpm 10.11.0 on Node 22. Build the common quality image, then the pnpm image: docker build -t oyzu-toolchain/node:quality tooling/images/node-quality docker build -t oyzu-toolchain/node:pnpm10.11.0-node22 tooling/images/node-pnpm oyzu --root path/to/project run list oyzu --root path/to/project build oyzu --root path/to/project inspect dist The build requires Docker and these explicitly provisioned images; Oyzu does not install them. --image pnpm=<image> selects an already provisioned compatible image. The image must include the owned runtime prerequisites, including yaml 2.8.1 at /opt/oyzu-pnpm/node_modules/yaml, and the Node quality tools. Its immutable image identity binds those tools. A project's exact packageManager, when present, must agree with the pnpm that runs. An exact stable release is a pinned tool, locked as oyzu:pnpm and run in place of the image's pnpm, so pnpm never downloads itself in the worker. A Corepack digest suffix such as pnpm@10.11.0+sha512.<hex> is accepted and ignored for that comparison. Native strict engine validation rejects incompatible Node requirements. Development tasks use installed host tools. oyzu run list exposes native package scripts and inferred test/quality tasks; oyzu run <task> uses the development environment. Captured builds run native build/test work and read-only lint/format checks. Node's native test runner receives JUnit and LCOV reporting through the existing Node builder; other supported framework reporting remains framework-specific. See Node quality for quality selection and provisioned defaults. Formatting during a build never rewrites the checkout.

Other Node versions are tested with verification toolsets in oyzu.toml, never in build.yaml (matrix.node is refused). Toolset verification runs execute on the native host executor; pnpm builds use the isolated executor, so a pnpm build that has verification runs fails with VERIFICATION_RUN_UNSUPPORTED until runs reach that executor. Workspace support is described below; private registry configuration remains unfinished. The admitted lock format is v9 with a root importer and, for workspaces, native member importers. pnpm 12 can write pnpm-lock.yaml as two YAML documents: an environment document whose root importer pins pnpm itself under packageManagerDependencies (with its pnpm and @pnpm/exe.* packages), followed by the usual v9 project document. Oyzu reads such a lock as follows: The project document is admitted and captured exactly as a single-document lock is. The environment document is validated but not captured, because Oyzu provisions the package manager itself. It may contain only lockfileVersion, importers, packages and snapshots, a single . importer, and only configDependencies and packageManagerDependencies in that importer. A non-empty configDependencies fails, because configuration dependencies would need their own captured inputs. Workspace version projection rewrites only the project document and writes the environment document back unchanged. A lock with more than two documents fails. This reading is in place. The provisioned default profile is pnpm 10.11.0, which cannot read a two-document lock. An exact packageManager release is a locked tool requirement when the tool provider offers it. The provider selects the publisher's platform executable package for both the older and pnpm 12 package families. The compiled CLI completed a full isolated build of the two-document fixture with pnpm 12.3.4, including tests, coverage and a package (see implementation status). Other pnpm 12 projects, versions and platforms remain unqualified. Every registry package in the project document's packages section is admitted and checked for an exact SHA-512 integrity value. Native frozen pnpm installation in the selected build image requests the archives it needs; acquisition captures only those requests through the scoped npm-public route to https://registry.npmjs.org/. Optional archives for other platforms are not fetched unless native pnpm requests them for the selected image and declared configuration. The lockfile remains unchanged. Acquisition disables project lifecycle scripts. Unsupported pnpm configuration and hook files are rejected before any native invocation, including the version query. Preparation verifies archive digests before handing bytes to pnpm. The snapshot contains content-addressed tarballs in lock identity order for the selected native requests; it does not retain pnpm's timestamped mutable store. Repeated native requests for one archive share a single broker fetch. Native pnpm requests at most eight packages concurrently, matching the broker client bound. Its acquisition-only loopback wait is 120 seconds so a broker request can complete within its existing 55-second client window; replay of captured local bytes retains the 15-second wait. Neither setting raises the broker's network deadline or byte allowance. An unknown route or failed broker or integrity check fails preparation even if native pnpm would tolerate a missing optional package. For installation, the adapter creates a fresh private store and serves exact captured archives on an ephemeral loopback port. For pnpm 12, it also serves full publisher packuments for the admitted locked package names. Native admission runs on a private copy of the project first; Rust captures the publisher responses through the active scoped npm-public broker before freezing the prepared tree. Native pnpm may also request attestation responses for exact admitted locked name/version pairs. The bridge captures only those native requests through the same broker; Rust validates their source and 200 or 404 status, stores the returned bytes and digest, and binds the selected responses in extensions["oyzu.dev/pnpm"].attestations. A source-backed 404 records absence; broker denial or timeout cannot become absence. pnpm evaluates its own attestation policy and cryptographic evidence. The dependency snapshot's policyMetadata also lists each captured packument's sourceId, URL, locked versions, SHA-256 digest and size; the preparedTree digest binds the raw bytes. This is source and content evidence, not a complete authenticity or runtime SBOM claim. The isolated worker has no external network. During acquisition its loopback server asks the broker only for exact admitted locked archive and attestation identities; during execution it serves only the frozen selected subset and never forwards requests. A native HEAD probe receives headers only when its exact route already has captured metadata or archive bytes; it never fetches or selects an archive. The server holds no registry credentials, and unknown routes and methods fail. Native pnpm needs HTTP access to this local server, so its own --offline switch is not used. Native supply-chain policy evaluation remains enabled; Oyzu does not set trustLockfile. Execution mounts no acquisition broker, rechecks captured response identity, and enables native lifecycle behavior. Its private pnpm store uses an invocation-scoped scratch mount and is discarded afterward. Explicit Oyzu build --offline still rejects this builder before preparation; online capture followed by network-isolated execution is the verified mode. pnpm 10's dependency-script approval rules still apply; Oyzu does not silently approve dependency scripts. Native lock/manifest checks run with --frozen-lockfile. The adapter checks that the lock bytes remain unchanged and requires the same pnpm/Node versions during preparation and execution. Credentials are absent from the inventory and loopback endpoint. Managed/private registry routes remain unimplemented for this profile.

Checked-in patchedDependencies settings are supported in a single project's pnpm-workspace.yaml or the native pnpm object in package.json. For example: patchedDependencies: is-number@6.0.0: patches/is-number@6.0.0.patch Use native pnpm patch and patch-commit to generate the patch, settings and updated lock; commit those inputs together. Oyzu needs no additional setting. A pnpm-workspace.yaml containing these settings does not itself require multiple projects. A packages list enables native workspace discovery; patch-only settings retain single-project planning. The workspace settings below are also admitted; other configuration keys remain unsupported. All declared and locked patch paths must reference regular files inside the captured project. Absolute paths, parent traversal, backslashes, symbolic links, missing files and patches over 4 MiB fail admission. Native pnpm verifies lock/configuration agreement and patch hashes, selects matching dependencies and applies the patch to its private installation. Oyzu does not parse diff hunks or implement its own patch engine. Modified patch bytes with a stale lock fail before project lifecycle hooks run. Source files and the content-addressed registry archives remain unchanged. Registry inventory records continue to identify the original downloaded archives. The oyzu.dev/pnpm.sourcePatches extension separately records each locked patch selector, captured relative path, SHA-256 digest, size and native lock hash. The source digest binds the patch inputs, and the dependency-snapshot digest includes the patch evidence. This distinguishes source modifications from pristine upstream archive identity; it is not a complete runtime SBOM.

Successful builds produce a snapshot-versioned native .tgz package under dist/, with its embedded package version matching the artifact version. The manifest records actual artifacts and collected test/coverage reports; native logs and the dependency snapshot accompany the bundle. Failed tests retain collected reports and block packaging. oyzu inspect dist checks recorded content integrity, not release eligibility or producer trust. Dependency records use adapter layout 1, inventory every captured archive with its name, version, source ID, size and SHA-256 digest, and record lockfile-sha512 verification in oyzu.dev/pnpm. Package purpose currently means build input; runtime/test classification and registry dependency edges are not modeled. Workspace captures additionally retain native local package edges for planning and version projection. No complete runtime SBOM is claimed. A stale lock requires regenerating and committing the lock with the intended native pnpm version before rebuilding. Digest mismatch, denied acquisition, missing captured archives, packuments or selected attestation responses, or changed runtime versions fail rather than refetch during execution. The current captured registry inventory uses layout version 1, including a dependency-free pnpm 12 project with empty response allowlists. Project sources remain unchanged by the captured build.

The EX-020 pnpm variation has a private root, a native pnpm-workspace.yaml, a committed v9 lock and locally linked app/shared packages. Run oyzu build from that root without an Oyzu configuration file. run list exposes build/test/lint/format-check; direct host build dispatch uses native pnpm --recursive run build, while direct tests use the workspace report collector. Acquisition runs native frozen installation with scripts disabled, then asks pnpm to list its members. Workspace commands use the first provisioned pnpm executable on PATH, including a standalone executable; they do not fall through to a lower-priority pnpm when that executable is selected. Corepack pnpm shims are refused because they can acquire a manager. JavaScript pnpm layouts continue to run through the selected Node interpreter. Workspace lock projection uses the same provisioned YAML module path required by the pnpm image (/opt/oyzu-pnpm/node_modules/yaml by default), independently of the selected command shape. Local links come from the validated importer records and must resolve to captured members or a named, publishable workspace root. A private root is not a link target. The common Node workspace planner orders the root and members, freezes their snapshot identities and declares package-owned JUnit/LCOV. Execution projects root and member versions, workspace dependency selectors and matching importer specifiers in its private tree before a fresh frozen installation. Native pnpm pack converts workspace selectors to published snapshot dependencies. The publishable root is packed once, separately from member packages. The committed source and lock remain unchanged. For an opaque root build, Oyzu keeps the native root script once instead of guessing which member scripts it covered. Before packing, the selected Node runtime resolves each concrete public import and require entry from its package and requires the selected file to be regular. It also checks concrete declaration files selected by Node's types condition, and a literal legacy declaration path; these checks establish file presence, not TypeScript validity. A missing declared JavaScript entry fails the build; no JavaScript entry is invented for types-only or assets-only packages. Null exclusions and native conditional alternatives remain Node's decision. Wildcard-only public entries without a concrete specifier cannot be certified. For pnpm, one native pack --json result binds the archive's name, version, filename and included files; an archive omitting a selected public file is refused before its artifact receipt is written. Compiled fixture checks cover missing and omitted public files, and the pinned Hono product proof produced all nine packages. Other managers retain their existing packing behavior. Browser/custom conditions, declaration validity and every wildcard path remain outside this gate. Root scripts retain stage ownership. Otherwise member build scripts run in dependency order and member tests/quality use native scripts or inferred defaults. Required test/quality failures block artifact collection, with available reports retained in the failed bundle. Shared task scheduling owns overrides, prerequisites and hooks. Build formatting is read-only. Registry inputs use the captured loopback server described above; pnpm's HTTP transport to that local server does not permit external downloads. A root test script of the bounded form tsc -p <relative-config> && vp test --run keeps its native pnpm script and TypeScript preflight while forwarding Vitest JUnit/LCOV instrumentation to the final VP command. The runner's Vitest/Vite configuration comes from the selected Vite+ package graph; the coverage provider remains a declared project dependency and must match that runner's version. Other custom root scripts retain their existing report obligation without inferred flags. For the read-only formatting stage, a root format script consisting solely of vp fmt --check with directory-prefixed operands may serve as the native check when no explicit format-check or format:check script and no preformat/postformat hook exists. An opaque or mutating format script does not become a check. These paths have focused dispatch tests and real pinned Hono product evidence, including TypeScript preflight, native VP tests, JUnit/LCOV, lint and read-only formatting. The qualification record preserves earlier timeout failures and the later passing runs; it does not establish the underlying timing cause or a general timing guarantee. A small publishable-root fixture passed compiled isolated full builds on Windows and Linux: root, app and shared packages had projected local versions, the root build script ran once, JUnit/LCOV were collected and bundle inspection passed. The pinned Hono flow uses a package-local root producer and eight adapter producers in dependency order. Its ordinary product proof at 88e7ed09 produced nine usable packages and required reports. Two further fresh full products at 01cfff24 passed from one live held prepared input set, with separate installed workspaces, run identities and outputs, no restored action results, and unchanged source and tool lock. Each passed 5,196 tests with 44 skipped and no failures or errors. An offline consumer of the ordinary product's nine local archives resolved the checked public files and executed the root package through both import and require. This is a bounded Linux proof, not tar-byte reproducibility or every export/platform combination; a separate native peer-check command failed and remains an explicit limit. Current workspace regression and integration status is in the qualification record. Cyclic graphs, affected selection, member task groups and complete direct host build/quality composition remain functional gaps. Workspace registry dependencies, peer/alias combinations and framework variations still need their own scenario evidence. Native pnpm package layout and peer rules remain authoritative. python tooling/test-native-workspace-build.py --manager pnpm passed Windows native acquisition, fresh captured-input replay, two snapshot packages with matching local dependency versions, real JUnit/LCOV, lint/read-only formatting and failed-test reports using Node 24.14.1/pnpm 10.11.0. The same probe supports --manager yarn; host adapter checks alone do not prove worker isolation. The focused native-prepared binding proof at d816 verified that direct, nested bare and helper commands all selected locked standalone pnpm 12.6.0 and completed the YAML-backed version projection before its intentional consumer stop. Later compiled Hono product and held-input proofs are recorded separately, retaining attribution to their exact source and dependency subjects.

This increment supports single-project public registry packages with conventional integrity-only lock resolutions, native dependency patches and the decided workspace settings, and experimental captured workspace packaging. The pnpm 12.3.4 two-document fixture and a dependency-free single-document lock have measured end-to-end builds; other pnpm 12 projects, versions and platforms remain unqualified. For pnpm 11+, Oyzu passes native pmOnFail=ignore to prevent executable self-download and still checks the selected locked version. .npmrc, .pnpmfile.cjs, .pnpmfile.mjs, configuration other than packages, patchedDependencies and those settings, packageExtensions, explicit tarball/Git/file resolutions and private registries still require adapter work. Yarn Classic has a separate native adapter. This is an incremental implementation, not full pnpm compatibility. Pinned Hono f78a245abc393368583085e19c7f5b28b460bf51 now has the bounded nine-package full product, consumer and two-fresh-product evidence described above using Node 24.22.0/pnpm 12.6.0. The original Vite corpus still stops on hoistPattern, and Docusaurus on nodeLinker; those settings remain unsupported. The qualification record preserves the original admission, acquisition and native-test failures alongside the later Hono successes. This does not qualify other corpus revisions or complete pnpm compatibility. The Windows native probe in tooling/test-node-registry-acquisition.py --manager pnpm --native-cli <pnpm.cjs> exercises real pnpm with a direct and transitive package, repeated fresh captures, offline replay of captured bytes, lifecycle isolation, stale locks, corrupted archives and rejected source hooks. This replaces the former test-pnpm-acquisition.py --pnpm-cli entry point. The native manager probe also covers version/engine rejection, JUnit/LCOV and repeatable packages. These host probes do not prove container isolation. The Linux compiled-CLI Node suite builds the registry fixture, validates reports and dependency records, repeats snapshot packages and exercises failed tests; revision-specific CI results remain in implementation status. Full captured-build execution on Windows/macOS is not established by native adapter tests. Add --patches to the acquisition probe to exercise the native patch example, both native configuration locations, changed-patch rejection before hooks and denied patch paths. The Linux compiled-CLI suite includes that fixture's snapshot artifact, four JUnit cases, coverage, source-patch evidence, repeatability and preflight failure bundle. Consult implementation status for whether that revision has passed isolated acceptance.

On 2026-10-10 the maintainer decided that captured builds honour these pnpm-workspace.yaml settings as declared: catalog and catalogs, overrides, minimumReleaseAge, allowBuilds and trustPolicy. Each one is either fixed by the committed lock or makes acquisition stricter, so honouring it never widens what a build may fetch or run. They need no Oyzu configuration. For example: catalog: is-odd: 3.0.1 is-number: 6.0.0 overrides: is-number: 'catalog:' minimumReleaseAge: 1440 trustPolicy: no-downgrade allowBuilds: esbuild: false Oyzu never re-resolves dependencies for these settings. Before any native invocation, acquisition and execution check them as follows; native pnpm --frozen-lockfile then applies its own checks. Setting What Oyzu checks Effect with the provisioned pnpm 10.11.0 catalog, catalogs Each catalog maps names to specifier strings. catalog is the default catalog, so declaring catalogs.default too fails. Every lock importer dependency whose specifier is catalog: or catalog:<name> must have a lock catalogs entry whose specifier equals the declared one, as native frozen installation requires. Native pnpm compares the same entries and installs the locked versions. overrides The lock's overrides section must equal the declared map after native normalization: $name takes the root package.json specifier and catalog: takes the catalog entry for the override's target package. Overrides come from pnpm-workspace.yaml, or else from package.json pnpm.overrides merged over resolutions; declaring them in both places fails. A difference fails with pnpm lock overrides differ from configuration for <selector>. Native pnpm makes the same comparison (LOCKFILE_CONFIG_MISMATCH). The locked graph already reflects the overrides. minimumReleaseAge A whole number of minutes. Not read: pnpm 10.11.0 predates it (10.16). The frozen lock resolves nothing new, so no release-age decision arises; Oyzu fetches no registry metadata to evaluate ages. trustPolicy no-downgrade or off. Not read: pnpm 10.11.0 predates it (10.21). Releases that have it apply it during resolution, which a frozen install does not perform. allowBuilds Each value is true or false; a placeholder such as set this to true or false fails. When any entry is true, the provisioned pnpm must be 10.26.0 or newer, the first release that reads it; otherwise acquisition fails with pnpm allowBuilds approves <selector>, but provisioned pnpm <version> predates allowBuilds. Denials are honoured: pnpm 10 runs no dependency build scripts unless approved, and acquisition disables lifecycle scripts entirely. An approval needs a newer provisioned pnpm, which then runs only the approved packages' scripts during execution. In package.json, the native pnpm object may hold only patchedDependencies and overrides, because pnpm 10 reads the other settings only from pnpm-workspace.yaml. Any other key in either place fails with pnpm capture does not yet support configuration <key> in <file>. This includes the companion settings minimumReleaseAgeExclude, trustPolicyExclude and trustPolicyIgnoreAfter, the pnpm 10 build settings onlyBuiltDependencies and ignoredBuiltDependencies, and blockExoticSubdeps; admitting them needs a further decision. The message names the key, never its value. After native validation, the oyzu.dev/pnpm.workspacePolicies extension records the declared minimumReleaseAge, trustPolicy and allowBuilds values, which leave no trace in the lock, and the dependency-snapshot digest includes them. Recording a policy states what the project declared, not that the provisioned pnpm enforced it. Catalogs and overrides are bound through the recorded lock digest and the source digest. To recover from a catalog or override failure, regenerate and commit the lock with the native pnpm version the project declares. An undecided key must be removed until a maintainer decision admits it. Newer pnpm releases can evaluate minimumReleaseAge and trustPolicy against publisher metadata during frozen installation; the captured pnpm adapter supplies the full admitted publisher packuments and selected native attestation responses described in acquisition and execution. Native pnpm owns the policy decision; Oyzu does not synthesize acceptance or convert a broker failure into missing metadata. The registered pnpm-policy proof at f2e86155 used real pnpm 12.6.0: its ordinary release-age setting passed, while changing only the age to an intentionally unsatisfiable value produced ERR_PNPM_MINIMUM_RELEASE_AGE_VIOLATION before actions or artifacts. That one measured denial is not qualification of every policy combination or authenticity claim. The settings example declares a catalog dependency, a catalog-referenced override and the three policies; its committed lock uses pnpm 10.11.0's format. Supplemental admission, record and native-acquisition helpers remain available. The later pnpm-policy scenario qualifies the release-age flow on a task-owned copy declaring pnpm 12.6.0, with frozen source/lock records, genuine captured metadata, native positive and negative outcomes and a failed bundle containing no artifacts. Consult implementation status and the qualification record for revision-specific evidence; this does not imply every helper or corpus combination has passed. The corpus projects that use these settings also use undecided keys or .npmrc files and pin pnpm 10.33, 11.9 or 12.4, none of which is provisioned, so they still fail admission.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/publish.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Status: experimental OCI and GitHub Releases publication. The standalone path distributes selected finalized files without a platform account, requires preexisting signed provenance, signs publication intent, and retrieves the registry objects to verify their bytes. Native npm, Python, OCI image archives and mutable OCI tag publication remain outside this slice. Authored code and tests are not a deployed-provider qualification; measured evidence belongs in implementation status.

Run oyzu publish --manifest dist/manifest.json --destination sandbox, or omit --destination to use publish.default. Repeat the option for several named destinations or select a configured set. All selected destinations are required. The complete selection and evidence are checked and all publication signatures are verified before the first distribution. A later destination failure leaves earlier successful publications intact and reports unfinished destinations. Configure through the ordinary configuration cascade, in the project root's oyzu.toml (or oyzu.local.toml) only: a [publish] table in any other folder's file is a CONFIG_SCOPE error naming its file and line (root-only, OEP-0022 OD7): [publish] default = "sandbox" [publish.destinations.sandbox] kind = "oci" # Optional when the build bundle has exactly one artifact: artifacts = ["app/archive"] registry = "https://registry.example.com" repository = "team/artifacts" usernameEnv = "REGISTRY_USERNAME" passwordEnv = "REGISTRY_PASSWORD" [publish.sets] release = ["sandbox"] [publish.requirements.provenance] bundlePath = "evidence/build.sigstore.json" publicKey = "<base64 raw 32-byte Ed25519 public key>" builderId = "https://ci.example.com/builders/release" [publish.requirements.signing] keyEnv = "PUBLICATION_SIGNING_SEED" publicKey = "<base64 raw 32-byte Ed25519 publication public key>" This is an illustrative configuration: supply your own accepted public roots, preexisting signed evidence and independently provisioned credentials. Secret values never belong in the TOML. PUBLICATION_SIGNING_SEED contains a base64 32-byte Ed25519 seed. Its derived public key must match the configured public key. Registry username/password references are optional and must appear together. The same-origin registry bearer challenge flow is supported. HTTPS is required, with plain HTTP permitted only on loopback for local proof registries. kind is optional and defaults to oci. Explicit kind = "oci" uses the same publication path and normalized request as an existing destination that omits it; existing configurations need no migration. GitHub Releases uses the native adapter described below. npm, pypi and unknown kinds fail configuration validation with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE before evidence loading, credentials or network access. Remove the unsupported kind only when the destination is actually an OCI registry; omitting it does not enable a native package protocol. Unknown destination fields also remain errors. publish.destinations, publish.sets and publish.requirements each resolve as one atomic value: a later cascade source replaces that entire map/object. They do not merge nested entries. Profiles and existing mandatory configuration constraints apply. An evidence path is relative to the source declaring the effective requirements. Artifact paths are relative to the build manifest's bundle. Each destination may select distinct exact build output IDs with artifacts. The ID is the target for its primary output, otherwise target/name; it is not the file's basename or the manifest's internal artifact id. For example, artifacts = ["app/archive"] selects target app, output archive, while artifacts = ["app"] selects that target's primary output. Omission is valid only when the manifest contains one artifact. Empty or duplicate selectors fail configuration validation with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. Selectors are checked long before publishing (names that cross files): oyzu config validate, oyzu build --plan and every build refuse a selector or byArtifact key whose build does not exist, or whose @os/arch is not one of the build's declared platforms, with CONFIG_REFERENCE_UNKNOWN, the file, line and column, and the nearest build name; each build's Prepare refuses an output name the builds it prepares do not produce, listing their outputs, before the first action runs. At publication, unknown or ambiguous output IDs or omitted selection in a multi-artifact bundle still fail with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_SELECTION_INVALID before evidence loading, signing or upload. Correct the exact IDs in each selected destination. A bound chart needs its image in the same publication (OEP-0022 OD5). A helm/chart build whose bindings point its values at an image's with.repository is published only when the same oyzu publish invocation also pushes that image to that repository: an OCI destination whose registry host and repository equal with.repository and whose artifacts select the image. Otherwise publication fails with PUBLISH_BINDING_UNPUSHED before evidence, signing or upload, naming the chart destination and the destination to add. Mirrors elsewhere remain allowed. publish.default and each publish.sets entry are checked the same way when the configuration is read (CONFIG_BINDING_UNPUSHED). Explicit entries support several files and different files per destination, without implicit Cartesian fan-out. A selector may name one platform: output-id@os/arch, such as cli/bin-oyzu@linux/x86_64. The platform is the one the builder recorded for the file (its oyzu.dev/artifact-compatibility fact), written in the canonical spelling x86_64/arm64; amd64 and aarch64 are accepted and normalized. An unqualified selector such as cli/bin-oyzu selects every platform of that output in the bundle, each as a separate file with its own evidence, so a single-platform bundle keeps working unchanged. A qualified selector whose platform the bundle lacks fails with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_SELECTION_INVALID and lists the platforms present; so does a qualified selector for an output without a recorded platform, and two artifacts of one output and platform (the same platform in two bundles); toolset verification runs never add an artifact (see verification toolsets). Listing an output both unqualified and qualified, or the same platform twice, fails configuration validation with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. A bundle holds several platforms of one output only when its manifest lists them; today oyzu build writes one platform per bundle, and the release workflow publishes each platform's bundle to the same release. The manifest must record a succeeded build. The selected artifact must be a finalized regular file; its bytes and size must match its SHA-256 identity. Other outputs retain manifest validation but their files are not read or distributed. Publication never builds, scans, repackages, executes project hooks, or creates missing historical evidence. The evidence profile is a Sigstore v0.3 bundle carrying one DSSE application/vnd.in-toto+json envelope, an in-toto Statement v1 and SLSA build provenance v1, verified against an independently configured Ed25519 public root and exact accepted builder identity. This self-managed-key profile makes no transparency-log, trusted-time, keyless identity or SLSA-level claim. For a build with different provenance per output, replace the single [publish.requirements.provenance] fields with an exact output-ID map: [publish.requirements.provenance.byArtifact."app/archive"] bundlePath = "evidence/app.sigstore.json" publicKey = "<accepted base64 raw Ed25519 builder public key>" builderId = "https://ci.example.com/builders/package" [publish.requirements.provenance.byArtifact."cli"] bundlePath = "evidence/cli.sigstore.json" publicKey = "<accepted base64 raw Ed25519 builder public key>" builderId = "https://ci.example.com/builders/cli" These illustrative entries use the same output IDs as destination artifacts; only the selected output's profile is used. Its bundlePath stays relative to the source declaring the effective requirements, and its exact subject, public key and builder are verified before signing or distribution. Unselected bundle files are not read. The existing single form remains supported; it still must cover the selected file. Combining that form with byArtifact, using an empty map/ID, or supplying malformed profile fields fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE. A missing selected entry fails with PUBLISH_EVIDENCE_MISSING; add its exact profile rather than substituting another output's evidence. Mapping several profiles requires exact-subject evidence for each selected file. Signing settings are unchanged. byArtifact keys use the selector grammar above. Provenance is one bundle per file, so an output selected on several platforms needs one bundle per platform: either a qualified key per platform ("cli@linux/arm64"), or one unqualified key whose bundlePath contains the {artifact.platform} placeholder. The placeholder renders as the canonical platform, which is also a relative path: [publish.requirements.provenance.byArtifact."cli"] bundlePath = "evidence/{artifact.platform}/cli.sigstore.json" # evidence/linux/x86_64/cli.sigstore.json publicKey = "<accepted base64 raw Ed25519 builder public key>" builderId = "https://ci.example.com/builders/cli" {artifact.platform} is the only placeholder; any other { or } in bundlePath fails configuration validation. An unqualified key without the placeholder that would cover several selected platforms, or a placeholder on an output without a recorded platform, fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE before evidence loading. Qualified and unqualified keys for the same output together fail configuration validation. A missing bundle for one platform fails the whole plan with PUBLISH_EVIDENCE_MISSING naming the qualified key; nothing is published. Standalone publication rejects --no-upload and the governed --provenance and --policy-evidence options before configuration or network access. It takes existing evidence only from the resolved publish.requirements.provenance.bundlePath setting. The separately signed publication intent binds the exact artifact identity, media type, native coordinate, provenance digest, canonical plan digest, evidence placement and effect targets to the operation publish. It cannot assert a historical build origin or completed upload. Its deterministic contents exclude the invocation identifier, allowing identical republishing to reuse the native OCI coordinate. The signature is verified before distribution. The OCI artifact contains the unchanged file plus the preexisting provenance bundle and publication-intent bundle as retrievable layers. The coordinate is registry/repository@sha256:<manifest-digest>. Tags are unsupported: a mutable tag's preflight read cannot prevent a concurrent writer from replacing it. Matching existing content is already-present; a wrong digest header, manifest, layer or declared artifact identity is a conflict. Success requires independent native GETs of the manifest, config and all layers with digest/size checks. Upload acknowledgements and HEAD responses alone never establish success. Human output identifies the operation, selected artifact output ID, each destination outcome, exact reference and retrieved artifact digest. --json returns a v1alpha1 receipt with operationId, status, planDigest, artifacts and destinations. Each destination has kind and entries with artifact ID, coordinate, reference, payload/native-asset outcomes and evidence storage/verification. Artifact id is the exact selection key: output-id@os/arch for a file with a recorded platform (cli/bin-oyzu@linux/x86_64), the output ID otherwise. Such an artifact also carries compatibility (kind target, native or independent, and the canonical platform), which the signed intent binds. When other outputs exist, unselectedArtifacts lists their keys in sorted order. Human output lists them as unselected and not published. Each destination distinguishes published, already-present, failed and unfinished, and records the manifest/artifact/evidence digests actually verified. A failed or unfinished receipt exits 2; successful publication exits 0. Retry the unchanged plan after resolving the failure; successful destinations are reconciled by their digest. Preflight operation errors such as missing evidence, a wrong subject or a conflicting existing asset exit 1 through the shared CLI error path; JSON diagnostics carry the same exitCode. Invalid command syntax exits 2. Publication needs network access. There is no offline publication success. Artifacts and GET responses are currently held in memory; streaming and larger artifact qualification are deferred. The implementation is shared across host platforms; only explicitly recorded native runs establish platform coverage. The Linux standalone selection proof built two real binaries and verified the selected output, its original provenance and signed intent through a disposable OCI registry. It also verified that the unselected payload was absent, matching repeat/recheck behavior and early refusals. That anonymous loopback run does not qualify authentication or governed execution.

The GitHub adapter uses the same configuration, whole-plan evidence acceptance, signing and restricted worker as OCI. The bounded GitHub.com proof passed on Windows x64, including native downloads, exact evidence/signature checks, matching/conflicting assets and controlled partial recovery. The GitHub qualification record records exact revisions and limits; broader hosts, enterprise routes and deployed platform execution remain unqualified. Replace the destination in the preceding example with this illustrative entry: [publish.destinations.sandbox] kind = "github-release" apiUrl = "https://api.github.com" repository = "your-owner/your-test-repository" tokenEnv = "GITHUB_SANDBOX_TOKEN" artifacts = ["app/archive", "cli"] [publish.destinations.sandbox.evidence] mode = "destination"

A GitHub destination commits no tag (OEP-0022 OD6). oyzu publish attaches to the release at: --tag <tag>, when given: for example a manually started release, or a release whose tags version inference does not read. It applies to every selected GitHub destination of that publication. Otherwise, the exact version tag that version inference recorded for the packages the destination publishes: the exactTags of each published artifact's version decision in its target record's extensions["oyzu.dev/versioning"]. The decision is the one for the package the artifact records (extensions["oyzu.dev/versioning"].package, written by the Rust builder and for Node workspace package archives), else the build's only decision, else the one whose version is the artifact's. A single-package repository tagged v1.4.0 at the built commit publishes to release v1.4.0; the api package of a workspace tagged api/v1.4.2 publishes to api/v1.4.2, even when worker in the same workspace has the same version. The tag is decided before evidence, signing or any network access, and then frozen in each entry's signed coordinate. Without --tag, publishing refuses and sends nothing when: Code When Remedy PUBLISH_TAG_UNKNOWN A published package records no exact version tag: the built commit carries no version tag that applies to it. Tag the built commit with its version (v1.4.0, or <package>/v1.4.0 for one package of a workspace), rebuild and publish again; or pass --tag. PUBLISH_TAG_CONFLICT The destination publishes packages whose exact version tags differ, a package records several tags, or one has a tag and another has none. The message lists each tag with its packages; when the tags all name one version (v1.4.0 and 1.4.0 on one commit) it says so. One release has one tag: give each independently versioned package its own destination, delete a duplicate tag, or pass --tag. PUBLISH_TAG_AMBIGUOUS Several packages of a build share the artifact's version with different tags, and the build did not record which package produced it (another builder, or a build by an older oyzu). Rebuild with this oyzu, or pass --tag. PUBLISH_TAG_COMMIT_MISMATCH The derived tag points at another commit than the one the build recorded: in this checkout (when it has the tag), or on GitHub (resolved through annotated tags, checked before any write). Also when the packages record the tag on different commits. Build the tagged commit and publish again, or pass --tag to publish to that release anyway. PUBLISH_UNSUPPORTED --tag is given but no selected destination is a GitHub release, or the publication is governed. Drop --tag. --tag is not tied to the built commit. When it replaces a different recorded exact version tag, publishing warns with PUBLISH_TAG_OVERRIDDEN and continues. A committed tag in a github-release destination is refused in every command that reads the configuration (oyzu config validate, oyzu build, oyzu publish, ...) with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE: publish.destinations: PUBLISH_DESTINATION_TAG_REMOVED, naming publish.destinations.<name>.tag: delete it. There is no compatibility path. One-time rebuild of oyzu. An oyzu built before this change requires the key, so it cannot read a configuration without it: every command, and an oyzu shim standing in for cargo, fails with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE: invalid value for publish.destinations. In this repository run tooling/bootstrap-oyzu.sh once. It detects an oyzu that cannot read the configuration (oyzu config validate) and builds oyzu and oyzu-shim from source into .oyzu/bin, using that older oyzu's managed Rust with a temporary configuration holding only [tools] and oyzu.lock when cargo does not run on its own; then put .oyzu/bin first on PATH or reinstall from it. Limits. The recorded tags are local observations of the checkout that was built, not authenticated source-control facts; the adapter still requires the tag and its release to exist on GitHub and never creates either. The tag is tied to the recorded built commit, not to a clean tree: a build of the tagged commit with uncommitted changes still records the tag (its source digest and version suffix differ) and is published to it. Provision the tag/release separately and supply a repository-scoped Contents read/write credential by environment reference. The adapter never creates refs or releases, finalizes releases, changes metadata or deletes assets. It freezes the API root, observed repository/release IDs, resolved tag commit, upload route, draft/prerelease state and exact filenames, then refuses changed identity before writes. Reported draft/private visibility does not imply public distribution. Asset names are derived at publication from the file's local name and the compatibility its builder recorded, so one release holds several platforms of one operating system family. Bytes and local dist/ filenames never change: Recorded compatibility Asset name Example target (built for one platform) <stem>-<os>-<arch><ext> oyzu for linux/x86_64 → oyzu-linux-x86_64; oyzu.exe for windows/x86_64 → oyzu-windows-x86_64.exe; app.tar.gz for linux/arm64 → app-linux-arm64.tar.gz independent (no platform restriction) the filename site.tar.gz native (a package whose own name encodes the platform, such as a wheel) the filename pkg-1.0-cp312-cp312-manylinux_2_28_x86_64.whl pending, unknown or missing refused with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_SELECTION_INVALID the builder must record what the file is for The platform uses the canonical spelling (x86_64, arm64, never amd64) and carries an ABI only when it differs from the OS's naming default ABI (GNU on Linux, MSVC on Windows, none elsewhere): a GNU (glibc) Linux build is oyzu-linux-x86_64, a musl one oyzu-linux-x86_64-musl, a GNU Windows build oyzu-windows-x86_64-gnu.exe; sidecars follow the derived name. The resolved ABI is always recorded in the artifact's compatibility, which the plan digest, signed intent and receipt carry. Qualified selectors and output IDs (cli/bin-oyzu@linux/x86_64, cli/bin-oyzu@linux/x86_64/musl) and {artifact.platform} evidence paths use the same published form, so a GNU and a musl build of one output coexist. A selector naming the default ABI (@linux/x86_64/gnu) can never match and is refused with the form to write. Two artifacts whose published platforms are identical are refused with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_SELECTION_INVALID before evidence or network access. {artifact.platform} in an evidence bundlePath renders a non-nesting path form: linux/x86_64 for the default ABI, linux/x86_64-musl otherwise. Each artifact's identity also records the executor that built it (executor: host, cross-toolchain with its target, container) in the plan digest, signed intent and receipt. The record is read strictly from the manifest: an unknown kind or field is PUBLISH_MANIFEST_INVALID, and a cross toolchain whose target triple does not build the artifact's platform is PUBLISH_EXECUTOR_INVALID (also checked again by the publication worker). A release publication refuses a platform-specific (target or native) artifact without an executor record with PUBLISH_EXECUTOR_UNKNOWN; rebuild it with this oyzu. Publication does not otherwise judge the executor: refusing cross-built or native output is a policy constraint planned for build intent slice 7. ext is the longest case-insensitive match from .tar.gz, .tar.xz, .tar.zst, .tgz, .zip, .exe, .msi, .dmg, .pkg, .deb, .rpm, .dll, .so, .dylib, keeping its original case; without a match the platform is appended. A target file is qualified even when the release holds one platform, and names carry no version, so releases/latest/download/oyzu-linux-x86_64 stays stable as long as each release builds Linux with GNU (the native Ubuntu runners do); a musl release build would publish oyzu-linux-x86_64-musl instead. Extending the extension list renames matching assets. Derived names must use ASCII letters, digits, dot, underscore or dash, at most 220 bytes, without a leading dot, and must not end in a reserved evidence suffix. Reserved evidence names follow the derived name: <asset>.provenance.sigstore.json and <asset>.publication.sigstore.json. Two planned names that are equal ignoring ASCII case collide. These checks fail with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_SELECTION_INVALID before evidence loading, signing or network access. The plan freezes each derived name in the coordinate's assetName, which the signed intent binds; the worker re-derives it from the frozen artifact facts and refuses any other name. Earlier assets under unqualified names (oyzu) are left alone; they are never renamed or removed. Before any upload, the complete plan checks planned name collisions, aliases and independently retrieved existing assets. Matching content is reused; different bytes fail with PUBLISH_CONFLICT without overwrite or deletion. Original provenance and verified signed intent are uploaded and retrieved before their corresponding payload. Success requires exact native GET bytes, sizes/digests and evidence claims, rather than an upload acknowledgement. The default and only supported evidence placement for both OCI and GitHub is evidence.mode = "destination". receipt and managed cannot be used to weaken remotely retrievable evidence requirements. This does not imply npm/PyPI support. GitHub.com admits the configured API origin, exact release upload route on uploads.github.com and asset downloads on release-assets.githubusercontent.com. API path prefixes are preserved. Same-origin requests stay within that prefix; upload routes bind the repository and release ID. Redirected asset downloads remain anonymous, including a return to the API origin. Tokens never follow arbitrary redirects. Enterprise endpoints are initially limited to same-origin routes within the API prefix; translating /api/v3 to /api/uploads is unsupported. No enterprise, GitHub Actions artifact or GHCR qualification is implied. An uncertain upload can leave a remote asset. Receipts retain verified completed, failed and unfinished native asset outcomes. Retry the unchanged plan under current authority: matching assets remain, and only missing work is attempted. Changed subjects, coordinates or evidence require a new plan; same-name different evidence is a conflict, not permission to replace it. Release metadata remains mutable by other writers; read-back is an observation, not permanent immutability. The unreleased v1alpha1 worker, receipt and intent evolve in place to file sets, typed coordinates and entries. Old singular-subject worker bodies are rejected; there is no parallel legacy protocol.
