Existing OCI configuration still defaults to oci, but derived wrapper coordinates can differ because intent claims changed. Use a fresh proof namespace when comparing historical OCI qualification. Release asset naming changed every destination kind, not only GitHub: when a file has recorded compatibility, its receipt artifacts[].id, entry artifactId and unselectedArtifacts use the qualified key (cli/bin-oyzu@linux/x86_64), and its artifact identity, plan digest and signed intent include compatibility. An OCI destination still accepts files without recorded compatibility.

A build records the platforms each target declares (platforms: in build.yaml) in its manifest (oyzu.dev/platforms, under the logical target that every platform variant shares). Standalone publication (every destination kind) compares them with the platforms its selected artifacts record, combining the variants of one target: a declared platform of a published target with no selected artifact is a gap, whether it was never built (a build on one runner) or simply not selected (cli/bin-oyzu@linux/x86_64 only). In the release context a gap refuses the whole publication with PUBLISH_PLATFORMS_INCOMPLETE before evidence loading, signing or network access, naming each missing target and platform; in any other context it is a warning and the gaps are recorded without a reason. A target that declares no platforms is not checked. A bundle whose manifest has no platform records (built before they existed) is refused in release with PUBLISH_PLATFORMS_UNKNOWN and warned about elsewhere. A platform the project never ships belongs out of its declared platforms; an allowance is for one publication, not a standing exception. To publish anyway, name each missing platform with a reason: oyzu publish --destination github \ --allow-incomplete darwin/x86_64=no-intel-mac-runner \ --allow-incomplete windows/arm64="arm64 runner not qualified yet" Each value is <platform>=<reason> (aliases accepted; the reason is 1 to 200 printable characters). A malformed value, a repeated platform or a named platform that no published target is missing is CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE, so the record never claims a gap that does not exist. Every gap (target, canonical platform and the allowance's reason, or null for a warned gap) is bound into the plan digest, recorded in every signed publication intent as incompletePlatforms and returned in the receipt. Governed publication does not check completeness yet and refuses the flag (PUBLISH_UNSUPPORTED). Several bundles as one publication. A release built one platform per job publishes every platform at once by repeating --manifest, one bundle each: oyzu publish --destination github \ --manifest bundles/linux-x86_64/dist/manifest.json \ --manifest bundles/darwin-arm64/dist/manifest.json \ --allow-incomplete windows/arm64=runner-unavailable The bundles' artifacts are selected, checked for completeness (their target records combine, so the variants of one target cover its declared platforms together) and published in one plan. Each artifact keeps its own bundle's files and executor record. A bundle given twice is PUBLISH_REQUEST_INVALID; governed publication takes one manifest (PUBLISH_UNSUPPORTED). The release workflow uses this.

When a published build's configuration requires tool lines (verification.<tool>, usually from policy; OEP-0022 OD1 rule 3, R8), standalone publication (every destination kind) checks them against the verification evidence the given bundles recorded, after selection and completeness and before evidence loading, signing or network access. Each line must be outside the build's native range (not applicable), covered by the build's own passing tests on a version in the line, or covered by a passing verification run of the same build that verified its source or the published artifact, from any --manifest bundle. Otherwise the publication fails with PUBLISH_VERIFICATION_MISSING, naming each line, why it is not covered and the commands of the runs the build left to other jobs. The requirement is resolved when publishing, in the build's folder and the publication's context. Pass a dedicated verification job's (oyzu build --verify-only) bundle beside the platform bundles: it is evidence only, and publication takes no artifact from it. The receipt lists how each line was settled under verification. See required tool lines. Governed publication does not check verification evidence yet.

For preparation without publication, see the native Linux candidate review record. Its private covered-source rebuild proof demonstrates changing an embedded shell component and emitting it from a rebuilt CLI, with exact source/material identities and explicit cache/delivery limits. CLI distribution remains subject to the compliance gate; the workflow below does not grant distribution clearance. Publishing a GitHub release triggers .github/workflows/release.yml. It runs one build job per platform runner; each job downloads the newest earlier release's oyzu for its platform (tooling/bootstrap-oyzu.sh --release), builds the release tag with it natively (oyzu build cli), signs provenance with the witness (--artifact cli/bin-oyzu@<platform>; on Linux that is the GNU build, the naming default, while a musl release would need @linux/<arch>/musl) and uploads its bundle (dist/, its evidence and a status) as a workflow artifact. The bundle is staged under the runner's temporary directory, outside the checkout, so checkout's cleaning cannot delete it and the witness's source state stays clean. Build jobs have read-only repository access (contents: read); only the publish job can write the release (contents: write). One publish job then downloads every bundle and runs oyzu publish once in the release context with one --manifest per built platform, so the declared platform set is complete; the completeness check (incomplete platform sets) refuses a release that leaves a declared platform out. The publish job chooses its oyzu by the Linux x86_64 bundle's status: the executable this run built when that platform was built, otherwise (a re-run where it was already published) the release's own oyzu-linux-x86_64 through the bootstrap. Before publishing it checks that this oyzu publish --help offers --allow-incomplete, repeatable --manifest and --tag, and fails with that reason if not. It publishes to the committed [publish.destinations.github] with --tag "$TAG", the release that started the run, and writes no oyzu.local.toml. The release tags so far (v0.0.2) are repository-wide: version inference reads only oyzu/v<version> tags for the oyzu package of this multi-package Cargo workspace, and a tag naming a version other than Cargo.toml's 0.1.0 would stop the build with version-conflict, so the bundles record no exact version tag to derive the release from. The maintainer decided on 2026-10-20 that releases are tagged oyzu/vX.Y.Z on a commit whose Cargo.toml already says X.Y.Z (decision); a follow-up switches the workflow to tag-triggered releases without --tag. The committed destination names oyzuai/oyzu and oyzu has no per-run repository override, so a run in a fork (another GITHUB_REPOSITORY) stops before publishing: a fork edits repository first. tooling/test-release-workflow.py (run in CI) keeps the workflow, oyzu.toml and, with --cli <oyzu>, the CLI's publish flags in agreement. Each of the six declared platforms has a GitHub-hosted runner that builds it natively (ubuntu-24.04, ubuntu-24.04-arm, macos-15-intel, macos-15, windows-2025, windows-11-arm); the repository variable OYZU_LINUX_RUNNER (a JSON runs-on value) moves Linux x86_64 and the publish job to another runner. Paid hosted minutes are used for releases only; pull request and push checks stay on the self-hosted runner. After publishing, the publish job attaches the configuration schemas build.yaml.schema.json and oyzu.toml.schema.json, printed by the same oyzu with oyzu config schema, with gh release upload --clobber. They are generated documents rather than build artifacts, so they carry no provenance sidecars, and a re-run replaces them with identical files. Editors reach them through https://github.com/oyzuai/oyzu/releases/latest/download/<asset> (editor schemas), so that URL follows the release GitHub marks as latest. A job whose platform's payload and both sidecars are already on the release skips its build, and the publish job names that platform with --allow-incomplete <platform>=already-published-on-<tag>. A platform deliberately not built in a release is named in the workflow's incomplete input (<platform>=<reason>, separated by ; or new lines, for example gh workflow run release.yml -f tag=<tag> -f incomplete="windows/arm64=runner unavailable"): its job is skipped and the reason goes to --allow-incomplete; nothing is allowed by default. Every build job validates the whole input before doing anything else: each entry needs a = and a non-empty reason, and its platform must be one of the six canonical names (linux/amd64 and other aliases are refused). linux/x86_64 cannot be named, because the publish job runs that platform's oyzu. If any build job fails, nothing is published; re-run the failed jobs (GitHub keeps the successful jobs' bundles for the run, and a re-run job replaces its own bundle). Bundles are kept for 7 days. A re-run after that finds no bundle for the expired platforms and stops with that reason; start the workflow again (gh workflow run release.yml -f tag=<tag>), which skips the platforms already on the release. When no earlier release has the qualified executable for the runner's platform, the workflow builds oyzu from the tag's source instead; that happens once per platform. When the earlier release's oyzu predates platform records (it has no publish --allow-incomplete), each build job also builds oyzu from the tag's source, because the publish job needs every bundle's platform and executor records: this is the case on the first release after build intent slice 6. The same replacement happens when the earlier release's oyzu has no publish --tag: such an oyzu requires a committed release tag, so it cannot read this oyzu.toml; tooling/bootstrap-oyzu.sh detects that and builds oyzu from the tag's source (the first release after OEP-0022 D7). A failed bootstrap stops the job; no step ignores it. The bootstrap maps the host to its asset and verifies the digest GitHub reports before installing it as .oyzu/bin/oyzu (or oyzu.exe) with mode 755, since raw downloads lose the executable bit: Host Asset Linux x86_64 / aarch64 oyzu-linux-x86_64 / oyzu-linux-arm64 macOS x86_64 / arm64 oyzu-darwin-x86_64 / oyzu-darwin-arm64; under Rosetta (sysctl.proc_translated is 1) it takes arm64 Windows x86_64 / ARM64 (MSYS/MINGW) oyzu-windows-x86_64.exe / oyzu-windows-arm64.exe, read from PROCESSOR_ARCHITEW6432/PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE because uname -m reports x86_64 under emulation tooling/bootstrap-oyzu.sh --print-asset prints the name for the current host. It does not look up the unqualified oyzu/oyzu.exe names of earlier interim releases; without a qualified asset it builds from source. Sidecar verification in the bootstrap is later work. Create and publish the release (and its tag) first: the adapter attaches assets to an existing release found by tag, and GitHub's tag lookup does not return a draft, so a draft fails with PUBLISH_GITHUB_API: inspection returned HTTP 404. A prerelease on a private repository is visible only to collaborators and its assets need a token to download. Re-run a release with gh workflow run release.yml -f tag=<tag>. Until a protected builder exists, the evidence comes from a local test-builder witness, tooling/release-witness.mjs. It signs SLSA provenance for the built outputs with a self-managed Ed25519 key. It is not a protected build, a trusted timestamp or a SLSA level claim. The accepted public keys are in oyzu.toml; the seeds are the repository secrets OYZU_RELEASE_BUILDER_SEED and OYZU_RELEASE_PUBLISHER_SEED in CI, or files in a directory outside the checkout: node tooling/release-witness.mjs keys --key-dir <dir outside the checkout> # once gh secret set OYZU_RELEASE_BUILDER_SEED < <dir>/builder.seed gh secret set OYZU_RELEASE_PUBLISHER_SEED < <dir>/publisher.seed To release by hand, build, then sign with --started/--finished timestamps taken around the build (without them the witness falls back to approximate dist/ file times), then publish: oyzu build cli node tooling/release-witness.mjs sign --key-dir <dir> --artifact cli/bin-oyzu --artifact cli/bin-oyzu-shim node tooling/release-witness.mjs publish --key-dir <dir> --arg --manifest --arg dist/manifest.json --arg --destination --arg github --arg --tag --arg <tag> The witness takes the same selectors as oyzu publish (cli/bin-oyzu signs every platform of that output in the manifest, cli/bin-oyzu@linux/x86_64 exactly one) and writes each bundle to .oyzu/release-evidence/<os>/<arch>/, the path the {artifact.platform} placeholder in oyzu.toml renders. Signing the same bundle again yields byte-identical evidence: the invocation ID derives from the manifest and artifact digests, and the build times and source state are recorded once per manifest in .oyzu/release-evidence/witness-run.json and reused. A retried publish over the same bundle therefore reuses the sidecars already uploaded. Limitations: Optimized executables are not yet observed in a release run. The workflow's build step sets OYZU_CONTEXT=release (a release event's tag already implies it; a workflow_dispatch re-run runs on a branch ref), and since build intent slice 5 a release build is optimized (cargo build --release). No release has run with this yet; earlier published executables were development builds and report debug in --version. Optimized is not a publication-eligibility claim. Hosted platforms are not yet qualified. Linux arm64, macOS and Windows jobs are configured for GitHub-hosted runners but have not completed a release run; until one does, treat those platforms as unqualified. Linux x86_64 has run on the self-hosted runner. A partial platform conflicts on rebuild. A platform is skipped only when its payload and both sidecars are present. If an earlier attempt uploaded part of a platform, the re-run rebuilds different payload bytes under the same asset name, which is PUBLISH_CONFLICT; publish the same bundle again by hand, or delete the partial assets before re-running. Publishing a combined bundle handed off from build jobs is later work (build intent slice 6).

With explicit --server, --account, --project (or the corresponding environment selection), the CLI stages/registers the build, then submits a durable publication operation. Pass --provenance FILE with the preexisting Sigstore bundle. The platform selects requirements and destinations centrally; caller-selected roots or signing credentials cannot grant governed authority. --destination cannot be combined with governed routing. The first slice requires one staged file artifact; --no-upload cannot satisfy this path. Optionally pass --policy-evidence FILE with an existing signed policy report bundle when the central policy requires one. The CLI reads UTF-8 JSON and sends the original string unchanged as policyEvidence.bundle; omitting the flag omits that optional object. It does not verify the report signature, evaluate customer facts, select trusted roots, or treat report contents as approval. Central admission determines accepted producer, predicate, root and account/subject scope. A report that observes an issue is open is an observation, not an approval claim. The operation POST is /publish/v1/accounts/{account}/projects/{project}/operations, carrying schemaVersion, registrationBuild, exact staged artifact identity/reference, and provenance.bundle. The CLI follows GET /operations/{operationId}. Build registration or staging success alone is never presented as completed distribution. The durable operation remains inspectable when following it times out; inspect that operation before submitting another request. Server URL path prefixes are preserved for staging, registration, operation submission and status following, with or without a trailing slash. The complete governed flow and publisher isolation qualification are deferred by the maintainer's 2026-10-17 implementation-merge decision and tracked in issue #541. The standalone proof and component checks do not establish those governed guarantees in a live deployment. Protected workers invoke the same built-in implementation through the hidden __publication-worker --request FILE bridge. This is an internal fixed contract, not a plugin ABI. The request freezes the exact file set, entries, native coordinates, evidence, signing references and operation/executor authority. Before signing and each registry mutation, the worker requests current central authorization bound to the exact operation, executor, subject, destination, provenance and signing intent. Mutation requests have no automatic transport replay. Roots and secrets are provisioned by the protected host, never returned to the caller. The following sections document the existing registration/staging transport used before that operation, including its CI credential discovery.

In CI, governed oyzu publish first reads the completed build manifest (dist/manifest.json), stages its file artifact and registers its outputs and component versions. This registration uses the same output contract as platform build completion. The command then requests publication with the preexisting provenance and follows the durable operation. Its final result reports that operation's decisions, execution and verified receipts. Registration alone does not authorize external distribution. Publishing is optional. oyzu build and everything else stay local and work without an account.

A finished oyzu build whose manifest records status: succeeded. A failed, cancelled or interrupted build is refused before anything is sent (PUBLISH_BUILD_NOT_SUCCEEDED). The platform URL, account and project, as flags or environment variables. A credential the project accepts: the pipeline's OIDC token for a trusted CI connector, or a publish token issued on the project's CI connector. See credentials. Registration routing uses flags/environment; commit, repository and ref come from the CI system's environment or flags. Standalone publication uses the cascade above.

oyzu build oyzu publish --server https://oyzu.example.com --account acme --project web --provenance evidence/build.sigstore.json Flag Environment Default Meaning --server URL OYZU_URL required The platform's URL. Must be https, except http://localhost, http://127.0.0.1 or http://[::1] for a local devstack, so a token never crosses a network unencrypted (PUBLISH_INSECURE_SERVER). --account ID OYZU_ACCOUNT required The account to publish to. --project ID OYZU_PROJECT required The project to publish to. --manifest FILE dist/manifest.json The build manifest, relative to the directory (-C). Repeat it to publish several bundles (one per platform) as one standalone publication; see incomplete platform sets. --provenance FILE required for governed publication Original preexisting signed provenance bundle, read as UTF-8 without rewriting its bytes. --policy-evidence FILE omitted Optional original signed policy report bundle for central admission; governed only. --version VERSION none The build's version, when the pipeline names one. --commit SHA from CI The built commit. --repository OWNER/NAME from CI The repository the build came from. --audience AUDIENCE OYZU_AUDIENCE oyzu The audience requested for OIDC tokens the CLI asks a CI system for. --token-env NAME none Read the OIDC token from this environment variable instead of discovering one. --no-upload OYZU_PUBLISH_UPLOAD=0 upload Historical registration-only transport control. Governed publication requires staging and rejects an artifact without an immutable staged reference. A flag wins over its environment variable. Account and project identifiers follow the platform rule: lowercase letters, digits and inner hyphens, 1 to 63 characters, starting and ending with a letter or digit. The global --json flag prints the final operation record with registrationBuild. If following the operation times out, the CLI reports status: "unfinished" and a recovery message; the platform operation remains inspectable. Transport errors follow the usual {"error": …, "exitCode": 2} shape.

jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-24.04 permissions: contents: read id-token: write # lets oyzu publish request an OIDC token steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - run: oyzu build - run: oyzu publish --server https://oyzu.example.com --account acme --project web --provenance evidence/build.sigstore.json

oyzu publish uses the first credential it finds, in this order: --token-env NAME, else OYZU_ID_TOKEN: an OIDC token the pipeline already holds. A --token-env variable that is unset or empty is an error, not a fall-through. GitHub Actions: when ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL and ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN are set (the job has permissions: id-token: write), the CLI requests a token for the audience (GET $ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL&audience=oyzu, authorized by the request token) and uses the answer's value. Bitbucket Pipelines: BITBUCKET_STEP_OIDC_TOKEN (a step with oidc: true); CircleCI: CIRCLE_OIDC_TOKEN_V2, then CIRCLE_OIDC_TOKEN. Buildkite: when BUILDKITE is set and buildkite-agent is on PATH, buildkite-agent oidc request-token --audience oyzu. OYZU_PUBLISH_TOKEN: a scoped, revocable publish token (oyzp_…) issued on the project's CI connector, for CI tools without OIDC. A source that is present but fails (GitHub refuses the token request, the Buildkite agent fails) stops the command (PUBLISH_CREDENTIAL_UNAVAILABLE) instead of falling through to another credential. With none found the command fails with PUBLISH_NO_CREDENTIAL and, in GitHub Actions, names the missing id-token permission.

The platform accepts a CI OIDC token once for each privileged publish operation (the build registration, the upload grant, and publication create or retry). A token sent again for the same operation is refused with HTTP 401. GitHub Actions and Buildkite can issue tokens on request, so Oyzu requests a new token for every request attempt, including each retry after a connection failure or a 502, 503 or 504, (reads, such as polling a publication operation, do not consume a token and mint none). Discovery requests one first so a missing permission or a failing agent stops the command before anything is sent. A failure to issue a later token stops the command with PUBLISH_CREDENTIAL_UNAVAILABLE. A fixed token (--token-env, OYZU_ID_TOKEN, Bitbucket, CircleCI, OYZU_PUBLISH_TOKEN) is sent as it is on every attempt. If a retry is refused with a 401 (or the platform's reason is replayed), the command fails with PUBLISH_CREDENTIAL_REPLAYED: a reused token is the likely cause and the earlier attempt may already have taken effect, so check the platform before publishing again, with a new token. The Buildkite helper has a fixed 30-second deadline, including output capture. If it stalls, Oyzu attempts to kill the local helper and returns PUBLISH_CREDENTIAL_UNAVAILABLE with external command deadline exceeded; it does not wait indefinitely for a descendant holding an output pipe open or fall back to the publish token. Token output stays in memory and is not included in timeout diagnostics. There is no timeout setting or automatic helper retry. Check the Buildkite agent and its OIDC service/policy, then rerun oyzu publish, or explicitly select an already issued credential with --token-env. An absent agent still allows the normal discovery fallback. Killing the local helper does not guarantee remote work or descendants stopped, and the helper deadline does not bound the complete HTTP publication flow. Offline publication is unavailable. Deadline-runner regressions are authored but unexecuted on this desktop; see verification status. How each CI system provides its token: CI system How GitHub Actions permissions: id-token: write on the job; discovered automatically. GitLab CI/CD id_tokens: on the job, for example OYZU_ID_TOKEN: {aud: oyzu}; read from OYZU_ID_TOKEN (or name another variable with --token-env). Bitbucket Pipelines oidc: true on the step; BITBUCKET_STEP_OIDC_TOKEN is discovered. Its audience is fixed by Bitbucket; the project's trust must accept it. CircleCI CIRCLE_OIDC_TOKEN_V2 / CIRCLE_OIDC_TOKEN are discovered. Their audience is the CircleCI organization; for an oyzu audience, mint one with circleci run oidc get --claims '{"aud":"oyzu"}' into OYZU_ID_TOKEN. Buildkite Discovered through buildkite-agent oidc request-token; the pipeline's OIDC policy must allow it. Jenkins with the OIDC provider plugin Bind the plugin's credential to a variable and pass --token-env (or bind it as OYZU_ID_TOKEN). Jenkins without OIDC, TeamCity OYZU_PUBLISH_TOKEN from a credentials store / secure parameter. Which tokens a project accepts is the platform's decision (the trusts on the project's CI connector), not the CLI's. The token is sent only in the Authorization header of the publish request. It is never printed, logged or written to disk; progress names only where it came from (for example "a GitHub Actions OIDC token").

Before the build is POSTed, every artifact without an oci_digest (anything but an OCI image or index) is uploaded to the platform's registry as an OCI artifact, unless --no-upload or OYZU_PUBLISH_UPLOAD=0 is given. Images and indexes are not uploaded by the CLI; they keep their oci_digest. Check the files. Only an artifact whose path is a regular file in the bundle, of the recorded size and SHA-256 digest, is uploaded. A directory artifact is skipped with one warning and published without an oci_ref. A missing file or one whose bytes changed since oyzu build stops the publish with PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_CHANGED before any credential is requested. With no artifact left to upload, steps 2 to 4 are skipped. Upload grant. POST {server}/publish/v1/accounts/{account}/projects/{project}/builds/uploads with the same credential and headers as the publish: {"artifacts": [{"path": "artifacts/api/default/binary/server", "media_type": "application/octet-stream", "digest": "sha256:…", "size": 123}]} path is the artifact's path in the bundle as the manifest lists it (1 to 1000 entries, only the artifacts being uploaded). The platform answers 200: {"registry": "https://registry.example", "repository": "acme/web/artifacts", "token": "<jwt>", "expires_at": "2026-10-11T12:00:00Z"} 404 means the platform has no artifact storage: one warning is printed and the build is published as without upload, with no oci_ref. 401, 403 and 422 fail the publish with the platform's problem, as for the publish itself; 502, 503 and 504 are retried the same way. Registry sign-in. The standard registry token flow: GET {registry}/v2/ answers 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="…",service="…"; the CLI calls the realm with ?service=<service>&scope=repository:<repository>:pull,push and HTTP Basic authentication (user oyzu, password the grant's token) and uses the answer's token (or access_token) as the bearer. The realm must be on the registry's own origin (scheme, host and port), so the grant token never goes elsewhere. The registry must be https, except plain http on loopback. Push. The empty config blob {} once (application/vnd.oci.empty.v1+json, sha256:44136fa355b3678a1146ad16f7e8649e94fb4fc21fe77e8310c060f61caaff8a, size 2), then for each artifact: its file's bytes, uncompressed, as one blob whose digest is the artifact's digest, after HEAD /v2/<repository>/blobs/<digest>; a 200 skips the upload; this manifest, serialized once in exactly this form and put to /v2/<repository>/manifests/sha256:<SHA-256 of those bytes> with Content-Type: application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json (never a tag): {"schemaVersion":2,"mediaType":"application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json","artifactType":"<media_type>","config":{"mediaType":"application/vnd.oci.empty.v1+json","digest":"sha256:44136fa355b3678a1146ad16f7e8649e94fb4fc21fe77e8310c060f61caaff8a","size":2},"layers":[{"mediaType":"<media_type>","digest":"<digest>","size":<size>,"annotations":{"org.opencontainers.image.title":"<file name>"}}],"annotations":{"dev.oyzu.output":"<output name>"}} <output name> is the target for its primary artifact and target/name otherwise, as components name build outputs. Registry requests that fail with a server error or in transport are retried up to three attempts; any other refusal fails the publish with PUBLISH_UPLOAD_FAILED and nothing is published. Each uploaded artifact's output then carries "oci_ref": "<registry host[:port]>/<repository>@sha256:<manifest digest>" (no scheme).

POST {server}/publish/v1/accounts/{account}/projects/{project}/builds with Authorization: Bearer <credential>, Content-Type: application/json and Accept: application/json: { "version": "1.4.2", "commit": "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567", "repository": "acme/web", "ref": "refs/heads/main", "run_url": "https://github.com/acme/web/actions/runs/42", "outputs": [ {"path": "dist/manifest.json", "kind": "manifest", "media_type": "application/vnd.oyzu.build-manifest.v1alpha1+json", "digest": "sha256:…", "size": 2101}, {"path": "dist/image-index/any/image.oci.tar", "kind": "artifact", "media_type": "application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json", "digest": "sha256:…", "size": 123, "target": "image-index", "name": "primary", "version": "0.1.0-dev.g111111111111", "oci_digest": "sha256:…"}, {"path": "dist/api/linux/x86_64/server", "kind": "artifact", "media_type": "application/octet-stream", "digest": "sha256:…", "size": 123, "target": "api", "name": "binary", "version": "0.1.0-dev.g111111111111", "oci_ref": "registry.example/acme/web/artifacts@sha256:…"} ] } Optional fields are omitted when unknown. outputs matches a platform runner's FinishOutput (runner contract): one manifest output for the manifest file itself: its media type, the SHA-256 of its bytes and its size; one artifact output per artifact the manifest lists, with the manifest's path, mediaType, digest, size, target, name and version, plus oci_digest (the manifest's ociDigest, the digest a registry addresses it by) for oci-image and oci-index artifacts only, or oci_ref for an artifact the CLI uploaded. oci_ref is the one field beyond the runner's FinishOutput. Directory artifacts carry their tree digest. Paths are relative to the checkout root, as a runner reports them: the manifest's directory relative to -C (dist/ by default) followed by the artifact's bundle path. A --manifest outside the directory reports paths relative to its own bundle. Artifact digests are the ones oyzu build recorded; files that are uploaded are checked against them, and oyzu inspect checks the whole bundle. The CLI checks the platform's limits before sending (PUBLISH_MANIFEST_INVALID): at most 1000 outputs, paths up to 1024 bytes, media types 255, targets 256, names 64 and versions 255; every artifact has a target, name and version, a sha256 digest, a safe relative path and, if it is an OCI image or index, a sha256 ociDigest. Commit, repository, ref and run link come from the first CI system that announces itself: CI system commit repository ref run_url GitHub Actions GITHUB_SHA GITHUB_REPOSITORY GITHUB_REF $GITHUB_SERVER_URL/$GITHUB_REPOSITORY/actions/runs/$GITHUB_RUN_ID GitLab CI_COMMIT_SHA CI_PROJECT_PATH refs/tags/$CI_COMMIT_TAG or refs/heads/$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH CI_PIPELINE_URL CircleCI CIRCLE_SHA1 CIRCLE_PROJECT_USERNAME/CIRCLE_PROJECT_REPONAME CIRCLE_TAG / CIRCLE_BRANCH CIRCLE_BUILD_URL Buildkite BUILDKITE_COMMIT (not HEAD) from BUILDKITE_REPO BUILDKITE_TAG / BUILDKITE_BRANCH BUILDKITE_BUILD_URL Bitbucket BITBUCKET_COMMIT BITBUCKET_REPO_FULL_NAME BITBUCKET_TAG / BITBUCKET_BRANCH https://bitbucket.org/<repo>/pipelines/results/$BITBUCKET_BUILD_NUMBER Jenkins GIT_COMMIT from GIT_URL GIT_BRANCH without origin/ BUILD_URL TeamCity BUILD_VCS_NUMBER (use --repository) none none

The platform answers 200 with the build, its eligibility (candidate or snapshot), one entry per component and the outputs that belong to no component: Build registered · 01jab7v3k9m2q8r4t6w0y1z5c7 (candidate) ✓ published api 1.4.2 (candidate) = already published web 2.0.0 ! skipped worker 0.3.0: the build did not publish [worker/config] Outputs in no component (never shipped) web/build-metadata This registration response describes recorded components and does not establish external distribution. The public command proceeds to the durable publication operation; its final receipt and independently verified outcome control success. The displayed final result is the operation result described above. A successful HTTP status alone is insufficient: the response must name the build, use candidate or snapshot eligibility, and provide components and unassigned outputs arrays. Every component names its component and version, uses published, already-published or skipped, and includes a reason when skipped. Malformed responses fail with PUBLISH_RESPONSE_INVALID in human and JSON modes. The server may already have published the build; inspect its state and check platform/client compatibility. Retrying the same build is safe.

Every failure exits 2 and prints one diagnostic; nothing is retried that the platform refused. Code Meaning PUBLISH_NOT_CONFIGURED A server, account or project is missing or malformed. PUBLISH_INSECURE_SERVER The server uses plain http and is not localhost. PUBLISH_MANIFEST_MISSING / PUBLISH_MANIFEST_INVALID No manifest at the path, or it breaks a rule above. Nothing is sent and no token is requested. PUBLISH_BUILD_NOT_SUCCEEDED The manifest records a build that did not succeed. PUBLISH_ARTIFACT_CHANGED An artifact to upload is missing, not a regular file, or no longer has its recorded size or digest. Nothing is sent; build again. PUBLISH_UPLOAD_FAILED The registry refused or failed a sign-in, blob or manifest request (after retries for server errors). Nothing is published. PUBLISH_RESPONSE_INVALID The platform's upload grant or answer is malformed, or names a registry that is not https (plain http only on loopback). PUBLISH_NO_CREDENTIAL / PUBLISH_CREDENTIAL_UNAVAILABLE No credential found, or a CI system did not issue one. PUBLISH_CREDENTIAL_REPLAYED (401) The platform refused a fixed CI token on a retry (any 401), or said it was reused (reason replayed). After a retry, the earlier attempt may already have taken effect: check the platform, then publish again with a new token. Only fixed tokens can be reused; GitHub Actions and Buildkite send a new token per attempt. PUBLISH_UNAUTHENTICATED (401) The platform did not accept the credential: expired, wrong audience or revoked. 403 (PUBLISH_<code>) "Oyzu refused this pipeline's token": the token is valid, but no trust on the project's CI connector accepts this pipeline (repository, branch or workflow). other PUBLISH_<code> The platform's RFC 9457 problem: its detail, each errors[] entry as field: message, and the platform request id. PUBLISH_UNREACHABLE The platform could not be reached after retries. Connection failures and 502, 503 and 504 answers are retried up to five attempts with backoff, honoring Retry-After (at most 30 seconds). Each retry carries its own token where the credential source can issue one (see One token per request attempt).

Not qualified against a deployed platform; the endpoint is being built. The first explicit publication slice accepts one finalized file. OCI images, indexes and directory publication require later native destination support. Each uploaded file is read into memory for its push; very large files need that much memory. Streaming is a later refinement. A registry whose token endpoint (realm) is on another origin is refused. Commit, repository and ref are what the CI system says; the platform decides what it trusts from the token's claims. Windows and macOS runners use the same code; the integration test runs on Linux CI.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/python-applications.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. An explicit python/app target with static PEP 621 metadata and one console script produces a runnable, versioned .pyz application alongside the native wheel and source distribution. The application contains the built wheel's files and captured runtime dependencies. It does not copy arbitrary checkout files or rebuild the project for packaging. builds: api: uses: python/app The native pyproject.toml supplies application intent: [project] name = "example-api" version = "0.1.0" dependencies = [] [project.scripts] example-api = "api:main" [build-system] requires = ["setuptools==80.9.0"] build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta" [tool.setuptools] packages = ["api"] api.main is an ordinary console callable. Oyzu does not invent a server, port, health check or supervisor. Multiple scripts or missing scripts fail planning with a focused diagnostic; an entrypoint-selection override remains pending. Auto-detected python/package projects retain package semantics and may contain multiple console scripts.

oyzu run list oyzu build oyzu inspect dist python <application-artifact-path-from-manifest> Read the application artifact's path from dist/manifest.json. Its filename is <target>-<snapshot-version>.pyz, using the package's PEP 440 snapshot version, such as 0.1.0.dev0+g0123456789ab. wheel and sdist remain separate artifacts. Existing consumers must select artifacts by identity rather than assuming an application emits exactly two files. Version inference combines native metadata with applicable exact tags, nearest first-parent release tags and Conventional Commits. A v1.4.2 baseline plus a feature change can produce 1.5.0.dev0+g... across all three artifacts without editing the checkout. The plan and manifest retain the decision. Requirements-only applications use SemVer coordinates instead of inventing Python distribution metadata. Neither a tag nor a local build grants release authority. The pipeline prepares captured dependencies, invokes the selected native backend once, assembles the application, tests sources extracted from that archive, and runs lint/read-only formatting gates. Shared collection retains JUnit and Cobertura in dist/ with paths, digests and summaries in the manifest. See Python testing for collection, overrides, empty-suite behavior and coverage thresholds. Direct development tasks retain native commands; they do not assemble application archives or collect build evidence automatically. Assembly checks the native wheel's identity and selected console entrypoint against the plan. Native pip installs only captured runtime wheels into the payload offline, without dependency resolution; build/test tools remain outside the payload. Installer-local provenance and interpreter-specific launchers are removed. A generated launcher uses native distribution entrypoint metadata. The internal oyzu-application.json records source identity, version, project source files, runtime package identities, selected entrypoint and original wheel digest. Archive entries have sorted paths and normalized ZIP metadata. Shared archive validation rejects unsafe paths, case collisions, symlinks and oversized payloads. Packaging verifies the archive's tested digest and unchanged native wheel/sdist inputs. Tests, missing reports, quality failures and changed artifacts block successful collection. Inspect retained logs/reports in dist/ to correct the failing step. These checks bind the normal lifecycle; they do not confer production trust or protect against malicious tests rewriting private build state.

For the native pip wheel path, Oyzu can resolve and install CPython from pyproject.toml requirements or .python-version. That path produces a wheel, without assembling the runnable .pyz described here. Requirements-only, uv, Poetry and legacy projects retain the captured path. See fresh-checkout qualification for measured native wheel results and host limits. Captured application builds use provisioned Linux container images through Docker, as described in the CLI overview, with Python 3.12 and pip, uv or Poetry backend integration. The image supplies the interpreter and native tools; installing CPython on the host does not replace it. Preparation uses existing broker routes; assembly and tests use captured inputs with networking disabled. Full private registry support remains pending. Correct missing inputs during preparation rather than adding a network fallback to the build. The archive requires pure Python wheels and zip-compatible code/data. Native extensions, .pth startup behavior and libraries needing real filesystem resources are not generally ZIP-compatible. Native-wheel and forbidden-payload checks fail explicitly; native tests must establish the application's resource-loading behavior. Python itself is not bundled: running the artifact requires a compatible interpreter. Legacy setup.py applications, dynamic console metadata, editable installs, general entrypoint overrides and native application layouts remain unfinished. Package builders retain native-extension support where implemented. Requirements-only applications continue using conventional app.py or __main__.py without invented distribution metadata and retain their existing 0.0.0-dev.g<source> snapshot versions. Both application paths share archive writing, archive-source tests and packaging checks. No Oyzu test/output configuration is required. Optional Dockerfile-free Python container assembly now consumes this exact tested archive through a captured CPython 3.12 profile. Its new native acceptance case remains pending CI. Runtime overrides, application-container matrices, image startup smoke tests and full profile/policy qualification remain unfinished.

python tooling/test-python-distribution-app.py --wheels <prepared-native-wheel-directory> python tooling/test-python-application.py --wheels <prepared-native-wheel-directory> Supply wheels for the host interpreter: packaging 24.2, build 1.2.2.post1, setuptools 80.9.0, wheel 0.45.1, pytest 8.3.5, pytest-cov 6.0.0, Ruff 0.11.13 and dependencies. The probes do not download them. The distribution probe builds a real setuptools wheel, executes the archive without site packages, replaces checkout code before testing, checks runtime-only inclusion and repeated artifact identity, and rejects entrypoint mismatch and post-test changes. Windows native verification does not establish Linux isolation. CI separately exercises EX-012 through the compiled CLI, quality failures, root/configured suites, reports and repeatability. Consult implementation status for revision-specific results.

Python lifecycle orchestration, broker transport, archive assembly and report sequencing now run in compiled Rust. Embedded Python bindings are restricted to packaging/marker, Poetry export, setuptools, pytest/coverage and quality-tool APIs. They run in the selected Python toolchain and are not project-supplied helpers. Ruff remains a native executable. The CLI itself requires no Python interpreter. Captured builds require images containing the matching compiled worker. The Python, legacy, uv and Poetry toolchain images below require explicit provisioning; they are outside the current published toolchain image set. The shared builder-worker image can be acquired from that published set; the first command shows how to build it locally instead: docker build -f tooling/images/builder-worker.Dockerfile -t oyzu-toolchain/builder-worker:v1 . docker build -f tooling/images/python.Dockerfile -t oyzu-toolchain/python:3.12 tooling/images docker build -f tooling/images/python.Dockerfile --build-arg PYTHON_BASE=python:3.12-bookworm -t oyzu-toolchain/python-legacy:3.12 tooling/images docker build -f tooling/images/python.Dockerfile --build-arg PYTHON_BASE=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.12.21-python3.12-trixie-slim -t oyzu-toolchain/uv:0.12.21-python3.12 tooling/images docker build -f tooling/images/python-poetry.Dockerfile -t oyzu-toolchain/poetry:2.5.1-python3.12 tooling/images Custom build images must provide /usr/local/libexec/oyzu/oyzu as well as their native tools. Older build images must be rebuilt. The delivered application's runtime container still uses plain python:3.12-slim-bookworm; it does not need the Oyzu worker. This migration does not expand supported Python versions, platform qualification, package sources or provisioning policy.
See native local builds for the bounded host profiles, prerequisites, artifact differences and multi-target evidence behavior. This is separate from the isolated packaging contracts above.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/python-containers.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The captured build path accepts the python/app builder option with.container: true. It packages the already-tested pure-Python application archive into an OCI image without a source Dockerfile or second application build. Linux CI has verified the default and override profiles, repeated identities and failure gates at revision 69b4d04, after correcting an initial report-schema defect. It does not yet provide application startup smoke tests, additional language runtime profiles or full EX-012 acceptance. builds: api: uses: python/app with: container: true with.container is a python/app option: the builder owns and validates it (OEP-0022 M2). oyzu config validate and every command that reads the build inventory check it. Another builder's with.container, including python/library, is refused, and so is the earlier top-level container: build field, with a message naming with.container. Run oyzu run list, oyzu build and oyzu inspect dist as usual. Native application build/test/lint/read-only-format tasks remain visible and retain their existing overrides and hooks. Image build, assertion and package actions appear under a derived api-container target in the plan and manifest. These derived actions are internal build actions; direct oyzu run invocation and overrides/hooks for them are not implemented. A source target colliding with the derived name fails rather than being overwritten.

Provide the native Python toolchain/dependencies required by Python applications, plus python:3.12-slim-bookworm and oyzu-toolchain/docker:buildkit0.25.0 in the local Docker image store. The latter comes from tooling/images/docker-metadata.Dockerfile, and Oyzu pulls its published, digest-pinned copy when it is missing (see Published toolchain images). Provision the appropriate AppArmor profile where required. The CLI does not pull any other missing image, install Docker or change host security settings. Build with oyzu build --isolated: on every host the native build refuses a container request (native build does not support these declared relationships; select --isolated explicitly). The earlier Linux captured-build acceptance predates two planning regressions (2026-10-03 and 2026-10-06) that broke the derived container actions on every host until 2026-10-20. The registered python-container scenario passed again on Windows 11 with Docker Desktop 29.8.1 (status); Linux and macOS have not been re-run since. The language-owned python-pure-zip-3.12-v1 profile requires captured CPython 3.12 preparation facts and a pure, ZIP-compatible application artifact. Preparation probes the provisioned runtime's implementation/minor version without network access, captures its immutable image identity and OCI content, and rejects a changed image between probing and capture. This is integrity and compatibility evidence, not registry authentication or production authority. Base bytes must be provisioned through an appropriate trusted process. Pinned base approval and centrally configurable runtime profiles remain further work. The default runtime layout is: /app/application.pyz, numeric user/group 65532:65532, working directory /app, and exec-form entrypoint ["python", "/app/application.pyz"]. Inherited CMD is cleared. No ports, health checks, server lifecycle, deployment settings or secrets are inferred. No build tools or project dependencies are installed inside the image assembly action; the archive already contains its captured pure-Python runtime closure.

Use an object only when the defaults need to change. The following example requires the named base to have been provisioned locally with a compatible CPython 3.12 runtime: builds: api: uses: python/app with: container: base: registry.example/python-runtime:3.12 user: "1000:1001" workdir: /srv/api entrypoint: [python, /app/application.pyz] Each field is optional; {} has the same packaging defaults as true. base is a literal image reference (up to 512 bytes), resolved to immutable local content and subjected to the same platform/CPython probe and captured-base admission as the default. Missing or incompatible bases fail; no pull or public fallback occurs. user is numeric UID:GID, each within the unsigned 32-bit range; named accounts and negative identities fail. The same identity owns the copied archive. workdir is an absolute literal image path (up to 1,024 bytes, ASCII letters/digits and /._-, without parent escapes). It does not relocate the archive from /app/application.pyz. entrypoint is an exec-form array of 1-64 nonempty literal arguments (up to 4,096 bytes each, no control characters). No shell or variable expansion is implied. Unknown keys, wrong types and explicit null fields fail configuration validation. Overrides are target intent in the frozen build.yaml inventory, not additional TOML precedence layers. They are bound by the source/plan identity, while execution settings still use the resolved configuration snapshot. The selected native application entrypoint and ZIP payload must already be unambiguous; changing the image entrypoint does not resolve multiple native console scripts. A custom argv is declared launch metadata, not evidence that its executable exists or that the service starts. The existing runtime compatibility probe always runs, even with a custom entrypoint. Base approval and mandatory runtime-user policy remain future integrations; these overrides confer no production authority.

The original application, wheel and sdist artifacts remain available for a distribution application; requirements-only applications retain their application artifact. The derived target adds an image artifact at a manifest-declared path such as api-container/artifacts/api-0.1.0-dev.g<source>.oci.tar. OCI image versions use the existing semver snapshot spelling, independently of Python's PEP 440 wheel/archive version. The manifest records the file digest and OCI publication digest. Packaging starts after the application package action, which already depends on its tests, required reports and quality gates. Shared materialization checks and copies the exact retained archive into an otherwise empty private image context and links the producer's test/coverage evidence. Generated image definitions never enter the checkout. Image content/platform assertions produce a separate JUnit report; image packaging assertions do not fabricate application coverage. A failed application prerequisite blocks image assembly; failed OCI assertions block image publication into the bundle. Inspect retained logs and reports, fix the native error and rebuild. The normal configuration engine owns precedence and policy checks. Docker tool eligibility is checked alongside the application before preparation. docker.apparmorProfile comes from the resolved owner snapshot and is frozen into the image action. No execution-time environment override replaces it. Profile names do not grant signing/publication rights. Managed application acquisition remains subject to the existing connector-binding restrictions; this feature introduces no managed download fallback. Boolean configurations retain their existing meaning. Previously rejected option objects are now supported with the finite contract above. No generated Dockerfile or extra project task is required.

with.container: false disables the option and counts as no container everywhere (native builds, independent scheduling and version hooks treat the build as having no image). Legacy/native Python application layouts, application-container matrices, other language runtime profiles and image startup smoke execution remain unimplemented and must not be inferred from this path. Unsupported options/profiles fail explicitly. Application startup behavior is not established merely by passing archive tests or OCI assertions. Discovery does not infer container intent for every Python application. The Python captured CI suite runs the authored python-api/variants/container.build.yaml and container-overrides.build.yaml cases. It requires exact application bytes in the image, a compatible captured runtime, nonroot launch metadata, application reports and image JUnit, unchanged sources, repeatable plan/artifact identities, a failed-test case that blocks image generation, and incompatible custom-runtime rejection. The override case checks actual image metadata, exact unchanged application bytes, captured custom-base identity and repeatability. CI provisions tools before invoking the compiled CLI. Local Rust profile tests and existing shared acquisition/worker checks establish narrower contracts; consult implementation status for actual native results. Those variants use with.container since the configuration split D2 change; the CI runs above used the earlier top-level spelling. The initial Python job 110889424053 at 9b84d6a failed on missing required and subject fields in the generated plan report declaration. Report intents now use the same typed contract as native and custom tasks, with a regression against the checked-in plan schema. The corrected Python job 110898263768 at 69b4d04 passed the complete registered Python container acceptance group, including exact payload bytes, default/custom runtime capture, overrides, reports, repeatability, failed-test blocking and incompatible runtime rejection. This verifies the implemented packaging profiles; the remaining smoke-test, matrix and broader EX-012 requirements are still outstanding.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/python-preparation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. A captured python/package or python/app build first prepares its Python dependencies: a worker with access only to the public PyPI broker routes downloads binary wheels, then every build, test and quality action installs them offline. This page describes which authored inputs preparation reads and how it treats dependency-group includes, editable references to the project itself, dynamic versions and locked packages that must be built from source. Native pip, uv and Poetry semantics stay with those tools; Oyzu reads only the declarations listed here.

The worker collects these declarations from the captured source: Input Purpose recorded project.dependencies in pyproject.toml runtime build-system.requires (or native locked legacy tools, with fixed defaults for unselected tools) build The dev dependency group, with its includes test requirements.txt runtime Default test and quality tools not already declared or locked build or test A uv project contributes its native uv export --locked closure and a Poetry project its native lock export. That complete hashed export owns the selected project and group closure. Supplemental backend, requirements-file and injected tool requirements are resolved by native pip with the native registry lock as constraints, retaining their original extras and transitive dependencies. A pip project continues to resolve its complete declarations. Every original root remains available to native dependency inventory validation; separating download roots does not remove extra activation, closure/version checks or the guard against downloading a package already selected for a source build. Every wheel is digest-recorded in the dependency snapshot. An authored build-system.requires remains authoritative, including native conflicts with a lock. When it is absent, the implicit setuptools/wheel backend uses active requirements already selected by the native lock. Only an unselected tool receives the fixed fallback (setuptools==80.9.0 or wheel==0.45.1). Native packaging interprets names and environment markers; every active locked constraint is retained for pip to resolve. No lock is refreshed and no authored requirement is dropped to make a conflict disappear.

A captured package/library can itself provide the selected native quality tool, as when building Black with Black formatting. The offline build installs the project's wheel before quality checks, so those checks use the installed tool. Oyzu omits only the implicit quality fallback whose native canonical name equals the current package name; it does not download a second public copy of that package. Explicit requirements and native locked constraints, build/test-runner defaults, ordinary tool acquisition and required failure/report gates remain unchanged. This does not change app or runtime-only preparation or execute project/backend code during acquisition. The affected native Black replay passed offline preparation/build and actual installed self-formatting; its required coverage and lint failures still block full package delivery. See the qualification result.
documents.s: The current package as a quality tool

documents.t: [dependency-groups] follows PEP 735. An entry is either a requirement string or an { include-group = "name" } table, and an include is expanded in place. Group names compare after PEP 503 normalization, so Runtime_Checks and runtime-checks name the same group: [dependency-groups] dev = [{ include-group = "tests" }, "pytest-cov==6.0.0"] tests = [{ include-group = "runtime-checks" }, "pytest==8.3.5"] runtime-checks = ["packaging==24.2"] Preparation captures packaging, pytest and pytest-cov as test inputs. An include of an undefined group, a group defined twice under equivalent names, a cyclic include or any other table entry fails preparation with a diagnostic naming the group. Only the dev group is selected, matching uv's default; for uv projects the native export applies the same includes.

Requirements files commonly install the project under development, as in -e .[cli], and dependency groups commonly reference the project with extras, such as name[tests]. The project is built from the captured source, so preparation never downloads it. Such a reference is replaced by the requirements that installing the project adds: project.dependencies and the project.optional-dependencies tables for the selected extras, following extras that reference the project again. Extra names compare normalized. An undefined extra fails preparation, and a reference whose environment marker does not apply to the build interpreter is skipped, as pip skips it. The editable forms accepted in requirements.txt are -e ., -e ./, --editable . and --editable=., each optionally followed by [extras]; the project needs a static project.name. Every other directive, including -r, -c, an editable path to another directory and option lines, still fails with Unsupported requirements directive; no alternate source fallback.
documents.s: The project itself as a requirement

documents.t: In a package/library build, an exported dependency can itself require the current project, including an extra: for example, a Litestar plugin requires litestar[cli]>=2.0.1. The current project is built from captured source, so it is a provider for that dependency without being downloaded or represented as an external package ID. Native inventory checks its declared base requirements, requested optional groups and their captured closure using native marker and extra semantics. Unknown extras, missing dependencies, unapproved direct URLs and a duplicate downloaded/source identity fail. Dynamic dependency metadata cannot establish this closure without backend execution and is refused. The original source version is not assumed equal to the final snapshot version. Active back-edge constraints remain explicitly pending in private prepared metadata. At the start of the existing package prepare action, after the private project version is bound to the shared version decision, native PEP 440 checks compare every pending constraint with actual OYZU_VERSION. A missing planned version, identity mismatch or incompatible constraint fails before creating the venv, installing dependencies or running a source backend. Acquisition does not run project code or invent a version for dynamic metadata. This provider is not available in app or runtime-only dependency contexts.

A project may list version in project.dynamic instead of declaring it. For the selected pdm.backend, this native declaration supplies a version without running the backend or importing project code: [project] name = "example" dynamic = ["version"] [build-system] requires = ["pdm-backend"] build-backend = "pdm.backend" [tool.pdm.version] source = "file" path = "example/__init__.py" Oyzu reads that captured UTF-8 file and follows PDM's default syntax: the first line matching __version__ = "1.2.3" or VERSION = '1.2.3' wins, including an optional trailing comment. Native packaging.Version validates and normalizes the literal, and the existing shared version inference selects its source snapshot. The recorded nativeVersion retains the native value; wheel/sdist metadata carries the selected snapshot. Actual native PDM metadata, installed-artifact tests/coverage and an independent offline delivered-wheel consumer passed on Linux; see the bounded proof. The path must be relative, contained in admitted captured source, free of links or reparse points, and name a regular file no larger than 4 MiB. Unsafe or missing paths, invalid UTF-8, a missing default literal and an invalid PEP 440 version fail preparation; correct the native declaration or version file and rerun. No project code in the file executes while facts are acquired. Other dynamic forms retain name-only facts and tag-based inference: setuptools [tool.setuptools.dynamic] version = { attr = ... }, Hatch file/VCS providers, PDM call/SCM/custom-pattern providers, and PDM projects with backend-path, a configured tool.pdm.build.custom-hook or conventional pdm_build.py. These providers are not executed during preparation or claimed as native file facts. Without applicable tags their base remains 0.0.0, giving a PEP 440 snapshot such as 0.0.0.dev0+g0123456789ab; the native strategy fails with version-needs-native when no native version is available. In its private build tree the build removes version from project.dynamic, removes tool.setuptools.dynamic.version when present and writes the selected snapshot as the static project.version, so the wheel, sdist and their metadata carry the same version. The checkout keeps its dynamic declaration. A pyproject.toml without either a static or a dynamic version still fails with Python project version must be static or listed in project.dynamic.

Some locked packages have no wheel to download: a uv.lock package whose source is a Git repository pinned to a commit, and a uv workspace member or path dependency, which uv export lists as -e ./PATH or ./PATH, and a registry package that uv.lock locks with only a source distribution (sdist) and no wheel. Following the maintainer decision of 2026-10-10, these are built from source, but the build runs only inside the isolated, network-denied build worker, never during preparation: Preparation splits these lines from the native export. Only registry lines are downloaded with their hashes; a project or group declaration that names such a package is satisfied by its source build and is not downloaded. This includes a declaration that repeats the source as a direct URL, such as advanced-alchemy @ git+https://github.com/... in an extra or dependency group, when uv.lock pins that package to a Git commit or member. A direct URL for a package that is not built from a locked source is still refused. A registry package with an sdist and no wheels in uv.lock is removed from the wheel download and treated as a source package of kind sdist. Its sdist is downloaded from the files.pythonhosted.org route of the scoped broker, checked against the SHA-256 in uv.lock (a missing hash or a URL outside that route fails preparation), and unpacked by Oyzu without running any of its code. Only regular files are written, names must be portable with one top-level directory, and archives are limited to 256 MiB. The tree is stored under sources/ and then follows steps 3 and 4. A package with any wheel keeps the wheel download. Each Git source is fetched at the commit uv.lock records, with the native Git client through a read-only route of the scoped broker. Only public HTTPS GitHub repositories have routes, as for Cargo Git sources. The checkout's tree, without Git metadata, is stored under sources/ in the prepared tree. No hooks, filters, submodules or credentials are used. Preparation reads each source's build-system.requires from its pyproject.toml (or native locked legacy tools, with fixed fallbacks, for a setup.py package without it) and captures those requirements as build wheels, resolved with the lock's constraints. No backend or package code runs. In the build worker, after the captured wheels are installed, each source is copied into the private build state and built with pip wheel --no-index --no-deps --no-build-isolation, so the backend and its requirements come only from the captured set. A build requirement missing from that set fails before the build runs. The wheel must carry the locked name and version; the wheels are then installed from a manifest of their digests with --require-hashes, and the project builds and tests against them. For example, with this declaration uv locks sampleproject at the commit, and preparation records it with sourceId python-git-0: [project] dependencies = ["sampleproject"] [tool.uv.sources] sampleproject = { git = "https://github.com/pypa/sampleproject", rev = "621e4974ca25ce531773def586ba3ed8e736b3fc" } The dependency snapshot records each Git source as a package whose digest is that of its captured tree, with verification digest-only, and lists every source package with its kind, path, commit, purpose and build requirements in the oyzu.dev/python-sources extension; an sdist source also records its URL and SHA-256, and its package record uses sourceId pypi. Workspace members are part of the captured project source and have no separate package record. Because Git metadata is not captured, SETUPTOOLS_SCM_PRETEND_VERSION is set to the locked version during the source build, so backends that read the version through setuptools-scm or hatch-vcs use it. A source whose build requirements include maturin or setuptools-rust needs a Rust toolchain and Cargo crates, which Python preparation does not capture. Preparation fails naming the requirement before any build runs, as for the maturin-built pydantic-core workspace member of pydantic. Python applications (python/app) whose runtime closure includes a package built from source fail at packaging, because application archives install captured wheels only; runtime dependency contexts for Docker refuse such packages during preparation.

The build worker keeps everything it creates for a Python target outside the project tree, in /out/.oyzu-python of the target's private output root: Path Contents venv/ Build environment with the captured wheels and source builds installed dist/ Native wheel and sdist before packaging copies them sources/, source-builds/, source-wheels/ Copies and wheels of packages built from source application/, application-project/, application.pyz, test-application/ Application staging, archive and its extracted test copy The output root persists across the target's actions and is never inside /workspace, so a project at the workspace root is covered too. Native build backends therefore cannot pack the build environment into the sdist (hatchling and other backends that include untracked files did, issue #315), and Ruff, Black and Flake8 check only project files without an added exclusion. Packaging still copies artifacts to the target's bundle directory /out/<target>/<platform>/ (named to the adapter as OYZU_OUTPUT) and reports are written to its reports/ directory, so bundle locations follow the shared bundle layout. The state is private to the worker and not an input or output contract. Project hooks that ran against the former .oyzu-build/ folder inside the project no longer see it there. A Python target has no stage contract, so the action cache reuses it only as a whole target and never needs to restore this state.

Preparation failures stop the build before any action runs and retain the worker diagnostic. Correct the authored input and start a new build. Diagnostic Cause and recovery Dependency group NAME is not defined / includes itself Fix the include in [dependency-groups] Project extra NAME is not defined Declare the extra in project.optional-dependencies or correct the reference An editable project reference needs a static pyproject.toml project name Declare project.name statically Source package NAME needs build requirement maturin... The source builds Rust code; no Rust toolchain or Cargo inputs are captured. Not supported (below) Source package NAME build requirement REQ is not in the captured dependency set A source's build requirement was not captured; the isolated build stops before running its backend Isolated source build of NAME failed The backend failed offline with only captured inputs; pip's native output is in the action log Locked path requirement PATH: only workspace members and path dependencies inside the captured project can be built The export names an absolute path, a parent directory or a file: URL Git sources currently require a public HTTPS GitHub repository / Git source must lock a full commit identity The uv.lock Git source is not admitted; pin a public GitHub repository by commit Git source NAME uses submodules, which preparation does not fetch The locked commit has a .gitmodules file Git sources need the git client in the Python preparation image The preparation image has no git; the provisioned images install it Packages built from source are supported only for uv projects with uv.lock / ...not supported in runtime dependency contexts Source builds from a Poetry export or for a Docker runtime context uv.lock sdist-only package NAME: has no locked SHA-256... / ...outside the approved registry file route The lock's sdist entry cannot be trusted as a hashed input; re-lock from PyPI The sdist of NAME does not match the SHA-256 recorded in uv.lock The downloaded archive differs from the lock; nothing is built Python applications cannot package runtime dependency NAME built from source yet A python/app runtime dependency is built from source Direct URL requirements need an approved source adapter A declaration or requirements file pins a direct URL or Git source outside uv.lock Current project dependency REQ is incompatible with planned version VERSION A back-edge does not accept the actual snapshot; the original native version is not proof of compatibility Current project extra is not defined: NAME / Current project dependency closure requires static metadata The requested current-project closure cannot be established from admitted captured metadata Poetry lock is missing or stale; update it with poetry lock The lock does not match pyproject.toml; run poetry lock and commit the result

Source builds. Git sources, sdist-only registry packages and local members are built from source only for uv; Poetry Git and path sources and pip requirements-file Git or path lines are still refused. Git sources need a public HTTPS GitHub repository and a full commit; sdist-only packages need files.pythonhosted.org sdists in uv.lock and are refused in runtime contexts and applications like other source builds; submodules and Git LFS content are not fetched. Sources that build Rust (maturin, setuptools-rust) and other non-Python build toolchains beyond what the build image provides are not captured. A source package that is itself the build requirement of another source is refused, environment markers on member lines are refused, and virtual members are skipped as uv skips them. These choices are provisional and conservative. Source build evidence. The source-built wheels are not reproducibility checked; their bytes come from the backend run in the build worker, and only the source tree and captured build requirements are digest-recorded. Stale Poetry locks. A lock whose content hash no longer matches the project is rejected, as poetry install rejects it; Oyzu does not refresh or tolerate it. Confirmed by the maintainer on 2026-10-10. Dynamic version evidence. Only the selected PDM default file form above supplies declarative native version facts; other computed versions use tags. Other dynamic metadata, such as dynamic dependencies, is not computed. Groups. Only dev is selected; selecting other groups is not configurable.

python tooling/test-build-scenarios.py --suite python --only python-captured --cli <compiled-cli> selects full checks and captured execution through its registered wrappers. It builds pip and uv fixtures with dependency-group includes, a pip project whose requirements.txt installs itself with an extra, a setuptools project with a dynamic version, a PDM default file-version project with an independent delivered-wheel consumer, explicit optional prerequisites/native formatter scope, uv workspace and local-path dependencies, a uv Git source pinned to a pypa/sampleproject commit, a uv sdist-only registry package (pyperclip 1.9.0), a real registry wheel depending on that locked source build, legacy root/member backends with native locked setuptools, and a positive Poetry main/dev export. Each successful build must retain unchanged source/lock bytes, deliver wheel/sdist artifacts, and collect passing installed-artifact tests and coverage with measured hits. Git dependency tests also exercise the project's installed module. Refusal cases cover cyclic includes, missing extras, external editable paths, unapproved direct URLs, maturin members, and stale uv/Poetry locks; they must retain unchanged authored inputs and deliver no successful artifacts. Fixture lock setup uses the provisioned uv/Poetry images with --pull=never; network access there authors a native lock before the captured build starts and is not an execution fallback. When fixture setup needs a custom certificate authority, explicitly set SSL_CERT_FILE to a readable regular CA bundle. The harness mounts it read-only for native lock acquisition and supplies its path to uv, Requests/Poetry and Git, preserving TLS validation. An invalid explicit path fails before Docker starts. This fixture setting does not change captured-build trust or add the CA to an image. The registered captured/full group passed all 22 expected outcomes on Linux: 14 successful artifact flows each collected passing installed-artifact tests and coverage, seven required preparation refusals emitted no actions/artifacts, and one required formatter failure retained real passing tests/reports while blocking every artifact. Source/lock guards and compiled inspection passed. The PDM flow additionally executed its delivered wheel independently offline. For stale uv declarations, the pinned native tool refuses offline resolution before its stale-lock diagnostic; a separate freshness guard is not claimed from that case. All eight affected pinned corpus baselines ran; Attrs completed its installed artifact/test/report/package flow, while the other repositories retained explicit failures or refusals. The captured helper, backend, transitive-source and Poetry fixtures passed. Litestar's real offline prepare/build corrections passed, but its own snapshot parser blocks collection/reports/package exports; that remains a named upstream compatibility outlier. Configured FastAPI selects its declared all extra and native formatter scope, clearing the earlier optional-CLI failure. Its installed tests report 3595 passed, one telemetry prerelease conflict and 22 skips; native Ruff rejects three translation-test Markdown fixtures and one skills reference document. Required reports are retained and packaging remains blocked. Black's implicit self-tool correction passes native prepare/build and actual installed Black formatting. Its 556 passing native tests and three skips still yield a failed test action because mandatory Cobertura is missing: native coverage configuration omits installed site-packages. Native Flake8/pycodestyle also crashes on its existing invalid-escape token fixture. No Black artifacts are exported. These distinct configured replays do not replace the original pinned baselines or imply corpus success. See captured Python completion for exact revisions, tools, native evidence, remaining scenarios and corpus obligations. The Rust unit tests in src/builders/python/adapter/requirements.rs cover include expansion, normalized names and the accepted editable forms, and those in src/builders/python/adapter/sources.rs cover Git source admission, export splitting and member lookup. Unit checks supplement the compiled native proof; they do not qualify the remaining source forms or pinned corpus.

Installed-artifact tests measure the installed package, not the checkout. A native coverage configuration such as [tool.coverage.report] with omit = ["*/site-packages/*"] can therefore exclude every measured package file: native assertions may pass while coverage reports No data to report and the required Cobertura report is missing. The test action fails and packaging stays blocked. Narrow or remove that exclusion in the project's native coverage configuration so the installed package remains eligible, then rerun and retain the configuration change as an explicit captured input. Do not substitute checkout-only coverage, suppress the required report or infer coverage success from pytest's passing assertion count. This recovery guidance does not claim a configured Black coverage rerun has passed. See Python artifact testing.
documents.s: Native coverage omits the installed package

documents.t: CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/python-sessions.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Oyzu can prepare pip and uv acquisition automatically through oyzu exec and activated Bash. An Oyzu-owned subprocess keyring helper supplies a session's password to the native tool in memory. No Python keyring package or per-project authentication file is needed. This opt-in prototype uses a fixture local agent; it does not implement platform login or captured oyzu build integration.

Configure an agent in user or administrative Oyzu configuration and provision Python/pip or uv on PATH: [python] sessionEndpoint = "http://127.0.0.1:43199/session" The port is illustrative. The endpoint is absent by default, leaving standalone behavior unchanged. The normal configuration cascade resolves it. Project, local, invocation and profile settings cannot select agent authority. User configuration is excluded in CI under existing rules.
