The laboratory endpoint must use numeric loopback HTTP with no credentials, query or fragment. oyzu exec -- python3 -m pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt oyzu exec -- uv lock oyzu exec -- uv sync --locked eval "$(oyzu activate bash)" pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt The measured native versions are Python 3.12.14, pip 25.0.1 and uv 0.12.21 on Linux. Native Windows/macOS execution is unqualified; managed-session Windows shell shims are not implemented. The shell installs launch aliases for python, python3, pip, pip3 and uv when their native executable is present. Explicit exec also recognizes versioned Python/pip executable names. Plain interpreter execution is unchanged; python -m pip is routed through pip admission. Managed operations are pip install, download, wheel; uv lock, sync, pip install, pip sync. Help/version bypass admission. Other operations fail explicitly. uv run, Poetry and arbitrary Python scripts that internally invoke package managers are not qualified by this adapter. Publication belongs to oyzu publish; native uv publish is rejected.

Each supported invocation requests admission with its working directory, tool and arguments before starting native acquisition, including warm/offline operations. Directory is an unverified context hint. The experimental response supplies index, username and numeric-loopback credentialEndpoint. The index must be credential-free HTTP(S) with no query or fragment. Oyzu adds the username alone to the native index URL and stages its own executable under the keyring name. The helper implements keyring get <service> <username> and asks the agent for a password for that service and username. The agent must validate the request against its admitted source; native URL handling remains native-owned. This is an explicit single-index configuration replacement mode: Pip receives PIP_CONFIG_FILE set to the null device, PIP_INDEX_URL and PIP_KEYRING_PROVIDER=subprocess. It uses noninteractive acquisition. Uv receives UV_NO_CONFIG=1, UV_DEFAULT_INDEX and UV_KEYRING_PROVIDER=subprocess. Inherited alternate-index/find-links variables are removed; UV_CONFIG_FILE is removed. Explicit source, provider, config-file, isolation and directory override arguments are rejected instead of combined with managed settings. Persistent resolver configuration is not merged, including unrelated options inside disabled pip/uv configuration. Ordinary package metadata remains native; Oyzu does not rewrite requirements, pyproject.toml, uv.toml or locks. Native CLI/environment options unrelated to routing remain native-owned. This choice uses pip's documented null-config behavior and uv's configuration controls. Passwords are returned through the native helper pipe, never placed in generated configuration, launcher arguments or launcher environment. The session locator is access-sensitive; this fixture transport is not production authenticated IPC. Native processes can read credentials in memory. Read-only access is enforced by the upstream identity, not client network filtering or hostile-code containment.

Native results and exit status follow oyzu exec; --json captures native output in the structured result. Package caches, installed packages and generated locks remain native-owned. Temporary helper files live until the child exits and are removed after normal success/failure. Abrupt-termination cleanup is deferred. NATIVE_SESSION_* identifies authority/admission failures; PYTHON_SESSION_INVALID identifies malformed session data; PYTHON_ROUTING_CONFLICT rejects explicit configuration conflicts; PYTHON_OPERATION_UNSUPPORTED identifies an unsupported command. Helper errors are generic. Denied/unavailable admission prevents native work without a direct or cached offline fallback. Restore agent availability before retrying. The qualified flow is ordinary named packages from one admitted index, including hash-pinned requirements and uv locks retaining upstream wheel URLs. Direct URL, VCS/path dependencies, requirements-file source directives, uv source/workspace overrides, alternative credentials in existing netrc/native auth stores, and arbitrary native parser aliases are not qualified source-policy enforcement. Disabling persistent resolver configuration is not a network sandbox. These inputs need explicit admission/configuration composition before broader support is claimed; the agent must never grant credentials solely because a client asks. See the launch qualification. Platform and CI identity integration remain deferred. No Oyzu schema version was introduced.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/python-testing.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Python builders expose an implicit test task for pip, uv and Poetry projects. It remains callable and part of the default build even without a tests/ or test/ directory. Native pytest selects tests at execution time, including root-level tests and configured paths. Oyzu does not import conftest.py, execute Python or collect tests during static discovery.

oyzu run list oyzu run test oyzu build oyzu inspect dist The static pytest detector records evidence from pytest.ini, .pytest.ini, [tool.pytest.ini_options] in pyproject.toml, [pytest] in tox.ini, or [tool:pytest] in setup.cfg. With no explicit evidence, it records pytest as the profile default. This identifies intent; it does not parse native selection rules or decide which tests exist. Native pytest owns configuration precedence, testpaths, filename patterns, markers and collection errors. Multiple pytest configuration files remain inputs for the same framework, not competing frameworks. For example, this native configuration requires no Oyzu test section: [pytest] testpaths = checks python_files = spec_*.py Development execution uses the detected manager: Manager Implicit command pip python -m pytest uv uv run --locked pytest Poetry poetry run pytest Provision Python, the manager and project dependencies before using these commands. Development execution retains the native manager's environment and behavior, including any native synchronization; it is not an isolated build. Explicit TOML task replacements and Oyzu pre/post hooks retain their normal task-engine behavior. Additional arguments can be forwarded with oyzu run test -- <pytest arguments>.

oyzu run test now wraps the supported exact pytest command with compiled Oyzu orchestration and an embedded native pytest adapter and finalizes JUnit/Cobertura in a test-only dist bundle. This applies to pip, uv and Poetry: the manager selects the interpreter/environment, and native pytest owns collection. The listed implicit command above describes the native operation; execution supplies reporting through that interpreter. Python 3.11+ is required by the adapter, with current verification on Python 3.12 and pytest 8.3.5, pytest-cov 6.0.0 and coverage 7.16.2. Reporters must already be available in the selected environment; Oyzu does not install them. See direct test reports for shared hook, override, retention, inspection and host-provenance behavior. The host adapter measures checkout source, not an installed build artifact. It preserves native coverage configuration selected by COVERAGE_RCFILE or the supported coverage configuration files, including source settings, branches, exclusions and thresholds. Without configured source settings it measures the task's working directory, including unimported Python modules. Collected tests, native pytest filename patterns, conventional test filenames, conftest files and internal .oyzu/.venv paths are excluded from application coverage. Arbitrary test-support modules are not inferred as tests merely because another test imports them; use native coverage exclusions where needed. Each invocation uses a temporary coverage configuration and data file. An existing .coverage file or ambient COVERAGE_FILE cannot supply old hits and is not overwritten. The reporter pins its required output locations and coverage configuration; pytest-cov source/output command-line options do not override those assignments. Native test selectors such as -k remain supported. Normal pytest/manager caches and Python bytecode can still be written in this host workflow. Missing application coverage remains missing evidence rather than being synthesized. Only supported exact commands and their exact shell shorthand are instrumented. Explicit python -m pytest uses that interpreter on PATH even in a uv/Poetry project; the implicit manager command retains its manager. Bare pytest uses python on PATH. Custom shell programs and other replacements retain their original bodies and must produce the required reports via declared paths or the supplied report environment variables. Native assertion/collection errors, coverage thresholds and missing reports fail the invocation while retaining available evidence. Empty suites retain pytest's exit code 5 and zero-test JUnit; an emitted zero-denominator coverage report is not rewritten to 100 percent.

oyzu build requires the provisioned container toolchain and dependency preparation described in the CLI overview. Preparation includes pytest 8.3.5 and pytest-cov 6.0.0 when the project/native lock has not selected those packages. Reporter preparation no longer depends on a guessed test directory. Project declarations and native lock constraints keep their versions; incompatible integrations fail rather than downloading a replacement during tests. Current Python acquisition uses the public PyPI broker routes; complete private-source integration remains pending. The package test adapter runs pytest against the installed snapshot distribution with importlib mode. It derives measurable Python sources from installed wheel metadata and preserves native coverage settings, including thresholds. The application adapter measures source extracted from its generated application artifact. Native pytest/pytest-cov create JUnit and Cobertura; shared collection retains them under the target's reports in dist/ and records paths, digests and parsed summaries in dist/manifest.json. No test/output YAML is needed. Successful test and quality gates permit the builder's snapshot artifacts to be collected. Captured package tests can import ordinary captured test helpers, including namespace directories such as docs_src and regular test packages with relative imports. Pytest keeps the original working directory, collection paths and test resources. A private helper import view excludes the current installed distribution's import identities from its wheel RECORD: flat modules, regular packages, whole namespace roots and native extension names. Missing installed submodules cannot fall back to the checkout. Coverage continues to measure the installed wheel's Python files; helper availability does not change coverage scope. Native pytest resolves configured pythonpath directories; the adapter maps in-capture paths to equally filtered helper views before conftest imports. Relative paths and absolute paths inside the captured project are supported. Paths outside the capture, file/ZIP import paths and paths entering an installed import identity fail explicitly. Selected tests or conftest files beneath a protected artifact import identity also fail visibly; move those tests into a separate test directory. Oyzu retains importlib mode even when forwarded package-test options request another mode. These package boundaries do not change direct host tests or extracted-application testing. Rust owns the temporary helper-view lifetime. The native pytest hook creates shallow helper links, with a helper-copy fallback where Windows symlink privileges are unavailable. Helpers and their resources remain test inputs; this does not grant network access, install packages or modify captured source. An assertion failure, collection error or failed coverage threshold blocks final artifact collection. An empty suite keeps pytest's native exit code 5 and any emitted zero-test JUnit report; it is not rewritten as successful test evidence. Coverage that was not produced remains missing, while emitted coverage retains its actual denominator and hits. A suite containing explicitly skipped tests retains native skip counts and the native exit outcome. A zero exit code from a custom replacement cannot satisfy missing required reports by itself. No-tests behavior is a compatibility change: projects previously excluded from the test stage by the directory heuristic now invoke pytest and can fail the build when it collects no tests. Add tests or correct native collection configuration; an empty directory is not a successful test result. Direct tests now also require their report obligations; zero exit status alone is insufficient if a replacement command omits reports. Explicit python/app distribution projects now add a console application archive and test its extracted sources. See Python applications for entrypoint selection, artifact identities and format limits; package builders continue testing the installed distribution.

python tooling/test-python-tasks.py --cli target/debug/oyzu python tooling/test-python-direct.py --cli target/debug/oyzu python tooling/test-python-reporting.py python tooling/test-python-adapter.py Use target/debug/oyzu.exe on Windows. The probes need installed pytest/pytest-cov; acquisition-boundary checks also need pip. Local verification uses Python 3.12.14, pytest 8.3.5, pytest-cov 6.0.0 and coverage 7.16.2 on Windows. CI runs direct task/reporting checks on Windows, macOS and Linux, then separate captured-build cases on Linux. See implementation status for revision-specific results; configured CI is not evidence that a pending job passed. The native probes verify root and configured suites, nonexecuting listing, assertion failures/skips, empty-suite exit/JUnit, installed-source coverage and native coverage threshold failure. The direct-bundle probe additionally requires uv 0.12.21 and Poetry 2.5.1. It creates empty native manager projects and exposes the explicitly provisioned reporter packages through PYTHONPATH, while native managers still select/create their environments. It checks real test-only bundles, source coverage including unimported files, test exclusion, forwarded arguments, thresholds, native collection/failure, and preservation of existing coverage data. It does not establish all native manager synchronization or dependency profiles. Captured scenarios additionally require snapshot wheel/sdist artifacts, report collection, unchanged checkout bytes and rejection of artifacts after an empty suite. Native reporter tests alone do not verify container isolation or packaging. The helper import view passed 20 compiled native reporting/import-path probes on Linux with host Python 3.12.14, both pytest 8.3.5 and 9.1.1, pytest-cov 6.0.0 and coverage 7.16.2. The captured/full group passed 12 usable wheel/sdist flows and seven required preparation refusals. Its new helper fixture uses native Python 3.12.15 and produces JUnit 2/2 plus installed-only coverage 3/3. The affected pinned FastAPI rerun cleared helper collection and passed its nine identified tutorial/client/OpenAPI cases during the full suite; two independent assertions and its format gate still block package export. Attrs retains its complete installed-artifact flow on the same candidate. Earlier Windows reporter verification does not establish this new path; captured helper verification on Windows and macOS has not been recorded. See captured Python qualification for exact candidate identities, native tool versions and failures. For no tests, check pytest's native filename patterns and configuration, then run the same manager command to inspect collection. For missing reporters, correct the declared dependencies or provisioned environment and repeat preparation. For report/coverage failure, inspect the native logs and report records retained in dist/. Native test configuration and plugins execute during testing, so they are subject to the build's offline execution boundary, or ordinary host permissions for direct tasks. This integration uses pytest as the supported default. Pytest can run supported unittest.TestCase suites, but a dedicated unittest runner preserving every unittest feature is not implemented. Other frameworks, general custom-runner adaptation, full configuration inheritance, distributed pytest execution and all pytest/pytest-cov versions remain separate work. The host adapter's pytest-cov controller integration is exercised against the provisioned version; native version incompatibilities fail instead of fabricating results. Missing measurable Python source remains an evidence failure; native-extension coverage is not claimed from Python line measurements. Native references: pytest configuration and pytest exit codes.

Oyzu selects commands, creates private coverage files and launches the selected interpreter in Rust. Embedded pytest/pytest-cov code is limited to native configuration, source metadata and framework hooks. It is carried inside the compiled executable; Oyzu never searches the project for its own reporting scripts. Python is required because this is an explicitly selected Python build, not as an Oyzu CLI dependency. Native pytest exit codes and report obligations are unchanged. For captured package helpers, the native adapter normalizes only pytest's resolved pythonpath list before its native consumers insert paths. This boundary is needed because pytest may apply those paths before loading plugins or conftest files; configuration resolution and test selection remain native pytest responsibilities. It also delegates native conftest imports through a narrow private-API guard: pytest can import an enclosing application package before loading conftest, so the guard refuses a protected checkout identity before either executes. Native selection and the original importer retain their arguments and behavior for allowed conftest files. This integration is exercised against pytest 8.3.5 and 9.1.1; a changed native API fails the invocation and requires qualification.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/release-check.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Status: experimental client. oyzu release check implements the CLI side of the platform's would-ship route (deployments.v1 checkWouldShip, POST /api/v1/accounts/{account}/projects/{project}/ship-checks). It is verified against a scripted local server (tests/integration/release_cli.rs) and unit tests. The platform does not yet route deployments.v1 at its edge, so the command is not yet qualified against a deployed platform.
documents.s: Checking whether a build would ship

documents.t: Run oyzu release check after oyzu build to ask Oyzu, before anything is published, what a release of this build would do in each of the project's environments: would ship: nothing waits on a person or a gate; would wait: it would enter once the named approvals, gates or blockers clear; refused: a policy or fact would refuse it, named with the reason. The platform derives the same plan a release would get now, from the project's saved facts and policies. Nothing is published, saved or started. A coding agent can ask the same question through assist's MCP endpoint (deployments_check_would_ship).

A finished oyzu build whose manifest records status: succeeded (dist/manifest.json by default). platform.url and platform.account, as for oyzu secrets, and a platform credential from the shared provider: the oyzu auth login session or a bearer in OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN. The check runs as that person: they need to be able to read the project. The project, as --project or OYZU_PROJECT.

oyzu build oyzu release check --project web oyzu release check --project web --environment production oyzu release check --project web --json Flag Meaning --project The project to check in (or OYZU_PROJECT). --environment Answer for this environment only; repeat for more. Default: every environment. --manifest The build manifest to check (default dist/manifest.json). --version Every component's version, instead of each artifact's own. --commit The built commit; defaults to the checkout's HEAD.

The manifest's artifacts, as a publish would name them: each artifact's output is its target, or target/name for an artifact other than the target's primary one, and an OCI image or index is addressed by its OCI digest. The body also carries the commit, the GitHub repository the checkout pushes to when there is one, and the requested environments. No eligibility is sent, so the platform checks the build as a candidate.

People see one line per environment and, under it, each reason with the policy behind it: Would this build ship? · web (checked as a candidate build) ✓ qa would ship … production would wait Approval from release-managers (1) (promotion policy prod-approval) ✗ eu would refuse it api has not been verified in staging (verification policy eu-staged-check) Once published (start policies) agents: joins the open batch of jobs (2 versions so far) and rides the release cut at 2026-10-11T15:02:00Z; 2 releases already wait in the queue ahead of it The last section appears when a start policy covers the build. It says whether publishing would join the policy's open batch, open a new one, or cut a release at once, and how many of the release scope's releases already wait in its start queue, so an agent knows its change rides the next release rather than starting one. --json prints the platform's answer as a ship-check record with account added. The command exits 1 when any environment would refuse the build; waiting on a person or a gate is not a failure. The answer must identify the project and classification and contain components, unassigned outputs and environments arrays. Each environment must name its environment, tier and digest, provide reasons with kinds and text, and use one of the three verdicts above. Missing fields or unknown verdicts fail with RELEASE_CHECK_RESPONSE_INVALID and a nonzero exit in human and JSON modes; they never authorize shipping. Check platform/client compatibility before retrying.

Code Meaning RELEASE_CHECK_NOT_CONFIGURED No project, or no platform.url / platform.account. RELEASE_CHECK_UNAUTHENTICATED No credential is available (run oyzu auth login from a terminal, or set OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN; unattended runs never use a stored session on their own), or the platform refused it. RELEASE_CHECK_NO_COMMIT Not a Git checkout with a commit, and no --commit. RELEASE_CHECK_NOTHING_TO_SHIP The manifest lists no artifacts. RELEASE_CHECK_RESOURCE_NOT_FOUND The project does not exist, or the person cannot read it. PUBLISH_MANIFEST_MISSING, PUBLISH_MANIFEST_INVALID, PUBLISH_BUILD_NOT_SUCCEEDED The manifest is read exactly as oyzu publish reads it, with the same errors.

deployments.v1 has no route at the platform's edge yet, and deployments checks Access only for calls made through assist; a person's token sent straight to it is not yet verified there. Until both land, the command is proven only against a scripted server. The build is always checked as a candidate.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/remote-runs.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Status: experimental client. oyzu build --remote and oyzu run <task> --remote implement the CLI side of the draft remote runs contract (design page). Client checks use a scripted local server and the contract mock. The bounded connected Linux build flow also has recorded qualification; broader host/service support remains incomplete. Sign-in is the experimental oyzu auth, verified only against a local conformance fake.

--remote runs the same invocation on a platform pool instead of this machine: the pool checks out the exact pushed commit, runs oyzu build or oyzu run <task> there with full checks in isolation, and streams the output back. The CLI follows it to the end and exits with the remote exit code. Everything else Oyzu does stays local and works without an account; --remote is the optional platform path.

A Git checkout whose HEAD is pushed to a github.com repository linked to a project in your platform account. git must be on PATH. platform.url and platform.account in user/global, machine or administrative configuration. Project/local scope is rejected with a diagnostic naming the key: oyzu config set --global platform.url https://platform.example.com oyzu config set --global platform.account payments CI can supply OYZU_PLATFORM_URL and OYZU_PLATFORM_ACCOUNT through the configuration contract. These invocation sources override ordinary files and remain subject to administrative constraints. A checkout cannot redirect a developer's platform credential, even when its environment is trusted. A platform credential from the shared credential provider: the session stored by oyzu auth login (used when you run from a terminal or select it with platform.authentication.provider), or a bearer supplied in OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN (never stored or refreshed; it is a credential, so it is read from the environment and never from a configuration file). Unattended runs with neither fail with REMOTE_UNAUTHENTICATED instead of looking for a developer's session.

Command Runs remotely oyzu build --remote Every target oyzu build cli web --remote Targets cli and web (and what they depend on) oyzu build --affected origin/main --remote Targets affected since the merge base of origin/main and HEAD oyzu run policy-check --remote Task policy-check (target:task also works) … --remote --download out The same, then downloads every output into out/ oyzu build --remote --plan previews a remote build locally without creating a run; see planning a remote run. The CLI resolves the repository from the current branch's remote (else origin), the full HEAD commit and the checked-out branch ref. For --affected it sends the full merge-base commit, never a local ref name.

Text mode uses the same linear view as a local build. Each log line the pool streams is attributed to the target or task that wrote it (scope in the contract), so task starts, native output and task results look like local ones. The runner's own lines (checkout, start, finish) appear under runner. The receipt on stdout leads with the outcome, then the run id, commit, project, Oyzu version, portal link when there is one, and the outputs the run produced: ✓ Remote build succeeded Run 01jab7v3k9m2q8r4t6w0y1z5c7 Commit 3f2a9c1d4b5e (main) Project oyzu/platform Oyzu 0.9.0 Outputs manifest dist/manifest.json 4.0 KiB sha256:aaaaaaaaaaaa report dist/cli/linux/x86_64/reports/junit.xml 2.0 KiB sha256:bbbbbbbbbbbb Use --download <DIR> to fetch outputs; nothing was written locally. With --json, stderr carries the same structured events a local build emits (output events keep the remote scope as operationId) and stdout carries one remote-run record: run (the final run resource), result (state, exit code, reason and outputs), downloads (path, digest, local file) and cancelled. The record also contains invocationId, the exact submission body (repository, commit and selection), observation and a cancellation object. After a run has been created, failure to follow or retrieve its result produces an unknown outcome with the last observed run state/time and log position; it does not assert failed remote execution or start local work. The last run-resource state can predate subsequent scoped task log events. Known log gaps remain explicit in the result even after a connection recovers. Complete observation means the client received terminal records, not that every log entry or required artifact transfer is complete. Bounded retry notices describe observation loss and recovery. Submission, observation and requested artifact transfer are distinct phases. The current public contract supplies queued/running/final states and scoped task lifecycles; worker identity, assignment and detailed worker preparation/transfer telemetry are unavailable and are not inferred from illustrative studies.

Remote outcome Exit code Succeeded 0 Oyzu exited non-zero on the pool That exit code Failed before Oyzu ran, skipped, cancelled, timed out, or an unknown state 1 Refused before or while creating the run (configuration, Git, platform problem) 2 Interrupted with Ctrl-C 130 An unknown remote outcome after submission exits non-zero (1); an interrupt retains exit 130. Use the supplied Web link, or check the run ID with the platform operator when no link was supplied, before starting a replacement run. Reattachment and CLI retrieval of a previous remote run are not implemented.

The first Ctrl-C asks the platform to cancel the run and keeps following its log while the pool stops it; a second Ctrl-C exits at once with 130. The observer keeps following beyond the local cleanup grace period so it can retain the execution owner's confirmed outcome. Cancelling is retry-safe, so a cancel that races the run's own finish is harmless. There is no confirmation prompt, so cancelling works the same in CI. Closing the terminal (SIGHUP) is not a cancellation: it ends only the local follower, and the remote run continues on the pool. cancelled records that this invocation requested cancellation. It is not confirmation that execution stopped. cancellation.requested, acknowledged and confirmed expose separate facts; confirmation follows a terminal cancelled result. A finished-run conflict is followed to its actual outcome. The receipt preserves pending or unknown cancellation and any known log gaps. Assigned native workers use the same cooperative interruption lifetime as a local captured build. A running cancellation acknowledgement requires the execution owner's normal process wait and fresh finalized native build record; revoking a lease or receiving a success response alone is insufficient. Forced or unconfirmed stops remain explicit failures. The real Linux service/worker proof passed cancellation during the shared native action: the observer retained all three cancellation facts and exited 130 after confirmed cleanup. A second real run preserved an already accepted shared contribution while stopping API and preventing the final bundle from starting; see the distributed qualification record. resultAvailable distinguishes a fetched result from a partial observation. When the final run resource is already confirmed, losing access to its result retains that execution outcome and identifies unavailable metadata/outputs. The invocation still fails if requested observation cannot complete. Last-observed timestamps advance on actual responses; elapsed waiting is not execution progress.

Outputs are listed by digest and never written into dist/. --download <DIR> fetches each one through the platform's short-lived download link, which receives no platform credential, verifies its SHA-256 digest before writing, and writes it at its recorded path under DIR. A path that would leave DIR is refused. For accepted native split builds, these are the manifest, artifacts and required reports. The output projection excludes the private admitted plan, execution envelope and logs; it is not a complete local build bundle for oyzu inspect. The existing run log view retains remote observation separately. Native contribution validation precedes final platform success; downloaded file digests are checked again by the client. Reported native success does not guarantee platform acceptance. If the complete transferred contribution cannot be verified, the run fails with CONTRIBUTION_UNVERIFIED and no accepted outputs. This does not turn successful native actions into failed tests or grant permission to replay their commands. Inspect the run's diagnostic and retained native evidence before retrying. The result must contain an outputs array, including an empty array when there are no outputs. Every output supplies its kind (manifest, report or artifact), media type, nonnegative size, path and digest. A missing or malformed array or missing output metadata fails with REMOTE_RESPONSE_INVALID before downloads start, in human and JSON modes, even when the platform reports that the run succeeded. Check the platform's result and client compatibility; the remote run itself is not restarted.

Refusals never fall back to a local build. Platform problems keep their stable code with a REMOTE_ prefix and the platform request id, for example REMOTE_UNAUTHENTICATED (set a current token), REMOTE_REPOSITORY_NOT_LINKED, REMOTE_COMMIT_NOT_FOUND (push first) and REMOTE_VALIDATION_FAILED. Local checks fail before any request: REMOTE_NOT_CONFIGURED, REMOTE_NOT_A_CHECKOUT, REMOTE_REPOSITORY_UNSUPPORTED (not github.com), REMOTE_COMMIT_NOT_PUSHED (HEAD is on no branch of the remote) and REMOTE_AFFECTED_BASE_INVALID. Uncommitted changes produce a warning: they are not part of the run. Requests that fail in transport or answer 503 are retried up to five times with backoff, honoring Retry-After. Creation is retried under the same Idempotency-Key, so a retry never starts a second run. Logs are followed with 30-second long polls over plain HTTPS and resume from the last cursor, so the client works through proxies (HTTPS_PROXY, NO_PROXY, SSL_CERT_FILE) with outbound access alone.

Supply only a credential intended for this client, account and operation through the supported authentication setup. The environment input is a transport, not proof of how a token was issued or its allowed actions. It does not provide token creation, refresh or a safe way to share a person's session with an agent. Never copy a browser session token or put a bearer value in command arguments. The token is sent only to platform.url as a bearer credential. platform.url must be HTTPS; plain HTTP is accepted only for a loopback host, for local development against a mock. Run ids and digests from the platform are validated before they are used in a URL or a file name, and log text is escaped before it reaches the terminal like local child output.

The #479 implementation candidate connects internal admitted native preparation and assigned-plan verification separately from public read-only preview. This has passed the connected real-service flow on Linux, including distinct API/Web workers, an independent whole-build artifact/report comparison, cancellation, retained-byte upload retry, safe worker replacement, coupled prerequisites and required output/report/contribution refusals without implicit replay. The agreed finite cases and exact qualification limits are recorded in distributed build completion. No interactive login; the token comes from OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN. GitHub repositories on github.com only, matching the contract's github provider. Task arguments (-- args) are not supported remotely. --detach, listing runs and re-attaching to a run are not implemented. Broader platform/host qualification remains incomplete; see the linked distributed qualification record and RUNS-08/RUNS-09 in the design page.

oyzu exec -- cargo test --locked --test integration remote_runs: the compiled CLI against a scripted server for a successful build with scoped log replay and verified download, a failing task's exit code and JSON event stream, an expired token and an unpushed HEAD. python tooling/check-runs-contract.py: the contract and its mock, including scoped log entries. python tooling/test-remote-cli.py --cli <compiled-oyzu>: the compiled CLI against the contract mock end to end.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/runtime-matrices.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. A project tests its builds on other runtime versions with verification toolsets in oyzu.toml, and ships a build for several platforms with platforms: in build.yaml. The two never mix: a toolset changes only how a build was checked, a platform changes what ships (configuration split OD1, decided 2026-10-19; implemented in delivery step D4b, with the evidence publication checks in M6b). Runtime versions are never written in build.yaml: the former matrix.<runtime> axis is refused (see migration).

The shipped build is built and tested once, with the [tools] versions. Each toolset adds a verification run: the build's runtime-dependent stages, repeated with the toolset's tools, recording what they verified. A run never produces an artifact, so release selection and publication see one artifact however many toolsets run. # build.yaml: nothing about runtime versions builds: app: uses: node/app # oyzu.toml [tools] node = "22.14.0" # builds, tests and ships the app [toolsets.node24.tools] node = "24.14.1" # also tested on Node 24, in pr, ci and release oyzu pin # locks Node 22.14.0 and the node24 toolset's 24.14.1 oyzu build # local: the app alone oyzu build --verify-with node24 # local: the app and its Node 24 run oyzu build --context ci # ci: the app and its Node 24 run The EX-032 fixture is this project; its scenario runs every case below with the compiled CLI.

Contexts. A toolset runs in every context but local unless it lists contexts = [...] (local, pr, ci, release); contexts = [] turns it, or an inherited definition, off. oyzu build --verify-with NAME (repeatable) adds a toolset's runs in any context, whatever its contexts. Builds. A toolset applies to the builds in its folder chain whose builder uses one of its tools (the builder's tool requirements for its build and test stages): a node toolset adds nothing to a Go build in the same folder. The nearest definition of a name applies whole, as for --toolset. Platforms. One run per toolset, assigned to the build's first declared platform (the host's when the build declares none), unless the toolset lists platforms = [...], which makes one run per listed platform. A run is not multiplied by the build's platforms. Jobs. A job runs the runs assigned to the platform it builds: a plain local build runs the host's, and a job restricted with --platform runs that platform's. Runs assigned to other platforms are named in the build's details (Verification elsewhere) and in the plan, never silently dropped. What a run executes. The build's build and test stages, with the build's own hooks, with the toolset's tools; never lint or format checks (they do not depend on the runtime and run once, with the shipped build) and never packaging or publication. A run runs every check its levels do not turn off in any context, as --full does: it exists to test. Its outputs are not collected; its test and coverage reports are, apart from the shipped build's. What it verified. Each run records verifies: source or verifies: artifact. Every builder implemented today rebuilds and tests the source with the toolset's tools, so runs record source; a builder that installs and tests the built artifact instead (a Python wheel under another interpreter) would declare artifact. A named toolset that no selected build's folder defines fails with CONFIG_TOOLSET_UNKNOWN (listing the defined ones), and one whose tools no selected build uses fails with TOOLSET_NOT_APPLICABLE, before anything runs. A requested run never silently runs elsewhere: when none of a named toolset's runs of a build is assigned to the platform this job builds (the build's first declared platform is not the host, for example), --verify-with and --verify-only fail with VERIFICATION_RUN_NOT_HERE, naming each run, its platform and its command. A toolset whose tools policy refuses fails only a build that executes its run here (TOOLSET_INVALID): plans, --skip-verification jobs and jobs whose run is assigned elsewhere list the run with its requests as written and go on. The stages a run repeats are one shared set (build and test) for every builder. OD1 rule 4 and its cost section call for each builder to declare its own verification stage set; the shared set is a deliberate simplification, accepted in review, and builder-declared stage sets are a named follow-up.

A run is its own target, <build>-verify-<toolset> (with the platform appended when the toolset lists several), shown as its own Plan row: -- Plan ------------------------------------------------------------------------ format lint test build app off off run run app-verify-node24 off off run run The Tools block lists each tool once per version (node 22.14.0 and node 24.14.1). The manifest records the run's target with an oyzu.dev/verification extension: {"build": "app", "toolset": "node24", "platform": "windows/x86_64", "verifies": "source", "reason": "context", "tools": {"node": "24.14.1"}} reason is context when the toolset's contexts include the build's context and requested for --verify-with/--verify-only; tools are the toolset's requests as written, which oyzu.lock resolves. The run's target has no artifacts. A failing test in a run fails the build, with the shipped build's own evidence kept. Verification evidence. Every native build's manifest also records what its builds and their runs verified, under the extension oyzu.dev/verification-evidence, which oyzu publish checks: {"verifyOnly": false, "builds": [{"build": "app", "tests": "passed", "source": {"commit": "5f3b…", "tree": "9c1e…", "digest": "sha256:fc29…"}, "tools": [{"tool": "go", "id": "oyzu:go", "request": "1.24.13", "version": "1.24.13", "ranges": [{"dialect": "go-minimum", "expression": ">=1.24.0", "file": "go.mod", "field": "go"}]}], "notApplicable": [{"tool": "go", "line": "1.23", "native": "go.mod go >=1.24.0", "requiredBy": "project constraint (oyzu.toml [constraints])"}]}], "runs": [{"id": "app-verify-go125", "build": "app", "toolset": "go125", "platform": "windows/x86_64", "verifies": "source", "status": "here", "command": "oyzu build app --verify-only go125", "subject": {"source": {"commit": "5f3b…", "tree": "9c1e…", "digest": "sha256:fc29…"}}, "stages": ["build", "test"], "result": "passed", "tools": [{"tool": "go", "id": "oyzu:go", "request": "1.25", "version": "1.25.14"}]}]} A build entry is each shipped build this job built: source is the source revision its actions ran on, tools the tools its builder uses in the build and test stages with the version oyzu.lock resolves each request to and the native ranges that constrain them (package.json engines, go.mod go), tests whether its own test stage passed, failed or did not-run (a fast local build skips tests), and notApplicable the required lines outside those ranges. A run entry is every run of the selected builds, with its status: here (it ran in this job), other-platform or skipped (--skip-verification), and the command that runs it. A run that ran here adds its subject, the tool identities it ran with, the stages that ran and its result: passed only when every one of its actions passed and its tests ran. A verifies: source run's subject is the source revision it ran on; a verifies: artifact run's subject would be the digests of the build's artifacts in its bundle (no builder declares artifact yet). verifyOnly is true for a --verify-only job: its bundle is evidence only. Source revisions​ verifies: source evidence binds to the source revision (OD1 rule 5, R8). A source revision has: commit and tree: when the build's folder is in a Git work tree and no file of the build's source selection differs from HEAD (by Git's own comparison, after its line-ending conversion) or is untracked, the HEAD commit and the Git tree of the build's folder; digest: always, a SHA-256 over the selected files' paths and contents with CRLF line endings read as LF and executable bits ignored, taken before any action runs. Two revisions are the same source when their digests are equal and, if both record a tree, their trees are equal too. The digest is always required, so an edit Git's index does not show (git update-index --assume-unchanged, --skip-worktree, a filter) still makes a different source; the commit is recorded for provenance only, so another commit with the same tree and content (a change elsewhere in the repository) is the same source. A Windows checkout (core.autocrlf) and a Linux checkout of one commit are the same source, and so are an exported tree and a checkout with the same content. oyzu build --plan --json keeps .matrix for platform builds only and lists every run under a separate .verify key, each with id, build, toolset, platform, runner (OS and architecture), verifies, requested, source (the file defining the toolset), tools, status (here, other-platform, skipped) and the command a dedicated job runs: "verify": [{"id": "app-verify-node24", "build": "app", "toolset": "node24", "platform": "linux/x86_64", "runner": {"os": "linux", "arch": "x86_64"}, "verifies": "source", "requested": false, "source": "oyzu.toml", "tools": {"node": "24.14.1"}, "status": "here", "command": "oyzu build app --verify-only node24"}] The command adds --platform when the build declares platforms.

By default one job builds and then runs every verification run assigned to its platform. To give runs their own jobs, read .verify from a planning job (GitHub Actions reads it with fromJSON) and: run each entry's command in a job on its runner: oyzu build app --verify-only node24 runs only that toolset's runs of the build, not the build's own stages (the builds it depends on are still built); build the platform jobs with --skip-verification, which runs no verification run and names each one it skips as a VERIFICATION_RUN_SKIPPED warning with the command that runs it. --verify-with and --verify-only conflict with --skip-verification, --isolated, --all-platforms, --image and --remote. Pass every job's bundle to oyzu publish (--manifest once per bundle): the platform jobs' bundles supply the artifacts and their builds' evidence, the verification jobs' bundles the runs' evidence. A --verify-only job's bundle is evidence only: the builds its run depends on are built there too, but publication takes no artifact from it, so the same output is never offered from two bundles.

Policy requires tool lines, never toolset names (OD1 rule 3): the setting verification.<tool> lists the lines of a tool ("22", "3.12", "1.24": one to three numbers) a build must have passing verification evidence for before it is published. The tool is named without a namespace (verification.node, not verification.oyzu:node). It is an ordinary per-folder set, so central policy and a root oyzu.toml [constraints] table require lines with a required constraint, limited by when/unless like any constraint, and a project can list its own: # root oyzu.toml [constraints."verification.go"] required = ["1.23", "1.24", "1.25", "1.26"] when = { context = ["pr", "ci", "release"] } # optional For each line a build's builder needs the tool for (its build and test stages), in the build's own folder and context: Outside the native range: not applicable. A line no version of which satisfies the build's native range (package.json engines.node, the go.mod go minimum) is never run. The manifest records it under notApplicable, naming the requirement and the native file and range (go.mod go >=1.24.0), and publication accepts it. Other native ranges (requires-python, rust-version) are not evaluated: such a line runs, and its tool resolution reports the conflict. An organization that needs a support floor constrains tools.<name> instead. Covered. The build's own [tools] request in the line (its tests run with it) covers it everywhere. A toolset the build's folder sees whose request for the tool is in the line covers it only in the contexts its runs run in: a toolset with contexts = [] never does, one with contexts = ["release"] only in release builds (or when named with --verify-with/--verify-only). Otherwise a run is added as if a toolset policy-<tool>-<line> (policy-go-1_26, dots becoming _) requesting the line were defined in the root oyzu.toml: target <build>-verify-policy-<tool>-<line>, listed in .verify with requiredBy (verification.go = 1.26 (project constraint (oyzu.toml [constraints]))) and its command (oyzu build app --verify-only policy-go-1_26). It runs where a toolset's runs do: in every context but local (a required constraint whose when names the local context also runs it locally), in the contexts where no covering toolset runs, on the build's first declared platform; policy still binds its tool. --verify-with policy-go-1_26 adds it in any context. oyzu pin locks it in a set labelled toolset = "policy-go-1_26" when the requirement applies in the context pin runs in and some context it runs in has no covering toolset (pin with OYZU_CONTEXT=release oyzu pin for a release-only requirement); a build whose lock already pins other tools but lacks the line fails with TOOL_LOCK_STALE and the remedy oyzu pin. oyzu build --plan shows the requirement as a CONFIG_CONSTRAINT_OVERRIDE (or policy override) note; oyzu config explain verification.go shows where each line comes from.

oyzu publish resolves verification.<tool> again when it publishes, in each published build's folder and in the publication's context, so a requirement added between build and release still applies. For every published build, each required line of each tool its record lists must be settled by the evidence of the bundles given with --manifest: not applicable (outside the recorded native range); the build's own tests: its bundle records its tests passed with a version of the tool in the line (a fast local build skips tests; build with --full, or in a ci or release context); a run: a run of the same build in any given bundle that ran (status: here), passed, used a version in the line and verified the published build: its source subject is the build's source revision (verifies: source), or its artifact digests include the published artifact's (verifies: artifact). Otherwise publication fails before evidence loading, signing or any network access, with every unsettled line, why, and the commands of the runs the build left to other jobs (a run another given bundle ran and that settled a line is not listed): ✗ PUBLISH_VERIFICATION_MISSING: no passing verification evidence for app go 1.25 (required by project constraint (oyzu.toml [constraints])): no run with go 1.25 was given. … Run what is missing (the runs this build left to other jobs: oyzu build app --verify-only go125) and pass every bundle with --manifest. Nothing was sent A bundle without verification evidence (written by the isolated executor, which does not record it yet) does not say which tools its build uses, so publication refuses its build when any verification.<tool> line applies in the build's folder, whatever the tool. A published receipt lists how each line was settled under verification, and the human output under Required verification: Required verification app go 1.23 not applicable: outside go.mod go >=1.24.0 · required by project constraint (oyzu.toml [constraints]) app go 1.24 the build's own tests (1.24.13) · required by project constraint (oyzu.toml [constraints]) app go 1.25 run app-verify-go125 (1.25.14) · required by project constraint (oyzu.toml [constraints])

oyzu pin locks every toolset's tools beside the [tools] tools, each toolset's in its own set labelled toolset = "NAME", whatever the context and whether or not a build uses them; oyzu --toolset NAME pin locks one toolset. Plain oyzu update re-resolves [tools] and then every toolset. A build whose lock lacks a run's tools installs and locks them like any other tool request; the toolset lock rules apply. A toolset neither command can lock, one a nested folder defines (TOOLSET_NESTED_LOCK) or one whose tools policy refuses, is left out and named, with the reason, under Toolsets not locked (toolsetsNotLocked in JSON); the rest is still locked and the command succeeds. Decided before anything is written, so a command never locks one set and then fails on another. A build's run that needs such a toolset fails when it runs. Native ranges still constrain every run: a toolset Node outside package.json engines fails when its tools are resolved, naming the constraint.

Runs execute on the native host executor. A build that takes the isolated (captured) executor (--isolated, --image, --all-platforms, slices and remote pool builds, or a builder without a native host path, such as pnpm or Yarn Node builds) and has runs fails with VERIFICATION_RUN_UNSUPPORTED, naming them, and so does its --plan. Build natively where the builders allow it, or add --skip-verification, which lists the runs as skipped in the plan and warns VERIFICATION_RUN_SKIPPED for each in the build. oyzu build --remote cannot pass --skip-verification to the pool (the request carries no build options). A pool job is a CI build: it runs in the context it detects or is pinned to, normally ci (release for a release), never local. So a toolset with the default contexts makes a remote build fail; for remote builds, list contexts the pool does not use, for example contexts = ["local", "pr"] to verify locally on request and in pull requests built by a host CI job. oyzu build --remote --plan evaluates toolsets in the context of the machine running the plan (local unless --context says otherwise), so it does not predict the pool's refusal; pass --context ci to see what a pool job would reject. Running verification runs on the pool is a named follow-up. No builder declares verifies: artifact yet: every run tests the source, and the artifact binding is implemented but unexercised. Only the native host executor records verification evidence; an isolated build's bundle has none, so publication refuses it when any verification.<tool> line applies in the build's folder. The check that the work tree holds HEAD covers the build's folder: an uncommitted change to a declared inputs file outside it does not stop the revision from naming the commit. Not applicable is decided for engines.node and the go.mod go minimum only. Runs of a build whose platform this job builds with a cross toolchain are placed here as for any platform; whether tests run there follows the builder's cross-build rules.

build.yaml no longer accepts matrix (in either shape). A runtime axis is refused with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE and the toolset form built from the file's own values: CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE: app: matrix.node is no longer accepted: build.yaml says what ships, and tool versions belong in oyzu.toml. The build ships once, built with [tools]; each other version is a verification-only toolset that tests the build in pr, ci and release (add one locally with oyzu build --verify-with NAME). Remove matrix from build.yaml and add to oyzu.toml: [tools] node = "22.14.0" [toolsets.node24.tools] node = "24.14.1" See docs/reference/runtime-matrices.md The old axis built and kept one complete artifact per runtime, each in its own provisioned image; a toolset builds one artifact and verifies the others, so a release no longer holds two artifacts for one output. matrix.platform remains refused in favor of platforms:. Shipping a separate artifact per runtime ABI (OD11) is a different, deferred job.

builds: api: uses: go/app path: api image: uses: docker/image platforms: [linux/x86_64, linux/arm64] materialize: - from: api to: bin/server This authored EX-027 shape expands into two image variants, each bound to a producer variant for the same platform. Requirements propagate transitively through materialize, including named artifacts and directories. A producer's own platforms list constrains those requirements; conflicts identify the consumer's required platforms and the producer's allowed platforms. Ordering-only depends_on and foreign task prerequisites do not propagate platform requirements. Same-target task prerequisites retain their variant identity. An unconstrained producer retains a standalone instance for explicit commands such as oyzu build api. Selecting image selects only its matching producer variants. Building the whole workspace omits an extra standalone producer when its consumers already demand platform variants; an ordering/task dependency can still explicitly require that standalone instance. The selection record includes all concrete IDs and identifies excluded instances. Standalone instances also count toward the 256-instance bound. If a retained standalone instance cannot uniquely choose among a dependency's declared platform variants, selecting it fails with an ambiguity error before preparation. Its valid explicitly platform-bound instances remain usable. Resolve the ambiguity with a producer/consumer platform declaration; Oyzu does not guess from the host. Other invalid declarations and conflicting constraints remain workspace-wide validation errors. platforms is the only way to declare artifact platforms: the platform axis is internal to expansion, and the retired platform: <os/arch> and matrix.platform spellings are refused with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE naming platforms: [...] (configuration split M5). OS/architecture values with the usual aliases are accepted and stored canonically. Each builder admits those values separately against its actual executor capabilities. Native builders currently require matching toolchain execution, so the example above still fails before application actions when the only provisioned Go worker is amd64. Cross-compiling a binary would not prove ARM tests passed. Docker can assemble separate amd64/arm64 scratch images on its amd64 worker when no target code is executed; see Docker platform admission. Complete selected families produce separate versioned image archives plus a complete OCI index. Automatic platform-independent producer reuse, ABI/runtime compatibility, remote worker selection and full EX-027/050 acceptance remain unfinished. Local platform-specific toolchain selection is described in toolchain platforms. Equal bytes, a directory artifact or a successful cross-platform assembly do not establish any of those capabilities. Platform-constrained targets record a platform variant axis. Inferred producer variants receive deterministic concrete IDs, even for a single requested consumer platform. Resolve their identities through the selection mapping and materialization receipts instead of assuming that the logical producer name is its artifact target ID. A target that declares exactly one platform keeps its logical ID; several declared platforms give each instance a platform-qualified ID. Variant IDs are portable and deterministic, derived from the logical name and platform with a digest suffix when normalization is needed; expansion rejects case-insensitive ID collisions and bounds the workspace to 256 target instances and 16,384 copied tasks. A build's tasks and hooks are copied per instance, including the unqualified root hooks and stage replacements task binding gives it; in a workspace with one logical target, a root workspace task (neither a hook nor a stage) that an instance reaches through a prerequisite uses an internal root- task alias. Expansion uses the frozen build inventory and never rewrites build.yaml. Complete selected OCI image platform families produce an additional OCI index artifact. Partial dependency selections keep their individual images without synthesizing an incomplete index. Aggregate targets are derived plan records outside the source-variant selection list.

Verification runs: build::verification_runs tests (contexts, --verify-with, --verify-only, --skip-verification, platform assignment, nearest definition and contexts = [], unknown and inapplicable toolsets, the isolated-executor refusal and pin instances), build::variants tests (a run's tasks, bound root hooks and stage replacements and dependencies; a run is never a producer), config::sources toolset parsing, config::build_model matrix refusal, and the compiled-CLI configuration_cli tests for .verify, contexts and platforms. The EX-032 scenario runs the example with real Node 22 and 24 downloads: oyzu pin, a ci build with one artifact and a Node 24 run recording verifies: source, a local build without the run and with --verify-with, the --skip-verification and --verify-only fan-out, a test failing only on Node 24, and the refused matrix.node. Measured results are in the D4b status entry. Verification evidence and required lines (M6b): config::verification tests (native ranges, lines, selectors), build::verification_runs (a required line no toolset covers becomes a labelled run, locally only on request), build::verification_evidence (which evidence settles a line), the publication presentation test, and the compiled-CLI publish_cli::a_build_lacking_evidence_for_a_required_tool_line_is_refused. The EX-032 scenario checks the evidence of the ci build and that the dedicated --verify-only job's run verifies the platform job's source. The compiled-CLI proof (a Go app built, verified on Go 1.25 in a separate job and on a policy-added Go 1.26 run, refused and then published to a local OCI registry) is in the M6b status entry. Platform matrices: tests exercise transitive propagation, explicit constraint conflicts, ordering versus artifact dependencies, local/foreign task binding, stable IDs and standalone selection against the authored EX-050 project. The captured Docker suite requires two actual OCI images with matching architecture, separate JUnit/quality evidence and repeated snapshot identities; it also checks EX-027's missing target-execution and conflicting producer failures. The Go suite checks EX-049's inferred producer variant and named artifact bytes. OCI index assembly and its pending native verification are described in the index reference.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/rust.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. The in-development native local build is selected by plain oyzu build for one inferred or explicitly declared Rust target. Use oyzu build --isolated for the captured behavior below. Adding --plan produces a read-only preview, not dependency capture. The native bootstrap milestone is not yet acceptance-verified. Rust build, test, doctest and packaging orchestration runs in compiled Oyzu adapters. Host and isolated plans select the private compiled entry point; the former Python adapter files have been removed. Rust requirement discovery does not list Python. Cargo, Nextest, LLVM coverage tools and the applicable linker/SDK remain prerequisites. Explicit task overrides retain their own requirements. Broader host report-gate and rebuilt isolated-suite qualification remain pending; the registry-backreference corpus proof below qualifies that specific rebuilt flow. See the migration checkpoint. The experimental Rust builder discovers Cargo.toml without Oyzu configuration. Cargo owns workspace membership, native package metadata and dependency resolution. Captured builds currently support single packages and contained local workspaces, including libraries, binaries, proc macros and build scripts. Locked crates.io dependencies are captured before execution. Private/alternate registry and Git acquisition, and cross-compilation, remain unfinished. Artifact version selection now uses the shared version inference resolver for native, exact-tag and nearest-tag/commit snapshots. Release authorization remains separate and unimplemented. Workspace members resolve independently using their native path-dependency closure. A relevant dependency commit participates in the consumer's version analysis; an unrelated member's commit does not. Root workspace inputs conservatively affect all members. Private manifests and packaged local dependency requirements use each member's selected version; equal native version strings do not establish a release group. Captured builds preserve a member's original declared version when Cargo's resolved registry graph contains a dependency on a registry package with that member's name. Cargo package verification re-resolves through the workspace's private packaging registry; a projected prerelease can otherwise conflict with the registry dependency's release range. Only affected members retain declared versions, and local path requirements use those retained versions. Unaffected members still receive their normal snapshot versions. Inactive dependency declarations alone do not trigger preservation. These artifacts remain snapshots. The existing oyzu.dev/versioning evidence records reason: cargo-registry-backreference, the source digest and captured Git/input-scope facts, intent: snapshot and productionEligible: false even when the archive uses a release-shaped declared version. Use the build bundle's source identity and artifact digest to distinguish snapshots with the same native version. This correction does not authorize publication or repair other Cargo dependency cycles. See native qualification. Local development-dependency cycles can be packaged in captured builds when their ordinary and build-dependency edges remain acyclic. Oyzu groups only members involved in a development cycle and asks native Cargo to package that group together. Its provisional package command uses --locked --offline --exclude-lockfile --no-verify; the provisional archives are admitted only to an invocation-private registry after native index identities and archive checksums match. Oyzu then packages every member separately with native verification enabled, --locked --offline --exclude-lockfile, and requires each final archive to be byte-identical to its provisional counterpart before admitting any group member as a final artifact. Acyclic members retain ordinary per-member packaging and their existing archive contents. Affected cycle archives omit Cargo.lock, so a consumer cannot use cargo install --locked against such an archive; use the source workspace with its original lock or resolve the published package normally. Declared versioned development dependencies remain in the normalized manifest. Ordinary/build dependency cycles, unsupported registry backreferences in a cycle group, changed external identities and native verification failures still stop packaging. See the measured qualification. When the original lock contains a different registry version of an affected member, the packaging adapter lets native Cargo align its invocation-private lock with checksum-verified workspace archives after their promotion. It uses the original native registry package IDs and precise retained versions, offline; package verification remains --locked --offline. Every resulting identity must be an original captured input or a verified owned archive. Native pruning is reported, and the execution copy's original lock/configuration are restored on success or failure. Source checkout files and the captured registry remain unchanged. Same-version archive collisions, incompatible native ranges or uncaptured external changes still fail and block final artifacts. Native Windows drive/UNC path prefixes are translated only at the Cargo configuration boundary; non-UTF-8 registry paths fail rather than losing identity. The pinned clap corpus now completes oyzu build --isolated --full using the rebuilt worker image and exact image override recorded in qualification, delivering eight native crates, a working Linux binary and all three required reports. Installed/default images and public distribution were not updated. Three members retain their declared versions while five retain normal snapshot projection; all eight decisions retain snapshot identity and no release authority. Coverage collection passed at zero of 73 lines, which is not positive application coverage. See the commands, artifacts and limits. Plain local oyzu build selects the host and retains quality gates. Use --platform <os/arch> to cross-compile one other platform natively, or --all-platforms for the declared matrix through the captured executor. See build selection and checks.

oyzu build --platform <os/arch[/abi]> builds a Rust target for another platform with this host's pinned toolchain: cargo build --target <triple> with the target's linker. Oyzu decides from host facts and file lookups alone (nothing is installed or run while planning) and shows the result in Plan for every declared platform (platforms and executors): Target platform Triple Linker Available when linux/<arch> (default, published as -musl), linux/<arch>/musl <arch>-unknown-linux-musl rust-lld (self-contained, ships with every Rust toolchain) always; pure-Rust crates only linux/<arch>/gnu <arch>-unknown-linux-gnu <arch>-linux-gnu-gcc it is on PATH windows/<arch> on a Windows host, windows/<arch>/msvc <arch>-pc-windows-msvc MSVC Visual Studio's VC/Tools/MSVC/<version>/lib/<x64 or arm64> is installed windows/<arch> elsewhere, windows/<arch>/gnullvm <arch>-pc-windows-gnullvm <arch>-w64-mingw32-clang (LLVM MinGW) it is on PATH windows/<arch>/gnu <arch>-pc-windows-gnu <arch>-w64-mingw32-gcc it is on PATH darwin/<arch> <arch>-apple-darwin Apple clang the host is macOS; elsewhere needs a macOS runner The defaults are musl for Linux, MSVC on a Windows host and LLVM MinGW elsewhere; an ABI in the platform name (linux/arm64/gnu) overrides them. The host's own machine (and its default ABI: GNU on Linux, MSVC on Windows) builds as a host build; a musl build of the host's machine is a cross build. The target's standard library must be in the pinned toolchain: a cross-built target adds rust-std@<triple> to its tool requirements, and preparation refuses with PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE when rustc --print target-libdir --target <triple> has none. Outputs go to dist/<target>/<platform>/ with the target's executable suffix, and static executable verification checks the format and architecture against the target platform without running it. Limits: a crate that compiles C code (the cc crate) needs a C cross compiler the rust-lld route does not provide; tests, coverage and doctests are not run for a cross-built platform here (--full with --platform would try to run foreign executables); and cargo-zigbuild is not used. A project can require a cross build for a platform with build.executors; a release then cross-compiles it as declared or fails. Demonstrated on Windows 11 x86_64 for linux/arm64 (see the status entry).

A [tools] rust = "1.95.0" declaration in oyzu.toml selects the matching oyzu.lock environment for the captured target scope and profile. The current container worker consumes a linux/<architecture>/gnu installation from the workspace's .oyzu/tools store. This is the compiler's execution platform; artifact platforms in build.yaml do not change it into a macOS or Windows tool. Only a Rust-only declared tool selection is supported by this initial handoff. Before package acquisition or Cargo execution, OYZU verifies the locked request, current backend/installer identity, complete installation receipts and payload contents. It leases the installation while copying it into the private dependency snapshot, then verifies the copied tree against the receipt. Preparation and build actions use its Cargo, rustc and rustdoc; the plan fixes their command environment. The dependency evidence records the request, selection, installation, backend, lock and copied-tree identities. The live tool store is not mounted in containers. Missing or stale locks, missing worker distributions, absent installations, unsupported layouts and changed payloads fail without falling back to image Rust. This path does not resolve versions, install tools, edit the lock or use the network for tool restoration. Provision the matching worker installation first. Existing oyzu install currently provisions its host only; installing Linux compiler selections from a Windows host is still unfinished. No new project-specific build flag is required. Builds without explicit tool requests retain the existing provisioned-image behavior. The image continues to provide native OS prerequisites, format/lint and reporting utilities; this handoff does not qualify those as locked tools or establish cross-compilation support. On Unix controllers, the Linux restoration container runs as the owner of its private input directory, following the shared executor's user mapping. Its input remains read-only and private; restoration keeps networking disabled, a read-only root filesystem and all capabilities dropped. This avoids permission failures when the controller's temporary files are inaccessible to the image's default user. Windows retains its existing Docker user behavior. A bounded Linux Rust 1.99.1 app proof passed two full isolated builds, native crate verification, JUnit 1/1 and application coverage 6/9 lines. The delivered binary ran read-only without networking and printed Hello, Oyzu!; both artifact digests and original source bytes were unchanged on repeat. The flow reused a previously verified packaged compiler, then restored it into a read-only action volume. The new controller and unchanged worker have separately recorded source identities. See the qualification and limits; this does not establish fresh installation on every build, the full Rust corpus or Windows/full-Bookworm worker qualification. Verification: on a Linux controller using the local Docker engine, python3 tooling/test-build-model.py --cli <compiled-cli> --locked-rust <Rust-1.95-sysroot> uses a real compiler with explicitly synthetic test lock/receipt provenance. It proves plain oyzu build produces and executes the feature-enabled binary, records compiler 1.95 despite image Rust 1.94, and rejects missing/stale locks and a corrupted payload before actions. This fixture does not prove installation or download provenance. Native Windows cannot attest the Linux executable modes in its NTFS store; automatic Linux worker provisioning remains unfinished.

The CLI accepts builds.<name> with the shared fields listed in build inventory migration and builder-owned with. Rust accepts with.features, a list of unique Cargo feature names. Features apply to native metadata resolution, builds, lint, tests, doctests and package verification. Native default features remain enabled. Unknown options fail; options are not arbitrary command strings. with.artifacts selects all (the existing default) or binaries. On the captured path, all delivers the discovered binaries and eligible workspace crate archives; binaries delivers only enabled Cargo binaries and does not schedule crate packaging. Native local builds already deliver binaries; the explicit binaries choice additionally refuses an empty enabled-binary inventory on both paths. Feature-gated binaries require their native Cargo features. This choice preserves compilation, selected checks, required reports and executable validation. It does not change Cargo publication rules or permit failed build outputs to be exported. In particular, publishable workspace packages with unpublished path dependencies can fail ordinary crate packaging because Cargo does not register unpublished dependencies in its packaging registry. A target whose required output is an executable can explicitly select binaries. builds: cli: uses: rust/app platforms: [linux/x86_64] with: features: [integration] artifacts: binaries Run oyzu build for the native host, or oyzu build --all-platforms for the declared matrix. The existing captured execution path still requires the provisioned Linux Rust builder image described below and captures crates.io inputs before offline execution. Outputs and reports remain in the verified dist bundle. An omitted platform uses the existing executor platform; an explicit list expands every declared platform on the captured path. The native local default selects the current host from that list; --platform selects another one, built natively by a cross toolchain when this host has one. Explicit Rust requests now use the locked-tool handoff below. Pinned public GitHub acquisition is implemented through the scoped broker; private Git remains unsupported. The repository's six-platform self-build is not yet working. Other proposed shared fields and other builders' with options fail explicitly until their adapters implement them. The rust: object is gone (configuration split M4): Cargo features are with.features and cross-compilation targets are platforms entries, below. New named builds reject legacy language objects, tool versions, runtime matrices, unknown shared fields, and empty, repeated or suffixed platform declarations. tooling/test-build-model.py --cli <compiled-cli> exercises the new authoring through a real Linux build, feature-required compilation, reports, packaging, bundle inspection and execution of the collected binary. It is not six-platform self-build evidence.

A Rust build names the platforms it ships in platforms, never as Cargo target triples. The former rust: object, whose targets list generated <target>:build-<triple> tasks for oyzu run, is refused with CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE naming this replacement; nothing generates those tasks any more (configuration split M4). builds: cli: uses: rust/app with: features: [mise-integration] platforms: [linux/x86_64, linux/arm64/musl, windows/x86_64, darwin/arm64] Former rust.targets triple platforms entry x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu linux/x86_64 on a Linux x86_64 host (its compiler's own target), otherwise linux/x86_64/gnu aarch64-unknown-linux-musl linux/arm64 cross-built (musl is the cross default) or linux/arm64/musl x86_64-pc-windows-msvc windows/x86_64 on Windows, or windows/x86_64/msvc x86_64-pc-windows-gnu, -gnullvm windows/x86_64/gnu, windows/x86_64/gnullvm aarch64-apple-darwin darwin/arm64 oyzu build --platform <os/arch[/abi]> builds one of them on this host: the host platform as a host build, another one with the native cross toolchain. Routing checks only that the target's linker is present: a crate whose build script compiles C (ring, through the cc crate) also needs a C cross compiler for the target, which the rust-lld route does not provide, so such a build fails in that build script. Build those platforms with the container executor instead (--isolated, or "linux/arm64" = "container" under build.executors), whose oyzu-toolchain/rust-cross:v1 image supplies the C cross compilers, or on a runner of that platform. oyzu build --plan --json lists every declared platform with the runner and executor it needs, so a CI matrix builds each on its own runner; this repository's release workflow builds its six platforms that way. A project that needs a particular executor declares it with build.executors. The Cargo features in with.features apply to every platform's build, test, lint and archive stages. Outputs go to dist/<target>/<platform>/. Limits: only x86_64 and arm64 on Linux, Windows and macOS have platform names, so a triple outside them (for example riscv64gc-unknown-linux-gnu) has no replacement yet; a build is not a raw cargo build --target, so it applies Oyzu's admission, tool requirements and artifact collection; and one run builds one native platform per target.
documents.s: Platforms instead of Cargo target triples

documents.t: oyzu run list oyzu run build oyzu run test oyzu run lint oyzu run format-check oyzu build --plan oyzu build oyzu inspect dist Development tasks use already provisioned Cargo, rustfmt and Clippy on the host. Static task listing reads native manifests without executing Cargo. Implicit tasks include fetch (cargo fetch --locked), executable installation (cargo install --path . --locked), workspace build/test, Clippy, formatting, formatting checks and archive. Fetch and install are explicit development tasks, not automatic build stages. oyzu run format modifies source; captured builds use read-only format-check. Direct test execution uses native host state and the shared test-only dist/ report collector; platform-specific evidence is recorded below. Native Cargo workspace ownership is distinct from separate Oyzu target groups.
