Native test plans use the same platform-qualified output contract as captured plans: JUnit, Cobertura and doctest reports belong under dist/<target>/<platform>/reports/. The shared host executor translates that output contract to its private bundle and honors declared report destinations; report paths are not relative to the Cargo workspace. Required collection and the 16 MiB report limit still apply. Captured builds require Docker and this explicitly provisioned Linux amd64 image: Run the following from the repository root: the image build copies Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock and src/ to compile its worker. The repository provisioning script uses the same root build context. Host development execution does not use this image. docker build -f tooling/images/rust.Dockerfile -t oyzu-toolchain/rust:1.99.1-nextest0.9.146-llvmcov0.9.1 . The image recipe selects Rust 1.99.1, rustfmt, Clippy, LLVM tools, cargo-nextest 0.9.146, cargo-llvm-cov 0.9.1 and the compiled Oyzu worker at /usr/local/libexec/oyzu/oyzu. Its separate image-build stage compiles that worker with Rust 1.99.1; Python is not installed. Custom --image cargo=<image> profiles must supply the same capabilities, including a compatible worker. Rebuild older images before using these plans. Tool/image provisioning is explicit and separate from project execution. Oyzu does not download a missing toolchain image. The updated image recipe has not yet completed isolated-build qualification. Docker dependency contexts use the narrower rust/cargo provider. Its standard Rust 1.94.0 consumer image needs no Python, nextest or llvm-cov. It validates the original lock/workspace and exports only the native registry, without artifact version projection or report setup. The tool requirements above still apply to ordinary rust/app and rust/library builds. The CLI supports Windows, macOS and Linux; that does not imply a native captured-build executor on each host. Current isolated Rust acceptance runs on Linux with Docker. The native artifact probe also runs separately on all three CI hosts. See implementation status for revision-specific evidence.
documents.s: Ordinary tasks and isolated build prerequisites

documents.t: A checked-in Cargo.lock is required. Preparation admits its complete registry inventory before issuing any requests. The current standalone source profile permits crates.io index entries through https://index.crates.io/ and archives through https://static.crates.io/crates/, using the shared host transport and its redirect/size/request limits. A different registry or an unsupported Git host fails explicitly; there is no direct Cargo network fallback. This fixed public profile is not yet enterprise connector routing or private Cargo authentication. Public GitHub sources must carry a full commit identity in Cargo.lock. Native Cargo and Git fetch through repository-scoped broker routes inside a container with networking disabled. The broker admits only smart-HTTP discovery and upload pack requests, with the existing size, redirect and request limits. Cargo checks out the pinned objects and resolves the package graph; OYZU captures the bare object database and reconstructs checkouts privately for offline build actions. This preserves Git repositories containing Unix symlinks on Windows controllers. Git evidence records object identity, not a publisher signature. Private Git, other hosts, submodule routing and Git LFS are not qualified. Only publishable workspace packages are archived. A publish = false package (an empty publish list) never gets a .crate: a private application delivers its executables instead, even when its only binary is feature-gated off (a test fixture or development tool is then neither archived nor shipped), and a private library is workspace internals that no registry accepts. Private packages still build, lint and test with the workspace. Before 2026-10-20 private libraries were archived too, which failed whenever one depended on another (this repository's oyzu-plugin-sdk on oyzu-plugin-protocol: no matching package named oyzu-plugin-protocol found), because Cargo leaves unpublishable packages out of its packaging registry. Publishable packages retain native Cargo packaging and verification; one that depends on a private library still fails with Cargo's own message. The archive inventory and the plan select the same packages. tooling/test-build-git.py exercises a real dependency from the pinned mise fork, compiles offline, executes the resulting binary and checks the build bundle. The Windows-hosted proof produced the binary and three reports; it is not evidence of the complete CLI platform matrix. Each locked registry package must have a SHA-256 checksum. Acquisition requires matching index metadata and archive bytes, then captures the archive and only the locked version's index entry in Cargo's native local-registry format. If a cached index entry omits a locked version, online preparation fetches that entry once through the approved broker source and checks it again. Offline preparation fails with a hint to rerun online; it never refreshes from the network. Duplicate matching entries and checksum disagreements remain errors. Cargo owns extraction, checksum revalidation, resolution and compilation. No project code runs during host acquisition. This avoids implementing a second Cargo resolver or unpacking untrusted crates on the host. When the lock contains only local workspace packages, preparation writes no registry replacement into the private Cargo home. Locked offline execution still applies. This preserves Cargo's native temporary registry for packaging unpublished workspace dependencies; replacing crates.io with an empty registry prevents that resolution. Single packages with captured registry dependencies retain source replacement. For a workspace combining local path dependencies and registry inputs, the Rust adapter packages acyclic members in dependency order using a private writable copy of the captured registry. Each acyclic member runs native cargo package --locked --offline --allow-dirty --registry crates-io --package <name> with verification enabled. Cargo generates the normalized archive and its temporary registry entry; the adapter checks their planned name/version and matching SHA-256 before admitting them into that private copy for dependent members. It does not generate Cargo index entries or resolve dependency versions. Local ordering uses native manifest paths, including renamed/optional dependencies. Development-cycle groups use the conditional native staging and verification flow described above. Ordinary/build dependency cycles and paths without a workspace owner fail planning explicitly. The original captured registry is immutable. The adapter restores the action's Cargo source configuration and removes its temporary registry on ordinary success or failure; sandbox cleanup owns abrupt termination. Captured packages remain inputs, while only the workspace's planned artifacts can reach dist/. Identity/checksum conflicts, a collision with an already captured name/version, an index over 4 MiB or an archive over 128 MiB fail packaging. Repair the native package input or manifest and rebuild; there is no network fallback. The conditional provisional native command skips verification only while staging an affected development-cycle group; every final member archive must pass native verification and byte comparison before admission. Registry publication restrictions in native manifests still apply to this explicit crates.io packaging profile; private-registry publication remains unfinished. Preparation then checks the original lock using native offline Cargo resolution, projects workspace package versions and contained workspace dependency requirements into private manifests, and regenerates the private lock with Cargo. Source files remain unchanged. Unresolved paths and paths outside the captured target fail preparation. Registry packages keep their locked versions and remain inputs; they do not become this workspace's published artifacts. Prepared input records contain each archive's name, version, digest and size. digest-only verification means matching recorded content, not a publisher signature or release authorization. Dependency edges and per-package purpose distinctions are not yet modeled in this inventory. Acquisition currently requires the approved upstreams to be reachable on each fresh preparation; persistent offline acquisition reuse is not implemented. Once preparation succeeds, build execution reads the captured registry with network access denied. Versions retain each package's base version and use a source-derived suffix, such as 1.2.3-dev.g<source-prefix>. Different workspace packages retain their individual base versions. These are snapshot versions; they do not establish release eligibility or production trust. Build execution runs workspace release compilation, native tests with reporting, Clippy, rustfmt checking, native verified crate packaging and final collection. Commands use locked offline inputs and the shared executor denies networking. Build scripts and proc macros execute inside that environment and must work with the captured inputs. The selected compiler host target, .oyzu-build/target output root, private Cargo home and offline setting are fixed plan facts; a task environment cannot redirect them. The owned command wrapper installs captured source configuration into that private home so Clippy, nextest and coverage subprocesses inherit it. Custom native source overrides are not supported by this public profile and can fail offline resolution; other native Cargo settings remain in the captured project. Tests run through cargo llvm-cov nextest; native JUnit and Cobertura are retained under dist/ and indexed with paths, digests and summaries in dist/manifest.json. Test execution and coverage generation retain independent failure outcomes. Missing or invalid required reports fail collection. inspect dist checks bundle integrity, not release authorization. The native Cobertura export uses --skip-functions to omit redundant per-function records while retaining source-line and branch details. Oyzu's coverage gate consumes covered and valid source-line counts; the report collector's 16 MiB limit is unchanged. A real Windows MSVC full self-build accepted an 11,775,479-byte report. A same-profile export without --skip-functions was 23,068,338 bytes; all 595 source files and their complete source-line/branch records and metrics matched, including the collected report. Native branch totals were zero, so this does not qualify nonzero branch instrumentation. The full-build proof records pinned tools, driver/source attribution, unchanged controls and the earlier failed attempts. Cargo doctests run as part of the same implicit test gate because nextest does not execute them. Prepared native Cargo metadata selects workspace packages with a doctest-enabled target, honoring native doctest = false. Each selected package runs cargo test --doc --locked --offline --package <name> in the captured workspace. Binary-only targets and registry dependencies do not create doctest invocations. Preparation layout version 5 retains the native doctest selection and relocatable binary inventory; old prepared metadata must be regenerated. The additional required doctest.xml report has one case per Cargo invocation, identified by package name, with bounded native diagnostics. Its suite properties explicitly describe this scope. Counts are invocation outcomes, not the number of individual documentation examples: a doctest-enabled package with no examples can have a successful invocation. Stable Cargo owns assertion semantics; Oyzu does not parse human console text into invented case counts. Native nonzero exits produce failures; launch errors produce errors. Native doctest stdout and stderr stream through the host executor while the report retains bounded diagnostic prefixes. Compilation and doctest execution have no separate per-package timer; any enclosing executor deadline still applies. Other selected packages still run after a package fails. Each invocation starts with fresh report output; prior success cannot satisfy a failed launch. Doctest failures block artifact collection even if nextest and coverage generation succeed. Inspect the named report and native diagnostics to repair the example, compilation or provisioned rustdoc/linker environment, then rebuild. Task replacement retains this additional report obligation. The existing coverage report measures nextest execution only: doctest coverage and individual doctest JUnit cases remain unfinished, as do every custom nextest configuration and broader framework support. Compilation, tests, lint, formatting and archive verification are required gates. Their failures block final artifacts. Native logs and available reports explain the failed stage. Repair the native input and rerun; an earlier successful bundle is retained under .oyzu/history, not reused as this build's successful output.

oyzu run test produces nextest JUnit, native LLVM Cobertura coverage and Cargo doctest invocation reports, followed by oyzu inspect dist. The real app/workspace reporting step passed on Windows MSVC, Linux and macOS in run 37049720609 at bfa2b7c. This verifies the direct reporting step, not the entire still-running workflow. The local Windows GNU Rust 1.94.0 compiler lacks profiler_builtins; its earlier coverage failure remains a toolchain limitation. Provision Rust/Cargo with its llvm-tools-preview component and compiler profiler runtime, cargo-nextest 0.9.146 and cargo-llvm-cov 0.9.1. Existing Windows product qualification uses an MSVC compiler and its native linker/SDK for coverage; the local windows-gnu compiler is not supported by this flow. A separate windows-gnullvm tiny-project coverage experiment succeeded without MSVC; see native build prerequisites for its scope and remaining qualification limits. Dependencies must already be installed for locked offline Cargo resolution. Tools are not installed by the product. Missing LLVM tools fail before llvm-cov can request a download; explicit LLVM_COV/LLVM_PROFDATA paths can identify provisioned binaries. After shared task admission, Cargo's native metadata --no-deps --locked --offline supplies workspace membership and doctest-enabled packages. Static run list never invokes Cargo. The exact implicit cargo test --locked --workspace command receives automatic instrumentation. Arbitrary task replacements retain their bodies and required JUnit/coverage/doctest obligations; they do not waive evidence collection. No Oyzu build/test configuration is needed for the default flow. A temporary nextest profile inherits the project's default configuration and supplies fresh JUnit output; the native .config/nextest.toml is not edited. This uses nextest's native profile inheritance. Project coverage/reporting state is not reused: compilation and coverage use private temporary target directories. Native nextest may retain its ordinary store output on the host. Extra command arguments go to the nextest invocation; doctest selection remains the metadata-selected workspace packages. Alternate nextest profiles, arbitrary Cargo test argument compatibility and filtered doctest selection are not implemented by this initial direct adapter. The compiled Rust adapter is shared by captured and direct execution. It runs nextest, attempts coverage generation independently of a failed test, and runs stable Cargo doctests. Any failed phase fails the task. Doctest reports count package invocations, not individual examples, and doctest execution is not included in nextest coverage. Custom native settings, build scripts and proc macros retain their normal execution semantics. Direct reports disclose host execution and unverified tool identity; Cargo's offline flags are not a host network sandbox. See direct test bundle boundaries. python tooling/test-rust-direct.py --cli <compiled-path> uses EX-021 and EX-022: implicit task listing, default-profile settings, native JUnit/Cobertura, successful and failed tests, independent doctest failure, unchanged source/configuration and bundle inspection. It requires tooling/design-requirements.txt for report-contract validation. CI explicitly provisions the pinned reporters with tooling/provision-rust-reporting.py after downloading the compiled CLI. The three-host direct-reporting steps passed at bfa2b7c; broader native profile and argument combinations remain outside that probe.

With the default captured with.artifacts: all, selected publishable workspace packages produce native <package>-<selected-version>.crate archives. Packages declaring publish = false or an empty publish list do not produce crate archives. Each enabled binary additionally produces <binary>-<selected-version>-<compiler-host>. Explicit with.artifacts: binaries selects only executable outputs and refuses a library-only inventory. The selected version is normally a projected snapshot; resolved registry backreferences retain the affected member's declared version as described above. Manifest names use the existing scoped crate- and bin- identities. Under the default choice, a publishable library-only package has a crate artifact without an invented executable. Duplicate binary names currently fail planning instead of colliding in the output bundle. Cargo's resolved features determine whether a binary with required-features is enabled. An unmet feature gate omits that binary from the artifact plan; enabling the feature through native defaults or with.features includes it. This does not add a feature matrix or new CLI feature-selection syntax. Cargo documents required-features as native target selection. The build adapter consumes Cargo's JSON compiler messages. It matches opaque package IDs and binary target names against a prepared inventory and takes executable paths from native compiler-artifact events. It accepts fresh Cargo cache results as well as newly compiled binaries, requires a successful native process and build-finished event, rejects missing/unplanned/conflicting outputs and verifies each executable is a regular file contained in the target root. It does not guess executable filenames or publish intermediate test binaries. The adapter clears its reserved staging directory before invoking Cargo. Only after all expected binaries are verified does it stage them for the shared final collection step. This prevents a previous executable from satisfying a disabled feature or failed compilation. Native source archive contents are checked in the scenario harness to exclude private .oyzu-build files. Cargo does not automatically exclude arbitrary custom output directories; the captured profile fixes its private output location. Exhaustive custom Cargo include/exclude packaging behavior remains unverified. Task overrides and pre/post hooks retain their existing shared owners. Replacing a native build task must still satisfy its planned artifact obligations; an override does not waive collection checks. No registry publication, signing or promotion is performed by this builder increment.

python tooling/test-rust-artifacts.py --cli <compiled-oyzu> --cargo <provisioned-cargo> python tooling/test-rust-doctests.py --cli <compiled-oyzu> --cargo <provisioned-cargo> python tooling/test-rust-packaging.py --cli <compiled-oyzu> --cargo <provisioned-cargo> These Python programs are repository test harnesses, not shipped runtime adapters. They invoke the compiled CLI; --cli defaults to target/release/oyzu (with .exe on Windows). Historical results below predate the compiled migration; current qualification is recorded in implementation status. The artifact probe checks gated binaries disabled/enabled by Cargo defaults, exact executable bytes, launching collected executables, fresh cache results, source archive exclusions, missing outputs, redirected output paths and compiler failures. The Rust example variants supply the native inputs. Rust planner checks cover per-package versions, feature resolution and fixed output facts. The doctest probe runs real stable Cargo against a local workspace, checking successful examples, assertion/compile failures, independent package outcomes, missing-tool stale-report replacement and unchanged inputs. Its --cargo option accepts a command on PATH or an executable path; relative paths are anchored before changing into the fixture, and symlinks retain the Cargo invocation name required by rustup. Unix probes additionally execute through a temporary Cargo symlink. Windows verification passed with Rust 1.94.0; the local GNU toolchain required its provisioned linker setting in RUSTDOCFLAGS as well as RUSTFLAGS. Run 36971869232 passed all three CLI jobs, including the corrected native doctest probe and local-workspace packaging test. The captured Linux suite requires failed doctests to block artifacts despite successful nextest results; isolated doctest acceptance is still pending. The Rust test suite also gives native Cargo a fresh home and an acquired fixture registry, then runs tests, Clippy and verified packaging offline. It checks unchanged source lock bytes and rejection of corrupted archives from a fresh cache. Acquisition checks reject unsupported sources before fetching and mismatched index/archive checksums. The mixed-packaging probe uses native Cargo to create a registry fixture, then packages a three-member snapshot workspace against it with no downloads. It checks archive contents, locked external dependencies, repeatability, source/registry/configuration preservation, rejected index tampering and failures during native verification. GitHub Actions runs it on each CLI host. The checked-in EX-022 registry variation additionally exercises the captured CLI build, reports, delivered binary and failure-gated collection; passing the host probe alone does not prove that isolated scenario. The compiled-CLI Linux scenario suite additionally builds applications, libraries and local workspaces, executes delivered binaries, checks snapshot crate contents, measures application coverage, verifies repeatability and confirms failed tests/formatting block collection. The registry example adds a locked public dependency with no Oyzu configuration; its CI checks require retained dependency identity, versioned outputs, JUnit/coverage, unchanged inputs and rejection of a modified lock checksum. New registry and feature-gate scenarios must pass that suite before being described as verified captured behavior. Native host checks alone do not prove isolated build acceptance. Remaining work includes private/alternate Cargo registries, private Git sources and credentials, persistent acquisition reuse, full feature/profile/platform matrices, doctest coverage/individual-case reporting and broader test-framework support, custom task artifact production, release policy, publication, remote caching and complete authored-scenario acceptance. The build goal remains broader than this implementation increment. Native binary capture now identifies a planned binary by its target-relative Cargo manifest path and target name. This preserves ownership when a prepared target rooted at /workspace executes under /workspace/<target> in a mixed repository. Cargo package IDs remain opaque; Oyzu does not rewrite or parse them. The change fixes the nested-target failure observed by the live logging acceptance probe. The sole version-1 inventory records relative manifest paths; the superseded package-ID inventory reader has been removed.

Explicit artifact platforms select the local Linux cross-compilation image. The six supported selections are linux/x86_64, linux/arm64, darwin/x86_64, darwin/arm64, windows/x86_64 and windows/arm64 (the image builds musl and LLVM MinGW; another ABI is refused). The curated native baselines are musl for Linux, Apple Darwin with a macOS 13 deployment target, and LLVM MinGW for Windows. These baselines remain experimental until the real CLI flow has passed; they do not establish older operating-system compatibility. After building the standard reporting image above, provision the cross worker: docker build -f tooling/images/rust-cross.Dockerfile -t oyzu-toolchain/rust-cross:v1 . This is local environment setup. The build command uses that image automatically for explicit platforms; a missing image fails with a provisioning diagnostic. The image contains the native cross linkers and SDK prerequisites, while the project's locked compiler and target standard libraries are restored separately. The compiler must be declared in oyzu.toml and installed into oyzu.lock. oyzu install on Windows also provisions the local Linux compiler distribution when the project declares a Rust build. The worker uses the embedded mise library; no separate mise executable is invoked. Within one build, equivalent locked selections share compiler verification. The verified archive is extracted once per archive digest and worker image into a build-owned Linux volume, mounted read-only for preparation and execution. Each mount checks its archive digest; Cargo homes, outputs and workspaces remain private. Normal build completion or failure releases the volume; the persistent oyzu-tools-* volumes are reused by identity and superseded ones are pruned (see build logging). Execution runs without network access. The complete project entry point remains oyzu build, with platforms and builder options in build.yaml. Explicit cross-platform Rust actions currently reserve 8 GiB and allow up to two hours per action. The executor caps target concurrency using Docker's available memory, retaining 25% for engine/controller headroom; a Docker engine needs about 11 GiB to admit one such action. These are builder-declared execution resources recorded in the plan, not additional project flags. Locked compiler preparation reserves 4 GiB. The CLI project's native Cargo test profile retains line-level debug information instead of full type debug data, reducing linker pressure from the embedded mise dependency graph. Coverage instrumentation and required test/report gates remain enabled. An earlier cold self-build exceeded a one-hour test-action limit while linking and starting tests; that failed run is not a successful build. Tests and coverage execute on the Linux worker. Cross-compiled executables are checked for the requested binary format and architecture before collection; this is compilation evidence, not a claim that tests ran on each target OS. macOS and ARM runtime qualification remain separate. Rust uses a private Linux scratch filesystem for Cargo extraction and Git checkouts. It keeps a 2 GiB minimum size ceiling and grows to match larger action memory reservations; the reservation itself does not increase. Where cgroups are available, their limit covers process and tmpfs use together. Git acquisition copies back only the bare object databases, keeping registry extraction and upstream symlinks off Windows host mounts. This accommodates the CLI's measured 1.27 GiB of unpacked locked registry inputs without imposing a smaller fixed scratch ceiling. Captured build inputs and execution workspaces live under the repository's .oyzu state directory, on the same volume as the project, rather than filling the operating system's temporary volume. They remain private run state and are excluded from source snapshots and published bundles. Formatting uses the same read-only locked compiler mount as compilation, tests and lint; it never adds Cargo feature-selection arguments to cargo fmt. Shared compiler restoration is automatic and does not add build YAML options. Reuse is scoped to one invocation; it does not deduplicate target metadata, crate acquisition or complete preparation, and does not provide a persistent compiler cache.

Build manifests now include oyzu.dev/tool-requirements for selected Rust targets. The static detector reads literal package.rust-version and Rust toolchain channel constraints with source digests and field locations, in every toolchain-file form rustup accepts (details). It reports compiler components, platform standard libraries, and selected formatting, lint and test requirements. Fast builds omit unselected quality helpers; explicit toolchain components remain requirements. Inherited Cargo MSRV currently requires workspace metadata and fails with an explicit diagnostic rather than being ignored. For a declared, locked Rust compiler, captured preparation uses the same resolved build-stage requirements as pinning and preflight when choosing its recipe. A test-enabled build therefore requires the locked llvm-tools-preview component, even when the lock also contains a smaller fast-build recipe. A fast build can still select that smaller recipe. An incomplete lock refuses preparation; adding an environment override or relying on the image's different compiler does not satisfy the declared Rust selection. Requirement records alone do not prove installation. The selected compiler recipe goes through normal admission and materialization before capture. The current captured test helpers (cargo-nextest and cargo-llvm-cov) remain supplied by the provisioned worker image. The bounded exact-engine proof verified Rust 1.99.1 full-recipe selection, accepted native reports and a runnable Linux x86-64 artifact while preserving both locks.

oyzu run list discovers Rust install and fetch tasks without running Cargo. For a single Rust target, oyzu run install runs cargo install --path . --locked in that target's directory. With several targets, qualify the task, for example oyzu run cli:install. Explicit task overrides retain their existing precedence. This replaces the previous misleading install mapping to dependency fetching; use oyzu run fetch for cargo fetch --locked. oyzu run install -- --root /path/to/bootstrap --force oyzu run fetch -- --offline Trailing arguments are forwarded as argv to Cargo. Installation uses Cargo's release profile by default; Cargo chooses package binaries and reports native errors for packages without installable binaries or virtual workspace roots. Use --bin to select a binary, and --force explicitly when replacement is wanted. --root and CARGO_INSTALL_ROOT choose the installation root; otherwise Cargo's configured/default destination applies. Its bin directory must be on PATH. Cargo and native build prerequisites must already be usable under Oyzu's existing tool-installation policy. A lock selects dependencies but does not make Cargo offline: forward --offline when caches suffice. Native output and failures use the existing task output/JSON contracts. oyzu install still provisions development tools. oyzu build does not execute this installation task unless explicitly connected by authored task dependencies or hooks. This is not a substitute for required build/report gates or publication eligibility. The inferred Windows Oyzu self-install with an explicit root uses staged bootstrap replacement: the current binary remains available during compilation, and successful results replace it while preserving an adjacent backup. Generic Cargo installations keep native behavior.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/scan.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. oyzu scan runs policy-selected SonarQube, Trivy, Gitleaks and/or Grype adapters against an existing successful dist build bundle. This is a development experiment, not the complete managed scanning service. No platform account is required. The experiment plan owns the acquisition and handoff acceptance scenarios.

The five first-flow native Gitleaks cases have passed on Windows at the recorded checkpoint. The local administrative container fixture is a test configuration, not a requirement for ordinary standalone builds or a public platform policy wire model. Optional managed execution follows the client boundary. scan remains explicit: it does not rebuild, run test tasks, or publish. Builder test overrides and their reporting integrations remain owned by the task/build lifecycle. This command replays the build manifest's frozen whole-tree source.selection or host source.projections, including authored inputs and effective ancestor rules. Whole-tree and aggregate host projection digests retain their existing meanings and must match exactly. Replay does not rediscover declarations or load current ignore rules. Nested host replay retains and binds authored sibling inputs in its staged repository, but adapters receive the workspace path; scanning those external sibling inputs remains unqualified. It does not retrieve Git revisions or prepare build-coupled scanner instrumentation. Such layouts are not qualified by the Java fixture and must not be described as supported by this experiment. Artifact copies remain scan-owned, digest-verified inputs; they do not mutate the producer bundle or implement new build materialization syntax.
documents.s: Scope relative to current build and task contracts

documents.t: The first native Gitleaks selection flow is demonstrated under #533. The typed project settings scan.gitleaks.enabled and scan.gitleaks.failOnFindings are booleans, both defaulting to false, and use the ordinary configuration cascade and enforced constraints. Native installation/execution is connected and has compiled on Windows at the recorded checkpoint: it uses the shared tool owner's acquired installation, lease and exact executable, with no PATH or container fallback. Native acquisition, reuse, finding rejection, informational findings and execution failure passed through genuine Rust build bundles. The complete harness also passed the exact source-mismatch refusal before scanner launch. No selected scanner produces SCAN_SELECTION_REQUIRED, with the minimal setup instruction. Existing administrative container selections remain required and cannot be replaced by these project settings; enabling failOnFindings can only tighten Gitleaks' finding criterion to zero. The native selection uses ordinary project TOML: [scan.gitleaks] enabled = true failOnFindings = true Omit failOnFindings to retain findings without a finding-based rejection criterion; execution failures still fail. Native Gitleaks uses an explicit tool request under [tools] when present, a compatible captured pin, or the shared resolver's default otherwise. A first unpinned operation prepares portable tool metadata under a temporary private lock owner and installs only the host payload. Verified installation/leases and remembered selections remain owned by the shared tool subsystem. This does not edit project/global configuration or oyzu.lock. oyzu scan --store <DIR> selects the native tool store for that invocation, using the same path semantics as install/build/exec. Relative paths resolve from the project root. Omitting it keeps the shared user store. Store location does not change tool identity, required verification, policy or lock authority; container images remain in Docker's store. This permits a separate initially empty scanner store without changing routine project configuration. With --offline, a compatible recorded installation or pin and cached inputs must already be available; an unpinned empty store refuses before online resolution. The native Gitleaks qualification record owns the runnable first-flow proof and its measured results and limits. The command reads configuration through the normal session. Only administrative configuration may supply scan.policy; project Gitleaks enablement uses the typed settings above. Tool version requests belong under [tools], not scanner settings. This initial fixture is not an OPA or server wire contract. In the existing protected admin-settings.json format: { "schemaVersion": 1, "kind": "local-admin-policy", "settings": { "scan.policy": { "locked": true, "value": { "sonar": { "image": "sonarsource/sonar-scanner-cli@sha256:a3f4215076706c95a17a68c19322ee916e40a3acd081a8c1a1e839e0194afa57", "endpoint": "https://sonarqube.example.com", "projectKey": "example", "sources": ["app/src/main/java", "library/src/main/java"], "requireClasses": true }, "trivy": { "image": "aquasec/trivy@sha256:af6acf9a6b85dfe389a1941505c0ce9efef52a4719635e1a962f022a3d855daa", "maximumFindings": 0 }, "requireQualityGate": true } } }, "profiles": {}, "requiredCapabilities": [] } Provision Docker and the SonarQube project and service. Preflight acquires missing policy-selected, digest-addressed scanner images through the shared container-tool provider and verifies/reuses existing images. Docker owns image storage; this is not native archive-tool installation. Managed acquisition, nonpublic tool catalogs and configured registry routes are rejected until connector projection is connected; there is no direct-download fallback for those configurations. Provide SONAR_TOKEN in the invoking process environment; do not put a token in the policy file. It needs analysis submission and permission to read task, quality-gate and project-issue data. The isolated experiment supplies a temporary development token and revokes it afterward; this is not credential brokering qualification. HTTP is supported for the isolated local service proof. oyzu build oyzu scan oyzu scan --json Each call starts a separate scan. Global --json works before or after scan. The current source tree is captured with the build's recorded snapshot selection and must match the build's recorded tree digest. A Git HEAD value alone never satisfies that check. Changed source fails before scanner launch; restore the matching inputs or explicitly build again. This initial path does not yet fetch source from Git or retrieve remote bundles. Cross-host filesystem differences can prevent a digest match and are not silently normalized. A bundle without either source replay contract fails with SCAN_SOURCE_SELECTION_MISSING; malformed or ambiguous contracts fail with SCAN_SOURCE_SELECTION_INVALID. Build explicitly with the current CLI to record the required selection, then scan that bundle. There is no guessed selection for earlier development bundles. Source replay, native execution and exact mismatch refusal passed in the recorded Windows proof; consumer regression tests passed in this branch's full workspace suite. This does not establish cross-host scan qualification. Source paths are relative directories. requireClasses selects this adapter's retained-class mode: it requires classes extracted from digest-verified JARs. It is not a claim that all SonarQube Java analysis requires bytecode. There is no Maven invocation, implicit build or scan during build. Original dist is verified before and after scanning and is not modified by scan.

Completed attempts are finalized at .oyzu/scans/<run-id>/manifest.json. plan.json records frozen policy, resolved tool identities and prepared subjects; events.jsonl retains execution progress. Their digests are included in the result. Each check records tool.disposition (installed/reused). Container tools record tool.image; native tools record the exact tool, version, platform, backend, selection digest and installation key. Established run preparation failures retain a failure manifest and journal with the failed phase; invalid configuration rejected before establishing a run does not create evidence. Scanner acquisition does not pin tools or write the project oyzu.lock. Human output uses the shared build-style terminal renderer: a scan heading, Preflight installation/reuse and readiness, a distinct Scan phase, scoped scanner activity and completion with elapsed time. The final aligned table identifies each scanner, analysis type, subject, execution result and duration. Separate details show findings, provider gates, acceptance, report links and the result path. Narrow terminals use lossless stacked rows. Redirected output preserves chronological readable text; NO_COLOR disables color and quiet mode suppresses progress without hiding the result. JSON stdout contains only the result; structured progress events go to stderr. The terminal view is finalized before reporting preflight errors or the final result. Native output is retained as sonarqube/native.log rather than interleaved with progress. sonarqube/provider.json retains the provider response snapshot. The native CLI exiting zero is only submission success. Oyzu waits up to three minutes for the server task, then obtains the analysis-specific quality gate. Any execution failure skips aggregate acceptance while independent scanners still run and retain their evidence. Otherwise the fixture can require a passing provider gate and a maximum Trivy finding count. Exit zero means accepted; exit one means execution failure or rejected acceptance. Ordinary input-preparation and finalization errors also use the shared command failure classification: SCAN_SOURCE_MISMATCH is exit one, supported flag/specification diagnostics are exit two, and CONFIG_*/POLICY_* diagnostics are exit three. Other diagnostics retain their shared categories. The specific diagnostic code remains available in human and JSON modes. No incomplete attempt is reported as a finalized success. oyzu scan --offline permits local Trivy checks when their images and inputs already exist. Missing images fail with TOOL_OFFLINE; SonarQube selections fail with SCAN_OFFLINE before analysis. Checks are never omitted to make an offline invocation succeed. The project dashboard and issue search are current project views, not immutable analysis references. The result labels that distinction, retains the analysis/task IDs and records issue-snapshot truncation above 500 issues. Issue snapshots do not drive this experiment's acceptance decision. A passing provider gate does not mean zero findings or permission to publish.

sonar and trivy are independent optional selections; at least one is required. requireQualityGate requires SonarQube and defaults to false. Trivy runs source secret detection only, with no vulnerability database, network, upstream credentials or Docker socket inside the scanner. It uses the same verified source snapshot. This does not qualify container, dependency-vulnerability or infrastructure scanning. Trivy's native JSON is retained at trivy/report.json, its stderr at trivy/native.log, and file digests in the result manifest. Each check carries its own resolved tool identity. Finding counts are facts; maximumFindings is the administrative acceptance threshold (omission means no count limit). Native findings never alone imply an execution failure. A nonzero native exit or malformed report is an execution failure. Repository trivy.yaml, ignore files and secret rules do not supply this administrative configuration. Administrators may supply trivy.rules, an array of native custom secret rules with id, title, regex and severity (LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH or CRITICAL). Built-in rules remain active. Native Trivy validates regex semantics; an invalid rule fails the check. This experiment uses a custom rule matching a harmless existing Maven metadata to demonstrate acceptance rejection without introducing an actual credential. Raw secret reports may contain sensitive source; protect the local result directory. Only counts, not matched secret text, appear in human output.

Independent container adapters run concurrently after all selected checks complete preflight. scan.jobs defaults to 2 and bounds active checks (1–65535); set it to 1 for serial execution through the normal configuration cascade. Administrative locks apply. SonarQube waiting for remote analysis occupies its slot while Trivy may run in another. Reports use separate scanner directories and results retain plan order regardless of completion order. A failed check does not cancel independent checks. Acquisition and input preparation remain sequential. Native tool installation, scanner-specific build extraction and immutable remote report storage remain unimplemented. Inputs retained under the experiment result include source and classes; treat that task-owned directory as sensitive project data. Local results provide content integrity, not authenticated provenance or RBAC. Docker administrators can inspect process environments. No scanner receives the Docker socket; the controller requires local Docker access. Linux Docker execution is the first qualification target; Windows/macOS native CLI qualification remains pending. See the qualification record for measured results and failed expectations rather than inferring support from this reference.

Add gitleaks to the administrative scan.policy alongside other scanners, or select it alone. For example: { "gitleaks": { "image": "zricethezav/gitleaks@sha256:691af3c7c5a48b16f187ce3446d5f194838f91238f27270ed36eef6359a574d9", "maximumFindings": 0 } } This example selects Gitleaks 8.30.0. Versions remain policy-controlled, acquired through shared preflight and recorded in the frozen plan. The adapter runs dir on the verified source snapshot, not Git history. It requires Docker and supports offline execution after image acquisition. scan.jobs bounds concurrency with other scanners; use three to admit all three together. config optionally supplies administrative native Gitleaks TOML. Omission uses bundled default rules through an explicit owned config. Project .gitleaks.toml, .gitleaksignore and inline gitleaks:allow comments do not override this selection. Native config errors are execution failures. The scanner has no network, upstream credentials or Docker socket, and reads source through a read-only mount. Native JSON and diagnostics are retained at gitleaks/report.json and gitleaks/native.log, with report digests in the result. Gitleaks is invoked with full native redaction; treat reports as sensitive source metadata nonetheless. Human output shows counts, not matched values. maximumFindings is optional; omission imposes no count limit. Findings do not make execution fail: acceptance compares their count to the configured threshold after required checks finish. A nonzero native exit or malformed report prevents acceptance evaluation. This qualifies snapshot secret scanning only, not history scanning, exhaustive secret detection, native archive installation or managed credential acquisition. See Gitleaks usage for native rule semantics. Oyzu does not copy or redistribute the scanner image.

Add grype to the administrative scan.policy. The initial adapter consumes all recorded application/java-archive artifacts from the verified build bundle: { "grype": { "image": "anchore/grype@sha256:af65fbc0c664691067788fe95ff88760b435543e45595eb2ca6f102fc476fbe1", "maximumFindings": 0 } } This selects Grype 0.110.0. Preflight acquires the policy-selected image, copies and verifies JAR digests, then invokes native grype db update without mounting source or artifacts. Each run owns its database; its tree digest is captured in prepared inputs. Analysis reads that database and the retained artifacts with networking disabled. Project Grype configuration is not loaded. Database age/hash validation remains enabled. Database download failures prevent analysis and retain diagnostics. Results identify dependency-vulnerability and artifact, retain native JSON at grype/report.json, diagnostics at grype/native.log and preparation diagnostics at grype/database.log. Native database metadata accompanies the evidence. Findings count vulnerability matches, not unique CVEs; omission of maximumFindings means no count limit. Execution failure skips acceptance; findings are evaluated afterward. Independent scanners share scan.jobs; four admits all four supported scanners. The current implementation downloads a fresh database for every run and retains it in the run directory. It can consume significant disk and network bandwidth. Offline invocation fails explicitly with SCAN_DB_OFFLINE; cache reuse is not implemented. Missing JAR artifacts fail with SCAN_INPUT_MISSING. This does not qualify OCI image, SBOM, source-lockfile, or transitive dependency coverage: only packages Grype catalogs from the recorded JARs are analyzed. A clean result is not a complete dependency audit. Native scanner installation and managed database routing remain outside this proof. See Grype database behavior and CLI reference.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/secrets.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Status: experimental client. oyzu secrets list|create|set|rm implement the CLI side of the draft secrets contract. They are verified against a scripted local server. That client evidence does not qualify CLI login or deployment against a live platform. Use the endpoint's advertised authenticated caller setup; this page does not establish deployment or provisioning status.

A secret is a named value your platform account keeps for the account, one of its organizations or one of its projects: a token a build job needs (build exposure) or a webhook secret the platform verifies deliveries with (internal exposure). Values are write-only: you set or replace a value and nothing ever shows it back, to anyone, including account owners. No command or API operation returns a stored value. For a custom webhook secret, --generate makes the value on your machine and shows it to you once, to paste into the sender. Everything else Oyzu does stays local and works without an account; these commands are an optional platform path.

The same settings and token as remote runs: platform.url and platform.account in configuration (user scope is the usual place), for example oyzu config set --global platform.account payments. A platform credential from the shared credential provider: the session stored by oyzu auth login (used from a terminal, or when platform.authentication.provider is session), or a bearer in OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN. The token is a credential, so it is read from the environment and never from a configuration file. The draft authentication contract describes the intended credential-provider behavior. A supplied token is used as is and never created or refreshed; do not obtain one by copying a browser session or hand a person's session to unattended automation. Unattended runs need an explicit provider or token and never use a developer's stored session. Possession alone does not authorize a Secrets operation. No Git checkout is needed.

Command Does oyzu secrets list The account's secrets: name, type, exposure, value version, description oyzu secrets list --project web A project's secrets (--org <org> for an organization) oyzu secrets create <name> --exposure internal Create a secret with no value. --exposure build for one jobs receive; --type file for exact bytes such as a key file (default text); --description oyzu secrets set <name> < value.txt Set or replace the value from standard input oyzu secrets set <name> --file key.pem Set or replace the value with a file's exact bytes oyzu secrets set <name> --generate Generate a value, set it and print it once oyzu secrets set <name> … --overlap 24h Keep the replaced value valid for 24 hours (at most 168h; h, m or s) oyzu secrets rm <name> --previous End an overlap now, for a replaced value that leaked oyzu secrets rm <name> Delete the secret and all its values --org and --project work with every command; without them the command acts on the account itself. Organizations and projects are named by their identifier within the account. set and rm look the name up in that scope (a secret id works too) and fail with SECRETS_NOT_FOUND, naming the create command, when there is no such secret; set never creates one. A typical custom webhook: oyzu secrets create release-webhook --exposure internal --description "Release tool deliveries" oyzu secrets set release-webhook --generate Rotating it without dropping deliveries: oyzu secrets set release-webhook --generate --overlap 24h, update the sender, then oyzu secrets rm release-webhook --previous once it uses the new value.

A value is read from standard input or --file, or generated with --generate; never from a command-line argument, so it does not land in shell history or process listings. Standard input must be piped or redirected: when it is a terminal, set fails with SECRETS_VALUE_REQUIRED instead of echoing what you type. The bytes are sent exactly as read, so echo token | oyzu secrets set x stores a trailing newline; use printf '%s' "$TOKEN" or a file without one. A value must not be empty and is at most 64 KiB; a text secret must be UTF-8 (the platform checks). Both are checked before anything is sent. --generate draws 32 bytes from the operating system's cryptographically secure random source and uses them as 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters, which every webhook sender accepts. The value is printed once, after the platform has stored it. If the platform refuses the request, the value is discarded and never shown.

Text mode leads with the outcome. A listing is a table; the Value column shows the version, and during an overlap when the previous one stops being valid, or not set: Secrets · project web of payments Name Type Exposure Value Description npm-token text build version 2 (version 1 valid until 2026-10-11T09:05:00Z) hook text internal not set Release tool Values are write-only: no command shows a stored value. Replace one with `oyzu secrets set <name>`. A generated value is shown once with a warning: ✓ Set the value of release-webhook (version 1) Generated value 3f9c…(64 hexadecimal characters) Copy it into the sender's webhook settings now. It cannot be shown again; if it is lost, set a new one. With --json, stdout carries one record with kind, account and scope: secrets (with secrets, the contract's metadata), secret-created and secret-overlap-ended (with secret), secret-value-set (with secret, and generated_value only for --generate) or secret-deleted (name, id). Treat the JSON output of --generate as sensitive: it holds the value.

Exit status is 0 on success and 2 on any refusal. Platform refusals keep the contract's code with a SECRETS_ prefix and the platform request id, for example SECRETS_RESOURCE_CONFLICT (name taken, no previous value, or a sign-only secret, which only the platform manages), SECRETS_PERMISSION_DENIED, SECRETS_UNAUTHENTICATED (run oyzu auth login, or set a current OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN) or SECRETS_VALIDATION_FAILED (with the failing field). Client-side failures are SECRETS_NOT_CONFIGURED, SECRETS_NOT_FOUND, SECRETS_VALUE_REQUIRED, SECRETS_VALUE_EMPTY, SECRETS_VALUE_TOO_LARGE, SECRETS_VALUE_UNREADABLE, SECRETS_OVERLAP_INVALID and SECRETS_UNREACHABLE. Listing retries a 503 or a transport failure with backoff, like remote runs. A create, set or delete is sent once: retrying a value could create a second version and, with an overlap, retire the value it was meant to keep. If one fails in transit, run oyzu secrets list to see what happened. Creation requires HTTP 201 and metadata with a valid id, the requested name, scope, type and exposure, a description and valid creation/update timestamps. Malformed responses fail with SECRETS_RESPONSE_INVALID in human and JSON modes instead of reporting creation. The server may have created the secret: use oyzu secrets list to check before retrying, and check platform/client compatibility. A returned secret value is rejected rather than printed.

No command reads a value back; the contract has no such operation. Values are never taken from arguments, never logged, and never written to disk by the CLI. A generated value exists only in memory until it is printed. The credential is sent only to platform.url, over the shared outbound transport (proxy and extra trust settings apply); redirects are not followed. sign-only secrets (the platform's own integration keys) are listed but cannot be created or changed with these commands.

Not qualified against a deployed platform; portal entry and per-project permissions are not implemented yet, and login is verified only against a local conformance fake. No interactive hidden prompt for typing a value; pipe it or use --file. Exposure, type and scope are fixed at creation; to change one, create a new secret.

cargo test --test integration secrets_cli runs the compiled CLI against a scripted server: stdin bytes reach the server exactly once and never appear in output, --generate prints exactly the value it sent, names resolve per scope, and refusals keep their code and request id. Unit tests cover value sources and limits, overlap syntax, generation, argument parsing (no value argument, no sign-only) and the human layout.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/shell-activation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Every Oyzu build includes the mise library integration. Build with Rust 1.95 using cargo build --locked --bins; no integration feature flag exists. This page describes the experimental shell activation implementation, not a production-qualified release. Its scoped lifecycle checks passed on Windows PowerShell and Linux/macOS Bash and Zsh. See implementation status for measured results. The opt-in OCI session prototype adds Unix launch shims for provisioned Helm/BuildKit clients. Activation itself does not contact its agent; the native invocation requests a session using its current context.

An environment-only project needs no tools, lock, install or account. Shell activation and oyzu exec apply its environment after the folder is trusted; explicit project tasks and builds always apply it: [env] APP_MODE = "development" _.path = ["./bin", "./node_modules/.bin"] The array prepends directories in order. To append as well, use this alternative: [env] _.path = { prepend = ["./bin"], append = ["./scripts"] } The reserved env._ table is metadata, never an exported variable. Values and paths are literal: no variable expansion, scripts, dotenv discovery or command substitution. Plain env.PATH assignments are rejected with a migration message. Relative paths belong to the file declaring them, including local/profile files. They do not change when you enter a subdirectory. Missing directories are allowed. Empty entries, NUL, unknown controls and an embedded host PATH separator are errors. Use "." explicitly for the declaring directory. Normal configuration precedence applies. Each winning _.path declaration replaces the entire inherited control; [] clears project additions. Arrays preserve order. Selected tool shims precede project prepends, inherited PATH, then project appends. Existing occurrences are preserved rather than claimed as project-owned insertions. Projects within Git use the repository root unless --root is explicit. Outside Git, the outermost applicable ancestor Oyzu configuration establishes the root. Nested files affect only their subtree. Installed tools live in the shared user store, independently of the project owning the configuration and lock. Activation can select an explicit store with --store; relative store paths resolve against the invocation directory. Use the same store for installation and activation. Relative parent components such as ../tools are normalized lexically on every host before the store's existing no-follow filesystem checks; normalization does not create directories or relax symlink/reparse-point validation. Development tasks can select that store with oyzu run <task> --store <path>. The path follows the same invocation-directory resolution as build and install, and applies to the whole task sequence, including hooks and prerequisites. Tasks verify installed selections; this option does not install missing tools or fall back to another store. Preparation failures retain their original error and causes; shared stderr diagnostics give recovery guidance without replacing the error code. oyzu run list --store <path> remains discovery-only and does not open or create the store. Place task arguments after --; a --store after that separator is forwarded to the task instead.

In PowerShell 7.5+: oyzu activate pwsh | Out-String | Invoke-Expression Set-Location ./project-a Set-Location ../project-b oyzu deactivate In Bash or Zsh: eval "$(oyzu activate bash)" # substitute zsh for Zsh cd ./project-a cd ../project-b oyzu deactivate Activation can start outside any project. Directory hooks apply before the next command; configuration edits refresh at the next hook. Call _oyzu_hook to refresh explicitly in an activated shell. Hooks never install tools, run tasks or access the network. Tools declared in [tools] must already have a usable frozen selection. Profile installation is explicit: oyzu shell install SHELL --profile-path PATH. Removing that profile block changes future loads; deactivate the current session separately. See the profile instructions. Each activated terminal owns its state. A nested shell can call activate to obtain its own record and change projects without modifying its parent's record. Deactivation restores its inherited baseline. No shared global tool selection is changed.

Switching first reverses the prior project delta. A scalar restores only when it still equals Oyzu's applied value; user edits and deletions are preserved. A new project's explicit assignment temporarily overrides that edited baseline, which is restored afterward. Empty strings and absent variables remain distinct. Explicit removals use the existing configuration control: [overrides] remove = ["env.APP_MODE"] The variable is unset for that project and restored on unload if the user has not changed it. PATH restoration preserves unrelated additions and removes owned unique entries even after reordering. Ambiguous duplicate edits are retained with a diagnostic. Invalid configuration or unavailable required selection unloads the previous project's changes and reports OYZU_TOOL_STATUS=unavailable. Fix the configuration or explicitly install/update tools; the next hook retries. No failing project is partially applied. A usable environment reports ready. Managed environment values and development secret references remain unsupported in this milestone and fail explicitly. Hooks do not authenticate, refresh credentials or fall back around authorization. Applying project/local literal values through activation, hooks, shims or exec requires folder trust, because shells, loaders and interpreters can execute the contents of environment variables.

Review the checkout's environment settings, then run oyzu trust [path]. With no path, this trusts the current project's root. oyzu trust --revoke [path] removes the record; oyzu trust --list lists records. Every form supports --json and human output. Trust is keyed by the canonical root folder, including resolution of symbolic links, and survives edits to oyzu.toml. It never writes into the checkout or contacts a service. Records live under trusted-projects in the native user state directory. Untrusted folders never prompt or block tool selection: activation still exposes the tools but skips project/local [env], env._.path, and their removals. User/global environment values remain effective. Prompt hooks, shims, exec and one-shot env --shell use the same rule. A short stderr hint names oyzu trust once per invocation, or once per activated shell session. run, build, build planning and the build configuration digest always include project/local env and PATH settings under normal configuration precedence, regardless of folder trust. These commands explicitly execute or plan the repo's declared code and must agree with CI. config inspection also retains the configured environment. User/global or administrative configuration can set [trust] enabled = false to disable the check, or parents = ["/absolute/projects"] to trust projects beneath selected canonical parent folders (for example E:\\CodexData\\projects on Windows). The default is enabled with no trusted parents. Project/local files cannot set these controls. OYZU_PROJECT_TRUST=false disables the check for an invocation; true enables it and overrides ordinary files. CI context is automatically trusted, including a true CI marker; platform executors run in that CI context. Local coding agents receive no exemption. Revocation removes only the explicit record: a parent rule, disabled check or CI exemption can still trust the folder. This changes earlier literal-environment behavior. Trust existing checkouts once, or configure their parent directory in user scope. Dedicated regression coverage tests scope rejection and the compiled CLI trust lifecycle; Windows native state and real shell qualification still require running the checks on that host.

oyzu env displays configuration sources, effective variable names and selected executables in separate tables. Names such as CARGO_HOME and cargo-llvm-cov are preserved literally. Configuration sources include env._.path, which is PATH metadata rather than a separate exported variable, and identify the winning source and profile from the resolved cascade (including oyzu.local.toml). Ordinary values are visible in human and JSON inspection. Credential-like names (including token, secret, password, API key, authentication and private-key names) and values rejected by the shared diagnostic sanitizer remain redacted. This is heuristic protection, not secret discovery: do not put secrets in innocuously named literal variables. Configuration/log inspection retains its separate, conservative redaction contract. Human output lists PATH entries in search order and removes Windows extended-path prefixes from displayed source paths. Tool-provided variables and inherited PATH also contribute to the composed environment. Inspection does not modify the calling shell. In an untrusted folder, oyzu env still shows configured values and provenance, with project entries marked skipped until trusted for activation, hooks, shims and exec. The displayed PATH describes the configured composition, including those entries; it is not a claim that activation has applied it. oyzu env --json lists inspected environment values and selected commands, with configuration provenance in the configuration array. projectEnvironmentSkipped reports whether shell/exec use withholds project environment, and affected configuration rows carry the same skipped until trusted status as human output. To apply directory changes in an existing PowerShell session, run oyzu activate pwsh | Out-String | Invoke-Expression. Then where.exe oyzu includes the project-local executable before the bootstrap if env._.path contains its directory. Leaving the project restores the prior PATH. For future shells, use the explicit shell profile installation. On Windows, directories Oyzu adds to PATH use ordinary drive or UNC notation, not the \\?\ prefixes used by internal filesystem canonicalization. Inherited PATH entries retain their original spelling for restoration. Windows PowerShell 5.1 can apply the initial activation, but the upstream directory-change hook requires PowerShell 7 or newer; use a supported PowerShell version for automatic switching (including the empty-variable requirement noted below). oyzu exec -- /absolute/path/to/program applies the trust-filtered environment, including unsets, to a child without changing the caller. Bare commands retain the existing declared-tool requirement. oyzu env --shell SHELL emits one-shot changes without installing lifecycle hooks; use activate for automatic rollback. PATH metadata does not become a task environment variable or a hermetic build input. The existing build/task contracts still own their explicit environment variables.

The repository's .oyzu/bin PATH declaration supports the in-development native CLI bootstrap workflow. Environment activation alone does not prove successful native compilation or repeated self-replacement. The activation wrapper dispatches ordinary CLI commands to the first oyzu application on the active PATH, falling back to the activating executable when none is found. Environment hooks and shell lifecycle commands retain the activating executable. This permits a successful local build to take over ordinary commands without reinstalling activation. The PowerShell lifecycle fixture verified this dispatch on Windows with the compiled limited-debug CLI on 2026-10-03. Native self-build and promotion remain separately unverified. Run python tooling/test-project-environments.py --cli PATH --shell pwsh or select bash/zsh. The fixture exercises real shell entry/switch/leave, nested scopes, unset/restore, config refresh, failure cleanup and child-session independence. It provisions no tools and checks that no project lock or tool store was created. The native CI workflow also compares ordinary and no-default-features command help. The intended shell matrix is Bash on Linux/macOS, Zsh on Linux/macOS and PowerShell 7.5+ where available. PowerShell 7.5 introduced support for preserving empty environment values; earlier versions cannot satisfy this environment contract (Microsoft documentation). Evidence is recorded separately; a test definition is not proof that every host passed. Additional shells, managed/secret integration, general shim expansion, active-installation retention, crash recovery, stress testing and performance tuning remain outside this activation milestone.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/target-workspaces.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Native oyzu build prepares a separate source workspace per selected target before native dependency preparation. Target hooks and stages share that target workspace; ordering dependencies do not expose another target's generated files. Direct oyzu run tasks retain their intentional checkout behavior. This is workspace separation, not enforced filesystem or network sandboxing. Host processes retain ambient host access. This behavior does not establish production publication eligibility.
documents.s: Host target workspaces and artifact inputs

documents.t: Named builds require explicit source inputs only for their selected targets and required dependencies, including task prerequisites and hooks. A missing prepared input belonging to an unselected target does not block the build or its read-only preview. For example, oyzu build cli needs no prepared docs input; oyzu build docs and an all-target build still require it. Missing inputs of a selected target or dependency fail before native execution. Affected selection observes inputs across the workspace to determine which targets changed. Captured source retains available authored inputs for prerequisites discovered during native preparation, such as archive hooks; their inputs become required when that target joins the selection. Existing snapshot boundary and link restrictions still apply to those retained inputs. The target's source directory is captured with current edits and eligible untracked files using the existing snapshot exclusions (including .git, .oyzu, dist, target, node_modules and virtual environments). Native project ownership still belongs to discovery. Files outside the target directory require explicit source inputs when not already part of that native ownership unit: builds: api: uses: node/app path: api inputs: [../../shared/schemas] inputs is a list of literal file/directory paths relative to the declaring build.yaml, not the target's path. Paths must resolve within the enclosing Git repository. Without a Git repository, the selected build root is the boundary. Absolute paths and boundary escapes fail. On the captured execution path the captured source is the boundary: an input must stay under the directory holding build.yaml and name at least one captured file, and it joins the target's action-cache scope and stage contracts (declared inputs). Snapshot link/reparse restrictions remain in force. Captures preserve repository-relative layout; each target receives its own copies. Additional source contents participate in recorded source-projection identity. This does not enable host action-result caching. Generated outputs from another build must use artifact relationships, not source inputs. A snapshot detects changes while copying individual files; it is not an atomic repository-wide snapshot. Unsupported native inputs fail through their native tools; arbitrary script dependencies are not automatically inferred. Source capture caches directory ignore decisions within one invocation; explicit inputs and mandatory metadata/repository exclusions keep their existing rules. Host workspace refresh walks each target's known source/input roots directly, without a preliminary whole-repository inventory for that target. It still hashes every admitted source file on each build. Files whose size, modification time and read-only state match the retained private copy are not rewritten; other files are copied again, and stale generated files are removed. This reduces preparation work on repeated builds without depending on Git's tracked-file list. Refresh uses a nonfollowing source-file handle for live metadata, hashing and the post-read change check, avoiding a separate path-based file metadata open. For Oyzu's own checkout, keep the source revision current when testing this behavior: a successful self-build promotes that checkout's compiled executables back into .oyzu/bin, including artifacts restored from cache. Replacing only the launcher cannot keep a fix absent from the sources being built. See local executable promotion. Temporary source captures and complete admitted-source copies used by dependency preparation preserve modification times and do not flush each file to durable storage. Complete copies keep already-admitted inputs without reapplying ignores. Content hashing, change detection and independent copies remain required. Prepared dependency/output snapshots and final bundle/store publication retain their durability boundaries. Completed prepared trees are inspected directly when only their validated identity is needed; no discarded duplicate is created for that observation.

builds: server: uses: rust/app path: server consumer: uses: node/app path: consumer materialize: - from: server to: inputs/server - from: server into: inputs/original from selects a producer. Optional artifact selects its logical output name; omission requires an unambiguous primary artifact. Exactly one destination is required: to: exact destination for a file, or contents-under-destination for a directory. into: destination directory for a file, preserving its exported basename. When the producer fixes the file name only as it runs (a native wheel), the collected name is used, not the planned one; see file name discovery. Directory artifacts use to. Optional runtime names a provisioned local image that must accept native files (such as a Python wheel) for this input; see native wheels. It is valid only with usage: runtime, the image must match the consumer's platform, and it is never pulled. Destinations are relative to the consumer target. No implicit archive extraction, source overwrite, overlapping destination, or scraping of old output trees is allowed. Producer platform compatibility and artifact identity are validated. materialize establishes ordering automatically; do not repeat depends_on. Native metadata and dependency preparation still precede action execution. Inputs that generate a consumer manifest or are needed by npm ci during preparation are not supported by this slice; handoff occurs before the consumer's first action. Artifacts are collected once all required producer actions and report obligations succeed, before its consumers run. Each consumer receives an independent copy verified against the collected digest. The manifest records handoff receipts. A failed producer blocks dependents; successful independent artifacts can remain in a failed bundle, without making that bundle successful. The producer's pre_build, build and post_build actions share its private tree. Post-hook changes to declared output are included in the artifact handed to the consumer. A failure in any of those actions prevents producer artifact publication, even if the build already wrote output files. Native failure diagnostics remain in the failed bundle; fixing the hook or command and rebuilding starts with a fresh private source tree. This is not a guarantee that post-hooks run on cancellation. A host-built (native local) Python output is a wheel directory named primary, so use to for it. A python/package target built in a worker image (--image pip=<image>) exports file outputs named wheel and sdist; select one with artifact: wheel and into. Typed image bindings remain separate work. Host-coordinated image execution is described below.

The experimental host coordinator admits docker/image alongside supported native targets. It reuses the existing captured Docker metadata and rootless BuildKit executor; ordinary host targets still run as host processes. Docker is required only when an image target is selected. No build container receives the host Docker socket, and no nested Docker daemon is started. Provision the existing worker image explicitly from this repository: docker build -f tooling/images/docker-metadata.Dockerfile -t oyzu-toolchain/docker:buildkit0.25.0 . Image bases must already be available to the provisioned Docker daemon. Preparation captures their identities; worker actions remain offline. This does not install Docker or change host security settings. Existing docker.apparmorProfile configuration and executor enforcement still apply. Explicit tool pins must be satisfied by their supported executor contract; an image tag does not verify pins. An intended Linux producer/consumer flow is: builds: package: uses: python/package path: package image: uses: docker/image path: image materialize: - from: package to: payload oyzu build image --plan includes the producer, artifact edge and each target's executor without contacting Docker. oyzu build image runs that graph. The image's Dockerfile can use COPY payload/ /wheels/ without predicting a versioned wheel filename. This assembles a wheel payload; installing it into an application runtime is a separate Dockerfile responsibility. Native source selection and Dockerignore filtering apply to the image's context; materialized artifacts are explicitly added. Additional source files outside that context do not become Docker COPY inputs. Artifact compatibility is separate from producer execution provenance. Captured matrix expansion selects the declared producer variant matching each consumer platform; it does not select by filename or matrix enumeration order. Host Python wheel directories are inspected after collection: every wheel must report pure Python and none-any tags before the directory is admitted across platforms. Python tags remain in evidence; the image's package manager must check interpreter and other runtime requirements. A host-built wheel whose tags all name one Linux x86_64 or aarch64 platform (linux_*, manylinux*, musllinux_*) is recorded as native and is consumed only as described under native wheels. Any other native wheel tags (for example Windows or macOS) remain unqualified and fail runtime handoff, including on the same OS. Platform-independent sharing of native wheels through captured matrix expansion is not implemented. Plain native builds still select host producer outputs. For a native binary matrix feeding a foreign-platform image, use --all-platforms; the CLI does not automatically switch that producer to a cross-compilation executor. materialize.usage defaults to runtime.
