Explicit usage: data permits deliberate inclusion without claiming runtime compatibility. It still requires a unique logical output, successful producer, verified bytes and safe placement. Data edges do not propagate consumer platform requirements into producers; ambiguous matrix outputs still fail. to and into retain their existing placement semantics. Artifacts carry extensions.oyzu.dev/artifact-compatibility: target records the resolved artifact platform, pending requires builder inspection before use, independent retains native runtime tags, native binds package files to one platform plus the builder that verifies them against the consumer runtime, and unknown explains absent qualification. Bindings/receipts record oyzu.dev/artifact-consumer platform and usage. Pending or unknown artifacts cannot satisfy runtime consumption. This extends the existing version-1 contracts; it does not certify arbitrary binaries or runtime ABIs.

A native wheel is accepted only after the consumer runtime check. For generic linux_x86_64 and linux_aarch64 wheels, Oyzu inspects ELF .so dependencies in the wheel and probes the exact consumer image's Python process. A positively identified glibc/musl mismatch is refused before the consumer image build, naming the wheel, ELF member, linkage and consumer image. If linkage or consumer libc is inconclusive, the check reports NATIVE_WHEEL_LIBC_UNVERIFIED and continues to pip. This includes wheels with no identifiable libc dependency and wheels with other unidentified .so members. A missing Python runtime remains an error. UNVERIFIED means Oyzu has no libc conclusion. Separately, for generic Linux wheels with a recognized interpreter-specific *.cpython-<version>-<platform>.so member, Oyzu compares that filename suffix with importlib.machinery.EXTENSION_SUFFIXES from the exact consumer Python. When its CPython-specific suffix is absent, or the consumer cannot report those suffixes, Oyzu emits NATIVE_WHEEL_EXTENSION_SUFFIX_UNVERIFIED in human and JSON diagnostics, naming the wheel, member, observed suffix and consumer. Pip still decides wheel tags and ABI, and a warning does not block the build. A plain .so or .abi3.so does not trigger this specific comparison. The member may be a helper or data library, so this check does not claim that every .so is a required import module. A warning calls for checking the module import in the final image and, if it fails, building the wheel with that consumer's Python and native toolchain. For manylinux* and musllinux_* tags, pip retains its existing decision without the extra ELF or suffix checks. Pure *-none-any wheels keep their independent handoff. Before a native wheel enters the consumer workspace, Oyzu runs pip install --dry-run --no-index --no-deps for it in that image with networking disabled. Pip decides whether the interpreter version, ABI and wheel tag fit; the extra refusal handles only positively identified libc mismatches for generic Linux tags. The suffix comparison is diagnostic only. The runtime image is, in order: the input's explicit runtime: <image> (a provisioned local image; it overrides the captured base and must match the consumer platform), else the consumer's captured pip dependency base (a requirements.txt consumed from the pinned base image; see Docker images). materialize: - from: package to: inputs runtime: registry.example/python:3.12-slim # only needed without a pip base A consumer with neither (for example a plain COPY into scratch) cannot receive a native wheel; usage: data still includes it without a runtime claim. A rejection fails the consumer with the wheel name, the image reference and either the linkage mismatch or pip's message. The human summary shows it as an ERROR line (terminal controls escaped, line breaks kept); --json carries it in diagnostics, and the action log keeps the full text. Wheel classification covers Linux wheels whose tags all name x86_64 or aarch64 (linux_*, manylinux*, musllinux_*), including abi3 wheels. The proof shows version-specific tags (cp313-cp313-linux_x86_64) accepted only by the matching Python and an abi3 wheel accepted by both Python 3.12 and 3.13. Because pip is the authority, Python versions need no Oyzu list. Not covered: a Linux arm64 consumer (classification is unit-tested; no arm64 build or execution was available), broader libc version and transitive library checks, and Windows/macOS tags, which stay unknown and are refused. These and the Windows/macOS host qualification are tracked in implementation status. Qualification: python tooling/test-native-wheel-abi.py --cli <compiled-oyzu> (needs Docker, a host C compiler and oyzu-fixture/python-abi:<version> images; the script header describes them). The producer's CPython is pinned with .python-version; Oyzu provisions it. These host-built cases need a Linux host: a Windows or macOS host builds win_*/macosx_* wheels, which stay unknown and are refused by a Linux consumer.
documents.s: Native wheels and the consumer runtime

documents.t: A Linux native wheel can be produced from any host with Docker by building it in a worker image: oyzu build --image pip=<image>, where the image is a Python image with a C compiler (not a -slim image) and the Oyzu worker at /usr/local/libexec/oyzu/oyzu. The wheel's tag comes from that image's interpreter, for example cp313-cp313-linux_x86_64. Collection finds it (below), reads its tags from the wheel's own WHEEL metadata and records native compatibility for the image's platform, so the consumer check above applies unchanged. The case is tooling/test-native-wheel-abi.py --worker-image <image>; on Windows add --captured-only to skip the host-built cases.
documents.s: Wheels built in a worker image

documents.t: A planned file output has an exact name and collection requires that file. The one exception is a builder-declared discovery, used when the name cannot be known until the build has run: It is consulted only when no file exists at the planned path, so an output that exists under its planned name, such as a pure py3-none-any wheel, is collected exactly as before and never reinterpreted. Python implements it for the wheel output of python/package: the single regular file {name}-{version}-*.whl next to the planned file. No match keeps the original missing bundle path failure; more than one match fails and names them. sdist, applications and other builders have no discovery. The result is a file name in the planned directory, never a path; symlinks are ignored and the usual containment, regular-file, digest and size checks still apply. The bundle's artifact record carries the file actually collected, and compatibility is inspected from that file's metadata, not from its name. The frozen plan, --plan output and plan digest keep the planned name (py3-none-any), so the planned and collected names can differ for a native wheel. materialize with into writes the consumer's file under the collected name; the receipt records where it was written. to names an exact file and therefore cannot address a name that is only known after the build; use into for a discovered file. Collisions with the collected name are detected when the file is written, not at planning, and an existing file is never overwritten. Limits: the lookup also applies to a legacy setup.py wheel whose planned tag is absent, so a mismatched tag there is collected and classified from its metadata rather than failing. The Windows/macOS wheel tags are not classified (below). Named image platform lists must include the resolved worker platform for this path; use the existing --all-platforms captured path for matrix execution. Worker task replacements and pre/post hooks run through the shared task executor and retain report obligations. Hooks share the private target workspace. Docker context membership is frozen during preparation: hooks may modify admitted files, but newly generated undeclared files do not automatically enter the context. --isolated continues to select the captured build path for the whole graph. Fast builds assemble and verify the OCI image without selecting optional checks. --full adds the existing image assertions, lint and formatting stages, with reports collected through the shared owner. Image content and platform integrity are always verified before publication, including fast builds. The bundle records worker image identity, dependency evidence and per-action enforcement; this does not imply that host producer actions were sandboxed or establish production publication eligibility. Windows image-only fast/full flows have passed. The Windows Python-to-Linux runtime fixture installs/imports the wheel in Linux and verifies exact materialized bytes. Failed-producer blocking, unknown native-wheel rejection and explicit data-only inclusion also passed. See the three-platform Rust-to-image proof, which independently exports Linux amd64, Linux arm64 and Windows amd64 binaries and executes only the matching Linux amd64 binary in its consumer image, in the qualification record.

During an executing build, Windows Ctrl+C or Unix SIGINT/SIGTERM requests coordinated cancellation. Oyzu stops admitting actions, terminates owned native process groups/trees or removes active named workers, retains available logs and a failed bundle, blocks pending dependents, and returns exit code 130. Normal private workspace cleanup then runs. Windows console, Linux SIGINT and Windows-coordinated image-worker flows are verified. Post-hooks are not guaranteed to run. Forced termination (SIGKILL), deliberately detached descendants, every acquisition phase and macOS runtime behavior are not qualified. Inspect remaining processes and build-owned storage after an unhandled termination; do not assume cleanup. oyzu build --plan shows declared shared source inputs and artifact relationships without tool installation, copying source, or running a build. Physical artifact selection and source admission are verified during preparation. Private trees use .oyzu/host-workspaces under the existing build transaction lock. They persist between builds as exact source copies: each build refreshes them in place, rewriting only files whose bytes changed and removing anything outside the selection, and at the end of a build removes what the build generated inside them. On Windows this avoids re-creating every source file per build, which on-access scanning made the slowest preparation step (about 46 seconds for this repository's 2,600-file CLI projection). Interrupted builds leave state that the next build reconciles under that same lock. Native Rust compiler caches remain in the original target's .oyzu/native/rust store with existing budget controls. Copies preserve modification times and use stable paths for repeat builds. Tool stores and native download caches remain shared. This does not promise unchanged cache keys after target selection or source layout changes. Offline runs still require tools and native dependencies already available. Fix an invalid input path, artifact selector, collision or failed native command, then rebuild. No manual copying into a consumer is required. Private workspace cleanup does not remove finalized bundles, tools, or compiler caches.

tooling/test-host-workspaces.py --cli <compiled-oyzu> exercises real host producer/consumer builds, shared parent inputs, edits, verified handoff, clean checkout behavior, preview, hook continuity, pre/build/post failure blocking, diagnostic retention, recovery and cleanup. Qualification results are recorded in implementation status. Linux/macOS runtime qualification and enforced sandboxing are not implied by Windows checks.

An explicitly selected python/package output named wheel can bind one producer to multiple consumer platforms when the producer declares no platforms. Collection inspects the actual wheel before runtime consumption; pure Python platform-independent wheels can be shared. Explicit producer platforms remain authoritative. A Linux native wheel is native and is accepted only after pip accepts it in the consumer runtime (native wheels); unknown wheel compatibility (for example Windows or macOS tags) still fails closed. A wheel built in a worker image keeps its real file name through discovery. materialize.usage: build selects compatibility against the execution platform, while the default runtime uses the consumer artifact platform and data carries no executable compatibility claim. The current build-tool path requires an unambiguous producer; selection from a multi-variant generator matrix remains unfinished. Its end-to-end qualification passed on Linux amd64 (2026-10-07): an amd64 generator ran on the executor and a linux/arm64 consumer built from its output. Rust recipe lookup selects the smallest pinned recipe that contains the requested components and still fails with TOOL_LOCK_AMBIGUOUS for incomparable recipes; a cross target's request includes its target-platform standard library. Windows, macOS and other Docker versions are not qualified. See the qualification record for measured portable-wheel and worker-hook results and remaining limitations.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-aqua.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Status: experimental, provisional. First install proof (A1) of the draft backend compatibility direction: Oyzu reads the aqua registry catalog that mise's aqua backend reads, inside oyzu.toml, and names each package with an Oyzu tool id. Error codes, field names and the pinned registry snapshot may change. Qualification is Linux x86-64 only; see qualification for what ran and what did not.
documents.s: Registry packages (oyzu: ids, from the aqua registry)

documents.t: oyzu install terraform@1.9.8 # a curated name oyzu install gh@2.49.2 # a catalog short name, stored as oyzu:gh oyzu install oyzu:burntsushi/ripgrep@14.1.1 oyzu install aqua:go-task/task@3.54.0 # mise spelling, rewritten to oyzu:task oyzu exec -- gh --version # runs the installed, verified binary oyzu tools info oyzu:gh # provider, source, commands, platforms, verification oyzu tools versions oyzu:gh # releases, newest first, with excluded ones explained oyzu uninstall oyzu:gh The declaration is the tool's canonical id: [tools] "oyzu:task" = "3.54.0" "oyzu:gh" = "2.49.2" terraform = "1.9.8" # curated names may also be written bare All the tool commands apply (scopes, --dry-run, --frozen, --offline, update, tools current, tools list). No account is needed and no mise executable is used.

mise's table form of a [tools] entry is accepted with one option, version, for every tool (not only registry packages). It means exactly the same as the plain string: [tools] "oyzu:gh" = { version = "2.49.2" } [tools."oyzu:jq"] version = "1.7.1" oyzu install gh@2.50.0 changes only the version inside such a table, so the file keeps its form and comments. (A table under an aqua: or core: key is replaced by a plain entry under the new key when that tool is installed.) Unknown options (os, exe, bin, asset_pattern, install_env, postinstall, ...) and unknown sub-tables are ignored with optional configuration warnings. Only version affects the request: ignored fields never run hooks or modify installation. Use oyzu config validate --strict to reject these warnings; declare a required capability when correct execution depends on new behavior. A table without a valid version string is still refused. Arrays of versions are not supported.

Maintainer decision of 2026-10-10 (naming): tool ids carry no aqua: prefix. Every spelling of a package resolves to one canonical id, and configuration and the lock store that id, so the spelling never changes the lock. Package Canonical id Also accepted In the curated set (for example hashicorp/terraform) oyzu:<name> (oyzu:terraform) terraform, oyzu:hashicorp/terraform, aqua:hashicorp/terraform Any other registry package oyzu:<owner>/<repo>[/<name>], lowercased (oyzu:burntsushi/ripgrep) aqua:BurntSushi/ripgrep; a catalog short name (ripgrep) with oyzu install A GitHub repository's release assets github:<owner>/<repo> (unchanged) Oyzu's own providers (Node, Go, Rust, ...) oyzu:<name> (oyzu:go) go, and the earlier core:go Curated names. The curated set is the proposed launch set (platform governed-tool-catalog-coverage.md, section C), each named by its primary name in the pinned mise catalog, except cli/cli, which is oyzu:gh (mise calls it github-cli; both short names install it). It is built into the client (src/tools/development_backend/names.rs), so curated names resolve without the network. A name that would collide with an Oyzu provider (kubectl, helm, k3d) or an admitted Cargo helper is not curated; those packages keep their owner/repo id. The public tool index is expected to supply these names later. aqua: is an input alias. aqua:<owner>/<repo> is accepted wherever an id is (commands, [tools] keys, policy) and rewritten; Oyzu never writes it. Installing a tool that is declared under an aqua: or core: key moves the declaration to the new key. Origin is provenance. Each lock resolution records the registry package in its components (package:<owner>/<repo>), next to registry: and tag:. Earlier locks. A lock written with aqua: or core: ids is stale. oyzu install reports TOOL_LOCK_STALE naming the rename; oyzu install --update drops those pins and re-pins the same tools under their oyzu: ids, re-reading each publisher checksum (exact versions resolve to the same archives and digests). oyzu install --frozen fails until then. [tools] keys written as aqua: keep working and are not rewritten by --update.

oyzu install gh@2.49.2 works as in mise: a short name that Oyzu neither provides nor curates is looked up in the catalog and expands to the first backend in its entry that Oyzu supports (aqua:cli/cli), which is then stored under its canonical id (oyzu:gh). oyzu:gh is looked up the same way. $ oyzu install gh@2.49.2 $ cat oyzu.toml [tools] "oyzu:gh" = "2.49.2" The catalog is the registry/*.toml data of the mise crate release 2026.10.5 (MIT), downloaded at run time from static.crates.io, checked against a pinned SHA-256 and cached as <store>/catalogs/mise-registry-<digest>.crate (re-checked on every read; offline use works once cached). None of it is stored in this repository, no mise code is compiled or run, and a core tool name that Oyzu already admits (node, go, ...) keeps resolving to Oyzu's own provider. Catalog short names are accepted by oyzu install; other commands and [tools] keys take a curated name or the canonical id. Situation Result Unknown name TOOL_NAME_UNKNOWN, naming the explicit oyzu:<owner>/<repo> spelling Listed only under backends Oyzu lacks (cargo:, npm:, asdf:, ...) TOOL_BACKEND_UNSUPPORTED, listing them Catalog cannot be fetched / digest differs TOOL_REGISTRY_UNAVAILABLE / TOOL_REGISTRY_DIGEST_MISMATCH

Request Meaning Needs the release listing 3.54.0 or v3.54.0 Exactly this release No latest Newest stable release the recipe covers Yes 2.49 Highest stable 2.49.x the recipe covers Yes An exact version tries the tag spellings <version_prefix>v<version> then <version_prefix><version> and takes the first whose checksum file exists, so pinned installs make no GitHub API request and cannot hit its rate limit. The release listing uses GitHub's releases API for the newest 300 releases. Set GITHUB_TOKEN to raise the anonymous limit; it is sent to api.github.com only. Drafts are never offered; pre-releases only when named exactly. The lock retains the original request and a concrete normalized release. Its validation uses the package selector's same exact-tag, version-prefix and stable latest rules; it does not compare the word latest literally with the selected version or consult a mutable release listing. An incompatible version or damaged resolution identity is still refused. Raw tags must agree with the normalized version; ambiguous numeric suffixes are refused. Registry tag prefixes ending in a digit are not qualified by this matcher.

Registry. One pinned snapshot, aqua-registry v4.573.0 (SHA-256 52a43b0b…0228), fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com, checked against that digest, and cached in the tool store at catalogs/aqua-registry-<digest>.yaml (re-checked on every read). A different snapshot is a reviewed source change. No registry data is copied into this repository or the binary. Resolution. Declaring or updating a tool evaluates the recipe for every default platform (linux/amd64/gnu, darwin/arm64/native, windows/amd64/msvc) with the recipe evaluator, reads the publisher's checksum file, and writes one lock resolution per platform. A platform with no build is recorded as unavailable, as for other tools. Recipe types. type: github_release (the asset of a GitHub release) and type: http (a direct download URL the recipe renders, such as https://releases.hashicorp.com/... or https://storage.googleapis.com/...). Both resolve exact versions without the release listing: the tag spellings above are rendered into the URL and checksum URL, and the first whose checksum file exists is taken. Other types (go_install, cargo, github_content, ...) are refused with SOURCE_KIND ("not a release download"); nothing is installed. Packaging. The recipe's format decides how the download is unpacked: format Installed as tar.gz, tgz gzip tar tar.xz, txz xz tar (pure-Rust decoder, lzma-rust2) tar.zst zstd tar, concatenated frames included (the ruzstd decoder Oyzu already uses) tar plain tar zip ZIP32 raw (or an asset with no archive extension) the asset is the executable: it is stored under the first command's name (<name>.exe on Windows) and marked executable off Windows; as in aqua, files[].src is ignored and every declared command runs that file Every tar kind is streamed through the same bounded extractor (entry, size, depth and a 200:1 expansion limit). Other formats (tar.bz2, tbz, single-file gz/bz2/xz/zst, 7z, dmg, pkg) are reported as TOOL_ARCHIVE_UNSUPPORTED, naming the supported list. The lock is the pin. Each resolution holds the archive URL and SHA-256, and in components the facts install needs: kind: (one of the kinds above, as the evaluator's layout kind: tar.gz, tar.xz, tar.zst, tar, zip, raw), bin:<command>=<path in the archive>, tag: (the release tag) and registry: (the snapshot digest). This reuses the existing components field; no schema changed. A locked tool restores and runs without the registry, and oyzu install --frozen into an empty store needs only the pinned archive URLs. Download. Only the host archive is downloaded and its SHA-256 must equal the locked value. Hosts: GitHub's release hosts and the registry file are fixed. A recipe that downloads from elsewhere (for example a vendor's release server) has that host admitted from its pinned URL: HTTPS on port 443, a public DNS name only (no IP literal, single label, or .local/.internal- style name), no credentials. A tool route configured for registry packages is refused (TOOL_ROUTE_UNSUPPORTED) because routing for this backend is not connected. Commands. The executables a recipe declares (files) become the tool's commands; a recipe without files gets one command named after the last segment of the package name (kubectl for kubernetes/kubernetes/kubectl), as in aqua. On Windows .exe is completed as the registry does (complete_windows_ext). When a package has several commands, every one is an entry point (oyzu exec -- <command>), each distinct command file must exist after unpacking and is marked executable, and each distinct command directory is put on PATH for child processes, the primary command's directory first. The primary command is the first by name, not by recipe order. Several names may share one file (superfly/flyctl declares flyctl and fly, both flyctl): each name runs through oyzu exec, but only the file's own name is found by a child process searching PATH, because Oyzu does not create links in the installed tree.
documents.s: What is installed, and from where

documents.t: Install verifies the publisher's SHA-256 checksum: the lock records the checksum the recipe's checksum file lists for each platform, and the downloaded archive must equal it. A per-asset checksum file whose whole body is one digest with no file name (dl.k8s.io's kubectl.sha256) is read as that asset's digest, as aqua does. This is the check the open-source backend performs today. Recipes may declare more (GitHub artifact attestation, cosign, SLSA provenance, minisign). Those checks are not performed yet and do not stop an install; for example oyzu install oyzu:gh@2.102.0 installs on its checksum even though the recipe also declares an attestation. tools info says so. A later milestone can add the verifiers, and a stricter, curated backend can require them; neither is part of this one. What the lock cannot hold yet is reported instead of installed: Code Cause TOOL_CHECKSUM_MISSING The recipe declares no checksum to lock and the package is not on the GitHub-reported digest allow-list TOOL_CHECKSUM_UNSUPPORTED The recipe's checksum is not SHA-256 (the lock records SHA-256 only) or its checksum file is regexp format TOOL_CHECKSUM_UNVERIFIABLE The checksum file does not list the archive, or lists conflicting values

A recipe that declares no checksum normally cannot be locked. For a short, curated allow-list of packages Oyzu instead locks the SHA-256 GitHub reports for the release asset the recipe downloads from the package's own repository (the evidence github: packages use). The list is GITHUB_DIGEST_ALLOWED in src/tools/development/aqua.rs; it currently holds protocolbuffers/protobuf/protoc, the one recipe proven end to end. The fallback is deliberately not available to every checksum-less recipe, because that would loosen acquisition checks for tools nobody reviewed. Any other checksum-less package reports TOOL_CHECKSUM_MISSING; for a tool a builder merely detected that is an attention row and the build continues, for an explicit pin it is an error. To add a package: open a PR that adds its registry name to the list, with a test or proof that the recipe downloads from the package's own GitHub releases and that GitHub reports a digest for the asset, and the rationale in the PR. Review of that entry is the approval; see third-party compliance for the notice rules that apply to any new tool. A successful install means the archive equals the checksum the publisher listed at resolution time; it does not prove the publisher or the checksum file is authentic.

Code Meaning and recovery TOOL_ALIAS_UNSUPPORTED Another backend (asdf:, vfox: …) is not supported; the message lists what is TOOL_SPEC_INVALID Not oyzu:<name>, oyzu:<owner>/<repo> (or <owner>/<repo>/<name>), github:<owner>/<repo> or the aqua: alias TOOL_NAME_UNKNOWN oyzu:<name> is not curated; use oyzu:<owner>/<repo> or oyzu install <name> TOOL_NOT_IN_REGISTRY The package is not in the pinned snapshot; check the spelling TOOL_VERSION_NOT_FOUND No such release for an exact version, or nothing matches a prefix in the newest 300 releases; run oyzu tools versions TOOL_RATE_LIMITED GitHub refused the release listing (anonymous limit or an access policy); set GITHUB_TOKEN, or request an exact version TOOL_ARCHIVE_UNSUPPORTED Packaged in a format outside the packaging table (for example tar.bz2, a single gzip-compressed binary or 7z); the message lists the supported kinds CONFIG_INVALID_VALUE A [tools] option table has no valid version string; see option tables TOOL_RECIPE_UNSUPPORTED The recipe uses a construct the evaluator does not implement; see recipe resolution TOOL_REGISTRY_UNAVAILABLE / _DIGEST_MISMATCH The pinned snapshot could not be fetched, or its bytes differ from the pin

tools versions oyzu:<name> lists the newest releases, newest first, evaluated for this host. A release the recipe does not cover, has no build for this platform, or whose verification this build cannot perform appears under excluded with its reason, so the list shows what install would accept. tools info shows provider, source, commands (after the tool is locked), platforms, eligibility under tools.allowed, declarations and the verification rule. Both support --json.

Linux x86-64 only has been run. Windows and macOS behavior (including the .exe completion, raw .exe assets and zip extraction) is covered by unit tests only. Archives: tar.gz, tar.xz, tar.zst, tar, zip and raw executables. Not tar.bz2 (41 registry entries; no bzip2 decoder is in the build), single-file gz/bz2/xz/zst executables, 7z, dmg or pkg. Only SHA-256 checksum files. Attestation, cosign, SLSA and minisign checks that recipes declare are not performed. A command name that differs from its file's name (an alias such as flyctl's fly) runs through oyzu exec but is not on the child PATH. Option tables honor only version; unknown options warn and remain inert. The other mise backends are not implemented (github: is separate and experimental; see tool-github); catalog short names resolve only to aqua registry entries and only for oyzu install. A hand-written declaration with no lock entry needs oyzu install <id> or oyzu install --update to resolve; plain oyzu install reports TOOL_LOCK_STALE, for the string form and table form alike. The snapshot is fixed per build; customer registries and a floating registry are not supported. A configured tool route is refused rather than honored. Version listing needs GitHub's API. The evaluator is independent and unverified against the registry's own engine beyond observed recipes; vars and musl builds are unsupported. Registry packages are admitted by their well-formed id, so tools.allowed matches the canonical oyzu: id; how an aqua: entry in that list is read was not exercised. Behavior of that policy for registry packages was not exercised (the setting is managed-scope only).

python tooling/test-tool-aqua-install.py --cli <oyzu> --workspace <dir> drives the compiled CLI against the pinned registry and real publishers; unit tests live in src/tools/development/aqua.rs, acquisition.rs and declare/spec.rs; tests/integration/recipe_resolve.rs covers rejected specs. Archive kinds are unit-tested in src/tools/store/archive.rs (xz, single- and multi-frame zstd), option tables in src/config/registry.rs and src/config/edit.rs. The 2026-10-10 live runs of tar.xz, raw, http and multi-command packages and option tables are in the qualification record. Results: qualification record.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-backend-inspection.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. See tool lock inspection for the lock entry point.

The draft backend descriptor schema encodes the OEP's closed identity record: exact source commit, patch-register digest, embedding ABI and adapter revision, nullable registry/plugin digests, verifier digest and unique string features. Nullable fields are required even when null. Positive revision integers stay within the canonical JSON safe range. Source pins and digests require exact whole-string matches; trailing newlines are rejected by both the schema and runtime parser. Shared malformed fixtures exercise all five identity fields. The synthetic fixtures are not compiled backend descriptors or approved pins. Run python tooling/check-tool-contracts.py with tooling/design-requirements.txt installed to check descriptor, layout and receipt shapes offline. The checker rejects duplicate JSON keys and nonlocal schema references. Descriptor fixtures cover four valid shapes and thirteen rejected shapes, including floating refs, omitted identities, open records and unsafe integers. Schema checks do not establish sorted feature order, provenance, canonical descriptor hashing, compatibility or admission. The Rust parser checks the shared fixtures and additionally requires features to be sorted and unique. No stable project configuration syntax is introduced. oyzu tools inspect-backend PATH reads a regular JSON file, bounded to 2 MiB plus one overflow probe. Relative paths use -C, then --root, then the current directory. It defaults to readable text; --json returns digest, source_pin and validation: "structure-and-identity-only". Success exits 0; malformed, oversized or unreadable input exits 2. It rejects unknown/duplicate fields, omitted nullable identities, malformed digests, floating source refs and unsafe revisions. It never reads project/mise configuration, accesses the network, executes backend code or changes files. Repair input explicitly and rerun on error. oyzu tools inspect-backend tests/fixtures/tool-backend/descriptor.json The example is synthetic and cannot authorize installation. The digest uses oyzu.backend.v1, a zero byte and canonical JSON through the shared record encoder. A checked-in golden identity and per-field mutation tests verify identity binding; formatting differences do not change it. Compiled descriptor admission, provenance validation, source licensing approval and compatibility remain separate unimplemented gates. A self-consistent malicious descriptor can pass inspection.

stage_tool_candidate accepts archive_kind: "zip" for bounded ZIP32 archives using stored or DEFLATE compression. The standalone tar materialization API is unchanged. This is a library staging capability, not a production installation command or backend qualification. It uses the same verified blob, admitted plan, path checks, required payload checks and receipt boundary as tar layouts. Inspection of the maintained fork's zip 8.6.0 dependency found that its high-level archive reader builds a filename-indexed map that collapses duplicate names, after allocating central-directory metadata. Checking only ZipArchive::len() and then applying Oyzu path checks would therefore miss duplicate records and apply resource limits too late. Its streaming visitor also ends central-directory parsing on an error, so successful visitation alone does not establish a valid complete directory. Oyzu therefore preflights the complete central directory before initializing the decoder. Entry counts, total local/central metadata (32 MiB), individual and total expanded sizes, and per-file expansion ratios are bounded. The expanded archive budget includes local headers, central metadata and the footer/comment as well as payload. Names must be ASCII or explicitly flagged UTF-8. Duplicate raw names, inconsistent local/central names, sizes, methods and CRCs, overlapping local records, unconsumed gaps and trailing data fail. Both signed and unsigned ZIP32 data descriptors are checked. Decoder output must reach EOF with the declared size and valid CRC; a corrupt payload never receives a receipt. Only ordinary files and empty directories from DOS/Unix originating systems are admitted. Unix executable bits are preserved in otherwise private file modes; Windows launch validation still uses receipt rules. ZIP64, encryption, split archives, self-extracting stubs, Unicode override extra fields, links and special entries are rejected. Archives requiring these features need further qualified implementation; they are never silently interpreted as another format. On any failure, discard the incomplete staging directory and retry with an admitted artifact in new empty staging. Extraction has no network access or subprocesses. The exact zip 8.6.0 dependency uses only deflate-flate2, with default features disabled. Original notices for it and its new transitive dependency typed-path are preserved in third-party notices. This does not approve the complete shipping dependency graph or establish publisher authenticity. Tests cover stored/DEFLATE staging and receipt publication, CRC corruption, header disagreement, duplicate metadata, limits, traversal, case collisions and both data-descriptor encodings. Real upstream archive parity and native platform qualification remain separate gates. Archive path admission is centralized under store/archive/paths: raw duplicate detection, strip-prefix validation, case/type collision checks, expanded entry and depth limits, and anchored destination traversal use one rule set. The 32 MiB name budget now includes original names retained for duplicate detection, even when stripping skips a prefix ancestor, as well as expanded destination names and link targets. Archives that previously escaped this accounting can fail earlier; no receipt is written on failure. TAR and ZIP use this same path owner.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-catalog.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Status: experimental, provisional. Milestone M4 of the tools catalog plan (client half), with the N3 governance additions (catalog-filtered tools versions, the kept copy for an unreachable edge, governed oyzu: providers). The client is implemented and has run end to end against the delivery edge from the platform repository. No production edge exists yet. Setting names, codes and the catalog document are drafts pending maintainer review.

An organization that manages its developers' tools approves which tools and versions they may install. Its delivery edge publishes that decision as the organization's catalog: the signed public tool index narrowed to the approved versions, with each entry's lifecycle state and how its bytes are delivered. A client configured with the catalog installs registry packages and Oyzu's own archive providers (oyzu:java, …) only from it: Only versions the catalog approves resolve. Any other version fails before anything is downloaded. A blocked or quarantined version fails with the organization's reason. The catalog is signed by the edge, and only a catalog signed by a key pinned in toolCatalog.keys is used, fetched or kept. The catalog can only narrow the index. An entry whose SHA-256 differs from the signed index record is refused, so the edge cannot substitute other bytes. Artifacts the catalog delivers through the edge are downloaded from the edge with the organization token. Artifacts it marks direct (a license that forbids redistribution) come from the publisher, and the client still checks the catalog's SHA-256. There is no local recipe fallback, and no registry file, GitHub release listing or provider publisher API (such as Adoptium's) is read. tools versions lists only what the organization approves and serves. Node's moving lts alias needs publisher LTS markers, which the signed tool index does not yet contain. Governed resolution refuses it with TOOL_LTS_METADATA_UNAVAILABLE; catalog-only checks report it unavailable. Select an approved exact version or named line (lts/krypton) instead. Without an organization catalog, an unpinned Node requests lts even with engines.node: select the greatest stable release whose publisher-index lts field is a non-empty string and that satisfies every engine constraint. If none matches, fall back to the greatest stable release satisfying them. The requirement reason in the plan explains this fallback rule. Standalone indexed resolution uses that same exact selection. Explicit latest, major, exact and named LTS pins keep their behavior and must satisfy engines; frozen lts locks validate offline without refreshing publisher LTS facts. When the edge cannot be reached, the last good catalog is used for a bounded time (toolCatalog.maxOfflineAge), with a warning. It never adds anything the edge did not approve. The edge's side is the platform repository's delivery service (dl edge).

A signed tool index (toolIndex.url). The catalog approves versions of index records; it is not an index on its own. An organization token from the edge's operator. The public key of the edge's catalog signing key (ed25519:<base64>), from the edge's operator (delivery catalog-keygen prints it when the key is made).

Setting or variable Value; default Meaning toolCatalog.url HTTPS URL (HTTP only on loopback); absent Base URL of the delivery edge. Unset: registry packages resolve from the index or locally as before toolCatalog.keys Array of one to eight ed25519:<base64> public keys; absent The keys the catalog must be signed by. Required whenever toolCatalog.url is set (TOOL_CATALOG_UNTRUSTED without it). Pin two while the edge rotates its key. User or machine scope only (CONFIG_SCOPE in a project file); lock it in admin-settings.json toolCatalog.maxOfflineAge 0, <n>h or <n>d (at most 366d); 7d How long after the edge built it the last good catalog may be used when the edge is unreachable. 0 never uses it. User or machine scope only (CONFIG_SCOPE in a project file); lock it in admin-settings.json to enforce a value toolCatalog.adminUrl HTTPS URL (HTTP only on loopback); absent; env OYZU_TOOL_CATALOG_ADMIN_URL Base URL of the delivery admin API, where tools request and --cancel go. User, machine or administrative scope only (a project file cannot set it: the sign-in token is sent there) OYZU_TOOL_CATALOG_TOKEN Environment variable The organization token, sent as Authorization: Bearer. Never a setting, so it cannot land in a committed file # ~/.config/oyzu/config.toml [toolIndex] url = "https://index.example.test/" [toolCatalog] url = "https://dl.example.test/" keys = ["ed25519:7sb4o1W0lRKR712+E7DQ8uYEeTX2sUXSzJMTpKc0lzI="] The client reads GET <url>v1/catalog once per command, sending the ETag of its kept copy so an unchanged catalog answers 304 and is not downloaded again. A proxied artifact is fetched from <url>v1/upstream/<host><path> for its original URL, so the edge can look it up. The client does not call v1/versions or v1/resolve; it applies the same rules to the catalog document, so a cached copy behaves exactly like a fetched one.

To make the catalog mandatory on a machine, set it as a locked administrative setting in the machine's protected admin-settings.json (see configuration). User and project files then cannot remove or change it: { "schemaVersion": 1, "kind": "local-admin-policy", "settings": { "toolCatalog.url": { "locked": true, "value": "https://dl.example.test/" }, "toolCatalog.keys": { "locked": true, "value": ["ed25519:7sb4o1W0lRKR712+E7DQ8uYEeTX2sUXSzJMTpKc0lzI="] }, "toolCatalog.maxOfflineAge": { "locked": true, "value": "3d" }, "toolIndex.url": { "locked": true, "value": "https://index.example.test/" } }, "profiles": {}, "requiredCapabilities": [] } Pair it with a network allowlist that permits the edge and the index host but not the publishers' hosts. Distribute both through device management.

The edge serves the catalog as a DSSE envelope, {"payloadType": "application/vnd.oyzu.tool-catalog+json", "payload": <base64>, "signatures": [{"keyid", "sig"}]}. Each signature is Ed25519 over the DSSE pre-authentication encoding, and its keyid is the hex SHA-256 of the 32-byte public key. The client accepts the envelope when one signature verifies under a pinned key; anything else (another key, an edited payload, a plain JSON document) fails with TOOL_CATALOG_UNTRUSTED. The payload is: Field Meaning org The organization the token belongs to revision SHA-256 of what the catalog says; changes exactly when the catalog does index {serial, sha256} of the signed public index the edge built it from policy_revision The organization policy's revision (0 for an edge reading policy files) built, expires When the edge signed it, and when a fetched copy stops being accepted (24 hours later by default) entries The approved entries: id, aliases, version, platform, sha256, delivery, state, refusal, upstream URL Checks, in order: the signature; for a fetched copy, that it has not expired (TOOL_CATALOG_STALE, which also points at a wrong clock); then, when the client's verified index has the same serial as the catalog's index, that both name the same SHA-256 (TOOL_CATALOG_MISMATCH). The edge and the client each pick up a new index release on their own schedule (the edge hourly, the client after an hour's reuse), so a catalog from a neighbouring serial is accepted; every entry is still matched against the client's own index record. The edge reuses one signed envelope until half its lifetime has passed or the catalog changes, and its ETag is the SHA-256 of the envelope bytes. To rotate the key, the edge's operator adds the new key beside the old one (the edge signs with both), clients move toolCatalog.keys to the new public key, and the operator then removes the old key.

For an aqua: package, after the lock: The index selects the version, considering only versions the catalog approves (on any platform), so every platform of a lock gets the same version. The record for each platform must be admitted: approved for that platform, not refused, and naming the index's SHA-256. A version approved for other platforms only is treated like a release without a build for this platform. A version the publisher did not build for some platform is judged the same way on the platforms it has; the missing platform is left out of the lock, as without a catalog. Downloading follows the catalog's delivery for the artifact URL: proxy through the edge, direct from the publisher. A URL the catalog does not list is refused. Reinstalling from a cached archive still checks admission against the current catalog before staging an installation. An admitted, verified blob is reused without another artifact download. If a portable lock omits the archive size, the store recovers it from the digest-verified cached bytes. With install --offline, admission uses the kept catalog under the age and signature rules below and never contacts the edge; both the catalog and archive must be available locally.

A version the signed index withdrew (its withdrawn reason; see the index) stays in the catalog with state withdrawn, the reason in withdrawn and a refusal, and the edge refuses to serve it. The client refuses it with TOOL_VERSION_WITHDRAWN, the reason and the newest version the catalog serves for this host: TOOL_VERSION_WITHDRAWN: oyzu:golang-migrate 4.20.0 was withdrawn from the tool index: upstream release assets were deleted (404). The newest version the acme tool catalog serves for linux/amd64/gnu is 4.19.1. With nothing else servable, the message says to ask with oyzu tools request. The same holds when the index withdrew the version and the catalog has not caught up. A prefix or latest skips withdrawn versions, and an existing lock naming one is refused on the next install (before reuse or download). tools versions lists it under excluded with TOOL_VERSION_WITHDRAWN and the reason, and tools check --catalog reports it as withdrawn. An older client refuses it through the refusal (TOOL_REFUSED). The lock is the same as without a catalog. It records the publisher URL and the published SHA-256, never the edge's host or the token. github: packages are refused under a catalog because the catalog does not list their artifacts.

Oyzu's archive providers (Java, Node, Go, Python, Maven, Gradle, kubectl, k3d, Helm, Liquibase, Tailscale, npm and pnpm) follow the same three steps under a catalog instead of reading their publisher's live metadata. The index carries them under their oyzu: id with origin core:<name> (oyzu:java from core:java); the catalog may name them by either. The version comes from the index narrowed by the catalog, the SHA-256 from the verified index record, and the provider only rebuilds the archive layout from the record's publisher URL. The lock records oyzu:java, the publisher URL and the SHA-256, exactly as without a catalog. Requests use the index's selection: an exact release (21.0.8), a release-line prefix (21, 1.25) or latest. For Java, lts and * select the newest approved long-term-support release (8, 11, and every fourth feature release from 17: 17, 21, 25, …). Node's named aliases (lts/jod, lts-iron) name their release line; the moving lts alias is refused under an organization catalog as described above. Any other request, such as a range (^20, ~1.24, >=3.12 <3.14), selects the newest approved release it matches. Native constraints (>=17) narrow every request. A provider the index does not carry is refused with TOOL_NOT_IN_INDEX. The client can now produce and consume records for all archive providers above. The separate index job must publish them before managed installations can use them. oyzu:rust uses an approved indexed channel manifest, its component digests and pinned rustup bootstrap. Each selected download is verified before entering rustup's local mirror; see indexed Rust. An unapproved exact version remains TOOL_NOT_IN_CATALOG, including on reuse. cargo: helpers (cargo:cargo-nextest, cargo:cargo-llvm-cov) remain refused with TOOL_NOT_IN_INDEX; governing their releases is deferred.

With toolCatalog.url set, oyzu tools check --catalog fetches the catalog (or, with --offline, reads the kept copy) and judges each declared registry package and provider as an install would: the request selects among the versions the catalog approves, and the selected version must be admitted for the host and every explicit tools.platforms entry. The default pin matrix is optional coverage: missing records for other hosts do not refuse an install on this host. Status Meaning Refused approved Installs version through the catalog no not-in-catalog The catalog approves no release the request matches; also every github: package yes refused The organization refuses version (the reason is the edge's), or the catalog names other bytes than the index; also cargo: helpers and unindexed Rust (TOOL_NOT_IN_INDEX) yes withdrawn The request names (or every match of it is) a version withdrawn from the tool index; the reason names the newest servable one yes not-in-index The index does not carry the tool, or has no verified record for it yes unavailable No build of the selected version for the host or an explicitly required platform, or approved for other platforms only yes excluded, blocked, unknown As without a catalog yes The JSON form adds catalog (org, built, source and any cached-copy warning).

oyzu tools versions <tool> lists, newest first, the indexed versions the catalog approves and serves for this platform, for registry packages and providers alike. A version the organization refused (blocked, quarantined, below a floor) appears under excluded with TOOL_REFUSED and the reason, and the human output shows it in a "Refused by the catalog" table; one whose catalog SHA-256 disagrees with the index appears as TOOL_CATALOG_MISMATCH, and one withdrawn from the index as TOOL_VERSION_WITHDRAWN with the reason. Versions the organization never approved are not shown. A tool the catalog does not list fails with TOOL_NOT_IN_CATALOG, the same error as installing it. The JSON source is organization catalog, and catalog gives the org, built and whether the copy was fetched or cached.

oyzu tools request <tool>@<version> [--reason TEXT] asks the organization's administrators to approve a version the catalog does not serve. The version may be a prefix (kubectl@1.31). It posts to the delivery admin API, which has its own host (not the platform gateway and not the edge): POST <toolCatalog.adminUrl>/v1/orgs/<org>/requests with {"tool", "version", "reason"}, where <org> is the organization named by the signed catalog the CLI already reads from the edge. The call is made as the signed-in person: it needs oyzu auth login (platform.url, platform.account) or OYZU_PLATFORM_TOKEN, and sends that access token as Authorization: Bearer to the admin URL, not OYZU_TOOL_CATALOG_TOKEN; the person needs the catalog.request permission. Without toolCatalog.adminUrl (or OYZU_TOOL_CATALOG_ADMIN_URL) it fails with TOOL_CATALOG_ADMIN_URL_MISSING; no URL is guessed. Reading the catalog for the organization still needs OYZU_TOOL_CATALOG_TOKEN. The command shows the request: its id, state (pending, or approved when one of the organization's auto-approve rules admits it at once) and what to do next. Asking again for the same tool and version returns the request already pending (HTTP 200, created: false); a new request is HTTP 201 (created: true). Both are success. A version the catalog already serves reports served. The admin API checks the tool against the signed index; a tool it lacks, or a version with no verified artifact, fails with TOOL_REQUEST_INVALID and its reason; a person without catalog.request (HTTP 403) fails with TOOL_REQUEST_FORBIDDEN; no or a refused sign-in fails with TOOL_REQUEST_UNAUTHENTICATED. TOOL_NOT_IN_CATALOG refusals name the command. Administrators list and decide requests through the delivery admin API. A request is pending until an administrator approves or denies it, its requester cancels it (cancelled), or it expires (expired). A pending request expires 30 days after it was made unless the organization configures another limit; the edge says when in expires_at (RFC 3339). An expired or cancelled request can no longer be decided, and the same tool and version can be asked for again. oyzu tools request --status <id> reads one of the organization's requests back from the edge (GET /v1/requests/<id>): its state (pending, approved, denied, cancelled or expired), created_at, expires_at, who asked, who decided and why, and what to do next. An id the organization does not have fails with TOOL_REQUEST_UNKNOWN. oyzu tools request --cancel <id> withdraws a pending request (POST <toolCatalog.adminUrl>/v1/orgs/<org>/requests/<id>/cancel with {}, as the signed-in person like the request itself) and shows it, now cancelled. Only its requester can: the platform refuses anyone else with TOOL_REQUEST_FORBIDDEN (HTTP 403). A request that is no longer pending fails with TOOL_REQUEST_NOT_PENDING (HTTP 409), naming its state when the edge gives it. oyzu tools requests lists the requests made from this machine, newest first, each with its state read from the edge now. The edge lists no requests by requester, so the client remembers the ids it was given (the newest 50, per catalog URL and token) in state/tool-catalog/<key>.requests.json of the default store; the file holds ids, tools and versions only, never a state. A pending request shows when it expires (pending, expires 2026-11-10). A remembered request the edge no longer has shows as unknown. Neither command polls; run it again to see a decision.

Each successfully fetched and verified catalog is kept in the default tool store, under catalogs/tool-catalog/<key>/catalog.json (~/.local/share/oyzu/tools/… on Linux): the signed envelope exactly as the edge served it, with the time it was fetched. The signature is checked again every time the copy is read, so an edited copy, or a copy after the pinned keys changed, is refused (TOOL_CATALOG_UNAVAILABLE naming TOOL_CATALOG_UNTRUSTED). The key is derived from the catalog URL and a SHA-256 of the token (never the token itself), because one edge serves many organizations: switching edges or organizations never reads another catalog's copy. In-process reuse includes this token-specific cache path, the resolved store, settings and offline mode, so loads from different user data roots cannot share a catalog. See the default store location for disposable-home isolation on Windows. A copy is replaced only by a newer fetched document; one the edge built earlier than the kept copy does not replace it. When fetching fails with a network error or an HTTP 5xx, the kept copy is used if the edge built it no longer than toolCatalog.maxOfflineAge ago (its signed built, not the local fetch time), and the command reports TOOL_CATALOG_CACHED with the copy's fetch time and age. Its signed expires does not apply offline; maxOfflineAge does. Its entries go through the same index cross-check: an entry whose SHA-256 differs from the signed index record is still refused. A copy older than the limit fails with TOOL_CATALOG_STALE. A refused token (401, 403), a missing catalog (404), a bad signature or a malformed document is the edge's answer and is never replaced by the copy. The built time of the newest catalog fetched from the edge is also kept, apart from the copy, in state/tool-catalog/<key>.json of the default store. A kept copy built earlier than that fails with TOOL_CATALOG_STALE ("older than the newest one this client fetched"), so a restored backup, a copy synced from another machine or an older copy put back into the cache cannot bring back a version the organization has since withdrawn. While a kept copy stands in, a command whose copy has less than a quarter of toolCatalog.maxOfflineAge left (under 42 hours at the default 7d) also reports TOOL_CATALOG_EXPIRING with the time left, before installs start failing with TOOL_CATALOG_STALE. oyzu tools versions --offline never asks the edge: it uses the kept copy under the same age and newest-seen rules, with the cached index, and reports catalog.source as cached. oyzu install --offline replays the lock and needs neither.

Code Meaning Recovery TOOL_CATALOG_UNAUTHENTICATED OYZU_TOOL_CATALOG_TOKEN is empty or the edge rejected it Get a current token from your administrator TOOL_CATALOG_UNAVAILABLE The catalog could not be fetched and no usable copy is kept (none yet, another catalog's, maxOfflineAge = "0"), or the edge has no catalog for the organization (404) Check the network path to the edge TOOL_CATALOG_STALE The edge is unreachable (or --offline) and the kept copy is older than toolCatalog.maxOfflineAge, or older than the newest catalog this client fetched; or the edge served a catalog past its signed expires Reconnect to the edge; check this machine's clock TOOL_CATALOG_UNTRUSTED toolCatalog.keys pins no key, or the catalog (fetched or kept) is not signed by a pinned key Pin the edge's current public key; report a bad signature to the edge's operator TOOL_CATALOG_CACHED (warning) The edge is unreachable; the kept copy was used None needed while it is young enough; reconnect to pick up changes TOOL_CATALOG_EXPIRING (warning) The kept copy in use has less than a quarter of maxOfflineAge left Reconnect to the edge before it runs out TOOL_NOT_IN_INDEX Under a catalog, a provider (or package) the signed index does not carry, oyzu:rust when the index has no Rust record, a cargo: helper, or no index configured Wait for the index to carry it, or ask an administrator TOOL_CATALOG_INVALID The catalog document is malformed Report it to the edge's operator TOOL_NOT_IN_CATALOG The organization has not approved this tool or version, or the artifact URL is not listed Ask for it with oyzu tools request <tool>@<version> TOOL_REQUEST_INVALID tools request was not given <tool>@<version>, or the edge refused the request (a tool the index lacks, no verified artifact) Fix the spec, or pick an indexed version TOOL_REQUEST_UNAVAILABLE The admin API has no such organization or request route (HTTP 404), or the edge takes no requests Check toolCatalog.adminUrl; ask an administrator directly TOOL_REQUEST_UNAUTHENTICATED tools request or --cancel without a person's sign-in, or the platform refused it (HTTP 401) Run oyzu auth login (the organization token is not accepted here) TOOL_REQUEST_NOT_CONFIGURED tools request or --cancel without platform.url or platform.account (the sign-in) Set them TOOL_CATALOG_ADMIN_URL_MISSING tools request or --cancel without toolCatalog.adminUrl / OYZU_TOOL_CATALOG_ADMIN_URL Set it to the delivery admin API URL TOOL_REQUEST_UNKNOWN tools request --status or --cancel with an id the organization does not have Run oyzu tools requests for the ids made here TOOL_REQUEST_FORBIDDEN tools request by a person without catalog.request, or --cancel for a request someone else made (HTTP 403) Ask an administrator for the permission, or ask the requester TOOL_REQUEST_NOT_PENDING tools request --cancel for a request already approved, denied, cancelled or expired (HTTP 409) Nothing to cancel; --status shows it TOOL_VERSION_WITHDRAWN The version (named, matched by every candidate of a prefix, or locked) was withdrawn from the tool index; the message gives the reason and the newest version the catalog serves for this host Install or lock that version instead (oyzu install --update <tool>) TOOL_CATALOG_NOT_CONFIGURED tools request (any form) or tools requests without toolCatalog.url Requests are for managed installs only TOOL_REFUSED The version is blocked, quarantined or otherwise refused, with the reason; or the edge refused the download Use another approved version TOOL_CATALOG_MISMATCH The catalog names other bytes than the signed index, or another index under the same serial Nothing was installed. Report it to the edge's operator

Native installation admits Linux amd64/arm64 GNU, macOS arm64 native and Windows amd64 MSVC. The five-platform index includes an unsupported macOS amd64 record. Tailscale provides standalone Linux archives only. Publication of new provider records belongs to the separate index repository. Provider/Rust catalog installation fixtures require Linux amd64. See implementation status for verification results; live evidence and native Linux ARM64 installation remain unverified. The kept copy is signed, so editing it fails, and an older genuine copy is refused. A person who can write both it and the newest-seen record in their own store can still put back an older genuine copy and use a withdrawn version offline, but only until maxOfflineAge after the edge built that copy. A replayed genuine catalog (someone between the client and the edge with a valid token) is accepted until its signed expires, 24 hours by default. While offline (or with the edge down) a withdrawal made after the last fetch is not seen until the next fetch, for at most maxOfflineAge. Only Linux x86-64 has been run.

tests/integration/tool_catalog.rs a_developer_asks_for_an_unapproved_version: the refusal names tools request; the request carries the person's token (not the organization's) to /v1/orgs/acme/requests with the tool, version and reason; a pending (201), an already-pending (200), an auto-approved and a refused answer, and a 403 are reported; a missing or organization token fails with TOOL_REQUEST_UNAUTHENTICATED. a_developer_follows_their_requests: tools requests lists the request made, pending then approved; tools request --status reads it back with who decided; an unknown id, a missing token and a spec given with --status fail. a_developer_cancels_a_request_and_sees_expiry: tools requests shows a pending request's expiry; tools request --cancel posts to /v1/orgs/acme/requests/<id>/cancel with the person's token and shows the cancelled request; an expired request reads back as expired; 403, 409 and 404 fail with TOOL_REQUEST_FORBIDDEN, TOOL_REQUEST_NOT_PENDING and TOOL_REQUEST_UNKNOWN; --cancel with --status is refused. a_withdrawn_version_is_refused_with_the_newest_servable_one: an entry with state withdrawn fails install with TOOL_VERSION_WITHDRAWN, the reason and the newest servable version and downloads nothing; tools versions excludes it with the reason; tools check --catalog reports withdrawn. a_version_the_index_withdrew_is_refused_under_a_catalog: an exact and a prefix request for a version only the index withdrew are refused, with the tools request hint when nothing else is servable. withdrawn_entries_are_refused_with_their_reason (unit): withdrawn, state or both mark an entry withdrawn. unindexed_rust_and_cargo_helpers_are_refused_under_a_catalog: with no Rust record in the index, rust@1.95.0 and cargo:cargo-nextest installs and tools versions rust fail with TOOL_NOT_IN_INDEX and fetch nothing. catalog_check_matches_what_install_would_do: tools check --catalog reports an approved prefix request with its version, an unapproved release (which install then refuses with TOOL_NOT_IN_CATALOG), Rust (with no index record) and a github: package as refused with exit 1, and a blocked release with the organization's reason. a_cached_copy_in_its_last_quarter_warns_before_it_runs_out (unit): the TOOL_CATALOG_EXPIRING threshold. Unit tests in src/tools/org_catalog.rs: admission, version approval, delivery lookup, proxied URLs and malformed documents; signatures (either of two pinned keys accepted; another key, an unsigned document, an edited payload, a forged key id and another payload type refused); key parsing; the index serial and digest check; an edited kept copy and a kept copy under other pinned keys refused; ETags. Unit tests in src/tools/org_catalog.rs for the kept copy: used while young enough with its age, refused when stale or disabled, never read for another catalog URL, never replaced by an older document, and refused when older than the newest catalog fetched (a_cached_copy_older_than_the_newest_fetched_catalog_is_refused). Compiled-CLI tests (tests/integration/tool_catalog.rs) against a stand-in edge and the signed terraform fixture index: an unapproved version is not downloaded, an approved one is requested from the edge by host and path with the token, a blocked version fails with its reason, a mismatched SHA-256 is refused, a missing or rejected token fails closed, and a version with no build for another lock platform is still judged on this one. tools versions lists only approved versions, shows the refused one with its reason and refuses an unlisted tool. With the edge answering 503, the kept catalog is used with a TOOL_CATALOG_CACHED warning; another token finds no copy; 401, 404 and a malformed document are not replaced by it; maxOfflineAge = "0" disables it. tools versions --offline lists from the kept copy without a request to the edge and refuses an older copy put back into the cache (offline_listing_uses_the_cached_catalog_and_never_an_older_one). Only a catalog signed by the pinned key is used: another key, an unsigned document and a missing toolCatalog.keys fail with TOOL_CATALOG_UNTRUSTED, and a project file cannot pin a key (only_a_catalog_signed_by_a_pinned_key_is_used). A catalog naming another index under the client's serial is refused for listing and install, and an expired one is refused (a_catalog_from_another_index_or_past_its_expiry_is_refused). A second command sends the kept copy's ETag and uses it on 304 (an_unchanged_catalog_is_not_downloaded_again). For oyzu:java (a signed fixture index with core:java records): tools versions java lists approved releases only, a refused release and an unapproved feature are not installed, and java@lts selects 21.0.8 over the approved non-LTS 24.0.2, downloads the archive through the edge, locks the publisher URL and the index SHA-256, and oyzu exec -- java runs it (Linux). The same for oyzu:node, oyzu:go and oyzu:python: node@lts/jod, go@~1.24 and python@3.13 select the newest approved release of their line, install it through the edge and run it, while a blocked release and an unapproved line are refused (Linux). install_through_the_delivery_edge (ignored by default) runs against the real edge. On 2026-10-10 it passed on Linux x86-64: with only 1.15 approved, terraform 1.16.5 was refused, and 1.15.3 installed through the edge, which filled it from releases.hashicorp.com; the lock held the publisher URL and SHA-256 and terraform version ran. managed_client_against_the_compose_stack (ignored by default) runs against the platform's whole Compose stack, driven by its deploy/compose/e2e.sh. On 2026-10-10 it passed on Linux x86-64 through the s3:// edge: jq 1.7.1 installed and ran, and the blocked jq 1.7 (with the organization's reason), the unapproved yq and a github: spec were refused. managed_client_installs_each_provider_through_the_compose_stack (ignored by default) runs against the same stack, which approves one version of each Oyzu provider. On 2026-10-11 on Windows x86-64 through the s3:// edge: an unapproved version of every provider was refused, and Maven 3.9.11, Gradle 9.1.0, Helm 3.19.0, kubectl 1.31.0, k3d 5.8.3, Liquibase 4.33.0, npm 11.6.2 (with Node 22.20.0) and pnpm 10.18.2 installed with the publisher URL in the lock. Rust 1.90.0 installs once the edge serves the components its channel manifest pins (oyzuai/platform#258); the full test passed with that change. On an edge with nothing stored, Gradle and Liquibase (134 and 354 MB) install on the first run once the edge answers 503 FILL_PENDING while it fills them (oyzuai/platform#263) and the client waits for it (#344); the test passed that way on 2026-10-11 with all three changes. Tailscale is checked on Linux hosts only.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-commands.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Status: implemented for the tools Oyzu admits today; the design is the accepted OEP-0021 tool commands proposal (design accepted 2026-10-07; implementation experimental). Syntax, error codes and the choices listed under accepted choices may still change. Platforms: developed and verified on Linux x86-64 only; Windows and macOS are unverified (see verification). These commands change what a scope requires ([tools] in configuration) and what it has locked (oyzu.lock) together, and inspect the result. They use the existing providers: node, go, python, java, maven, gradle, helm, kubectl, k3d, liquibase, tailscale, npm, pnpm, rust, the Cargo helpers cargo-nextest and cargo-llvm-cov, and, experimentally, registry packages written aqua:<owner>/<repo> (see the aqua: backend) or github:<owner>/<repo> (see the github: backend). No account is needed. oyzu install go@1.26 # this project: declare, lock, install oyzu install -g node@22 # your user configuration, all projects oyzu install go # declared: ensure installed; undeclared: go@latest oyzu update go # newer version within the requirement; config untouched oyzu uninstall go # remove the project declaration and lock entry oyzu tools current # what is in effect here oyzu tools list # what is in the store, and what references it oyzu tools versions go # what could be installed oyzu tools info go # provider, verification, eligibility
documents.s: Tool commands: install, update, uninstall and inspection

documents.t: oyzu pin kubectl@1.34 helm@3.22.0 edits the project's [tools] requests and locks their exact archives for the configured platforms in one transaction. All archive providers use this path, including Python, Maven, Gradle, npm and pnpm. --dry-run previews the result without writing. Explicit specs cannot be combined with --refresh or --offline; bare oyzu pin retains discovery-driven pinning, refresh and offline behavior. Normal configuration precedence and policy still apply, and overridden requests fail without changing files. Bare oyzu pin covers every toolset: it locks each toolset's tools in that toolset's labelled sets beside the [tools] sets, and oyzu --toolset NAME pin locks only that toolset's (toolsets). The result uses the shared declaration presentation: requested/selected versions, covered and unavailable platforms, configuration path and lock path. oyzu --json pin kubectl@1.34 helm@3.22.0 returns the same facts with status: "pinned". Pinning does not install payloads or prepare shims. Publisher metadata acquisition may verify archive bytes where its checksum format requires conversion; indexed pinning reads the index/catalog only (Rust also reads the approved manifest). Run oyzu install --frozen afterward to install. The defaults include linux/arm64/gnu; locks can carry it on any host. An unavailable provider/platform is omitted and reported. macOS amd64 and musl are not added to installation support. See implementation status for explicit-spec and ARM64 verification results.

Flag Configuration written Lock none, inside a project project oyzu.toml (created if absent) project oyzu.lock -g, --global the user configuration file (OYZU_USER_CONFIG or the native location) the oyzu.lock beside it --local oyzu.local.toml project oyzu.lock --toolset NAME (global option; install, update, uninstall, pin) that toolset's [toolsets.NAME.tools] in project oyzu.toml, or oyzu.local.toml with --local that toolset's sets in the project oyzu.lock; the [tools] sets are never changed (toolsets) A project is --root, or the workspace root when it holds oyzu.toml, oyzu.local.toml, build.yaml or a Git marker. Outside a project, a command without -g fails with TOOL_NO_PROJECT and writes nothing; it never guesses. --global and --local conflict, and --toolset is refused with --global. A profile never holds tools (toolsets): an explicit --profile on install SPEC or uninstall fails with TOOL_PROFILE_DECLARATION and writes nothing. A command acts on the selected scope only and prints a note when the same tool is declared elsewhere. -g ignores project files entirely, including when run inside a project.

install with no arguments installs everything declared in the effective configuration (--frozen, --offline, --update). oyzu install --global installs the global selection independently of the current project, using the user configuration and its sibling oyzu.lock. It accepts the same frozen, offline, update and store controls; it never edits project declarations or locks. For example, oyzu install --global --frozen --offline restores a previously locked global selection using locally available installation or acquisition data. Missing locks fail with TOOL_LOCK_MISSING; an offline installation still requires the needed cached data. With specs: A spec is [provider:]name[@version], split at the last @. go@1.26 is a prefix, go@1.26.8 is exact, go@latest is the newest eligible version, and go alone keeps a declared requirement (ensuring it is installed) or takes latest when undeclared. Several specs are applied together or not at all. Naming a tool twice is TOOL_SPEC_INVALID. Configuration stores what you typed ("1.26"); the lock stores the exact version. Core tools (node, go, python, java, maven, gradle, rust) are written under the name you typed; other tools (cargo-nextest) are written under their canonical ID ("cargo:cargo-nextest") so a later alias change cannot alter the file. An existing declaration keeps its spelling. Existing TOOL_ALIAS_UNSUPPORTED and TOOL_ALIAS_AMBIGUOUS behavior is preserved, and an ambiguous bare name fails listing the exact retry spellings. Order of operations: parse specs, evaluate tools.allowed, resolve every platform in the default set (Linux x64, macOS arm64, Windows x64 for archive tools; tools.platforms overrides), install only the host archive, then publish configuration and lock in one journaled transaction. Any failure leaves both files unchanged. Concurrent edits fail with PIN_EDIT_CONFLICT. Declared tools of the same lock that are not yet in the portable lock layer are resolved in the same run, keeping the exact version they already had, and are installed too, so the whole selection remains consistent. Replacing a requirement reports Replaced "1.25" (1.25.9) -> "1.26" (1.26.8) and reuses an installation already in the store. --dry-run resolves (reading publisher catalogs) and reports versions, files and platforms; it downloads no archive and writes nothing. Specs with --frozen, --offline or --update fail with TOOL_FLAGS_CONFLICT before any project, configuration or network access, as do --dry-run and --local without specs. Archive tools and Rust-family tools resolve through different contracts; one command cannot mix them (TOOL_FLAGS_CONFLICT: run two commands). Result (human, then the shape of --json: tools[] with tool, key, request, version, previous, status, platforms, otherScopes; plus configuration, lock, scope, store): ✓ Installed go 1.26.8 Declared "1.26" in ./oyzu.toml (project) Locked in ./oyzu.lock for 3 platforms (darwin/arm64/native, linux/amd64/gnu, windows/amd64/msvc)

install recipe:owner/name@version --artifact-set FILE [--artifact-set-digest sha256:D] supplies the tool from a resolved artifact set instead of a built-in provider, and tools info … --artifact-set shows the same eligibility without side effects. --dry-run reports eligibility only. Details, output and limits are in artifact sets; the flags are provisional, apply to the project scope only (-g/--local fail TOOL_FLAGS_CONFLICT) and the install downloads and verifies the artifact and writes the lock, but does not yet extract or activate a recipe tool. install --frozen replays locked recipe: tools from the lock alone.

update [TOOL...] re-resolves within the existing requirement, locks the result for all platforms, installs the host selection and never edits configuration. No arguments updates every tool of the selected scope. It takes names, not versions. In a project without --toolset it also covers every toolset (toolsets): the [tools] tools first, then each toolset's, each in its own lock sets; a named tool is updated wherever [tools] or a toolset declares it, and the table's Set column names [tools] or the toolset of each row (toolset in JSON). install --update remains as a deprecated alias with its old behavior (all scopes). A tool still missing from the portable layer is migrated, keeping its version. Hand-edited removals are not pruned from the lock.

uninstall TOOL... removes the declaration (comments elsewhere in the file are kept) and every lock record for the tool at the selected scope, in one transaction. Shared payloads are never deleted: they remain in tools list as unreferenced. A tool not declared at that scope fails with TOOL_NOT_DECLARED and names the scope that does declare it. --dry-run writes nothing.

All inspection is read-only, performs no installation, never re-hashes installed payloads (installs are verified once, then trusted) and prints the store path. tools current [-g] [--all] [--details]: one row per effective tool with the requested and selected versions, scope and status. --global shows only global declarations; --all adds declarations a more specific scope overrides. Statuses: ok, not installed (locked but absent from the store), blocked (tools.allowed, naming the rule), stale lock (no lock, no matching entry, or no entry for this platform or provider), ambiguous (conflicting lock records or names), and deprecated (reserved; no provider reports it yet). tools list: installations in the store with size and what references each: global (the user lock), project (this project's lock) or unreferenced. Other projects are not indexed, so an installation reported unreferenced may be used elsewhere. tools versions TOOL: selectable versions, newest first, from the publisher's catalog, or from the tool index when one is configured and lists the package (which also works offline from its cached copy). Otherwise requires network (TOOL_OFFLINE with --offline). Pre-release, snapshot and nightly versions are not offered by the adapters, so excluded is always empty today; a tool blocked by tools.allowed reports why. Rust and Cargo helpers have no catalog (TOOL_VERSIONS_UNSUPPORTED). tools info TOOL: provider, accepted names, commands, platforms, verification, eligibility, declarations by scope and current state. tools check --catalog and tools migrate [--write]: check declarations against the tool index, and move mise.toml tools and aqua: ids to Oyzu names; see the tool index reference.

Code Meaning TOOL_SPEC_INVALID Unparseable spec, empty version, duplicate tool TOOL_NO_PROJECT Project scope outside a project; use --global TOOL_NOT_DECLARED uninstall/update of a tool the scope does not declare TOOL_FLAGS_CONFLICT Specs with --frozen/--offline/--update; spec-only flags without specs; mixed resolution contracts; a declaration overridden in this invocation CONFIG_OVERRIDE_DENIED tools.allowed excludes the tool; names the rule, nothing written TOOL_NATIVE_MINIMUM_CONFLICT A tool version below the minimum a native file declares (Go's go.mod/go.work lines) was configured where it must agree: in the native file's folder or nearer, on the command line, by policy or in a matrix axis; names both sources, exit status 3 (Go version selection) TOOL_LOCK_STALE The lock has no pin for a request; for a native minimum that changed (go get rewrote go.mod), it names the file, the declared version and the pinned one.
