Run oyzu pin TOOL_ALIAS_*, TOOL_LOCK_*, PIN_EDIT_CONFLICT Existing codes, unchanged An interrupted configuration/lock publication is recovered before reading configuration when retrying oyzu install, oyzu update or oyzu uninstall. Install recovery precedes configuration preflight and artifact-set replay, including plain, --frozen, --offline, spec and artifact-set forms. Offline configuration reads also use the offline session policy. oyzu pin also recovers it. Read-only commands report PIN_RECOVERY_REQUIRED with the affected directory and a recovery command. Unexpected external edits stop recovery with PIN_EDIT_CONFLICT; the journal remains for investigation. Configuration and lock readers capture one consistent pair under the shared edit lock, then release it before acquiring or launching tools. A concurrent first edit or a change while capturing additional targets reports CONFIG_EDIT_CONFLICT; retry the command. Recipe-staleness errors identify the actual tool, version and lock path. Use oyzu pin --refresh to refresh recipes while retaining selected versions, then oyzu install to materialize them. Tool-preparation failures identify the tool, requested or pinned version, store path and recovery command. Windows paths in these diagnostics use the plain C:\... or \\server\share\... form in both human and JSON output; the extended \\?\ prefix remains an internal filesystem detail. Unix diagnostic paths are unchanged.

Recorded in the proposal's decision record (accepted 2026-10-07): no provider prefix beyond canonical IDs; core tools stored as typed; no allow-list patterns; no prerelease flag; tools versions has no offline source; no project index; bare oyzu tools unchanged. A platform for which the provider publishes no artifact for the requested version is omitted from the lock and reported as unavailable (a warning in the human view, unavailablePlatforms in --json). The other platforms lock and the host installs normally; selecting the unavailable platform fails. Example: oyzu install node@14 locks Linux and Windows only, because Node 14 has no macOS arm64 build. This applies when a tool is first declared or re-declared with a new request, and only for the Node, Go and JDK catalogs; an update re-resolves only the platforms already locked, and a tool with no artifact on any platform fails. Any other resolution failure (for example a missing checksum file) still fails the command.

Linux only verified. Mixed archive and Rust-family specs need separate commands. Installing one tool also installs the other declared tools of its lock group. Config and lock publication is journaled, with recovery as described above. Managed (enrolled) mode is rejected as for the other tool commands.
tooling/test-tool-commands.py drives the compiled CLI against real Go and Node downloads; tests/integration/tool_commands.rs covers the no-download cases. See the qualification record.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-github.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Status: experimental; implemented but not yet proven against live GitHub. The resolver, asset matcher and install path are covered by unit tests and a rejected-spec check; the live runner tooling/test-tool-github-install.py has not run successfully because the development sandbox cannot reach the releases API (see qualification). github:<owner>/<repo> installs a program from a GitHub repository's release assets, using the same [tools] syntax as mise's github: backend. No account and no mise executable are needed. $ oyzu install github:cli/cli@2.49.2 $ cat oyzu.toml [tools] "github:cli/cli" = "2.49.2" Prerequisites and platforms: network access to api.github.com, github.com and GitHub's release-asset host. The default lock covers linux/amd64/gnu, darwin/arm64/native and windows/amd64/msvc.

An exact MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH request reads the release tagged v<version> or <version>. latest and prefixes such as 2.49 list the newest releases and pick the highest stable match (oyzu tools versions github:owner/repo shows them). For each lock platform the asset is chosen by oyzu-asset-match, scoring names for OS, architecture and libc. An architecture mismatch is never a fallback, and checksums, signatures, packages (.deb, .rpm, .msi) and source archives are not candidates. The SHA-256 is the digest GitHub reports for the asset, else one in a checksum file published beside it. The asset is downloaded once per platform, checked against that digest, and searched for the command (the file named after the repository, else the only executable). The lock pins the asset URL, its SHA-256 and the command path. Restore (install --frozen) needs neither the API nor the matcher. Only the publisher's SHA-256 is checked, as for aqua:: no attestation, signature or SLSA verification is performed.
documents.s: How a release is chosen and pinned

documents.t: Code Meaning TOOL_RATE_LIMITED GitHub refused the request (anonymous limit or access policy); set GITHUB_TOKEN, which is sent to api.github.com only TOOL_VERSION_NOT_FOUND No release matches the request TOOL_CHECKSUM_MISSING The release publishes no SHA-256 for the chosen asset; nothing is installed TOOL_CHECKSUM_MISMATCH The downloaded asset differs from the published digest TOOL_ARCHIVE_UNSUPPORTED The chosen asset is not tar.gz or zip (for example a bare binary or tar.xz) TOOL_RECIPE_UNSUPPORTED The archive has no single identifiable command TOOL_SPEC_INVALID The id is not github:<owner>/<repo>

Not run live; Linux x86-64 behavior is unverified end to end. Windows and macOS are unverified. Bare-binary assets, tar.xz/tar.zst, option tables (asset_pattern, bin, version_prefix), private repositories and GitHub Enterprise hosts are not supported. tools versions lists releases without inspecting assets, so a listed version can lack a build for the platform. Resolution downloads each platform's asset once, which can be large. The asset matcher is adapted from mise (MIT); its compliance record is pending human review.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-go-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Indexed installation and pinning use the organization catalog contract. A matching verified index record is preferred without a catalog; with one, only approved indexed releases install. The provider evidence command uses the same metadata adapter as installation. Linux ARM64 GNU joins the native host/lock matrix (Tailscale remains Linux-only); macOS amd64 and musl are excluded. See implementation status for automated verification. Live publisher evidence and native ARM64 qualification remain pending. See tool management for shared prerequisites, command conventions and qualification limits.

For a Go project, configure: [tools] go = "1.24.13" oyzu install oyzu which go oyzu exec -- go version oyzu exec -- gofmt -l main.go oyzu exec -- go run ./main.go oyzu install --frozen --offline The internal oyzu-tool-metadata library supplies version selection and target archive facts, extracted from the pinned mise implementation. It consumes the official Go catalog and checksum bytes supplied by Oyzu's acquisition broker, checking release filename, catalog size/hash and checksum-sidecar agreement. It does not initialize mise, discover configuration or access the network itself. Unsupported request modes fail before catalog acquisition. Oyzu verifies the acquired bytes, publishes the installation and retains the existing version-1 lock and frozen reuse/restoration contracts. The lock records go-releases and digest-only verification, not publisher signatures. No Go executable is needed to install the prebuilt release. The Windows Go ZIP adapter allows up to 900:1 per-file expansion. This admits the 65,535-byte go/src/compress/flate/testdata/huffman-null-max.in entry in the official Go 1.27.2 Windows ZIP, measured at 829.56:1. Other archive types retain their 200:1 default, and Go's per-file, total-size, entry-count and depth bounds are unchanged. A lock authored with the earlier Windows Go layout retains its recorded layout identity; use oyzu update go to explicitly refresh it. Frozen commands never silently change the layout identity. Windows qualification of the fresh-resolution path extracted the verified official archive and compiled and ran a native Go program; it reused the cached verified archive bytes, so it does not qualify cold archive acquisition. See the qualification record. exec and shell activation prepend the selected installation's bin directory, set GOROOT to its payload and default GOTOOLCHAIN to local so normal execution uses the locked compiler without automatic toolchain acquisition. An explicit TOML environment setting can override GOTOOLCHAIN in this standalone development mode. Ordinary Go module/package acquisition remains native Go behavior; selecting a compiler is not yet managed module routing or hermetic build integration. oyzu update go explicitly resolves the configured Go request again. The install --update go and --update oyzu:go forms are supported aliases. Stale ordinary requests fail and frozen/offline commands do not resolve new versions. Node and Go projects can share an explicit store; a project can also declare both tools as described below. Public pinning reads the native go.mod/go.work Go minimum (the newer of the go and toolchain lines), requests it when [tools] go is unset and rejects incompatible requests; see Go version selection. A Go selection admitted under the current layout exposes both go and bundled gofmt as selected native commands. oyzu exec -- gofmt -l main.go prints the file name when it needs formatting and nothing when it is formatted; gofmt -w main.go edits the file. JSON mode represents the native output in its stdout field. Existing frozen installations with an older Go layout continue to run go, but do not acquire gofmt implicitly. Run oyzu update go to admit the current layout for the configured Go version, then use frozen commands as usual. oyzu pin --refresh updates portable resolution metadata, not the installed layout. Offline/frozen commands never perform that update. The observed Windows Go 1.24.13 update kept its exact version. Go's builder-owned formatting tasks retain their native path. Additional builder handoff qualification remains unfinished. Supported target tuples are Linux amd64/arm64 GNU, Windows amd64 and macOS arm64; native qualification is recorded separately below. Activation prepares native node and go shims, each with its own manifest. A shim resolves the currently configured tool and refuses a command absent from that selection. Existing retained frontend/shim versions are unchanged; deactivate and reactivate to use the new frontend. env --json identifies the selected canonical tool and protects sensitive environment values. Go accepts administrative tools routes scoped to go, oyzu:go or *, with the same explicit host binding file as Node. A Go proxy base must serve index.json containing the official all-release Go catalog, plus archive filenames and their .sha256 sidecars at that base. Without a configured route, the host fetches https://go.dev/dl/?mode=json&include=all and https://dl.google.com/go/ artifacts. There is no public fallback from a configured route. An authenticated local forwarding-proxy proof passed on Linux using real publisher bytes, including missing-binding denial, bad-credential denial and frozen reuse without credentials. This does not qualify a particular corporate service; managed mode is still unavailable. The real Go runner installs 1.24.13, checks frozen selection and GOROOT, and compiles and runs a program using only the standard library, with literal arguments and TOML environment. It can also exercise a native shell shim: python tooling/test-tool-go.py --cli PATH_TO_FEATURE_ENABLED_OYZU --workspace PATH --shell bash Add --pin --update to exercise public portable pins, native minimum-version rejection, second-project reuse, and exact/ranged updates through the real compiler. --store PATH reuses a proof store. Updates are online operations even when initial fixture replay uses --offline-check; each update is followed by a frozen offline installation and unchanged-lock check. The Linux assembled extraction passed this flow, including switching to Go 1.24.12 and back to 1.24.13. Retain the workspace and rerun with --offline-check --restore-cached under externally disabled networking to move installations aside and restore from cached archives. Use restoration once per workspace; the previous tree is preserved at installs-before-restore. The script's offline option does not itself disable networking. Use --shell pwsh on Windows or --shell zsh where available. Linux amd64 passed real acquisition, frozen reuse, version/GOROOT checks, actual compiler execution and Bash shim activation on 2026-10-02. At that checkpoint, Windows/macOS acceptance was still pending in CI; Windows subsequently passed the 2026-10-05 runner and the current Go ZIP proof above. The 2026-10-14 Linux fresh-checkout gate also passed the current no-pin Go build from an empty per-project store, with no Go tool on PATH. macOS was not requalified by this run. Native module constraints and corporate Go proxy behavior remain unqualified. Mixed-project evidence is separate below. The same Linux workspace then passed restoration from cached bytes and real compiler execution with container networking disabled, preserving lock bytes. On 2026-10-05 the extracted metadata path passed the real Go 1.24.13 runner on Windows with PowerShell and Linux Docker with Bash: acquisition, frozen offline reuse, which/exec, GOROOT/GOTOOLCHAIN, compiling/running the standard-library program with literal arguments/TOML environment, unchanged lock and native shim activation. Unit checks also cover all three admitted archive layouts, selector intersection, catalog membership and checksum disagreement. Native macOS and specific corporate-service qualification remain pending. See the extraction record.
CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-grant-inspection.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them.

docs/contracts/tools-v1/selection-grant.schema.json defines a proposed closed payload shape for a future compact signed grant. The fixture files under tests/fixtures/tool-grant/ are unsigned synthetic data and grant no authority. Run python tooling/check-tool-contracts.py with the existing pinned design requirements to check them offline; no agent, management account or signing key is needed, and no configuration or store data is modified. The shape requires protocol/request/context/decision identity, policy revision, selection digest, operation list, validity, offline flag, revocation epoch, issuer/audience/tenant/subject. It rejects unknown fields, missing bindings, duplicate/unknown operations, wrong audience/protocol, malformed digest/UUID and non-integer or unsafe numeric fields. An allow payload is the only grant shape; resolve cannot share an operation list with execution, and offline-enabled grants list only activate/exec/build. Times are proposed whole Unix UTC seconds. These are new draft wire choices, not an accepted or deployed service contract. The schema alone checks shape. The initial Rust VerifiedToolGrant::verify library API additionally verifies compact JWS signatures against a caller-supplied pinned Ed25519 key map and exact ToolGrantContext. The caller must obtain keys, issuer/tenant/subject, request/context identity, policy revision, revocation epoch and selection digest independently from authenticated agent state. Supplying these values from the token or project would defeat their binding. This API does not authenticate its caller or fetch keys, contact an authorizer or authorize a launch. Only alg=EdDSA is accepted, with a nonempty kid and optional typ=oyzu-tool-selection+jws; other headers, duplicate JSON and unknown payload fields fail. Limits are 128 KiB per token, 8 KiB decoded header, 64 KiB decoded payload and 256 trusted keys. Existing strict JSON depth/entry bounds also apply. The configuration-policy verifier retains its different alg=Ed25519 header and policy audience unchanged. Call verify(token, keys, context, unix_seconds, Instant::now()) on online receipt, then check(context, unix_seconds, Instant::now(), offline) before each use. Signed ordinary lifetimes cannot exceed 60 seconds. Offline-enabled grants permit only activate/exec/build and cannot exceed 900 seconds. Online receipt and online use are limited to the first 60 seconds of either kind of grant. Offline use requires its explicit flag and the same live object; no restart persistence is provided. Fixed monotonic deadlines use the remaining signed time at receipt, so neither mode changes nor wall-clock movement extend validity. Changed context bindings, expiry, backwards wall-clock movement beyond five seconds or monotonic reversal permanently invalidate the instance. An operation outside the signed list is denied. invalidate() handles explicit invalidation; the owning agent must call it on logout, key/policy changes and uncertain resume. Those notifications are not wired yet. Recovery requires a fresh online grant, never editing project/lock data or retrying a permanently invalidated instance. Tokens and verified objects have no persistence API and errors omit token data. The implementation uses portable Rust clocks/cryptography; focused tests use synthetic signatures and the shared valid/invalid payload fixtures. This remains an initial library boundary, with no deployed service interoperability, agent lifecycle integration or grant-backed launch path. The protocol remains a draft.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-helm-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Indexed installation and pinning use the organization catalog contract. A matching verified index record is preferred without a catalog; with one, only approved indexed releases install. The provider evidence command uses the same metadata adapter as installation. Linux ARM64 GNU joins the native host/lock matrix (Tailscale remains Linux-only); macOS amd64 and musl are excluded. See implementation status for automated verification. Live publisher evidence and native ARM64 qualification remain pending. Oyzu can pin and install helm, so a project that packages or deploys Helm charts needs no host-installed copy. See tool management for shared prerequisites.

[tools] helm = "3.16.2" # exact release # helm = "latest" # the publisher's current stable release oyzu install helm@3.16.2 # declares, locks for every platform, installs this one oyzu exec -- helm version --short oyzu which helm

Only an exact version (3.16.2 or v3.16.2) or latest is accepted. The Helm download host has no list of releases, so ranges, minor lines such as 3.16 and pre-releases are refused with a message naming the accepted forms, and oyzu tools versions helm fails for the same reason. latest reads the publisher's helm-latest-version marker, which currently names a 4.x release; pin an exact version when a project depends on 3.x behavior. The lock records the resolved version, so latest does not move until oyzu update.

Each release publishes one archive per platform on https://get.helm.sh/: a tar.gz for Linux and macOS and a zip for Windows, each containing a single <os>-<arch>/ directory with helm, LICENSE and README.md. Oyzu strips that directory, so helm (or helm.exe) is at the root of the installed payload. The digest for each platform comes from the archive's .sha256sum sidecar on the same host, which must name the requested archive; Oyzu locks it, downloads the archive through the tool broker and verifies the bytes before storing them. The digest comes from the publisher, not a signature. Oyzu does not redistribute the archive. Administrative tools routes scoped to helm, oyzu:helm or * use the same host connector bindings as the other tools; there is no public fallback from a configured route. Supported platforms are linux/amd64/gnu, linux/arm64/gnu, darwin/arm64/native and windows/amd64/msvc. The installed command is helm.

Verified against the live publisher on two hosts. On Windows 11 x86_64, oyzu install helm@3.16.2 and helm@latest locked all three platforms and installed the Windows zip, oyzu exec -- helm version --short printed v3.16.2+g13654a5 and v4.3.0+gbec5b06, and a range request and tools versions were refused. On Linux x86_64 (Ubuntu 24.04 container), oyzu install helm@3.16.2 installed the tarball and helm version --short printed v3.16.2+g13654a5. For macOS the locked digest was checked against the downloaded archive and its listing (a single darwin-arm64/ directory containing helm), but that binary was not installed or executed, and no chart was packaged. Not covered: offline replay with a cold store.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-index.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Status: experimental, provisional. Milestone M3 of the tools catalog plan. The client is implemented and tested against signed fixtures and a real public-good Sigstore bundle. By default it reads the public index published as GitHub releases of oyzuai/tool-index. Field names, settings, codes and exit statuses are drafts pending maintainer review.
documents.s: The public tool index (toolIndex, tools check --catalog, tools migrate, tools trust)

documents.t: Oyzu publishes one public, signed tool index built by a scheduled job in the oyzuai/tool-index repository: every registry package's versions, with per-platform download URLs and the SHA-256 Oyzu verified. install and tools versions for registry packages read it instead of the pinned aqua registry file, the GitHub releases API and the publisher's checksum file. Only the artifact download itself still goes to the vendor. The design is in the platform repository (OEP-draft-configuration-and-tool-lifecycle, public-tool-index.md). The file format is tool-index.schema.json.

The client accepts indexed Java, Node, Go, Python, Maven, Gradle, Helm, kubectl, k3d, Liquibase, Tailscale, npm, pnpm and Rust. Archive records name the exact URL the installation adapter uses. Rust records approve the channel manifest and carry its component digests plus a pinned rustup bootstrap; see Rust installation. Without an organization catalog, a matching verified index record is preferred over live publisher metadata. Under a catalog, a missing tool remains TOOL_NOT_IN_INDEX, and an unapproved version is TOOL_NOT_IN_CATALOG. Cargo helpers remain unavailable under a catalog. The index producer can obtain these records with oyzu --json tools evidence --provider <name> --version <exact-release>. The default evidence matrix has five entries: Linux amd64/arm64 GNU, macOS arm64/amd64 native and Windows amd64 MSVC. macOS amd64 is emitted as unsupported; Tailscale also emits unsupported macOS arm64 and Windows records. This preserves index coverage without adding unsupported installation hosts. The evidence reference owns the publisher sources and checksum formats. Client support does not publish index records. The separate tool-index job still needs its provider configuration and pinned Oyzu revision updated. See implementation status for automated verification; live publisher evidence and native ARM64 installation remain unverified.

Setting Value; default Meaning toolIndex.url HTTPS URL (HTTP only on loopback), or false; https://github.com/oyzuai/tool-index/releases/latest/download/ Base URL of the index: by default the assets of the newest index release. false reads no index, so registry packages resolve from the pinned registry by local recipe evaluation (refused under managed configuration) toolIndex.trustedRoot Absolute path; Sigstore's production trusted root (compiled in, or newer from oyzu tools trust refresh) A Sigstore trusted_root.json to verify signatures against instead, for a private Sigstore deployment. User or machine configuration only: a project file setting it fails with CONFIG_SCOPE toolIndex.identity https: URI; https://github.com/oyzuai/tool-index/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main The certificate identity the index must be signed by, for a customer-signed index. User or machine configuration only # ~/.config/oyzu/config.toml [toolIndex] # A mirror instead of the public index (or `false` for no index): url = "https://index.example.test/" # Only for an index signed by another workflow or another Sigstore instance: # identity = "https://github.com/example/tool-index/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main" # trustedRoot = "/etc/oyzu/sigstore-trusted-root.json" The index URL may point at an Oyzu host, a GitHub release download directory or a customer mirror. Trust comes from the signature and the pinned identity, not from the host. The default URL is GitHub's "latest release" download path. GitHub redirects it to the newest release's tagged download path (releases/download/index-v<serial>/) and then to its asset host, release-assets.githubusercontent.com; those are the only other locations fetched. A network that blocks the asset host needs a mirror.

Large indexes validate independent tool records with up to four workers, bounded by available CPUs. Every record digest is still recomputed; signature, freshness, withdrawal and rollback checks remain required. Failures are reported in document order. This changes preparation cost without adding a setting or trusting an unverified persistent parsed index. Each release is a few files in one flat directory: index.json, index.json.zst (the same bytes compressed with zstd, about a twentieth of the size; transport only) and index.json.sigstore.json, a Sigstore bundle v0.3 written by cosign attest-blob --statement in the index repository's release workflow, signing an in-toto v1 statement of predicate type https://sigstore.dev/cosign/sign/v1 that names index.json's SHA-256. The workflow signs keylessly: Fulcio issues a short-lived certificate for the workflow's GitHub Actions identity, and the signature is recorded in the public Rekor transparency log. Oyzu verifies the bundle itself (no cosign or network call) against the trusted root. Both Rekor generations are accepted, because the public Sigstore service decides which log cosign writes to and can move signing to Rekor v2 without notice: Rekor v1 entries (dsse 0.0.1) carry a signed entry timestamp (SET). The signing time is the entry's integrated time. Rekor v2 entries (hashedrekord 0.0.2, as cosign logs a DSSE envelope there) carry an inclusion proof up to a checkpoint the log signed, and no time. The signing time comes from an RFC 3161 timestamp in the bundle, signed by a timestamp authority in the trusted root. The checks: The bundle is v0.3 with exactly one log entry and one DSSE signature. The signing time: for Rekor v1 the integrated time; for Rekor v2 the first RFC 3161 timestamp whose CMS signature is by a trusted timestamp authority's certificate (valid for time stamping then, and within the authority's validity period) and whose message imprint is the hash of the DSSE signature. The log: the Rekor key whose log id matches the entry and that was valid at the signing time. For Rekor v1, its ECDSA P-256 SET over the entry verifies, and the entry records this payload, this signature and this certificate. For Rekor v2, the entry is rebuilt from the bundle (SHA-256 of the DSSE pre-authentication encoding, the signature and the certificate); its RFC 6962 inclusion proof leads to the root hash of a checkpoint whose origin is the log's host name and that the log key (Ed25519 or ECDSA P-256) signed. The certificate chains to a Fulcio CA valid at the signing time, for code signing, validated at that time, which must fall within the certificate's validity. The certificate names the expected identity: SAN URI toolIndex.identity, OIDC issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com and runner environment github-hosted. An index signed on a self-hosted runner is refused. The DSSE signature verifies with the certificate's key. The payload is an in-toto statement (cosign's https://sigstore.dev/cosign/sign/v1 predicate) whose subject has the SHA-256 of the exact index.json bytes. Then the document is checked strictly. Unknown fields are refused, tools must be sorted with lowercase oyzu: ids (names are matched without regard to case), and every record's digests must recompute with the artifact-set rules. Finally freshness: the document's expires must be in the future, and its serial must not be lower than the highest accepted one, nor equal to it with different bytes (rollback). Oyzu fetches index.json.zst and decompresses it (at most 256 MiB); only when the server answers 404 for it, as a mirror holding just index.json does, is index.json fetched. The signature is checked against the decompressed bytes, so the compressed file needs no trust of its own. The last verified pair is kept under <store>/catalogs/tool-index/<key>/ (the key covers the URL, trusted root and identity). The highest accepted serial and the SHA-256 of that copy are kept apart from it, in <store>/state/tool-index/<key>.json (keyed by URL and identity only), so deleting the cache or refreshing the trusted root does not reset rollback protection, and a cached copy older than that serial is refused too. Both paths are scoped to the resolved store: separate stores have independent histories, even for the same URL and signer. In-process reuse also includes the store, settings and offline mode. See the default store location for disposable-home isolation on Windows. A copy fetched less than an hour ago is verified again and used without any request (index.source is recent); the job publishes once a day, and without this every command downloaded the whole index. After an hour the source is asked again. When a newer copy cannot be fetched or fails verification, the cached pair is verified again and used while it is unexpired. Output says so: index.source is cached, and index.warning gives the reason. With --offline (tools versions, tools check --catalog, tools migrate) only the cached copy is read and nothing is fetched; install --offline replays the lock and resolves nothing. If no valid copy exists, the command fails with TOOL_INDEX_UNAVAILABLE, naming both the fetch failure and the cache state. Not checked: signed certificate timestamps from the CT log; for Rekor v1, the inclusion proof and RFC 3161 timestamps (the SET is the log evidence); for Rekor v2, the timestamp authority's ESS signing-certificate attribute (the signer is identified by its key, which must be a trusted authority's).

For a registry package (oyzu: ids and their aqua: aliases, not github:), after the lock: The index. The package matches an index tool by its origin. The request (1.16.5, v1.16.5, 1.16 or latest) selects a version that has a resolved record for the platform. Prefixes and latest skip pre-releases. The lock receives the record's artifact URL and its verified SHA-256, with no other request. Local recipe evaluation (standalone only), as before, when the index does not list the package, has no matching release, or has only a discovery-tier record without a verified SHA-256. With managed configuration, step 2 never runs. The miss fails with TOOL_NOT_IN_INDEX. An index the tool lists as excluded fails with TOOL_EXCLUDED. A listed version without a build for the platform fails as an unavailable platform. A configured index that cannot be verified is always an error and never falls back silently. With an organization tool catalog configured, step 1 considers only the versions the organization approved, and step 2 never runs.

The index can withdraw a version (its upstream assets were deleted, the release was broken). The version keeps its records, so a lock or digest still matches it by name, and gains a reason: { "version": "4.20.0", "released": {...}, "sets": [...], "withdrawn": { "reason": "upstream release assets were deleted (404)" } } The reason is 1 to 512 characters; an index without withdrawals has no such field. The index repository lists withdrawals in config/withdrawn.toml. A prefix or latest skips withdrawn versions, for registry packages and for Oyzu's providers that read the index (Java, Node, Go, Python). An exact request naming a withdrawn version, a prefix whose every match is withdrawn, and an existing lock naming one are refused, never handed to local recipe evaluation or the publisher's live metadata: TOOL_VERSION_WITHDRAWN: oyzu:golang-migrate 4.20.0 was withdrawn from the tool index: upstream release assets were deleted (404). The newest available version is 4.19.1. The last sentence names the newest stable, non-withdrawn version with a build for this host, and is left out when there is none. A lock is checked against the index the install can read (fetched, or with --offline the cached copy); when no index can be read, a locked install goes ahead as before. tools versions lists a withdrawn version under excluded with TOOL_VERSION_WITHDRAWN and the reason, and tools check --catalog reports it as withdrawn. Under an organization catalog the catalog marks the version withdrawn too, and the message names the newest version the catalog serves; see the catalog reference. tools versions aqua:owner/repo lists an indexed package from the index: newest first, with tags, release time (publisher or first-seen) and versions excluded for this platform. With --offline it reads only the cached copy, and it needs no GITHUB_TOKEN. The JSON source is tool index, and index describes the URL, version (the document's serial), expires and whether the copy was fetched or cached.

The command checks every tool declared here (project, or global outside a project) against the index. It installs and writes nothing. With toolCatalog.url set it judges governed tools against the organization catalog instead, with the statuses in the catalog reference. By default, availability is judged on this host. Explicit tools.platforms entries add required coverage; the default multi-platform pin matrix does not. An omitted record on another host does not prevent installation here. Status Meaning Refused indexed Installs from the index at version for the host and every explicitly configured tools.platforms entry no local Not in the index (or no matching release); would be evaluated locally no (standalone) refused As local, under managed configuration yes direct github:, or one of Oyzu's own providers, which uses a verified index record when the index carries one and its publisher's metadata otherwise no unavailable Listed, but no build for the host or an explicitly required platform yes withdrawn The request names a version withdrawn from the index (or every match of it is); reason gives the index's reason and the newest available version yes excluded The index excludes the tool yes blocked tools.allowed does not list it yes unknown The name is not a tool Oyzu recognizes yes Exit 0 when nothing is refused, 1 when something is, and 2 when toolIndex.url is false (TOOL_INDEX_NOT_CONFIGURED). The JSON form carries tools[], the refused count, outcome and index.

This command moves declarations onto Oyzu names. It reads mise.toml (or .mise.toml) [tools] and the project's oyzu.toml. By default it is a dry run: the result shows every change and the complete proposed oyzu.toml (after). --write replaces oyzu.toml atomically, keeping its comments and formatting. mise.toml is never modified. mise spelling Becomes node, go, … (built-in tools) and core:<name> The bare name A short name that resolves to a supported backend (gh, terraform) Unchanged; bare names resolve against the index aqua:owner/repo (also already in oyzu.toml) The tool's index name (terraform), or oyzu:owner/repo (lowercased) when the index does not list it or none is configured github:owner/repo Unchanged ubi:owner/repo github:owner/repo asdf:, vfox:, and short names available only through them Left out with the reason Other backends (npm:, pipx:, cargo:, go:, …) Left out with the reason A version array keeps its first entry, and a table keeps its version; anything dropped is noted. An entry whose name oyzu.toml already declares is reported as a conflict, and the existing declaration is kept. Running the command again after --write reports no change. Resolving short names reads the pinned mise name catalog, which is downloaded once into the store.

The trusted root compiled into the CLI is a copy of Sigstore's trusted_root.json (target version 14 of Sigstore's root-signing TUF repository). When Sigstore rotates a key or adds a log, oyzu tools trust refresh takes the newer root without an Oyzu release: oyzu tools trust refresh # from https://tuf-repo-cdn.sigstore.dev/ oyzu tools trust refresh --from /media/sigstore # from a copy, on a machine without network oyzu tools trust status # which root verifies the index now --from takes an HTTPS URL of a TUF repository mirror or a directory. A directory may hold the repository's files as Sigstore serves them (16.root.json, timestamp.json, 166.snapshot.json, 14.targets.json, targets/<sha256>.trusted_root.json) or be a checkout of github.com/sigstore/root-signing (metadata/…, targets/trusted_root.json). The refresh runs the TUF client checks, starting from Sigstore's TUF root version 15 that is compiled in (or from the last refresh): Each newer root (N.root.json, N+1, N+2, …) must be signed by the threshold of the previous root's root keys and of its own; the final root must be unexpired. timestamp.json, the snapshot it names and the targets file the snapshot names must be signed by the threshold of their role's keys in that root (ECDSA P-256 over the canonical JSON of signed), have the named versions, be unexpired, and not go below the versions accepted before. A targets version below the built-in root's (14) is refused. trusted_root.json must have the length and SHA-256 the targets file lists, and parse. The result is kept in <store>/state/sigstore-root.json (the rotated roots, the targets metadata and the bytes) and verified again, offline, every time it is read: its roots must chain from the compiled-in TUF root and its targets metadata must list the bytes, so editing the file cannot change trust (it fails with TOOL_TRUST_INVALID; delete it to return to the built-in root). It verifies the index instead of the built-in root only while its targets version is newer; a later Oyzu release with a newer built-in root takes over again. toolIndex.trustedRoot, when set, wins over both. refresh reports status (refreshed or unchanged), the TUF root and targets versions with their expiry, the trustedRoot SHA-256 and whether it is inUse (refreshed or built-in). status reports inUse (built-in, refreshed or configured), the built-in root and the kept refresh. Expiry is checked only when refreshing: Sigstore's timestamp expires within about a week, so an offline copy must be recent when it is used. Every command that loads the index with Sigstore's production root also warns with TOOL_TRUST_ROOT_EXPIRING while the newest TUF root it holds (the compiled-in version 15, or the one a kept refresh rotated to) expires within 30 days, or has expired. Index verification does not depend on it; the warning says to run oyzu tools trust refresh while the anchor it starts from is current.
documents.s: oyzu tools trust refresh and status

documents.t: Code Meaning TOOL_INDEX_UNTRUSTED The toolIndex.trustedRoot file cannot be read or is not a trusted root; inside a TOOL_INDEX_UNAVAILABLE reason, the bundle did not verify TOOL_INDEX_URL_INVALID The URL is not HTTPS (or loopback HTTP) TOOL_INDEX_UNAVAILABLE No verified, unexpired copy could be obtained TOOL_INDEX_INVALID The signed document is malformed (wrong format, no serial or UTC expires, unsorted, digests do not recompute) TOOL_INDEX_NOT_CONFIGURED tools check --catalog with toolIndex.url = false TOOL_INDEX_EXPIRING (warning) The index in use expires within three days: the job that publishes it daily has stalled. After expires, commands that need it fail with TOOL_INDEX_UNAVAILABLE TOOL_TRUST_ROOT_EXPIRING (warning) The TUF root tools trust refresh starts from expires within 30 days; run the refresh TOOL_NOT_IN_INDEX Managed configuration and the index lacks the package or release TOOL_EXCLUDED The index lists the tool as excluded TOOL_VERSION_WITHDRAWN The requested or locked version was withdrawn from the index (or every match of a prefix was); the message gives the reason and the newest available version. Install that one, or oyzu install --update <tool> for a lock TOOL_MIGRATE_NOTHING / TOOL_MIGRATE_INVALID Nothing to migrate / a TOML file cannot be parsed TOOL_TRUST_REFRESH_FAILED tools trust refresh could not fetch or verify the TUF repository (the reason names the file and the check) TOOL_TRUST_SOURCE_INVALID --from is neither an HTTPS URL nor a directory TOOL_TRUST_INVALID The kept refresh no longer verifies against the compiled-in TUF root

A release published within the last hour can go unseen until the hour is up; there is no flag to force a fetch. The two files are fetched separately from the latest release. If a new release is published between the two requests, the pair does not verify and the cached copy is used (with its warning) until the next run. The compiled-in trusted root is Sigstore's production root as published through its root-signing TUF repository on 2026-10-10 (third_party/sigstore-rs/). It is updated with Oyzu releases or by oyzu tools trust refresh, never fetched automatically. The refresh has been run against a checkout of root-signing (2026-10-10); a run against tuf-repo-cdn.sigstore.dev has not been recorded yet. tools evidence still verifies GitHub attestations against the compiled-in root. The trust anchor of tools trust refresh is TUF root version 15, which expires 2026-11-20; a refresh after that needs the repository to carry version 16 or later (Sigstore re-signs its root before expiry). Commands warn with TOOL_TRUST_ROOT_EXPIRING from 2026-10-21 until a refresh rotates past it. Rekor v2 support is verified against bundles built in the tests (and checked with sigstore-go), not yet against a public-good Rekor v2 bundle: none existed for a cosign DSSE signature when it was written. Only ECDSA (P-256 or P-384) timestamp authorities are supported. Oyzu's archive providers carried by the index (oyzu:<name>, origins core:<name>) resolve from it under an organization catalog; their records are oyzu tools evidence --provider <name> output (see recipe resolution and evidence). Without a catalog, a provider request takes the newest verified index record it matches and reads the publisher's live metadata only when the index has none (no index, a provider the index does not carry, or no verified record for the request). Once an exact indexed version is selected, an omitted or unsupported platform is unavailable; it does not trigger a publisher lookup. A version the index lists with no records at all (not yet verified, or older than the versions whose records the index keeps) falls back to the publisher like a version the index does not list. Portable pinning keeps that version's available platforms, so a missing Linux ARM64 record does not prevent installation on another supported host. This matches standalone registry-package resolution. An index that cannot be verified is an error, as for registry packages. A registry package matches an index tool by the tool's id (oyzu:terraform) or by the package of its origin (oyzu:hashicorp/terraform, aqua:hashicorp/terraform), ignoring case. Release dates come from the index (released). There is no minimum-release-age rule yet. Only Linux x86-64 has been run.

Verifier tests (src/tools/index/sigstore/tests.rs) on a real public-good bundle (a cosign v3 DSSE in-toto bundle, kubewarden-controller release.yml@refs/tags/v1.34.0) with Sigstore's production trusted root: it verifies for its subject digest and signer, and is refused for another identity, issuer or runner environment, another digest, a tampered payload, signature, SET, log entry body, integrated time or certificate, and a trusted root without the CA or the Rekor key. Rekor v2 tests (src/tools/index/sigstore/rekor_v2_tests.rs) build a bundle the way cosign v3 logs a DSSE signature to Rekor v2: a Fulcio-style certificate, an Ed25519 log with a signed checkpoint and an RFC 6962 proof (from an independent tree builder), and an RFC 3161 timestamp. It verifies at the stamped time, and is refused without a timestamp, with no trusted timestamp authority, for a timestamp over another signature, after the certificate expired or before the authority was trusted, with a tampered timestamp, checkpoint, proof hash, log index or log origin, without an inclusion proof or a trusted log key, and for an edited or unsigned payload. On 2026-10-10 the same fixture verified with sigstore-go v1.3.0 (WithTransparencyLog(1), WithSignedTimestamps(1), the pinned identity and the artifact digest), and sigstore-go refused it with one proof hash flipped. The production trusted root parses with its Rekor v2 log (log2025-1.rekor.sigstore.dev, Ed25519) and its timestamp authority. Withdrawals: withdrawn_versions_are_skipped_and_refused_by_name and withdrawal_reasons_are_bounded_and_strict (src/tools/index/tests.rs); the compiled CLI against a signed fixture index with terraform 1.16.5 withdrawn (tests/integration/tool_index.rs withdrawn_versions_are_skipped_listed_and_refused: tools versions excludes it and offers 1.15.3, install of it fails before anything is locked, tools check --catalog reports withdrawn for the exact version and for 1.16), and a_locked_withdrawn_version_is_refused (ignored, downloads terraform; run on 2026-10-11): an installed, locked 1.16.5 is refused once the index withdraws it. Client tests (src/tools/index/tests.rs): lookup and version selection, malformed documents, fetch and cache, tamper fallback, rollback (lower serial, same serial with other bytes), expiry of the fetched and the cached copy, foreign trusted roots, other identities, self-hosted runners and offline cache reads. Bundles are signed in-process by a test-only Sigstore instance (tests/support/tool_index_fixture.rs: a P-384 CA chain, P-256 leaf and log key). Rollback state (rollback_state_survives_deleting_the_cache_and_holds_old_cached_copies_to_it): after serial 5, deleting the cache and serving serial 2 is a rollback, and so is an older genuine copy put back into the cache (offline, or looking freshly fetched). Trust refresh (src/tools/index/trust_root_tests.rs): with real root-signing metadata (root 14 to 15 rotation, timestamp 804, snapshot 166, targets 14 and the compiled-in trusted_root.json, tests/fixtures/sigstore-tuf/) the refresh verifies and reports the built-in root unchanged, and refuses the same files a week later (expired timestamp). Throwaway repositories with generated keys cover a root rotation that replaces the built-in root, a tampered kept file (TOOL_TRUST_INVALID), a short threshold, rollback of targets, targets older than the built-in root, wrong target bytes, a root signed only by its own keys and one key listed under two ids. On 2026-10-10 the compiled CLI refreshed from a checkout of root-signing at fa6fe20 and reported targets 14, the built-in root. the_tuf_root_warns_thirty_days_before_it_expires checks the TOOL_TRUST_ROOT_EXPIRING window against the compiled-in root 15. Expiry warnings: an_index_within_three_days_of_expiry_warns (unit) and the compiled-CLI an_index_close_to_expiry_warns (tests/integration/tool_catalog.rs): an index two days from expires reports TOOL_INDEX_EXPIRING, a 14-day one does not. Compiled-CLI tests (tests/integration/tool_index.rs): the index is real tools resolve + tools evidence output for terraform 1.16.5 and 1.15.3 (tests/fixtures/tool-index/terraform.index.json), signed with the test instance and served over loopback HTTP. The tests cover tools versions, the tamper fallback, expiry, the trust settings' scope rule, an index from another identity, tools check --catalog and tools migrate. install_resolves_from_the_index_and_locks_its_digest (ignored by default; needs releases.hashicorp.com) installs terraform 1.16.5 from the index and runs it. On 2026-10-10, with the earlier TUF-signed fixture, it passed through a proxy that refused github.com, raw.githubusercontent.com, api.github.com, release-assets.githubusercontent.com and static.crates.io. The only hosts contacted were releases.hashicorp.com and, from terraform itself, checkpoint-api.hashicorp.com. It passed again on Linux x86-64 with the Sigstore-signed fixture the same day (that run did not restrict GitHub hosts).

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-java-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Indexed installation and pinning use the organization catalog contract. A matching verified index record is preferred without a catalog; with one, only approved indexed releases install. The provider evidence command uses the same metadata adapter as installation. Linux ARM64 GNU joins the native host/lock matrix (Tailscale remains Linux-only); macOS amd64 and musl are excluded. See implementation status for automated verification. Live publisher evidence and native ARM64 qualification remain pending. Oyzu can prepare a JDK, Maven and Gradle itself, so a fresh checkout of a Maven or Gradle project needs none of them installed. See tool management for shared prerequisites and native host builds for which projects use them.
documents.s: Tool Java, Maven and Gradle Installation

documents.t: Pinning is optional. For a project the native Maven build supports, oyzu build resolves a JDK and Maven, writes oyzu.lock, installs them into the shared tool store and builds: oyzu build # no Java or Maven on PATH, no pin needed oyzu pin --dry-run # preview: oyzu:java 17 and oyzu:maven 3.9, with their sources oyzu exec -- mvn -version An explicit request in oyzu.toml takes precedence: [tools] java = "21" # latest 21.x; "lts" (the default without a declared level) or "21.0.8" maven = "3.9" # latest 3.9.x; any Maven release range

Tool Request Source JDK The literal maven.compiler.release, maven.compiler.target, maven.compiler.source or java.version in the root POM (1.8 means 8), raised to 17 when lower; otherwise lts, the newest long-term-support release [tools] java overrides Maven 3.9, the conservative line, which supports Java 8 and newer [tools] maven overrides A property that is not a literal number is treated as undeclared. The declared level is a floor, not a JDK to run: a project declaring release 21 gets a JDK 21 and not the newest one, while a project declaring 8, 9 or 11 gets JDK 17, the oldest release Maven, Gradle and Oyzu's Java integration run on. JDK 17 compiles those older levels faithfully (--release 8 checks against the Java 8 API). Gradle levels follow the same rule. The lock records the exact build. The same selection runs isolated builds: preflight locks it and the captured worker restores that JDK instead of the image's (see Maven). An explicit [tools] java below 17 still installs for host use, but an isolated build refuses it with TOOL_UNSUPPORTED_VERSION, naming the selected JDK.

JDK: Eclipse Temurin through the Adoptium API (available_releases and the newest asset per feature release and platform). The API declares each archive's SHA-256; the archive is downloaded from the adoptium GitHub organization and verified against it. Maven: the release index (the maven-3 and maven-4 directory listings), the archive and its SHA-512 sidecar all come from the Apache distribution server, the publisher of record, which does not throttle shared addresses the way Maven Central does. Pinning verifies the archive against the publisher's SHA-512 and records the SHA-256 of the verified bytes in the lock. The one archive serves every platform and is downloaded once per resolution. Archive downloads are fetched in 2 MiB ranges, each with its own 45-second deadline, so a slow publisher server (Apache's archive has measured about 180 KB/s) slows a first build but does not time it out. Digests come from the publisher, not a signature. Oyzu does not redistribute these archives. Administrative tools routes scoped to java, maven, oyzu:java, oyzu:maven or * use the same host connector bindings as Node and Go; there is no public fallback from a configured route. Gradle: the release catalog at services.gradle.org/versions/all lists each release's distribution URL and SHA-256; the zip is downloaded (the publisher redirects to its GitHub release assets) and verified against that digest. One archive serves every platform. Defaults to Gradle 8, or 9 when the project declares a Java level above 24. A project with a committed gradlew provisions no Gradle: the wrapper downloads its own. The installed JDK sets JAVA_HOME to its verified payload so no ambient JDK is used (on macOS the payload root is Contents/Home). Commands launched through shims are java, javac, mvn and gradle. A build task sees JAVA_HOME, MAVEN_HOME and GRADLE_HOME from the provisioned tools; an ambient value is never inherited, so a machine-wide JDK cannot change which Java a build uses.

The native build covers Maven reactors only when every jar's name can be read from the POMs: literal or inherited versions, jar packaging, no finalName or classifier. Otherwise the project keeps the isolated (Docker) path. Ant is not native. Ant projects (build.xml) have no native host build: Oyzu does not provision Ant, and an arbitrary build.xml does not declare its jar outputs statically the way POMs and Gradle's model do. Without Docker, oyzu build refuses before doing any work, naming the oyzu-toolchain/ant image it needs and pointing to native host builds; with Docker and the image provisioned the isolated path builds it as before. Native Ant is deferred work. Wrappers (mvnw, gradlew): a committed wrapper is run instead of mvn/gradle and Oyzu provisions only the JDK, exposed as JAVA_HOME. The wrapper downloads its own Maven or Gradle with its own tooling (the Maven wrapper in bin form needs only Java plus unzip or tar; the only-script form also needs curl or wget on PATH). That download is the wrapper's own transfer, not the Oyzu broker, so connector routes, credentials and Oyzu's digest verification do not apply to it; pin distributionSha256Sum in gradle-wrapper.properties or distributionSha256Sum in maven-wrapper.properties to verify it. The native Gradle build uses Gradle's own model (an Oyzu-supplied init script reports each project's archive tasks and test tasks), runs gradle --no-daemon --console=plain build, publishes the model's jar and archive outputs and collects each tested project's JUnit XML. An archive kind Oyzu does not register is refused with a reason; same-named archives are qualified by project path. Quality stages share the Maven limitation below. The build runs Maven's own verify, as the authored build task and the isolated path do, so tests run inside the build. Each module with test sources owes its Surefire XML from the default target/surefire-reports directory, shown as Tests N passed · M failed; a failing test fails the build with Maven's output and publishes no artifacts. The build also runs JaCoCo 0.8.13 (prepare-agent before verify, report after) and collects each tested module's target/site/jacoco/jacoco.xml as its coverage. A module whose POM declares maven-failsafe-plugin and whose test sources hold an IT*, *IT or *ITCase class also owes its target/failsafe-reports XML, collected as that module's integration tests. Custom report directories are not collected, and an authored build command supplies its own reports. The native Gradle build applies the same Oyzu coverage init script as the isolated path (Gradle's JaCoCo plugin 0.8.13) and collects each tested project's JUnit results and build/reports/oyzu/<test task>/jacoco.xml. Gradle's own integration-test source sets are collected only when they are Test tasks Gradle's model reports. Coverage tooling is downloaded by Gradle or Maven from Maven Central, so a failed or throttled download fails the build; offline builds need those artifacts already cached. --full lint and format checks still require the separately provisioned quality tools (OYZU_JAVA_QUALITY_HOME, Java quality); the failure names Checkstyle and google-java-format, the provisioning command and the alternatives, and is proven by the fresh-checkout harness. Maven on Windows uses mvn.cmd; this launcher and the Windows JDK zip are unverified. Verified on Linux x86_64 only (2026-10-07): the java-maven-reactor fixture built both module jars from an empty store with no Java or Maven on PATH in about 90 seconds, most of it downloading a 193 MB JDK and Maven from Apache's slower distribution server, and its two tests ran and passed. The java-gradle-multi-project fixture built its three jars and ran its test (Gradle 8, JDK 17 from the declared level) in about 40 seconds from an empty store. Windows, macOS, offline restoration, connector/proxy routing and review of the licenses of the downloaded distributions are not verified. Maven itself still resolves dependencies from Maven Central, which can throttle shared addresses. Pinning derives Java requirements for every Maven target, including projects that later use the isolated path. See the fresh-checkout record.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-k3d-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Indexed installation and pinning use the organization catalog contract. A matching verified index record is preferred without a catalog; with one, only approved indexed releases install. The provider evidence command uses the same metadata adapter as installation. Linux ARM64 GNU joins the native host/lock matrix (Tailscale remains Linux-only); macOS amd64 and musl are excluded. See implementation status for automated verification. Live publisher evidence and native ARM64 qualification remain pending. Oyzu can pin and install k3d, so a project that runs a local Kubernetes cluster in Docker needs no host-installed copy. See tool management for shared prerequisites. k3d needs a running Docker engine to create clusters; Oyzu installs only the k3d binary.
[tools] k3d = "5.7.4" oyzu install k3d@5.7.4 # declares, locks for every platform, installs this one oyzu exec -- k3d version

Only exact versions are accepted (5.7.4 or v5.7.4). Oyzu does not call the GitHub API, so it has no list of k3d releases to search; ranges, minor lines such as 5.7, latest and pre-releases are refused with a message naming the accepted form. oyzu tools versions k3d fails for the same reason.

Each release publishes one binary per platform (https://github.com/k3d-io/k3d/releases/download/v<version>/k3d-<os>-<arch>, with .exe on Windows) and a checksums.txt listing their SHA-256 digests. Oyzu reads the digest for each platform from that list, locks it, downloads the binary through the tool broker (GitHub redirects to its release-asset host, which the broker also allows) and verifies the bytes before storing them. The digest comes from the publisher, not a signature. Oyzu does not redistribute the binary. Administrative tools routes scoped to k3d, oyzu:k3d or * use the same host connector bindings as the other tools; there is no public fallback from a configured route. Supported platforms are linux/amd64/gnu, linux/arm64/gnu, darwin/arm64/native and windows/amd64/msvc. The installed command is k3d.

Verified on Linux x86_64 against the live publisher: oyzu install k3d@5.7.4 locks all three platforms and oyzu exec -- k3d version runs the installed binary. The darwin and windows binaries are locked but not executed, and no cluster was created. Not covered: offline replay with a cold store and Windows or macOS installation.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-kubectl-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Indexed installation and pinning use the organization catalog contract. A matching verified index record is preferred without a catalog; with one, only approved indexed releases install. The provider evidence command uses the same metadata adapter as installation. Linux ARM64 GNU joins the native host/lock matrix (Tailscale remains Linux-only); macOS amd64 and musl are excluded. See implementation status for automated verification. Live publisher evidence and native ARM64 qualification remain pending. Oyzu can pin and install kubectl, so a project that deploys to Kubernetes needs no host-installed copy. See tool management for shared prerequisites.

[tools] kubectl = "1.31.2" # exact release # kubectl = "1.31" # newest 1.31 patch the publisher marks stable # kubectl = "latest" # the publisher's current stable release oyzu install kubectl@1.31 # declares, locks for every platform, installs this one oyzu exec -- kubectl version --client oyzu which kubectl

The Kubernetes project publishes no list of every release, so Oyzu cannot resolve ranges. A request is one of: Request Resolved through 1.31.2 (or v1.31.2) Itself; no lookup 1.31 https://dl.k8s.io/release/stable-1.31.txt latest or * https://dl.k8s.io/release/stable.txt Ranges such as >=1.30 and channels are refused with a message naming the accepted forms. oyzu tools versions kubectl fails for the same reason. Pre-release versions cannot be selected. The lock records the exact version, so 1.31 stays on the patch it resolved to until oyzu update moves it.

Each release is one binary per platform at https://dl.k8s.io/release/v<version>/bin/<os>/<arch>/kubectl (kubectl.exe on Windows) with a .sha256 sidecar beside it. Oyzu locks the sidecar digest, downloads the binary through the tool broker and verifies the bytes against it before storing them. The digest comes from the publisher, not a signature. The host redirects to cdn.dl.k8s.io, which the broker also allows. Oyzu does not redistribute the binary. Administrative tools routes scoped to kubectl, oyzu:kubectl or * use the same host connector bindings as the other tools; there is no public fallback from a configured route. Supported platforms are linux/amd64/gnu, linux/arm64/gnu, darwin/arm64/native and windows/amd64/msvc, the same set as the other core tools. The installed command is kubectl; no environment variable is set.

Verified on Linux x86_64 against the live publisher: exact, minor-line, latest and v-prefixed requests install and lock all three platforms, and oyzu exec -- kubectl version --client runs the installed binary. The darwin and windows binaries are locked but not executed. Not covered: offline replay with a cold store, publisher outages, oyzu update behavior across minor lines, and Windows or macOS installation.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-liquibase-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Indexed installation and pinning use the organization catalog contract. A matching verified index record is preferred without a catalog; with one, only approved indexed releases install. The provider evidence command uses the same metadata adapter as installation. Linux ARM64 GNU joins the native host/lock matrix (Tailscale remains Linux-only); macOS amd64 and musl are excluded. See implementation status for automated verification. Live publisher evidence and native ARM64 qualification remain pending. Oyzu can pin and install liquibase, so a project that applies database changelogs needs no host-installed copy. See tool management for shared prerequisites. Liquibase runs on Java: pin a JDK beside it (see Java and Maven installation). The installed JDK sets JAVA_HOME, which the Liquibase launcher reads, so no ambient Java is consulted.

[tools] java = "21" liquibase = "5.0.4" # exact release # liquibase = "latest" # the newest stable release oyzu install java@21 oyzu install liquibase@5.0.4 # declares, locks for every platform, installs this one oyzu exec -- liquibase --version oyzu exec -- liquibase --url=jdbc:h2:file:./db/app --username=sa --changelog-file=changelog.xml update

Only an exact version (5.0.4 or v5.0.4) or latest is accepted. Ranges, minor lines such as 5.0 and pre-releases are refused with a message naming the accepted forms, and oyzu tools versions liquibase fails because Oyzu does not list releases. latest is the release API's newest non-draft, non-prerelease release; the lock records the resolved version, so it does not move until oyzu update.

Liquibase 5.x is FSL-1.1-ALv2, source-available. Provider evidence records this license explicitly. It does not classify 5.x as Apache-licensed/open-source or choose the index serving class. License obligations and serving decisions remain with their respective owners. The publisher ships no checksum file. Oyzu reads the release document from api.github.com/repos/liquibase/liquibase/releases/ and locks the digest GitHub records for the platform's archive: liquibase-<version>.zip on Windows (launched through liquibase.bat) and liquibase-<version>.tar.gz on Linux and macOS (launched through the liquibase script). The archive has no top-level directory. Oyzu downloads it through the tool broker (GitHub redirects to its release-asset host, which the broker also allows) and verifies the bytes before storing them. That digest is computed by GitHub when the asset is uploaded; it is not a signature from the Liquibase project. Oyzu does not redistribute the archive. Administrative tools routes scoped to liquibase, oyzu:liquibase or * use the same host connector bindings as the other tools; there is no public fallback from a configured route. GitHub records asset digests only for recent uploads. Releases 4.33.0 and later (including 5.x) were seen with one, and 4.32.0 and every earlier release checked had none. Oyzu refuses a release with no recorded digest, naming the missing digest, instead of installing it unverified. Unauthenticated GitHub API requests are limited to 60 per hour per address, and an install reads the release document once per platform. The Oyzu HTTP client sends User-Agent: oyzu/<version> on every request, which the GitHub API requires. Supported platforms are linux/amd64/gnu, linux/arm64/gnu, darwin/arm64/native and windows/amd64/msvc. The installed command is liquibase.

Verified against the live publisher on two hosts, each with no Java on the host. On Windows 11 x86_64, oyzu install liquibase@5.0.4 and @4.33.0 installed, @latest resolved to 5.0.4, and oyzu exec -- liquibase --version ran under the pinned JDK (Java Home pointed into the Oyzu store) and applied a changeset to an H2 file database with update. @4.29.2 (no recorded digest), a range and tools versions were refused. On Linux x86_64 (Ubuntu 24.04 container) the tarball installed and the same --version and H2 update succeeded under the pinned JDK. For macOS the locked tarball digest equals the sha256 of the downloaded archive and the archive holds an executable liquibase at its root, but that was not installed or executed. Not covered: database drivers other than the H2 driver bundled with Liquibase, cold-store offline replay, and the liquibase.bat launcher under a Windows shell that puts a POSIX find ahead of find.exe on PATH (the launcher calls find /i; run it from a normal Windows shell).
CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-lock-inspection.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them.

All Oyzu tool locks now use format = 1. One document can contain resolved_environment/resolution records for planned tools and environment/tool records for verified installation graphs, plus optional requirements discovery evidence. These record types do not imply each other's verification status. One parser validates both; unsupported format numbers fail. Pin updates resolution records without discarding installed records, and install preserves resolutions. Older development formats have no compatibility reader. Regenerate development locks deliberately; existing cache payloads are not deleted. Every resolved_environment and environment entry may carry toolset = "NAME": the set was locked for that toolset ([toolsets.NAME.tools]). The [tools] sets carry no toolset. The label scopes which sets a command changes (a toolset's commands change only its own sets); it is not part of request_digest, so the same requests have the same identity in every scope. A name follows configuration identifier syntax. Entries have no scope or profile field; the lock JSON schema no longer lists them. The request/tool/selection identity domains are also version 1; earlier identity keys are not silently admitted as equivalent. Provider identity is owned by src/tools/identity.rs: the digest domain is oyzu.tool-provider.v1 and its descriptor is {"provider":"oyzu","contract":1}. It identifies the maintained provider contract, not an upstream revision or the binary's dependency graph. Source provenance remains in the upstream notices. The maintainer explicitly retired compatibility with unreleased development identities. Old locks are rejected: run oyzu pin --refresh, then oyzu install. These operations retain old payloads rather than relabeling receipts. Normal payload, recipe and selection verification still applies. The schema stays at version 1; no migration branch or automatic acceptance of old identities exists. oyzu pin --dry-run previews discovered requirements and resolved tool recipes; oyzu pin publishes complete resolutions without installing tools. See requirement discovery. Optional [[requirements]] records remain discovery evidence only: their resolved and installed fields must both be false, and their digest binds the inventory. Inspection reports installation and resolution record counts separately. oyzu tools inspect-lock [PATH] validates an experimental version-1 tool lock without resolving, downloading, installing or running a tool. PATH defaults to oyzu.lock relative to -C, then --root, then the current directory. An explicit absolute file path is also supported. Output defaults to readable text; --json returns the structured result. Success exits 0 and validation/read errors exit 2. See the CLI output contract for JSON errors. oyzu -C /path/to/project tools inspect-lock oyzu tools inspect-lock tests/fixtures/tool-lock/valid.toml The second example uses synthetic identity data, not an installable artifact. The command requires a regular UTF-8 TOML file and reads at most 8 MiB plus one byte to detect overflow. All tool-record readers verify the opened object is a regular file; Unix uses nonblocking open so a FIFO is rejected without waiting for a writer. Explicit symlinks to regular metadata files remain supported; this is not the installation store's no-follow containment boundary. It does not read project configuration or mise files, use ambient mise settings, make network requests, or modify the lock. Profiles and other configuration options do not filter inspection: the whole document is validated. Scope paths are checked lexically; filesystem containment and current configuration compatibility are not assessed by this command. Validation rejects unknown/duplicate fields, unsupported formats, malformed digests, record-key mismatches, verification subjects that differ from artifact digests, duplicate sets (installation sets by request digest; resolution sets by request digest, roots and toolset), missing dependencies, cycles, excessive depth, unreachable tools, conflicting canonical IDs in a closure and missing platform distributions. Different scopes may lock different versions. Limits are 1,024 environments, 4,096 tools, 64 distributions per tool, 16,384 edges, depth 64 and 256 roots per environment. Toolset names use configuration identifier syntax. Logical source/artifact identifiers currently reject colon and path separators in addition to controls; they cannot carry URLs or filesystem paths. Output includes format, environment/tool counts, the sorted platform inventory and selection digests for each environment's common supported platforms. Each digest binds the exact transitive platform closure, including artifact bytes, verification metadata, layout and backend identities. Comments and set-like array ordering do not affect it. Changing a dependency artifact changes the selection digest even when its tool ID and version are unchanged. Each selection also contains installation_keys, mapping tool keys to recursive installation identities. A dependency change invalidates its own installation and dependent installations. Adding an unselected platform leaves the existing platform's installation identities unchanged. These keys name intended content; they do not establish that an installation exists or is authorized. validation: "structure-and-identity-only" is deliberate: success does not prove publisher authenticity, legal clearance, policy authorization, installed content integrity or backend admission. Request digests are checked for shape, not recomputed against current configuration/native constraints. Backend option allowlists, version canonicalization and package-closure admission require the future pinned backend adapter. A self-consistent malicious lock can pass this inspection; it is not an execution capability. The current CLI does not yet install, activate, switch or execute tools through mise. Those operations remain work under OEP-0003. No automatic migration of experimental format 1 is provided. For invalid input, repair the source records or restore a known valid lock; do not change digests merely to suppress validation failures. Inspection does not repair files. Unit tests cover graph failures, bounds and semantic identity. The CLI test checks an independently computed golden digest, ignores malformed adjacent mise and Oyzu configuration, preserves file bytes and rejects tampering. Local results and platform limits are recorded in implementation status.

Node and Go projects can also use oyzu pin --dry-run, oyzu pin, then oyzu install --frozen. Set the runtime request in [tools] (node or go; a Go module's go.mod minimum is a request by itself); the selected builder reads native runtime constraints without executing the tool. Node checks package.json's engines.node; Go reads the Go minimum (the newer of the go and toolchain lines) in go.mod/go.work and requests it when [tools] go is unset (Go version selection). A missing configured version produces an incomplete preview with an actionable diagnostic and exit 2; it never publishes an empty successful pin. Version selection uses the extracted upstream catalog semantics. Pin records the selected version, publisher archive SHA-256 and URL; it does not download or install the runtime archive. Portable Node/Go records retain the configured request (including numeric prefixes and ranges) separately from the exact resolved version. Lock validation checks that version against the request using the provider's selection rules, including Node aliases; an incompatible resolution is rejected. Frozen reads do not refresh the publisher catalog. Rust and Cargo helper requests remain exact versions. The current Node/Go archive adapter admits linux/amd64/gnu, darwin/arm64/native and windows/amd64/msvc. These three are the defaults for those tools; tools.platforms restricts coverage to admitted tuples. Unsupported tuples fail rather than borrowing another platform's artifact. Metadata coverage does not qualify execution on an unavailable host. Installation consumes the pinned host recipe and preserves the portable lock; repeat offline installation reuses its verified user-store payload. Offline pin requires matching recipes. Existing installed-record locks remain readable and are not silently relabeled. The first Node public pin/install/exec/frozen-offline flow passed on Windows. The expanded cross-host runner is tooling/test-tool-management.py --pin; see the extraction audit for completed checks and outstanding qualification. oyzu pin now resolves Rust metadata for Linux GNU, macOS and Windows on AMD64 and ARM64. Windows compiler recipes distinguish MSVC and GNU/LLVM; GNU/LLVM recipes also pin the rust-mingw component. Windows amd64 installation selects MSVC; the GNU/LLVM recipes remain pinned metadata. Defaults cover eight tuples: linux/{amd64,arm64}/gnu, darwin/{amd64,arm64}/native, windows/{amd64,arm64}/msvc and windows/{amd64,arm64}/gnullvm (brace notation here is explanatory, not accepted configuration syntax). Restrict coverage through the configuration cascade, independently of build targets: [tools] rust = "1.95.0" platforms = ["windows/amd64/gnullvm", "linux/arm64/gnu"] The list must be nonempty and use supported exact tuples. Pin resolves every requested compiler platform and its components before publishing. Missing publisher metadata fails without publishing a partial lock. Offline pin requires existing matching compiler records for all requested platforms. No tool payloads are downloaded or installed by pin. Exact stable Rust versions remain required. The existing supported helper versions are nextest 0.9.146 and cargo-llvm-cov 0.9.1. Their platform URLs and SHA-256 digests come from their published GitHub release asset metadata. Windows helper executables are published as MSVC binaries; they retain that identity even alongside a GNU/LLVM compiler. This is explicit metadata selection, not permission to install an MSVC compiler or SDK. macOS nextest uses its published universal binary. Compiler recipes and output-target standard libraries remain separate facts. This extends lock metadata coverage, not native installation qualification. Windows GNU/LLVM component installation and real ARM64 execution remain unproved; existing install paths are not automatically made portable by these records. Backend digests retain current compatibility checks and are not executable hashes. See the portable-lock design.
Store inspection. Request identity and frozen selection. Backend inspection. Grant inspection. Worker contract.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-management-development.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Node, Go and Rust installation use Oyzu configuration, internal tool mechanics, version-1 locks and the shared installation store. The mise application and fork are not runtime dependencies. Adapted code retains its upstream notices. This remains development functionality, not a distribution-qualified release. All archive providers now share indexed pin/install governance, including npm and pnpm. Native host support includes Linux ARM64 GNU alongside Linux amd64 GNU, macOS arm64 and Windows amd64 MSVC. Node ARM64 archives use the vendor's linux-arm64 spelling. Historical proofs below do not establish native ARM64 qualification. See implementation status for current verification. See provider coverage, indexed Rust and pin declarations. Build with Rust 1.95 or newer using cargo build --locked --bins. A private Oyzu worker installs Rust from frozen inputs; Node and Go use internal metadata and archive mechanics through the acquisition broker. No separate mise executable is used.
