The provider contract now has an Oyzu-owned identity. Unreleased locks from the retired adapter must be regenerated with oyzu pin --refresh, followed by oyzu install. There is no legacy compatibility reader or receipt relabeling; existing payloads are retained. See provider identity.

Pin output separates managed tool requirements from executor prerequisites. Inventory JSON includes category (managed-tool, executor-prerequisite or constraint); category does not claim provider support or installed availability. Pinning records managed resolutions, not observed machine paths or SDK inventory. Installation remains limited to admitted tool providers and never installs OS components. Native project dependencies retain their native manifest/lock owner. See native build readiness and the design boundary. Native npm execution uses the selected Node installation's bundled npm/npx through Oyzu's verified execution environment. No aube installer or mise application is embedded. Native npm retains its own registry, authentication and cache semantics; Oyzu controls prerequisite selection, execution and evidence. Bundled commands need no separate tool declaration. Explicit npm/pnpm releases use their own providers; selecting npm overrides Node's bundled copy. Python similarly exposes its interpreter aliases and bundled pip through the selected Python, including Windows module-only layouts. Developer commands use the shared composed-PATH lookup, including host commands; controlled builds retain their separate admission rules. Mise's aube-dependent Node workspace task provider is omitted; Oyzu owns its own task discovery and execution.

The shared-store/portable-lock realignment is in progress. Resolution records now contain request facts and recipe roots without scope/profile labels. Rust lookup uses version, execution platform and required components and selects the smallest pinned recipe that contains them; incomparable matching recipes fail with TOOL_LOCK_AMBIGUOUS. A cross target's request includes its target-platform standard library. Configuration continues to own profile and directory precedence. Installation records are also keyed by effective requests, and store leases consume an exact selection digest rather than a directory or profile. Schema version remains 1. Earlier development records containing scope/profile or the obsolete requirements inventory are rejected by the strict decoder rather than silently reused. Regenerate these unreleased locks with the current CLI; retain existing payloads until reuse is verified. User-origin requirements use the lock beside the user configuration file; project-origin requirements use the project lock. An arbitrary invocation directory does not acquire a lock for user defaults. A project overriding one tool retains unrelated user defaults. Configuration chooses the owner before lock matching; owner labels and paths are not persisted in portable records. OYZU_USER_CONFIG can select an absolute user configuration file without changing machine policy locations; see the configuration reference.

oyzu tools list oyzu tools current oyzu tools current --details oyzu tools current --json oyzu which node tools list reads installation receipts in the selected store independently of project configuration. tools current resolves effective configuration and its locks, showing selected versions, missing installations, configuration provenance and component purposes. Both support --details for full locations, identities and cross-compilation targets, --store, and the global --json flag. Inspection does not install tools, update locks or acquire over the network. A nonexistent store remains nonexistent. Human output uses a concise aligned summary with configuration filenames; --details includes full paths. JSON always retains the complete structured records. These inventory commands report stored metadata, not freshly verified payload integrity. which and execution use verified installation selections and can therefore reject an installation whose receipt was visible in inventory. A missing lock is reported as stale lock; stale, ambiguous or incompatible locked selections fail rather than selecting an unrelated installed version. Install the declared selection explicitly to resolve missing payloads. Declaring, updating and removing tools and browsing versions are covered by tool commands, which also defines the current status words (ok, not installed, blocked, deprecated, stale lock, ambiguous); pruning remains separate follow-up work. Successful installation output reports installed or reused for each selected tool, its version and Rust components. Reuse still verifies the selected payload; these result labels do not change lock selection or acquisition. Errors retain their failure exit status and do not produce a successful installation summary. Native installer diagnostics use the shared invocation logger on stderr, including structured records under --json; stdout remains the command result. Use oyzu build --store <path> when building with a store selected by oyzu install --store <path>. Omitting the override always selects the shared user store, not a store remembered from an earlier command. See local builds.

Create oyzu.toml at the workspace root: [tools] node = "22.15.0" [env] APP_MODE = "development" Then run the Oyzu binary: oyzu install oyzu install --frozen oyzu install --frozen --offline oyzu which node oyzu env --json oyzu exec -- node --version oyzu exec -- node -e 'console.log(process.env.APP_MODE)' The shell quoting in the last example is suitable for Bash and PowerShell. -C DIRECTORY, explicit root and profile selection use the existing configuration resolver. Installation supports Node, Go and Rust selections at the workspace root. The Node selector is interpreted by the extracted metadata library against the actual Node catalog. Existing locks retain the exact version unless an update is explicitly requested. If a maintained adapter changes an installation layout (for example, adding the bundled npm entrypoint to Node), ordinary or frozen reuse reports TOOL_LAYOUT_STALE. Run oyzu install --update node to explicitly rebuild the selected layout from verified archive inputs. This uses the normal online update contract: version constraints still apply and metadata refresh requires access. Repinning alone does not replace an existing installation. The replacement is staged and verified before publication; the older installation and its receipt remain intact, including for existing leases. Subsequent selection prefers the currently admitted layout and still verifies its payload. Updating a different tool does not authorize changing Node's layout. Duplicate equally eligible receipts remain an ambiguity error. No schema migration or receipt relabeling is performed. Tool names are resolved locally from the admitted adapter definitions, with upstream alias provenance retained in the extracted registry. Name resolution does not start a backend worker, inspect an installation or access the network. Version/catalog resolution and acquisition still use their existing backend and verification contracts. For the currently admitted backends, node and "oyzu:node" identify the same tool, as do go and "oyzu:go", and rust and "oyzu:rust". Oyzu's own providers were named core:<name> before 2026-10-10; core:node is still accepted as an input alias for oyzu:node (in configuration, commands and route scopes), but the lock and every report use oyzu: ids. Registry packages follow the same rule; see tool ids. Quote canonical TOML keys containing a colon. Changing only between these names preserves the normalized request identity and existing lock; it does not require installation or relocking. Defining both names for one tool fails with TOOL_ALIAS_AMBIGUOUS, even if their versions agree. Unknown registry names fail with TOOL_ALIAS_UNSUPPORTED. This does not enable additional backends or make alias names executable commands: use node, go, cargo, rustc or rustdoc for exec. Selective updates accept the same registry names. Administrative tools.allowed values are compared through that same alias map; this setting remains admin-only. The real acceptance runner is python tooling/test-tool-aliases.py --cli PATH --workspace NODE_ACCEPTANCE_PATH; it reuses the two-version Node workspace above without changing its projects. Add --update for online canonical-name resolution. On a disposable root Linux host only, --disposable-linux-host temporarily creates an administrative policy to check both allowed-name spellings and denial; it refuses an existing policy and removes its own file afterwards. Linux offline replay with networking disabled and the separate online update passed on 2026-10-02. Native CI remains pending. After editing the Node requirement in TOML, run: oyzu install --update node oyzu exec -- node --version For a Node-only project, bare --update and --update oyzu:node select the same root. The command resolves through the Oyzu provider, prints the previous and proposed exact version, installs the result and then commits the lock using the existing compare-and-swap transaction. It never edits TOML. Ordinary install rejects changed requirements with TOOL_LOCK_STALE and an update remedy. --update conflicts with --frozen and --offline; unsupported tool names fail. A failed update leaves the previous lock intact. An unchanged resolution preserves lock bytes. A newly configured Node/Go project can reuse an exact installation even before it has its own installation lock. After backend version resolution, installation looks up the matching user-store receipt before downloading an archive to learn its size. It validates the layout and verifies the payload through the same publication/lease contract, then writes the project's portable lock. Version resolution can still require catalog metadata; this is distinct from downloading or extracting the tool again. Offline/frozen installation still requires pins. Updates operate on effective requests grouped by their configuration-owned lock. Replacing a request set preserves other request sets and platform distributions; conflicting acquisition facts for the same exact identity/platform fail rather than being overwritten. Other projects sharing the store keep their own locks and versions. Publication is atomic per lock owner, not across user and project locks together. Installation prepares the current host selection; it does not materialize every platform recorded in a portable lock. The default store is user-level: %LOCALAPPDATA%/Oyzu/tools on Windows, ~/Library/Application Support/Oyzu/tools on macOS, and ${XDG_DATA_HOME:-~/.local/share}/oyzu/tools on Linux (relative XDG values use the home fallback). On Windows, an absolute HOME different from the native profile selects <HOME>/AppData/Local/Oyzu/tools; unset HOME or use the normal profile to retain the native LocalAppData location. All default consumers resolve this location independently of the project directory. Explicit --store PATH overrides remain available for install, which, exec and environment commands; relative overrides resolve from the invocation directory. Use --store .oyzu/tools explicitly to inspect/reuse a previous project-local store. Existing contents are not automatically moved or deleted. Store routing is implemented; complete context-independent lock matching, automatic existing-content reuse and user-global selection remain under the active implementation brief. Installation requests metadata and the archive through Oyzu's existing HTTP host fetcher, using https://nodejs.org/dist/ unless an administrative connector route applies (see below). It checks the archive against Node's declared SHA-256, derives the layout from the extracted metadata library, stages and publishes the installation, then commits the lock through the existing lock-edit transaction. The lock explicitly records digest-only verification; it does not claim a verified publisher signature. An existing incompatible lock fails rather than being silently replaced. A failed installation does not publish a new lock. install --frozen requires an existing compatible lock and never resolves a new version. Both ordinary and frozen installs reuse an already installed selection after verifying its receipt and contents; this path needs no network and leaves the lock unchanged. If the installation is absent, Oyzu first verifies the cached archive against the locked digest and size, then restores the installed tree. Only a missing archive requires acquisition from the selected route; invalid cached content fails instead of silently downloading a replacement. install --offline forbids metadata and artifact networking. It requires an existing compatible lock and either a verified installation or its cached archive. Combine it with --frozen to explicitly prohibit lock edits. Missing locks or archives fail with an online-install remedy. Run ordinary install online to create the initial lock and acquire the required bytes. which node prints the selected receipt entrypoint. Trusted PATH overrides can choose another program during exec. Inspection shares read-only developer selection and verified installation lookup, makes no network request and does not install or launch anything. A missing installation fails instead of returning a system PATH executable. Without a compatible pin, inspection can reuse matching recorded installations; it never creates a lock. Developer exec composes configured tools with ordinary executable lookup on PATH. Missing configured tools install on invocation by default through Oyzu's existing acquisition, lock and receipt machinery. Compatible locked versions are retained; a new configured selection may publish oyzu.lock. This behavior is separate from controlled build admission: system PATH cannot satisfy a locked build requirement. See invocation controls. The selected installation leases remain held during native execution. Arguments, streams, cwd and native exit status pass through; no shell expression is inferred. exec also accepts an explicit absolute or relative executable path. It resolves relative paths against -C/the invocation directory and applies the same developer selection, configuration eligibility and environment. For example: oyzu exec -- ./bin/development-runner "argument with spaces" oyzu exec -- /usr/bin/python3 scripts/check.py On Windows, use a full executable path such as oyzu exec -- C:\Python313\python.exe scripts\check.py. Drive-relative paths such as C:python.exe are rejected as ambiguous. A program started this way can find the selected Node at the front of PATH; the explicit program itself is a requested development command, not a verified locked tool. This is ordinary development execution, not the hermetic build executor. Invoke an interpreter explicitly for scripts that need one. No implicit shell parsing is added. Bare commands use the composed PATH, including ordinary globally installed executables. Commands absent from PATH fail with COMMAND_NOT_FOUND. Explicit missing paths and directories fail lookup; invocation preparation may first install configured tools when automatic installation is enabled. which npm returns the bundled npm JavaScript entry point; exec npm and the npm shim launch it with the same verified Node interpreter. Managed execution and process-tree/signal supervision remain unfinished. Exercise the actual explicit-path flow against the retained two-project acceptance workspace with: python tooling/test-tool-exec.py --cli PATH_TO_FEATURE_ENABLED_OYZU --workspace PATH Linux amd64 passed this scenario with container networking disabled on 2026-10-02. Native Windows/macOS explicit-path execution acceptance remains pending in CI.

oyzu exec -- bash scripts/check.sh and oyzu exec -- sh scripts/check.sh use the same developer selection, composed PATH, tool environment and child-stream/exit contracts as other exec commands. Configured tools follow invocation install controls; Oyzu does not install the host shell or add implicit shell parsing. Linux/macOS resolve these shell names normally on PATH. Trusted project PATH prepends precede selected tool directories. On Windows, bare bash/sh select a native shell in this order: bash.exe/sh.exe on the composed PATH, excluding %SystemRoot%\System32 and %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\WindowsApps WSL launchers/aliases. Git for Windows' bin\bash.exe/bin\sh.exe, derived from git.exe found on PATH under cmd, bin, mingw64\bin, mingw32\bin or usr\bin. Git\bin under %ProgramFiles% or %ProgramFiles(x86)%, then %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Git\bin. If no native shell is found, the error describes the search and requires Git for Windows' shell. Make an existing Git installation discoverable or supply its explicit executable path. No WSL fallback occurs. Explicit paths still select exactly the requested executable. The host shell itself is not a locked tool. Git Bash/MSYS converts ordinary Windows PATH entries to its POSIX form on startup; Oyzu continues exporting ordinary drive paths, not verbatim \\?\ paths or a manually rewritten POSIX PATH. The same resolver serves host tasks, including shell-string tasks. tooling/test-tool-exec.py also checks bare bash/sh, argv tasks and shell-string tasks against the real pinned Node executable in its provisioned acceptance workspace. These additions still need desktop/CI execution on Windows, Linux and macOS; earlier explicit-path results do not establish this coverage.

A project can request both tools in the same TOML file: [tools] node = "22.15.0" go = "1.24.13" oyzu install oyzu which node oyzu which go oyzu exec -- node --version oyzu exec -- go version oyzu install --update node Installation resolves the configured roots, prepares missing installations and publishes one version-1 lock only after the complete selection is available. Existing content-addressed installations can be reused across single-tool and mixed projects. Failure leaves the previous lock intact; acquired cache entries may remain for reuse. --update node or --update oyzu:node resolves only Node and retains Go's exact record, version and artifact identity. The equivalent Go names preserve Node. Multiple update names select those roots; bare --update selects all configured roots. Adding a tool requires an update that includes it. Removing a tool from TOML requires bare --update. Changing an unselected request fails with TOOL_LOCK_STALE; include that tool in the update or restore its requirement. The command never edits TOML. Unchanged requests/records retain their existing text through the lock-edit contract. For portable pins, updates refresh the selected tool's recipes for every platform already recorded for that request. Unselected recipes retain their identities; the host installation is verified before the candidate portable lock is committed. Exact requests and Node/Go ranges use the same provider selection rules as pinning. The candidate passes the same native-constraint and component validation as frozen execution; updates do not bypass that contract. Adding a tool resolves its recipes using the same platform defaults and tools.platforms selection as oyzu pin. Ambiguous prior requests still require explicit pinning. Removing a configured tool changes the active selection; it does not delete shared installations or portable pins that another selection may use. Exec and shell activation acquire one verified lease for the complete selection. Both bin directories are prepended in deterministic configuration-key order, and each backend adds its environment. A Node process can therefore launch the selected Go, and vice versa. An incomplete or stale environment fails as a whole; execution does not silently use one valid tool while replacing another from ambient PATH. Shell selection identity includes every selected executable, so changing either locked tool causes the next hook to recompute the environment. env --json now includes tools (canonical IDs to executables) and executables (command names to executables). The existing tool and executable fields remain for single-tool projects; mixed projects use the maps. Sensitive environment values remain protected; ordinary configured values are visible. which accepts either selected command and still returns its path. The real runner installs both tools, changes only Node, verifies the complete Go record is unchanged, and runs Node with a Go child under the composed environment: python tooling/test-tool-mixed.py --cli PATH_TO_FEATURE_ENABLED_OYZU --workspace PATH Use --store PATH to reuse an existing shared store. Retain the workspace and repeat with --offline-check under externally disabled networking to verify frozen reuse and both tools without acquisition. Add --pin for portable pinning, multi-platform recipe refresh, exact/ranged Node updates and unchanged Go recipes. Add --add-tool with --pin to start with Node alone, add Go through a selected update, remove Go from configuration, and restore it using frozen offline reuse. Ambiguous scoped/profile selections still require explicit pinning. Add --shell bash, --shell zsh or --shell pwsh to exercise both commands through an activated shell. Linux frozen replay, Node-to-Go child execution, redacted inspection and mixed Bash activation passed with networking disabled on 2026-10-02. Windows mixed execution and Linux portable add/remove/update flows also passed during extraction on 2026-10-05; native macOS remains unverified.

Host target mapping currently covers Linux amd64 GNU, Windows amd64 MSVC and macOS arm64. On 2026-10-02, Linux amd64 under Rust 1.95 passed both versions, shared-store project switching, frozen/repeat installs, which/exec agreement, arguments, cwd, TOML environment, unchanged locks and exit status. The same projects then passed replay under Docker --network none. A separately mounted store also passed installation/publication. Removing the installed trees while retaining their real archives then passed install --frozen --offline restoration and execution for both versions with networking disabled; an empty cache failed as expected and locks remained byte-identical. The original install/exec scenario at revision 73bb33d passed on macOS arm64 and Windows amd64 in CI run 37045134221. Frozen/which/restoration then passed on macOS at 01e81be in run 37047681781 and Windows at 1acb16f in run 37048375166. Run the real user acceptance scenario with Python 3.11+ and public Node access: python tooling/test-tool-management.py --cli PATH_TO_FEATURE_ENABLED_OYZU The runner creates two projects selecting Node 22.15.0 and 22.14.0, installs into one store, checks frozen version selection, literal arguments, cwd, TOML environment and exit-code propagation, and revisits both projects. These are actual downloads and executions, not mocked backend or store behavior. Use --workspace PATH to retain these projects, then rerun with the same path and --offline-check in an environment with network access disabled. The replay checks frozen and ordinary install reuse, which/exec executable agreement, unchanged locks and both project versions. --offline-check itself does not disable networking; the surrounding environment must enforce that condition. Add --restore-cached to move the retained installed trees to WORKSPACE/installs-before-restore and restore them through install --frozen --offline, then verify actual execution and empty-cache errors. Use this restoration check once per retained workspace; the backup is preserved. With online access and a retained workspace, exercise explicit updates with: python tooling/test-tool-updates.py --cli PATH_TO_FEATURE_ENABLED_OYZU --workspace PATH The runner changes the first project's requirement from 22.15.0 to 22.14.0, checks stale-selection rejection, updates and executes the new version, then restores 22.15.0 through an explicit update. It checks that the second project is unchanged and a repeated update preserves lock bytes. On failure it retains the workspace at the failing step for diagnosis. This complete update scenario passed on Linux amd64 with Rust 1.95 on 2026-10-02 and Windows amd64 at 1acb16f in CI run 37048375166. Native macOS update acceptance passed at e335d70 in run 37051685318. The complete Linux mixed runner also passed from a fresh project on 2026-10-02: initial installation, Node-only update preserving the exact Go record, rejection of a changed unselected requirement, frozen reuse and cross-tool execution. This extends the offline replay evidence above; native mixed CI remains pending. Remaining functional work includes other tools, native constraints, scoped/profile/multi-platform updates, managed connector grants and selection, npm entrypoints, full shim/shell lifecycle qualification and build handoff. Managed configuration is explicitly rejected by this standalone proof. Child stdio currently carries internal metadata; authenticated worker IPC, full process tree cleanup and further hardening are deferred. Transitive notices/SBOM and distribution approval remain separate from the authorized development import. Native checkpoint: at 1c2bd16, CI run 37056475928 passed Windows PowerShell profile installation/removal and explicit-path exec on both Windows and macOS. Its Linux job passed Go installation, compilation, cached restore and shell execution. Windows Go and macOS profile failures were corrected subsequently; the corrected native results remain pending. See the consolidated review checkpoint for the remaining functional scope and evidence boundaries.

oyzu pin --dry-run and oyzu pin show one requirement row per kind, name and constraint across the selected matrix, with an affected-target count. Different constraints remain distinct. Rust components retain their formatting, linting and coverage purposes. Installation support describes the current host's capability, not proof that the tool is installed: pin does not check availability. Use oyzu tools current for that metadata observation. The JSON inventory includes consolidated requirements with targets and sources, while retaining the original per-target facts. Native and isolated build diagnostics use the same summary, emitting a request only once even during replanning. This presentation consolidation does not merge lock identities, platform recipes, constraints or execution requirements. Unsupported discovery remains explicit. External linker/SDK prerequisites remain separately provisioned. Human tables wrap long cells within columns at ordinary terminal widths; only very narrow terminals use labeled records. Pin platform coverage uses OS, architecture and ABI columns. A dry-run success does not mean tools were installed. Pin shows the requested version separately from the tool name. It uses the resolver-selected request before lock metadata resolution, including configured requests and builder defaults. Components marked With Rust share the selected Rust toolchain; they are not independently pinned. Multiple target requests remain visible. JSON retains these requests by tool and target in requested_versions.

Pinned Rust distribution inputs use 8 MiB HTTP range requests. Each request keeps the broker's 45-second deadline, source/redirect authorization and bounded retries; a progressing large download no longer has to fit into a single request deadline. The response ranges must be contiguous, match the requested offsets and lengths, and agree on the total size. The complete artifact must still match its locked SHA-256 before rustup can use it. The existing 256 MiB artifact and 1 GiB session byte limits include partial/failed transfer bytes as before. A server that ignores ranges may return a complete first response, still subject to the ordinary request timeout and byte limit. A full response after partial segments, inconsistent ranges or digest mismatch fails closed. No alternate source or unpinned download is used. Errors identify the pinned Rust input name without including upstream URLs or credentials. Other acquisition paths retain their existing request behavior.

With Node configured in oyzu.toml, a fresh oyzu install records both Node and its bundled npm in the verified installation. oyzu exec -- npm ci and bare npm ci in an oyzu activate shell use that installation. Persistent native shims produced by activation can also run without an active shell session; they resolve the current project on each invocation. No global npm is selected. oyzu which npm reports the JavaScript entry point, not a standalone Windows executable; use exec npm rather than attempting to execute that path directly. npm's existing version is the one bundled with the selected Node release. There is no separate npm request or version pin for that bundled copy. An explicit npm selection can override it. Known bundled npx and Python/pip aliases are discovered inside an already leased installation, so accepted existing receipts and frozen locks do not need edits or reinstalling. This does not revive rejected legacy lock/receipt formats. which pip reports the backing Python interpreter; exec pip and the pip shim supply -m pip. Ordinary environment configuration is passed to npm through existing execution and shell contracts. The local broker experiment sets proxy and CA variables without storing upstream tokens in npm configuration. This is a laboratory integration, not automatic platform connector discovery or authorization. Without the experimental session setting below, explicit native command-line settings can still override environment routing. No machine-wide network enforcement or prevention of deliberate bypass is claimed. Publishing is supported only through oyzu publish. Developer sessions must use an upstream read-only identity and never receive a publish connector. The npm launcher is not itself a method filter or a security boundary against a user who owns the host. The publishing command's platform integration is outside this proof. The Node/npm layout covers Windows and Unix distributions; measured results and OS qualification belong in the linked qualification record, not inferred support.

For the isolated local-agent experiment, configure this once in user configuration: [npm] sessionEndpoint = "http://127.0.0.1:43100/session" This is an opt-in laboratory integration, not a working platform login workflow. The local agent must already be running and supply the experimental session contract. The compiled CLI has no developer login command; existing managed-mode enrollment safeguards remain unchanged. Remove the setting to return to standalone behavior. npm.sessionEndpoint is absent by default and follows normal configuration precedence/constraints. It accepts numeric-loopback HTTP only, with no credentials, query or fragment. No project-specific proxy settings are required. After installing the requested Node into a fresh store, use oyzu exec -- npm ci or activate the shell and run npm ci. Each invocation resolves its current project and contacts the endpoint; shell activation itself remains offline. User transport settings are intentionally excluded when Oyzu detects CI. This user-level setup therefore covers local developer sessions, including non-TTY shells, but does not configure CI jobs. CI needs an eligible job/administrative configuration source and its own authorized agent session; automatic CI bootstrap is not implemented by this experiment. An absent effective endpoint retains standalone behavior; it is not a managed fail-closed configuration. The experiment supports command-first install, i, ci, run, run-script, view and session-approved audit. Help/version skip the agent. Other command spellings, flags before the command, and native npm publish are unsupported in this mode. Publishing requires oyzu publish, whose integration is not part of this experiment. These restrictions do not certify that arbitrary npm scripts cannot bypass Oyzu; developers still control their machines. The child receives proxy, registry/scope, audit and public CA settings, never an upstream credential from this adapter. No .npmrc is generated. The installed npm resolves its effective configuration before execution; conflicting proxy, registry, bypass, audit or TLS overrides stop with NPM_ROUTING_CONFLICT. Remove the conflicting option/configuration and retry. Nonempty inherited NO_PROXY also conflicts. Approved environment values can legitimately supersede project settings through npm's normal precedence. Audit defaults to disabled because it submits dependency names; an unapproved explicit audit returns NPM_AUDIT_DENIED. NPM_SESSION_UNAVAILABLE means the agent is absent, denies access or cannot prepare it. Start/restore the agent and retry; there is no direct network fallback, even for cached dependency commands. NPM_SESSION_INVALID identifies an invalid response or missing public CA file. NPM_CONFIG_UNAVAILABLE means native effective config could not be inspected. npm execution retains native exit status after preparation. Native caches and installed packages persist normally; child settings do not modify the parent shell. Working directory association is unverified local context. Nested npm lifecycle commands re-enter the shim and request their own session; frontend recursion markers end at the verified native tool handoff. This proves neither hostile-host isolation nor production IPC authentication/TLS provisioning. Upstream ACLs must supply narrow read-only authority. The Linux merge regression covers managed installation, private retrieval and Bash with Node 22.15.0 using a loopback HTTP fixture. macOS, broader Linux transport coverage, other npm versions and real local-agent/account lifecycle need qualification. Measured outcomes and failed attempts are recorded in automatic-session qualification.

oyzu install uses the shared linear progress display: a checking status per tool followed by a ready or failed marker. Interactive terminals update the active status and show bounded installer output beneath it; redirected output retains a start and completion line without repeating intermediate verification messages. --json retains structured diagnostics on stderr and a machine-readable result on stdout. -q suppresses progress. Verification is still performed before a tool is marked ready.

Pin/build requirement resolution includes explicit tools from each selected target’s resolved configuration, even when that target’s builder does not request them. For example, repository tools.rust remains a resolvable configured requirement inside a nested Node project. Builder requirements retain their components and native constraints; configured entries do not fabricate build stages. Unsupported tool adapters still fail explicitly. This does not supply missing versions for other tools or add native multi-target execution support.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-npm-pnpm-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Indexed installation and pinning use the organization catalog contract. A matching verified index record is preferred without a catalog; with one, only approved indexed releases install. The provider evidence command uses the same metadata adapter as installation. Linux ARM64 GNU joins the native host/lock matrix (Tailscale remains Linux-only); macOS amd64 and musl are excluded. See implementation status for automated verification. Live publisher evidence and native ARM64 qualification remain pending. Oyzu can pin and install npm and pnpm as their own tools, oyzu:npm and oyzu:pnpm, separate from the npm that ships inside Node. A project selects a release with [tools], or with packageManager in package.json, and the lock records it with the registry's integrity. See tool management for shared prerequisites.

[tools] node = "22.12" npm = "11.6.2" # exact release, a range such as "11", or "latest" # pnpm = "10.20.0" oyzu install npm@11.6.2 # declares, locks, installs oyzu exec -- npm --version oyzu exec -- npx --version oyzu install pnpm@10.20.0 oyzu exec -- pnpm --version oyzu tools versions npm and oyzu tools versions pnpm list the registry's stable releases. Selecting Node also exposes its bundled npm and npx commands, when their native CLI modules are present in that installation. They work through oyzu exec -- npm ..., oyzu exec -- npx ..., activated shells and refreshed shims without a separate npm declaration. Both run on the selected Node. Use an explicit npm declaration only to select a different npm release; its npm and npx take precedence over the bundled copy. Existing installed Node records and frozen locks work without reinstallation or receipt edits. After upgrading both Oyzu binaries, run oyzu reshim to refresh the fixed shims directory and existing activation launchers owned by that frontend. Installation and shell activation use the same bundled command discovery. The ordinary shim still resolves the current project or global selection at invocation time; a shim file does not select a tool version. For pnpm, versions combine the official older and pnpm 12 platform packages; latest follows the unscoped pnpm publisher's tag. A tagged release unavailable on the selected platform fails latest selection, while available exact pins and ranges still work.

A Node target whose package.json declares an exact stable npm or pnpm release for its own manager, such as "packageManager": "pnpm@10.20.0", gets that release as a tool requirement. It is a native default: build preflight locks it beside Node when the project has no oyzu.lock yet, and an explicit [tools] selection must agree with it. A Corepack digest suffix (+sha512.<hex>) is accepted and not compared; the lock records the registry's integrity instead. When an oyzu.lock already exists without the release, oyzu install npm@<version> (or pnpm@<version>) adds it. Ranges, tags and pre-releases in packageManager select nothing; the build then checks the declaration against the image's manager as before. Yarn is not a pinned tool. engines.node instead constrains Node's LTS default and any explicit runtime pin; see Node selection.

The isolated build worker restores the locked release read-only beside the locked Node and runs it in place of the image's copy for acquisition and every action: pnpm's executable is restored at /scratch/pnpmtool and comes first on PATH. npm is restored at /scratch/npmtool. Oyzu's npm integration runs its bin/npm-cli.js through OYZU_NPM_CLI, and acquisition writes npm and npx launchers into the prepared tree, which every action finds first on PATH at /dependencies/manager/bin. The dependency record lists the release under the oyzu.dev/locked-manager extension with its lock evidence, and the manager version it reports is the locked one. A changed digest in oyzu.lock is refused. Only linux/amd64 workers are admitted, and an offline build needs the archive already cached. On a Windows controller, pnpm's Linux workspace links remain in the private captured workspace for the provisioned Docker worker. Action tracking reads those Linux link targets without following them on the host; it does not restore link-containing action deltas from cache. An earlier CLI failed during prepare with Unsupported reparse point type; retry with the corrected CLI without changing native workspace configuration. See the Windows workspace qualification for the exact recipe, executor and consumer evidence and remaining limits.

Both tools come from https://registry.npmjs.org/, the publisher of record. Resolution reads the package's abbreviated metadata document and refuses a release whose metadata names any tarball other than <registry>/<package>/-/<file>-<version>.tgz or carries no SHA-512 integrity. Oyzu downloads the tarball through the tool broker, verifies it against that integrity and locks the SHA-256 of the verified bytes, as it does for Maven. Administrative tools routes scoped to npm, oyzu:npm, pnpm, oyzu:pnpm or * use the same host connector bindings as the other tools. Tool Releases through 11 Releases from 12 Commands npm npm, one tarball for every platform Same package npm (bin/npm-cli.js) and npx (bin/npx-cli.js), run on the selected Node pnpm on linux/amd64 @pnpm/linux-x64 @pnpm/exe.linux-x64 pnpm pnpm on linux/arm64/gnu @pnpm/linux-arm64 @pnpm/exe.linux-arm64 pnpm pnpm on darwin/arm64 @pnpm/macos-arm64 @pnpm/exe.darwin-arm64 pnpm pnpm on windows/amd64 @pnpm/win-x64 @pnpm/exe.win32-x64 pnpm.exe npm's bin/npm, bin/npx and their .cmd and .ps1 forms are installer shims that run the npm bundled with Node, so they are left out of the installed tree. npm's scripts need a Node: with oyzu:npm selected, oyzu:node must be selected too, and npm and npx run on it. When both are selected, npm is the dedicated tool's and Node's bundled npm is not used. A lifecycle script that calls npm through PATH during oyzu exec still finds Node's bundled npm; inside the build worker it finds the locked one.

Unit tests cover the registry metadata, archive facts, integrity verification and the packageManager requirement. The compiled Windows CLI selected and locked pnpm 12.3.4 for the two-document fixture, and completed a full isolated build with captured publisher policy metadata, native tests, coverage and a package. Two further no-cache builds repeated all actions with the same captured metadata digests and stable plan/package identities. Explicit offline dependency preparation and cross-platform installation remain unqualified. The broader declared package manager build scenario and nested npm calls from lifecycle scripts remain unverified.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-proxy-acquisition.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. See tool management for shared prerequisites, command conventions and qualification limits.

Administrative registries.routes can select an opaque connector for Node. The existing protected admin-settings.json contract accepts this entry inside its settings object: "registries.routes": { "locked": true, "value": [{"protocol": "tools", "scope": "oyzu:node", "connectorId": "corp-node"}] } Routes remain administrative-only; they cannot appear in project TOML. Exact node or oyzu:node scopes take precedence over *; specifying both exact aliases is ambiguous and fails. Other protocols do not route Node acquisition. tools.allowed is enforced before selecting or installing Node. Non-public tools.catalogs remain unsupported and fail without public fallback. Supply a host-owned TOML binding file explicitly to install: format = 1 [connectors.corp-node] base_url = "https://proxy.example/node/" authorization_env = "CORPORATE_NODE_AUTHORIZATION" oyzu install --connector-bindings /absolute/path/to/host-bindings.toml Relative binding paths are resolved from the invocation directory (including -C). This file is not automatically discovered in a project. base_url must end in / and serve the Node distribution layout: index.json, versioned SHASUMS256.txt and archives. HTTPS is required except for loopback HTTP used by local proxies. authorization_env is optional and names a host environment variable containing the complete Authorization header value. Set that variable through your host credential provisioning; do not put credentials in project TOML, binding files or command arguments. The binding file also serves artifact set routes: a tools route whose scope is an exact host selects a connector whose optional redirects = "server" | "client" field states who follows redirects (ignored by the Node and Go adapters). Both mise metadata requests and archive acquisition use the host broker and the same binding. The mise child receives response bytes, not connector credentials or endpoints. Existing broker redirect admission applies. This is an explicit standalone development binding, not an agent-issued managed connector grant or an OS network containment claim. Managed mode is still rejected. Missing bindings, unavailable credential variables or denied requests fail; there is no retry against the public source. Correct the binding or authorization and rerun installation. Failed acquisition does not commit a new lock. Locks retain the logical node-releases source and content identity without transport endpoints or credentials. Frozen reuse and restoration from cached archives load no bindings and require no proxy credentials. A missing cached archive in offline mode fails without contacting the proxy. The real proxy acceptance runner forwards actual public Node metadata and archive bytes through an authenticated loopback proxy, installs and executes Node, checks missing/denied binding failures, then reuses the frozen installation offline. Run it only as root on a disposable Linux host; it temporarily provisions /etc/oyzu/admin-settings.json, refuses to overwrite an existing policy and removes its policy afterward: python tooling/test-tool-proxy.py --cli PATH_TO_FEATURE_ENABLED_OYZU --disposable-linux-host This scenario passed on Linux amd64 on 2026-10-02. Native Windows/macOS proxy acceptance remains pending; the shared implementation has not yet been qualified against a production corporate proxy.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-python-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Indexed installation and pinning use the organization catalog contract. A matching verified index record is preferred without a catalog; with one, only approved indexed releases install. The provider evidence command uses the same metadata adapter as installation. Linux ARM64 GNU joins the native host/lock matrix (Tailscale remains Linux-only); macOS amd64 and musl are excluded. See implementation status for automated verification. Live publisher evidence and native ARM64 qualification remain pending. Oyzu can prepare CPython itself for a Python build, so a fresh checkout needs no Python installed. See tool management for shared prerequisites and native host builds for which projects use it.

Pinning is optional. For a project the native Python build supports, oyzu build resolves a CPython release, writes oyzu.lock, installs it into the shared tool store and builds with it: oyzu build # no Python on PATH, no pin needed oyzu pin # optional: preview or refresh the selection oyzu exec -- python --version Pin explicitly with a request in oyzu.toml; an explicit request takes precedence: [tools] python = "3.12" # latest 3.12.x; ranges such as ">=3.11 <3.14" also work

Source Role [tools] python in oyzu.toml The request, when present .python-version (one release such as 3.12 or 3.12.4) The default request [project] requires-python in pyproject.toml A constraint every selection must satisfy Neither The greatest stable release available The selection is the greatest stable CPython satisfying the request and every constraint. Pre-releases, free-threaded and debug builds are never selected. requires-python is translated with PEP 440 meaning (<=3.12 is exactly 3.12.0, ~=3.10 is >=3.10, <4). !=, === and local/pre-release specifiers cannot be expressed as a tool range and fail with the specifier named; set [tools] python to choose a version instead. A request nothing satisfies names the tool, the request, each constraint and the file it came from.

Distributions come from Python Build Standalone (install_only archives for Linux amd64/arm64 GNU, macOS arm64 and Windows amd64). Oyzu reads the publisher's latest-release.json, then that release's SHA256SUMS, and records the archive URL (which embeds the release tag) and declared digest in oyzu.lock. A pinned lock restores without network access to the catalog. Digests come from the publisher's checksum manifest, not a signature; downloaded bytes are verified against them. Oyzu does not redistribute these archives. Administrative tools routes scoped to python, oyzu:python or * use the same host connector bindings as Node and Go: a base serving latest-release.json and the release assets under the same relative paths. There is no public fallback from a configured route.

The distribution bundles a terminfo database whose entries differ only by letter case (for example 2621A and 2621a). No case-insensitive filesystem can hold both and the store refuses such archives, so the layout declares exclude_paths: ["share/terminfo"] (see archive layout). The exclusion is part of the digest-bound layout, applies to tar archives only, and may never remove a required path, launcher or executable. CPython's curses finds terminfo on the system at run time; builds do not need the bundled copy. The python command launches the real interpreter (bin/python3.X); bin/python, python3 and pip remain in the tree and on PATH.

The installed CPython is verified when it is installed (archive digest and layout) and trusted afterwards; later builds, tasks, oyzu exec and shells do not re-hash it (see the decision). Python therefore runs normally and may write __pycache__ bytecode beside the standard library, as it does in any install, without affecting later builds. Earlier builds re-hashed the installed payload on every run, so the first bytecode write made the second build fail with installed payload differs from receipt, as root and as an unprivileged user. Editing or damaging the installed tree is not detected up front. A broken interpreter fails when it runs; delete that tool install to reinstall it. A store whose earlier build hit the old failure works again without being discarded.

Only the native pip wheel path uses this today (pyproject.toml with the pip manager). requirements-only, uv, Poetry and legacy projects still use the isolated executor, which needs Docker. Python supplies python, python3 and its python3.X alias through frozen execution and shims. When the installation includes pip, pip, pip3 and pip3.X run the selected interpreter with -m pip; Windows does not need a Scripts/pip.exe launcher. No separate pip declaration is required. Existing installed records and frozen locks remain valid. After upgrading Oyzu, refresh an existing fixed shims directory with oyzu reshim. pip fetches the project's build backend from the package index during the wheel build; --offline builds fail when it is not already cached. The newest stable CPython is chosen when a project declares nothing, which can be a very recent release; declare requires-python or pin to avoid surprises. Two consecutive builds against one store pass as root and as an unprivileged user on Linux x86_64 (2026-10-07); tooling/test-fresh-checkout.py --project python repeats the second build. macOS and Windows are not verified. Verified on Linux x86_64 only (2026-10-07): the python-api fixture built a wheel from an empty store with no Python on PATH in about 20 seconds, and an explicit python = "3.12" selected 3.12.15. Windows, macOS, offline restoration, proxy/connector routing and real third-party license review of the bundled components are not verified. See the fresh-checkout record.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-request-identity.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. See tool lock inspection for the lock entry point.

The experimental Rust project_tool_requests boundary consumes an already captured EffectiveConfig, a caller-trusted unambiguous alias map, builder-owned native constraints and required capability IDs. The caller must obtain that map from an admitted catalog; project settings cannot add aliases or rebind canonical IDs. The implementation does not yet load the maintained fork's catalog. Effective tools.* strings become canonical requests; reserved tools.allowed and tools.catalogs are policy/catalog inputs, not version requests. Unknown aliases and multiple configured names for one canonical tool fail. Canonical IDs present in the catalog may be requested directly. Expressions are preserved verbatim for the backend; this function does not parse semver, pick versions, intersect constraints or admit an installation. Effective profile overrides have already been applied by the configuration resolver. The returned identity hashes the complete object requests, native_constraints and required_capabilities in domain oyzu.tool-requests.v1. Constraint arrays and capability arrays are sorted; duplicates fail. Environment values, secrets, origins and policy revisions are excluded. Policy must still be enforced for every use even when this identity stays unchanged. The golden fixture for only oyzu:node = "22" with empty constraints/capabilities is independently computed and checked against Rust. Limits are 4096 alias entries, 256 root requests, 4096 constrained tool IDs, 16384 total native constraints, 256 capabilities, 16 KiB per text value and an 8 MiB aggregate text budget. Capabilities are at most 256 ASCII letters, digits or -_.:/. Invalid/oversized values fail before cloning the bounded collections. Nothing is read from disk, downloaded, executed or modified by projection. ToolRequestIdentity::parse(json_bytes, admitted_ids) reads the serialized identity record for an internal consumer. The caller supplies canonical IDs from a trusted catalog, not from the record. Exactly requests, native_constraints, required_capabilities and digest are required; extra fields and duplicate JSON keys fail. It shares projection's normalization and identity calculation, requires already sorted sets and checks the supplied digest against the recomputed value. Literal version syntax remains unchanged. Decoding is bounded to 8 MiB, nesting depth 32 and 10,000 JSON entries before typed conversion, followed by the limits above. No files, network or tools are accessed. Catalog membership is only a consistency check, not source trust or permission to use a backend. A caller must also bind the record's digest to its trusted operation context; anyone can compute a digest for a different request. This parser supplies the normalized request portion of a future worker payload, not the complete resolve-operation schema, broker session or catalog provenance. ToolRequestIdentity is immutable after projection or checked parsing. Rust consumers use requests(), native_constraints(), required_capabilities() and digest() to borrow its contents. This replaces the experimental public fields; callers needing a changed request must project or parse a new identity so its digest is recomputed. JSON field names and digest calculation are unchanged. Frozen selection uses these accessors to compare the same validated request map and digest. Immutability preserves consistency, not policy approval or freshness. The draft request-record schema and tests/fixtures/tool-requests/ share malformed-shape cases with the Rust parser. Run python tooling/check-tool-contracts.py with the design requirements installed to check the schema fixtures. Schema string lengths count characters; the runtime additionally enforces UTF-8 bytes, aggregate budgets, sorted order, catalog membership and digest recomputation. Passing shape checks does not prove those semantic checks or qualify a backend. After projection, prefer select_for_tool_requests(workspace, directory, profile, requests, platform): it checks both the computed digest and canonical request map against one captured lock. A lock with a matching digest but an altered request map fails TOOL_LOCK_STALE. Alias catalog loading, native builder constraint production, backend resolution and worker wiring remain unfinished.

The experimental Rust select_locked_environment(workspace, directory, profile, request_digest, platform) boundary chooses from workspace/oyzu.lock after the caller has resolved effective configuration and computed its request digest. It does not read Oyzu or mise configuration itself. Workspace and working directory must exist as directories; both are resolved physically and an outside working directory fails. Internal directory aliases select the physical scope. Locked scope aliases are resolved physically too; two matching scope records for the same physical ancestor fail TOOL_LOCK_AMBIGUOUS. Existing locked scope directories for the selected profile must stay inside the workspace. Missing unrelated scopes do not prevent using a present scope. Among locked environments for the exact profile, the longest complete ancestor scope wins. app does not match application. A nearer scope with a different request digest fails TOOL_LOCK_STALE, even if the root entry would match. No matching scope/profile fails TOOL_LOCK_MISSING; no complete selection for the requested platform fails TOOL_PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE. These failures require an explicit resolution/update action, not a fallback to another profile, parent or platform. The whole lock is validated before selection, including unrelated dependency graph errors. Nothing is installed, downloaded, executed or edited. Success returns the existing LockedSelection identity and installation keys. The caller must still check current policy, compiled backend admission and installed receipts and retain leases before use. This boundary is not a stable new CLI command, a resolver, an authorization grant or race-proof filesystem containment. This lower-level entrypoint checks the supplied digest only; use select_for_tool_requests to also bind the projected canonical request map. Worker integration remains pending.

The experimental Rust API tools::ToolLockEdit supports the publication part of an explicit version-1 update. It does not resolve versions, authorize sources, install tools or enable an oyzu lock CLI command. The caller supplies a complete resolved candidate after applying its update scope and policy; records absent from that candidate are deliberate removals. Existing frozen selectors never call this API. No platform account or network is used. let edit = oyzu::tools::ToolLockEdit::capture(lock_path)?; let proposal = edit.propose(&resolved_format_2_bytes)?; // Review proposal.changes() and proposal.preview(). For combined install, // complete verification and installation before committing this proposal. proposal.commit()?; Capture accepts an existing parent directory and an absent or valid version-1 regular file. Existing source and candidate are independently bounded to 8 MiB and validated by the same whole-graph parser used by inspection. Format 1 is rejected; this API does not implement migration. File symlinks/reparse points and nonregular inputs are rejected. Parent paths are canonicalized at capture; this is a workspace edit boundary, not the store's hostile-filesystem containment API. changes() returns ordered environment (scope, profile) or tool-key records tagged added, changed or removed. Formatting/order-only differences are excluded. preview() returns the exact proposed output bytes. Unchanged records retain their TOML spelling and comments, including inline-array records. Changed records use candidate formatting; editing may normalize line endings. A semantic no-op retains the complete original bytes. The editor validates the final output and compares its normalized graph with the candidate before returning a proposal. Commit uses a permanent sibling .oyzu-tool-lock-edit.lock for cooperating writers (excluded from source snapshots, so whether a checkout has written its lock does not change action keys) and compares the current file with the captured bytes both before staging and immediately before publication. Missing-file creation uses no-replace publication. Updates use a flushed same-directory temporary file and atomic replacement, preserving existing permissions; Unix also syncs the parent directory. Windows sharing/lock violations, including replacement access denial, are retried for at most two seconds, with a fresh source comparison on each retry. Read-only Windows sources fail before staging. Temporary files are cleaned up on ordinary failure; the permanent coordination file remains and must not be deleted while writers may be active. A build that records tool identities therefore leaves it beside oyzu.lock in the project root; ignore it in version control. An observed source change, active writer or failed replacement reports TOOL_LOCK_EDIT_CONFLICT. Capture a fresh source and regenerate/review the proposal to retry; never force a stale proposal over external changes. Invalid graphs fail before publication. A directory-sync error after replacement explicitly reports that the lock was published; inspect the current file before retrying. Dropping an uncommitted proposal does not write the lock. This is optimistic concurrency: a noncooperating process can still race the last comparison, and replacement of the parent directory is outside this boundary. It is not a filesystem compare-and-swap primitive or an authorization grant. tests/integration/tool_lock_edit.rs covers actual temporary-workspace publication, retained comments, no-op byte identity, empty-lock transitions, semantic diffs, stale edits, active-writer exclusion, invalid graphs and format rejection. Unix tests cover symlink/FIFO denial; Windows exercises bounded sharing-denial recovery and read-only-source cleanup. Complete resolver/update orchestration, migration, install-before-lock lifecycle and native CI qualification remain separate OEP requirements.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-resolve.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Status: experimental, provisional. First proof (P1) of the draft recipe ingest engine; command names, field names, the exit code for partial results and every limit value are drafts pending maintainer review. Nothing here installs a tool. See the qualification record for exactly what ran.
documents.s: Recipe resolution and evidence (oyzu tools resolve, oyzu tools evidence)

documents.t: Many tools are single-binary releases described only by community recipe data (the public aqua registry). For an exact version and platform, a client needs the URLs to fetch, the evidence the publisher offers and whether the platform has an asset at all. tools resolve evaluates a recipe snapshot offline and emits one record per (tool, version, platform): a discovery-tier artifact set. It reads two things — the snapshot file you name and the flags — and writes stdout. tools evidence takes such a document, downloads each resolved artifact and its checksum file from the real publisher hosts, records sha256 and size, compares them with the published checksum and fills the verified tier. With --provider java it builds the discovery records of Oyzu's Java provider from the publisher's listing first, so the public index can carry Java the same way. Both are read-only with respect to configuration, locks and the tool store. Neither needs an account. They ignore oyzu.toml, oyzu.lock, -C and --root.

# 1. Fetch a registry snapshot yourself (resolve never fetches one) curl -sSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aquaproj/aqua-registry/v4.573.0/registry.yaml # 2. Offline evaluation, pinned to the snapshot digest oyzu --json tools resolve --registry registry.yaml \ --registry-digest sha256:52a43b0b2817a56fe7566625809d7cca41a1178ccae2b152941221b516e70228 \ --snapshot-tag v4.573.0 \ --tool hashicorp/terraform --version v1.16.5 > terraform.discovery.json # 3. Download and check the real bytes (needs the network) oyzu --json tools evidence --set terraform.discovery.json > terraform.verified.json Without --json both commands print a readable summary (outcome, a table of records, unsupported platforms and errors with reasons, next steps). Colour follows NO_COLOR and terminal detection; the plain text carries the same meaning.

Flag Meaning --registry FILE The merged registry.yaml. A directory (the per-package tree form) is rejected with SNAPSHOT_INVALID; tree form is deferred --registry-digest sha256:HEX Reject the snapshot before evaluation unless its SHA-256 matches (SNAPSHOT_DIGEST_MISMATCH) --snapshot-tag, --snapshot-commit Caller-asserted labels recorded in the document; never checked --tool NAME (repeatable), --tools-file FILE Registry package names such as hashicorp/terraform. A file has one name per line (# comments allowed) --version V (repeatable) Exact upstream version as the recipe sees it, including any prefix (v1.16.5). Required: there is no default and no listing --platform OS/ARCH/ABI (repeatable) Default: linux/amd64/gnu, darwin/arm64/native, windows/amd64/msvc, independent of the host. Operating systems linux, darwin, windows; architectures amd64, arm64. Only the default ABI of each OS is modeled; others (for example musl) yield an error record PLATFORM_ABI_UNSUPPORTED --limit NAME=VALUE (repeatable) Lower a counted limit (recipe_nodes, recipe_bytes, recipe_depth, recipe_overrides, string_bytes, expression_steps, url_bytes, record_urls, regex_bytes, snapshot_bytes, output_bytes). Values above the default ceiling are rejected Every (tool, version) pair is evaluated for every platform. Flag order and repetition do not change the output, which is sorted by (tool.id, version.requested, platform). Tool ids are aqua:<registry package name>, the same backend spelling mise uses (aqua:cli/cli), so a declaration written for mise's aqua backend keeps its form. Provisional until install is wired to it.

github_release and http packages. The evaluator is a closed, Oyzu-owned interpreter of the registry's data format, implemented in the oyzu-recipe crate: Version branch: the entry's version_constraint, otherwise the first version_overrides item whose constraint is true (the record's version.branch is top-level or override[N], or null when no branch was selected); version_prefix and version_filter. Expression language: Version, SemVer, string and list literals, semver("…"), ==, !=, in, matches, startsWith, endsWith, contains, not/!, and/&&, or/||. semver() is false for a version that is not a semantic version, so recipes fall through to exact Version == "…" branches. Pre-release versions satisfy only constraints that name a pre-release. Templates: {{.Version}}-style fields, pipes, parentheses, if/else/end and the functions trimV trimPrefix trimSuffix replace title semver regexFind index splitList eq ne. supported_envs (with rosetta2 / windows_arm_emulation), replacements, platform overrides (first match), no_asset, error_message, complete_windows_ext, files, checksum, cosign, minisign, slsa_provenance, github_artifact_attestations. Anything else is reported, never guessed: a loop, an unknown function or the recipe vars feature gives RECIPE_FEATURE_UNSUPPORTED for that record.

One JSON document (format 1, kind artifact-sets), validated by artifact-set.schema.json and described field by field in the draft. It contains the engine, the snapshot (its computed digest plus your labels), the effective limits and the records. A record has status: Status Meaning Exit resolved URLs (artifact, checksum, signatures …), archive facts and declared evidence 0 unsupported A normal result: PLATFORM_EXCLUDED, NO_ASSET, RECIPE_MESSAGE, SOURCE_KIND (build-from-source packages), VERSION_NOT_COVERED, PRIVATE_PACKAGE 0 error The engine could not decide: LIMIT_EXCEEDED, RECIPE_INVALID, RECIPE_FEATURE_UNSUPPORTED, RENDER_FAILED, URL_NOT_HTTPS, PLATFORM_ABI_UNSUPPORTED 3 Digests use the domain oyzu.artifact-set.v1, a zero byte and RFC 8785 canonical JSON. recipe_digest covers the parsed entry (so comments and key order do not matter); digests.declared covers the record without verified, tier and digests; digests.full covers everything except digests. The document carries no time, host, user or path, so the same snapshot digest, request, limits and engine build produce byte-identical output on every run. A GitHub release download is stored as the recipe renders it (github.com/…). The signed redirect target is never stored.

Exit Meaning 0 Complete document; every record is resolved or unsupported 1 Evidence problem, no records: SNAPSHOT_INVALID, SNAPSHOT_DIGEST_MISMATCH (and, for evidence, SET_INVALID, SET_SCHEMA_INVALID, SET_FORMAT_UNSUPPORTED, SET_DIGEST_MISMATCH). With --json the shared error envelope (error, code, nextStep, exitCode) is on stdout 2 Usage problem, no records: FLAGS_CONFLICT, REQUEST_EMPTY 5 Not found, no records: TOOL_NOT_IN_SNAPSHOT 3 Complete document in which at least one record is error (resolve) or a resolved record stayed at the discovery tier (evidence). Exit 3 is provisional A process killed by the environment (memory, wall clock) emits no document. Run one tool per process when you need that blast-radius control.

Flag Meaning --set FILE / - A tools resolve document (or standard input). Every record's digests are recomputed first; a mismatch is SET_DIGEST_MISMATCH and nothing is fetched --allow-host HOST (repeatable) Permit a host beyond those named by the set's own URLs --verify METHOD (repeatable) Run only these methods; the rest are reported not-run --provider NAME java, node, go or python: instead of reading a set, build the records of an Oyzu provider from its publisher, then verify them the same way. Excludes --set --version V (repeatable, with --provider) Exact provider release, such as 21.0.8. Required with --provider; anything else is FLAGS_CONFLICT before any download --platform OS/ARCH/ABI (repeatable, with --provider) Default: linux/amd64/gnu, linux/arm64/gnu, darwin/arm64/native, darwin/amd64/native, windows/amd64/msvc; unsupported installations get an unsupported record

For Java (Eclipse Temurin) the command reads the publisher's GA release listing of each feature release once (api.adoptium.net/v3/assets/feature_releases/<feature>/ga, at most 16 MiB, the newest 20 releases) and writes one record per version and platform: tool.id is core:java (the index tool oyzu:java carries it as its origin), source_kind is github_release, and version.requested and version.normalized are both the release (21.0.8). A resolved record names the archive and the publisher's per-archive SHA-256 file (….tar.gz.sha256.txt) on github.com/adoptium/temurin<feature>-binaries, with one checksum#0 evidence entry for the archive's file name. These are the archive URLs the Java provider installs from, so the record matches what a client locks. release carries the publisher's release time when the listing has one. A platform the Java provider does not install (anything outside the four installation defaults) is unsupported with PLATFORM_UNSUPPORTED; a release without a build for the platform is unsupported with NO_PLATFORM_ARTIFACT; a release missing from the listing is an error record (VERSION_NOT_FOUND), and an unreadable listing gives error records (SOURCE_UNAVAILABLE). The document's snapshot is {source: "api.adoptium.net", form: "merged-file"} with the SHA-256 of the listings read; recipe_digest names the provider's record rules. The resolved records are then downloaded and checked exactly as for a set, and exit codes are the same. oyzu --json tools evidence --provider java --version 21.0.8 --version 17.0.16 > java.verified.json

The other index providers follow the same rules (tool.id is core:<name>, the platform and error codes are Java's, and each record names the archive the provider installs from): Node reads nodejs.org/dist/index.json (at most 16 MiB) for the release and its day, which becomes release.time (precision: "day"), then each release's SHASUMS256.txt (at most 1 MiB). The evidence entry names the archive in that manifest. Go reads go.dev/dl/?mode=json&include=all (at most 16 MiB). A release must be a stable catalog release that lists the platform's archive; the record's checksum is the archive's .sha256 sidecar on dl.google.com (file_format: "raw"). Python reads python-build-standalone's current-release pointer (raw.githubusercontent.com/astral-sh/python-build-standalone/latest-release/latest-release.json), then that release's SHA256SUMS on github.com. Only versions that release ships as install_only builds for all four installation platforms are recorded; any other is VERSION_NOT_FOUND. The archive URL carries the release tag, so a lock restores it without the pointer.

--provider also accepts Maven, Gradle, Helm, kubectl, k3d, Liquibase, Tailscale, npm, pnpm and Rust (lowercase names, optionally prefixed with oyzu: or core:). Versions are exact stable three-part releases. Human output and global --json use the same records and exit semantics. Omit --platform to emit all five index platforms: linux/amd64/gnu, linux/arm64/gnu, darwin/arm64/native, darwin/amd64/native, windows/amd64/msvc. macOS amd64 remains unsupported. Provider Publisher authority and check Maven Apache archive directory listing, binary tarball and SHA-512 sidecar Gradle services.gradle.org release catalog's SHA-256 and binary ZIP Helm get.helm.sh archive and SHA-256 sidecar naming that archive kubectl dl.k8s.io binary and SHA-256 sidecar k3d GitHub release binary and its checksums.txt entry Liquibase GitHub release API's asset digest; no publisher checksum file Tailscale pkgs.tailscale.com stable Linux tarball and SHA-256 sidecar npm, pnpm npm registry tarball metadata and SHA-512 SRI, converted to SHA-256 only after verifying the archive Rust static.rust-lang.org channel manifest and SHA-256 sidecar; all available xz component URL/digest pairs, plus a versioned, checksum-verified rustup bootstrap Archive names, layouts and publisher-document parsing use the same oyzu-tool-metadata adapters as installation. Checksum entries with params.file_format = "provider" are re-read using those adapters during verification; params.provider selects the adapter. Registry metadata is bounded at 64 MiB; ordinary checksum files retain the 4 MiB limit. Liquibase 5.x records carry params.license = "FSL-1.1-ALv2", a source-available license. This is a license fact, not a serving-class or legal approval. For Rust, the artifact is dist/channel-rust-<version>.toml, not the generated installed sysroot. The checksum entry's params.rust_distribution contains inputs keyed by component/target, each with url and digest, and rustup with its versioned bootstrap URL and digest. Evidence verifies the manifest checksum, checks that the complete map matches the downloaded manifest, and verifies the bootstrap bytes against its publisher sidecar. Component tarballs are checked when selected for installation, not all downloaded by the evidence job. This supports extra components and targets without inventing a second authority. The existing artifact-set and tool-index schemas are unchanged. Examples of provider evidence collection: oyzu --json tools evidence --provider kubectl --version 1.34.1 oyzu --json tools evidence --provider helm --version 3.22.0 oyzu --json tools evidence --provider rust --version 1.95.0 Live publisher evidence is not yet recorded; see implementation status for automated verification. An unreachable publisher produces error/discovery records, never verified success. Human output lists unsupported and failed discovery platforms with their reasons; JSON retains the complete records and existing evidence exit semantics. For each resolved record it downloads the artifact (streamed and hashed, never stored; at most 2 GiB) and the checksum file (at most 4 MiB, fetched once per URL), and records verified.artifact.{digest,size,publisher_digest,agree}. Redirects are followed manually, at most five, and every hop must be an allowed host or the reviewed pair github.com → release-assets.githubusercontent.com; the hosts seen are reported in verified.observed_redirect_hosts (host names only). Transport follows the broker's proxy and CA rules (HTTPS_PROXY, NO_PROXY, SSL_CERT_FILE; see acquisition transport); each transfer is retried at most twice on transport failures and 408/429/5xx. Per evidence entry, verified.results[].outcome is: verified: for checksum, the checksum entry for the artifact's file name exists and equals the computed digest (sha256 or sha512). For github-attestation, see GitHub artifact attestations; for slsa-provenance, see SLSA provenance files. failed: the checksum file lacks the name, lists conflicting values, is not a hexadecimal value of the right length, could not be fetched, or disagrees with the artifact; or no attestation GitHub lists for the artifact verifies; or the provenance file or its Rekor entries could not be read or do not verify (the detail says which). verifier-unavailable: this build has no verifier for the method (cosign, minisign, openpgp), or the checksum algorithm (md5, sha1) or file format (regexp) is unsupported. The evidence is declared but unchecked and is never counted as verified. not-run: excluded by --verify. A record becomes tier: verified only when at least one entry verified and none failed; verified.lock then carries the strongest verified kind in the lock's verification shape: attestation when an attestation verified (its evidence_digest is the SHA-256 of the verifying bundle; for a SLSA provenance file, of the file; a GitHub attestation is preferred when both verified), else digest-only (the checksum file's SHA-256). Otherwise the record stays discovery with verified.status: failed and the reasons in results, and the command exits 3. A checksum-verified record establishes that these bytes equal what the publisher's checksum file listed at fetch time. It does not prove the publisher is who the recipe says, that the checksum file is authentic, that a signature holds, or that use is permitted. An attestation-verified record also establishes that a GitHub Actions workflow of the release's repository attested these exact bytes (below), or, for SLSA provenance, that a slsa-github-generator release built them from that repository; it says nothing about whether the workflow's source is trustworthy.

For github-attestation evidence (aqua's github_artifact_attestations), evidence asks GitHub's API for the attestations of the artifact's digest, GET https://api.github.com/repos/<owner>/<repo>/attestations/sha256:<digest>?predicate_type=https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1, where <owner>/<repo> comes from the artifact's GitHub release URL (other artifact URLs fail the evidence). A GITHUB_TOKEN in the environment is sent to api.github.com only, to raise the anonymous rate limit (60 requests an hour); listings are memoized per repository and digest. A 404 means no attestation. Each listed Sigstore bundle (v0.3) is read inline from the response or, when GitHub offers it only through bundle_url (as for the GitHub CLI's own releases), downloaded from that pre-signed https URL without the token and without following redirects, snappy-decompressed (block format, at most 8 MiB) and parsed the same way. Each bundle is verified offline, with the same verifier as the tool index's signature (tool index) and Sigstore's public-good trusted root compiled into the CLI: one Rekor entry whose signed entry timestamp verifies against a Rekor key of the trusted root, and a certificate chaining to a Fulcio CA valid at the entry's integrated time; the certificate's OIDC issuer is https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com, its source repository (Fulcio extension 1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.12) is https://github.com/<owner>/<repo> (case-insensitive), and, when the recipe names a signer_workflow, its SAN starts with https://github.com/<signer_workflow>@ (that workflow file at any ref), as with gh attestation verify --repo --signer-workflow; the DSSE signature, the log entry's payload hash and signature, and an in-toto v1 statement with predicate https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1 whose subject names the artifact's SHA-256. The first bundle that verifies wins; identity reports its signing workflow and verifier is sigstore-public-good.
