Not checked: SCTs, Merkle inclusion proofs, RFC 3161 timestamps (so bundles from GitHub's own Sigstore instance, used for private repositories, do not verify), the runner environment, and the provenance predicate's contents.

For slsa-provenance evidence (aqua's slsa_provenance, typically {type: github_release, asset: "{{.Asset}}.intoto.jsonl"}), evidence downloads the record's provenance URL (at most 4 MiB, same host and redirect rules as checksum files). The file is what slsa-github-generator publishes: one DSSE envelope whose signature carries its Fulcio certificate, with no transparency-log entry in the file. As slsa-verifier does, the log entry is looked up in Rekor's public API by the artifact's digest: POST https://rekor.sigstore.dev/api/v1/index/retrieve with {"hash":"sha256:<digest>"}, then GET https://rekor.sigstore.dev/api/v1/log/entries/<uuid> for at most 16 returned UUIDs (memoized per digest; no credentials are sent). Nothing Rekor returns is trusted unverified; verification is offline against the same compiled-in trusted root: the envelope is an in-toto statement (v0.1 or v1) with predicate https://slsa.dev/provenance/v0.2 or v1, and a subject whose name is the artifact URL's file name and whose SHA-256 is the artifact's; some returned entry has a signed entry timestamp from a Rekor key of the trusted root (the canonical {body, integratedTime, logID, logIndex}, as for bundles) and records this envelope: an intoto 0.0.1 entry with the envelope's certificate and its payload (or envelope) hash, an intoto 0.0.2 entry also recording its signature, or a dsse 0.0.1 entry; its integratedTime is the signing time; the certificate chains to a Fulcio CA valid at that time and was itself valid then; the OIDC issuer is https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com; the SAN is a workflow of slsa-framework/slsa-github-generator at a release tag, https://github.com/slsa-framework/slsa-github-generator/.github/workflows/<file>.yml@refs/tags/v*; the source repository extension is the recipe's source_uri (github.com/<owner>/<repo>), else the release's repository from the artifact URL, else the recipe's repo_owner/repo_name; and with source_tag, the source repository ref (1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.14) is refs/tags/<source_tag>; the DSSE signature verifies with the certificate's key. identity reports the builder workflow and verifier is sigstore-public-good. Not checked, as for bundles: SCTs and the Merkle inclusion proof (the signed entry timestamp is the log evidence), and the provenance predicate's contents (builder id, build type, materials). Unlike slsa-verifier, any generator workflow at a v* tag is accepted rather than a fixed builder list; for a delegated (BYOB) build the certificate names the generator's delegator workflow, and the builder it delegated to is not checked.

resolve has no network, process or file-write capability by construction: the oyzu-recipe crate depends on no HTTP client, TLS stack, process or temp-file crate and its sources name no such API (checked by a unit test and by the proof runner with cargo tree). The bare command adds no operating-system sandbox; supplying one (for example an empty network namespace) is the caller's job. The qualification run used unshare -rn. Recipes are untrusted data. Recipe text shown in human output is control-character escaped. The registry's license obligations are open; see licensing and provenance. The evaluator is written independently against the registry's public data format and contains no registry data or code from another project. Credentials are never sent to publisher hosts.

Merged-file snapshots only; the per-package tree form, --registry-tested-version, supplements (origin: supplement) and the curated batch are not implemented. Verification: checksums, GitHub artifact attestations and SLSA provenance files. No cosign, minisign or OpenPGP verifier exists. The attestation check was proven with real bundles in unit tests; a live run against api.github.com happens in the tool index job (the development sandbox cannot reach the API). The provenance check was proven in unit tests on slsa-verifier v2.6.0's real provenance file against the production Fulcio CAs, with Rekor entries built in Rekor's response shapes and signed by a test log key: Rekor was unreachable from the development sandbox, so the live lookup and a real Rekor entry's body shape are unverified. Rekor's index search is best effort; an artifact whose entries it does not list fails the evidence. evidence runs sequentially, has no stall timer, and does not refuse private/loopback addresses after DNS resolution; its host allow-list is derived from the set's own URLs. Windows executable-suffix handling for files is not applied (only raw assets get .exe). semver() follows one specification implemented in this repository. Differences against the registry's own engine on pre-release and build-metadata edge cases are unmeasured (deferred differential testing). Aliases and YAML tags are handled by the YAML parser; duplicate keys fail the whole snapshot; alias-expansion bombs are limited only by snapshot_bytes before parsing (hardening deferred). Linux x86-64 only has been run. Output is designed to be identical on Windows and macOS; that is unverified. --provider java has not run against the live Adoptium API from this repository's sessions (no network route); its parsing is tested on a fixture listing in the API's documented shape. The listing covers the newest 20 GA releases of a feature, so an older release is VERSION_NOT_FOUND. Only Temurin JDK images are recorded; providers other than the supported provider list are FLAGS_CONFLICT. --provider node and --provider python verified real releases from this repository's sessions (2026-10-10: Node 21 to 26 and CPython 3.10 to 3.15 on the three platforms, through the tool index job). --provider go has not run against go.dev from here (no network route); its records are tested on a fixture catalog in the publisher's shape. version.branch is null when no branch was selected (PLATFORM_ABI_UNSUPPORTED, a limit trip on the whole entry, VERSION_NOT_COVERED). This differs from the client contract outline, which required a string; see the implementation notes.

python tooling/test-tool-resolve.py --cli <oyzu> --workspace <dir> --registry <registry.yaml> drives the compiled CLI against the pinned snapshot and real publishers; compiled-CLI tests are in tests/integration/recipe_resolve.rs (including the --provider input checks); the Java provider's records are unit-tested in src/tools/recipe_evidence/java.rs (Node, Go and Python in providers.rs) and its listing parser in crates/oyzu-tool-metadata/src/jdk/tests.rs; schema fixtures in tests/fixtures/tool-artifact-set (python tooling/check-tool-contracts.py). Results and revisions are in the qualification record.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-rust-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. See tool management for shared prerequisites, command conventions and qualification limits.

The current implementation uses Oyzu's compiled worker to invoke rustup with broker-verified frozen inputs. Its command mechanics are adapted from the pinned mise source, without initializing mise settings, loading backends or consulting mise configuration. Cargo/Rustup homes remain private to the installation; rustup uses a minimal profile, explicit components/targets and disabled self-update. Both native streams go to diagnostics while the worker's stdout remains a private protocol. The returned sysroot must reside inside the private Rustup home. This extraction is undergoing real-host qualification; earlier evidence below describes the former embedded implementation and does not qualify this replacement. The Rust integration is being verified through the same install, which, exec, environment and shell contracts as Node/Go. It requires a current Oyzu frontend and a Rust selection declared in native toolchain files or Oyzu TOML: [tools] rust = "1.95.0" oyzu install rust oyzu which cargo oyzu exec -- rustc --version oyzu exec -- cargo build oyzu install rust --frozen --offline An explicit install name must already be configured. It validates the name and installs the complete configured project selection, retaining one environment lock rather than creating a separate Rust installation workflow. Bare install continues to install all configured tools. Rust recipes use exact three-part stable versions. Pinning and isolated first-build resolution also accept the native stable channel, resolving it to one exact release before acquisition and plan freeze. Windows amd64 installations select the MSVC compiler (the host's platform, like Linux and macOS) and consume the matching pinned recipe, including its formatting, lint and coverage components. Windows selections retain a separate native platform identity for each helper; see discovered helper installation. The experimental Linux compiler profile also installs rustfmt, Clippy, LLVM coverage tools and standard libraries for the six binary targets supported by the Rust builder. Native rustup owns component and target installation. Discovery reads every rust-toolchain file form (see Rust toolchain files); resolving beta/nightly, partial-version or dated channels remains subsequent functional work. For stable, the resolver first uses the admitted signed index and organization catalog. Standalone publisher fallback, when allowed by existing controls, reads the checksum-verified official stable channel manifest only to select the exact version. Its versioned manifest, components and installer still pass the existing exact recipe/acquisition checks. The lock retains request stable and its exact selection. Offline reuse and pin --refresh retain that selection; they do not move the channel. A fresh offline request without locked metadata remains unresolved. The original source and Cargo minimum remain binding. See the original stable qualification for the observed gap and current native verification status. This addition covers pinning, frozen reuse and isolated first-build selection; direct install/update entry points still require an exact configured Rust release. The worker performs rustup installation in private homes. Oyzu packages the completed compiler sysroot into its existing cached archive/store format, retaining bundled notices; the receipt identifies the published Cargo/rustc/rustdoc commands. The lock's digest-only evidence covers that generated snapshot, not a claim of signed publisher verification or a captured bootstrap download closure. Frozen cached restoration does not invoke rustup. If both installation and archive are absent, restore online through explicit update; do not silently regenerate a different archive for an existing digest. Pinned Rust installation captures and verifies each recipe input through Oyzu's broker, then gives rustup a private local distribution mirror. An organization catalog now governs indexed Rust releases and every selected component; see below. Configured Rust connector routes remain unsupported, with no direct fallback from an enforced route. Cargo package/Git acquisition remains ordinary Cargo behavior. Mutable Cargo cache/configuration is separate from the committed compiler payload. Execution sets RUSTC and RUSTDOC to selected native binaries and prepends their bin directory; no ambient rustup installation supplies the compiler. A compatible system linker is a prerequisite: Windows MSVC requires Visual Studio Build Tools with the C++ workload (no IDE) and its Windows SDK; macOS requires command line tools. A GNU/LLVM recipe, if selected explicitly, requires externally provisioned LLVM/MinGW. Installing Rust does not install MSVC, Windows SDKs or other system prerequisites. Acceptance is exercised by tooling/test-tool-rust.py. At 9ddf621, Linux amd64 passed real installation with ambient Rust removed from PATH, store-owned Cargo/rustc/rustdoc version checks, dependency-free compilation and program execution, frozen reuse with unchanged lock bytes, and building the actual Oyzu checkout's default frontend using the installed compiler. The last check reused the provisioned Cargo dependency cache; it does not establish dependency capture or an isolated Oyzu build. A subsequent run with container networking disabled restored the removed installation from its cached snapshot and compiled the sample project again. Native Windows/macOS Rust qualification remains pending.
documents.s: Rust installation through the frozen native worker

documents.t: Native Linux arm64 GNU is admitted. Remote arm64 installation uses the explicitly provisioned oyzu-toolchain/worker:v1-linux-arm64 sibling and verifies its actual architecture. Oyzu does not provision images or emulators. Native ARM64 and this worker sibling still need qualification. Ordinary oyzu install now installs only the native development selection; it never provisions a Linux compiler worker merely because build.yaml declares Rust targets. Isolated build preparation remains a separate execution path. Earlier acceptance proved Windows-to-Linux provisioning through a prebuilt oyzu-toolchain/worker:v1 image. That historical flow is no longer part of ordinary installation. The captured-build machinery and its image prerequisites remain independent; native installation does not qualify isolated builds. The remote Linux installer uses a private 6 GiB executable tmpfs and an 8 GiB container memory limit with two CPUs. Rustup keeps downloaded inputs, expanded components and transaction scratch concurrently; the earlier 2 GiB scratch limit failed the repository's 12-component Rust 1.99.1 recipe during extraction. The larger bound completed that installation during qualification. Network denial, the read-only root and distribution inputs, dropped capabilities and no-new-privileges remain required. The separate restoration worker also uses 6 GiB scratch and an 8 GiB memory limit: its verified private archive, cached archive and extracted tree coexist. The measured repository recipe required at least 3,276,915,836 bytes before filesystem overhead and exhausted its earlier 3 GiB bound. That recipe completed restoration under the larger limit; this does not qualify the full isolated build. Neither stage removes locked components. Hosts must have sufficient container resources.
documents.s: Local Linux Rust worker from Windows (experimental)

documents.t: For a Rust-only Windows amd64 project, run oyzu pin, oyzu install, then oyzu run install. The last command is the Rust builder's executable installation task; it does not provision tools. An older MSVC or differently pinned installation requires explicit oyzu install --update rust; stale records are never relabeled. The native compiler's platform is windows/amd64/msvc. The pinned recipe's cross-target standard libraries may also be installed; their presence does not establish that cross-linkers are available. Installation uses the existing verified store and records the recipe digest in the tool record's options. After publication, install --frozen --offline verifies and reuses the installed selection or restores its cached archive. Missing cached payloads fail. The version-1 lock retains its other platform resolution recipes. oyzu run obtains verified tools from the default user-level store using discovery's resolved configuration snapshot. It holds installation leases for the complete task/hook sequence and prepends verified tool binaries to PATH; Rust also supplies explicit RUSTC/RUSTDOC paths. Other task-specific environment values are retained. Missing verified selections fail before task hooks, with an oyzu install remedy; listing/help do not acquire tool leases. Custom stores are available through oyzu exec --store, not through oyzu run in this slice. Native linker, CMake and other package-specific prerequisites remain external. Managed task environments and wider native platform qualification remain pending.
documents.s: Pinned native Rust and task execution

documents.t: Before a new Rust installation, the admitted tool broker fetches the exact stable channel manifest and its published SHA-256 checksum. The adapter verifies the manifest and checks that every requested compiler component has a published URL and digest. Missing components or mismatched checksums fail before launching rustup. Metadata parsing itself installs nothing and creates no state. Metadata acquisition also pins a versioned rustup installer using its published checksum. The broker verifies every selected input before the compiled worker invokes rustup. Existing locked offline archive reuse does not invoke this new-install metadata preflight.

oyzu tools evidence --provider rust --version 1.95.0 produces the existing artifact-set shape for all five index platforms, marking macOS amd64 unsupported. The approved artifact is the official channel manifest. Its checksum params carry all available xz component URL/digest pairs and a checksum-verified, versioned rustup bootstrap. The evidence collector checks rustc, Cargo, host rust-std, Clippy, rustfmt and LLVM tools availability. Cross-target standard libraries and target-independent components such as rust-src remain selectable from the same indexed manifest. Under toolCatalog.url, pin/install/build acquisition selects an approved, verified indexed release. The manifest download must match the index's SHA-256, and its complete component map must equal the indexed map. Native declarations in rust-toolchain.toml select components/targets from those inputs. Every selected component and the bootstrap must match an indexed URL and digest; the broker then hashes their downloaded bytes before copying them into the temporary mirror. Rustup uses this local mirror, private homes, a minimal profile and disabled self-update. Missing mirror inputs fail; no live publisher fallback can add them. This retains rustup's native installation semantics instead of reimplementing them. The release catalog entry governs delivery of its manifest and admitted component URLs: direct entries use the fixed publisher hosts, proxy entries use the edge's existing upstream URL route. The edge must serve those approved component URLs. Frozen recipes are checked against current catalog/index metadata before installing or reusing a selection. Installed payloads are trusted and never rehashed on reuse. Offline operations use the existing signed caches and archive/store rules. Unapproved releases fail with TOOL_NOT_IN_CATALOG; absent tools or records without component metadata fail with TOOL_NOT_IN_INDEX; differing indexed/locked inputs fail with TOOL_CATALOG_MISMATCH. A downloaded input with the wrong digest fails before rustup starts. Older Rust index records need regeneration, without a schema version change. cargo: helpers still refuse under a catalog; their governance is deferred. Unit tests cover the indexed component map and extra target/component selection. The compiled-CLI installation fixtures require Linux amd64 and check protocol and digest enforcement with a stand-in installer. They do not qualify real rustup, compilation or native platforms. See implementation status for verification results.

After an embedded backend update, oyzu pin --refresh reacquires installation metadata for the already selected versions and configured execution platforms. It preserves version selection; it does not upgrade Rust, install tools, edit oyzu.toml, or reinterpret an old installation receipt as a new backend identity. Use oyzu pin --refresh --dry-run to review the proposed lock without writing it. Refresh requires online metadata acquisition and conflicts with --offline. An incomplete or failed resolution does not publish a replacement lock. Then run oyzu build. Build looks up the exact refreshed recipe in the shared user store and installs it if missing. Historical installation records embedded in a development lock do not override portable resolution records. Existing installations remain intact; reuse requires the exact current recipe identity. The native build retains the installation's verified lease through task execution instead of hashing the payload again to activate it. No invocation re-hashes an already installed payload: tools are validated when installed and trusted afterwards, and this is not a same-user tamper boundary.

Mise-enabled builds now expose oyzu pin --dry-run (optionally --offline). The command discovers the full project's quality-stage requirements, expands platform declarations using the build planner, and prints a concise tool summary with unresolved explanations. Use --json for requirement provenance, available compiler metadata, and detailed diagnostics. A matching version-1 selection retains its exact compiler version and is checked against native constraints. New selections accept an exact stable version or the native stable request in configuration or a native toolchain declaration. Pinning is optional. With no explicit [tools] rust, no rust-toolchain.toml channel and no oyzu.lock, oyzu pin or the first build resolves the requirement stable to the greatest stable release (which must satisfy any Cargo rust-version minimum, otherwise resolution fails) and records it in oyzu.lock. An explicit pin or a toolchain-file channel takes precedence. Offline resolution needs an existing lock, as for any stable request. Verified 2026-10-18 with the compiled CLI: an unpinned tiny Cargo project (rust-version = '1.80', committed Cargo.lock) built natively on Windows, locking Rust 1.99.1 and producing its executable. The experimental resolver supports exact stable Rust selections, resolution of stable to an exact release, and the Rust adapter's supported helper defaults: cargo-nextest 0.9.146 and cargo-llvm-cov 0.9.1 for Linux amd64 execution. Their versioned archives and checksums are the same inputs already declared by the Rust worker recipe. Other helper versions remain unsupported; these metadata records do not establish installed availability. A complete preview includes the exact proposed oyzu.lock text in JSON proposed_files and exits 0. Incomplete resolution exits 2 and proposes no files. oyzu pin revalidates discovery/configuration, then publishes a complete version-1 lock through the recoverable transaction. It does not install tools or change native files or TOML, preserving comments and avoiding duplicate declarations. --offline reuses existing matching version-1 compiler metadata and built-in helper metadata, or reports missing inputs without acquisition. The build handoff supports a pinned Rust compiler; native installation of the complete pinned component selection remains unfinished. Configuration reads, frozen selection and installation lease acquisition reject an unfinished .oyzu-pin-journal.json. Pin recovery checks every destination against its recorded old/new bytes before rolling the entire set forward. Unexpected external changes retain the journal and fail with PIN_EDIT_CONFLICT. This is recoverable publication, not atomic replacement of multiple files. The transaction engine has focused stale-edit/interruption coverage. Pin captures the original lock before metadata acquisition and checks discovery/configuration again before commit.

The decoded TOML schema defines the sole tool lock contract. resolved_environment and resolution record exact plans before installation; environment and tool retain verified installation graph facts. Optional requirements records hold discovery evidence. All sections are validated by one parser. Missing sections mean no records, never permission to execute an unresolved tool. Pinning retains installation records and updates resolution records. Installation retains resolution records. Resolution recipes are not receipts. The private materialization graph uses this same contract, with only installation records. No schema-version dispatch, legacy pin mode, or format migration is supported. Native installation of pinned components remains separate functional work. Version conflicts in ordinary pin output show the two source files and versions, an explanation, and confirmation that no files changed. Generated matrix IDs and content hashes remain in structured evidence rather than the normal message. --json represents a conflict as a schema-versioned object with complete: false and a conflict record, retaining the native field and content digest. The experimental preview treats native Rust toolchain channels as defaults. An explicit tools.rust (or canonical tools."oyzu:rust") selection overrides that channel. Cargo minimum Rust versions remain mandatory compatibility checks. Structured requirements distinguish native-default from compatibility origins. The accepted pinning direction preserves authored TOML and records exact selections in the lock. Ranges and other rolling or dated channels are not yet supported by this experimental resolver.

The mise-enabled build handoff can now read an exact Rust compiler from a version-1 lock and provision its declared components. It checks explicit versions, native defaults and Cargo compatibility using the same compatibility function as pin. The local Linux worker must be rebuilt with this protocol; the controller requires confirmation of the requested component set. Generated archives are hashed after installation. A private materialization graph under .oyzu/tools/resolutions/<resolution-digest>/oyzu.lock binds the resolution ID to those actual archive bytes. This graph uses the existing version-1 receipt and lease verifier; it is not a conversion of the public resolution lock into an installation receipt. Publication follows successful Linux restoration and lease validation. Subsequent captures verify the cached archive through that same path. The two-platform dependency-free fixture has passed a real build from an empty project tool store after pinning, followed by bundle inspection and ELF architecture checks (amd64 and arm64). A subsequent build and inspection also passed using the cached compiler without invoking rustup. Automatic first-build resolution and explicit offline build behavior are described below. Native helper installation is described below; isolated helper materialization is not qualified by that flow. Do not interpret a successful pin as installed-tool evidence.

For a mise-enabled build with no oyzu.lock, preflight now sends the selected captured targets to the same tool planner used by pin. It publishes a complete resolution lock before capturing source, then uses the materialization path above. Authored TOML stays unchanged. Local fast builds select only their required stages; pin still selects all configured applicable gates. Existing locks retain their selections rather than being silently migrated or replaced. This path supports exact Rust versions from configuration or native declarations. Without either, the Rust adapter supplies its supported default, Rust 1.99.1; discovery exposes that default and pin records the exact recipe in the lock. It does not select a compiler from PATH or copy the default into TOML. Native declarations take precedence over this fallback, and explicit TOML selections take precedence over native defaults. A missing-lock affected build is rejected until a full selection establishes the environment. The first run published the lock and installed the selected compiler, but exposed an unconditional coverage probe in Cargo preparation. Preparation now probes nextest and coverage only when the test stage is enabled by the captured configuration. The corrected fast build passed in 289.7 seconds using the cached compiler; bundle inspection and ELF checks confirmed amd64 (machine 62) and arm64 (machine 183). No nextest or coverage probe ran. A dry run on the repository's dependency-free Rust example also resolved the supported default successfully and proposed only oyzu.lock. The frozen compiler acquisition proof is recorded below.

oyzu build --offline requires an existing tool lock and a cached compiler archive. It does not resolve new versions or publish lock changes. The compiler still passes normal archive, receipt and lease verification before execution; an absent installation or archive fails without starting an installer. This first offline path supports standalone Rust projects with dependency-free Cargo locks (including local workspace packages). Registry and Git package replay is not connected and fails before fetching those inputs. Other builders and managed configuration acquisition reject explicit offline mode. Worker images must already be provisioned, as for online builds. These limitations are explicit errors rather than permission to fall back to online acquisition. The missing installation CLI check passed: exit 1, unchanged lock, and no tool store created. Cached build replay passed in 270.25 seconds, with both ELF architectures verified, successful bundle inspection, an unchanged lock and no installer invocation. The latest CLI also passed pin --dry-run --offline against an existing full resolution lock without edits. The repository example (examples/builds/rust-app/project, with a two-platform build declaration) passed plain oyzu build from an empty project tool store and without oyzu.lock, oyzu.toml or a native toolchain declaration. The run selected the adapter default, installed it through embedded mise and produced Linux amd64 and arm64 binaries. Bundle inspection and ELF machine checks passed. The measured run took 648.15 seconds on the available Windows/Docker host; this is functional evidence, not a performance claim. The successful offline replay used this exact example and retained its original Cargo manifests and source bytes.

The current controller stages every locked Rust acquisition input through its broker and checks its SHA-256 digest before launching installation. A private read-only distribution directory is passed to the embedded mise Rust installer through install_rust_from_directory; the Linux installer worker runs with --network=none. Bootstrap HTTP is answered from the same verified inputs. Unlisted requests fail rather than falling back to public acquisition. The existing store still records and verifies the actual generated compiler archive. This uses mise revision 0105e9222972c0e5c6bd89f24aff1550f460de16, which changes the admitted backend identity. Prior backend locks are not silently rewritten or reused. Both controller and worker compiled successfully. A fresh copy of the dependency-free repository Rust example, with no lock or tool store, passed plain oyzu build in 522.51 seconds. Bundle inspection passed and ELF headers confirmed Linux amd64 and arm64 outputs. Source files remained byte-identical. Installer network mode none and the read-only input mount were captured during the run. The first isolated run installed the compiler but failed when rustup attempted an unpinned self-update. The frozen-directory method now disables that update; the bootstrap version remains fixed by the recipe. The corrected run passed; the original failure remains recorded in implementation status. The subsequent oyzu build --offline passed in 254.27 seconds, with successful bundle inspection, both ELF architectures, an unchanged lock and no installer invocation. The final binary also passed pin preview/publication/idempotence and missing-offline-input checks. This completes the bounded dependency-free Rust workflow, not all builder or helper-tool installation coverage.

Pin now publishes platform-specific Rust and helper records as described in the lock reference. Earlier Linux-only pin descriptions above are superseded for metadata resolution. Native installation and worker paths retain their existing qualification limits; this change does not complete portable installation or backend compatibility work.

With a portable oyzu.lock, native preparation combines builder requirements with the effective configuration instead of installing only literal [tools] entries. You do not need to repeat inferred helpers in TOML. Use oyzu pin, then oyzu install to prepare the containing target's full enabled tool selection, or oyzu build --full to install and execute the selected quality stages. Ordinary oyzu build prepares compile requirements only unless configuration requires additional checks. oyzu run test consumes the same pinned test selection but requires it to be installed first. The admitted release archives are cargo:cargo-nextest 0.9.146 and cargo:cargo-llvm-cov 0.9.1. Their short names are also accepted in [tools]. Explicit configuration overrides builder defaults and still must satisfy native compatibility constraints and policy. Other helper versions/backends fail with a named unsupported or stale-pin error; there is no implicit cargo install, source build, or separate mise executable. Archives use the existing broker, published checksum verification, bounded extraction and installation lease contracts. Configured tool routes do not fall back to public downloads on failure. The shared user store contains the installations; project locks remain portable version-1 resolution records. Reusing a compatible installation does not copy it into the project. Windows GNU/LLVM Rust and native MSVC helper executables retain their separate artifact platforms. This does not install MSVC or a Windows SDK. The selected Rust sysroot also binds rustup's RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN so Cargo subcommand proxies in a user Cargo home cannot select a different global Clippy or rustfmt. tools current, which, exec and shell activation recognize the inferred selection for the nearest containing target. Descendant targets do not change a parent shell's tool versions; native builds prepare each target against its own configuration. Existing explicitly provisioned flows without portable pins remain available. Missing pins require oyzu pin; build never silently repins them. Missing installations require online preparation; --offline reuses verified installed payloads and cached archives and cannot acquire missing inputs. Windows native coverage is the first runtime qualification; Linux/macOS and isolated helper installation are separate qualification work. See implementation status for commands and results.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-shell-environment.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. See tool management for shared prerequisites, command conventions and qualification limits.

oyzu env and oyzu env --json inspect available selected installations and report selected executables and effective environment variables. Ordinary values are visible; credential-like fields and detected sensitive values are redacted. See shell activation for provenance and PATH views. Missing tools are omitted without installation; invalid locks, corrupt receipts and enforced denials retain their errors. Explicit project pins and commands with no configured tools do not read unrelated remembered developer selections. Those snapshots are loaded and validated only when an unpinned requirement actually needs installed-selection fallback. An invalid remembered snapshot still fails that fallback; it is never accepted as a usable pin or silently deleted. The environment composition is shared with exec: literal TOML values plus the selected binary directory prepended to inherited PATH. An already leading selected directory is not prepended again. exec --json captures application output in stdout and stderr fields alongside exitCode; default execution passes the streams through. Place Oyzu flags before the child argument separator --. To explicitly print assignments with their actual values, select a shell: # Bash eval "$(oyzu env --shell bash)" node --version For Zsh use --shell zsh. For PowerShell 7 use: oyzu env --shell pwsh | Out-String | Invoke-Expression node --version --shell with --json returns the rendered code in a script field alongside the shell name. Without --json, code remains directly evaluable. See the CLI output contract. Environment patches use the extracted mise diff operations in the internal oyzu-shell library. Bash, Zsh and PowerShell rendering run directly through that library, without initializing a mise backend worker. Windows POSIX path normalization retains the pinned upstream utility. It performs no network or installation. Values remain literal, including quotes, dollar signs and shell metacharacters; they are not interpreted as config code. Shell activation (including env --shell), prompt hooks, shims and oyzu exec require project/local environment and PATH additions to pass folder trust: environment consumers can interpret literal values as executable instructions. Untrusted projects keep their selected tools and skip those additions without prompting. oyzu run, oyzu build, build planning and the build configuration digest always retain those settings. oyzu env shows configured values and provenance, marking project entries skipped until trusted when shell/exec use would withhold them. PowerShell literals escape ASCII apostrophes and all four Unicode single-quote delimiters, including values and frontend/profile/shim paths. Rendering requires UTF-8 environment values. Pass the same --store used for installation when using a shared store. This is a one-time application to the current shell. It does not install prompt hooks, automatically switch on directory changes or restore old values. Use the activation commands below when testing automatic transitions instead. The lookup/rendering lease ends when the command returns; this does not establish an active-shell retention lease. Those lifecycle capabilities remain unfinished.

From an installed project, start a session in Bash or Zsh: eval "$(oyzu activate bash)" # use zsh for Zsh node --version cd ../another-installed-project node --version oyzu deactivate For a shared store, pass --store /absolute/store to activate. Without that option each hook uses the default user-level store. Root/profile options from activation are retained for the session. The PowerShell equivalent is oyzu activate pwsh | Out-String | Invoke-Expression. The original PowerShell activation/switching/deactivation scenario passed on Windows at 83049fa in run 37050580618; native acceptance with the newly added shims remains pending. The internal oyzu-shell library renders Bash, Zsh and PowerShell prompt/directory hooks and deactivation using extracted mise mechanics. Oyzu adapts the generated namespace before inserting the real frontend path through the renderer's literal quoting. The hooks call this same Oyzu binary, never a separate mise executable. A missing command may install its configured provider on invocation, subject to the controls below. The shell retries with the refreshed environment. Prompt/directory hooks use read-only local selection, with no network, installation or project task execution. PowerShell missing-command acquisition requires the command name to appear as a token in the initialized PSReadLine session's latest typed line, matching Mise; noninteractive script lookups do not trigger that hook's installation path. Explicit exec/tasks and already invoked native shims retain their separate invocation controls. Changing directories applies the new project's locked Node and literal TOML environment. Unchanged selection emits no environment changes. Unchanged prompts compare the working directory, relevant environment inputs and source/lock metadata before resolving configuration or reading lock contents. Creation and deletion of sources also invalidate the cached selection, including changes to the user's trusted-project records. Installed executables, payloads and receipts are not watched or hashed: installation verifies them once, and subsequent use trusts the installation. The hook observes each prompt without a time-to-live delay or background service. Old records without freshness data refresh once. Unreadable inputs force resolution. Failed selection still clears the previous environment and reports unavailable. This is prompt freshness, not an integrity cache: metadata checks do not detect all hostile/backdated content edits. exec, shim dispatch, tasks and builds continue obtaining verified leases. oyzu env also retains verified inspection; it can take longer than config show. Neither consumes a prompt cache as execution authority. The embedded mise revision is part of backend identity; after changing it, refresh pins and install through oyzu pin --refresh and oyzu install, never by rewriting receipts. Oyzu records changed variable values and PATH under its native per-user state directory's shell-sessions folder; the environment carries a random token. Unix directories are private (0700), with ownership and ancestor protection checked; linked directories are rejected. Windows uses the user's LocalAppData state directory and rejects reparse points. Session files are atomically replaced. Deactivation removes the record after rendering cleanup; JSON deactivation is a preview and retains the record. Missing or unreadable records produce a warning and hook/marker cleanup, while shims fall back to ordinary configuration options. Values from a lost record cannot be reconstructed: open a new terminal for a clean environment, or activate again to begin a fresh session. On activation, records older than 30 days are reclaimed only when their shell is gone (or the activation was never consumed); records belonging to live shells are retained. Scalars are restored only when they still equal the value Oyzu applied, preserving user edits. An unchanged PATH is restored exactly. On Windows POSIX shells, restoration preserves the saved mount spelling when its ordered native entries match the rolled-back PATH (for example, /bin versus /usr/bin in Git Bash). This spelling restoration never replaces a changed list of paths. Compiled-CLI Git Bash qualification passed as recorded in the extraction audit. Unique owned entries can be removed after user additions or reordering; ambiguous duplicates are retained with a diagnostic. Invalid configuration or denied selection clears the preceding project's delta, sets OYZU_TOOL_STATUS=unavailable and emits a diagnostic once per changed failure. Missing installations alone do not prevent applying a valid environment: existing selected executable directories lead the native shim fallback and inherited PATH. Trusted project PATH prepends precede selected tool directories, matching Mise; controlled build preparation retains tool directories first. The status ready describes a composed environment, not proof that every tool is installed. Use oyzu tools current to inspect availability. A command may install its configured provider when invoked; cd alone never installs or writes a lock. Deactivation removes the session's PATH insertion and restores the previous environment.

Profile editing is explicit; activate alone never edits a file. Choose the profile your shell loads, or use the default: oyzu shell install bash oyzu shell remove bash --rc-file ~/.bashrc Use zsh with your .zshrc, or PowerShell: oyzu shell install pwsh --rc-file $PROFILE oyzu shell remove pwsh --rc-file $PROFILE --rc-file PATH selects a shell startup file; the old --profile-path spelling remains a hidden alias. Global --profile NAME still selects an Oyzu configuration profile and never selects a shell startup file. Without --rc-file, Bash uses ~/.bashrc, Zsh uses $ZDOTDIR/.zshrc or ~/.zshrc, and PowerShell 7 uses its current-user console profile: the Windows Documents known folder followed by PowerShell/Microsoft.PowerShell_profile.ps1, or $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/powershell/Microsoft.PowerShell_profile.ps1 on Unix (fallback ~/.config/powershell/Microsoft.PowerShell_profile.ps1). For another PowerShell host or version, pass --rc-file $PROFILE. Override roots must be absolute. An explicit relative path resolves against -C/the invocation directory. Oyzu creates missing parent directories and files, appends one marked block, and preserves surrounding UTF-8 content and existing permissions. The block invokes the absolute running Oyzu frontend with shell-specific quoting. Keep that frontend available; rerunning installation after moving/upgrading it replaces an intact block. Repeated installation with the same frontend is a no-op. Success explains how to open a new terminal or activate this one, and suggests oyzu which cargo (substitute another installed command) to inspect selection. --json reports changed, shell, profile_path, installed, shims, activation, check and nextStep. The block uses ordinary activation defaults: the shared user tool store and configuration at shell startup. Install the project's locked tools before opening a new shell. It does not embed a project, profile selection, credentials or shared store path. Shell profile editing itself performs no networking or activation. To use an explicit store (oyzu activate <shell> --store PATH) or custom activation options, keep a separately maintained initialization command outside the managed block. oyzu tools list --json reports the effective store; pass the same --store to installation, inspection and activation when overriding the default. Installation/removal refuses modified, incomplete, duplicate or differently owned blocks. Preserve any manual customization elsewhere and restore/reconcile the managed block before retrying. Symlink profiles require the explicit real target; non-UTF-8 profiles require conversion before use. Removal deletes only the intact block, including its inserted separator, preserving surrounding content byte for byte. A newly created profile remains as an empty file after removal. Removing the block affects future loads; run oyzu deactivate to end the current active session. The real acceptance runner installs Node, loads each managed profile in its shell, executes the locked Node through its shim, deactivates, and checks idempotence, edited-block preservation and byte-exact removal: python tooling/test-shell-profile.py --cli PATH_TO_FEATURE_ENABLED_OYZU --shell bash --shell zsh Use --shell pwsh for PowerShell. The runner requires public Node access for its fresh installation and never edits the user's actual shell profile. Linux Bash and Zsh passed this complete flow on 2026-10-02. Native macOS and PowerShell profile acceptance remain pending in the three-host CI workflow.
documents.s: Install activation in a shell profile

documents.t: Install and activation provision launchers for every command recorded by installed tools, including pnpm, kubectl, Helm and interpreter companion commands. Windows requires oyzu-shim.exe beside oyzu.exe; build/install both binaries. Its upstream-derived entry point calls the shared Oyzu execution library directly, preserving native arguments, exit status, invocation selection and installation leases without starting another oyzu process. The launcher is consequently larger than the earlier forwarding-only image. Windows defaults to one native image per release per shim directory, shared through internal hardlinks (copies when unavailable). Unix uses symbolic links to Oyzu. Windows also supports the configured publication modes below. Shims live in STORE/shims/native/FRONTEND_PATH_ID/shared or .../cwd, shared by shell sessions. An adjacent pointer records the owning frontend; per-command manifests record the command, publication release and store mode. These are version-1 local records, not lock identities. Rebuilding at the same frontend path reuses the location. Run install or activate to refresh launchers. Missing companion executables fail explicitly. The main package currently builds both Cargo binaries on every platform; Unix uses links and does not need the companion to dispatch tools. Dispatch validates the manifest/name and Unix link target, without reading or hashing launcher contents. Publication hashes its source image once, serializes writers, atomically replaces changed metadata and leaves identical records alone. On Windows, publication retries transient access/sharing failures for up to one second while readers finish. Readers continue to see complete records; publication never removes the old metadata first. A persistent failure is still reported. On Windows an executing launcher is renamed aside before replacement; a later refresh reclaims retired images once processes release them. Install also refreshes existing activation launchers, so newly installed commands become available in an already activated shell. A shim resolves the current directory, configuration and lock, and retains verified installation leases. --store chooses a fixed store; otherwise the shared user store is selected. Active root/profile/toolset options come from the session. Outside a session, default configuration selection applies. Invocation-time acquisition uses the controls below and the existing verified installer. After selecting a verified installed tool, execution clears the private frontend recursion markers from that native child's environment. A tool may therefore invoke the same shim again (for example, a Node script launching another managed Node process), with fresh invocation selection and the nested command's exit status preserved. The Windows launcher's checks still reject an actual dispatch loop before tool selection. Resolved system and explicit-path children also have private dispatch markers removed, so nested commands can enter their own shim normally. Prompt hooks do not provision shims. Old full-image shim/session directories are not automatically deleted, since existing shell references must be preserved; reactivate old shells and clean only identified unused or byte-identical data. The generated oyzu shell function evaluates deactivation output. Invoking the absolute binary with deactivate only prints it. No profile file is modified. Leading global flags such as oyzu -q deactivate are supported. Options taking values retain their original order; lifecycle commands use the frontend that activated the session even when another oyzu is on PATH. As with the bare CLI, --log-level and -q are incompatible: a rejected invocation leaves the session active. Use oyzu --log-level error -C /project deactivate or oyzu -q deactivate. --json deactivation is a preview: the wrapper prints the JSON without evaluating it and the active session record remains available. Run oyzu deactivate to apply the restoration and end the session. Help and failed commands are never evaluated. Environment-only and nested-shell activation are described in the shell activation reference. Active-shell installation retention and fully reversible PATH alignment remain unfinished. Profile installation/removal is explicit as described above. This is a controlled development integration. The real Linux Bash/Zsh acceptance passed with networking disabled: activation, automatic cd switching between Node 22.15.0 and 22.14.0, unchanged-hook output, missing-selection cleanup, user-edited scalar preservation and deactivation. The subsequent native-shim replay also passed on Linux Bash/Zsh, including literal arguments and exit status. A direct offline probe put a real Node later on PATH and confirmed the former restrictive missing-selection behavior. That historical contract is superseded by issue #424; see the current invocation controls below. Native macOS and Windows native shim acceptance passed at e335d70 in CI run 37051685318, including their native activation/switching flows. Run it against the retained two-project workspace: python tooling/test-tool-activation.py --cli PATH_TO_FEATURE_ENABLED_OYZU --workspace PATH --shell bash --shell zsh Linux Bash and Zsh application passed with networking disabled on 2026-10-02: the shell launched the same Node executable as exec, literal metacharacters were preserved, inspection values were redacted and the lock was unchanged. PowerShell environment application passed on Windows at 3eefcc2 in CI run 37049209850; macOS Bash/Zsh environment application passed at e335d70 in run 37051685318. Reproduce against a retained acceptance workspace with Python 3.11+: python tooling/test-tool-environment.py --cli PATH_TO_FEATURE_ENABLED_OYZU --workspace PATH --shell bash --shell zsh Use --shell pwsh to require the real PowerShell interpreter. Requested shells must be installed; the runner does not skip a missing interpreter. Tool-only directories do not require a native build manifest to select already pinned tools. Portable-lock lookup uses optional native discovery: present project manifests and explicit build declarations are still validated. Build and task commands retain their normal project-discovery requirements. Qualification of this extraction fix is tracked in the audit.

Non-interactive processes such as IDEs, CI jobs and scheduled tasks never run a prompt hook. For them, put the store's shims folder on PATH. It holds one launcher for each command of each installed tool, and each launcher resolves the project it runs in on every call, exactly as activation's shims do: oyzu reshim # refresh launchers and print the fixed folder eval "$(oyzu activate bash --shims)" # put it first on PATH in this shell oyzu shell install bash --shims --rc-file ~/.bash_profile oyzu shell install zsh --shims --rc-file ~/.zprofile The folder is STORE/shims/bin. The PATH line removes any copy of the folder already on PATH and puts it first, so an unmanaged copy of a tool earlier on PATH cannot win, and an empty PATH gains no empty (current-directory) entry. A store whose path contains the PATH separator (; on Windows, : elsewhere) is refused with SHIMS_PATH_INVALID, because on PATH it would split into other entries. Windows Bash/Zsh lines use the active MSYS/Cygwin mount mapping; when generated from a native terminal they use Git Bash drive spelling such as /c/Users/.... The rendered path is checked against : as well, so a Windows drive cannot create a relative C entry. Generate Cygwin profiles inside Cygwin to retain its mount table. Each launcher keeps its tool's command name exactly, .exe included. oyzu install keeps it current when it exists and belongs to the same Oyzu frontend; oyzu reshim refreshes it and makes the running frontend its owner. A launcher without a usable selected command searches eligible non-shim PATH entries by default; the strict setting below disables that fallback. activate --shims only emits PATH code: it does not inspect installations or republish metadata at shell startup. Run oyzu reshim once before using that mode and after moving/upgrading the frontend. shell install --shims performs that initial refresh when it writes the profile. On Windows, put the folder on your user PATH so every new process finds it: $shims = (oyzu reshim --json | ConvertFrom-Json).directory [Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('Path', "$shims;" + [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('Path', 'User'), 'User') oyzu-shim.exe must sit beside oyzu.exe; copy both when installing a build. oyzu reshim also refreshes existing shims/native/FRONTEND_PATH_ID/cwd and shared activation launchers owned by the running frontend. Use it after updating both Windows binaries so an already activated shell can use the new launcher. It does not edit startup files or change the parent shell's PATH. --store PATH selects a store; otherwise the normal store selection applies. --json reports the fixed folder as directory and the recorded installed command names as commands. Refresh uses local installation records without acquiring tools; missing Windows launcher templates and publication failures return an error. The shim refresh command is top-level reshim; the former shell shims spelling is removed without an alias. shell contains profile install and remove only.

Activation adds the Oyzu executable's directory if it is absent from PATH, matching Mise when activation is called by absolute path. That directory remains after deactivation; project tool directories and environment changes are restored. Installation records a validated selection snapshot in the store's developer-selections directory. Developer shell/exec/task preparation and env/which inspection can reuse matching installed versions in a project without a compatible pin, through the same provider selector and verified receipt lease. This does not write a project lock. An existing compatible pin always wins; a missing pinned payload cannot be replaced with another stored version. Equivalent installed records from different selectors can be reused when their host artifacts, layout, verification and dependency facts agree; differing recipes remain ambiguous and require an explicit pin. Controlled builds continue through their admitted locked preparation. Older stores can record these reusable facts by running an explicit oyzu install; directory/prompt refresh does not upgrade store metadata or acquire tools. Standalone developer commands follow the pinned Mise v2026.10.10 reference. Configure the controls through Oyzu's typed cascade, including profiles and administrative constraints: [settings] auto_install = true offline = false exec_auto_install = true not_found_auto_install = true not_found_auto_install_registry = false not_found_system_fallback = true auto_install_disable_tools = [] windows_executable_extensions = ["exe", "bat", "cmd", "com", "ps1", "vbs"] windows_shim_mode = "exe" [settings.task] run_auto_install = true The shown values are defaults. auto_install = false disables the subordinate exec, missing-command and task mechanisms. exec_auto_install prepares the configured exec environment; not_found_auto_install prepares the provider of an invoked shim or a command the shell could not find. The disabled-tool list accepts short or canonical Oyzu tool IDs and leaves explicit oyzu install available. Direct tasks use task.run_auto_install; controlled build preflight continues requiring its complete locked selection regardless of developer toggles. Registry installation stays off by default. When enabled, a shell missing-command hook requires a unique advertised provider and uses the existing global declaration transaction to install and record it. Ambiguous names are skipped. Project declarations override the resulting global selector through the shared configuration cascade, including when the project uses a different admitted alias. Like Mise, this operation prefers the highest compatible installed version and retains latest as the global selector. Unlike Mise's extra stdout config status line, Oyzu keeps status/progress on stderr and leaves child stdout unchanged. The maintainer approved this narrow difference on 2026-10-14 so command substitution and machine consumers do not need to filter prose from native output. An already intercepted stale shim does not invoke registry discovery, matching the pinned Mise behavior; configured-provider installation remains available through either entry point. Registry support is limited to Oyzu's admitted provider catalog; broader upstream backends remain unqualified rather than implicitly authorizing another installer. not_found_system_fallback controls shim fallback, not ordinary oyzu exec PATH lookup. To make unresolved shims fail, set it and not_found_auto_install to false. Lookup skips Oyzu shim farms and retains PATH order. A failed admitted installation, invalid lock/receipt, denied tool or unavailable managed integration is an error; it is not silently converted into ambient execution. oyzu exec --offline or settings.offline = true can use admitted cached bytes but cannot download missing inputs. Node supplies bundled node, npm and npx; a configured separate npm owns npm and npx ahead of that bundle. Companion scripts use the selected Node interpreter. Separate npm installations include digest-bound native shell companions for ordinary activation. Windows developer PATH lookup uses native PATHEXT order, matching the pinned Mise implementation's which lookup even when windows_executable_extensions lists a different order. Receipt-recorded managed commands retain their exact executable/interpreter descriptions. PowerShell/VBScript use their native interpreters; Rust's native process API owns batch argument encoding. Bare bash/sh on Windows select native Git for Windows shells. WindowsApps aliases on inherited PATH are excluded even when the invocation uses a disposable HOME/AppData directory, keeping selected Windows tools available to that shell. Native Windows qualification found that Mise v2026.10.10 does not resolve an unmanaged bare .ps1 command. The maintainer approved Oyzu's native PowerShell execution as an explicit exception; see the qualification record below. windows_shim_mode selects publication on Windows. exe is the default native launcher; hardlink links each command to the frontend and requires a compatible filesystem on the same volume; symlink links to the frontend and requires Windows symlink permission (typically Developer Mode); file publishes CMD and Git Bash forwarders. File forwarders call the private native shim entry point, which owns selection and execution, and recover native arguments from a dedicated CMD /c invocation. Interactive CMD and batch call retain their shell argument semantics. PowerShell's default Windows argument-passing mode uses legacy rendering for CMD files, which can change empty arguments and embedded quotes before dispatch. Direct CMD file forwarding applies delayed expansion, which changes caret and exclamation characters, matching the pinned Mise file-mode oracle. The differential runner also exercises Standard argument passing explicitly. No mode starts the public oyzu exec command. Other hosts retain their native symlink publication. The setting uses the regular configuration/profile cascade; rerun oyzu reshim --store PATH to replace the publication mode in the fixed farm and existing activation farms owned by this frontend. Publication reports unavailable link permissions/filesystems without silently choosing a different mode. Native qualification is recorded in the linked report. An invocation may create a missing configured lock or materialize a newer admitted companion layout at the same exact selected version. It never upgrades a compatible pin merely to run a command. Prompt/directory refresh, env, which, and build --plan never acquire tools. which remains selected-receipt inspection; a shell finding a shim does not prove that the selected tool is installed. A build prepares, per selected target, the tools its builder detects for the selected stages plus the tools pinned in that target's folder oyzu.toml chain (a root pin reaches every target; a pin in docs-site/ reaches only targets at or below it). Targets sharing a folder share its pins. Pins elsewhere are not prepared, so oyzu build cli does not download a tool only docs uses; oyzu exec, shells and oyzu install still provide every pinned tool. Host prerequisites are checked, never installed. Rationale and acceptance: which tools a build gets. No system fallback is accepted as a locked build tool or as a way around an enforced acquisition/management denial. Approved npm sessions require the selected Node-backed npm; npx uses that same routing inspection rather than bypassing it. Native execution retains binary streams and OS-native arguments. Unix execution forwards interrupts to the child group, retains terminal foreground ownership, and preserves signal termination; captured JSON reports its numeric shell status. Windows execution uses the existing suspended job owner. See parity qualification for actual commands, measured cases and remaining native-host requirements. Full issue completion requires Windows/macOS evidence and the remaining differential acceptance matrix.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-store-inspection.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. See tool lock inspection for the lock entry point. Archive providers and indexed Rust use this same store. Linux ARM64 GNU has its own platform entries, so locks created on any supported host can carry it. Acquisition verifies indexed/publisher digests before publication; installed payloads are then trusted. Catalog/index metadata may refuse an unapproved or withdrawn release on installation/reuse without rehashing installed files. Explicit tree inspection below remains an observation requested by the caller, not an automatic integrity check. ARM64 native installation is unqualified.

oyzu tools inspect-tree /absolute/path/to/payload This reads an existing directory and emits its sorted manifest, content byte count, domain-separated tree digest and canonical manifest blob digest. It never executes payload files, follows payload symlinks, writes a receipt or modifies the tree. As with lock inspection, output is JSON, success exits 0 and errors exit 2. Relative paths are based on -C, --root or the current directory. Use a physical path without symlink/reparse-point ancestors; redirected roots are rejected rather than silently resolved. Parent .. components are rejected. File records include content digest/size and Unix executable bits. Directory entries and relative symlink targets are included. Windows executable bits are zero because Windows does not provide Unix mode bits. Timestamps, owner IDs, ACLs and host inode/file IDs do not enter the portable manifest. The scanner checks hardlink identities locally and rejects links to files outside the tree; internal hardlinks produce explicit file records for each path. The reader anchors Unix child access to directory descriptors with no-follow opens. Windows holds all ancestor directories without delete sharing and rejects reparse points when opening regular files/directories. Link chains are resolved against the manifest component by component: escaping, cyclic, dangling or non-directory chains fail. Portable member names reject Windows devices, ADS, trailing-dot/space aliases, controls and case collisions on every host. Root directory names may be host-native; payload member names must be portable UTF-8. Limits are 200,000 entries, 8 GiB of file content, 1 GiB per file, path depth 64, 64 symlink expansions, 16 KiB link targets and a 32 MiB aggregate path/target budget. Hashing streams through a 64 KiB buffer. Special files fail before reads; observable file size, identity, link-count or executable-mode changes during verification also fail. Limits cannot be raised by project input. validation: "payload-observation-only" does not claim an atomic snapshot against a malicious same-user writer. The scanner reads all bytes and uses no mtime-only cache, but a trusted receipt comparison, healthy monitor or private managed materialization is still required at the selection/execution boundary. Those admitted-selection and private managed-execution operations remain unfinished.

The Rust library's tools::materialize_archive accepts an archive source, an empty operation-owned staging directory, the expected SHA-256 and exact byte size, and whether the archive is gzip compressed. This is a store implementation boundary, not a CLI install command or a stable external plugin interface. It does not acquire bytes, authorize a backend, execute anything, write a receipt or publish an installation. Failed staging must be discarded by the caller. Source and staging paths must have physical, non-symlink ancestors. The source path must therefore use the physical temporary directory on systems where a temporary-directory ancestor is an alias (for example macOS /var). The source must be a regular file; no-follow opens reject symlinks and special files before reads. The source is copied through a bounded buffer into a private unnamed file while checking its locked identity. Extraction reads that verified file, never a reopened source path. Unix writes use descriptor-relative no-follow operations; Windows holds ancestor directories against replacement and creates new files without following reparse points. Existing staging content is rejected. The tar implementation accepts regular files, directories, bounded GNU long-name/link extensions and local PAX path/linkpath records in tar or gzip-compressed tar. The PAX names use the same containment/conflict validation as ordinary names; this supports non-ASCII filenames in official Go archives. Other PAX fields and global PAX records remain unsupported. Symlinks are delayed until all file writes finish, then checked against the complete payload graph. Windows symlink materialization, hardlinks, sparse entries, ZIP and other formats remain unsupported and fail; backend admission must account for these limits. Ownership, set-ID and archive directory permissions are not imported: directories are private and traversable, files are private with Unix executable bits retained. A reviewed layout plan is still required for final permissions. Bounds include 200,000 raw and expanded entries, 8 GiB input/expanded bytes, 1 GiB per file, depth 64, 16 KiB GNU/PAX extension bodies and a 200:1 gzip expansion ratio. The decoder is drained after tar's end marker so gzip trailers and trailing expanded data are checked. Paths reject traversal, absolute names, case aliases, Windows devices/ADS and conflicting parent types. The returned tree observation still does not attest policy, receipt authenticity or an atomic snapshot against a malicious same-user writer. This is partial TM-04/MISE-13 evidence, not a complete installation or backend acceptance result.

The Rust library's tools::verify_installation_selection reads a version-1 lock, an exact scope/profile/platform, a tool store root and a caller-trusted installer release digest. It requires installs/<installation-key-hex>/receipt.json and payload/ for every tool in the selected closure. It returns the selection digest only after all records and payloads match. It does not download, repair, execute, publish or acquire leases, and is not an execution authorization API. Receipts use the exact fields specified by OEP-0003, with format 1 and explicit null package_closure_digest when absent. Unknown fields and duplicate JSON keys fail. Every locked field, publisher-verification record, sorted direct dependency installation-key list and installer release identity must match. Every payload is rehashed through no-follow handles; no mtime cache or upstream installed-version status can satisfy this operation. The current composition budget is one million tree entries and 32 GiB of payload content across the selection, with the existing per-tree limits also applied. Receipt JSON is capped at 2 MiB and uses the existing strict JSON depth/entry limits. Larger tuples require reviewed limits rather than project-controlled overrides. The initial resolved launch records are closed tagged objects: Native: kind: "native", payload_relative_path, ordered prefix_args. Interpreter: kind: "interpreter", payload_relative_path, interpreter, ordered prefix_args. Installation path: installation_key, relative_path. Argument: kind: "literal" with value, or kind: "path" with an installation path. Environment value: kind: "literal" with value, or kind: "paths" with ordered installation paths. Entrypoints must resolve to existing files; interpreters must also be executable on Unix targets. Directory environment references and file/directory arguments may use the exact current or direct-dependency installation only. . denotes that installation's payload root for directory references. Symlinks resolve through the already-verified manifest, not through unchecked filesystem opens. Command/environment case collisions, invalid environment names, NUL literals, excessive arguments and literal PATH replacement fail. Literal arguments remain data; no shell is invoked. The draft format-1 receipt schema defines the closed JSON shape, tagged launch/environment records, required nullable closure field and structural bounds. Validate it offline with python tooling/check-tool-contracts.py after installing the pinned tooling/design-requirements.txt in a validation environment. The same command checks layout records. It uses only local schema references and changes no store content. The shared receipt fixture is synthetic; it is rebound to real fixture payload hashes by the Rust receipt tests, never executed as an installed tool. Both validators reject the shared malformed-record corpus. JSON Schema measures character lengths, whereas runtime applies UTF-8 byte limits and additionally checks portable paths, case collisions, sorted dependencies, exact lock identity, payload hashes, file types and executable permissions. Schema success alone does not establish receipt validity or authority. This verifies receipt/content binding, not receipt authenticity or compatibility with an admitted layout plan. A caller must separately check backend/layout admission, verification evidence, policy, leases and current authority before using the data. A self-consistent altered receipt and tree is not an authorized installation. The initial publication/OS-lease operation is described below; admission, lifecycle integration and recovery remain separate unfinished work.

tools::lease_installation_selection accepts the same exact selection and installer identity plus optional staging. The caller must provision trusted, private, physical store/staging roots and complete policy and backend/layout admission first. The library does not choose an application state root, grant authorization or turn arbitrary supplied receipts into approved installations. Staging uses installs/<installation-key-hex>/{receipt.json,payload/}. Extra root entries, redirected objects and hardlinked receipts fail. Installed tools are validated when installed and trusted afterwards; tamper-proofing them is not a goal (see the decision). Acquiring a lease on an installation that is already committed checks only its directory shape and that its receipt matches the lock, installer release and dependencies; it does not hash the payload or check entrypoints against it. A staging installation about to be published is fully inspected against its receipt first, so extraction and layout problems are caught at install time. A tool damaged or edited afterwards fails when it runs. The explicit tools::verify_installation_selection operation described above still rehashes every payload on request; no command calls it automatically. The lease retains the receipt snapshot verified during acquisition. Call lease.command("node") to obtain borrowed LeasedToolCommand metadata from that exact selection: selection/tool/installation identities, tool ID, version, platform and a typed ToolLaunch. Native launches retain a payload-relative file and ordered prefix arguments. Interpreter launches additionally retain an explicit interpreter installation/path. ToolArgument distinguishes literal UTF-8 arguments (including empty strings) from typed installation-relative paths; no quoting, shell parsing or wrapper inference occurs. Lookup searches the entire selected closure. When several receipts supply the requested command, the one whose tool is named for it (oyzu:npm for npm) wins; otherwise lookup fails TOOL_COMMAND_AMBIGUOUS. Unknown commands fail TOOL_COMMAND_MISSING; path-like or invalid names fail TOOL_COMMAND_INVALID. It never searches ambient PATH or adds/removes .exe. Windows-target lookup uses the receipt validator's uppercase command comparison; Unix targets use exact spelling. A syntactically supported foreign target can be inspected this way, but the metadata does not imply it can run on the current host. The result borrows the lease and contains symbolic paths, not executable host paths or execution authority. Lookup does not reopen receipts, rehash payloads, run tools, contact a service or observe later edits. A new lease acquisition rechecks current receipts only; a retained lease is not a change monitor or protection against same-user mutation. Future launch consumers must separately enforce current authorization/content validity, resolve paths within leased payloads and supervise the child tree. No which/exec command is enabled by this library API. Mutation locks live permanently under locks/<key-hex> and are acquired in lexical order. All selected existing/candidate receipts and payloads are checked before any new member is published. Regular files and receipts are flushed once at this final boundary, rather than also during extraction/layout staging; Unix also syncs directories. Linux uses renameat2(RENAME_NOREPLACE), macOS uses renameatx_np(RENAME_EXCL), and Windows uses a write-through MoveFileExW without replacement or cross-volume copying. Raw Windows publication uses extended-length paths, including UNC paths, so a deep custom store is not limited by MAX_PATH. Failure never deletes an existing install. Windows directory fsync is unavailable; missing/damaged state after a crash must still fail subsequent verification. macOS execution of this new native path remains pending qualification. Publication is atomic per installation, not across the whole closure. An error after an earlier member committed may leave valid unreferenced entries; the source lock is never edited. Handled install failures remove their owned staging; interrupted stages are reclaimed as described below. Existing valid entries are reused, while corrupt installations fail without automatic replacement, quarantine or public download fallback. Publication takes shared OS lease locks under locks/<key-hex>.lease before mutation locks are released. Read-only selection instead takes shared leases directly and validates its receipt snapshot while they are held. It does not acquire exclusive mutation locks or write/fsync a diagnostic journal. The returned InstallationLease must remain alive until the whole consumer action ends. Both lock kinds use a bounded 30-second contention deadline. Lock files are never removed/replaced during ordinary operation. InstallationLease::selection_digest() borrows the identity from the verified receipt snapshot used for command lookup and lease journaling. There is no separately mutable digest field. Experimental Rust callers must replace lease.selection_digest with lease.selection_digest(); lock, receipt, journal and CLI formats are unchanged. This identity describes the acquired snapshot, not current policy authorization or protection against later same-user edits. An installed-environment lookup scans and parses installation receipts once per invocation, indexing them by tool identity and platform for all selected tools. It reads the project lock from the same frozen capture as configuration and shares its validated representation through selection and materialization. Projection validates the in-memory graph without TOML serialization round trips. These caches do not hash installed payloads and do not replace final receipt validation under the selected installations' leases. Unix lock initialization first attempts exclusive no-follow creation. If the entry already exists, it opens that same name without creation or truncation, then requires a regular single-link inode. This preserves permanent lock identity under concurrent initialization. Recovery's existing-only opens never create missing lock evidence. Prune must acquire mutation first, then try an exclusive lease; this protocol has not yet been connected to a prune command. Process exit releases kernel locks. Before returning a publication lease, the store atomically publishes a flushed format-1 leases/<lease-id>.json record while holding its mutation and shared lease locks. The closed writer records format, lease_id, owner_pid, created_unix_nanos (decimal string), selection_digest and sorted unique installation_keys.
