InstallationLease::lease_id() exposes the diagnostic ID; read-only leases have an in-memory ID with no durable record. IDs use PID, timestamp and a process-local counter, with exclusive creation and no-replace publication; they are not secrets or authorization tokens. Records contain no workspace paths, environment values or credentials. Ordinary lease destruction removes its own record before explicitly unlocking its journal guard and installation leases. Explicit unlock prevents a transient fork-inherited descriptor from extending the completed supervisor lifetime; closing the handles remains the fallback if unlock fails. Callers must still retain the lease until the entire supervised child tree ends. Cleanup errors conservatively leave a stale record; destruction cannot report them to the caller. Forced termination can also leave a final record, and a crash during writing can leave a .pending file. Neither PID/timestamp nor a record's presence establishes liveness: recovery must use OS locks and the relevant reference/owner checks, never PID alone. Each new lease holds an exclusive locks/lease-<lease-id> journal guard until destruction, including empty records. These unique guard files are removed on normal destruction after closing the handle. Permanent installation mutation/lease lock files are never removed. A journal creation/publication failure rejects selection and releases locks; already committed installations remain valid but unreferenced. Unknown or redirected lease directories fail without following links or replacing content. The parent and file flush behavior has the same platform limits as publication. tools::recover_tool_leases(store, dry_run) reaps stale process-lease records, unfinished records protected by an idle canonical guard, and orphan guard files. Install staging creation invokes this maintenance operation too; no CLI prune command is enabled. The root must be a trusted physical store. It opens existing directories and lock files without creating missing lock evidence. It requires a canonical record ID, matching closed format-1 data, valid digests, sorted unique keys and a regular single-link record. It then tries the journal guard, sorted mutation locks and exclusive installation leases without waiting. Busy locks retain the record. Older records lacking a guard, unknown names, malformed data, redirected files and unverified entries remain for manual review. Only unique journal guard files are removed; permanent installation locks remain. No PID polling or installation deletion occurs. This is a cooperative store contract, not protection against same-user malicious writers. The returned counts are stale, removed, active_or_busy and unverified_or_failed, plus dry_run. Dry-run performs the same transient lock checks but removes nothing. More than 4,096 directory entries fails before processing; record reads are capped at 512 KiB each and 32 MiB aggregate, with an extra byte probe for overflow. Unverified or failed records increment the last counter without exposing record text. The sweep is not one transaction: an I/O failure may follow earlier removals, and a failed directory sync leaves durability uncertain even if unlink succeeded. Reinspect and retry after correcting storage errors; never infer an active process solely from that counter or a leftover file. Recovery attempts to explicitly unlock each transient journal, mutation and installation lock before closing it on every return path, including an invalid record or a busy later lock. When unlock succeeds, a duplicate descriptor inherited by another process cannot extend that recovery attempt's lock lifetime; closing remains the fallback if unlock fails. This does not make an unverified record safe to delete. This is a cooperative-store foundation. Persistent shell-session references, operation owner/start-time journals, workspace reference tracking, prune, shell-session retention and supervised child-tree lifetime integration remain outstanding. A lease alone neither prevents same-user file tampering nor kills descendants when a supervisor dies. The complete MISE-05 fault-injection and power-loss matrix is not yet satisfied.

tools::cache_tool_blob(store, source, digest, size) takes a caller-authorized reader and exact SHA-256 identity. The existing store root must be private, physical and trusted. Blobs are stored under blobs/sha256/<digest-hex>; permanent locks/blob-<digest-hex> files serialize publishers with a 30-second contention deadline. A cache hit is fully rehashed into a private temporary snapshot and never reads the acquisition source. Under the same blob mutation lock, a corrupt archive is moved to quarantine/ and treated as a cache miss. Online installation can acquire fresh verified bytes; offline installation names the missing digest/path and requires an online retry. Externally hardlinked cache entries still fail without replacement or reacquisition. For portable recipes that pin a digest without a size, installation uses the verified cached blob's on-disk size before considering a download. This lookup does not grant catalog admission; the installer checks admission before staging. On a miss, the stream is copied and hashed using a 64 KiB buffer, with a maximum size of 8 GiB. At most the expected size plus one byte is consumed; truncation, excess, wrong digest and reader failure publish nothing. Interrupted reads retry. The caller must implement transport timeouts and cancellation: an arbitrary blocking Read cannot be interrupted by the store. The store neither chooses a source nor performs HTTP, credentials, signature verification or policy decisions. The install, artifact-set replay and locked build-archive download paths stream HTTP bodies to temporary files before digest verification and cache publication; small metadata responses remain buffered. This bounds archive download memory independently of archive size while retaining transport byte/deadline limits. Only fully verified bytes are copied to an exclusively created temporary under staging/, flushed and atomically moved without replacement to the blob path. The same native publication primitives and durability limitations described above apply. A handled publication error removes only this operation's temporary file; a destination collision is never overwritten. Process death before rename may leave unselected staging. Install and blob staging now use owned install-* directories under staging/, protected for their complete lifetime by a shared locks/staging OS lease. New staging creation first attempts an exclusive lease: only when no writer is active does it recursively reclaim abandoned install-* entries through no-follow directory operations. Busy staging is preserved. Untracked staging from older binaries (.tmp* and top-level blob-*) remains for manual review because it has no liveness evidence. Quarantined archives are also retained for inspection. Temporary names are collision-resistant identifiers, not credentials. The returned VerifiedBlob exposes read/seek access and digest/size, with no write or raw-handle API. Its bytes are an independent private snapshot: subsequent cache mutation does not change the returned content. tools::materialize_tool_blob consumes that snapshot into an empty staging payload without reopening the cache. It applies the same tar/gzip limits and graph checks as materialize_archive, which now uses the shared snapshot verifier. Extraction and final observation retain the same native directory handle. This proves byte identity and safe materialization only; backend/layout admission, publisher verification, receipts and execution authority remain separate requirements.
documents.s: Verified blob cache and extraction handoff

documents.t: tools::stage_tool_candidate consumes a VerifiedBlob, bounded format-1 layout JSON and ToolCandidateRequest. The request identifies the exact lock selection, tool key, trusted installer identity, empty operation-owned candidate directory and an admitted layout digest obtained from compiled release data. Project input must never supply the admission digest. There is no production descriptor registry or automatic backend admission yet; this library operation cannot grant them. Layout identity is domain oyzu.archive-layout.v1 over the complete canonical plan. It must match both the supplied admission digest and locked distribution. Backend digest, target platform, single input blob digest and size must also match; package-closure distributions are not admitted by this archive-only finalizer. Unknown/duplicate JSON fields, omitted nullable fields and unsupported formats fail. The initial JSON Schema records the closed field names. Rust adds portable path, byte, graph, identity and content checks that JSON Schema cannot establish. Currently supported plans use tar, tar.gz, the ZIP subset described below, or raw single-file artifacts. Archives allow an optional strip_prefix and, for tar archives, optional exclude_paths; raw plans require null. All require payload_subtree: ".". Other archive kinds and subtree projection fail explicitly. On Unix, executable_paths may contain at most 4096 sorted, unique portable payload-relative file paths. Each must resolve through ordinary directories to a regular file with one hardlink; symlinks are rejected at every component. The finalizer sets exactly private mode 0700 through the opened handle, and recomputes the payload tree before authoring the receipt. It never executes the file. Windows requires an empty list because Unix permissions are not a Windows launch contract. A transform failure leaves uncommitted staging without a receipt; discard that staging and retry in a new empty directory. Entries outside the strip prefix are rejected, including a prefix ancestor that is not an ordinary empty directory. Strip-prefix removal does not rewrite symlink targets; the final contained link graph must remain valid. Required paths are a sorted unique list of exact payload paths and file, directory or symlink types. extraction_bounds has positive integer max_entries, max_bytes, max_file_bytes, max_depth and max_expansion_ratio fields. Entry, byte and depth ceilings remain fixed. The default expansion ratio stays 200:1; an explicitly admitted layout can request up to the hard ceiling of 1024:1, as allowed by the OEP's descriptor-specific bounds. This ratio is part of the hashed layout identity, not a project option or a value inferred from an archive. Production descriptors need review before admitting larger bounds. Existing default-200 plans are unchanged; older binaries reject layouts above their supported ceiling. max_bytes caps both total payload bytes and the expanded archive stream (including archive metadata). All runtime fixtures exercising smaller bounds must still fail before a receipt is written. The schema permits the broader proposed archive vocabulary; schema validity does not mean a tuple is currently implemented or admitted. Entrypoint templates have kind, payload_relative_path, explicit nullable interpreter_tool_key / interpreter_relative_path, and ordered prefix_args. Native entrypoints require null interpreter fields. Interpreter entrypoints use self or an exact direct dependency tool key, avoiding a circular self identity. Path arguments and environment path lists use owner (self or an exact direct dependency tool key) plus relative_path. Typed literal strings are never evaluated. Resolution substitutes installation keys, never absolute paths. Names, collisions, literals, declared dependency references, own payload path types and own executable permissions are checked before receipt creation. Success leaves only payload/ and canonical receipt.json in the candidate, and returns its installation key. It never edits oyzu.lock, publishes, performs network operations or invokes tool code. Whole-selection publication then checks all dependency references, receipts and current payload bytes before committing. Failure can leave an incomplete candidate; callers must not adopt it. Receipt creation does not itself verify publisher signatures or attestations: callers must establish that evidence before invoking this boundary. Recovery, production worker wiring, compiled descriptors and native backend parity are still required.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-tailscale-installation.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Indexed installation and pinning use the organization catalog contract. A matching verified index record is preferred without a catalog; with one, only approved indexed releases install. The provider evidence command uses the same metadata adapter as installation. Linux ARM64 GNU joins the native host/lock matrix (Tailscale remains Linux-only); macOS amd64 and musl are excluded. See implementation status for automated verification. Live publisher evidence and native ARM64 qualification remain pending. Oyzu can pin and install tailscale and tailscaled on Linux, so a project or CI job that joins a tailnet needs no host-installed copy. See tool management for shared prerequisites. Oyzu installs only the two binaries; it does not start the daemon, authenticate, or grant any network capability. tailscaled normally needs root or a TUN device, or its userspace-networking mode, which is the caller's decision.

[tools] tailscale = "1.78.1" # exact release # tailscale = "latest" # the stable track's newest tarball version oyzu install tailscale@1.78.1 # declares, locks, installs on Linux oyzu exec -- tailscale version oyzu exec -- tailscaled --version

Platform Result linux/amd64 Installed from the publisher's static tarball. linux/arm64/gnu Admitted from the publisher's arm64 tarball; native qualification pending. macOS No artifact: the publisher ships a GUI app bundle and a .pkg, not a command-line payload. Windows No artifact: the publisher ships .exe and .msi installers, not a command-line payload. A platform with no artifact is reported as unavailable (NoPlatformArtifact) and omitted from the lock. On macOS and Windows oyzu install tailscale therefore fails with TOOL_PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE and changes nothing, because the host platform is the one selected for installation; a lock created on Linux still resolves the Linux platform for CI. Linux arm64 GNU is also admitted. Other Linux architectures and musl remain outside the supported native host set.

Only an exact version (1.78.1 or v1.78.1) or latest is accepted. Ranges, minor lines and pre-releases are refused with a message naming the accepted forms, and oyzu tools versions tailscale fails because Oyzu does not list releases. latest reads the TarballsVersion of the stable track's JSON index at https://pkgs.tailscale.com/stable/?mode=json; the lock records the resolved version.

The Linux tarball is https://pkgs.tailscale.com/stable/tailscale_<version>_<arch>.tgz, where arch is amd64 or arm64. It holds one tailscale_<version>_<arch>/ directory with tailscale, tailscaled and systemd unit files; Oyzu strips that directory so both binaries are at the payload root. The digest comes from the .sha256 sidecar on the same host. Oyzu locks it, downloads the archive through the tool broker and verifies the bytes before storing them. The digest comes from the publisher, not a signature. Oyzu does not redistribute the archive. Administrative tools routes scoped to tailscale, oyzu:tailscale or * use the same host connector bindings as the other tools; there is no public fallback from a configured route. The installed commands are tailscale and tailscaled.

Verified on Linux x86_64 (Ubuntu 24.04 container, Oyzu built from this branch) against the live publisher: oyzu install tailscale@1.78.1 locked the one Linux platform, printed a warning that darwin/arm64 and windows/amd64 have no artifact, and installed both binaries. oyzu exec -- tailscale version and tailscaled --version printed 1.78.1, and oyzu which resolved both into the store payload. tailscale@latest resolved to 1.104.1 and tailscale@1.56.1 installed. A range request was refused with the accepted forms. On Windows 11, oyzu install tailscale@1.78.1 failed with TOOL_PLATFORM_UNAVAILABLE and left oyzu.toml unchanged, as described above; macOS was not run. Not verified: the daemon (tailscaled was not started and no tailnet was joined, so the tarball's systemd units are untouched), other Linux architectures, cold-store offline replay, and oyzu update.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/tool-worker-contract.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Maintainer reference for the private worker protocol, not public CLI syntax.

ToolWorkerChannel<T> provides the initial private-channel byte framing for OEP-0003. It takes an already established duplex Read + Write transport; it does not discover a channel, start a subprocess or read worker stdin/stdout. The supervisor must authenticate and restrict inherited channel handles and enforce deadlines/cancellation independently. A blocking Read or Write is not made interruptible by this codec. This is an unstable internal interface, not a public worker/plugin compatibility promise. The sequential ToolWorkerChannel is suitable only when no read/write overlap is needed. For cancellation while waiting on a response, use split_tool_worker_channel(read_handle, write_handle) to obtain a ToolWorkerReceiver and ToolWorkerSender. Supply already established halves of the same trusted channel; this function neither creates nor duplicates handles. Each half can be owned by a separate thread. There is one shared atomic byte budget and failure state, and no synchronization lock spans transport I/O. The sender can therefore transmit a cancel while the receiver is blocked. The receiver reserves prefix bytes before reading them and body bytes before allocation/read; the sender reserves its complete frame before writing. In-flight reservations count against the same limit and are not refunded after failure. Failure in either half prevents subsequent successful operations in both. abort() on either half marks the shared state closed, and an in-flight read that later completes cannot return a successful frame. It does not interrupt the underlying syscall or retract bytes already written. The supervisor must still apply OS deadlines and explicitly shut down/cancel the underlying transport on timeout; dropping or invalidating a framing object is not process cancellation. Neither half is cloneable, so callers cannot accidentally interleave multiple framed writers through this API. Construct one channel per operation with ToolWorkerChannel::new(transport). send(json_bytes) validates one UTF-8 JSON object, writes a four-byte big-endian length and the original bytes, then flushes. receive() reads exactly one frame and returns an untrusted JSON value. Both directions share a 32 MiB lifetime budget, including length prefixes; each body is at most 8 MiB. Empty bodies, non-object roots, duplicate keys, malformed/nonfinite values and excessive nesting fail. The shared strict JSON parser also caps aggregate entries at 10,000. Oversized lengths and exhausted budgets fail before allocating or reading bodies. Malformed outgoing JSON emits no bytes. All failures permanently invalidate the channel instance. This includes clean EOF, short reads, invalid input and write/flush failures; retry requires a new supervised operation rather than attempting stream resynchronization. Errors use TOOL_WORKER_* codes without payload or transport-error text. No files, network connections or credentials are created by the codec itself. Framing success is not envelope admission. ToolWorkerExchange, described below, adds closed outer envelopes and response correlation; operation-specific payload admission and worker-side dispatch remain unimplemented. Complete authenticated bootstrap, handshake/operation deadlines, embedded backend dispatch and executor containment are also absent. Windows restricted process inheritance is implemented separately below; Unix process creation remains outstanding. The native allocation API creates local endpoints only. Tests exercise fragmented reads/writes, exact frame bounds, combined budgets, invalid/truncated JSON and terminal errors; they do not qualify a running worker or complete TM-05. Concurrent tests additionally hold a receive pending while sending cancellation, then check shared abort and budget exhaustion. A Unix-only test exchanges control frames over a real close-on-exec socketpair. It does not launch a process, verify inherited descriptor restrictions or establish Windows handle-list support.

native_tool_worker_channel() creates two connected NativeToolWorkerEndpoint values without stdin/stdout, an environment token, a filesystem socket name or a listening network port. Unix uses a socketpair, with duplicate descriptors for independent read/write ownership. Windows uses two anonymous pipes through the existing standard-library pipe API. No new crate dependency or executable is added. Creation checks FD_CLOEXEC on Unix or absence of HANDLE_FLAG_INHERIT on Windows and fails if any returned handle is inheritable. Dropping an endpoint closes its owned handles. An endpoint implements Read + Write for sequential framing. Its split() consumes it and returns NativeToolWorkerReader and NativeToolWorkerWriter without additional duplication. Pass those to split_tool_worker_channel for concurrent framing with a shared budget. The halves expose borrowed native descriptors/handles through AsFd or AsHandle for future explicit supervisor inheritance and cancellation; they do not transfer ownership or reopen a name. This API allocates blocking transports. It does not spawn a worker, authenticate an inherited channel, configure a Windows process handle list, install an OS deadline, interrupt pending I/O or contain backend code. A dropped peer produces EOF, which framing treats as terminal failure. A blocked read/write with a live peer still requires supervisor-owned OS cancellation/deadline enforcement. The factory must not be presented as a deadline-bounded production worker. Windows and Linux tests transfer a 2 MiB JSON payload in both directions using the native factory and framed split transport, then verify peer-close failure propagates to both framing halves. Creation itself checks non-inheritance. Additional Windows/Linux regressions leave a length prefix incomplete or write a 2 MiB frame while the peer never drains the transport. Closing the peer then causes each pending operation to fail and makes the other framing half terminal. These tests depend on all peer endpoint handles closing. They do not prove that killing a child closes handles inherited by descendants, or that a live peer can be interrupted; the supervisor must establish those lifecycle properties. The test watchdog bounds the test harness, not production I/O. macOS uses the Unix implementation but native verification of this increment remains pending. The Windows process primitive below now implements explicit cross-process inheritance. Unix inheritance and actual worker dispatch remain unfinished.

NativeToolWorkerIo::new(endpoint) takes ownership of one private native endpoint and wraps the existing shared framing budget. This experimental supervisor API provides one dedicated read thread and one dedicated write thread at most, with no frame queue. start_receive() and start_send(owned_bytes) begin a frame; try_receive() returns None while its read is pending and try_send() returns false while its write is pending. Completed operations are joined before results are returned. Another send can therefore deliver a cancel while a response read is blocked. A second start in the same direction before collecting completion fails with TOOL_WORKER_IO_PENDING; polling without a started operation fails with TOOL_WORKER_IO_NOT_STARTED. The existing 8 MiB frame, 32 MiB session and JSON shape limits still apply. Send input is validated before creating its thread; invalid input closes the operation. Results are untrusted JSON, not admitted worker responses or installation receipts. This API has no network, backend, filesystem configuration or process-spawn effects. The supervisor calls shutdown(absolute_monotonic_deadline) after cancellation, expiry or transport failure. It permanently closes framing, interrupts native I/O, discards racing results and joins both threads. Unix shuts down the retained socket; Windows repeatedly requests synchronous I/O cancellation against the owned, dedicated thread handles until completion is observed. Those threads never execute an unrelated operation or return to a thread pool. No peer closure is required. This follows Microsoft's synchronous I/O cancellation guidance: requesting cancellation alone does not establish completion. TOOL_WORKER_IO_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT means cleanup is still incomplete: the owner retains pending threads and handles, permits another shutdown attempt and refuses all result retrieval or new I/O. Do not report successful cleanup or publish a result on this path. Dropping the owner also interrupts and joins; it can wait if the operating system fails to complete cancellation. It never deliberately detaches pending I/O threads. This is not a guarantee against a stuck OS driver. Shutdown uses at most 5 ms polling sleeps, shortened to the remaining deadline. Tests exercise simultaneous partial-frame read and backpressured write with a live peer, duplex request/cancel traffic, cancellation independent of another channel, discarded completed results, pending-operation rejection, joining on drop and retained ownership after cleanup timeout. Run cargo test --locked --lib tools::worker::io. Native process creation and job termination are separate Windows components described below. These I/O tests do not establish channel authentication, deadline scheduling, backend dispatch or authorization to use a backend. The six tests pass on Windows GNU with Rust 1.94 and Linux with Rust 1.95 (network disabled). At commit 63e8073, the full locked unit/integration test, strict Clippy and formatting steps also passed on Windows, macOS and Linux in native CI. That observation covers those completed steps, not every downstream CI job or later process-lifecycle changes. The development backend entry point normalizes the LLVM coverage runtime's __LLVM_PROFILE_RT_INIT_ONCE startup marker before validating the inherited installer environment. LLVM can inject it even after the supervisor clears the child environment. No other variable is removed by this normalization or added to the installer's allowlist; profiling is not disabled. Normalization precedes installer environment validation. On 2026-10-17, Linux qualification with managed Rust 1.99.1 reproduced the pre-fix worker's exit 1 after LLVM inserted that marker into an otherwise cleared environment. At source 0c3bbdda, the unchanged tool_catalog::governed_providers::governed_rust_installs_from_indexed_inputs_and_refuses_unapproved_or_changed_bytes fixture passed against a CLI built with oyzu exec -- cargo rustc --locked --offline --bin oyzu --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu -j 1 -- -C instrument-coverage. The integration fixture was compiled first and then executed directly, preserving its compiled-in CLI path and original assertions. Main-binary instrumentation activates the actual LLVM startup runtime; the library was compiled normally. This qualifies installer startup and admission with fixture payloads, not a Rust compiler installation or full-workspace coverage run. The earlier instrumented failure and later memory interruption remain failed observations. Separate plain workspace tests passed 1,851/0 failures/35 ignored; strict workspace/all-target Clippy, formatting and documentation checks passed on Linux.

Cleanup retains handles to job members observed before requesting termination. Success requires both zero active job members and signalled retained process handles, under the existing deadline. A zero accounting count alone can precede Windows signalling a descendant's handle. Retries retain those original handles; a membership-capture error still requests termination but cannot claim confirmed cleanup. Neither worker handle restrictions nor deadlines are relaxed. On Windows, WindowsToolWorkerJob::new() creates an unnamed, non-inheritable job with kill-on-last-handle-close enabled and no process breakaway permission. The native spawn adapter must create the initial worker suspended, call assign_suspended(process_handle), and only then resume its primary thread. Assignment is permitted once, including when the native assignment fails. If it fails, the caller must terminate and reap the still-suspended initial process; it must never resume it or retry assignment on that job. This API does not verify the image, inspect suspension, transfer the supplied process handle, establish a sandbox or authenticate a control channel. terminate(absolute_monotonic_deadline) requests termination of every process in the job, then queries native job accounting until no active processes remain. This includes descendants and any associated console-host processes. Success requires an empty job, not just a successful termination request. A repeated termination call is permitted. Assignment is permanently closed once termination starts, even for an initially empty job. The supervisor must independently join control I/O and finish handle/receipt cleanup before reporting operation cleanup. TOOL_WORKER_JOB_CLEANUP_TIMEOUT or a native query/termination error means exit has not been confirmed. The owner retains its job handle so cleanup can be retried. Closing the last handle requests job-wide termination as a fallback; dropping this value alone does not claim observed exit. Native errors preserve their OS cause under stable TOOL_WORKER_JOB_* diagnostic context. The Windows-only tests launch the test executable suspended, assign it before resuming, and have it create a real descendant. They check breakaway denial, membership of both known processes, confirmed exit of both after termination, empty job accounting, independence of another live worker, last-handle-close termination, failed-assignment sequencing and empty-job shutdown. Console hosts were observed as additional job members on Windows; the tests intentionally require cleanup of all members rather than assuming a fixed process count. Run oyzu exec -- cargo test --locked --lib launch::windows_job. The ignored child fixture is invoked by those tests; it is not a product worker entry point. All four lifecycle tests pass on Windows GNU with Rust 1.94, as do the full locked suite, strict all-target Clippy, formatting and real CLI task scenarios. At commit d9c18de, the locked unit/integration tests, strict Clippy and formatting also passed on native Windows MSVC in CI run 37032992735. The same checks passed on Linux and macOS; the Windows-only job tests do not run on those hosts. The complete workflow was still running when these completed steps were recorded; downstream build/task acceptance is not inferred from them. This is the Windows job component. The process primitive below supplies pinned same-binary creation and an explicit inherited handle list. Combined process/I/O deadline scheduling and backend dispatch remain unimplemented. Unix process groups and their equivalent cleanup verification remain outstanding. The implementation follows Microsoft's job-object lifecycle contract.

WindowsToolWorkerProcess::spawn_current(expected_image_digest, arguments, environment, directory, inherited_handles) is an experimental native supervisor primitive. It resolves the running executable from the OS, never PATH or a project image setting. The expected sha256: digest must come from independently trusted release admission; computing a hash of whatever file happens to be present does not establish that admission. This API does not approve the release, admit backend capabilities, authenticate a protocol bootstrap or expose an install/exec command. Before creation it opens the image and all canonical parent directories without following reparse points at those opens. Parent handles deny directory replacement; the image handle denies writes/deletion while held. It hashes the opened image in bounded chunks and requires the expected digest and exact observed length. Images larger than 512 MiB are rejected by this initial implementation. The handles stay owned for the process owner's lifetime. A changed release fails with TOOL_WORKER_IMAGE_DIGEST_MISMATCH; retry requires trusted release selection, not accepting the newly observed hash. No image or parent directory is modified. Image pinning is owned by worker/windows_process/image.rs. Disposable-file tests exercise write, delete, image rename and parent-directory rename denial while a pin is held, then successful replacement after release. A digest rejection must release every acquired handle so the update/retry path remains available. These tests use ordinary temporary files rather than a loaded executable, so the Windows loader's own image lock cannot substitute for the pin's protection. The path-taking helper is private; production still selects only the running executable. Run cargo test --locked --lib tools::worker::windows_process::image. These two pin-lifetime tests pass on Windows GNU Rust 1.94. Native MSVC verification of the extracted image module and its new tests remains pending. The caller supplies an absolute, admitted private working directory and literal bootstrap arguments. Arguments are quoted for native Windows parsing, without a shell. There are at most 256 arguments and 32,767 UTF-16 code units in the encoded command line including its terminator; NUL values are rejected. An explicit environment map replaces the inherited environment. It permits at most 256 ASCII alphanumeric/underscore names of 1-256 bytes, rejects case-insensitive duplicates and embedded NULs, and bounds the complete UTF-16 block to 32,767 code units. The empty map produces an empty environment block. The supervisor must supply only admitted settings; the primitive does not interpret or authorize their values. At most 16 caller-owned capability handles are consumed by launch. Their raw values remain unchanged for bootstrap arguments; the caller must bind their kinds and purpose independently. The child receives only these selected handles and one null-device handle used for its standard streams. Standard streams carry no control traffic and inherit no parent console output handle. Parent copies of the consumed handles close before the child is resumed. This uses the native process handle-list attribute, not broad inheritance into this child. Selected handles are temporarily inheritable in the parent during launch; coordination with any concurrent broad-inheritance launchers remains a supervisor integration obligation. The worker bootstrap must validate and clear inheritance on received handles before executing backend code. Creation is hidden and suspended. The process is assigned to its private job before its primary thread resumes. A failed assignment/resume terminates and waits for the initial process instead of leaving a suspended orphan. Earlier failure closes consumed handles without resuming a child. Native startup itself is synchronous; automatic handshake/operation deadline scheduling is not supplied by this primitive. try_wait() reports the full native DWORD exit code of the initial process. terminate(deadline) confirms an empty job and initial-process exit; it does not join I/O. Call the I/O owner's shutdown as part of the same supervised cleanup. Dropping the process owner requests job termination through kill-on-close, without claiming observed exit. Tests spawn this same test binary through the primitive. They verify literal argument parsing, explicit environment, access to a selected event but no access to an unrelated inheritable event, request/response traffic on private pipes, termination with a descendant retaining those pipes and blocked I/O, partial-frame child exit, preservation of a high-bit DWORD exit code, wrong-image rejection and handle closure after failed native creation. A separate native Windows argument parser checks empty, quoted, Unicode and trailing-backslash argument round trips. Run cargo test --locked --lib tools::worker::windows_process. All four native process tests pass on Windows GNU Rust 1.94, together with the full locked suite, strict all-target Clippy, formatting and real CLI task scenarios. At b68b983, the locked unit/integration suite, strict Clippy and formatting also passed on Windows MSVC in run 37036054434. Those steps passed on Linux/macOS too, where Windows-only tests are excluded. That observation predates the extracted image module and its two pin-lifetime tests, and does not establish success of the still-running full workflow. The focused Tool worker lifecycle workflow runs formatting, strict all-target Clippy and cargo test --locked --lib tools::worker on Windows, macOS and Linux with Rust 1.94. It runs for relevant changes on main and the active integration branch, and supports manual dispatch. Native tests launch their own ignored subprocess fixtures; ordinary --ignored execution is not required. This workflow does not run archive qualification, CLI task scenarios or captured builds. The full CLI and scenarios workflow remains the broader regression/acceptance suite; a green worker workflow cannot establish full OEP-0003 completion. The tests are lifecycle qualification, not mise execution. Release-manifest admission, the product worker entry point and authenticated bootstrap, automatic deadlines, backend dispatch, Unix spawning and the complete supervisor remain unfinished. No separate mise executable is used.

ToolWorkerExchange::new(request_bytes) checks a closed outer request: exact protocol, canonical UUID, context/backend-release digests, a recognized target platform, operation enum, sorted unique capability IDs and an object payload. Use one exchange per supervised operation. operation() exposes the selected operation; untrusted_payload() deliberately does not imply payload admission. Recognized platform syntax does not establish backend/platform support, and capability names do not prove executor capabilities. Both ToolWorkerExchange::context() and ToolWorkerSession::context() return a borrowed ToolWorkerRequestContext containing request_id, context_digest, backend_release_digest, target_platform and the sorted capability IDs. These are the fields from the validated original request, not a second parse or a separately mutable identity. Use them to compare the request with independently trusted supervisor state before dispatch. They remain inspectable after the operation ends; inspecting this snapshot does not renew the operation, authenticate the channel, admit a capability or grant execution permission. No wire format or request validation rule changes with this accessor. finish(response_bytes) compares protocol, request ID and context digest with the original request. It accepts exactly one ok response with an object result, or error/cancelled with a closed diagnostic containing only code. Codes are 1-64 uppercase ASCII letters, digits or underscores; arbitrary worker message text is not accepted. Even successful results use the explicitly named ToolWorkerOutcome::UntrustedResult variant and require operation-specific validation, containment/digest checks and current authorization before use. Call cancel() once to obtain a correlated envelope with the same protocol, request ID and context digest and operation="cancel". It marks cancellation before transport; any write failure requires aborting the operation. A later success response is discarded rather than allowing a cancelled operation to publish. abort() handles timeout, transport loss or supervisor cancellation. Any response attempt, including malformed or mismatched input, terminates the exchange; a second response is rejected. This state machine does not send bytes, interrupt a blocking transport, cancel a process or authenticate the channel. The outer-envelope schema and shared fixtures cover request/response shapes. Sorting, response correlation and lifecycle rules are runtime checks. Cancel encoding, code-only diagnostics and cancellation-race handling are initial draft wire choices requiring contract review. Operation-specific request/result records and backend cancellation remain outstanding; this is not the complete typed worker schema or a deployed worker protocol.

On Windows, WindowsToolWorkerLifecycle::new(process, io) joins ownership of an already-created process and its control channel. The trusted caller must associate the matching endpoint; this constructor does not authenticate their relationship. Use control() for protocol I/O and try_wait() for the initial process status. shutdown(absolute_cleanup_deadline) permanently denies further control access, interrupts both I/O directions, terminates and observes the job, then attempts I/O joining even if process cleanup failed. Both phases use the same deadline. Success returns the native initial-process exit code and confirms job-wide exit and joined threads. Failure retains ownership for another shutdown attempt; TOOL_WORKER_PROCESS_CLEANUP_FAILED, TOOL_WORKER_CONTROL_CLEANUP_FAILED or TOOL_WORKER_CLEANUP_FAILED preserve the relevant causes. A retry never reopens the protocol. Synchronous native calls are not preempted by this deadline. Dropping the lifecycle interrupts I/O and releases the process/job owner before the I/O owner joins its threads. Job close requests descendant termination; only explicit successful shutdown confirms process cleanup. Drop may still wait if native I/O cancellation fails to complete. Native tests cover descendants holding both control pipes, exhausted-budget retry, denial of protocol reuse and drop cleanup with a live transport peer. This Windows-only composition adds no backend dispatch, launch authorization, bootstrap protocol or Unix supervisor. For bounded synchronous collection of an already-started native I/O operation, NativeToolWorkerIo::wait_receive_frame(deadline) and wait_send(deadline) use an absolute std::time::Instant. They check expiry before polling and before returning a completed result. Expiry returns TOOL_WORKER_IO_DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, closes both directions and requests native interruption. An already-completed result collected after expiry is discarded. No elapsed-time extension occurs between polls; sleeps are at most one millisecond, subject to OS scheduling. The caller must still terminate the worker process and call shutdown with its separate cleanup deadline to confirm that all I/O threads joined. Expiry is not proof of process exit or completed cleanup, and the closed instance cannot be reused. These optional blocking waits do not schedule protocol defaults or a cancellation grace period. A supervisor that must concurrently observe process exit or user cancellation should use the nonblocking collection methods instead. Native tests keep peers open during incomplete reads and backpressured writes, then verify deadline failure, rejection of reuse and confirmed thread cleanup. ToolWorkerExchange::request_digest() commits to the exact validated request body using SHA-256 over oyzu.tool-worker.request.v1 followed by a NUL byte and the request bytes. The four-byte frame prefix is excluded. The supervisor must compute this expectation from its independently admitted request before launch. ToolWorkerSession::from_committed_request(bytes, expected_digest) validates the digest format and envelope, then rejects a mismatch with TOOL_WORKER_REQUEST_COMMITMENT_INVALID. This binds payload bytes as well as the outer identity. Even semantically equivalent JSON with different whitespace or field ordering fails against the original commitment; send the original bytes. After failure, tear down the operation rather than replacing the expectation with a digest computed from received input. For this startup path, ToolWorkerChannel::receive_frame() and the receiver's equivalent return ToolWorkerFrame, preserving the bounded original body through bytes() alongside untrusted_value(). NativeToolWorkerIo::try_receive_frame() collects the same single pending read as try_receive(); collecting through one consumes it for both. Existing value-only receive APIs remain available. Frame limits and shared accounting are unchanged. These APIs perform no network access or persistent writes, and require no new configuration or lockfile fields. The digest is an integrity commitment, not a credential. Supplying both request and expectation from an untrusted source establishes no authority. Authenticated launch context, capability-handle validation and typed payload admission remain separate requirements. Tests cover an independent digest vector, payload substitution, changed JSON spelling and exact-byte exchange over native channels between test threads; they do not exercise a product worker entrypoint. ToolWorkerSession::new(request_bytes, expected_operation, expected_context) applies the same bounded outer-request validation as the supervisor exchange, then requires exact equality with independently trusted supervisor state before creating a session. It compares operation, request ID, context digest, backend release digest, target and the complete ordered capability list. A mismatch returns TOOL_WORKER_REQUEST_BINDING_INVALID; neither adding nor dropping capabilities is accepted. Expected values must come from the supervisor operation, never from the received request. This is identity binding, not channel authentication or validation of payload values and capability handles. operation() and untrusted_payload() expose only the validated operation name and untrusted payload. One session represents one operation; it does not authorize serving multiple workspaces in a persistent worker process. accept_cancel(bytes) accepts exactly the correlated cancel envelope once. Unknown fields, duplicate JSON keys, another initial request, foreign identities, malformed JSON and repeated cancellation permanently end the session. A valid cancel prevents later success output. The dispatcher must still interrupt or stop backend work; accepting the envelope alone has no process effect. finish(ToolWorkerOutcome) encodes one correlated terminal response and reuses the supervisor's validation, including frame limits, object results, code-only diagnostics and cancellation-race rejection. Invalid output consumes the attempt; it cannot be replaced with a second response. abort() ends the session after transport loss or dispatcher failure. A send failure requires teardown, with no retry or new context in the same worker. Result contents remain untrusted and require independent supervisor validation before any publication or execution. Before recursive response serialization, the shared JSON tree validator checks the same depth-32 and 10,000-entry limits used on input. Encoding then writes into a bounded buffer and stops before an append would exceed 8 MiB, counting JSON escaping and envelope fields. Geometric buffer reservation is capped at that frame size; output is not fully serialized into an unbounded temporary first. This bounds the encoded buffer, not memory a backend already used to construct its result. Encoding failure ends the session and emits no response bytes. Focused tests cover all three terminal outcomes, invalid/oversized output, malformed/foreign/duplicate cancel, repeated response and success-after-cancel. A native private-channel test sends a request and cancel, receives the correlated cancellation diagnostic and observes peer closure. The 15-second test watchdog does not implement production deadlines. Run cargo test --locked tools::worker; no mise dependency, network or backend execution is required. Worker process composition and channel authentication, actual dispatch, OS deadline scheduling, backend cancellation and typed operation payloads remain absent. The Windows native process primitive above separately implements image pinning and restricted inheritance; the session itself does not perform those operations.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/toolchain-platforms.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Captured builds can select a matching provisioned execution image for an explicit or inferred artifact platform. Builders declare their execution requirement through an internal contract. Language builders require matching OS/architecture; the Docker assembly builder can use a different worker for operations that do not execute target code. This adds no project configuration or tool installation.

The native tool host set is Linux amd64/arm64 GNU, macOS arm64 native and Windows amd64 MSVC. Archive-provider locks carry linux/arm64/gnu even when resolved on another host. Each provider owns its vendor architecture spelling and reports missing releases as unavailable. Tailscale has Linux standalone archives only. macOS amd64 and musl remain outside this host expansion. The Rust installer worker also admits an explicitly provisioned oyzu-toolchain/worker:v1-linux-arm64 image, checked for Linux/arm64 identity. This does not provision a linker, emulator or build image. Automated tests cover host/metadata mappings; native ARM64 installation and remote worker execution still need qualification. Rust's broader portable compiler-metadata coverage is retained independently of the native installation host set. After matrix expansion, Oyzu resolves the builder's usual runtime-specific image and inspects its immutable identity and platform. If its platform satisfies the execution requirement, that image is used. Otherwise, for a default tagged image, Oyzu inspects one platform sibling named <default-reference>-<os>-<arch>. The sibling must actually have the requested platform; a matching tag is insufficient. Both the default and any needed sibling must already be available in the selected Docker daemon. There is no pull, image build or emulator installation in this selection path. Examples of currently provisioned CI siblings: Default image Linux ARM sibling oyzu-toolchain/go:1.24-mod0.25.0 oyzu-toolchain/go:1.24-mod0.25.0-linux-arm64 oyzu-toolchain/node:npm11.11.0-node22 oyzu-toolchain/node:npm11.11.0-node22-linux-arm64 The same suffix rule follows an exact Node runtime selection. Other ecosystem images are eligible for the common resolution rule but their platform-specific native integrations still need provisioning and verification. The current executor accepts Linux images only. For example, after explicitly provisioning Docker and any required ARM execution support: docker build -f tooling/images/go.Dockerfile -t oyzu-toolchain/go:1.24-mod0.25.0 . docker build --platform linux/arm64 -f tooling/images/go.Dockerfile -t oyzu-toolchain/go:1.24-mod0.25.0-linux-arm64 . oyzu build image oyzu inspect dist The authored Go container matrix requests two image platforms; materialization infers two matching Go producers. Each executes its language build, test and quality commands in its selected toolchain. Docker can then assemble both scratch images on its existing worker, and the engine creates their complete OCI index. --image manager=reference is an explicit override for all selected variants using that manager. Oyzu does not rewrite it or try siblings. An override with the wrong platform fails before preparation; one image generally cannot satisfy both sides of a native platform matrix. Omitted platforms retain existing defaults. Development oyzu run commands continue to use host tools and do not select container images.

Plans and dependency records bind the actual selected image identity and execution platform independently of the artifact target and CLI host. Go preparation additionally verifies native Go OS/architecture against the image. Successful image inspection alone does not establish that commands can execute: preparation/actions must run successfully under the existing sandbox and timeout limits. Unsupported execution or a missing/mislabeled sibling fails instead of silently using the wrong architecture. Provision the required image/execution support or correct an explicit override before rebuilding. These records do not attest physical native hardware versus emulation, discover remote worker pools, or authorize production publication. The Docker host must supply any emulation; Oyzu does not infer permission to install it. Docker documents native nodes, emulation and cross-compilation as different strategies. Executing target-language tests in an ARM image is required here; simply cross-compiling an ARM binary does not replace those tests. Dockerfiles with foreign-platform RUN remain separately restricted by Docker admission. Toolchain selection itself uses only the local daemon. Existing native dependency acquisition and offline build replay retain their own rules. Source snapshots, private target workspaces, report gates and failure-bundle retention are unchanged. Cross-platform ABI/base compatibility, automatic platform-independent output reuse, policy-controlled worker pools and comprehensive platform coverage remain unfinished.

Rust tests exercise matching/default selection, one verified sibling, explicit override preservation, missing/mislabeled siblings and the distinction between language execution and Docker assembly. The Linux Docker CI job separately provisions ARM emulation through a pinned setup action and builds matching Go/Node toolchain images, checking actual Go and Node architecture before invoking Oyzu. The captured suite now runs the authored EX-027 Go and EX-050 frontend platform graphs, requiring native-language JUnit/coverage and quality gates for both architectures, Go ELF architecture checks, exact materialized file/directory bytes, complete indices and repeatable plans/artifacts. Node fixture formatting is explicit setup before the immutable source check; builds do not rewrite source. These checks passed at revision ad6cbf1 in Docker job 110868387899. This does not claim all cases in either scenario, especially managed policy, ABI and cache requirements, have passed.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/version-inference.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Version inference is being connected to the captured build path. The current increment supports Cargo, Node and Helm package snapshots from native SemVer, exact local tags, nearest first-parent release tags and Conventional Commit impacts. Full OEP-0013 release/candidate operation authorization is not implemented. Go applications and Docker images use the same tag/bump inference without requiring a native version. Python maps compatible native PEP 440 versions into the same logical inference, then encodes the result for its wheel, source archive and application artifact. Maven, Gradle and Ant now consume the shared resolver through native JVM metadata.

Run oyzu build in a supported project with its existing native inputs and the corresponding provisioned build image. No new Oyzu configuration is required. Git must be available on the host. Git metadata is observed locally before native preparation; no automatic fetch occurs. An exported directory without Git uses native source snapshots, or 0.0.0 snapshots when the builder has no native application version. See Rust builds and build verification for native preparation and execution prerequisites. The implementation uses portable Git subprocesses; cross-host acceptance is pending. An ordinary single-package repository at version 1.4.2, with ancestor tag v1.4.2 and a subsequent feat: add endpoint commit, resolves the next base to 1.5.0. Artifacts receive 1.5.0-dev.g<12-character-source-hash>. The suffix remains content-derived, not the Git commit SHA. No wall-clock counter is used. Artifact digests, not version strings, identify final bytes. Versions finalized after hooks (captured Node builds, OEP-0011 handoff K2). For a target with a pre_build hook that declares outputs, the hash covers the target's source scope without the hook's own script plus the digest of the files the hook wrote under its declared outputs. The hook therefore counts as a generator: editing its script without changing what it writes keeps the version, and a change in what it writes changes the version and the package. The script stays in the hash when a builder stage reads or writes it, or when it is not named as an argument of the hook's command. plan.json records the pre-hook source version (the hash without the hook output), which the actions before the hook run with; the final version is recorded in the target's post-hook plan (plans/<target>.post-hooks.json) and the manifest. See hooks as always-run actions. The same version results with and without --no-cache. Other builders, other hook phases and the native host path keep the plain source hash.

On the captured Unix executor path, a target can refine its development source suffix after preparation and final command selection. Every selected command must have a complete, bounded, confinable stage contract and remain cacheable. The source membership is the union of shipping-command reads, declared inputs, and configuration/build/lock paths captured by their existing inventory owners. Check-only reads can leave the version scope only when their complete writes cannot reach a shipping read, directly or through another check. This is a positive native read boundary: unowned shared files need a consumer instead of changing every eligible target's version. Literal optional reads stay in the boundary while absent, so creating the file changes its consumers' source suffix. Source identity and native dependency captures remain whole-tree facts. The existing builder version-revision and plan compiler bind the revised version before execution, including independent target branches. Membership and command contracts must remain stable when the plan is rebuilt; otherwise the original plan, dependencies and versions remain together. Acquisition is not repeated. Reuse-disabled execution retains the same private views and source boundary. Windows, unsupported host paths, cross-target prerequisites, hooks, authored replacements, projected sources and materialized artifact inputs retain their established conservative scope. Missing captured control provenance or incomplete command evidence also keeps that scope. Existing hook finalization remains a separate supported path. The connected shared-source candidate is still awaiting its unchanged Linux acceptance run; see the qualification record.

The captured Node cross-target flow is demonstrated on Windows with Linux Docker workers, and ordinary native Go and Rust pairs are demonstrated on Windows. The authored/deleted/transitive and frozen historical-root regressions pass. F2's agreed functional scope is complete on those recorded profiles, including full workspace tests, strict Clippy, the current captured pair and all nine real CLI task behaviors. Broader hosts, native check-selection qualification and hardening remain separate; this does not complete F1, F3 or F4. Its existing depends_on, task and artifact relationships supply the prerequisite closure, and build.yaml inputs supply authored paths, including paths authored by a prerequisite outside that prerequisite's directory. Each consumer retains its own native package scope and tag baseline; a producer feature can advance the consumer against that baseline without advancing an unrelated target. No import inference or coordinated release-group policy is added. Commit impact intersects native/declared ownership with the build's frozen source selection, including authored ignore overrides. Deleted paths are tested against captured rules rather than dropped because they are absent from the current tree. Git paths remain relative to the repository root even when the workspace is nested. Editing live ignore rules after capture does not change the inference inputs. Plan/manifest source.selection and version-history evidence retain replay inputs; version decisions record inputScope.declaredPaths. Inputs in a different Git repository fail with version-inputs-outside-repository; keep the declared closure within the captured repository. History acquisition and release authority remain unchanged. The bounded real-Git scope/history and Source execution regressions pass in the full workspace run at 5d22a8ac: 1,838 passed, zero failed, 37 existing prerequisite skips and zero filtered. Every workspace/doc-test target completed. Corrected artifact, prerequisite and timing cases pass with their original assertions; the shared path-wrapping regression and unchanged environment-inspection assertion also pass. Strict workspace/all-target Clippy passed at c503a2d8 with warnings treated as errors. The final captured regression against the manifest-verified 82400b4d CLI passes, as do all nine original real CLI task behaviors using that same pair at 718a350b. Earlier failures and revision-specific evidence remain in the completion record. The real tooling/test-cross-target-version.py captured pair passed with the 82400b4d CLI and unchanged compiled inputs at 68026056: Declared relationship Producer base Consumer base Unrelated base Consumer depends on producer 1.5.0 2.4.0 4.1.0 Edge removed 1.5.0 2.3.1 4.1.0 Both builds produced snapshot coordinates derived from these bases, using each subject's own baseline. The pair passed in 218.0 seconds. Each executed 21 actions, passed nine native checks and seven tests, collected three JUnit and three LCOV reports and delivered three npm archives. Bundle inspection and installation and execution in independent offline native consumers passed. Authored files, Git state and tool locks remained unchanged by each build. This fixture declares no authored inputs, so it does not qualify authored ignore overrides. See the F2 proof boundary for the required native artifact, independent-consumer and unchanged-input proof. The prepared probe explicitly selects captured execution with --isolated --full --jobs 1 --no-cache, checks collected native test/coverage reports and bundle inspection, then installs the delivered archives into an independent native consumer. It requires a provisioned npm/Node quality image, its captured executor and Oyzu-managed Python/Node/npm. The first attempt failed before execution with NEEDS_USER_NAMESPACES (exit 3) when its session could not access Docker and automatic isolation selected Linux-only crun. The pair passed from a Docker-capable managed runner with the same CLI, fixture and lock. Verify Docker access from the actual managed runner session on Windows. Captured proof does not establish ordinary native-host version behavior. Supply a genuine already-provisioned node = "22" tool lock with the probe's required --tool-lock argument and its matching managed store with --store. The harness copies the original lock before creating Git baselines and preserves it in both the producer checkout and independent consumer; it never pins or installs tools. A captured Linux build alone does not prove that the pinned Node/npm is installed for the consumer's host platform. The probe writes generated JavaScript with LF line endings on every host so Windows fixture authoring preserves the mandatory native format-check contract. The separate prepared native probe is tooling/test-native-cross-target-version.py --cli <compiled-cli> --store <managed-store> --tool-lock <genuine-go-lock> --evidence-dir <new-directory>. It requires already-installed Go 1.24.13 and managed Python, uses the ordinary host build with --full --no-docker --jobs 1 --no-cache --offline, and executes the exported binaries outside the generated checkout. It checks native reports, per-subject baselines, artifact filenames and unchanged source/lock bytes with and without the declared edge. Go versions are artifact coordinates; this probe does not require application version injection. Source's frozen host source.projections contract is now integrated, preserving its aggregate identity. The imported contracts pass the structural checker after its earlier nonlocal-reference failure. The native Go implementation now receives original local Git history, the configured strategy and the declared closure's frozen projection admission and captured bytes. It uses the shared resolver and binds its decision to the native output filename and command, plan and manifest. History records are frozen into the plan before its digest is computed. The version-scope digest does not replace Source's aggregate projection identity. This wiring compiled on Windows at 6428b146; both CLI exports matched their manifest hashes, and preserved-bundle inspection passed. The native probe then passed both cases in 58.3 seconds: the consumer base was 2.4.0 with the edge and 2.3.1 without it, while the producer remained 1.5.0 and the unrelated subject 4.1.0. Each build executed 12 actions, passed four native tests, collected three JUnit and three coverage reports, and delivered three versioned binaries. Both bundle inspections and all six copied binary executions outside the checkout passed. Source, Git and locks remained unchanged. The native output still reports incomplete check-selection evidence; this proof does not establish complete selected-check coverage. Rust native projection is demonstrated on the Windows three-application pair. Private native Cargo paths reuse the existing manifest/dependency projector, private lock reconciliation runs offline, and native metadata supplies artifact versions. Stable executable names remain unchanged. Full/CI, explicit tags/conventional strategies, optimized and distributed builds stamp the inferred version into CARGO_PKG_VERSION. Local fast development builds retain declared Cargo package identities for incremental reuse and record the actual compiledVersion beside the source-specific artifact version; see local compilation versions. Run tooling/test-native-rust-cross-target-version.py with the same required probe arguments and already-installed Rust 1.99.1, rustfmt, Clippy, LLVM tools, cargo-nextest and cargo-llvm-cov. The probe checks actual binaries, native reports and per-subject decisions with and without the edge; it never installs tools. The new wiring compiled on Windows at 4ede08d1; both CLI exports matched their manifest hashes, and preserved-bundle inspection passed. The native Rust pair then passed in 44.3 seconds: consumer base 2.4.0 with the edge and 2.3.1 without it, producer 1.5.0 and unrelated 4.1.0 in both cases. Each build passed 12 actions and four tests, collected three JUnit and three Cobertura reports, and delivered three binaries. Both inspections and six independent binary executions passed. The binaries' compiled CARGO_PKG_VERSION matched the inferred snapshot versions and artifact metadata, including the producer's new capability. Authored manifests, native/tool locks and Git remained unchanged. The launcher restored child-only Temp and compiler-job environment values and their presence. Native check-selection evidence is still incomplete; this fixture has no authored inputs. Other host adapters retain their existing version behavior.

The default is auto. An optional ordinary setting in oyzu.toml selects one of four fixed strategies; this is not an expression language: [version] strategy = "tags" Strategy Base selection auto Reconcile native metadata, exact tags, nearest stable tags and Conventional Commit impacts; fall back to native metadata or 0.0.0 when history cannot supply a baseline native Use the native version and ignore tag/bump selection; fail if the project has no native version tags Use an exact applicable tag, otherwise the nearest stable first-parent tag; do not infer a bump or require native metadata to match conventional Use the auto reconciliation rules, requiring complete history and an applicable baseline or exact tag; reject unclassified relevant commits after the baseline All four still generate source snapshots. A strategy never changes publication or signing authority. The setting follows the normal configuration cascade, profiles, local-override eligibility and administrative constraints. Builders consume the frozen effective value, and it participates in computation identity. Omit the setting for existing behavior. Unknown values fail configuration validation. version-needs-native, version-needs-tags and version-needs-history identify missing strategy inputs. Supply the native declaration or complete local Git history/tags, or select a suitable strategy. version-unclassified-commits requires clarifying commit intent or selecting a less strict strategy. For native version schemes without a supported logical mapping, auto and native retain native snapshots; tags and conventional fail with unsupported-version-strategy.

Git history is observed once per repository per build, shared by every target in it. How much commit detail is read depends on what can change the result: Bounded (CI, --full, a ci profile, and the tags and conventional strategies). Commit messages and changed paths are read only for commits after the oldest of every tag subject's nearest stable first-parent release tag. Resolution excludes ancestors of each baseline, so older history cannot change a decision; the bounded read gives the same decisions as reading everything (tested against the full history, including merges and subject-scoped tags). Without any stable release tag no baseline exists and no commit detail is read. A shallow clone is read as it is. Head only (local fast builds on the default auto strategy, and native). The head commit, prefix, shallow state and tag list are still recorded, and an exact tag on the built commit still sets the version, but no commit messages are read. The version falls back to the native version (or 0.0.0) plus the source suffix, with reason native-fallback-local-history-skipped and historyComplete: false; the history record's traversal is head-only. Use --full, the CI context or an explicit tags/conventional strategy for the commit-driven version a release build would stamp. A local artifact's version can therefore differ from CI's for the same commit. The first applicable stable tag walking first-parent ancestry is the baseline. Merged commits still contribute declared impacts: breaking change, feature and fix choose the maximum major/minor/patch increment once. Other conventional types have no bump. Unclassified relevant commits are retained in evidence; this increment never claims sufficient release evidence. A native version already ahead of the baseline is retained if it meets the computed minimum. Incompatible exact tags, ambiguous versions on one tagged commit and insufficient explicit version advances fail with version-conflict or ambiguous-version-tags diagnostics. Correct the native declaration/tag intent and rerun; the builder never edits checkout metadata. Exact local tags still produce source snapshots and cannot authorize publication. They do name the release: oyzu publish reads the exactTags a published build records as its GitHub release tag, so the version and the release tag come from the same fact and no tag is committed. Builds of one destination must agree, and oyzu publish --tag overrides; see which release. Only a tag that applies to the package is recorded (the tag namespace rules below): an unscoped v1.4.0 on a member of a multi-package Cargo workspace records nothing, so such a release passes --tag. Artifact records of the Rust builder and Node workspace package archives carry extensions["oyzu.dev/versioning"].package, naming the package whose decision they come from. An RC tag matching a stable native core retains its prerelease label in the snapshot. Shallow history conservatively falls back to native source snapshots with an explicit reason; users can provision complete history before retrying. No network request is made to repair history. An unresolvable repository error is reported rather than being interpreted as an unversioned export. Cargo evaluates original metadata and then projects inferred versions and local package references only in its private preparation tree. Node managers capture native package/workspace facts and project the same decisions during isolated execution, including the root and member package metadata and local references. The native package version, planned coordinate and collected artifact version agree. Build output explains each package decision. Target records in dist/plan.json and dist/manifest.json retain extensions["oyzu.dev/versioning"]: native version, resolved base/version, source digest, commit, baseline tag/commit, exact tags, contributing/unclassified commits, history completeness, reason, algorithm strategy, configured requestedStrategy, snapshot intent and denied production eligibility. These are local observations, not authenticated source-control facts. The plan and manifest also retain extensions["oyzu.dev/version-history"], keyed by build target. Each entry contains a digest and the captured local history record: HEAD, repository prefix, shallow status, local tag names/object IDs/peeled commits, annotated-versus-lightweight identity, and reachable commit parents/messages/paths. Decisions reference this record through historyDigest and record first-parent baselineDistance and scoped analyzedCommits. The plan digest binds these inputs. The record labels remote freshness unknown and verification local-observation; a full local clone is not proof of the remote tag inventory. Failed preparation retains any history already captured in the failed manifest. History records include commit messages and paths; treat bundles as repository information when sharing. Helm projects the root chart version in private preparation; appVersion and dependency chart versions keep their native meanings. Go uses inferred versions for application artifact names and the manifest; it does not inject a version variable into compiled application code. Docker uses the version in the OCI archive name, exported image reference and manifest. Go and Docker record nativeVersion: null: an exact tag supplies their base, while an ancestor tag supplies the baseline for impact analysis. Without either, the base is 0.0.0. Go resolves each native workspace module independently using captured import and test-import edges. Directory-scoped tags supply module baselines, binary coordinates use their owning module's decision, and module zip/mod/info outputs retain native v prefixes and RC snapshot qualifiers. A path-major fallback is permitted only without a selected version baseline; incompatible explicit versions fail native module validation. See Go versions. Python's native packaging.version.Version supplies normalized facts; the shared resolver does not parse PEP 440. Stable versions with up to three release components and alpha/beta/RC versions can participate in SemVer tag inference. For example, base 1.5.0-rc.2 becomes 1.5.0rc2.dev0+g<source-hash>. Unrepresentable tag prerelease labels fail rather than losing their qualifier. Native epochs, postreleases, existing development versions and longer release tuples retain a native snapshot with reason native-ecosystem-source; Git bump inference for those version schemes is pending. Snapshots use development counter zero and replace original local labels with source identity; the original normalized native version remains recorded. The native parser's version API owns normalization and validity. Static PEP 621 pip/uv/Poetry projects project the selected version in their private pyproject.toml. A project that lists version in project.dynamic has no native version during preparation: its base comes from tags (or 0.0.0) and maps to a PEP 440 snapshot, which the private pyproject.toml receives as a static version; see dynamic versions. Legacy setuptools captures native facts offline, then projects the version through its distribution metadata. Its sdist stages a generated setup.py wrapper containing the original program and a fixed version override so rebuilding the source archive retains the artifact's version. Checkout sources and the source used by test/quality tasks remain unchanged. The wrapper supports native setuptools and distutils setup entry points; arbitrary custom distribution construction is not a qualified version provider. Requirements-only applications have no native version and retain SemVer application coordinates, including tag inference. Python dependency captures use adapter layout version 2; recreate older captures for version evidence. JVM preparation removes the conventional native -SNAPSHOT suffix when the remaining value is SemVer, while retaining the original declaration in evidence. Other native version forms keep their existing base and receive a source snapshot with reason native-ecosystem-source; arbitrary Maven/Gradle qualifiers are not silently reinterpreted as SemVer. Gradle's unspecified version permits a tag-derived base. Ant retains its native metadata adapter's 0.0.0 fallback when no version property exists. Maven and Gradle first capture native models in an isolated preparation worker. The host resolves versions and writes a frozen version-plan.json; native tooling then applies it in the same private workspace before dependency capture is frozen. Maven makes inherited module versions explicit using its native raw model writer in the private copy, then uses the versions plugin for module/parent/dependency projection and checks the resulting reactor coordinates. Gradle uses project directory identities across the root and included builds; archive tasks consume each selected version again during offline execution. Ant reevaluates its native model using the selected version properties and records the version in the exported JAR manifest. Maven modules use unique artifact IDs as tag subjects, or groupId.artifactId when artifact IDs collide. Gradle projects use unique native names, or project directory paths when names collide. Root tags are admitted only for a single native project; multi-project builds use scoped tags such as library/v1.4.2. Equal native versions alone do not imply a coordinated group. Maven captures local upstream projects from the native reactor graph, including reactor parent relationships. Gradle captures resolved project-component identities across root and included builds, using native build-tree paths to distinguish projects. Both feed the same transitive input-scope resolver as Cargo and Node; no dependency resolver is recreated in Rust. Gradle resolves these edges only during captured preparation/execution, through its existing repository boundary. Lightweight host metadata observation does not resolve them. Unresolved Gradle graph results fail preparation rather than omit a dependency. This requires the provisioned Gradle 8.14.3 profile and the current Maven metadata extension. Reprovision an older Maven image if native reactor edges are missing. Maven/Gradle dependency adapter layouts are now 4/3 respectively; older captures must be recreated. Coordinated inherited-version release groups remain unfinished. Independent Cargo and Node members admit package-name tag namespaces. Unscoped root tags are used only for a single Cargo workspace package or standalone Node package at the Git repository root. Cargo and Node use captured native local dependency edges to compute each member's transitive input scope before commit analysis.
