Development, build, optional and peer edges participate when represented by the native model; this is conservative build-input impact, not a claim that every dependency change changes the consumer's public API. Cycles form a finite input closure and do not imply that packages share a release version. For example, with app -> bridge -> shared and a separate independent package, a feat changing only shared advances the first three bases from 1.4.2 to 1.5.0; independent remains 1.4.2. Each package evaluates impacts against its own scoped baseline. Native packaging projects each dependency's chosen version into the consumer's metadata, even when their versions differ. Checkout manifests and locks remain unchanged. The most specific native member directory owns a changed path. Paths outside member directories, such as workspace manifests, lock files and root build inputs, count as shared inputs for all members. This deliberately favors conservative impact over guessing file imports. The decision's inputScope records selected directories and workspaceDirectories, making the scope inspectable. A root package does not implicitly own every sibling member; its declared local edges select those inputs. This does not yet infer undeclared cross-member imports, Oyzu task-input closures across separate targets, or coordinated release groups. Other builders' native dependency closures and explicit tag namespace settings remain unfinished.
documents.s: What history is read, and when

documents.t: The implementation finish line is recorded in the audited completion checklist. It distinguishes missing functional behavior and its acceptance evidence from broader compatibility, hardening and the separate publication implementation. Native dynamic version providers beyond the captured native adapters, verified CI release/candidate versions, provider evidence, history acquisition, remote tag inventory verification and destination-specific mappings are pending. No release or publication capability follows from this increment. tooling/test-version-inference.py --cli <compiled-cli> --evidence-dir <new-directory> creates a real Git repository, invokes the compiled CLI, opens the resulting Cargo archive, verifies plan/manifest versions and reports, changes source without a commit, and checks exact-tag conflict failure. The default uses the provisioned Rust build image. --builder node runs the corresponding npm package flow and inspects the .tgz package metadata. --strategy native, tags or conventional writes the corresponding oyzu.toml setting and checks its recorded selection, artifact version, dirty-source identity and exact-tag behavior. The default leaves configuration absent to prove inference. --builder helm inspects packaged Chart.yaml; --builder go checks the produced binary and its versioned coordinate; --builder docker checks the exported OCI reference. Each compares plan/manifest versions, checks required reports and preserves checkout metadata. Go/Docker also exercise an exact tag without native version metadata, verifying that it still produces a snapshot. --builder python, python-uv, python-poetry and python-legacy inspect wheel METADATA and sdist PKG-INFO; python-pip checks the requirements application's embedded manifest. The native legacy probe separately rebuilds a wheel from the sdist offline and executes the installed artifact. java-ant, java-maven and java-gradle exercise Ant, a Maven reactor and a Gradle composite respectively, checking versioned artifacts, native Maven/Ant embedded metadata, module decisions and collected reports. Gradle archive filenames/coordinates are checked; arbitrary JAR manifest attributes remain native Gradle behavior. Native workspace inference and pnpm/Yarn packaging use the workspace probe below; measured results and remaining manager limitations are recorded in implementation status. Unit checks cover real Git ancestry, merged features, exact-tag conflicts and bump selection. Results are recorded in implementation status after execution; this description alone is not acceptance evidence. tooling/test-workspace-version-inference.py --builder node|rust --cli <compiled-cli> --evidence-dir <new-directory> exercises dependency changes, a separately changed member and a shared root input through real scoped-tag repositories. It checks independent native archive versions, rewritten local dependency references, plan/manifest scopes, reports, bundle inspection and unchanged checkout metadata. For Node, --manager npm|pnpm|yarn selects the native lock and packaging flow (npm is the default). pnpm and Yarn locks are generated offline using the explicitly provisioned host manager before capture; Node fixture sources are formatted with the provisioned native Prettier. The corresponding build images must also be provisioned. This is test setup, not installation during a build. The same probe accepts --builder java-maven|java-gradle --scenario dependency-feature for a Maven reactor or Gradle composite. It adds an unrelated module and scoped tags, changes a shared library, then checks consumers' inferred versions and unchanged unrelated bases. Maven checks seven POM/JAR artifacts, embedded package versions, parent and local dependency references; Gradle checks four versioned JARs, including the included build. Both check recorded scopes, reports, bundle inspection and unchanged native source files. This representative JVM acceptance does not claim the later independent-fix/shared-root scenarios have been executed on those managers.

The resolver uses semver 1.0.28, already present in Cargo.lock and now a direct dependency. Its registry source declares MIT OR Apache-2.0, Rust 1.68, and includes LICENSE-MIT and LICENSE-APACHE. No upstream source is copied or modified and no license alternative or distribution approval is selected. The factual compliance baseline tracks the direct dependency; release audit obligations remain unchanged.

CLI reference Published from the canonical docs/reference/yarn.md file. Features marked experimental remain experimental; check support limitations before relying on them. Oyzu discovers conventional single-project and workspace Yarn Classic projects from its native manifests and lockfile, without an Oyzu build file. The current adapter captures locked public-registry archives and lets Yarn install from a private offline mirror. Native Yarn owns dependency layout, peer behavior and lifecycle semantics.

The supported provisioned profile is Yarn Classic 1.22.22 on Node 22. Build the shared Node quality image first: docker build -t oyzu-toolchain/node:quality tooling/images/node-quality docker build -t oyzu-toolchain/node:yarn1.22.22-node22 tooling/images/node-yarn oyzu --root path/to/project run list oyzu --root path/to/project build oyzu --root path/to/project inspect dist The executor requires Docker and already provisioned images. Oyzu never installs a replacement manager during a build. --image yarn=<image> selects a compatible provisioned image; its immutable identity is recorded. The image includes @yarnpkg/lockfile 1.1.0 at /opt/oyzu-yarn/node_modules/@yarnpkg/lockfile, tar-stream 3.2.1 for archive normalization, and the shared quality tools. Rebuild older custom images to include the lock parser. An exact packageManager declaration must agree with native Yarn's version. A Corepack digest suffix such as yarn@1.22.22+sha512.<hex> is accepted and ignored for that comparison: it identifies Corepack's own download, while the provisioned image identity is what Oyzu records. Incompatible Node engine requirements fail. Native scripts appear as tasks. Conventional build/test work and read-only lint/format checks run during captured builds. Development oyzu run commands use host tooling; explicit formatting can modify source, while build formatting checks cannot. See Node quality for defaults and framework configuration. The existing Node test integration collects JUnit and LCOV for native Node test scripts; supported alternative frameworks retain their own adapters.

The adapter uses Yarn's published lockfile parser for Classic v1 syntax, including grouped selectors. It requires a successfully parsed lock, current direct dependency selectors, conventional HTTPS registry archive URLs and an integrity value for every entry. SHA-512 is the normal form. Older Classic locks also carry integrity sha1-... values for packages they locked before the registry published SHA-512; those entries are admitted only when the SHA-1 value agrees with the #<sha1> fragment of their resolved URL, are verified against that SHA-1 digest, and are named in the dependency record (see below). SHA-1 is a weaker digest than SHA-512; regenerate the affected entries with native Yarn if you need SHA-512 verification throughout. Multiple selectors for one archive share its captured identity; conflicting identities and ambiguous offline-mirror filenames fail. Every locked archive is captured, including optional and transitive entries. Git, file and other non-registry resolutions are not admitted. Preparation uses the existing scoped broker routes for https://registry.npmjs.org/ and https://registry.yarnpkg.com/, recorded as npm-public and yarn-public. Redirects remain subject to broker authorization. Source lockfiles keep their original resolved URLs and hashes. The archive inventory strips URL fragments from transport addresses and verifies the lock's SHA-512 value before native installation. Credentials never enter the inventory or mirror. The snapshot contains content-addressed archives and inventory, not Yarn's extracted mutable cache. Each install creates a fresh private mirror/cache and a temporary Yarn configuration outside project source. Native installation consumes that mirror, with development dependencies included and no external network in the worker. Before allowing lifecycle scripts, Oyzu runs native yarn install --offline --ignore-scripts --force in the private tree and compares the resulting parsed lock with the captured lock. Any dependency-resolution change fails. Cosmetic serialization changes are discarded, preserving the original lock bytes. During execution, a second native yarn install --offline --frozen-lockfile --force runs the lifecycle without a broker. Acquisition never enables scripts. The native Yarn/Node versions must match the captured versions. This native lock comparison is necessary because suppressing lockfile writes alone does not establish that changed resolutions agree with the lock. Yarn owns selective path matching, version selection and dependency layout. Registry version overrides in the native package.json are supported, including selecting a different transitive version while retaining a direct version: { "dependencies": {"is-odd": "3.0.1", "is-number": "6.0.0"}, "resolutions": {"is-odd/is-number": "7.0.0"} } Generate and commit the corresponding lock with native Yarn before building. The authored example has the complete project. Native Yarn's compatibility warnings and selective-resolution limitations still apply; Oyzu does not introduce a second override matcher. File, Git, URL and alias-protocol resolution values are currently rejected before native invocation. See Yarn's selective resolution documentation. This follows Yarn's documented offline mirror mechanism. No package resolver or Yarn cache layout is reimplemented.

Native Yarn Classic reads a project .yarnrc and .npmrc itself, so Oyzu admits these files only when every setting in them is on a fixed list that cannot redirect archive sources, the offline mirror, caches, credentials or the Yarn executable: File Admitted settings .yarnrc ignore-engines, save-prefix, save-exact, disable-self-update-check, version-tag-prefix, version-git-message, version-git-tag, version-sign-git-tag .npmrc package-lock, loglevel, progress, save-exact, save-prefix, fund, audit, update-notifier For example, webpack's .yarnrc contains ignore-engines true and its .npmrc contains package-lock=false; both are admitted and native Yarn applies them. Any other key, including registry, scoped @scope:registry, //host/:_authToken credentials, yarn-path, yarn-offline-mirror, cache-folder and ---prefixed command-line settings, fails acquisition with Yarn capture does not yet support <file> setting <key> before any native invocation. The message names the key, never its value. .yarnrc is read with Yarn's own lockfile parser and .npmrc as key=value lines; an ini section header is rejected as an unknown key. Settings files in workspace members remain unsupported. .yarnrc.yml is Yarn Berry configuration and fails with a message saying Berry needs its own adapter.

Other Node versions are tested with verification toolsets in oyzu.toml, never in build.yaml (matrix.node is refused). Toolset verification runs execute on the native host executor; Yarn builds use the isolated executor, so a Yarn build that has verification runs fails with VERIFICATION_RUN_UNSUPPORTED until runs reach that executor. Modern Yarn remains unfinished; Classic workspace behavior is described below. Successful builds emit native snapshot .tgz packages, normalized for repeatable archive metadata. The embedded package version matches the artifact version. dist/manifest.json records actual artifacts, tests and coverage, with dependency snapshots and native logs alongside it. Failed tests retain reports and block packaging. Bundle inspection checks content integrity; it does not establish release trust. Dependency adapter layout 2 records names, versions, source IDs, SHA-256 digests and sizes. The oyzu.dev/yarn extension records lockfile-sha512 integrity and all-locked-registry-tarballs inventory. This page describes the most important constraints a developer should know before choosing Oyzu.
The supported documentation path builds Oyzu from an authorized source checkout. A public one-line installer or public package-manager distribution has not yet been verified or documented.
Tool versions, operating systems, builder families, dependency acquisition and caching vary in support. The local-build reference and tool-management reference contain the specific qualified cases.
Reuse is currently an experimental local capability. Do not assume complete hermetic hashing, OCI/remote caching or distributed worker interoperability.
The remote client includes an experimental command surface but has not been qualified against a deployed production worker service. See remote runs.
